en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Elucidation of the Guide in the Minor Collection.
The Introduction to the Composition:
Having performed what is to be sacrificed, I pay homage to that which is to be honored;
by the power of such sacrifice and other merits, may I always abandon obstacles.
Whatever of the *Netti* was composed by him, whatever was approved by him,
and by whomsoever the commentary was made— all that rests upon their power.
Recalling here and there the transitions between the languid and the non-languid sections, and so forth;
I shall compose this clarification of the Guide for the benefit of the Conqueror’s discourses.
May he who is called the Great Dharma King, whose virtues are immeasurable,
be one who is marvelous and extraordinary, fulfilling the requisites for enlightenment.
The lord of many kingdoms, the best promoter of the Dispensation;
praised by King Pāsaṃsa, he whose thoughts are inconceivable to men.
The king who acts upon his intentions, the protector of Sirivaḍḍhamāla.
The conqueror of the unconquerable, the perpetual builder of the Great Shrine and other monuments,
was earnestly entreated by the venerable Assāmatta, who was learned,
a seeker of the Victor’s Wheel, and known by the name Anantasuti.
Granted, this commentary has been composed by the bull-like elders, yet because of its profundity, it is difficult for the sons of the Conqueror to fully comprehend.
Therefore, in accordance with your request, I shall now proceed with due respect; listen.
The "Exposition of the Guide" (Nettivibhāvana) follows the method for training disciples.
1. Exposition of the Meaning of the Section on Compendium:
Therein, it is the commentary on the meaning of the Teacher’s excellent dispensation, which is comprised of the Three Trainings and consists of nine divisions.
One who desires to compose this *Nettippakaraṇa* must first understand, through wisdom alone, the excellent teaching of the Supreme Teacher— the best among men—
who is always to be honored and worshipped by the three worlds together with the world-protectors, and whose teaching constitutes both the basis and the subject matter for this *Nettippakaraṇa*,
as well as that which is to be commented upon. Now, demonstrating that very excellent teaching:
In order to define it for his father and for those wise ones who discern, and to illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem,
he spoke the first verse: “That which the world worships, and which the World-Protector always pays homage to—
this excellent teaching of that Best of Men should be known by the wise.”
For in this first verse, only the phrase “this excellent teaching (sāsanavara) should be known” is intended with the status of a specific object of action (*karaṇa*).
This is because, by means of this very specific action, the excellent teaching—which is the exclusive object of the guide (*netti*)—is shown.

Since it is precisely that excellent teaching, which is exclusively intended, that must be commented upon in the commentary on the *Netti*, the Master of the Commentary will state its object accordingly:

“This teaching, which is now the subject of our investigation into the *Paṭṭhāna*—the method for analyzing the factors to be analyzed—is excellent, supreme, and most sublime due to its perfection of qualities such as being good in the beginning;

and because it is the domain of subtle knowledge, it is to be experienced only by the wise. And: “Having subsumed these three types under the term ‘excellent teaching,’ that which is first among them is the means for the attainment of the others;
thus, it is the teaching of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*), which is the root of the entire dispensation and the specific subject matter of this own treatise.”

"Now, regarding what was stated—'The excellent dispensation is to be known by the wise'—in order to demonstrate, by means of another method, precisely that Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) which constitutes the object of the *Nettippakaraṇa* commentary," it is said:

"It is the root of the entire dispensation. By this, although the intended meaning is established even through the instrumental derivation (*kamma-sādhana*), the use of various forms of the word "root" (*mūla*) is for the purpose of leaving no room for diverse [contradictory] doctrines.

It has been said. However, the qualities of the Dhamma, such as being well-expounded (*svākkhāta*), are indicated either by the term "the Best of Men" (*naravara*)—who is the specific teacher of the Dispensation—or by the state of being the object that clarifies it, due to their inseparable connection.
Yet, because the "Best of Dispensations" requires a reference to its progenitor through a relationship of origin, the phrase "of the Best of Men" is used.

By this, the Supreme Person (*aggapuggala*), who is the progenitor of the Best of Dispensations, is expressed through the relationship of the signifier and the signified. [This refers to] the distinguished qualities such as Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and Omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), which are not shared with others.
However, the person who is related to the progenitor [of the teaching] is indicated either by the specific term "supreme man" (*naravara*) or by the state of being the illuminator of the meaning.
Is that supreme man, the progenitor of the excellent teaching, the ultimate reality (*paramattha*), or is he merely one who is to be honored and revered?
To this it is said: "Whom the world... reveres. By this, it is shown that the supreme man, the progenitor of the excellent teaching, is indeed the ultimate reality.
He does not exist; rather, he is praised and extolled as being always and at all times worthy of worship and homage by the world together with its world-protectors.

And here, by means of the words "worship" (*pūjana*) and "homage" (*namassana*), which denote the volition of worship and homage, the sense of the metaphorical application of the fruit [to the cause] is intended.

The state of being worthy of worship, which consists in the greatness of his merit, and the state of being worthy of homage, which consists in the qualities such as the knowledge of omniscience that has its proximate cause in the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*), have been illustrated by way of being the subject matter of the lamp. Therefore, the Master of the Commentary said:
"The Blessed One’s state of being worthy of worship and salutation by the world including the devas, and his state of being the Supreme Person, are being described..."
"...it illuminates the excellence of the qualities," and so forth.
Regarding such a supreme person, one might ask: "Is such a sublime teaching understandable by just anyone? To this it is said, "by the wise" (*vidūhi*).

By this, those who uphold the Three Piṭakas, who have become noble ones, or who are learned, are understood in the sense of being reciters; [this refers to] the qualities of the Saṅgha, such as its state of being well-practiced.
[The qualities of the Triple Gem] are illuminated either by the verbal root *vand* (to worship) or by way of being the subject of the illumination.

Having thus grasped them, he will say—referring to the qualities of the Triple Gem as they have been illuminated—"Having thus, in the first verse, performed an especially excellent exposition of the qualities of the Triple Gem," but this does not refer to the exhaustive meaning of the verse.
In that context, "thus" (*evam*) refers to [the verse] which consists in the manifestation of the supreme dispensation.
The meaning should be understood as referring to the first verse.

However, other teachers, without having thoroughly examined both the words that are intended and those not intended in this first verse, as well as the specific distinctions between the literal meaning (*vācakattha*) and the indicative meaning (*dīpakattha*), [merely rely on] the superficial appearance of the statement:
"Thus, by means of the first verse, the qualities of the Triple Gem have been most excellently illustrated."
They say: "In order to provide an exceptional exposition of the virtues of the Triple Gem, [the Blessed One] said, 'Yaṃ loko...';
and in order to demonstrate the preeminent virtues of the Triple Gem, they say, 'Yaṃ loko... Their assertion is not acceptable to us.
However, the reason for this should be understood according to what was stated by me above; such is the meaning of the connection (anusandhi) following the sequence of the words.

Alternatively, on one occasion, while sitting in the Jambu Grove reflecting on the welfare of his disciples and contemplating the excellence of his own resolve, Mahākaccāyana—having been praised by the Perfectly Enlightened One and commended by the Teacher—began the *Nettippakaraṇa*, a work of manifold meanings including the sixteen *hāras* and other categories, which provides an exposition of the ninefold teaching dependent upon the Dispensation; [beginning with]: "That which..."

He said, "The world," and so forth. If it is the case that one should have commenced the *Nettippakaraṇa*—consisting of the sixteen guides and so on, in the manner already described—then why was it not commenced, but instead something external to the *Nettippakaraṇa*, such as "That which the world," and so forth?
It would be like answering with a breadfruit tree when asked about a mango, or answering with an mango when asked about a breadfruit tree.
In the same way, when beginning the *Nettippakaraṇa*, does one begin something else? Nevertheless, in order to show that excellent Teaching—
which is the subject matter of the *Nettippakaraṇa* that he wishes to compose as a commentary on its meaning,
whether it be that which is accompanied by what is to be commented upon or merely that which is to be commented upon— he first presents that excellent Teaching by means of its generator.
In order to cause those who know to restrain themselves and to illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem, he said, "That which the world worships... and so forth.
This is the connection of the meaning, accompanied by the exhortation against further sinking.
"That which the world worships, and which the world-protector always pays homage to;"

“Of that Best of Men, this excellent teaching should be known by the wise”—this verse, composed with the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), is endowed with the characteristic common to noble meters (*ariyāsāmaññalakkhaṇa*). How so?
There are thirty morae (*mattā*) in the first half and twenty-seven morae in the second half; when combined, they amount to exactly fifty-seven morae.
In this verse, however, there are thirty-seven syllables. Among them, twenty are heavy syllables (*garu-akṣara*) and seventeen are light syllables (*lahu-akṣara*).
But the form “*tassetam sāsanavaran*” with the nasalized vowel (*sānunāsika*) is incorrect.

In that regard, the meaning of the detailed exposition (*niddesa*) should be understood according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*. The entire world of beings, together with the world-protectors (*salokapāla*), [should listen] with reverence.
Whether by recollecting his manifold qualities such as omniscience, or by worshipping those worthy of worship, or by worshipping through practice—
whosoever always and at all times reverently worships and pays homage to that Best of Men, the Teacher who is worthy of worship and homage,
the Best of Men, the Foremost One in the Three Worlds— to him [I shall speak] together with a descriptive praise of that Teacher.
Or rather, it is precisely that which is to be praised which must be known and understood by the wise. This is the domain of subtle knowledge;
this excellent teaching has been established by me as the subject matter of the *Nettippakaraṇa*, which I have undertaken to compose.
Having first shown what is to be known, I shall now undertake the *Nettippakaraṇa* as a commentary on its meaning. You [should listen to] that.
“O virtuous ones, listen and attend!”—this is the construction of the whole; the construction of the parts should also be made. How so?
“The world together with its world-protectors” (*salokapālo loko*) is a construction by way of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
It is not that the world remains after excluding the world-protectors; rather, it qualifies [the world] as “the world accompanied by the world-protectors. “The world worships... [and so forth].

The construction [of the phrase] “he both worships and pays homage” is based on the presence of the agent (*kattā*), the case-role (*kāraka*), the verb (*ākhyāta*), and the action (*kiriyā*), because it has been stated:
“He who acts is the agent. Let the world that acts be the agent. But as for the world that both worships and pays homage—how can that be the agent?
According to the sutta “He who acts is the agent,” one who acts—that is, brings about an action—is the producer of that action.
Because of the possibility of such a meaning, one who brings about all activities such as lying down and eating is indeed an agent (*kattā*).
And this world is precisely that which brings about the activities of honoring and revering. How is it that this world brings about activities?

Although the designation "world" (*loka*) does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), it is nevertheless designated for the sake of conventional description; it refers to that which proceeds within the continuum (*santāna*).
The arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) dependent on the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is to be understood;

it becomes a producer by way of being a condition—such as a root-cause, a predominance-condition, or a conascence-condition—as appropriate. Thus, the world’s state of being an agent and doer is to be known through the relationship of condition and that which arises from conditions.
This same method applies to such passages in all three Piṭakas.

The construction of the phrase “He who both honors and pays homage to that best of men” is based on the nature of the action expressed by the verb in its role as a *kammakāraka* (object-actor), because it has been stated: “That which one does is *kamma*. Let that which is to be done be *kamma*.
But how is that which he honors and pays homage to *kamma*? [It is so] according to the Sutta: “That which one does is *kamma*. “That which...”

Because the sense [of the definition] arises as "it is connected with an action; karma is that which is to be connected with an action," it follows that whatever is to be connected with any action—expressed by a term denoting the instrument (karaṇa), the object (vacanīya), or any other case—is indeed karma.
And this "best of men" (naravara) must necessarily be connected with the action of worshiping and paying homage by way of being the object (vacanīyabhāva).
How is this best of men the object? By way of being made the focal object (ārammaṇa) of the volition (cetanā) of worshiping and paying homage.
The "best of men" (naravara) is that which is to be expressed; volition (cetanā) is the expresser. Thus, the state of being expressed by the expresser is as follows:

although the "best of men" does not exist in an ultimate sense (paramatthato) as a conceptual designation (paññatti), it is spoken of as the five aggregates (khandhapañcaka) accompanied by mundane and supramundane qualities, proceeding by way of a continuum (santāna).

This [continuum] is the condition (paccaya) by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya); volition is the "conditioned" (paccayuppanna). Thus, they exist in the relationship of condition and conditioned.
The method of construction (*yojanā*). This same principle applies to such passages in all three Piṭakas.
In the phrase “of that best of men” (*tassa naravarassa*), the construction is made by way of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.

One qualifies [the subject] by showing that the "best of men" is not merely someone to be invited and so forth, but rather someone to be honored and venerated. And of that very one who is to be honored...
The connection is made through the relationship of the producer and the produced: "the excellent teaching of the Best of Men who is worthy of worship.
This specifies that the "excellent teaching" does not belong to the Pratyekabuddhas, the disciples, the Buddha-kings, or others;
rather, it restricts it to the excellent teaching of the Best of Men alone—the one worthy of honor and worship by the three worlds.

The construction is according to the absence of agent, instrument, object, and action in the phrase "to be known by the wise" (*vidūhi ñeyyaṃ*). The status of the agent has already been explained above.

By the term "by the wise" (*vidūhi*), there is referred to a mental state (*cittuppāda*) dependent on the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), which occurs within the continuum (*santāna*) and is accompanied by the knowledge that destroys delusion regarding the excellent teaching;
this is to be designated even though, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), the designation of a "being" (*satta*) does not exist. Such a state [is to be understood] as appropriate.

By way of conditions such as predominance (*adhipati*) and co-nascence (*sahajāta*), it would be the producer of the condition. Knowledge, which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root *ñā* (to know), would be the produced condition (*paccayuppanna*) that is to be produced; thus is the connection made by way of the relationship between condition and the produced condition.

The phrase “the excellent teaching is to be known” (*ñeyyaṃ sāsanavaraṃ*) is a connection by way of the qualifier and the qualified. The “excellent teaching” is not to be known by just anyone; rather, it qualifies it as the excellent teaching that is to be known only by the wise through subtle and refined knowledge.
The construction here is by way of the relationship between the qualifier (*visesana*) and the qualified (*viseyya*): “This is the excellent dispensation.
It qualifies [the dispensation] as follows: “That which is called the excellent dispensation was previously placed in my mind by me as something not to be set in motion;
now, as the subject matter of this *Nettippakaraṇa*, that same excellent dispensation—which is revolving in my mind—must be placed and set in motion. This is “this excellent dispensation.”

The construction should be made as "the subject matter of the *Nettippakaraṇa*. Therefore he said: "This is the Teaching (Sāsana), which is now the subject matter for our investigation of the *Paṭṭhāna* method of analysis that is to be divided.
Thus ends, in brief, the explanation of the meaning of the first verse of the *Netti*.

In that context, the word *yaṃ* is a relative pronoun (*sabbanāma*) accompanied by a demonstrative usage, denoting the Teacher, the Lord of Unrestricted Excellence. And the lack of restriction [is as follows]:...
This was stated because the act of worshiping and paying homage is not restricted [to humans alone], and not because it is impossible for other beings apart from the Best of Men (naravara).

This same principle applies to the three remaining Piṭakas that are not restricted. The world (*loka*) is so called because merit and demerit, as well as their ripening result (*vipāka*), are found (*lokyanti*) therein.
Herein, within this collection of beings (*sattanikāya*), merit and demerit are found—that is, they proceed—and their ripening result is also found—that is, it proceeds.

Thus, because it serves as the basis for the occurrence of the aggregates of beings (*sattanikāya*), their merits and demerits (*puññāpuññāni*), and their respective results (*vipāka*), the "aggregate of beings" indicated by the term "herein" (*ettha*) is called the world (*loka*).
"Pūjayate" is a verb (*ākhyātapada*) devoid of grammatical analysis; it means "he performs worship with due care.
They are "World-Protectors" (*lokapālā*) because they protect the world; they are worlds because they serve as the basis for the occurrence of merits and demerits and their respective results.

And who are they? They are either the four Great Kings—Inda, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kuvera—or the Kṣatriya Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Paranimmita, Vasavatti, Mahābrahmā, and so forth.

Here, "protection" (pālana) consists of the exercise of sovereignty and lordship over the respective worlds of beings, including the issuance of commands to prevent mutual harm and the granting of positions, dwellings, and other provisions along with their attendants.

One who functions together with these world-protectors is called *salokapāla*. Alternatively, it refers to those who, through moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), protect the world. Thus...

Because they protect, these two—moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*)—are the guardians of the world. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, these two bright qualities protect the world.
Indeed, it is because the world possesses these two guardians, moral shame and moral dread, that it is called “the world with its guardians.
For the virtuous person endowed with moral shame and moral dread is always and at all times honored and revered by the world with due respect, owing to his abhorrence of evil and his sense of shame.
And because of possessing the desire for the Dhamma.
Others, however, while worshipping and paying homage, worship and pay homage only at certain times, not at all times.
"Always" (*sadā*) is either a pronoun or a name expressing an alternative that is devoid of a grammatical construction denoting the time of worship and homage. "He pays homage" (*namassati*).
The verb form *sakkaccaṃ namassati* (he reverently pays homage) is a compound-free (viggahavirahita) expression. Regarding the word *tassa*:

here, *tassa* is a possessive pronoun (*sabbanāma*) denoting a specific application (*payogavanta*), which is likewise compound-free. Furthermore, this specification (*niyama*) is qualified by the act of worship and homage.
Therefore, it refers to that which is to be specified by the act of worship and homage—that which is to be worshipped and that which is to be paid homage to.

The meaning "of the best of men" is indeed appropriate. This same principle applies to the other remaining rules as well. The word *etaṃ* (this) is a pronoun (*sabbanāma*) possessing a specific application;

it is devoid of grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) and refers to the "excellent teaching" (*sāsanavara*), which is the subject matter for the Teacher’s investigation into the *Paṭṭhāna*—the method for analyzing the categories of the Abhidhamma.
It is called "teaching" (*sāsana*) because one teaches by means of it; that is, by means of this ninefold *Suttanta*, or together with the ninefold *Suttanta*, [it is] excellent (*vara*).

He instructs, exhorts, and disciplines beings as is appropriate for those capable of being trained in every respect, by means of the three vehicles, through the worldly, the supramundane, and the ultimate truths. Thus,

because it acts as the cause for the knowledge, practice, and realization of beings to be trained— following the process of instruction and exhortation— the ninefold Suttanta is indicated by the phrase "by this."
Or rather, the entire teaching (*sāsana*) consisting of the ninefold discourses (*navavidhasuttanta*) is excellent.

For through the teaching of the ninefold discourses, there arises for those to be trained (*veneyya*) a subsequent understanding based on a prior understanding; from that understanding comes practice, and from subsequent practice comes realization (*adhigama*);
and from a prior realization comes a subsequent realization. Therefore it was said: "Faith, virtue, learning, generosity..."
[Examples include: "Wisdom [is the cause] of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom," and "The preparation for the first jhāna is the first jhāna," and so forth.

In this context, the primary meaning of the word *desanā* (teaching) is the element of the Dispensation (*sāsana-dhātu*) and the arising of a state of consciousness associated with the knowledge of teaching that produces it;

while its secondary meaning refers to the understanding, practice, and realization of the goal by those to be trained, which are supported by that [primary meaning] as a decisive condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

The sense of the term *kāraṇūpacāra* (metaphorical designation of the cause) refers to the power of the supporting condition (*upanissaya-paccaya-satti*), which is reckoned as the instrumental capacity (*karaṇa-satti*) of the designation of name (*nāma-paññatti*) that constitutes the Teaching and is expressed by the word "by this.
The word *iti* likewise refers back to that very power of the supporting condition of the designation of name as being the cause.
The meaning of the suffix *-yu* is the designation of name which serves as the substratum for that power. It is precisely this...
This is the method regarding such passages in the three Piṭakas.
It is "excellent" (*vara*) and "supreme" (*uttama*) in the sense of being exclusively conducive to liberation and in the sense of possessing qualities not shared by others.

In the teaching of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*), it is so called because it delivers the fruit and because it serves as the cause for the path that leads to liberation. Furthermore, it is "unborn" (*aja*) because it cannot be overcome by disciples and others.
It is "excellent" (*vara*) in the sense of being uncommon and in the sense of being supreme; or else, it is "excellent" because it is to be chosen (*varitabba*).

Because it is the cause for the attainment of the prosperity desired by the wise regarding the aforementioned Teaching, and because it is to be chosen—that is, to be longed for—it is called the "Excellent Teaching" (*sāsanavara*).
Alternatively, in the sense already stated, it is both the Teaching and excellent, thus "Excellent Teaching. By the word "and" (*ca*), the variety [of its benefits] is indicated.
By the word *taṃ* (that), it indicates the non-difference of the referent.

They know, thus they are "knowers" (*vidū*). Those wise ones who know actions and their fruits, as well as phenomena distinguished as wholesome and so forth, according to their true nature—because they know in this way, those wise ones are called "knowers";
by them. That which is to be known is "the knowable" (*ñeyya*). [This is derived] from the verbal root *ñā* in its primary sense.

Knowledge with an object has been stated; by way of metaphorical designation (*ṭhānūpacārato*), the state of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccayabhāvo*) for the excellent teaching is shown, and by the word *iti*, that state of being an object-condition is referred to.
The excellent teaching, which is the substratum (*ādhāra*) of that state of being an object-condition referred to by the word *iti*, should be understood as the meaning of the suffix *-ñya*.
Alternatively, it is "knowable" (*ñeyya*) because it is worthy of knowledge (*ñāṇaṃ arahati*); [it is knowable] for those who possess wisdom.
The meaning is that knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is worthy of being known as an object of cognition. In this method, it should be understood as a derivative word (*taddhita*).
One who leads (*narati*), guides (*neti*), is a man (*naro*). That person who leads and guides himself to a high position among women is called a man because of his leading and guiding;
for even though he has become a son, he stands in the place of a father to his mother, and even though he has become a younger brother...
He stands in the place of a father toward his elder sisters. Alternatively, he is called *naro* because he is to be led (*netabbo*) or guided.
For from the time of his birth until he is capable of supporting himself by his own nature, he must be led by others; other beings, such as animals and so forth, are not like this.
In this context, however, he is called *naro* because, being within the domain of the Teacher, he leads (*narati*) those beings who are to be disciplined (*veneyyasatta*).
The meaning intended is "a leader" (*nara*). For the Teacher leads beings from the states of misery and so forth to a happy destination, or to the path, fruit, and *nibbāna*.
Because he is endowed with manifold qualities such as omniscience, he is excellent and supreme; or, he is called "excellent" (*vara*) because he is to be chosen or aspired to.
He is the foremost of the three worlds. By nature, a "leader" (*nara*) occupies a high station; being endowed with the highest of qualities, he is excellent, a leader.
And that "best" (*vara*) [together with] "man" (*nara*) makes "the best of men" (*naravaro*). The distinction in meaning between the particles *ca* and *ta* has already been stated;

this is a compound where the qualifying word follows the qualified word (*visesanapara-padasamāsa*). This is why it was said: "The meaning is 'of the foremost person' (*aggapuggalassa*). Others, however, say: "He is the best among men, or the best of men, thus he is the 'best of men' (*naravaro*).
I believe that statement contradicts the commentary’s explanation that "the meaning is 'of the foremost person'."

“Of that best of men”: thus, in brief, the explanation of the meaning of the words for the opening verse of the *Nettippakaraṇa* is complete. The literal meaning should be understood by following the grammatical construction, the contextual application, and the explanation of the words.

Nevertheless, it shall be stated again for the sake of thorough individual understanding: the word “yaṃ” (who/which) refers to one who is endowed with manifold qualities such as the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) not shared by others.
The one who teaches the excellent dispensation, the foremost in the three worlds, is to be honored and revered by the world together with its world-protectors; this is the literal meaning.
Regarding the word “world” (*loka*), the literal meaning includes the aforementioned world-protectors along with the entire world of sentient beings endowed with faith, generosity, and so forth.

Although the word “world” is used in the singular number, because it is a generic term (*jātisadda*), it encompasses all sentient beings without exception, just as in the expression “the great multitude” (*mahājana*).

In this context, although the word *loka* occurs even in reference to the "receptacles of formations" (i.e., the world as the field of experience) in such expressions as "knower of the world" (*lokavidū*), it functions here as a designation for the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*) because it serves as the basis for the acts of honoring and revering. Therefore, he said:

"by way of being the fit object for the act of honoring. Regarding the phrase "he honors": here, in the primary sense, the mental state of those who are honoring—which is itself designated as the "act of honoring"—is the literal meaning.

By way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*), all the aforementioned qualities of the Buddha—which serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and natural decisive support-condition (*pakatūpanissayapaccaya*) for that arising of consciousness—are the actual referents (*sarūpattha*).
Likewise, the world of the aforementioned kind, which accomplishes the act of worship through the case-ending suffix (*vibhattipaccaya*), is also the actual referent.
This being so, since there is no difference in the meaning (*atthabheda*), only one designator (*vācaka*) should be stated for both [designators]; why then [is it used] in a single sense?
Are two denotative words stated? This is not a fault, because the two denotative words function as both general and specific denoters.
For the word *loka* denotes that which accomplishes the act of honoring and that which accomplishes other acts; thus, it is a general denoter.
The word *pūjayati* denotes that which accomplishes the acts of honoring the world, honoring women, honoring men, honoring animals, and so forth; thus, it is a general denoter.

Therefore, the word *pūjayate* has the same meaning as the word *loka*, and it is restricted to the sense that it accomplishes the act of honoring (*pūjanakiriyā*) and does not accomplish any other act.
Furthermore, the word *loka* has the same meaning as the word *pūjayate*, and it accomplishes the act of honoring;

moreover, it is restricted to the sense that "the world" (*loko*) consists of women, men, animals, and so forth, who accomplish the act of honoring. This applies even in the case of the Three Piṭakas and others.
In such instances, this same method applies.

Regarding the term *salokapālo*: its literal meaning is a class of beings accompanied by the aforementioned supreme world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and capable of performing acts of worship and veneration.
Regarding the term *sadā*: its meaning is "at all times," referring to both day and night, as well as the period during which the Blessed One was living.

The "other time" (*parakāla*) refers to the period from the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*) until the disappearance of the Dispensation (*sāsana-antaradhāna*). Beyond that is the "other time" in its literal sense.

That, moreover, is the period when a future Buddha appears; just as people now worship and pay homage to past Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*), they will likewise worship and pay homage [to him].
Regarding the term "pays homage" (*namassati*), here, by way of the primary action of paying homage, it is designated as "homage."

The arising of the mind (*cittuppāda*) is the literal meaning (*sarūpattha*). By way of figurative application (*phalūpacāra*), all the aforementioned qualities of the Buddha—which serve as the objective support (*ārammaṇa*) and the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) for that arising of the mind—are also the literal meaning.

For the suffix of the third case (*tṛtīyā-vibhatti-paccaya*), the world consisting of the seven classes of beings as previously described, which accomplishes the act of paying homage, is the literal meaning; this occurs because two designators function [together] even in the absence of a difference in their referents.
This has already been explained above. Regarding the word *ca* (and): here, some [beings] do not pay homage even while making offerings, and others do not make offerings even while paying homage;
however, this world of sentient beings both makes offerings and pays homage—this is the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and the literal meaning (*sarūpa*).
As for the word *tassa* (of him): here, the pronoun *taṃ* refers to the one endowed with manifold qualities such as omniscience, who is worthy of being honored and worthy of being paid homage.
The Teacher, the foremost in the three worlds, is the primary related meaning (*padhāna-sarūpattha*) through his connection with the sixth case ending;
the excellent teaching of the Knower is connected to the progenitor, the best of men, as the secondary related meaning (*apadhāna-sarūpattha*).
This same principle applies to such instances throughout the Three Pitakas and elsewhere as well.
The literal meaning of the word *etaṃ* (this) is the Teaching (*sāsana*) which constitutes the subject matter for the Teacher’s analysis of the method of the *Paṭṭhāna*.
The literal meaning of the word *sāsanavaraṃ* (the excellent Teaching) is also that very same thing.

This excellent Teaching is threefold—consisting of the Teaching as study (*pariyatti*), the Teaching as practice (*paṭipatti*), and the Teaching as realization (*paṭivedha*)—yet it is specifically the Teaching as study that is intended here, because it is the root of all Teachings and because it is the subject matter of the *Nettippakaraṇa*.

Furthermore, it need not be stated by us that what is specifically intended [here] has already been shown in the commentaries on the Vinaya and elsewhere, as it is of great benefit because it constitutes the very root of that [teaching].
Even one who were to say so would have to be understood as saying this while being incapable of composing anything else that ought to be composed.
Moreover, that scripture (*pariyatti-sāsana*) is of one kind in terms of the essence of the flavor of liberation; it is of two kinds in terms of the Dhamma and the Vinaya.

It is threefold by way of the Vinaya Piṭaka, Sutta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka; it is threefold by way of instruction through command, instruction through exposition, and instruction through the ultimate meaning;
it is also threefold according to the distinction between instruction that reprimands according to the offense, instruction that conforms to the person, and instruction that accords with the Dhamma;
and it is also threefold according to the distinction between discourse on restraint and non-restraint, discourse on the unraveling of views, and discourse on the analysis of name-and-form.
In this context, there is a distinction: teaching depends on the teacher, the dispensation depends on those to be instructed, and discourse depends on the subject matter to be explained.
Furthermore, it is fivefold according to the division of the Nikāyas: the Dīghanikāya, Majjhimanikāya, Saṃyuttanikāya, Aṅguttaranikāya, and Khuddakanikāya;
and it is further divided by way of the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla.
Furthermore, it is ninefold; furthermore, by way of the division into aggregates of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*), it is eighty-four thousandfold.

There are four unmixed [categories]: pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), pertaining to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*), pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), and pertaining to those beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*). There are mixed pairs:

pertaining to defilement, pertaining to purification, pertaining to both defilement and penetration, pertaining to both defilement and those beyond training, pertaining to both purification and penetration, and pertaining to both purification and those beyond training.

There are four [sets]: those dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), those dealing with purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*), those dealing with the state beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*), and two mixed triads consisting of those dealing with defilement, those dealing with purification, and those dealing with penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*). There are twelve [sets] consisting of: those dealing with the defilement of craving (*taṇhāsaṃkilesa*), those dealing with the defilement of views (*diṭṭhisaṃkilesa*), those dealing with the defilement of misconduct (*duccaritasaṃkilesa*);

those dealing with the cleansing of craving (*taṇhāvodānabhāgiya*), those dealing with the cleansing of views (*diṭṭhivodānabhāgiya*), and those dealing with the cleansing of misconduct (*duccaritavodānabhāgiya*). Thus, it is sixteenfold through the division of these sixteen discourses (*sutta*).
“It is twenty-eightfold by way of the distinctions of: mundane and supramundane; based on beings and based on phenomena;

both based on beings and based on phenomena; knowledge of the knowable and knowledge of the unknowable; vision of the knowable and vision of the unknowable; cultivation of the knowable and cultivation of the unknowable; one’s own words and others’ words; one’s own words and others’ words regarding what is answerable and what is not answerable;

what is answerable and what is not answerable regarding kamma and its result; wholesome and unwholesome; wholesome and unwholesome regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited; and what is permitted and what is prohibited regarding what is praised and what is censured.”
The teaching of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*) consisting of these and many other such varieties is, in particular, the domain of the *Nettippakaraṇa*.

Since that [scriptural teaching] constitutes its domain, it should be understood that the two-fold teaching known as practice (*paṭipatti*) and realization (*paṭivedha*) are also, by way of metaphor, its domain because they are rooted therein.
Regarding the word "by the wise" (*vidūhi*), it refers to those who cause the aforementioned excellent teaching to proceed within their own continuums and cause it to proceed in others, and so forth.

The literal meaning of the word *vijānanasamattha* (capable of knowing) is a person such as a noble worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and so forth, who is endowed with qualities such as subtle and refined knowledge.
The literal meaning of the word *ñeyya* (to be known) is the excellent teaching, which is to be understood by such wise ones through subtle and refined knowledge and so forth.
The literal meaning of the word *naravarassa* (of the best of men) refers to the excellent teaching, which is divided into one kind and so forth.

Janaka is endowed with manifold virtues, the foremost in the three worlds, and the one whose purpose is his own true nature (*sarūpa*). Thus, the meaning of "own-nature" (*sarūpa*) in the opening verse of the *Netti* should be understood in brief.
Although the connection (*anusandhi*) and other such elements of that verse are thus to be known, [the author] asks as if not knowing them, and having raised an objection, [proceeds].
By means of the refutation as well, there will be a specific understanding of the profound intention that is free from confusion.
Therefore, having asked the question and having pointed out the fault, I shall explain by way of refutation, condensing the profound intention.
For what purpose did our teacher say, "That which the world... and so forth? It was in order to compose the *Nettippakaraṇa*. This being the case, that which constitutes the *Nettippakaraṇa*...
One should have stated only, "The *Netti* has sixteen sections," and so forth;

why then, instead of that, did he state something other than the *Nettippakaraṇa*, namely, "That which the world worships," and so on? Just as one going to the ocean goes to the Himālaya, and one going to the Himālaya goes to the ocean, even so, while composing the *Nettippakaraṇa*, [he] showed the excellence of the Teaching (*sāsana*).
Does it do so? Yes, it does. Nevertheless, wishing to compose the *Nettippakaraṇa* as a commentary upon that, he spoke the words beginning with "That which the world...
in order to first show that supreme teaching (*sāsanavara*). If this were the case, one might ask:

"Shouldn't he have said merely 'This is the supreme teaching'? Why did he say 'That which the world... and so forth? [The answer is: He specified that supreme teaching by means of its progenitor, the Supreme Man (*naravara*).

It was stated [in the commentary] that he is to be praised. Nevertheless, one might ask: "Since it would have been sufficient to say merely 'of that best of men' (*tassa naravarassā*), why was it said 'whom the world' (*yaṃ loko*) and so forth?

It was said "whom the world" and so forth in order to praise that progenitor, the best of men, as being worthy of worship and homage by the entire world, together with Lokapāla, the best of the world.
Furthermore, even when worshipping, people worship after first paying homage; therefore, [the word] "worships" (*pūjayate*) alone [would not suffice].
Is this not so? Nevertheless, even when some people perform acts of worship, honor, and the like for others, they do not pay homage because those qualities are not well known to them.

Thus, in order to show that one pays homage to the Blessed One precisely because his fame has arisen in accordance with reality, it is said: "and he pays homage. [This applies to] one who is worshipping and one who is paying homage.
The word "always" (sadā) is used to show that this is not merely at one time, but rather at all times.

To praise the sublime teaching—that such a sublime teaching for such a supreme person is to be known by the wise alone through subtle knowledge, which is endowed with subtle and refined wisdom—it is said: "to be known by the wise."

And here, by the words "he worships" (*pūjayate*) and "he pays homage" (*namassati*), numerous mundane and supramundane qualities—such as omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and others—which serve as the causes for the acts of worshiping and paying homage, are made manifest;
for it is by depending upon those qualities that the volition of worshiping and paying homage arises in all the world.
Among those qualities, some are recollected by the Elder Sāriputta and others both in their own form and by inference.
They honor and revere him. Therefore it was said: “Recall the Fully Enlightened One. Even those possessing only partial qualities are worthy of honor and worthy of reverence;

why then are all his qualities manifested? It is because, by showing all his qualities, [the Buddha] demonstrates his power in the cause—consisting of the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment, the application of great compassion, and the knowledge of relinquishment—and his power in the fruit—consisting of the perfection of the body, the inclination toward the welfare of others, the ripening of the faculties, the arrival of the proper time, and the knowledge of teaching. Regarding sentient beings—
Praise has been shown by way of the perfection of modes. By this, there is the practice for one’s own benefit and the practice for the benefit of others;

the non-approach and approach to that which is free from defilement; the non-transgression of worldly conventions; the perfection of conduct (*caraṇa-sampatti*) and the perfection of clear knowledge (*vijjā-sampatti*);
self-sovereignty and Dharma-sovereignty; being a lord of the world while not being a lord of self; and the gratitude for what was previously performed.

Furthermore, the state of not afflicting oneself, the state of not afflicting others, the accomplishment of the Buddha-nature through the qualities that constitute Buddhahood, the crossing over of others and one’s own crossing over, the mind intent on helping sentient beings,
and the mind detached from worldly things are all proclaimed. Thus, in every respect,
he has attained the status of a field for the performance of worship and homage toward one who is unsurpassedly worthy of offerings, most worthy of veneration, and most worthy of salutation.
It reveals. By this, it is revealed that the fulfillment of the purposes desired by those who worship and pay homage is attained; thus, all qualities are revealed.

Because it possesses the excellence of qualities such as being "good in the beginning" (ādikalyāṇa), it is "excellent" (vara), "supreme" (agga), and "most sublime" (uttama); and because it is the domain of subtle wisdom, it is "to be experienced by the wise" (paṇḍitavedanīya).

Therefore, by the expressions "the excellent object of knowledge" (varaṃ ñeyyaṃ) and so forth, all the qualities of the Dhamma, such as being well-expounded (svākkhāta), are revealed. Through the penetration of the Noble Truths...
Only those who have eradicated the defilements and dispelled delusion are, in the ultimate sense, wise, because they have transcended childhood and the other stages;
therefore, individuals who have cultivated the supramundane path and realized the fruits of recluseship are specifically called "the wise" (*vidū*).

For they are able to know and lead others to understand the aforementioned excellent teaching without error within their own and others' continuums. Therefore, those qualities such as being well-practiced...
The qualities of the Noble Saṅgha, which have been extolled by numerous scriptural passages, are also fully revealed by the word "by the wise" (*vidūhi*).
Thus, in the first verse of the *Netti*, having included the threefold dispensation by means of the phrase "this excellent dispensation," [the author] establishes that,
because the other two [of the three] serve as the means for its attainment, [the Saṅgha] is the root of the entire dispensation.

By way of showing the excellence of the formal teaching (pariyatti-sāsana), which is the subject matter of his own *Nettippakaraṇa*, all the qualities of the Triple Gem are also revealed through the method of praise.

For when all qualities are shown by way of method (*naya*), they are grasped without remainder, rather than being presented in their specific individual forms. Therefore, he said: "Setting aside the Blessed One, among those possessed of wisdom..."
Even the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma who was foremost among them, being devoted to discerning the qualities of the Buddha, said:
"Moreover, the inference of the Dhamma is known to me. And by the Blessed One himself it was said:
"Thus inconceivable are the Buddhas; Inconceivable are the qualities of the Buddhas."
“The ripening for those with faith in the inconceivable is itself inconceivable”—thus the verse was spoken.

In this context, “the qualities of the Buddha” refers to the virtues of the Buddha. Furthermore, it should be understood by the wise that we ourselves are utterly incapable of extracting and demonstrating the qualities of the Triple Gem in their true form, even though we exert ourselves to the utmost in proclaiming them throughout our entire lives; how much more so, then, is this the case for others?
Thus it is said:
"That which the world worships, and which the World-Protector always pays homage to—
that supreme teaching of the Best of Men should be known by the wise."
The connection and so forth, which were stated in brief by means of the verse spoken with the elision of the *niggahīta*,
are now complete: “That which the world worships, that the World-Protector always pays homage to—
let the wise know that to be the excellent teaching of that Best of Men.”
Others recite a different verse. The connection (*anusandhi*) of its meaning is according to the method already stated; however, the application (*yojana*) of the meaning is distinct.

For there, the world together with its world-protectors (*salokapālo loko*) honors and pays homage to that excellent teaching (*sāsanavara*)—whether it be that which is accompanied by what is to be praised or that which is itself to be praised—of that Teacher, the Best of Men (*naravara*), who is himself a world-protector (*lokapāla*); [this is] for that Teacher.
The construction is to be understood as follows: "It should be worshipped and honored; it should be known by the wise alone; this is the excellent teaching;
it is the domain of the *Nettippakaraṇa*—thus it should be grasped. The manner of the construction is indeed according to the method stated below.

However, there is a distinction regarding the analysis of the compound (*viggaha*). For according to this method, those who protect the world are the "World-Protectors" (*lokapālā*), such as the four Great Kings and others already mentioned.
Because he protects the entire world together with those World-Protectors (Lokapālas) by virtue of being the Leader of the World, the Blessed One is also designated by the term "World-Protector.
Here, he is referred to by the word "that" (*taṃ*) in the phrase "of that" (*tassā*);
therefore, the meaning taken is "of that Teacher, the World-Protector, the Best of Men. If this is so, then the World-Protector has become subordinate and thus secondary.
Having distinguished the world as being subordinate, how can it be referred to by the word *taṃ* (that)?

Although it is a qualifier of the world, because of its dependence on the excellence of the Dispensation (*sāsana-vara*), it is referred to as if it were the primary factor, since it is a specific relative standing in the relationship of progenitor and owner.
The Blessed One is grasped as the owner of the excellent Dispensation. How [is this] regarding the excellent Dispensation?
"Does the Blessed One, the Master, honor the sublime Teaching? There is no contradiction here. For the Blessed Buddhas are reverers of the Dhamma;
they dwell at all times honoring the Dhamma. Indeed, the Buddhas' state of being reverers of the Dhamma and their honoring of the Dhamma is shown by the passage:
"What if I... were to dwell depending on that very Dhamma, having honored it, revered it, esteemed it, and worshiped it."
Since it has been stated thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One, as a guardian of the world, honors the sublime teaching.

This being so, while the meaning "the Blessed One, as a guardian of the world, honors the sublime teaching" is appropriate, how is the phrase "the Blessed One, as a guardian of the world, pays homage to the sublime teaching" appropriate?
It is indeed appropriate; for by means of the act of honoring, the word "pays homage" implies that [the Blessed One] is inclined toward, bent toward, and leaning toward it.
Because the goal (attha) is also attainable. For the Blessed One dwells at all times leaning toward, inclining toward, and tending toward the Dhamma out of reverence for the Dhamma.
Indeed, this has been said: "By which [Dhamma] I indeed dwell throughout the entire cycle," and so forth.
The rest here should be understood either by the method explained below or by the method stated in the commentaries; therefore, we do not elaborate upon it.
Thus, having included all three types of dispensation by means of the phrase "the excellent dispensation" (*sāsanavara*) in the first verse,
he says "twelve words," etc., demonstrating that he restricts the scope of his own *Nettippakaraṇa* specifically to the dispensation of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*).
Alternatively, [he does so] along with the praise of the Triple Gem in the first verse, regarding the scope of the *Nettippakaraṇa*.

Since it must be asked whether "that excellent teaching shown by the Teacher" refers to the entire scope of the *Nettipakaraṇa* or only to the teaching of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*), he says, "The twelve words are the Sutta," and so forth,
showing that it is indeed the Sutta which constitutes the teaching of the scriptures. Therein, although it is stated in general terms as "the excellent teaching,"...
The meaning is that the *pariyatti-sutta* alone should be understood as the supreme teaching (*sāsana-vara*).
Since it must be asked, "But how many kinds is it?", it is said, "twelve terms" (*dvādasa padāni*); the meaning is that, in brief, according to its divisions, it is of twelve kinds.

To show that although it is of twelve kinds by way of division, it is nevertheless only twofold—namely, by way of the phrasing-term (*byañjana-pada*) and the meaning-term (*attha-pada*)—it says: "All of that, both the phrasing..."

And it was said: "and the meaning. Since one must ask, "Of those two, is it to be understood that only one, by way of its form, is the domain of the *Nettippakaraṇa*, or rather both?", it was stated, "That is to be understood as both," in order to show that it is both.
Regarding the relationship between the word and what is expressed by the word, that phoneme and that meaning upon which the designation "sutta" occurs—
The meaning is that both of these, in their formal aspect, are to be understood as the domain of the *Nettippakaraṇa*.

Since it must be stated, "How are they to be understood?", it is said: "What is the meaning? What is the phrasing? This is what is meant: the entire body of scripture (*pariyatti*), known as the Suttas, is twelvefold when divided into six types of phrasing and six types of meaning; it is twofold when categorized simply as phrasing and meaning.

It should be understood that the "excellent teaching" (*sāsanavara*) is the subject matter of my *Nettippakaraṇa*. Having asked [for it] according to its own form, the word for the meaning (*atthapada*) and the word for the phrasing (*byañjanapada*) should be known according to their own forms.

Thus, in the first verse, the Sutta spoken of as the "excellent teaching" possesses both the nature of the textual tradition (*pariyatti*) and the nature of the words for the meaning and the words for the phrasing.

Having shown the state of what is to be known, he now says "The sixteen modes of conveying" (*soḷasahārā*) and so forth, in order to show the *Nettippakaraṇa*—the method for investigating that Sutta—by means of an analysis of the meaning of its words.
Alternatively, after the excellent teaching, which is the subject matter of the *Nettippakaraṇa*, has been defined and shown in the second verse, it must be asked:
"What is this 'Netti,' and how many kinds are there? Therefore, [he speaks] to show that the name 'Netti' consists of this much.
To show this in brief, he said, "The sixteen bases," and so forth. Therein, it should be understood that the *Netti*— the commentary on the investigation of the meaning of that Sutta of the Teaching—
which was pointed out by me, Mahākaccāyana, consists of a collection of sixteen bases,
a collection of five methods, and a collection of eighteen root-terms.

In what sense are those strings (*hāra*) and so forth called a "guide" (*netti*)? The meaning—namely, that it is called a "guide" because it guides (*neti*) sentient beings who are to be trained toward the Noble Dhamma—is stated exactly as such in the commentaries.
Regarding this third verse as well, the reading "expounded by Mahākaccāna" is excellent.
Alternatively, the reading "expounded by Mahākaccāyana" is not excellent; for the grammatical characteristic was [already] explained by me below.
Regarding the word "stated": it was stated that "the *nettis* are a collection consisting of the sixteen *hāras*, etc.

Since those *hāras* are either an investigation of the phrasing (*byañjanavicaya*) or an investigation of the meaning (*atthavicaya*), and the *nayās* are also either an investigation of the phrasing or an investigation of the meaning, when this consideration arises, he says "the *hāras* are an investigation of the phrasing," and so forth, in order to show them after determining that "these are the investigations for this [particular *netti*]. Therein:

The strings (*hāra*) constitute an investigation into the phrasing (*byañjana*) of the discourse (*sutta*), not an investigation into its meaning (*attha*), because they consist of a commentary by way of the phrasing alone,
excluding the extraction of the root-terms of the sixteen strings. However, the three methods (*naya*) constitute an investigation into the meaning of the discourse,

because the discourse [is explained] solely by way of extracting the phenomena of its own nature— such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth— which are designated as the root-terms of the three methods.
Regarding the phrase "because of the nature of commentary on the meaning":

one must ask whether "both of those [the word-meaning and the meaning] should be applied to some part of a sutta only by way of being a commentary on the meaning, or rather should they be applied in every way and in every place?
Since this question must be asked, it follows that both of those are applied in every way to all suttas.

To show this, it is said: "Both are grasped. Both the strings (hārā) and the methods (nayā) are grasped completely and on all sides by way of determining the meaning of the discourse; thus, they are applied in every respect to the discourses. [The question arises:
"How does the discourse known as the *Netti*, which consists of a collection of strings and so forth, comment upon the discourse that is to be commented upon?"
It is said, "it is called a *sutta* according to the *sutta*," because it possesses the state of being something that must be spoken.

The meaning is this: the commentary-*sutta* known as the *Netti* is to be commented upon in accordance with the *sutta* to be commented upon; by whatever mode of teaching or by whatever other means it is to be explained, by those very means it is spoken—thus, "it explains. Alternatively, "how much of the *sutta* known as the *Netti* is to be commented upon?"
Because it must be said that "he expounds the Sutta," it is stated: "It is called 'according to the Sutta' (yathāsutta) as the Sutta.

In this context, "according to the Sutta" means that whatever Sutta was spoken by the Blessed One—all that Sutta is called the "Sutta" known as the *Netti*—and he expounds it, that is, he comments upon it, by way of showing the gratification (*assāda*), the danger (*ādīnava*), and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "By the method of the *Netti*..."
"For there is no discourse (sutta) whatsoever that cannot be commented upon.

Regarding the question, "Is that teaching which has been commented upon by the *Nettippakaraṇa-vaṇṇanā* to be further commented upon, or is it rather to be understood [as it stands]?"—because it must be stated [in response], he said, "And whatever the teaching... and so forth.
Both the teaching as it appears in the canonical text (*pāḷi*) and the various phenomena taught by that teaching—
both of these must be understood with absolute certainty by those cultivating them under the heading of the "teaching on the bases of liberation" (*vimuttāyatana*),
because both serve as the causes for the attainment of the final goal, which culminates in *parinibbāna* without remainder (*anupādisesa*). "In the understanding of both of these..."
Because it must be asked, "What is the sequence that serves as the cause for the knowledge of that which is to be accomplished?

it is said, "In this regard," and so forth. Therein, when that knowledge is to be accomplished, the search for the meaning and the investigation of the meaning of the ninefold teaching beginning with the Suttas—consisting of the *hāras* and *nayās*—is the sequence for the knowledge that is to be accomplished.

The meaning is that "sequence" (*anupubbī*) refers to the cause for understanding. Alternatively, when the understanding of both [the Sutta and its meaning] is to be accomplished, this sequence—consisting of the search for the meaning and the investigation of the meaning of the ninefold teaching beginning with the Sutta—is called the "sequence for understanding," as it serves as the cause for that which is to be accomplished.
Alternatively, it refers to the ninefold search for the Suttanta by means of the sequence of the *hāra* (modes of interpretation) and *naya* (guiding principles), which will be explained below.
They should be understood as being the causes for one who possesses discernment. It is in that very manner that they are stated threefold in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The exposition of the meaning of the Section on Compendium (*saṅgahavāra*) is finished.
2. Exposition of the Meaning of the Section on Enumeration (*uddesavāra*).

1. Thus, after the methods (hāra) and so forth have been shown briefly by way of the section on inclusion (saṅgahavāra), the teaching beginning with “In this regard, what are the sixteen methods? is now commenced in order to show them by way of detailed analysis.
Alternatively, it was stated that the *Netti*—the collection of the sixteen methods and so forth—was pointed out by me, Mahākaccāna;
since it must be asked, “Which are those sixteen methods?”, [this] was said.

“Regarding ‘therein, the sixteen modes of conveyance (*hāra*)’ and so forth: ‘therein’ (*tattha*) means among those sixteen modes of conveyance and the rest. The mode of conveyance of teaching, the mode of conveyance of investigation...
[and so on] ...the mode of conveyance of coordination—these are to be understood as the sixteen modes of conveyance.
In this context, because the term *hāra* is common to all of them, its etymological meaning must first be stated. In what sense are they called ‘modes of conveyance’ (*hāra*)?”

They are called *hāras* because by means of them [ignorance, etc. are carried away (*harīyanti*). By means of these specific modes of exposition, ignorance, doubt, and perversion are carried away from the Suttas, Geyyas, and so forth that are to be expounded;
thus, because they are the causes for carrying away ignorance and the rest, the specific modes of exposition indicated by the word "by means of these" are called *hāras*.
The term *hāra* consists of the verbal root *hara* (to carry away), referring to the teacher’s vocal expression and the mental state that originates it.
The primary meaning is the arising of a state of consciousness associated with the knowledge of understanding the meaning of the suttas to be expounded for those to be trained (*veneyya*).
The meaning of the metaphorical application of the cause is the arising of that consciousness.

The meaning of the metaphorical application of the fruit is the power of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) belonging to those specific expositions which serve as its decisive support condition. By the word *iti*, it is precisely that power of the decisive support condition which is referred to. Possessing that power...

The specific details of the commentary do not constitute the meaning of the grammatical suffixes. This same principle applies to such instances elsewhere as well; the full elaboration has already been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, it is called "teaching" (*desanā*) because by means of it [the meaning] is taught (*desiyati*).

By this commentary, the meaning of the suttas to be commented upon is taught—that is, it is explained and made known according to the commentary—thus, because it is the cause for making [the meaning] known, it is referred to as "by this."
The "teaching" (*desanā*) refers to the specific commentary indicated by the word [in the text], not the teaching of the canonical text (*pāḷidesanā*) itself;
or rather, it is called "teaching" because it accompanies the canonical teaching by way of being the commentary upon that which is to be commented upon.

Although other methods (*hāra*) accompany the "teaching" insofar as they constitute commentaries on the meaning of the Sutta—which is designated as the "teaching-text"—this method (*hāra*), however, is for the most part understood through the literal expression (*yathāruta*) alone.
It deserves to be called "practicing together with the textual exposition" (pāḷidesanā), but not so other [methods].

For there is no textual exposition devoid of the characteristics of demonstrating the gratification (assāda), the danger (ādīnava), and the escape (nissaraṇa), and this mode of interpretation (hāra) possesses the characteristic of demonstrating the gratification and so forth.

It is called "investigation" (vicaya) because by means of it things are investigated. By means of this particular method of commentary, the words, questions, and so forth in the Sutta are investigated.

Thus, because it is the cause for investigation, this specific method of commentary is called *vicaya* (investigation). The senses of the abstract noun (*katvattha*) and the locative case (*adhikaraṇattha*) are also applicable here.

The method of commentary characterized by the investigation of words, questions, and so forth, in accordance with the Sutta to be commented upon, is the *vicaya-hāra* (the mode of conveyance as investigation).

It is called *yutti* (reasoning) because by means of it, what is logical and what is illogical is investigated. By means of this specific method of commentary, [it serves as the basis] for all the modes of conveyance whose domain is the ground [of the teaching].

The investigation of what is appropriate and what is inappropriate is called *yutti* (the Mode of Conveying the Logical). Because it is the cause for such investigation, this specific type of commentary indicated by the term "by means of this" (*etāya*) is named *yutti*.

Here, one should understand that there is an elision of the latter member of the compound; it is the investigation of what is logical (*yuttiyā vicāraṇā*), or it is *yutti* because it is associated with the state of being an object of investigation.

The *yutti-hāra* is the specific type of commentary characterized by the investigation of what is appropriate and inappropriate regarding all the modes of conveying [the Dhamma] that have the planes as their domain.

That by which one goes and sets in motion the fruit is a *pada* (foot/step); it is a cause (*kāraṇa*). That wherein fruits stand and remain because their existence is dependent upon it is a *ṭhāna* (place/station);

it is a cause. Being both a *pada* and a *ṭhāna*, it is a *padaṭṭhāna* (proximate cause); it is an immediate cause. Because by means of this the proximate causes of the phenomena (*dhamma*) appearing in the Sutta are investigated, it is called *padaṭṭhānā*;
it is a specific commentary (*visesa-saṃvaṇṇanā*), with the word "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*) being elided. [This occurs] in the Sutta.

The *padatthāna-hāra* (the mode of conveying the basis) is a specific method of commentary characterized by the investigation of the bases (*padatthāna*) of the teachings (*dhamma*) that have been presented, as well as the bases of those very bases.
It is called *lakkhaṇa* because by means of this specific method of commentary, teachings possessing identical characteristics are indicated even when they were not explicitly stated in the Sutta.
It is characterized by the discernment of even those unspoken teachings that possess characteristics identical to the teachings already mentioned in the Sutta.
The *lakkhaṇa-hāra* (the mode of characteristic) is a specific kind of commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*).
Herein, the four—etymology (*nibbacana*) and so forth—which are shown in the Sutta, are "arranged" (*viyūhīyanti*); that is, they are analyzed and then synthesized.

It is called *byūho* because one arranges (*vāti*) by means of this; thus, it is the "fourfold arrangement" (*catubyūho*), which is the arrangement of the four: etymology, intention (*adhippāya*), and phrasing (*byañjana*). And of these, etymology...

The *catubyūha* (fourfold) method of interpretation is a specific mode of commentary characterized by demonstrating the connection between the beginning and the end of the introduction to the teaching.

The *āvatta* (turning back) method of interpretation is a specific mode of commentary characterized by turning back (*āvaṭṭana*)—that is, bringing together—those phenomena similar to or dissimilar from the phenomena grasped in the teaching;
it is called *āvatta* because "by means of this" (*etena vā*), those phenomena grasped in the teaching are turned back by way of their similar and dissimilar counterparts.

The *Vibhatti-hāra* (Analysis Mode) is a specific mode of commentary characterized by the analysis of phenomena—both those that are unique and non-unique, as well as those that are both common and unique—according to their defilement, purification, commonality and uniqueness, proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), and plane.

The *Parivattanā-hāra* (Reversal Mode) is a specific mode of commentary characterized by the reversal of the phenomena taught in the Sutta by way of their opposites; it is called "reversal" (*parivatta*) because [phenomena] are reversed here through their opposition.
"Vivacana" refers to various expressions that convey the same single meaning stated in the Sutta;

"vevacana" is simply a synonym for "vivacana. Thus, the "vevacana-hāra" (the method of synonyms) is a specific mode of commentary characterized by the application of numerous synonymous terms to a single meaning expressed in the Sutta.

The *paññatti-hāra* (the mode of presentation) is that specific method of commentary characterized by the manner in which the meanings stated in the Suttas are made known through various modes of presentation (*paññatti*), such that "by this" or "herein" [they are presented];

it is the characteristic of the way each individual phenomenon (*dhamma*) is to be presented through numerous modes of presentation. The *otaraṇa-hāra* (the mode of entry) is that specific method of commentary characterized by the entry into the meaning of the Suttas through the gateways of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and so forth, such that the phenomena contained in the Suttas "enter" or are "inserted" herein; thus, "by this" or "therein" they are entered.

In this [method], the undertakings of questions concerning the words and their meanings in the Sutta are purified (*sodhīyanti*) and settled (*samādhīyanti*); or, by means of this, there is purification (*sodhana*). Thus, the specific type of commentary characterized by the purification of the undertakings of questions concerning the words and their meanings in the Sutta is the "Purification" (*Sodhana*) Mode of Conveying.
In this [method], phenomena that constitute both the general and the particular are determined (*adhiṭṭhīyanti*) and set forth without conceptual differentiation (*vikappa*);

or, by means of this, there is determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). Thus, the [mode] characterized by the discernment of the general and the particular through the non-differentiation of the phenomena contained in the Sutta is the "Determination" (*Adhiṭṭhāna*) Mode of Conveying.
The mode of conveyance consisting of the specific distinction of the commentary is the foundation.
That which both causes and conditions prepares and constructs the fruit—this is the equipment consisting of cause and condition;
that which explains this equipment, as well as the cause and the condition, is the specific distinction of the commentary.
Thus, this specific mode of commentary is called the "Requisite" (*parikkhāra*).
The "Requisite" method of conveying is a specific mode of commentary characterized by the determination of the causes and conditions—termed "requisites"—of the teachings as they appear in the Sutta.

It is called "Arrangement" (*samāropana*) because the teachings appearing in the Sutta are arranged therein by way of their "footing" (*padaṭṭhāna*) and other such aspects, or because one arrives at them by means of it.

The "Method of Coordination" (samāropana-hāra) is a specific form of commentary characterized by the investigation of the word-meanings, synonyms, states, abandonments, and coordination of the teachings as they appear in the Sutta.
Since the meaning of the words must be stated everywhere according to the method of establishing the state (bhāva-sādhana), it should also be applied from that perspective.
The remainder is to be understood by following the detailed commentary.
In that context, the nature of the *hāra* (modes of exposition) was stated by the passage beginning, “What are the sixteen *hāras* of teaching?

Why, then, was the passage beginning with “Its *anugīti* (corresponding verse)” stated? It was stated again as “Its *anugīti*, teaching, investigation, and reasoning,” etc., for the purpose of easy comprehension through the *anugīti* verse.
Therein, “its” (*tassa*) refers to the enumeration of the *hāras*. “*Anugīti*” means a verse sung subsequently or afterwards. “Fifteen” (*pañcadasa*)... [etc.]

The fifteenth. The sixteenth is "the sixteenth. In meaning, they are "unmixed" (*asaṃkiṇṇa*), meaning they are free from confusion regarding the meaning of the words of the teaching, the meaning of their characteristics, and their intermixture.
Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "And that non-confusion of theirs is clearly evident in the exposition of their characteristics.
The remainder should be understood according to the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*). "Some modes (*hāra*) are mixed with certain other modes."
Since it must be stated, "Why should it be known as 'unmixed'? the text says, "Of these very [sixteen]," and so forth.
In that context, "it occurs of these" means that it occurs in the manner of those sixteen modes of conveying (hāra) such that there is no confusion;
it occurs by way of that non-confused mode. "Ayā" refers to the detailed exposition of the methods (naya), for it extends (ayati) and proceeds (pavattati).
In terms of its detailed exposition, the letter *ta* has been included for the purpose of removing the fault of confusion; it is a term expressing a specific classification of the method (*naya*).
"Classification by method" (*nayavibhatti*) means a classification according to the principle (*ñāya*).

It should be understood that the intention is this: such a classification by principle—which proceeds in detail through the five methods—occurs in that [text] in an unconfused manner, being known as such because it is not mixed up.

2. The sixteen modes of conveying (hāra) have been stated according to their specific forms and have been understood by us. However, because it was necessary to state what the "five methods" (naya) are, the passage beginning with "In this regard, what are the five methods?
was spoken after asking that question in order to recite them according to their specific forms. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, it is stated:
"Having thus recited the modes of conveying, the passage beginning with 'In this regard, what are... was now spoken in order to recite the methods."

Regarding this, the meaning of the term is explained in detail in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as follows: “They lead [one] therein toward defilement (*saṃkilesa*) and cause one to understand the distinction in purification (*vodāna*), thus they are ‘methods’ (*naya*); or else, those [states] are led by means of them, or [one] is led by them, thus they are ‘methods.

According to this, the primary meaning is the arising of consciousness associated with knowledge that proceeds by taking hold of both defilement and purification in accordance with the methods such as the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa*. Of these methods, such as the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa*...
The power of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is taken here by way of figurative application to its fruit; the word "iti" refers to that power taken figuratively as the fruit.
The methods such as the "turning of delight" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*) together with that power are not the meaning of "condition.
[This applies] to the discourse on the side of defilement through craving and ignorance, and to the discourse on the side of purification through serenity and insight.
The method characterized by guidance through the door of the application of the Four Truths is the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. In this context, "the Four Truths" refers as follows:
craving and ignorance constitute the truth of the origin because they are the root of existence; all remaining phenomena belonging to the three planes constitute the truth of suffering;
serenity and insight constitute the truth of the path; and the unconditioned element to be attained by means of that [path] constitutes the truth of cessation.

*Tipukkhalo* means "threefold-clear" (*tipukkhalo*), being clear (*pukkhalo*)— that is, beautiful— by way of three factors on the side of defilement, such as greed and so forth, and by way of three factors on the side of purification, such as non-greed and so forth.

It is a specific type of commentary characterized by the guidance of the meaning of the Sutta through the application of the Four Noble Truths, [showing] the side of defilement via the unwholesome roots and the side of purification via the wholesome roots.
The "Lion’s Play" method (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*) is so called because it leads one here by means of the Blessed One’s lion-like play.

It is a specific mode of commentary characterized by the leading [of the meaning] through the application of the Four Truths to the subject matter of the sutta— namely, the entire defiled side by way of the perversions such as the perception of beauty,
and the purified side by way of the faculty of faith and so forth.

"Surveying the directions" (*disālocana*) means the surveying of wholesome and other phenomena by way of the directions consisting of the eightfold method (*atthanaya*), the threefold method (*nayattaya*), and so forth.
Regarding the explanations of the meaning of the Sutta provided for the purpose of applying each respective method:
