those phenomena that constitute the "directions" (*disā*) of each respective method—such as purification (*vodāna*) and so forth, as well as defilements (*saṃkilesika*)—which have been extracted from the Sutta and explained, [the following is said] of those aforementioned phenomena:
“Direction-observation” (*disālocana*) is the observation by means of the mind, [perceiving] "this is the first direction," "this is the second direction," and so forth.

Because it brings together the phenomena thus observed by applying them to the three methods of meaning (*atthanaya*), it is like a hook; thus it is a "hook. The method that brings together the wholesome and other phenomena which constitute the directions of each respective method is the "hook-method" (*aṅkusanaya*).
It is called "lañjaka" because it marks (*lañjeti*); the method which marks—that is, makes manifest—the meaning of the Sutta is so called because of this marking and making manifest.
That method is called *lañjaka*; that which is both a method and a *lañjaka* is thus "method-*lañjaka*" (*nayalañjaka*). It should be applied as follows:
the first method-*lañjaka* is named *Nandiyāvaṭṭa*, the second method-*lañjaka* is named *Tipukkhalo*, and the third method-*lañjaka* is named *Sīhavikkīḷita*.

"Uttama" means "most exalted" because it is especially exalted among those that are exalted; it refers to that which is supreme. "Gata" means "known," with the sense of "matured" (*mata*); alternatively, the reading is "matā. The remainder here should be understood according to the method already stated and according to the commentary.
In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), which provides an exposition according to the method already stated:
"The nature of conventional designation (*sammutisabhāva*) is the state of being a mere worldly convention established by means of aggregates and so forth;

the nature of ultimate reality (*paramatthasabhāva*) is the characteristic of hardness, touching, and so on, belonging to earth, contact, and the rest. This is the summary here: that in which, when broken..."
Or, when exclusion (apoha) is performed by the mind, the cognition does not arise in that way;
this is conventional truth (sammutisacca), as in the case of a pot, or water with its constituent parts, and by contrast, the opposite is ultimate truth (paramatthasacca).

In this statement, [the term "pot"] refers to a collection such as the pot, shards, water, mud, and so forth, which is established for the world through prior convention regarding the pot, shards, water, mud, and so on.

The conventional nature (*saṃvṛtisabhāva*) consists merely in the conceptual designation (*vohāramatta*) of things such as a pot, a stone, water, or mud; it is not false by virtue of its conventional agreement (*saṅketa*).

The ultimate nature (*paramatthasabhāva*), however, is the characteristic of hardness and so forth in the case of earth and the rest, and the characteristic of touching and so forth in the case of contact and the rest.

“If this is so, [then] when a pot or the like is not present—either because it has not yet arisen, or because it has ceased, or because it is not occurring in a manner corresponding to its [expected] deficiency, or in the case of water and so forth...”

Granted that there may be a conventional nature (*sammuti-bhāva*); but how could there be a conventional nature when things are broken or deficient? For even earth, contact, and so forth are subject to breaking.
Furthermore, since hardness, touching, and so forth are not distinct from earth, contact, and so forth, how could they possess an ultimate nature (*paramattha-sabhāva*)?
By what summarized meaning do we [distinguish] between conventional nature and ultimate nature?
Because it must be said, "it is to be known," he said, "This, then, is the summary here," and so forth. In that context, "here" refers to these conventional natures and ultimate natures;
this method being explained should be understood as the summarized meaning.
When a jar or similar object is broken, that which is other than the jar—namely, the state of shards and so forth—is [produced] by the mind through what was previously done.
Just as, by whatever conventional designation such as "potsherd" a thing comes to be, when the primary substance— such as clay or water—
is present in a state of deficiency, another state such as "mud" arises from that [clay] due to a prior mental formation;
so too, by that very designation, there is the cognition that perceives the intrinsic nature of the potsherd and so forth.

The generation of the intrinsic nature of mud and so forth occurs; whether it be an unbroken jar or the like, or broken shards and the like, or water and the like in full measure, or mud and the like in deficient measure—all this is indeed conventional truth (*sammutisacca*). Because there is the state of being a question to be asked:
"When the mud is broken, or when the mud is deficient, what remains is the other conventional nature," [it refers to] the jar...
And it is said: "and in the water of the requisites.
The nature of conventional truth has been stated by you and understood by us; because it must be asked, "What is the nature of ultimate truth?", it is said:
"ultimate truth is the opposite of that. [This is known] from the fact that earth and so forth have the characteristics of hardness and so forth.
The intended meaning is that since contact and the others possess the characteristics of touching and so forth, while for anything else the characteristics of hardness and so forth are impossible,
and since earth, contact, and the rest possess the characteristics of solidity and touching, they must indeed be ultimate truths; thus,
when this summary meaning is accepted, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
3. The five methods (*pañca naya*) were taught by the Teacher according to their specific forms and have been understood by us.

Because it was asked, "Which are those words that were taught as the eighteen root-words (*aṭṭhārasa mūlapada*)?", he spoke the passage beginning with "In this regard, what are the eighteen root-words? in order to show them according to their specific forms.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, after thus teaching the methods as well...
It is said: "Now, the section beginning with 'In this regard, which are... is commenced in order to enumerate the root-terms (*mūlapada*). Herein, the construction should be understood as follows:
there are nine wholesome terms and nine unwholesome terms; thus, eighteen root-terms (*mūlapada*) are to be seen.

They are called "roots" (*mūla*) because by means of them the methods (*naya*) and the classifications of their foundations (*patiṭṭhāna-vibhāga*) are established (*patiṭṭhahanti*). They are called "terms" (*pada*) because they are established therein.
The terms are "methods," "divisions of the *Paṭṭhāna*," and "attainments. They are called "root-terms" (*mūlapada*) because they are both roots—by way of the sense already stated—and terms.
They are "wholesome" (*kusala*) because they cause one to adhere to what is blameworthy or evil; they are "wholesome" because they cut away lust and the other defilements at the *kusa* grass;
they are "wholesome" because they cut like *kusa* grass; and they are "wholesome" because they are to be taken up and practiced by means of the *kusa*-like knowledge.
They are wholesome. "Opposites of the wholesome" means unwholesome; here, the prefix *a-* has the sense of opposition.
Nine phrases are wholesome and nine phrases are unwholesome; these have been stated according to numerical limit and according to the distinction of their classes.
Since it must be asked, "Which are they?", the nine unwholesome phrases [are presented] by way of proximity.
In order to show them according to their specific forms, it was said: “Which nine terms are unwholesome? and so forth. However, in the Commentary it is stated:

“Having thus shown the root terms by way of numerical limit and by way of classification of type, he now shows them according to their specific forms; first, he recites the side of defilement beginning with ‘craving’ (taṇhā).
In that context, craving (taṇhā) is so called because it thirsts for and fears the aggregates such as form. Unfindable (avindiya) refers to bodily misconduct and so forth.

It is ignorance (*avijjā*) because it does not find; it is ignorance because it does not find what is to be found, such as bodily good conduct; or it is ignorance because it is the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*). It is greed (*lobha*) because they are greedy by means of it;
or it is greed because it is itself greedy; or it is greed because it is the act of being greedy. The same method applies to hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*).

Perception of beauty (*subhasaññā*) is the perception that occurs regarding the aggregate of form and so forth as "beautiful" when they are actually impure. [The same applies to] the perception of suffering regarding what is actually painful, and so forth.

“Perception of pleasure” (sukhasaññā) is the perception that arises as “pleasure. “Perception of permanence” (niccasaññā) is the perception that arises as “permanent” regarding conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāradhamma) which are actually impermanent.
“Perception of self” (attasaññā) is the perception that arises as “self” regarding the aggregates such as the eye, etc., which lack the nature of a self.
“Wherein” (yattha) refers to those locations in which the entire unwholesome side (akusalapakkha) is included and converges; those are the terms [to be understood].
The construction is: "unwholesome" (*akusalāni*). "Compendium" (*saṅgaha*) means enumeration (*gaṇana*). "Convergence" (*samosaraṇa*) means coordination (*samāropana*).

It is "tranquillity" (*samatha*) because it calms (*sameti*) and pacifies (*vūpasameti*) opposing states such as restlessness and the hindrances by way of their specific factor-counteraction (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
It is "insight" (*vipassanā*) because it sees conditioned phenomena through various aspects such as impermanence and so forth. It is the opposite of greed.

Non-greed (*alobha*). Non-hatred (*adosa*) is the opposite of hatred (*dosa*). Non-delusion (*amoha*) is the opposite of delusion (*moha*). Here too, the intention is that the prefix *a-* has the sense of "opposite," not the sense of "non-existence" and so forth.

Perception and the primary mental states that arise with regard to what is foul—namely, the aggregate of form and so forth, or the eye and so forth—are called "perception of the foul" (*asubhasaññā*);
specifically, this refers to the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhāna*).

Among the [three kinds of] suffering, such as the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*), the perception and the primary mental states that arise as "suffering" constitute the perception of suffering;

specifically, this is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings. Regarding the impermanent aggregates and so forth, which are subject to change, the perception and the primary mental states that arise as "impermanent" constitute the perception of impermanence;
specifically, this is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the mind. Regarding that which has the nature of non-self...

The perception of non-self (*anattasaññā*) consists of mental states dominated by the perception that the aggregates, or the eye and so forth, are "non-self"; it is specifically dominated by mindfulness in the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*).
For this teaching proceeds under the heading of wisdom and mindfulness. Therefore, it was said by the Blessed One:
"And how, bhikkhus, is the power of mindfulness to be seen? In the four foundations of mindfulness; herein..."

"The power of mindfulness is to be seen. Regarding the phrase "wherein" (*yattha*): the construction is that those states in which the entire side of the wholesome (*kusalapakkha*) finds its inclusion and convergence are themselves "wholesome" (*kusala*).
"Summary" (*uddāna*): "Uddāna" means giving protection above; the meaning is a statement of summary. When [the summary] has not been stated...
The meaning stated previously might become as if scattered; therefore, the intention is that the summary (uddāna) is given for the purpose of preventing such scattering.
"And the four perversions" refers to the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self.
"Defilements exist here in nine locations" means "ground" (bhūmi); thus, the ground of defilements is "defilement-ground" (kilesabhūmi), meaning the places where defilements arise.
"Nine terms" is what is meant.

"The four foundations of mindfulness" refers to the perceptions of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self. "The ground of the faculties" means the grounds, the spheres of activity, and the meeting places for the faculties that ripen liberation, beginning with faith.
By means of the nine wholesome terms, the wholesome side is joined and conjoined; by means of the nine unwholesome terms, the unwholesome side [is joined].
They are joined (*yujjanti*) and are being joined (*yojīyanti*). The wholesome factors are joined with the nine wholesome terms; as they are being joined, they come to be [associated].

The unwholesome factors are joined with the nine unwholesome terms; as they are being joined, they come to be [associated]. The remainder not stated in the section on enumeration (*uddesavāra*) is to be understood according to the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*).
Thus ends the exposition of the meaning of the Section on Enumeration (Uddesavāra), composed according to the strength of one's faculties. 3.
Exposition of the Meaning of the Section on Exposition (Niddesavāra).
The Exposition of the Description of the Sixteen Modes (Soḷasahāraniddesavibhāvanā). 4.
Regarding the modes and so forth: the summary of the *Nettippakaraṇa* as a whole has been recited and is known by us;
however, because it must be asked, "What is the exposition?", the following is stated—"In this regard, the *Nettī* in brief," etc.—in order to explain the modes and so forth that were recited.

It has begun. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: "When [the summary] has been thus recited, the following beginning with 'Therein, in brief' was commenced in order to explain the *hāras* and so forth.

Therein, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to that recited text of the summary beginning with: "In this regard, what are the sixteen *hāras*? Teaching, investigation," and so on. "In brief" (*saṅkhepato*) means concisely.
"The Guide" (*nettī*) refers to the *Nettippakaraṇa*. "Recited" (*kittitā*) means spoken; now, by way of detailed exposition...
"I shall explain"—this is what is meant.
"The gratification, the danger, and the escape; the fruit and the means;
and the command of the Blessed One—these are the requisites for the teaching of yogis."
The construction of the meaning in this verse is as follows: that specific mode of commentary by which— whether through the commentary on a Sutta— the gratification (*assāda*),
the danger (*ādīnava*), the escape (*nissaraṇa*), the fruit (*phala*), the means (*upāya*), and the instruction of the Blessed One for the benefit of yogis are shown,
commented upon, and made known by way of such commentary— that specific mode of commentary is what is called the "nutriment of teaching" (*desanāhāra*).
The meanings of the terms and so forth have already been explained in detail in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary); therefore, I shall explain only a small portion here.

It is called *assāda* (gratification) because it is tasted (*assādiyati*). What is it? It is pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*somanassa*), and the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) when they serve as desirable objects.
Or, it is called *assāda* because one tastes by means of it. What is it? It is craving (*taṇhā*) and the perversions (*vipallāsā*). For it is through the influence of the perversions that some...
Beings relish even an undesirable object by way of an agreeable aspect.
It is called *ādīnava* because it blows (*vāti*) intensely through the power of karma, proceeding as something miserable such as suffering; thus, it refers to suffering and the like.
Alternatively, it is called *ādīnava* because it proceeds by blowing excessively, being wretched (*ādīnaṃ*); thus, it refers to a miserable person, owing to that state.
And those states belonging to the three planes are so called because they are connected with impermanence and the rest.

It is "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) because one escapes by means of it; thus, it refers to the Noble Path. Alternatively, it is "escape" because one escapes [to it]; thus, it refers to Nibbāna. The word *pi* has the sense of inclusion. The various divisions of escape have indeed been stated in many ways in the Commentaries.
It "bears fruit" or "proceeds," hence it is "fruit" (*phala*); this is the fruit of the teaching. Even though the teaching itself does not produce the fruit [directly], [it leads to it].
Nevertheless, upon hearing the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, accumulations of merit arise;

because of the cause of these accumulations of merit, the fruit comes forth. Therefore, it is said that the teaching has a fruit. What is that fruit? It consists of the excellence of lifespan, beauty, happiness, strength, retinue, sovereignty, and requisites among gods and humans;

the glory of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*); the glory of kingship over the devas; the four perfections; the perfection of the wheels of virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*); the higher knowledges (*vijjā*), the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*); and the enlightenment of disciples (*sāvaka-bodhi*), the enlightenment of paccekabuddhas, and the perfect enlightenment of a fully awakened one (*sammāsambodhi*).
It is called *upāya* because, having attained the convergence of conditions (*paccayasāmaggi*), one goes toward it; that by which the fruit proceeds. What is it?

It is the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) of the Noble Path. For the preceding practice is the means for attaining the succeeding practice, and it is the means for the successive attainment of the Path and Nibbāna.
Some say, "The Path itself is also the means"; according to their opinion, it is Nibbāna alone [that is the goal].
It might be said that "escape" (nissaraṇa) has been mentioned. However, [the author] will later state that the noble path is the escape by saying, "Having abandoned those, cross the flood";
therefore, the opinion of some should not be accepted.

"Command" (āṇatti) means the enjoining or ordering of those to be trained by the Blessed One—who is worthy of commands—for the sake of accomplishing their welfare: "Practice right conduct in this way; do not practice wrong conduct. This is called a command.
They "strive" and "apply themselves" to the development of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths; thus they are "yogis.
Having supplied the ellipsis by stating "for the sake of those yogis who are to be trained," the construction should be made.

From the *Niddesa*, the specific distinction of the commentary that analyzes all the [factors] such as gratification (*assāda*) mentioned in the Sutta—even those occurring only in part—is called the "mode of teaching" (*desanāhāra*).
That mode of analysis should be understood, and since it will appear in the *Vibhaṅga* of the "Nutriment of Teaching," it is not shown here.

The exposition of the "Nutriment of Teaching" has been explained and is known by us; however, because it must be asked, "What is the exposition of the 'Nutriment of Investigation'?", [the following is said]:
"That which was asked and that which was answered, and whatever verse follows the sutta."
“The investigation of the discourse is designated as the ‘mode of investigation’”—this verse was spoken.
Therein, that which is questioned of the discourse and the questioning itself, as they are being investigated;

that which is answered of the discourse and the answering itself, as they are being investigated; and the investigation of the discourse’s words and so forth, as well as the investigation of its gratification and so forth—[all this constitutes the mode of investigation].
And there exists that specific method of commentary by which those aforementioned types—investigation, questioning, and so forth—are investigated;
this specific method of commentary is indicated as the "method of investigation" (*vicaya-hāra*). This is how the construction of the meaning should be understood.

*Pucchīyate* means "it is questioned"; *vissajjīyate* means "it is answered. These should be regarded as having the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāva-sādhana*), not the sense of an object (*kamma-sādhana*). Therefore, it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "He says 'in the sense of an abstract noun'—namely, 'answered' means answering."

Because of the restriction by the phrase "of the Sutta," it should be understood that what appears in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) by way of detailed exposition (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) is not to be taken [as the primary meaning]. That method of investigation (*vicaya-hāra*) has indeed been stated in the commentary.

How so?—“This question is one for the illumination of the unseen, for the correlation of what has been seen, for the cutting off of doubt, a question for assent, a question from a desire to speak, based on beings, based on phenomena (*dhamma*), based on a single [category], based on many [categories], within the domain of conventional truth (*sammuti*), and within the domain of ultimate truth (*paramattha*).”
The investigation of questions should be understood through such passages as: "having past objects, having future objects, having present objects," and so forth.
The investigation of answers is [understood] through such passages as: "this answer is a categorical response, an analytical response, a response by counter-question, a response by setting aside;
it is with remainder, without remainder, surpassable, unsurpassable, mundane, or supramundane," and so forth.
“Investigation” (*vicaya*) is the investigation that brings together the meaning of what has been asked, determining: “This question corresponds with this; it does not correspond with that.

Furthermore, “investigation of before and after” (*pubbāparavicaya*) is the investigation that correlates what precedes with what follows. “Investigation of the subsequent verses” (*anugītivicaya*) is the investigation [of the verses] by way of such categories as:
“This subsequent verse summarizes the stated meaning, summarizes the unstated meaning, summarizes both meanings, summarizes wholesome meanings, or summarizes unwholesome meanings,” and so forth.
Regarding the gratification and so forth: pleasant feeling is defined by such terms as "having the characteristic of experiencing a desirable object";
craving by "having the characteristic of grasping at an object"; the perversions by "having the characteristic of distorted grasping";
and the remaining phenomena of the three planes by "having their respective characteristics," and so on—according to the terms found within all twenty-two triads and more than four hundred dyads.
The investigation of gratification (*assādavicaya*) is the discernment of the specific distinctions of gratification in each respective case.

[This occurs] by way of [defining] painful feeling as "having the characteristic of experiencing the undesirable," and so forth; the truths of suffering as "having the characteristic of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*), and so forth;
impermanence and the rest as "impermanent" and so forth, by virtue of their having a beginning and an end and their being subject to destruction; and [the investigation of all] mundane phenomena.

The investigation of danger (*ādīnavavicaya*) occurs through the discernment of the specific stages of the path of practice—such as those partaking of defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and those partaking of decline (*hānabhāgiya*)—by way of the occurrence of danger and by means of the extraction of the syllable *o*.

The investigation of escape (*nissaraṇavicaya*) occurs by way of the discernment of the specific distinctions in the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*), such as the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), because the Noble Path arrives at the state of escape;
and by way of the discernment of the specific distinctions in the various methods already mentioned regarding Nibbāna itself. Thus is the investigation of escape.

Investigation should be understood as the discernment and determination of the fruits and so forth to be accomplished through the teaching of this or that sutta, as well as the means thereto and the specific injunctions found in those various suttas.
Thus, the "investigative method" (*vicaya-hāra*) should be understood as having the characteristic of investigation by way of determining the distinctions in the questions,
answers, prior and subsequent inquiries, and the verses, as well as the distinctions in the gratification and other [aspects] such as the danger.
It has been stated thus.
However, the distinction regarding the mode of answering is explained in the *Ṭīkā*.
How so?—When asked, "Is the eye impermanent? the categorical answer, "Yes, the eye is indeed impermanent," is an answer by way of a single alternative (*ekamsavyākaraṇa*).

When asked, “Should the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) be developed, and should it be realized? the answer given by analyzing the matter—stating that “that which is included in the path should be developed, and that which is included in the fruit should be realized”—is an analytical categorical response (vibhajjabyākaraṇa). When asked, “Is the faculty of final knowledge wholesome (kusala)?
one should first ask in return, “Does ‘wholesome’ mean the sense of being blameless, or does it mean having a pleasant result? and so on.
An answer by way of counter-question (*paṭipucchā-byākaraṇa*) is the non-answering and setting aside [of a question], such as when it is asked, "Is the self eternal or non-eternal?

and one replies, "This has not been declared," and so forth. Furthermore, the question, "Are these terms 'wholesome' (*kusala*) and 'phenomena' (*dhamma*) synonymous, or do they have different meanings?

is one that leaves something remaining to be asked. Regarding the fact that an answer may leave something remaining, this is due to the inclination of those to be trained (*veneyya*) within the teaching.

It should be understood that what lacks the miracle is surpassed, while what possesses the miracle is unsurpassed; the rest is indeed easy to understand from the exposition of the Mode of Conveying Investigation (*vicayahāra-niddesa*), as has already been stated.

It should be seen that the meaning stated in the commentaries (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) is unconfused, clear, and understood by those who are like young novices; therefore, it need not be analyzed by us in every instance.

The exposition of the Mode of Conveying Investigation has been explained and is known to us; however, because it must be asked, "What is the exposition of the Mode of Conveying Junction (*yuttihāra-niddesa*)?", [the following is provided].
“The ground and the range of all the modes (hāra), as well as the investigation of what is appropriate and inappropriate—this is designated as the Mode of Conveying the Method (yuttihāra).
This verse was spoken. Therein, “of all” refers to the sixteen modes; their “ground” is the phrasing that serves as the basis for their occurrence.

The meaning is to be construed as follows: whatever is the domain (*gocara*) and the meaning of the suttas—that is, the investigation (*parikkhā*) of what is appropriate and inappropriate regarding those domains of the letter known as the "planes" (*bhūmi*) and the meaning of the suttas known as the "domains"—and the exposition (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) consisting of the deliberation (*vicāraṇā*) upon that which is appropriate and inappropriate;
this specific type of exposition, characterized by the investigation of what is appropriate and inappropriate, is designated as the "Mode of Conveying the Logical" (*yutti-hāra*).

Regarding those strings (*hāra*), the logical consistency (*yuttibhāva*) of the phrasing (*byañjana*) that has come down in the Sutta as the "ground" is twofold: its nature as natural expression (*sabhāvaniruttibhāva*) and its nature as expressing the intended meaning (*adhippetatthavācakabhāva*).

However, the logical consistency of the phrasing that has come down in the Sutta as the "object" (*gocara*) is its non-contradiction with the Sutta, the Vinaya, and the nature of phenomena (*dhammatā*).
The lack of logical consistency (*ayuttibhāva*) should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.

The exposition of the Mode of Conveying the Logical Reason has been explained and understood by us. Since it must now be asked, "What is the exposition of the Mode of Conveying the Footing?", [the answer is given]:
"The Victor teaches the Dhamma, and whatever is the footing for that Dhamma—thus, as far as all phenomena extend, this is the Mode of Conveying the Footing."
The verse has been spoken. Therein, "the Dhamma" refers to whatever wholesome and other states (dhammas) the Victor teaches in the Sutta;
and "its foundation" refers to whatever foundation is to be determined for those wholesome and other states taught as Dhamma by the Victor in the Sutta.
In this manner, according to the stated method, [this applies] to all those states whatsoever that have been taught in the Sutta by the Victor.
Whatever foundation (padatthāna) of all phenomena is to be determined, and whatever foundation of that foundation is to be determined—
each such foundation, and in this manner according to the stated method, until as many foundational phenomena as there are to be determined have been determined—
all those foundations of phenomena (dhammapadatthāna) are to be applied accordingly.

The construction of the meaning is as follows: having extracted [the factors], that specific method of commentary by which they are explained is designated as the "basis of the word" (*padaṭṭhāna-hāra*).

This refers to such things as wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), hearing the true Dhamma (*saddhammasavaṇa*), and reliance upon virtuous friends (*sappurisūpanissaya*) regarding the wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) taught in the Sutta.

The proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) should be determined as follows: for unwholesome states taught in the Suttas, the proximate causes are improper attention, listening to what is not the true Dhamma, reliance on unworthy persons, and so forth;
for indeterminate states, the proximate causes are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate states as appropriate, and so on.

The exposition of the Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes has been explained and understood by us. Now, since it must be asked, "What is the exposition of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāraniddesa*)?"—
“When a single teaching has been stated, whatever teachings share that same characteristic are thereby stated as well;
this is the Mode called ‘Characteristic.
This verse has been spoken. Therein, when a single teaching has been stated by the Blessed One in the Sutta and determined in the Commentary:

Or, when there exists some property (*dhamma*) by which whatever phenomena possess a single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇa*), all those phenomena—even if not explicitly stated in their own form within the Sutta—should be brought forward by virtue of their shared characteristic as being subject to exposition;
that specific mode of exposition by which they are thus described is designated as the "Mode of Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇo hāro*). This is the construction of the meaning.
“Those which have one common characteristic (lakkhaṇa) are ‘single-characteristic’ (ekalakkhaṇā), meaning they possess a common characteristic;
or, by virtue of their co-occurrence, their common function, their common cause, their common fruit, or their common object, they are determined even though not explicitly stated. How so?
For instance, in such passages as, “With diversity of bodies and diversity of perceptions, through non-attention to the diversity of perceptions,” it is [determined] by way of co-occurrence.

Phenomena associated with perception (*saññā*) have been determined. In such passages as “Giving binds friends,” both the identity of function and the identity of purpose—namely, affectionate speech and beneficial conduct—are determined.
In such passages as “Feeling has contact as its condition,” perception and the other factors are also determined by way of their common cause.
In such passages as “Volitional formations have ignorance as their condition,” craving, clinging, and so forth are also determined by way of their common fruit.

When it is determined that "one relishes and delights in form, and with that as an object, lust arises," then because they share the same object, the feeling and other factors associated with it are also determined;
the meaning is that they must be stated after having been so determined. The detailed exposition will follow in the section on the *Vibhaṅga*.
The Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*) has been demonstrated and understood by us. Now, since it must be asked, "Which is the Fourfold Array Mode (*catubyūha-hāra*)?"—
“The etymological analysis, the intended meaning, the phrasing, the purpose of the teaching, and the connection between what precedes and what follows—this is the fourfold method of exposition.
Thus the verse is spoken. Therein, “etymological analysis” refers to the grammatical derivation of the words of the discourses belonging to the Buddhas for each respective sutta.

The intention of the teachers or disciples, the purpose and the phrasing, the source of the teaching through the medium of the phrasing, and the connection between what precedes and what follows—these, such as the analysis of language (*nirutta*), are that specific method of commentary by which they are clarified;

this specific method of commentary is designated as the "Fourfold Array" (*catubyūha-hāra*). It is the cause for the occurrence of the teaching, consisting of the teacher’s underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) and so forth.

This is called the source for the teaching. Since the Fourfold Array (Catubyūha-hāra) has a wide range of scope, we shall explain it after establishing its characteristic accomplishment in the analysis (vibhaṅga).
The exposition of the Fourfold Array has been demonstrated and is known by us; however, since it must be asked, "What is the exposition of the Conversion (Āvaṭṭa-hāra)?", [it is said]:
"In one basis, he seeks the remaining basis;..."
"It turns toward the opposite; that is the mode of conveyance called 'Turning' (āvaṭṭa-hāra).

This verse was spoken. In this context, when one basis for the terms such as the "striving element" (parakkama-dhātu) and so forth—namely, the "initiation element" (ārambha-dhātu) and so on—is presented in the teaching, [the mind] either seeks the remaining basis because of its dissimilarity, or because the teaching does not explicitly grasp it in its own form.
Or, when one seeks the "basis of the word" (padaṭṭhāna) for the remainder— by means of which specific method of commentary, having sought it and applied it,
one turns oneself and causes others to turn the teaching toward the opposites such as laziness, which serve as the basis for negligence and so forth—
that specific method of commentary is designated as the "converting method" (āvaṭṭa-hāra); such is the construction of the meaning.
“‘In the opposite’ (paṭipakkhe)”: this is merely an illustration, because turning back (āvaṭṭana) applies to the rest as well, even when they are similar.

For when the elements of initiative (ārambha-dhātu) and so forth have been introduced in the teaching, the teaching does not turn back only toward their opposites such as indolence (kosajja); rather, it turns back toward the remaining factors of the initiation of energy and so forth as well.
The exposition on the method of turning back has thus been explained and understood by us; however, since it must be asked, “What is the exposition on the method of analysis (vibhatti-hāra)?”—
“The Dhamma, the proximate cause, and the plane—this is the Mode of Conveying Analysis.
It should be understood as the analysis of both the common and the uncommon.
Thus the verse was spoken. Therein, the manifold intrinsic-nature Dhamma by way of the wholesome and so forth, and the proximate causes such as giving, virtue, and so forth—

The application of the meaning is as follows: that specific mode of commentary by which one analyzes the stages—such as "the stage of seeing" (*dassanabhūmi*) and "the stage of development" (*bhāvanābhūmi*)—as well as those qualities that are common and those that are uncommon, is the "mode of analysis" (*vibhattihāra*), and this is the "guidable" (*neyya*). [This is illustrated by:
"In this sutta, the wholesome states taught pertain to the side of purification; in this sutta, the wholesome states taught pertain to the side of penetration," and so forth.
The Dhamma, by way of such passages as "the unwholesome states mentioned in this sutta belong to the category of defilements," and so forth;

the proximate cause (*padatthāna*), by way of such passages as "this virtue is the proximate cause for this sublime distinction; this virtue and this jhāna are the proximate causes for this supramundane state," and so forth;

and the plane (*bhūmi*), by way of such passages as "the worldling is the plane for that which is to be abandoned by vision; stream-enterers and the rest [are the planes] for that which is to be abandoned by cultivation."
The manner of analysis should be understood in detail through such passages as: "by the words *bhūmi* and so forth, [he analyzes] the plane";
"by the words *sensual lust and ill will are common to worldlings and stream-enterers* and so forth, [he analyzes] what is common";

and "by the words *sensual lust and ill will are uncommon to non-returners and arahants* and so forth, [he analyzes] what is uncommon"—that by which he analyzes is called the Mode of Conveying Analysis (*vibhatti-hāra*). Thus the mode of analysis is to be grasped.

The exposition of the Mode of Conveying Analysis has been demonstrated and understood by us. Since it must now be asked, "What is the exposition of the Mode of Conveying Reversal?", [the answer is given]:
"When wholesome and unwholesome states have been demonstrated, developed, and abandoned, they are reversed by their opposites; this is the Mode of Conveying Reversal."
The verses have been spoken. Therein, when the wholesome, blameless states that are to be developed and cultivated have been demonstrated, explained, or praised;
and when the unwholesome, blameworthy states that are to be abandoned have been demonstrated, explained, or praised;

or when the contrary, opposite states which are the antidotes to those [former] states are demonstrated through a particular mode of exposition, by means of which it turns back—[that is the "turning-back"].
The application of the meaning is as follows: that specific method of exposition which turns [the teaching] around should be understood as "the Mode of Conveying the Reversal" (*parivattano hāro*).
This is illustrated by such passages as, "For a person of right view, wrong view is worn away," and so forth;

and by such passages as, "For one who abstains from taking life, taking life has been abandoned," and so forth; and [by the passage], "Sensual pleasures are to be enjoyed... [etc.]... by means of sensual pleasures."
And since the Vibhaṅga section will explain the state of being the opposite by means of reversal through such passages as, "Abstention from those is non-dhamma," it has not been elaborated here.
The exposition of the Mode of Conveying Reversal has been demonstrated and is known to us; however, because it must be asked, "What is the exposition of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms?"—it is said:
"Many synonyms indeed for a single dhamma are spoken in the Sutta."
“The wise one who knows the Sutta understands that which is called the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (vevacana-hāra).
This verse was spoken. Therein, for a single meaning or term stated in the Sutta, there are indeed many synonyms;
by means of that particular method of commentary, the wise one who knows the Sutta—having known it—[applies it] to even a single [term].

The construction of the meaning is as follows: for that expert in the Suttas who applies [the words] to their respective meanings, that particular excellence of commentary is designated as the "Mode of Conveying Synonyms" (*vevacana-hāra*).
Furthermore, since the words *yo* (who) and *so* (that) have identical referents, after stating "the expert in the Suttas," it is said "that particular excellence of commentary.
Regarding the word *bhagavā*, within the single referent of the Blessed One, [it is used for] "the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
The Blessed One is one perfected in true knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, and a Lord; he has reached the fulfillment of the fruit, attained self-confidence, mastered the analytical knowledges,
abandoned the four yokes, transcended the going upon wrong paths, extracted the thorn, healed the wound, crushed the thorns, and extinguished the obsessions.
He has transcended bondage, untied the knots, passed beyond all underlying tendencies, shattered the darkness, and possesses the eye.

He has surmounted the worldly conditions, is free from attraction and aversion, and has reached a state of non-conceptualization regarding agreeable and disagreeable phenomena. Having transcended bondage, he has laid down his arms;
he is most excellent, a bearer of the torch, a maker of light, a maker of radiance, a dispeller of darkness, one who has abandoned strife, and possesses immeasurable beauty.
Many synonyms have been applied, such as: "of immeasurable beauty, of incalculable beauty, maker of light, maker of radiance, illuminator of the splendor of the Dhamma," and so forth.
A detailed exposition will follow in the Vibhaṅga section.
The demonstration of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms has been explained and understood by us; however, since it must be asked, "What is the demonstration of the Mode of Conveying Descriptions?"—
“The Blessed One teaches one dhamma by means of various designations;
that mode should be known as the Mode of Designation. Thus the verse was spoken.
Therein, the Blessed One [teaches] one dhamma, such as the aggregates and so forth, by means of various [methods] such as the designations of presentation, origin, and so on.

The meaning of the construction is as follows: by whatever mode a thing is to be made known through designations (*paññatti*), he teaches it; that mode of being made known is elucidated by a particular method of exposition (*saṃvaṇṇanāvisesa*);
that particular method of exposition is to be understood as "the Mode of Conveying Designations" (*paññatti-hāra*).

In this context, by means of various designations—namely, the designation of presentation (*nikkhepa-paññatti*), the designation of origin (*pabhava-paññatti*), the designation of full understanding (*pariññā-paññatti*), and the designation of abandonment (*pahāna-paññatti*)—[it is explained].

The specific mode of commentary characterized by the manifestation of the various modes in which a single referent is to be made known through such designations as "designation by way of cultivation," "designation by way of realization," "designation by way of cessation," and "designation by way of disenchantment" is called the "Mode of Designation" (*paññatti-hāra*). In this context,

the designation "This is suffering" (*idaṃ dukkha*) is a "designation by way of presentation" (*nikkhepa-paññatti*) for the five aggregates, the six elements, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the ten faculties.
“Bhikkhus, if there is lust for physical nutriment, if there is delight, if there is craving, consciousness becomes established there and comes to growth.
Wherever consciousness becomes established and comes to growth, there is the descent of name-and-form.
Wherever there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the increase of formations.”
Such passages as these are designations of the origin of suffering and its arising.
“Bhikkhus, if there is no lust for physical nutriment, no delight, and no craving,” and so forth—such passages are designations of the full understanding of suffering;
“the designation of abandoning is for the arising [of suffering], and the designation of development is for the path.”

And the detailed exposition in the Vibhaṅga will come as follows: "The 'description by realization' refers to cessation," and "the 'description by relinquishment' refers to wisdom consisting of what has been heard, the 'description by realization' refers to the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,' and the 'description by occurrence' refers to the Wheel of Dhamma.
Such is the elaboration.
The exposition of the Mode of Conveying Designations has been demonstrated and understood by us.

Since it must now be asked, "What is the exposition of the Mode of Conveying Ways of Entry?", [the answer is given]: "That which is dependent arising, the faculties, the aggregates, the elements, and the bases—whatever one enters by means of these is the Mode of Conveying Ways of Entry."
The verses have been spoken. Therein, that specific method of exposition by which dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*),

the faculties (*indriya*), the aggregates (*khandha*), and the elements and bases (*dhātu-āyatana*) are determined— by means of these [factors] of dependent origination, faculties, aggregates, elements, and bases,
as they are being determined through the gateway of the meanings of the words as they appear in the Sutta— that specific method of exposition enters into and penetrates [the teaching].

The syntactical construction of the meaning is as follows: when one enters into [the teaching] on dependent origination and so forth, either by way of expressing it there or by way of making it known there, that specific mode of commentary is called the "Entrance" (otaraṇa) method.

In this context, "faculties and aggregates" (indriyakhandhā) means both faculties and aggregates; "elements and bases" (dhātuāyatanā) means both elements and bases. How is it an entrance? By such a reading as: "Released above, below, and in every direction," and so forth.

He digs up both the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*). "Washed clean" (*adhota*) refers to the sense-desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Completely liberated in every respect" (*sabbadhi vippamutta*) refers to this liberation of one beyond training (*asekkhāvimutti*) within the three realms.

These very same five faculties of one beyond training constitute the entry by way of the faculties (*indriya*). These very same five faculties of one beyond training are true knowledge (*vijjā*); with the arising of true knowledge comes the cessation of ignorance... [and so on] ...until the cessation of the mass of suffering; this is the entry by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
Those same five faculties of one beyond training are comprised within three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom;

this is the entry by way of the aggregates. Those same five faculties of one beyond training are included among formations; those formations which are without taints and are not constituent parts of existence are comprised within the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*); this is the entry by way of the elements.

"That element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu) included within the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana), which is that base that is taintless (anāsava) and not a life-continuum (bhavaṅga)—this is the entry by way of the bases. This will appear in the Vibhaṅga under such headings as "the entry by way of the bases.

Thus, the exposition of the Mode of Conveying the Entry has been demonstrated and understood by us. Since it must now be asked, "What is the exposition of the Mode of Conveying the Purification?", [it is said]:
"When the question has been answered, that upon which the verse was based is asked again in the verse."
“The investigation of the pure and the impure: that is the purificatory Mode of Conveying (hāra).

Thus the verse was spoken. Therein, regarding the question set forth in that verse, when the meaning desired to be known has been answered by the Blessed One in the answering verse—concerning which meaning of the discourse that verse was originally asked and established for the purpose of inquiry—[that constitutes the Mode of Conveying].

The application of the meaning is as follows: that specific method of commentary by which an investigation into the purity or impurity of the meaning of a sutta occurs, that specific method of commentary is called the "Purifying Mode" (*sodhano hāro*). How so?

The phrase “The world is shrouded by ignorance” (*avijjāya nivuto loko*) has been purified, but the introduction (*ārambha*) has not been purified. [The text continues: “Through lack of discernment and negligence... (*vivicchā pamādā*)...

The phrase "it does not shine forth" has been clarified, but the underlying motive has not been clarified. The phrase "I call craving its smearing" has been clarified, but the underlying motive has not been clarified.
The phrase "suffering is its great terror" has both been clarified and its underlying motive clarified.
Thus, the investigation into the state of being clarified or unclarified regarding phrases and so forth is the mode of conveyance known as "Clarification. [This is] in detail.
"But it will come in the Vibhaṅga.

The exposition of the "supporting condition as sustenance" has been explained and is known to us; however, because it must be asked, "What is the exposition of the 'basis as sustenance'?"—[the following is said]:
"The phenomena by way of unity, and those also which are expounded by way of diversity."
“They should not be conceptualized; this is the Mode of Conveying Resolution.

Thus the verse was spoken. Therein, those phenomena such as the Truth of Suffering which have been demonstrated both by way of their unity through generality and by way of their diversity through particularity—that specific mode of exposition by which the phenomena such as the Truth of Suffering have been demonstrated—[is the Mode of Conveying Analysis].

It should be formulated because it does not remain fixed as a conventional expression through the formulation of common and specific characteristics, and because its establishment depends on relativity, like the distinctions of time, direction, and so forth.
The construction of the meaning is this: "this particular method of commentary is the mode called 'the basis' (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*).

In that context, "on account of unity" (*ekattatāya*) means: the state of being one or common is "unity" (*ekatta*); the state of being unity itself is "unity-ness" (*ekattatā*); [the phrase is used] by means of that. The word "one" (*eka*)...
And here [the word] expresses a similar meaning, not a numerical one. Regarding "by way of difference" (*vemattatāya*): a distinct measure (*mattā*) is a "different measure" (*vimattā*);
the state of being different is "difference" (*vematta*); the abstract state of that difference is "differenceness" (*vemattatā*), by means of which.
For just as specific times expressed as "today" or "tomorrow" are non-fixed, so too are specific directions expressed as "the eastern direction" or "the western direction."
Thus, both the general and the specific are the intrinsic natures (sabhāva) of the meaning.

For instance, that which is called "this is suffering" is common (sāmañña) when considered in relation to birth and so forth, yet it is a particularity (visesa) when considered in relation to the Truth [of Suffering]. This same method applies to the Truth of Origination and the others as well.
"Suffering" is a state of unity; "birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering"—such is the state of diversity (vemattatā).
“‘The origin of suffering’ is its unity; ‘craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust,’ and so forth, is its diversity”—such details will be found in the *Vibhaṅga*.
The exposition of the “support” and the “nutriment” has been demonstrated and is known to us; however, since it must be asked, “What is the exposition of the ‘requisite’?”—[the following is stated].
“Those phenomena which, as conditions, produce another phenomenon in succession;
having drawn out the cause—this is the Mode of Conveying Requisites.
This verse was spoken. Therein, those conditional phenomena beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*) [produce] that resultant phenomenon beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
The specific distinction in the commentary is that which— having drawn out from the Sutta, by means of the *sahajātapaccaya* (simultaneous condition),

[the factors] that produce [their effects] through a succession of mutual conditions; and having extracted from the Sutta both the uncommon productive cause (*janakahetu*), such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth,

which has arisen previously and serves as the requisite condition for that fruit consisting of formations (*saṅkhāra*) and the rest, as well as the common causal condition (*paccayahetu*), such as improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) and so forth.
The construction of the meaning is as follows: that which proceeds by way of praising the requisites (*parikkhāra*) is this specific kind of praise called the "Requisites Mode" (*parikkhāra-hāra*).
For ignorance and so forth are the uncommon causes (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*) of ignorance and so forth, whereas improper attention and so forth are common conditions (*sādhāraṇa-paccaya*).
Therefore it was said: "A cause has the characteristic of being uncommon; a condition has the characteristic of being common."
And there is the analytical statement beginning with: “Ignorance is the cause of ignorance; improper attention is its condition.
The exposition of the Mode of Conveying Requisites has been demonstrated and is known by us. Since it must be asked, “What is the exposition of the Mode of Conveying Coordination?
[the answer is: “Those phenomena which have a particular root, and those which are shown by the Sage to have a single meaning...”
“Those [qualities] are to be superimposed; this is the Mode of Conveying Superimposition (samāropana-hāra).

Thus the verse was spoken. Therein, those qualities such as virtue (sīla) which have a certain root—that is, which are the roots of concentration (samādhi) and so forth—those qualities such as virtue are to be superimposed upon those [qualities] such as concentration by way of a specific mode of commentary consisting in their being the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for them.

Furthermore, those terms such as "fading away from lust," "mind-liberation," "fruit of the trainee," and "transcending the sense-sphere" (kāmādhātu), which were proclaimed by the Buddha-Muni as being identical in meaning and synonymous with the state of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala)—terms such as "lust," etc., up to "transcending," etc.—should be applied to one another as synonyms.
This specific method of commentary is called the "Method of Synthesis" (samāropano hāro); such is the application of the meaning.
And here, the fulfillment of the exposition of the three aggregates beginning with virtue is fully explained;

and since the fulfillment of development occurs through the abandoning of what is to be abandoned, both the application of development and the application of abandoning are also shown. Thus, there are four kinds of application:
application as the proximate cause, application of synonyms, application of development, and application of abandoning.

Therein, bodily good conduct and verbal good conduct constitute the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*); non-covetousness and non-ill will within mental good conduct constitute the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*);
and right view constitutes the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*). The aggregate of virtue is the proximate cause for the aggregate of concentration;
the aggregate of concentration is the proximate cause for the aggregate of wisdom. [Thus] the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration...

Concentration is the proximate cause for serenity; the aggregate of wisdom is the proximate cause for insight. Serenity is the proximate cause for the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust;
insight is the proximate cause for the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance—such is the application of proximate causes.
The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the fruit of training; the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the fruit of one beyond training. This is...

Synonyms: Liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the fruit of non-returning; liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the supreme fruit, which is arahantship—this is a synonym.
Liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the transcendence of the sense-sphere realm;
liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the transcendence of the three realms—this is a synonym. The faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the training in higher wisdom.
"The aggregate of wisdom" and so forth—this is a synonym; such is the application of synonyms.
For one who dwells contemplating the body in the body, the four foundations of mindfulness reach fulfillment through development;
when the four foundations of mindfulness are being developed, the four right endeavors reach fulfillment through development; when the four right endeavors are being developed...
"The four bases of psychic power reach the fulfillment of development," and so forth—this is the application of development.
Dwelling contemplating the body in the body, one abandons the perversion that perceives the foul as "beautiful"; one attains full understanding of physical nutriment;
one becomes non-clinging with respect to the clinging to sensual pleasures; one becomes dissociated from the yoke of sensual pleasure; and [one is freed] from the bodily tie of covetousness.

He becomes dissociated from it, he becomes free from the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), he has crossed over the flood of sensual desire (*kāmaugha*), he becomes free from the barb of lust (*rāgasalla*),
his station of consciousness based on form (*rūpūpikā viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) comes to full understanding,
his lust for the form element (*rūpadhātu*) is abandoned, and he does not fall into a wrong course through desire; such is the application of abandonment regarding "feelings" and so forth.
Thus, the method of coordination (*samāropana-hāra*) is concluded.
This exposition of the sixteen methods (*soḷasa-hāra*), composed according to the strength of one’s own capacity, is finished.

The Exposition of the Exposition of the Methods (Nayaniddesavibhāvanā) 17. The expositions of the Modes (Hāraniddesa) have been explained and understood by us; however, because it must be asked, "Which are the expositions of the Methods? the passage beginning with "And craving...
is stated. Alternatively, having thus explained the Modes according to the sequence of the summary (uddesa), [the text] now proceeds to explain the Methods (naya).

“Craving, and... and so forth is stated. Therein, that specific distinction of commentary—which leads craving and ignorance, as they are taken by way of analytical determination from what has come down in the Sutta, toward the side of defilement—is [accomplished] either by means of serenity (samatha) as it appears in the Sutta, or by means of insight (vipassanā) as it appears in the Sutta, taken by way of analytical determination.
By means of serenity, one leads the insight that has been grasped toward the side of purification; and while leading it, one leads it by yoking it with the truths.
This specific mode of exposition is the method named "the Conversion of Relishing" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*). This is the construction of the meaning.
And here, both the ground of the method of meaning and its exposition are called "method" (*naya*) in the verse; therefore, [the phrase] "this specific mode of exposition" is used.
It has been said. For the method of meaning (*attha-naya*) is not the commentary itself; rather, the method of guidance prior to the penetration of the Four Truths is indeed the method of meaning.

As for the commentary on that method of meaning—which proceeds as a construction of the ground of the methods by way of craving and so forth, according to the types of persons such as those who understand through a brief statement—that commentary is designated by the term "method" (*naya*).
This will be explained in detail in the section on the Modes of Conveying (*Hāra-sampāta*).
The exposition of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method has been explained and understood by us. Since it must now be asked, "What is the exposition of the Tipukkhalā method?", [the answer is]:

"That which leads one away from the unwholesome together with its roots, and leads one toward the wholesome together with its wholesome roots—true, such as it is, and not otherwise—that they call the Tipukkhalā method."

The verse has been spoken. In this regard, the specific distinction of the commentary is that it leads one’s own unwholesome state toward the side of defilement by means of its three roots—greed and the others—along with their underlying tendencies;
and it leads the wholesome state toward the side of purification by means of the three wholesome roots—non-greed and the others.
And in leading, it leads what is real, whether wholesome or unwholesome, and not what is unreal, such as illusions, mirages, and so forth; it leads what is true.
It leads to what is wholesome and unwholesome; it does not lead to a mere conventional truth like a jar or similar objects. It leads to the non-false wholesome and unwholesome, not to the false.
Because the intrinsic nature of the wholesome and unwholesome exists, they are "real" (bhūta) due to being ultimate truths (paramatthasacca), and thus "suchness" (tathā).
Furthermore, because the unwholesome lacks a desirable ripening, and the wholesome lacks an undesirable ripening, [they are suchness] with respect to their ripening.

Because they are non-deceptive when present, they are "not otherwise" (*avitatha*). For it should be understood that the terms "real" (*bhūta*), "true" (*tatha*), and "not otherwise" (*avitatha*) serve as qualifiers for the wholesome and unwholesome among these three [types of speech].
Alternatively, this method [of explanation] is "real" (*bhūta*) because it leads [to the understanding that] unwholesome states arise from unwholesome roots and wholesome states from wholesome roots.

Having determined the four truths as "thus," "not otherwise," and "not so," he applies them. For suffering and the rest are "real" (bhūta) because they are not otherwise than their state of being afflictive and so forth;
they are "thus" (tathā) because they possess the intrinsic nature of truth; and they are "not otherwise" (avitathā) because they are non-deceptive.
Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, these four are thus, not otherwise, and not different."

(Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1090; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.8). The definition of "guiding" (nayana) is the application of the meaning of suttas such as those on the unwholesome (akusala), by way of connecting them with the Four Noble Truths.
They say that they "guide" that specific mode of commentary (saṃvaṇṇanāvisesa) by means of the "three-fold beautiful" (tipukkhalam).

Regarding the etymological construction: there, because it is "beautiful" (pukkhalo) by way of three reasons (hetu), it is "three-fold beautiful" (tipukkhalo); thus, the specific mode of commentary on the meaning of the unwholesome and so forth, through the metaphorical designation of its locus, is called the "Three-fold Beautiful Mode" (tipukkhalanaya). A detailed exposition, however, will follow in the section on the Modes of Conveying (hārasampāta).
The exposition of the Tipukkhalanaya has been explained and understood by us; however, since it must be asked, "What is the exposition of the Sīhavikkīḷitanaya?", [the answer is given]:
"That method which leads away the defilements from the true Dhamma by means of the faculties through the inversions—that method the experts in methods call the Sīhavikkīḷita."

The verses have been spoken. Regarding that, those who know the methods of exposition—those skilled in the methods of the true Dhamma, or indeed those proficient in the method of meaning—expound this particular method of exposition as the "Lion’s Play" (*sīhavikkīḷita*).

This method leads, by means of the perversions mentioned in the Sutta, to the side of defilement regarding the corruptions; and by means of the faculties mentioned in the Sutta, it leads to the side of purification regarding the true Dhamma. Such is the application of the meaning.

In this context, "by way of perversions" means by way of the four perversions: [perceiving] the beautiful in the ugly, pleasure in suffering, the permanent in the impermanent, and a self in the non-self.
"By way of faculties" means by way of the faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*). "In the True Dhamma" refers to the True Dhamma of practice and penetration.
The rest here is exactly according to the method already stated. The detailed exposition, however, will follow in the *Hārasampāta*.
The exposition on the “lion’s sport” eye has been explained and understood by us. Since it must now be asked, “What is the exposition on the ‘surveying the directions’ eye?”, [the answer is]:

“Whatever wholesome and unwholesome states are mentioned here and there in the analytical expositions (veyyākaraṇa), when one surveys them with the mind—that indeed is called the surveying of the directions.”

The verse has been spoken. The reading "sīhalocanaṃ āhu" has been written down, but it should be understood that this is not the reading of the Elder, because its grammatical characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) differ.

In that regard, those wholesome and unwholesome phenomena which have been stated here and there in the analytical expositions (*veyyākaraṇa*) as being the directions of the method (*naya*), those wholesome and unwholesome phenomena—the directions of the method—exist neither outside nor inside, but only within the mind itself.
The construction of the meaning is as follows: "Whatever observation one makes, that observation is indeed an observation; it is called 'surveying the directions' (disālocanā).
In that context, "in the commentaries" (veyyākaraṇesu) means in the expositions of the meaning of the Sutta composed for the purpose of applying various methods of meaning.

"Wholesome" (kusalā) means those conducive to purification. "Unwholesome" (akusalā) means those pertaining to defilement. "Stated" (vuttā) means explained by extracting them from the Sutta. "While surveying" (olokayate).

They examine and investigate those wholesome and other states with the mind itself by way of their directional nature according to each respective method, thinking, "This is the first direction, this is the second direction," and so forth;
this is the meaning. The word *kho* is a particle used for emphasis;
by it, he shows that there is no specific difference in meaning regarding the method of discerning directions.
21. The exposition of the method of the "surveying of directions" has been explained and is known to us.
Because it must be asked, "What is the exposition of the method of the 'hook'?", the verse beginning with "having surveyed" (*oloketvā*) was spoken.

Therein, having surveyed all wholesome and unwholesome states—which constitute the various directions of the method—by means of the surveying of directions, and having extracted them from the Sutta by lifting them up, that which brings them together, that which performs the act of bringing them together, [is the hook].
The application of the meaning is as follows: this method known as "bringing together" (samānayanasaṅkhāta) is called the "hook method" (aṅkusanaya).

Herein, a "hook" (aṅkusa) is a specific kind of material object made of iron or the like, possessing a sharp point and being straight or curved, which serves as the cause for bringing elephants to a desired place;
and this method is called a "hook" in the sense that it is like a hook. By this—

For according to this method, it leads to the intended meaning of the sutta. Primarily, however, it is called an *aṅkusa* (goad) because it is raised at the place of piercing on the hook (*aṅka*) and, when there is no [obstruction], enters within.
This is derived from the prefix *upa*, the word *aṅka*, and the verbal root *as*, with the suffix *ap*.
This method also does not result in any particular difference in meaning.

The sixteen expositions (hāra-niddesa) and the five methods (naya-niddesa) have been pointed out by the Teacher. We too understand them; however, because it must be asked whether the sixteen expositions or the methods should first be applied to the suttas to be commented upon, [the following is said]:

“The sixteen expositions come first; having surveyed the directions by means of the surveying of directions, one should then explain the sutta by means of the three methods, having condensed it with the hook.”

He spoke a verse. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "Having thus demonstrated [the suttas] by way of the *hāras* and the *nayās*, he now speaks the words beginning with ‘The sixteen *hāras* first’ in order to show the sequence of their application (*yojanakkama*).

Therein, the sixteen *hāras*—because they consist of the search for the phrasing (*byañjanapariyeṭṭhi*)—must be applied first as the nature of the commentary upon the sutta to be commented upon; they are demonstrated by the one applying them according to the very sequence of the *hāras*.

They should be applied, not out of sequence. Having first commented upon the material according to the order of the commentary on the modes (*hāra*), one should subsequently examine it by way of the directions, lead it forward by the method of the hook (*aṅkusa-naya*), and then demonstrate it by means of the three methods of meaning (*attha-naya*); this is the intended sense.
Thus, it has been composed in accordance with the strength of one's faculties.
The Exposition of the Description of the Bases is completed.
The Exposition of the Twelve Bases has thus explained the suttas to be commented upon, which constitute the excellent teaching within the scope of the *Netti*, along with their phrasing and meanings.
Because it was stated in the section on the summary as "the twelve terms constitute the Sutta," and because it must be asked, "Which are they?",
they are pointed out according to their specific forms:
"Phoneme, term, expression, etymology, and likewise exposition."
"The statement of the six aspects (ākāra) and the word 'all' constitute the entirety of the phrasing.
Exposition (saṅkāsanā), manifestation (pakāsanā), opening up (vivaraṇā), analysis (vibhajanā), making clear (uttānīkamma),
and designation (paññatti)— by these six terms, both the meaning and the action are demonstrated."

Two verses were spoken. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: "Now, in order to explain those words—both phonetic and semantic—by virtue of which it was stated that 'a sutta consists of twelve words,' he says, beginning with 'the word consisting of syllables' (*akkharapada*). In this context, in what sense are they called "syllables" (*akkhara*)?

They are so called in the sense of being "unchanging" (*akkhara*), that is, in the sense of not moving away. For the phonemes beginning with the letter *a* [are so called] because they do not move from the letter *a*, etc.
It does not move, it does not shift, and it does not pass on from the beginning of the vowel *i* and so forth. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary:
"Because a phoneme (*vaṇṇa*) does not move, does not shift, and does not pass on by way of transition (*pariyāya*) while the word is not yet completed.

And regarding the phrase "while the word is not yet completed," this refers to words consisting of one, two, or three syllables that have not yet reached the state of having case endings (*vibhatti*).
Regarding the term *akkhara* (syllable): the intended meaning is that it refers only to a word (*pada*) when it is complete, and not to individual phonemes.

A word, however, seems to move through various meanings by way of its application (*pariyāya*), as it enters into different contexts; this is not the case for phonemes such as *a*, because they lack such semantic variation (*avevacanatta*).

Furthermore, in expressions such as "Do not think thus" (*mā evaṃ maññasī*), the single-syllable words beginning with the letter *mā* are called syllables (*akkhara*), whereas a word ending in a grammatical case suffix (*vibhatti*) is simply a word (*pada*).
That by which a meaning is reached (*pajjati*) is a "word" (*pada*). It is fourfold, being divided into noun (*nāma*), verb (*ākhyāta*), prefix (*upasagga*), and particle (*nipāta*).
Among these, a noun-word (*nāmapada*) has substance as its primary referent, such as "contact," "feeling," or "consciousness.

For in that case, the substance is manifest in form, while the activity is unmanifest. A verb-word (*ākhyātapada*) has activity as its primary referent, such as "he touches," "he feels," or "he cognizes."
[This is] the name [category]. For therein, actions such as touching (*phusana*) have a manifest form (*āvibhūtarūpa*), whereas substance (*dabba*) has a non-manifest form.
A prefix-word (*upasaggapada*) consists of terms such as *pa-*, *upa-*, and *iti-*, which serve as the cause for understanding specific types of action.

Indeed, in expressions such as “he dwelt having lived abroad for a long time” (*cirappavāsiṃ upavutthaṃ*), words like *upa-* and so forth indicate the distinction of the action of dwelling, such as its separation [from the object]. As for the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*), however, it applies to both noun-words (*nāmapada*) and verb-words (*ākhyātapada*).
One should understand that *upasaggā* (prepositions) are so called because they "attach themselves" (*upagantvā*) to the meaning of those two words [verb and noun].

Furthermore, particles (*nipātapada*) such as *evaṃ* and *iti*, which serve as the cause for manifesting the specific nature of both the action and the substance, are intended here because they are desired both in the [root] word and in its commentary.
If it is asked, "How then are these included by means of the syllable?"—[the answer is: while the syllables are being heard...
Because a specific distinction has been made for those who hear it, there is a full comprehension of the meaning of the words at the conclusion of each word.
Therefore, it should be understood that even by means of a single syllable, the mode of the meaning is grasped. Thus it was said:
"He makes it known by means of syllables, he makes it manifest by means of words, and he causes it to be condensed by means of both syllables and words."
*Vivaraṇā* means expansion. *Vibhajanā* (analysis) and *uttānīkamman* (making plain), along with *paññatti* (description), form the compound *vibhajanuttānīkammapaññatti*;
this is a collective *dvanda* compound. In that context, "analysis" (*vibhajana*) refers to the act of dividing.
That aspect of meaning which is demonstrated through the modes of phrasing is indicated by the two terms "expansion" (*vivaraṇa*) and "analysis" (*vibhajana*).
Making manifest is called "explanation" (*uttānīkamma*). Making known by various means is "definition" (*paññatti*).

Whatever aspect of meaning exists as it is being clarified by the phrasing and words known as etymological analysis (*nirutti*) and exposition (*niddesa*), that aspect of meaning is further demonstrated by the explanations and definitions.
By these six terms for meaning—beginning with "making known"—the meaning of the discourse (*suttattha*) is grasped, as well as its function (*kamma*).

The meaning is that the act of "condensing" (*ugghaṭana*) and so forth has been demonstrated. That meaning of the discourse by which the production of the act of condensing—consisting of the activity of awakening the mental continuum of one who is to be awakened by condensation (*ugghaṭitaññū*)—occurs, that meaning of the discourse takes the form of "indicating" (*saṅkāsanā*) and "explaining" (*pakāsanā*).
That meaning of the discourse by which the act of expanding—the activity of awakening the mental continuum of one who is to be awakened by expansion (*vipañcitaññū*)—[occurs]...

The arising of the meaning of the sutta is the mode of exposition and analysis. It should be understood that the meaning of the sutta by which the awakening of the mental continuum of the one to be guided—the activity known as the work of guidance—occurs, is the mode of the manifestation of the act of clarification.
Therefore, the Master of the Commentaries said: "For when the teaching proceeds by means of the meaning of the sutta..."

The production of the activity that awakens the mental continuum of those to be trained—such as those who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and others—is the meaning of the discourse, and it takes the form of the proclamation and so forth. Since it must be asked:
"Is there any meaning whatsoever that is not connected with the three aforementioned methods of meaning and the six terms of meaning, or is every meaning necessarily connected?"—
“Three methods are not deficient, and six steps of meaning have been enumerated.
The meaning of the Blessed One’s word is fully joined with nine terms”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “three” (*tīṇi*) is an expression using a change of gender; however, it should be stated as “three” (*tayoti*) to express its natural gender.
The three methods (*naya*) of the meaning are enumerated without omission, and the six phrases of the meaning are explained without omission.
The construction should be made as follows: "By means of the explained phrases of meaning, the entire meaning of the Blessed One’s word is fully joined;

there is no meaning whatsoever that is unjoined. "Of the meaning" (*atthassa*) refers to the meaning of the discourse (*sutta*). "Methods" (*nayā*) refers to the methods of the meaning of the *Netti*. "Phrases" (*padāni*) refers to the phrases of the meaning of the *Netti*.

26. Having grouped together those strings (*hāra*) and so forth that have been pointed out, and having defined them by way of enumeration for the purpose of easy comprehension of the meaning of the words in the *Nettippakaraṇa*, he says, beginning with "of the meaning" (*atthassa*).

Therein, the ninefold divisions of the meaning-words (*atthapada*), which constitute the components of the collection of meanings, [are for] the investigation of the meaning of the suttas and the phrasing (*byañjana*).
By way of enumeration according to the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*), there are twenty-four word-phrases (*byañjanapada*).
