When both the meaning-phrase and the word-phrase are condensed and combined together, there are thirty-three; the construction is that there are exactly thirty-three kinds, and the guide (*nettī*) is of these very thirty-three kinds.
In this context, "nine phrases" refers to the three methods of meaning (*atthanaya*) and the six meaning-phrases. "Twenty-four" refers to the sixteen modes of conveying meaning (*hāra*).

The six modes of expression (*byañjanapada*), the two methods of directional orientation (*disālocana-naya*) and the method of the goad (*aṅkuśa-naya*): thus, the *Netti* consists of thirty-three types.
The meaning should be understood as follows: there is no other referent for the term *netti* apart from these.

“In this way, among the *hāra* and *naya* of the *Netti* consisting of thirty-three referents, which is the *desanā-hāra* and which is the *vicaya-hāra*? and so forth, [is explained] according to the sequence of the teaching.
The word *siddha* (established) indicates that even though this is established, the opening statement, “The sixteen modes of conveying are first,” clarifies this meaning:
“All these modes of conveying (*hāra*) and methods (*naya*) must be applied by way of commentary to those suttas whose sequence has been shown here, and not out of order.
It makes this known by following the hearing of the words of clarification; therefore, thus...
The object has been shown; the gratification, the danger, and the escape are the supports for the teaching of the Dhamma;
the fruit is the fruit of the teaching of the Dhamma; the means is the means of the teaching of the Dhamma; and the command is the body of the teaching of the Dhamma.
This is because the food of the teaching has as its essential nature the manifestation of those [categories]: the gratification, the danger, the escape, the fruit, the means, and the command.

Even without an explicit extraction (*niddhāraṇa*), because the term *anarūpa* is easily understood among all the suttas to be commented upon by its very nature, and because it serves as the basis for the specific modes of commentary such as the "Investigation" (*vicaya*) and other "Modes" (*hāra*), the Mode of Teaching (*desanāhāra*) is presented first.

Following the Mode of Teaching, the Mode of Investigation (*vicayahāra*) is presented; this is because the meanings of the words in the Mode of Teaching—such as the "attractiveness" (*assāda*) and so forth—are subjected to investigation through word-questions, answer-questions, and the restatement of the words.

Following the Mode of Investigation, the Mode of Reasoning (*yuttihāra*) is presented; this is because there is an examination of what is logical and what is illogical regarding the meanings already investigated by the Mode of Investigation.

The Mode of Conveying Footings (padaṭṭhānahāra) follows immediately after the Mode of Conveying the Logical (yuttihāra), because it determines, through a succession of reasons, meanings that are either logical or illogical in accordance with their actual occurrence.

The Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇahāra) follows immediately after the Mode of Conveying Footings, because its characteristic is the grasping of even those phenomena not explicitly mentioned as having identical characteristics, provided their individual essences have been determined through a succession of reasons regarding what is logical or illogical.
By means of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics, the etymologies and other details of those phenomena must also be stated, even if they have already been determined in meaning from other Suttas.

The Fourfold Array (Catubyūha) method follows the Mode of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇa-hāra) for the purpose of showing that it is not only those teachings explicitly mentioned by their own form in the Sutta that are intended.
For in this way, there is a complete understanding of the meaning without remainder.

Through the Fourfold Array method, together with the etymologies, intentions, and origins stated therein, the meanings of the words in the Sutta are connected with other Suttas—this being what is known as "cross-referencing" (suttantarasaṃsandana).

When the investigation of the preceding and following [sections] has been shown, it is possible to easily demonstrate the turning toward other similar and dissimilar phenomena of the word-meanings of those suttas;
therefore, the method of "Turning" (Āvaṭṭa-hāra) follows immediately after the method of the "Fourfold Array" (Catubyūha-hāra).

For, since the turning toward other similar and dissimilar phenomena is the means for the correlation with other suttas, [it is applied] to the verse beginning with "Exert yourselves, strive... (*Ārambhatha nikkamatha*).
Having extracted the faculties of energy, concentration, and wisdom by means of undertaking, exertion,
and shaking off attachment to the Buddha’s teaching, it is shown in another sutta that negligence (*pamāda*) is the root of non-application toward those very undertakings,
exertions, and shake-offs; thus, negligence is turned back.
Following the Mode of Conveying the Conversion (āvaṭṭa-hāra), there is the Mode of Analysis (vibhatti-hāra).

By means of the conversion of similar and dissimilar phenomena, the classification of defiled and purified phenomena according to their common and uncommon bases, as well as their respective planes, can be easily applied;
thus, the Mode of Analysis follows immediately after the Mode of Conveying the Conversion.

When the distinction between the phenomena of defilement and purification has been made by means of the Mode of Distinction (vibhattihāra), it is possible to transpose the phenomena appearing in the sutta to be commented upon from their opposites with ease;
thus, the Mode of Transposition (parivattanahāra) follows immediately after the Mode of Distinction. For by means of the Mode of Distinction, it is stated:
"In a person possessing right view, wrong view is worn away."
The analysis of the method of reversal (*parivattanahāra*) will be illustrated by means of phenomena whose individual natures are distinct.

Following the method of reversal, the method of synonyms (*vevacanahāra*) is presented in order to show that even phenomena reversed from their opposites must be understood through synonymous expressions, and not only those phenomena appearing in the suttas to be commented upon.

Following the method of synonyms, the method of description (*paññattihāra*) is presented because it is possible to easily understand the classification of phenomena revealed synonymously by way of their various designations.

Since the classification of phenomena such as dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and the truths (*sacca*) can be demonstrated by way of the analysis of designations—through the method of designation (*paññattihāra*) consisting of the full understanding of their origin and so forth—it is possible to show how the phenomena mentioned in the Sutta enter [into that analysis] by way of dependent origination and so on; therefore, immediately after the method of designation comes the method of entry (*otaraṇahāra*).

Since it is possible to easily accomplish the inquiry, the undertaking, and the resolution of the word-meanings (*padattha*) in a Sutta that is to be commented upon once they have been introduced into the elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth by means of the method of entry, immediately after the method of entry comes the method of resolution (*sodhanahāra*).
The Mode of Conveying Determination (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) follows immediately after the Mode of Purification (sodhana-hāra).

This is because, once the words and their meanings have been purified by the Mode of Purification in the suttas to be extolled, it is easy to demonstrate the state of commonality and distinction—whether through identity or difference—that obtains here and there.
Thus, when the qualities that constitute commonality and distinction, both shared and unshared, have been made known by the Mode of Determination, [the Mode of Conveying Synonyms follows].
The classification of the fuel that is the cause of conditions—consisting of both common and uncommon forms designated as "requisites" (parikkhāra)—is easy to understand;
thus, after the mode of conveyance called "the foundation" (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra), there follows the mode of conveyance called "requisites" (parikkhāra-hāra).
When the uncommon and common causes have been shown by means of the "requisites" mode of conveyance, [it serves] regarding their respective fruits...
The Mode of Causality (*kāraṇākāra*) is the mode of teaching through the differentiation of those causes and fruits.

Since the Modes of Coordination (*samāropana-hāra*)—which are stated after having extracted the cultivation and abandonment of the states to be cultivated and abandoned—lead to the realization of the suchness of the meaning of the Sutta that is to be properly expounded, the Mode of Coordination is shown immediately after the Mode of Requisites (*parikkhāra-hāra*). This is to be understood as the reason for the sequence in which these Modes are presented.

Just as the summary (uddesa) conduces to the benefit of one who gains knowledge through a condensed presentation, so too does the method of the "turning of delight" (nandiyāvaṭṭanaya) conduce to the benefit of one who gains knowledge through a condensed presentation;
therefore, the method of the turning of delight was shown first.

Just as the exposition (niddesa) conduces to the benefit of one who gains knowledge through an expanded presentation, so too does the method of the "three-pointed" (tipukkhalanaya) conduce to the benefit of one who gains knowledge through an expanded presentation.

Therefore, after the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method comes the Tipukkhalā method. Just as the detailed exposition leads to the benefit of the one to be guided (neyya), so too does the Sīhavikkīḷita method lead to the benefit of the one to be guided.

Consequently, the Sīhavikkīḷita method is shown immediately after the Tipukkhalā method; thus, the sequence for the presentation of the three methods of meaning (atthanaya) should be understood. Of the methods of meaning...

Having looked toward the ground in a particular direction, there is the bringing together [of the elephant] from that direction to that ground. For it is not possible to bring it together without looking;
thus, after demonstrating the method of determining the direction, the method of the goad (*aṅkusa*) is shown.
Skilled elephant-riders mounted on their elephants look for a place for the elephant to go in all directions and, with the goad, bring it to the desired spot.
Some clever people guide [the text] without even looking; their is merely a leading, not a bringing together [of the parts].
In the same way, when the wise explain the meaning of the Sutta, they should be seen as guiding by means of the method (naya) after having looked with the mind alone.
[The types of commentary are: commentary on the origin, commentary on the intention, commentary on the word-meaning, and commentary on the injunctions and prohibitions.

Alternatively, it is the commentary on the conclusion; or else, the commentary on the purpose, the commentary on the summarized meaning, the commentary on the connection, the commentary on the objection, and the commentary on the resolution;

or else, the commentary on the introduction, the commentary on the analysis of words, the commentary on the examination of the meaning of words, and the commentary on the manifestation [of the meaning].
Likewise, there is the "single-stalk" discourse and the "four-cornered" discourse.
Or it is called the "Discourse on Sitting in a Circle" (*nisinnavattikākathā*).

In this context, the "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) is simply the "source" (*nidāna*). The "explanation of the rule" (*vidhi-anuvāda*) is simply the "statement of the distinction" (*visesa-vacana*). The "introduction" (*upogghāṭa*) is simply the "source" (*nidāna*). The "shaking up" (*cālanā*) is simply the "accusation" (*codanā*). The "presentation" (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) is simply the "resolution" (*parihāra*).
The commentary consisting of the explanation of the meaning of each individual word after reciting the text is called the "Single-Straw Discourse" (*ekanāḷikākathā*).

The exposition consisting of discourse—showing the opposite side, showing a simile for the opposite side, showing one's own side, and showing a simile for one's own side—is called "four-cornered discourse" (*caturassakathā*).

The exposition consisting of reaching the conclusion by way of dissimilar phenomena alone, and then again reaching the conclusion by way of similar phenomena alone, is called "discourse on the sitting-in-a-circle" (*nisinnavattikākathā*).
All these expositions are included within the *Netti* commentaries, such as the "Exposition of the Modes of Teaching" (*desanāhāra*) and so forth. Therefore he said: "As many as..."
"For indeed, all the specific expositions of the Sutta depend upon the *Netti-upadesa*. Thus, up to this point, it should be understood that this is the limit.
As for the methods concerning cause and fruit, the stages, the proximate causes, the similar and dissimilar, and the characteristics, these have been explained in detail in the *Aṭṭhakathā*;
therefore, I shall not elaborate on them here.
Thus ends the Exposition of the Meaning of the Section on Exegesis (Niddesavāra), composed according to the strength of one's faculties. 4.
Exposition of the Meaning of the Section on Further Exegesis (Paṭiniddesavāra).
1. Exposition of the Analysis of the Modes of Conveying (Desanāhāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā). 5.
Thus, the modes of conveying and so forth have been stated by the Teacher in their essential form through the summary (uddesa), and they have been explained through the detailed exposition (niddesa);

and we too have understood them. Now, if it is asked: why has the section beginning with "In this context, what is the mode of conveying by teaching" (desanāhāra) been commenced again? It is for the sake of those who are to be trained (veneyya).
Because of their threefold nature. For those to be converted are of three types: those of very sharp wisdom, those of moderately sharp wisdom, and those of dull wisdom.
Of these, the methods (hāra) and so forth were taught by way of summary for one of very sharp wisdom;

they were explained by way of exposition for one of moderately sharp wisdom; now, in order to show the methods and so forth by analyzing them for one of dull wisdom, [the text says]: "In that regard..."
The section on the analysis (vibhaṅgavāra) beginning with “What is the mode of conveying by teaching? has commenced. However, in the Commentary it is stated:

“Having thus pointed out the modes of conveying and so forth in their own form by way of verse composition for the sake of easy comprehension, [the author] now begins the section beginning with ‘Therein, what is the mode of conveying by teaching?
in order to analyze them first among those modes by way of detailed exposition.”
Regarding that, among the modes of conveyance (*hāra*) and so forth which have been specified in the enumeration and the exposition:

if one asks, "Among those modes of conveyance and so forth, what is the mode of conveyance of the teaching (*desanāhāra*)?"—it is this verse beginning with "The state of gratification and danger" (*assādādīnavatā*) that has been spoken; this verse, by way of its exposition, is called the mode of conveyance of the teaching.

Now, as for the exposition of that [verse] beginning with "The state of gratification and danger," which is being stated by me here, [one might ask]: "What is this mode of conveyance of the teaching?"
The specific detailed commentary beginning with “desayati” (it teaches) is to be understood as the analysis of the nutriment of teaching (*desanāhāra-vibhaṅga*).
Since it must be asked, “What does this nutriment of teaching teach?”, the question is established;

then, in order to determine and show that “it teaches this,” it is said: “What does this nutriment of teaching teach? It teaches the gratification (*assāda*), the danger (*ādīnava*),” and so forth. Therein, this...

If it is asked what the "nutriment of teaching" teaches: it teaches, extols, and elaborates upon the gratification (*assāda*); it teaches, [extols, and elaborates upon] the danger (*ādīnava*)... [and so on]...
it teaches, [extols, and elaborates upon] the escape (*nissaraṇa*)... [and so on]... it teaches, [extols, and elaborates upon] the fruit (*phala*)...
[and so on]... it teaches, [extols, and elaborates upon] the means (*upāya*)... [and so on]... it teaches, extols, and elaborates upon the injunction (*āṇatti*). This is the application.
And here, it should be understood that the expression “this is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching” (*desanāhāra*) is dependent upon what precedes and follows.

Since one might ask, “In which of the canonical teachings (*pāḷidhamma*) to be commented upon do these gratifications (*assāda*) and so forth shown in the verse beginning ‘Gratification, danger, and escape’ appear?”—therefore, the passage beginning “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma” was spoken.
[The gratifications and so forth] shown in the verse beginning “Gratification, danger, and escape”...

Since it must be asked, "Wherein among the canonical teachings to be praised are the gratification and so forth found?", [the answer is] those [teachings] which, among the canonical teachings to be praised as promised when [the Buddha] declared,
"Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;
I shall reveal the holy life, complete and pure, with its meaning and its phrasing."
The enjoyment and so forth have arrived; the intention is that this "conveyance of the teaching" (desanāhāra) conveys them.

In this context, although the word *dhamma* occurs in many senses—such as the scripture (*pariyatti*), the truths (*sacca*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), nature (*pakati*), merit (*puñña*), attainment (*āpatti*), and the knowable (*ñeyya*)—it should nevertheless be understood here as referring specifically to the *dhamma* of the scripture.
As for the exposition of the meaning (*atthuddesa*), it is found in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
It has already been stated; therefore, it is not stated here by me.

The syllable *vo* is seen in the senses of the accusative case, the instrumental case, the completion of a phrase, and the dative case; nevertheless, it should be understood here as being used specifically in the sense of the dative.

They are called *bhikkhus* because they beg (*bhikkhanti*) for the aggregates of virtue and so forth, or for the requisites through bodily intimation; or alternatively, because they see (*ikkhanti*) and contemplate the fear within *saṃsāra*.
"Monks. He addresses those monks as "monks"; it should be understood that he addresses them in order to encourage them with great zeal toward listening to the Dhamma by turning his face toward them.
"I shall teach the Dhamma": this means, "It is not out of a desire for lordship that I would compel you to do anything else; I shall teach only the Dhamma."
And when teaching, he does not teach by following the knowledge derived from hearing after having heard the Dhamma from others;
rather, because of his direct realization regarding all knowable phenomena through unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*), he declares: "I shall now teach the Dhamma being set forth by me alone.
It is "good in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*); or, it is "good in the beginning" because its beginning is good. The same applies to the other [two] cases as well.
The same method applies here. Furthermore, it should be understood that "good in the beginning" and so forth are stated by way of "good in meaning" and so forth. Therefore he said:
"It is good in the beginning through virtue, good in the middle through concentration, and good in the end through wisdom.

Or else, it is good in the beginning because the Buddha is perfectly enlightened; it is good in the middle because the Dhamma is well-expounded; and it is good in the end because the Saṅgha practices rightly."
Alternatively, it is "good in the beginning" by way of training those who understand through a concise statement;
"good in the middle" by way of training those who understand through an exposition; and "good in the end" by way of training persons who must be led.

This very meaning is intended here. The meaning is that it is "noble" (ariya) because it is known (arīyati); etymologically, the verbal root *ara* refers, in its primary sense, to a cognitive state of mind directed toward an object, wherein knowledge is predominant.

"Meaning" (attha): from the perspective of the metaphorical designation of the locus (*ṭhānūpacārato*), the "meaning" is the capacity of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for that which is to be known.

By the word *iti*, that very same capacity is referred to. The "meaning" of the suffix *ta* is the meaning to be known—designated as the "object-condition"—which is accompanied by the capacity of the object-condition;
this should be seen as the specific distinction in meaning among the primary roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*paccaya*). "It exists when it does not exist" (*asati bhavatīti*).
Or, "possessing meaning" (sāttha) means that the Dhamma which exists together with its meaning is "possessing meaning"; or, the Dhamma endowed with meaning is "possessing meaning";
or, it is "possessing meaning" due to its connection with the six types of purposeful words beginning with "proclaiming" (saṅkāsanādi).

This very sense is intended here, as it is the domain of the *Netti*. "Possessing phrasing" (sabyañjana) refers to that Dhamma whose phrasing is complete. It is complete because of its perfection in being loose, hard, long, short, heavy, light, connected, distinct, released, and suppressed.

Because it is endowed with the singular number and other grammatical features of feminine nouns ending in vowels such as *a*, and because it is free from errors of omission and the like, its constituent parts are complete;

thus, by virtue of being a collection of those parts, the Dhamma is said to have "complete phonemes" (*sabyañjana*). Alternatively, it is "with phonemes" (*sabyañjana*) due to the combination of syllables, consonants, and words. This is precisely the meaning intended here.

Since there is nothing to be added—meaning that in this [Dhamma] there is no deficiency of this or that which would need to be brought in or inserted—it is called "without anything to be added" (*upanetabbābhāvato*).

It is entirely fulfilled, either by the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
or it is entirely fulfilled by the perfection of these five aggregates. Having stated that "this excess here must be removed," it is pure because there is nothing to be removed.
Alternatively, it is pure because it functions for the purpose of crossing over the four floods, or because it proceeds with indifference toward worldly gain.

Because it is the best, or because it is the conduct (*cariya*) of the noble ones (*brahmā*), who are the best, it is called the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*). Among the various types such as the holy life of renunciation, the holy life of the path, and the holy life of the teaching (*sāsana*), I shall clarify and fully illuminate the holy life of the teaching—this is the meaning.
When the word "dhamma" occurs in the canonical text following the promise, "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma... I will clarify it," [it refers to this].
The teacher stated "the teaching-provision (desanāhāra) teaches, extols, and elaborates" using the general term *sāmañña* alone;

therefore, one should not understand specific distinctions such as "here the teaching-provision teaches this gratification (assāda) mentioned in the text" or "here it teaches this danger (ādīnava) mentioned in the text," because it must be asked, "How is this to be understood?"
Having determined the distinction by way of specific definition—stating, “This is the gratification (assāda) found here in the text;

this is the danger (ādīnava) found here in the text”—the passage beginning with “In that regard, what is the gratification? For one who desires sensual pleasures... is undertaken as a method of illustration.
Therein, the phrase “therein” (tattha) refers to the various objects and subjects of experience specified in the verse beginning with “The state of gratification and danger.”
Regarding gratification: what is the gratification therein? Having asked where it is found in the texts among those scriptural passages, [the answer is]:
“When one who desires sensual pleasures succeeds in obtaining them, that mortal surely becomes joyful, having gained what he wished for.”

Here, in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the gratification that has appeared as the object is this very gratification to be relished; it is the object of the teaching as nutriment. However, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it says:
"The Teaching of the Dispensation (*sāsanadhamma*) thus taught and expounded by the Blessed One proceeds by way of showing the gratifications and so forth;
those gratifications and so forth, which constitute the objects of the teaching as nutriment, are stated in particular detail in various passages of the text."
It is said: “In order to extract [the meaning] from here and there, bring it here by way of examples, and demonstrate it, the passage beginning ‘In this context, what is gratification?

is commenced. In this regard: that which is gratified is *assāda* (gratification); it is the sensual object (*vatthukāma*) that is to be relished. That which is desired is *kāma*; it is the sensual object as well.
One who desires that is *kāmayamāna*, i.e., a sentient being (*satta*). One whose mind (*mano*) is joined with rapture (*pīti*) is *pītimano*. It knows (*manati*).

One is called "mortal" (*macca*) in the sense of the verbal expression "he knows" (*jānāti*), and so forth. For that being who desires an object of desire, if that desired object is successfully attained, then that being will certainly be glad at heart.
The meaning of the verse should be understood as follows: whatever object a mortal desires, having obtained that object, that mortal will certainly be glad at heart.
One should understand that the meaning here is more extensive than merely saying, “He is gladdened in mind whenever he obtains what he desires”;
rather, because it is stated, “Having obtained what a mortal wishes,” it implies that a mortal is not gladdened in mind only upon obtaining an object of greed,
but is indeed gladdened in mind when he has obtained everything that is to be aspired for and honored.
The Master has analyzed that the "pleasure" (assāda) which is to be relished as an object is what appears here in the verse of the Pāḷi, and this is understood by us.

However, because it must be asked, "Among the dangers (ādīnava) categorized as suffering, mental distress, and so forth, which danger is presented in which part of the Pāḷi Dhamma?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is the danger? If he, desiring sensual pleasures... is commenced.

Regarding the phrase "in this and that": having asked which disadvantage (*ādīnava*) among those such as suffering and mental distress (*domanassa*) specified in the verse beginning with "the state of gratification and disadvantage" is found in which part of the scripture (*pāḷi*) among those scriptural teachings, [it is said]:
"If for that person who desires sensual pleasures, who has conceived a longing..."
“Those sensual pleasures fade away; one is afflicted as if pierced by an arrow.
Here, in this verse of the text, the danger consisting of mental distress (*domanassa*) that has been presented is the objective domain of the "nutriment of teaching" (*desanāhāra*).
Furthermore, in the verse, one who desires or seeks is called *kāmayāna*. Alternatively, that which moves or goes is a "vehicle" (*yāna*); [thus, one driven] by desire...
For one who desires sensual pleasures; for one in whom desire has arisen—such a person is "one in whom desire has arisen.
"Pierced" means struck through. A "dart" (salla) is so called because it enters like a barb.
When, for a person who desires and in whom desire has arisen, those sensual pleasures that ought to be obtained are lost due to some obstacle, then that person...

It is afflicted (*ruppati*). In what manner is it afflicted? It should be understood that just as a deer pierced by an iron arrow is afflicted, so too is a person whose desire has been frustrated afflicted.
Furthermore, it should be understood that by the word "is afflicted," the arising of mental distress (*domanassa*) is shown here.

The Teacher has analyzed that the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) consisting of mental distress is what is presented in this passage, and this is also known to us. [This occurs] by way of the Path and Nibbāna...
Since it must be asked, "Of the two kinds of escape, which escape is taught in which part of the Canon?", the passage beginning with "In this regard, what is the escape?

He who avoids sensual pleasures... is commenced. Therein, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to the two kinds of escape—namely, the Path and Nibbāna—as specified in that verse beginning with "The gratification and the danger... (*assādādīnavatā*).
"What is the escape from them? In which of those canonical teachings is it found? Having asked this, [he replies]:
"He who avoids sensual pleasures as one would the head of a snake with his foot, being mindful, overcomes that attachment in the world."
Here, in this verse, that which is called "emergence" (*nissaraṇa*)—consisting of the path characterized as the means of transcending—is the objective domain of the "nutriment of teaching.

In the verse, "he" (*yo*) refers either to one who has attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*) or to a noble one (*ariya*). "Sensual pleasure" (*kāma*) refers to the sensual objects (*vatthu-kāma*) of the type already mentioned.
Among those, he avoids them either by suppressing or by eradicating the desire and lust that have arisen. What does he avoid? He avoids them just as one avoids a snake.
Just as a man with keen vision, seeing a head upon a head [of an antelope], avoids it step by step with his feet, so too does that person avoid it.
Being mindful and possessed of mindfulness, he thoroughly transcends and moves beyond this craving—the attachment to forms and other objects in the world—by means of the path;
this "act of transcending" (samativattanaka) is a portion of what is designated as the path.
The word *nissaraṇaṃ* should be construed as "by way of escape. Where it should have been said *pādā*, the vowel *ā* has been shortened to *a*, and thus it is stated as *padā*.

And the term *pādā* [is used] by means of a part [of the whole], just as in the expression "due to non-delusion" (*amohabhāvā amohabhāvena*). Therefore, the Master has analyzed it, saying "by one's own foot," and we too [have done so].
Here, in this text, only a single part—the gratification (*assāda*)—which is designated as the object, has been presented; this is how the Master has explained it. And by us...

Since it must be asked, "Where in the scripture is that portion designated as the 'object' (visayī) which is called gratification (assāda)? the passage beginning with "In this context, what is gratification?
Fields, lands," and so forth, was commenced. Alternatively, why was it commenced in this way—namely, "In this context, what is gratification?
Fields, lands," and so forth—rather than by the passage beginning with "In this context, what is gratification? For one who desires sensual pleasures"?

Is gratification analyzed? True; however, gratification is twofold, by way of the object (*visaya*) and the subject (*visayin*). In that regard, the gratification consisting of the object was analyzed previously;
now, in order to analyze the gratification consisting of the subject, the passage beginning with “In this context, what is gratification?
Fields, lands,” and so forth, is commenced. Therein, “in this context” (*tattha*) refers to that verse beginning with “The gratification, the danger, and the escape.”

Having asked, "Among the gratifications distinguished as objects and subjects that have been pointed out, which gratification is found in those teachings of the Pāli, and in what part of the Pāli does it appear? [the following is stated]:
"Fields, lands, or gold, cattle, horses, slaves, and servants;..."
“Women are kin; many are sensual pleasures—for the man who is addicted to them.

Here, in this verse of the Pāli, the gratification (*assāda*) characterized as addiction that has been mentioned is this very gratification of the sense-object (*visaya-āssāda*) characterized as addiction, which is the object of the teaching (*desanāhāra*).
In the verse, “field” (*khettam*) means a place where seeds are sown; it is the act of sowing for people who are sowing.
The primary meaning of "khipa-dhātu" (the field-element) is the mental state that generates the act of throwing;
the meaning as a metaphorical fruit is the power of that mental state—which serves as the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*)—to cause growth in a rice paddy.
By the word "iti," it is precisely that power of causing growth which is referred to; the locus for that power is the place designated as the "paddy."
This is the meaning of the suffix *-ta*. This same method should be applied and understood as appropriate for such verbal meanings within the three Piṭakas.
That wherein things are sown—that is, established—is called *vatthu* (a site or foundation). The primary meaning of the verbal root *vap-* is "the establishing of other crops and so forth.
The power to establish a location is a figurative sense based on the result; by the word *iti*, that power of establishment [is indicated].
It is grasped. The meaning of "condition" (paccaya) is the place where that spear is established. A field (khetta), however, is the place for the growth of grain;
a site (vatthu) is the place for the growth of other crops.
It is called "hi" because joy and gladness (pītisomanassa) increase and proceed therein; what is that? It is joy and gladness. It is called "rāti" because it causes gold (jātarūpa) to proceed.
*Raṃ*: what is that? Gold (*jātarūpa*). *Hiṃ ranti hiraṃ*: this is a second-order tappurisa compound. *Ñāpeti tosetīti ñaṃ*: it makes known and satisfies; thus it is *ñaṃ*. What is that? Gold.
Having become *hiraṃ*, it is *hiraññaṃ*; the meaning should be understood as:
"having brought about joy and gladness while circulating, it especially satisfies people. The word *vā* has the sense of collecting both the stated and unstated meanings. They go.
"By way of distinction" means cattle (*gāvo*); "they live and eat by way of distinction" means horses (*assā*). Cattle and horses are *gavāssaṃ*.
"Giving first what is to be given" means *dā*; "living and eating" means *asā*. *Dāsā* means those who, having given, then live and eat;
the meaning is that they live and eat after first giving to their owners what is to be given. Or, they live on what is given by their owners.

They are called *dāsā* because they eat (*bhakkhanti*); or alternatively, they are called *dāsā* because they dwell (*asanti*) with difficulty and toil. They are called *purisā* because they fill (*purenti*) the hearts of their parents;
or they are called *purisā* because they seek (*isanti*) or search for what is beneficial (*puraṃ*).

"Pura" refers to the karma that precedes the state of being a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a Cakkavatti; what is that? It is powerful karma. Or, they are called *purisā* because they seek that "pura" through virtue (*sīla*). Thus, they are *purisā*.
For it is indeed in this way that they attain the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), a Solitary Buddha (Paccekabuddha), or a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti).

Alternatively, "men" (*purisa*) are so called because they dwell in a high place (*puri*). For men stand in the position of fathers to their mothers; these etymological explanations are indeed appropriate because the meaning is possible.
"Slaves and men" is *dāsaporisaṃ*; the compound is formed with the middle term expanded. And here, by the inclusion of the word "slaves,"...
A female slave is also included. The distinction should be understood as follows: male slaves are people of ill-fortune, while men are people of happiness.
Women (*thiyo*) are so called because sons and daughters stand (*tiṭṭhanti*) or are established (*patiṭṭhanti*) in them. The analytical meaning of the word *nara* has already been stated above.
The Master has explained that in this canonical verse, a specific portion—the danger (*ādīnava*) consisting of mental distress—is presented; [this] has been analyzed by us.
And because it was asked, “Where in the Pāḷi is the danger (ādīnava) characterized as suffering found? the passage beginning, “In this regard, what is the danger?
The weak overpower him,” was commenced. Alternatively, why was the passage beginning, “In this regard, what is the danger?
The weak overpower him,” commenced in this way, rather than [beginning] with, “In this regard, what is the danger? For one who desires that…”?
"Is the danger analyzed? Yes, it is true. However, the danger is manifold by way of suffering, mental distress, and so forth.
Of that manifold danger, one portion—the danger designated as mental distress—was already analyzed previously.

Now, in order to analyze the danger designated as physical suffering, the passage beginning "In this regard, what is the danger? The weak are overpowered by the strong," and so on, is commenced. Therein:

Regarding the word "therein" (*tattha*): among the disadvantages (*ādīnava*) such as suffering and mental distress indicated in that verse beginning with "the state of gratification and disadvantage," which disadvantage is present there?
Having asked, "In which of those scriptural teachings (*pāḷidhamma*) is it found?
[it is replied]: "The weak are overpowered by the strong; dangers crush them."
“Then suffering follows him, like water into a broken boat.

Here, in this verse of the Pāḷi, that portion of the danger which is reckoned as suffering has been mentioned; this portion of the danger reckoned as suffering is the domain of the “nutriment of teaching.
In the verse, “they have no strength among these defilements,” they are called “weak” (*abalā*). Why are the defilements weak? Because of the wholesome states (*kusala*).

Because they are to be abandoned. They "overpower" (abhibhavanti) that person who craves after sensual pleasures such as fields and the like—meaning they overcome that weak person due to his lack of the powers of faith and so forth.

Although the defilements are weak because they are to be abandoned by wholesome states, nevertheless, they are capable of overcoming one who craves after sensual pleasures and is devoid of the powers of faith and so forth.

"Crushing dangers" (*parissaya*) means that they "go toward" (*ayanti*), that is, they proceed by completely (*pari*) and all around (*samantato*) afflicting this man who is greedy for sensual pleasures, seeking sensual pleasures, and guarding sensual pleasures;
thus they are called "dangers. Both lions, tigers, and the like, as well as bodily misconduct and so forth, crush him.
Consequently, suffering such as birth and so on follows and pursues that man who is overcome by those dangers.
What does it follow after? It follows after just as water follows a broken boat; such is the meaning of "it follows.
The Master has analyzed that in this canonical verse, only a single part of the escape known as the Path is mentioned, whereas the whole is understood.
[One might ask: "Where in the canonical Dhamma is the escape known as Nibbāna mentioned as a single part?"
Because it was to be asked, the passage beginning with “In this regard, what is the escape? Therefore, a person should always be mindful” has been commenced.

Alternatively, why was the passage beginning with “In this regard, what is the escape? Therefore, a person should always be mindful” commenced in this way, when the escape has not already been analyzed by means of the passage beginning with “In this regard, what is the escape? He who avoids sensual pleasures”?
Truth is indeed [the means], but renunciation is twofold, by way of the path and Nibbāna. Among those two kinds of renunciation, that which is reckoned as the path has been analyzed previously;
now, in order to analyze that which is reckoned as Nibbāna, the passage beginning with "In this regard, what is renunciation?
Therefore, a person should always be mindful" is commenced. Therein, "in this regard" (tattha) refers to that [truth].
Regarding the escape [from suffering] consisting of the Path and Nibbāna indicated in the verse beginning with “by way of gratification and danger,” one might ask:
among those canonical teachings, in which specific canonical teaching is the escape known as Nibbāna found? Having asked this, it is said:
“Therefore, a person who is always mindful should avoid sensual pleasures;”
"Having abandoned those, one crosses the flood, like one who has boarded a boat and reached the further shore.
Here, in this verse of the Pāḷi, that which is called Nibbāna—the escape—is presented; this escape is the domain of the "nutriment of teaching.
In the verse, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means: because suffering follows a person who is greedy for sensual pleasures, therefore a person should always, at all times...

By devoting oneself to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, being mindful and possessed of full awareness, one should avoid and abandon sensual pleasures—those defilements that are sensual—either by way of suppression or by way of total eradication.

Having abandoned those sensual pleasures through the Noble Path, one would cross, or be able to cross, the fourfold flood (*oghā*). Who, like crossing over, would cross it? The owner of the boat, entering the boat.

Just as one who, having baled out water and sprinkled it outside, crosses over to the further shore by easily crossing in a light boat, so too, having baled out the water of the defilements occurring within oneself and removed it by means of the Noble Path, one would go to the further shore—the peace of Nibbāna—by means of a light personal existence through the Nibbāna-element without residue; such is the meaning. This...
Why is Nibbāna the escape? It is called the escape because it is the escape from all that is conditioned (*saṅkhata*).
This escape is included here in the Pāḷi Dhamma; this was analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us.
Since one might ask, "Which fruit is included in which part of the Pāḷi Dhamma?", [the text continues]: "In that regard, which is the fruit?"
The passage beginning with “Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives according to Dhamma” is commenced. Therein,
regarding the phrase “tattha tattha,” having asked which fruit among those fruits— protection, accomplishment, deathlessness, crossing over, and so forth—
indicated in that verse beginning with “assāda-ādīnava-tā” is found where, in which specific texts of the Pāḷi Dhamma?— [the following is stated]:
“Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by Dhamma, like a great umbrella in the rainy season.

This is the benefit when Dhamma is well-practiced: the one who lives by Dhamma does not go to a state of misery.”—In this canonical verse, that which has come down as the fruit of Dhamma’s protection from misfortunes is the bringing of protection.
And that which has come as the fruit—the accomplishment of prosperity—is this fruit of accomplishment through protection;
it is the domain of the "nutriment of teaching. In the verse, "dhamma" refers to that merit consisting of various types such as giving, which has been produced by a particular person;
that dhamma protects that person who practices dhamma and produces dhamma from harmful things. Like what? At the time of rain.
When it rains, a large umbrella must be held by one who is skillful; that person protects those holding it from the rain just as they do.
In the same way, the Dhamma must be protected through right self-application;
for only when one is heedful and properly guards the Dhamma does it protect them. Such a practitioner of the Dhamma alone does not go to a state of woe.
“This is the benefit” means that this is the benefit of the well-practiced Dhamma for one who has well practiced the Dhamma.
The Master explained that only a portion of the fruit is included here in the canonical Dhamma, as we also know this because it must be asked:
“Which method is found in which part of the Canon? To this, [the answer is]: “In that regard, what is the method? All conditioned phenomena...”
The passage beginning with “impermanent,” etc., has been commenced. Therein, regarding the phrase “tattha tattha”:

having asked which method among those methods—such as renunciation preceded by insight—indicated in that verse beginning with “the state of gratification and danger,” etc., is found where, that is, in which textual teachings (pāḷidhamma) among those [teachings], it occurs;—
“When one sees with wisdom: ‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’... [and so on]...

‘All phenomena are non-self’”—here, in these verses of the text, that which is called the knowledge of revulsion preceded by insight, which has come down as the path because it is the cause for the attainment of purification, is the means that constitutes the objective domain of the "nutriment of teaching."

In the verses, when one sees with wisdom that all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-saṅkhārā*)—without exception—are constructed by karma, consciousness, and nutriment, and are impermanent in the sense of non-existence, then one becomes disenchanted with what is impermanent and has the nature of suffering.

This state, characterized by the knowledge of disenchantment and preceded by insight (*vipassanā*), is the path to purification. Thus it is said in such passages as "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
The conditioned nature of formations has already been stated in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*.
Without consulting that *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, some teachers say, "Because they are objects of insight-knowledge, they are only phenomena belonging to the three planes.
If this were so, then the phenomena of the Path and Fruition would be permanent and so forth; therefore, it is only in accordance with the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* [that the correct view is maintained].

The meaning should be understood. "Suffering" means they are suffering by way of the nature of the suffering of pain (*dukkhadukkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*), and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*).

"Non-self" means they are non-self in the sense of being coreless, because they are devoid of the core of permanence, the core of substance, and the core of a self; or alternatively, they are non-self in the sense of not being subject to one's own control.
The Master has analyzed how a partial aspect of the means (*upāya*) is included here in the Dhamma of the scriptures, and this is also known to us: "Which..."
Since it must be asked, "Where in the canonical Dhamma (pāḷidhamma) is the injunction (āṇatti) found?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is the injunction?

Like one with eyes avoiding uneven ground," etc., is commenced. Therein, "therein" (tattha) refers to which injunction among those specified in the verse beginning with "The gratification and the danger," namely, the injunction to avoid evil misconduct and the injunction to practice wholesome good conduct, and so forth. Among those [injunctions], which injunction is it? In that context...
Having asked, "In which parts of the Pāli Dhamma does this appear?",
[he replied]: "Just as one with eyes would avoid uneven ground,
So should the wise man in the world of the living Avoid all evil deeds, provided he has the power to do so."
Herein, regarding the textual doctrine (pāḷidhamma), the instruction concerning the avoidance of evil misconduct that has come down is the domain of the "nutriment of teaching" (desanāhāra).
Just as a man with sight, when there is effort to be exerted,
avoids uneven ground or wild elephants and the like while still carrying his body, so too does the wise person in the world of the living.
One avoids evil, base, and wrong conduct. "Command" (āṇatti) refers to the command of the Blessed One, the King of Dharma who is worthy of commands;
that command is manifold. Therefore, in the verse beginning with "One should do what is wholesome," the practice of good conduct is the command.
"Come for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of the Tathāgata."
In such verses as, “Take up the precepts; that will be for your welfare,” the instructions regarding going for refuge and taking up the precepts are presented.
Why, then, was it begun with, “Behold the world as empty,” and so forth? Is it not the case that [the fruit] has already been defined there: “In this context, what is the fruit?”

By the passage beginning with "Dhammo have," by the passage beginning with "Therein, what is the means? All conditioned phenomena," and by the passage beginning with "Therein, what is the instruction?

The One with Vision," the fruit, the means, and the instruction are analyzed. That is true; however, the fruit, the means, and the instruction as they appear individually in various suttas have already been analyzed.
Now, in order to analyze the fruit, the means, and the instruction as they appear together [in this single context], [the following is said].
The passage beginning with “View the world as empty” (*suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu*) has been commenced.

Therein, “view the world as empty” means: view the entire world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāraloka*) as empty of self, either by way of observing its lack of mastery (*avasavattitā*) or by way of contemplating its hollowness (*tucchabhāva*).
This is the word of the Blessed One, because it is prescriptive in nature.

“Command” (āṇatti) means: he addresses him as “Mogharāja” because he is devoid of the essence of permanence, the essence of pleasure, and the essence of a self; or he is “vain” (mogha) because he is devoid of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and so forth. Regarding the phrase “ever mindful” (sadā sato):

since mindfulness spoken of here with reference to a person serves as the cause for clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) in the vision of emptiness (*suññatā*), mindfulness itself is the means, not the one possessing mindfulness (*satimā*); this is the intended meaning of “mindfulness” (*sati*) in this context. Regarding the phrase “having struck down the view of self” (*attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhacca*):
here, the “view of self” (*attānudiṭṭhi*) refers to [the views] such as “form is the self,” “the self possesses form,” or “in form... [is the self].”
The view consisting of twenty bases, such as "the self" and "form in the self," and so forth— having uprooted and completely severed this by means of the Path,
one would thus, according to the method described, be a "crosser over death," having transcended the domain of death. Herein, that which is the crossing over and transcending of the domain of death,
and the accomplishment of the preliminary practice for that transcending— this [is what is meant].

The intention is that the fruit of the Blessed One’s teaching is the objective domain of the "nutriment of the teaching. Although previously the various instructions regarding the fruits and their means were explained separately—as in:
“O Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as empty;
having uprooted the view of self, you shall thus be one who has crossed over death”—it is now presented here.

Furthermore, regarding the single verse, because they are analyzed together, one should understand the distinction that in all the suttas where fruits and so forth are shown together, or in all the verses, the fruits and so forth must be shown—just as the gratifications and so forth are—in some cases having been extracted individually.
Therefore, the commentator said: "But it should be understood how... an example is given together."
6. Regarding the gratification (*assāda*) and other factors that constitute the objective domain of the "nutriment of the teaching" (*desanāhāra*):

the Teacher has analyzed them in their specific forms through particular illustrations, such as, "In this portion of the scripture (*pāḷidhamma*), this gratification is presented; in this portion of the scripture, this danger (*ādīnava*) is presented.
But what did the Blessed One [intend] by these gratifications and so forth for the three types of persons—the one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), etc.—in common?
Since the following inquiry could arise—"Does he teach [the same thing] to everyone, or does he teach one person according to what is appropriate for them?

What exactly does he teach?"—in order to show how the gratification (*assāda*) and other factors are analyzed according to the distinction between individuals by saying, "To this person he teaches this;

to that person he teaches that," the passage beginning with "In this regard, the Blessed One, for one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement... was commenced. Therein, "in this regard" (*tattha*) means...
Regarding those [qualities] such as gratification (*assāda*) and so forth: the Blessed One teaches the escape (*nissaraṇa*) to the person who understands through a brief summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*);
the Blessed One teaches both the danger (*ādīnava*) and the escape to the person who understands through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*);
and the Blessed One teaches all three—gratification, danger, and escape—to the person who is guided by instruction (*neyya*). This is how the meaning of the construction should be understood.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "Having thus shown the gratification (*assāda*) and so forth by way of example and in their own form, the passage beginning with ‘Therein the Blessed One’ was spoken in order to now show the classification of the teaching according to the classification of individuals (*puggala*).
Regarding that, *ugghaṭitaññū* means: that which is struck upon (*ugghaṭīyate*), penetrated, or set down along with its distinctions and details is *ugghaṭita*;
one who knows (*ñū*) that struck-upon meaning is *ugghaṭitaññū*. By a mere summary (*uddesamatta*) alone...
The meaning is that he penetrates the goal which is to be penetrated with its divisions and in detail.

A person who, by the mere recitation—that is, by the mere act of being taught—knows the goal and attains the accomplishment of the goal, is called one "who understands through a brief indication" (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

That which is expanded and detailed is "the expanded" (*vipañcita*); one who knows that is "one who understands through expansion" (*vipañcitaññū*). A person who, by the mere exposition—that is, by the mere act of being explained—knows the goal and attains the accomplishment of the goal, is called one "who understands through expansion."

That which must be led to or brought to its meaning through further exposition is "to be led" (*neyya*). A person who, having understood the meaning exactly as it has been analyzed—either through further exposition or by way of reverse order—has attained the accomplishment of that meaning, is called "one to be led.

For one who gains realization through a concise teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*), the breakthrough to realization (*abhisamaya*) is accomplished solely through the teaching on escape; whereas for others, it is accomplished through both the teaching on danger and the teaching on escape.

The intended meaning to be understood here is that the penetration and realization of one who gains knowledge through exposition (*vipañcitaññū*) is accomplished, and the penetration and realization of one who is guidable (*neyya*) is accomplished by means of the teaching on gratification (*assāda*), the teaching on danger (*ādīnava*), and the teaching on escape (*nissaraṇa*).

However, the "one who dwells on the words" (*padaparama*) is not included here because he lacks the capacity for the division of penetration and realization. And since he is not included, [the following applies].

The third, sixth, and seventh of the seven methods of the *Paṭṭhāna*—namely, the gratification (*assāda*), the danger (*ādīnava*), the escape (*nissaraṇa*); the gratification and danger; the gratification and escape;

and the danger and escape—are included, while the remaining four methods are not. Indeed, the inclusion or exclusion [of these methods] should be understood as being due to the absence of those to be trained (*veneyya*) who could be disciplined by them.

The "disciplining of those to be disciplined" (*veneyyavinaya*) refers to the arising of the Noble Path within the mental continua of those to be disciplined, and not merely the disciplining of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

Furthermore, since the arising of the Noble Path is accomplished only through the three aforementioned methods of the "basis of the method" (*padaṭṭhānanaya*), the other methods are not mentioned here. For it is said in the *Peṭaka*: ... [text continues] ...
“In that regard, what is the gratification and what is the danger?
‘Whatever a person does, they see those results within themselves:
the doer of good sees the good, and the doer of evil sees the evil.’”
“In this regard, that a doer of good experiences what is good is the gratification (*assāda*). That a doer of evil experiences what is evil is the danger (*ādīnava*).

“Monks, there are these eight worldly conditions (*lokadhammā*). Which eight? ‘Gain,’ and so forth. In this regard, gain, fame, pleasure, and praise—this is the gratification. Loss, disrepute, pain, and blame—this is the danger.
“In this regard, what is the gratification and the escape?
‘The ripening of meritorious deeds is pleasant, one’s intention succeeds,
and one quickly attains the supreme peace, Nibbāna.’—
This is the gratification and the escape.
“Bhikkhus, there are these thirty-two marks of a Great Man possessed by which a Great Man has only two destinations...
[as in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta] ...he is one whose veil is rent. This entire Lakkhaṇa Sutta constitutes both the gratification and the escape.
“In this regard, what is the danger and the escape?
‘The five aggregates are indeed a burden; the bearer of the burden is the person.
The taking up of the burden is suffering in the world; the laying down of the burden is happiness.’”
“Having laid down the heavy burden, not taking up another burden,
having uprooted craving with its root, one is free from hunger and fully extinguished.”—
This is the danger and the escape.
“In this regard, what are the gratification, the danger, and the escape?
‘Sensual pleasures are indeed variegated, sweet, and enchanting; they agitate the mind in manifold forms.
Therefore, O King, I have gone forth; the life of a recluse is certainly better.’”

“This is the gratification, the danger, and the escape,” it was said; therefore, these same methods should be extracted and understood here as well. This method is indeed applicable to the fruits and so forth as well.
For in the *Peṭaka*: “In this regard, what is the fruit and the means? The verse beginning ‘A wise man, established in virtue’—this is both the fruit and the means.
In this regard, what is the fruit and the instruction?”
“If you fear suffering, if suffering is not dear to you,
do not perform an evil deed, whether openly or in secret.
This is both the result and the injunction.
“In this regard, what is the means and the instruction?
‘Having understood this body to be like a jar, and having established this mind to be like a city, fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom;
guard what has been won, and be one who dwells nowhere.’”
It is said: "This is both the means and the instruction. Therefore, the illustration of the fruit and so forth should also be understood by way of suffering.
Regarding the three types of persons—those who understand through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and the others—it is said: "To this person he teaches this;
to that person he teaches that. Those persons to whom the teacher has analyzed the gratification and so forth as appropriate are [the ones referred to].
Since it is possible to consider that those practices by which [beings] are distinguished become renowned, and that the persons distinguished by them are likewise renowned,
the passage beginning with "In this regard, there are four practices" was undertaken in order to show, by way of enumeration, how many such practices and how many such persons there are.
"In each of those" means among those persons, such as the one who gains knowledge through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth.
The construction should be made thus: "Those persons who are distinguished by whichever paths, those paths are four, and those persons are four.

Which four? The path of practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; the path of practice that is painful with quick direct knowledge; the path of practice that is pleasant with sluggish direct knowledge; [the path of practice that is pleasant with quick direct knowledge].
There are four [types of persons]: those for whom the way of practice is easy and direct knowledge is swift, and so forth. Which four?
The dull person of craving-disposition, the keen person of craving-disposition, the dull person of view-disposition, and the keen person of view-disposition—these are the four.
Even the classification made by way of the ways of practice and direct knowledges is indeed called a classification made by way of the ways of practice, because they are inseparable.
Having taken this into account, they are not called "the four paths with direct knowledge" (*paṭipadā-abhiññā*), but are instead called simply "the four paths.
Furthermore, these are distinguished by way of serenity (*samatha*) and also distinguished by way of insight (*vipassanā*). How are they distinguished by way of serenity?
From the very first moment of attention directed toward the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, beginning with "earth, earth," and continuing until the attainment of jhāna...
The wisdom that occurs from the time access concentration arises until it reaches absorption is called "the way" (*paṭipadā*).
However, the wisdom that occurs from the moment of access concentration until absorption is reached is called "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*),
because it is a state of wisdom attained beyond the lower level of wisdom.
And that path is painful and difficult for some because of their grasping at the manifestation of adverse states such as the hindrances;
for others, due to the absence of those [states], it is pleasant and easy. Furthermore, direct knowledge is slow and not quick in its occurrence for some because of their lack of clear knowledge;
for others, it is swift and quick in its occurrence because of their clear knowledge.
How is it by way of insight (vipassanā)? For one who, intent on insight by way of the material and immaterial,
discerns the four great elements and then discerns derived matter and discerns the immaterial, yet— while discerning both the material and the immaterial—
is able to discern them only with difficulty, through hardship, and with exhaustion, for him there is what is called the "difficult path of practice" (dukkhāpaṭipadā).

For one who has already grasped both the material and immaterial [realms], because of the slowness in the manifestation of the path during the preparatory stage of insight (vipassanā-parivāsa), there is what is called "slow direct knowledge" (*dandhābhiññā*).

By way of its opposite, the other two [types of direct knowledge] exist. However, here the modes of practice and direct knowledge (*paṭipadā-abhiññā*) should be understood as distinct according to insight, since the context concerns clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
for in the Commentary, it says: "Thus, with reference to those individuals..."

The classification of the teaching has been shown; in order to show those persons by classifying them according to their modes of practice (*paṭipadā*), it was said, “There are four modes of practice,” and so forth.
The method of application should be understood according to the same method already stated.
By means of the four modes of practice and the four direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), all four persons—without exception—are [liberated] from the suffering of saṃsāra; what then?

Is it that they simply emerge, or is there the possibility of investigation—such as "by this specific path and direct knowledge this person emerges" or "by this specific path and direct knowledge this person emerges"—in terms of a definite emergence? [In response to this:

"This person, having obtained these supports and the decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), by means of this specific path and direct knowledge, [emerges] from the suffering of saṃsāra..."
Having thus determined [the meaning], it was said, "The one of craving-temperament is dull-witted," and so forth,
in order to demonstrate it. Therein, the dull-witted person of craving-temperament, having obtained the decisive support condition through the foundations of mindfulness as supports,

by means of the faculty of mindfulness— surpassing the faculty of mindfulness through the Noble Path— [is liberated] from the round of suffering via the practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge.
The person of exalted temperament who is driven by craving, having obtained the decisive support through the jhānas as the necessary condition,
departs from the suffering of the round via the Noble Path— which is predominant in the faculty of concentration and possesses the practice that is difficult but swift direct knowledge—
by means of the faculty of concentration. The person of dull temperament who is driven by views, having obtained the decisive support through the right efforts as the necessary condition...

Having obtained [the path] through the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), with the faculty of energy predominant, one who is of a faith-character (*saddhācarita*) and of gentle temperament (*mudupuggala*) issues forth from the suffering of saṃsāra by means of the Noble Path characterized by the easy practice and sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*).
A person of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) and of exalted nature (*udattapuggala*), having obtained the decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*) through the various bases of truth,

issues forth from the suffering of saṃsāra by means of the Noble Path characterized by the easy practice and quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*), with the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) predominant.
The construction should be made as: "He goes forth from the suffering of saṃsāra. However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Regarding 'four persons'—these are the four types of individuals practicing according to the aforementioned classification of the path. To show that classification of the path together with its causes, methods, and fruits, the passage beginning with 'one of craving-temperament' was spoken.
Therein, "one of craving-temperament" (*taṇhācarito*) means one whose temperament (*carita*) is produced by craving (*taṇhā*).
"One who is endowed with dullness (*manda*) and the dullness of ignorance (*avijjā*) is *mando*; he is a person in whom delusion (*moha*) predominates.

*Udatta* means *udaatto*, which signifies one of exalted wisdom (*uḷārapañña*). It is called *udo* because it bestows an exalted fruit (*uḷāraṃ phalaṃ*); what is that? It is investigation (*pavicaya*).

It is called *atto* because it is produced within oneself (*attani nibbatto*). The etymological meaning of *udatta* should be understood as 'that person in whom *udo* (exalted investigation) is *atto* (produced)'."
For the first way of practice, the cause is being of a craving temperament and having dull wisdom; the means is the faculty of mindfulness;
and the fruit of all of them is indeed deliverance. For the second way of practice, the cause is being of a craving temperament and having keen wisdom;
the means is the faculty of energy. For the third way of practice, the cause is being of a view-temperament and having dull wisdom.

And the means (*upāya*) is the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*). For the fourth way of practice (*paṭipadā*), the cause (*hetu*) consists of being of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicaritatā*) and possessing exalted wisdom (*udattapaññatā*);
the means is the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*). Thus, the causes, the means, and the fruits are to be understood.

Furthermore, in this context, a person of speculative temperament who is exalted is called one who understands through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*); whereas one of speculative temperament who is dull and also of craving-temperament...
There is the person of noble disposition who is one to be known through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), and the dull-witted person of craving-disposition who is one to be led (*neyya*).

Therefore, by way of showing the distinction among these three types of those to be trained—beginning with the phrase, "In that regard, the Blessed One teaches the escape for the person who is one to be known through a brief indication" (*ugghaṭitaññū*)—he teaches the escape;
he teaches both the danger (*ādīnava*) and the escape, as well as the gratification (*assāda*).

"and he teaches both the danger and the escape"— thus the analysis of the teaching is shown. Therein, by showing the distinctions in the ways of practice through the passage beginning "four ways of practice," the fourfold division of those whose temperament is dominated by craving—
namely, the person of dull temperament with a craving-temperament, the person of keen temperament with a craving-temperament,
the person of dull temperament with a view-temperament, and the person of keen temperament with a view-temperament— is indicated.
It should be understood that the fourfold classification of persons (*puggalacatukka*) has been shown.

Now, in order to show—by means of the second method of exposition through the application of the meaning—the mild quartet of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*) divided fourfold by way of the four paths and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the passage beginning with "both those of craving-temperament" was stated. In that context, because craving is the opposite of concentration (*samādhi*)...

Both types of persons—those of craving-temperament and those of dull-faith temperament—having obtained the necessary support for insight preceded by serenity, proceed toward the wisdom of the path that leads to the fading away of lust, to the liberation of mind, and to the state of the fruit of training.
Deliverance occurs through right concentration accompanied by right view, not through right concentration alone; therefore, [this applies to] those of view-temperament and dull-faith temperament.

Both types of persons are led out by serenity preceded by insight, through the wisdom of the path for the fading away of ignorance, toward liberation by wisdom and the state of the fruit of one beyond training; thus it is said that all four types of persons are of only two kinds.

Regarding "for the fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāgāya*): it is called *rāga* because one is colored by it; it is called *virāgā* because lust fades away by means of this; the fading away of lust is *rāgavirāgā*.

It is for the fading away of lust through that [concentration]. "Cetovimutti" (liberation of mind) refers to concentration by way of its classification as "mind," as in the expression, "Develop the mind and wisdom. It is called "liberation" because it is liberated from its opposite by means of subsiding.

Thus, it is "liberation of mind" because one is liberated by the mind—that is, by concentration—or liberation of the mind itself is "liberation of mind"; this refers to the concentration of the fruit of non-returning.
For the non-returner (anāgāmipuggala), by fulfilling his practice in concentration, he goes forth toward the liberation of mind (cetovimutti).

Regarding the phrase "for the fading away of ignorance" (avijjāvirāgāya): ignorance (avijjā) is so called because it finds (vindati) what is not to be found (avindiya), such as bodily misconduct; or, according to the method of etymology (niruttinaya), it is ignorance because it does not find (na vindati) what is to be found (vindiya), such as bodily good conduct.
It is called fading away (virāgā) because one fades away from it (virajjati etāya). Thus, "fading away of ignorance" means the fading away from ignorance (avijjāya virāgā). By that [fading away].

For the fading away of ignorance. It is called *paññā* (wisdom) because it knows by way of various modes; it is called *vimutti* (liberation) because it is liberated; thus, "liberated by wisdom" is *paññāvimutti*.
Alternatively, wisdom itself is liberation, hence *paññāvimutti*, which refers to the wisdom of the fruit of Arahatship;

[the text speaks] by means of that *paññāvimutti*. Since it must be stated, "Among those, which persons are to be abandoned by which method of meaning?", it says: "In that regard, those for whom serenity is the precursor," and so forth.

It has been said. Therein, "therein" means: among those persons classified by the passage beginning with "both are of craving-temperament," those persons of both craving-temperaments who are dull-witted and are led by the method of the "turning of delight" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*)—those persons of both craving-temperaments who are dull-witted are to be made to progress, to be conveyed, to be led.
Those [persons] of both view-temperaments who are dull-witted... [are to be led] by the method of the "hook" (*aṅkusa*).

“Individuals who are guided by insight... [and] those who are guided by serenity—both these types of individuals with a speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) and a dull sense of urgency (*mandauttā*)—are to be abandoned, led, and conducted by means of the method of the lion’s play (*sīhavikkīḷita*); this is the meaning. 7.

“In that regard, ‘the four modes of progress’ (*catasso paṭipadā*), etc., by way of the teaching-method (*desanāhāra*), [demonstrates] the classification of the craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*) and so forth through the division of the painful mode of progress (*dukkhāpaṭipadā*).”

The person has been analyzed and is known to us; therefore, because it must be asked whether this "mode of teaching" (desanāhāra) occurs in some way or another within the Dhamma to be praised immediately after that analysis, he said, "Where does this mode occur?
and so forth. Regarding the Dhamma that the Teacher teaches to one endowed with the nine marks of excellence: in that [Dhamma]...
Regarding the phenomena to be praised, the three kinds of wisdom— beginning with that consisting in inquiry and beginning with that consisting in what has been heard—

which have been analyzed, and the three types of persons— beginning with those who understand through a brief indication— who have been analyzed by means of those wisdoms: it should be understood that this "mode of teaching" (desanāhāra) exists within the phenomena to be taught by the Teacher in the form of such an analysis.

In this context, "this method" (hāra) refers to the method of teaching (*desanāhāra*), by which the classification of individuals to be trained (*veneyyapuggala*) is shown through the analysis of the path (*paṭipadāvibhāga*).
As for the phrase "this method of teaching": where does it arise? It arises in relation to the Dhamma that is to be expounded, by way of being an exposition (*saṃvaṇṇanābhāva*).

"Of whom" (*yassa*) means of that person to be trained who is liberated from the eight unfavorable conditions (*akhaṇa*), such as being born in a border region and so forth, and who possesses the qualities of hearing, retaining, and so on.
And he is endowed with the attainments for that person to be trained. "Teacher" (*satthā*): he instructs and guides the world together with its devas, thus he is a teacher.
"Dhamma": the Dhamma that has been taught and is worthy of being praised. "Teaches" (*deseti*): he speaks by means of both concise and detailed methods. "A certain one" (*aññatara*):
a disciple among the Blessed One’s disciples who is capable of teaching the Dhamma in this way. "Worthy of veneration" (*garuṭṭhāniya*): [one who stands in the position of a teacher].
One who possesses the distinguished qualities of virtue, learning, generosity, and so forth—which are the grounds for reverence—is honored and his word is to be trusted.
A *sabrahmacārī* (fellow practitioner of the holy life) is so called because he practices or engages in the "holy" (*brahma*), namely the Teacher’s instruction, together with or equally with others.
He gains faith [thinking]: "The Teacher who teaches the Dhamma is a Perfectly Enlightened One. Regarding the Teacher...

Thinking, “This Dhamma is indeed well-expounded—possessing both meaning and phrasing, absolutely complete and absolutely pure, bringing welfare, bringing benefit, bringing happiness, producing jhāna, the path, the fruits, and Nibbāna—and it must be believed by us,” one gains unwavering faith in the Dhamma thus taught, and repeatedly generates that state of belief within one’s own mental continuum. Likewise, “Whoever... [text continues]”
“The disciple teaches the Dhamma; that disciple, a venerable fellow-practitioner whose word is to be trusted, is indeed capable of teaching the Dhamma either in brief or in detail.
Thus, regarding the teacher and the disciple, [one reflects]: “The Dhamma taught by such a disciple is meaningful, well-phrased, entirely complete, and entirely pure.”
"It brings wealth, it brings welfare, it brings happiness, and it produces meditation, the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna;
it must be believed in by us"—this is the meaning of repeatedly generating within one's own continuum the faith that believes in the Dhamma taught by the disciple.
"Therein" means in that Dhamma which must be believed, both that taught by the Teacher and that taught by the disciple.
The investigation of a person to be trained who has faith; the encouragement of one who is investigating; the weighing of one who is encouraged;

and the scrutiny of one who is weighing—this wisdom beginning with investigation is called "wisdom consisting of what is heard" (*sutamayī paññā*), because it proceeds by way of following through faith (*saddhānusāra*).
In this context, "investigation" (*vīmaṃsā*) is the act of investigating the scripture (*pāḷi*) and the meaning of the scripture.
Or, it is "investigation" (*vīmaṃsā*) because it investigates; it is the wisdom that examines a word by means of another word, or the meaning of a word by means of another meaning of a word.
Just as here, so too in the case of "exertion" (*ussāhana*) and the others, the explanations based on the abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*) and the agent (*kattu-sādhana*) should be made.
And exertion is the wisdom that supports the Dhamma through exertion and accomplishes its retention and mastery, not energy (*viriya*).
