And herein, that wisdom which proceeds merely upon what has been heard, but turns back without reaching the state of investigation and so forth, is not wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*).
Likewise, that which turns back after hearing and investigating, without reaching the state of exertion and so forth;

and that which turns back after hearing, investigating, and exerting, without reaching the state of weighing and so forth; and that which [turns back] after hearing, investigating, exerting, and weighing...
If it turns back without reaching the state of investigation, that wisdom should be understood as not being wisdom consisting in what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*).
However, for one who hears and believes, there is inquiry; for one who inquires, there is exertion; for one who exerts himself, there is weighing;
and for one who weighs, there is investigation—this is what should be understood as wisdom consisting in what has been heard.
The wisdom consisting in what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*) has been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us.

Since it must be stated, "What is the wisdom consisting in reflection (*cintāmayī paññā*)?", immediately after the analysis of the wisdom consisting in what has been heard, he says, "In that way, with the hearing as a support," etc., in order to analyze the wisdom consisting in reflection.
In this context, "heard" (*suta*) means that which is heard, namely the Dhamma of the scriptures; or alternatively, the hearing of the Dhamma of the scriptures is called "the heard."

Learning is of two kinds. "By means of" (*nissayena*) means "depending upon" (*upanissāya*). This [term] is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state already attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*), and thus the instrumental case is employed as "by means of learning" (*sutena nissayena*).
Here, however, [the meaning is]: "This abstention from killing and so forth is virtue (*sīla*) in the sense of being firm;
this one-pointedness is concentration (*samādhi*) in the sense of concentrating; these primary elements and derived matter are form (*rūpa*) in the sense of being subject to change."
Contact and the rest are "name" (nāma) in the sense of bending; these five factors beginning with form are "aggregates" (khandha) in the sense of a heap.
Wisdom that consists in the investigation of the intrinsic nature of those various phenomena—such as their state of oppression and so forth—is called "investigation" (vīmaṃsā).

Having asked for the etymological meaning of those very things such as virtue, concentration, and so on—namely, that virtue is so called because one is established (sīlati) therein—one [should explain] their common characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes.
"Balancing" (*tulana*) refers to the wisdom of grasping that functions as if weighing [the teachings].

"Investigation" (*upaparikkhā*), however, should be understood specifically as the wisdom of examination that investigates those very same phenomena—such as virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth—without abandoning their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), but rather by reflecting upon their aspects such as impermanence (*aniccatā*), suffering (*dukkhatā*), non-selfhood (*anattatā*), the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), and the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) along with its causal conditions. Through the retention and mastery of the Dhamma heard...

Because it proceeds [continuously], wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*) arises as if through exertion; however, wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī paññā*) does not proceed in that way due to the lack of continuous application based on the retention and mastery of what has been reflected upon.
Therefore, it is not called "exertion.
Both wisdom consisting of what has been heard and wisdom consisting of reflection have been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us. "Which..."

Because it is to be described as "wisdom consisting in cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī paññā*), [the author], after showing the two causal types of wisdom—consisting in hearing (*sutamayī*) and consisting in reflection (*cintāmayī*)—now analyzes the resultant wisdom consisting in cultivation. He says, "By means of these two," and so forth.

In that context, "by means of these two types of wisdom" refers to the two causal types of wisdom, namely those consisting in hearing and consisting in reflection. By means of the wisdom consisting in hearing...
Whether by means of wisdom born of hearing, wisdom born of reflection, or established in both, the practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara) initiates insight (vipassanā).

"Endowed with attention" (manasikāra-sampayutta) means being properly and thoroughly engaged through attention directed toward formations (saṅkhāra) by way of discerning [the aggregates] as form and non-form, and by way of [contemplating] impermanence and so forth. [This refers to] purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi), purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhā-vitaraṇa-visuddhi), and purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).

The meaning should be understood as follows: when a practitioner has brought insight to its culmination by accomplishing purification by knowledge and vision of the way, the noble path-knowledge—designated as purification by knowledge and vision—which arises in his continuum either on the plane of seeing Nibbāna or on the plane of development, is "wisdom consisting in development" (bhāvanāmayī paññā). This applies even to the knowledge of the first path.

It is called "vision" (*dassana*) because it first sees Nibbāna; however, because it proceeds by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it should be understood as "wisdom consisting in cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī paññā*).
The "planes of vision" (*dassanabhūmi*) are the first path and fruit; the remaining ones are called the "planes of cultivation" (*bhāvanābhūmi*). 8.
Our teacher has analyzed wisdom consisting in hearing and the others for you by means of the passage beginning, "For whom the Teacher... and so forth. Thus...
Reflecting on the objection that "without hearing [the teachings], there could be no wisdom consisting of reflection (cintāmayī paññā),

yet for the great Bodhisattvas there is indeed wisdom consisting of reflection even without hearing," he has included this in that [section] and speaks the words beginning with "from the voice of another" in order to analyze it by way of another method.
In this context, "the voice of another" (*paratoghosā*) means that which has its condition in the sound of the teaching proceeding from another; thus it is "the voice of another.

"Arising within oneself" (*paccattasamuṭṭhitā*) means arising separately within one's own self. "Proper attention" (*yonisomanasikārā*) refers to the attention proceeding by way of the method of discerning the intrinsic nature of various things to be contemplated, such as form and so forth, through their qualities of being subject to change, being mental, and so on; this is "wisdom consisting in reflection" (*cintāmayī*).

By the term "wisdom" (*paññā*), disciples are included by way of their commonality; nevertheless, because [the types of persons] such as those who understand through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth were specifically mentioned, it is the disciples who are intended here. Therefore, the former method is more appropriate.

"From another" means that knowledge which arises by reason of the sound of the teaching of the Dhamma proceeding from the teacher of the Dhamma, or by means of individual attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) arising within oneself.
And that knowledge which arises by means of a cause is called "wisdom consisting in cultivation" (bhāvanāmayī paññā) because it proceeds by way of cultivation;

by this term, disciples are also included in a general sense. Nevertheless, since [the suttas] speak specifically of those who understand through a brief indication (ugghaṭitaññū) and so forth, it is the disciples who are intended here;
therefore, the former method is more appropriate. "From another" means from the sound of the teaching of the Dhamma proceeding from the teacher of the Dhamma.
The wise should understand that the knowledge which arises by means of a cause— namely, that which arises from one's own internal emergence and the cause of wise attention (yonisomanasikāra)—
is called "wisdom born of cultivation" (bhāvanāmayī paññā) because it proceeds by way of cultivation;
having thus analyzed it, those desiring to know its profound meaning in detail should understand it through the passage beginning with "Thus, by way of the analysis of the path."
This is to be understood from the words of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The three types of wisdom beginning with that consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī-paññā*) have been analyzed by the Teacher through various methods, and they have been understood by us.
"Among those, what is the name of the person who possesses one or two types of wisdom? And what is the name of the person who does not possess even one?"
Because it must be asked, "Who is this?"— namely, which person possesses this wisdom or these [qualities],
and which person does not— it was stated, beginning with "For whom these...", in order to distinguish between individuals according to the classification of the wisdom of the path (*paṭipadā-paññā*).
In this context, one whose wisdom is exceedingly sharp possesses both the wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*) and the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī paññā*);
because this person of exceedingly sharp wisdom understands by a mere indication (*uddesamattena*), he is called "one who gains knowledge through a brief summary" (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

One whose wisdom is not exceedingly sharp possesses the wisdom consisting of what has been heard through both indications and detailed explanations, but lacks the wisdom consisting of reflection; this person is one of not exceedingly sharp wisdom.
One is called "one who gains knowledge through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*) because of knowing by means of the summary and the exposition.

As for the person of dull wisdom who possesses neither wisdom born of hearing (*sutamayī paññā*) nor wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī paññā*) through the summary and the exposition—this person of dull wisdom is called "one who is to be guided" (*neyya*), because he must be led by means of a complete and detailed teaching through the summary, the exposition, and the sub-exposition. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "Now..."
"In order to show that very classification of individuals to be trained (*vineyyapuggala*) for whose sake these insights (*paññā*) were set forth, the passage beginning with ‘For whom’ was spoken.

9. "Therein, by the words ‘The Blessed One [taught] for one who knows by a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*),' etc., he clarifies the teaching; and by the words ‘Therein, there are four ways of practice (*paṭipadā*),' etc."

Through the classifications of the practice (*paṭipadā*) and through the classifications of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) such as "this is the mode of conveying" (*svāyaṃ hāro*), the Teacher has analyzed the disciples who are the vessels for the teaching, and we too have understood it.

That textual teaching which was previously given—starting with "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma"—as the objective domain of the mode of conveying, so that one might connect it with the mode of conveying within the body of the teaching; [that is what has been analyzed].

Since it must be asked, "Now that the *pāḷidesanā* has been set aside, for what purpose does this teaching teach among the meanings such as 'gratification' (*assāda*) which have been determined by means of the 'mode of teaching' (*desanāhāra')?",
the passage beginning with "This is the teaching of the Dhamma" (*sāyaṃ dhammadesanā*) was commenced in order to demonstrate, having specified it, that "this meaning is taught. Therein,

"this teaching of the Dhamma" refers to that teaching of the Dhamma which is excellent in the beginning and so forth, and which was previously mentioned as the objective domain of the 'mode of teaching'.
Having set forth this teaching on the Dhamma, he asks—out of a desire to explain—for what purpose it teaches regarding gratification and so forth;
having asked, he answers, "It teaches the Four Truths. To show those [truths] in their specific form, it is said:

"Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. This is because they function respectively as the state of occurrence, that which causes occurrence, the state of non-occurrence, and the means for non-occurrence.
They are called "truths" because they are non-perverted in their nature.
It may be appropriate that in whichever teaching the truths are determined by way of the "mode of teaching," that teaching teaches the four truths.
However, it is not appropriate that in whichever teaching the gratification and so forth are determined, that teaching teaches the four truths.
It is not possible to say [that it is not so]. Since the gratification (*assāda*) and the rest have already been determined below, one might raise the objection:

"Therefore, they should also be called 'gratification and the rest'. Having taken this objection to heart, it was stated: "The danger (*ādīnava*) and the fruit (*phala*) are suffering (*dukkha*)," and so forth.

By way of the method of commentary according to the sequence of the teaching, that which was determined in the teaching as both the danger and the fruit is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the gratification is the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*).
The truth of cessation is the escape; the truth of the path is both the means and the instruction. Therefore, it must indeed be said that "he teaches the four truths.
Phenomena of the three planes, when tainted by craving, are suffering; and because they are oppressed by impermanence and so forth, they are indeed disadvantages. They bear fruit...
The fruit of the teaching is mundane, not supramundane; therefore, it must indeed be called "suffering.
As for "gratification," because the gratification of craving is included, it may also be called "the origin. A portion of gratification is suffering alone;
another portion of gratification is both suffering and the origin. Together with insight, there is the Noble Path and the Blessed One’s injunction regarding the teaching.
Because it serves as the means for the attainment of the fruit, it is said: “The path is the means and the instruction.
It should also be understood that the path is one part of the escape. Since it must be asked, “What is this teaching that specifically teaches these four truths?
the specific [teaching] is shown by defining it: “These four truths are this Wheel of Dhamma.”
It has been stated. The construction should be made thus: "This Dhamma-wheel, being spoken of here, specifically teaches these four truths.

Since it might be asked, "Why did the Blessed One say that this teaching, which specifically teaches these four truths, possesses the nature of a Dhamma-wheel?", the passage beginning with "As the Blessed One said" was stated. In that context, "birth also... [is as follows].

Because of such statements as "suffering," birth and the other factors of the three planes of existence, which are rooted in craving, are called "suffering" by virtue of being the basis for suffering and by virtue of being the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*) and so forth.
The construction is: "by me" (*meti*) means "promulgated by me.
"O monks" (*bhikkhave*) is an address intended to arouse enthusiasm for listening. "At Bārāṇasī" (*bārāṇasiyaṃ*) means in the vicinity of the city of Bārāṇasī. "At Isipatana" (*isipatane*)...
In the place where the Paccekabuddhas—who are designated as "seers" (*isi*) because they seek and strive for the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth—descend;
that is, in the hermitage (*assama*) built at Migadāya, the site where safety was granted to the deer.
"Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) means without a superior, being beyond all excellence. "Wheel of the Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) refers to the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
It is the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) because it is both *dhamma*—in the sense of upholding its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and so forth—and a *cakka* (wheel) in the sense of proceeding.
It is "irreversible" (*appaṭivattiya*), meaning it cannot be countered. Why? Because the Blessed One, the progenitor, is the Lord of Dhamma and the Perfectly Enlightened One;

and because for Koṇḍañña and the others, as well as for the eighteen crores of Brahmās, he has accomplished the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, which is unsurpassed among all that is to be known.
And because it was asked, "By whom is it irreversible?", he said, "By a recluse," and so forth. Therein, "by a recluse" (samaṇena) means by one who has merely gone forth into homelessness.
"By a brahmin" (brāhmaṇena) means by a brahmin by birth. For there is not even the arising of a thought to deny the ultimate sense of those who are true recluses and brahmins.
"By a deva" means by a deva of the six sense-sphere heavens. "By a Brahmā" means...

The Brahmās of the form realm (*rūpabrahmā*) are included. By using the expression “by anyone whatsoever” (*kenaci*), rather than saying merely “by a recluse... [or] by a Brahmā,” the remaining assemblies of kṣatriyas, householders, and common folk are also encompassed.

Therefore, it should be understood that even the eightfold assembly—consisting of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, householders, recluses, the Cātumahārājika gods, the Tāvatiṃsa gods, Māra, and the Brahmās—is entirely incapable of obstructing it. “In the world” (*loke*) means within the collection of beings who serve as the support for the Wheel of Dhamma.
Explaining the words of the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta* in accordance with the verse “Twelve words are the sutta,” he said:
“Therein, immeasurable...,” and so forth. Therein, “therein” (*tattha*) refers to the teaching of the Wheel of Dhamma.
Instead of saying “immeasurable syllables, immeasurable words,” he uses the reversed order of expression, “immeasurable words, immeasurable syllables,” which is generally the case.

This shows that they are "comprised within phrases. It should be understood that the terms *pada*, *akkhara*, and *byañjana* involve a shift in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). "Of this very meaning" refers to the manner in which it is to be expressed;
[it means] the revealing, the manifesting, the mode of manifestation, and the mode of designation, of the very meaning comprised of the Four Truths.
Thus, the genitive case is used in connection with the possessor of the mode (*ākāravanta*) and the mode (*ākāra*). "The mode of revealing" (*saṅkāsanākāra*)—[is explained as follows].
And it is the mode of the meaning that is to be proclaimed. This same method applies to the remaining [truths] as well. "Iti pi" means:
by this manner and by that manner, this suffering consisting of birth and so forth is to be understood as a noble truth (*ariyasacca*).

"Ayaṃ" refers to this craving (*taṇhā*) which is divided into the types beginning with sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*). It is the "origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya*) because it serves as the cause for the production of suffering.
The origin of suffering. "Aya" (this) refers to this unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*), which has escaped from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*).
The cessation of suffering: because it is the condition for the non-arising and the cessation of suffering—which is divided into birth and so forth—it is the cessation of suffering.
"Aya" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path beginning with right view. Because it has gone toward *nibbāna*, which is the cessation of suffering, by way of making it its object, [it is called the path].
And it is the "practice leading to the cessation of suffering" because it is the practice for the attainment of the cessation of suffering. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Therein, having analyzed the phonetic words (*byañjanapada*) and the semantic words (*atthapada*) starting with the phrase “In that regard, immeasurable...,” the passage beginning with “Therein, the Blessed One makes it clear through the syllables” was spoken in order to show the state of connection between them by way of their mutual relationship as subject and object. Alternatively:

In order to determine and demonstrate the relationship of subject and object—since it is possible to investigate whether the Blessed One reveals or elucidates by means of the common characteristics of syllables and so forth, or whether he reveals and elucidates them according to what is appropriate—the text states:
"Therein, the Blessed One reveals by means of syllables," and so on. Regarding that, "he reveals by means of syllables" means:
Why was it stated thus? Is it not the case that by the very term "the truth of suffering" (*dukkhasacca*) and so forth, the meaning of the truth of suffering and the rest should already be indicated?
True; however, through the apprehension of even a single letter that constitutes a part of a word, there occurs the apprehension of the entire word as a collection of letters.
And when the word is apprehended, the comprehension of the meaning of the truth of suffering and so forth necessarily follows. This being so, by the word alone—

Is it not the case that the syllable should not be grasped separately from its realization (*sijjhanata*)? No; for there occurs a specific arising of understanding regarding the meaning of the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca*) and so forth.
Indeed, by the syllable *du*, the sense of "contemptible" is grasped through its nature as the basis for manifold calamities;

by the syllable *kha*, the sense of "insubstantiality" is grasped through its lack of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood. Thus, there occurs a specific arising of understanding in this manner.
Therefore it was said: “The attainment of distinction through the grasping of the meaning of the words arises.
Because there is no completion of a sentence at the conclusion of each word, the meaning being indicated in brief by means of syllables is said to be “made manifest by the words.
But when the meaning has been made known and manifested at the conclusion of the sentence, it is said to be “opened out and disclosed. By means of the phonemes...
"By means of various modes (*pakāra*), when the division of the sentence has been made, that meaning is said to be 'analyzed' (*vibhatto*); thus it is said, 'he analyzes by means of modes (*ākāra*)'.
When the individual etymological analysis (*nibbacana-vibhāga*) of each of the constituent parts of the sentence—the words—has been performed, that meaning is made manifest;

thus it is said, 'he makes it clear by means of etymologies (*niruttī*)'. Or rather, by means of those constituent parts of the sentence whose etymologies have been established, through the method of detailed exposition..."
Because it brings complete satisfaction to the minds of those beings to be trained through teachings given without remainder, and because it sharpens their wisdom,
he says, "He makes known by means of explanations.
In such passages as "The Blessed One reveals by means of syllables," the restrictive particle *eva* applies either to "the Blessed One" alone or to "by means of syllables" alone.

If [the particle] *eva* were applied [to the word *sāvako*], the meaning would be: “The disciple does not clarify; he does not clarify by means of words and so forth. Yet, the disciple does clarify, and he clarifies by means of words and so forth.
If it is asked, “Where should the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) be applied?”—the restriction should be applied thus: “The Blessed One clarifies by means of syllables alone.
For if this were the case, then the meaning clarified by the disciple, or the meaning clarified by words and so forth, [would be excluded].
It is thus comprised. Furthermore, the diversity of the subject matter of the constituent phrases (atthapada) in terms of their syllables and so forth is established.
Therefore, in a discourse consisting of a single sequence of meaning, exactly six constituent phrases are to be extracted;
in a discourse consisting of multiple sequences of meaning, six constituent phrases are to be extracted separately for each distinct sequence.

Because it must be asked, "Among the six types of phonemes (*byañjanapada*), by which phoneme is which function accomplished?", [the Buddha] said, "In that regard, the Blessed One conveys [the meaning] by means of syllables (*akkhara*) and phrases (*pada*)," etc., in order to demonstrate this by specifying, "By this, this function is accomplished; by this, that function is accomplished.
In that context, "in that regard" (*tattha*) refers to among the phonemic phrases beginning with syllables.
“Unravels” (*ugghaṭeti*) means that it accomplishes the function of unraveling.

Although it is the teaching itself that accomplishes the function of unraveling, the Blessed One is nevertheless said to accomplish the function of unraveling because he is the generator of that teaching. This same sense should be understood for the remaining terms as well.

[The question arises: “Is it only the teaching that accomplishes the function of unraveling, or does the teaching also accomplish the functions of expanding and detailing because it is generated by him?”

Having determined that there is a separate teaching for each because it must be asked, "Or are there others that accomplish their respective functions individually?", he says, "In this regard, the summary (ugghaṭanā) comes first," and so on. Alternatively, since it must be asked, "What is the summary?
What is the expansion (vipañcanā)? What is the detailed exposition (vitthāraṇā)?", he says, "In this regard, the summary..."
"Beginning," and so forth. In this context, "therein" refers to the teachings that accomplish the functions of the brief summary (*ugghaṭana*) and the rest.

The meaning should be understood as follows: the teaching that accomplishes the function of the brief summary is the "initial teaching"; the teaching that accomplishes the function of expansion (*vipañcana*) is the "middle teaching"; and the teaching that accomplishes the function of detailed exposition (*vitthāraṇā*) is the "concluding teaching."
“Which person does the Dhamma-Vinaya—consisting of the meaning of the scriptures—guide when it is being summarized and recited?
Which person does the Dhamma-Vinaya—consisting of the meaning of the scriptures—guide when it is being analyzed and demonstrated?
Which person does the Dhamma-Vinaya—consisting of the meaning of the scriptures—guide when it is being expanded and explained?”
Because it was necessary to ask, "What is the trainer?", he said, "This is that Dhamma and Vinaya," and so forth. In the Commentary, however, it is stated:

"Having thus shown the function of the six phrasing-terms beginning with 'he makes known by means of syllables,' he now says, 'This is that Dhamma and Vinaya,' etc., in order to show the function of the meaning-terms."

In this context, when it is being condensed and recited—consisting of the recitation, mastery, and meaning of the teaching—this Dhamma-Vinaya disciplines the person who gains knowledge through condensation (*ugghaṭitaññu*).

Because it disciplines that person who gains knowledge through condensation, they call this Vinaya—which is being condensed and recited, consisting of the recitation, mastery, and meaning—"beautiful in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*). When it is being expanded and explained...

This Dhamma and Vinaya, which consists of the meaning of the exposition and the textual tradition (*pariyatti*), disciplines the person who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññu*);

because it disciplines such a person by means of that detailed exposition, the Vinaya—which is being detailed and demonstrated as consisting of the meaning of the exposition and the textual tradition—is called "beautiful in the middle.
Being expanded and further demonstrated, it consists of the meaning of the counter-exposition and the textual tradition.
Thus, this Dhamma-Vinaya guides the person who is to be guided and produces guidance;

because it guides the person to be guided, the Vinaya—which is being expanded and explained as the meaning of the explanatory scripture (*paṭiniddesapariyatti*)—is called "beautiful in its conclusion.
This should be understood as the meaning of the connection.
Alternatively, by the passage beginning with “he makes known by means of syllables,” the function of the six terms has been shown; in that case, the meaning (*attha*) would be devoid of function.
Yet, in the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*), the meaning itself must indeed possess function. Bearing this objection in mind, he says:
“This is the Dhamma and Vinaya,” and so forth. By this, it is shown that the meaning itself, in the primary sense, accomplishes the task of disciplining those who are to be trained.
However, it is shown that the word "attha" (meaning) accomplishes the task of training the three types of those to be trained through the metaphorical application of its location.
But because there is no foundation for the penetration of truth for one who takes words as the ultimate, such a person is not mentioned here.

Alternatively, by the inclusion of the "learner" (sekha), the inclusion of the "ordinary person of good quality" (kalyāṇaputhujjana) should be understood; and by the inclusion of the "one to be guided" (neyya), the inclusion of the person who takes words as the ultimate should also be understood.
In phrases such as *akkharehi*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*), not in the sense of cause (*hetvatthe*).
For syllables and so forth are indeed the means for the purpose of memorizing and so on; it is not the case that syllables and so forth are the means for the purpose of memorizing and so on.

Therefore, as in the expression "he dwells because of food" (*annena vasati*), the causal sense should not be understood here. For in that [latter] case, he dwells because of the cause that is food, and [one eats] food because of the cause that is dwelling.
“Obtained” (*laddha*) refers to the fruit of the action of dwelling, grasped by way of its being the cause for the action of dwelling.
This same method applies to such expressions as “he dwells because of a request” (*ajjhesanena vasati*). Therefore it was said: “And that for the sake of which there is an action, that is the cause.

In this context, “for the sake of which” (*yadatthā*) means that food and so forth are the purpose (*attha*) of that action of dwelling and so on; thus it is “that for the sake of which,” namely the action of dwelling and so forth. That [purpose], such as food and so forth—
The meaning should be understood as follows: the purpose is the cause for the activity of wearing it and so forth.

10. Having shown the threefold excellence—consisting of the perfection of twelve words—in the discourse introduced with "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma" by means of the passage beginning "Therein, immeasurable are the words," he now [explains] by way of the division into six-word phrases and six-syllable phrases.
Demonstrating the excellence of meaning, phrasing, and word-arrangement—what is termed "success"—he said, "In this regard, six phrases are the meaning," and so forth.

Alternatively, in accordance with what was stated as "twelve phrases constitute a discourse" (*sutta*), he demonstrated that the Pāḷi text announced by the words "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma" possesses twelve phrases through the passage beginning with "In this regard, immeasurable... and so on, up to "beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle..."
Having shown the threefold excellence of that text by means of the passage beginning with “In this regard,
the Blessed One [taught] by means of syllables,” which corresponds to what was stated as “good in the end,” he now shows the perfection of its six aspects— meaning, phrasing, syllables, and words—
in order to correspond to what was stated as “possessing meaning, possessing phrasing, entirely complete, and perfectly pure. In this regard, the six aspects are:

The passage beginning with “attho” and so forth has been stated. Therein, “tattha” (therein) refers to this scripture (*pāḷi*)—which is comprised of the teaching, the sustenance, and the object—which possesses six aspects of meaning (*attha*).
What are the six aspects? They are: announcing (*saṅkāsanā*), disclosing (*pakāsanā*), unveiling (*vivaraṇā*), analyzing (*vibhajanā*), making plain (*uttānīkammaṃ*), and defining (*paññatti*).
Because it has meaning, it is “sātthaṃ” (possessing meaning). Therein, “tattha” refers to this [scripture] which is comprised of the teaching, the sustenance, and the object.

In the Pāli, there are six categories of expression (*byañjana*). What are the six categories? They are: syllable (*akkhara*), phrase (*pada*), expression (*byañjana*), form (*ākāra*), language (*nirutti*), and exposition (*niddesa*).
These are the six categories. The construction should be made thus: "that which has expression is 'with expression' (*sabyañjana*).
"By that" means by way of that Pāli being endowed with the three kinds of excellence, and by way of its being endowed with the eight types of excellent phrases and expressions.
The meaning is: “Bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been taught by me... [as before] ...it is pure,” so said the Blessed One.
Since the word *kevala* denotes meanings such as "entire" and so forth, in order to specify the intended sense, it is said:
“*Kevala* means supramundane (*lokuttara*), not mixed with mundane (*lokiya*) phenomena. Regarding *paripuṇṇa*, even a single [factor] in the intended sense...

It is "complete" (*paripuṇṇa*) because there is no deficiency in meaning, and not even a single word among the expressive terms is superfluous or devoid of meaning; thus it is "without deficiency" (*anūna*) and "without excess" (*anatireka*).

It is "pure" (*parisuddha*): either pure because it is free from faults of expression and faults of meaning, or pure and radiant because it is the locus where the distinguished superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), purified of the stains of passion and so forth, are manifested.
It is "spotless" (*nimmala*) because the stain has departed from this Dhamma.

Or, it is "purified" (*pariyodāta*) because it is completely white (*odāta*), being free from all stains—whether through the absence of faults such as verbal corruption or through the absence of [defilements] such as lust.
It is "established" (*upaṭṭhita*); it is established because all excellences stand upon it, just as in the term "well-trodden" (*padakkanta*). A well-trodden place is what is meant by "well-trodden."

They are called *visesā* (distinguishing qualities) because they distinguish one from human states (*manussadhammehi*). All distinguishing qualities are "all-distinguishing qualities" (*sabbavisesā*); alternatively, they are "all-distinguishing qualities" because they distinguish [one] from everything else;
these are the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhammā*). The construction is: "established in those all-distinguishing qualities.

"This" refers to the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*), which comprises the three trainings. The "footprint of the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One" (*tathāgatapada*) is the footprint of the Tathāgata.
And they tread upon the seizing of the defilements either by way of practice or by way of teaching. It is also said and proclaimed that it is a place traversed after having been covered over;
likewise, it is said and proclaimed that it has been frequented and resorted to by the Tathāgata through the cultivation of his range or through the cultivation of meditation.
It has been trampled by the Tathāgata with the treads of his great thunderbolt-like knowledge and omniscience.

It is also called "the place of striving" (*ārañjitaṭṭhāna*); therefore, because it can be described as having the nature of the Tathāgata’s footprint and so forth, this holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*) is recognized.
"Holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means the conduct (*cariya*) of the Blessed One, who is the Supreme Being (*brahma*) among all beings;
or, the conduct that is supreme (*brahma*) and most excellent is the holy life. "Is recognized" (*paññāyati*) should be understood to mean that it is known in the manner already stated.
“Since it must be said: ‘How shall we know, free from doubt, that this compendium of the three trainings— the dispensation—
is the state of being the Tathāgata’s footprint, the state of being the Tathāgata’s footprint, the state of being frequented by the Tathāgata,
the state of being cherished by the Tathāgata, and the state of being made known by him in those various ways?’— therefore he said:”
The passage beginning with “the Blessed One” was spoken; it means that you should understand, free from doubt, by means of the words spoken by the Blessed One which illuminate that very state.
If the Blessed One summarizes by means of syllables and phrases, and elaborates by means of phonemes and modes, [you should understand].

He expands [the teaching] by means of definitions (*nirutti*) and explanations (*niddesa*). If this were so, there would be no need for the "nutriment of the teaching" (*desanāhāra*) composed by the Teacher;
for the meaning of the Blessed One’s very teaching would be established even without the nutriment of the teaching.
Bearing in mind such an objection, he asks, “For whom is this teaching of the Dhamma? and answers, “For yogis. Therein, “for yogis” means:
"Yogins" are those who apply themselves to the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths; [the term refers to] "of those yogins.

It should be understood that because this discourse of the Blessed One—described in the manner stated—is adorned by this "nutriment of the teaching" composed by me, it accomplishes the functions such as comprehension, and thus the nutriment of the teaching is indeed purposeful for yogins.
[This concludes the section on] the state of the nutriment of the teaching as being the gratification and so forth of the nutriment of the teaching.
Because it must be said, "By what means are we to know and believe this?", it was stated:

"Therefore the Venerable One... [etc. ...the Mode of Teaching. In that context, by that statement which the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke—namely, "The Mode of Teaching consists in the gratification, the danger, and so forth"—you [should understand] through that speech the nature of the Mode of Teaching as consisting in the gratification, danger, and so forth, for yogis.
"It must be known and it must be believed" is what is meant.
However, since one might ask, "Is the nutriment of teaching (desanāhāra) complete at this point, or is there no other [nutriment] assigned?", it is said, "The nutriment of teaching is assigned.
In that regard, in whichever teaching the gratification and so forth have been determined by whichever nutriment of teaching—
In this teaching, the meaning should be understood as follows: that "nutriment of teaching" has been extracted and applied.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Exposition) composed in accordance with the powers of beings, within the *Vibhaṅga* of the Nutriments of Teaching.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
2. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Investigation (Vicayahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā) 11.

By whichever specific mode of commentary, namely the analysis of the Mode of Teaching (*desanāhāra*), the Teacher [has explained] the meanings of the Sutta such as gratification (*assāda*) and so forth...

The analysis of the modes of teaching (*desanāhāra*), which constitutes a specific form of commentary, has been fully explained. Since it must be asked, "What is the mode of investigation (*vicayahāra*)?", the passage beginning with "In this regard, what is the mode of investigation?
was stated. Therein, the phrase "in those" (*tattha*) refers to those sixteen modes of teaching, such as the modes of teaching already specified;
"what specific form of commentary is the mode of investigation? refers to the analysis of the mode of investigation (*vicayahāravibhaṅga*).

“Name,” he asks. The construction is as follows: “This specific commentary on the explanatory verse beginning with ‘That which was asked and answered,’ now being spoken by me, is called the ‘Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Investigation’ (vicayahāra-vibhaṅga).
By the phrase “What does this mode of conveying investigation investigate? one should investigate that very object of investigation which is to be investigated by means of this investigation.

Because he asks [this question], it is said, "He investigates the word; he investigates the problem," and so forth, in order to show that the object of investigation must be determined and demonstrated separately.
By stating, "What does he investigate? He investigates the word," rather than saying, "What is investigation?
It is the investigation of words," he demonstrates that the term *vicaya* (investigation) has the sense of an agent-noun (*kattusādhana*). In that context, the word...

"Discerns" means that he discerns every word of the ninefold Sutta, from the beginning up to the conclusion, by way of nouns and so forth, generic terms and so forth, feminine gender and so forth, words ending in long vowels and so forth, nominative case endings and so forth, and singular numbers and so forth.

"He discerns the question" means that he discerns it by way of the seven types of questions—such as those for the revelation of the unseen—and by way of their bases, such as the sevenfold basis of beings, their objects, such as conventional reality, and their temporal scope, such as the past.
"He discerns the answer" means [he discerns] the categorical answer and so forth, and the answer requiring further elaboration and so forth.
He investigates by way of answering questions with a superior answer (*sauttarabyākaraṇa*), answering questions with a worldly answer (*lokiyabyākaraṇa*), and so forth.

"He investigates the sequence" means he investigates by correlating what follows with what precedes. "He investigates the gratification" means he investigates by way of the craving that constitutes gratification, the pleasure that is to be gratified, and so forth.

"He investigates the danger" means [he investigates] by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*), and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*).
Or he investigates by way of being subject to defilement, such as the experience of the undesirable, having a beginning and an end, and so forth.

"He investigates the escape" means he investigates it either by way of the Path, or by way of Nibbāna, or by way of the Path’s coming-to-be, or by way of the synonyms for Nibbāna such as the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).
"He investigates the fruit" means [he investigates it] by way of the absence of going to a miserable destination through the practice of Dharma, or by way of crossing over death, and so forth.
He discerns the fruit of the teaching, and by means of the teaching, he discerns the fruit of conduct.

"He discerns the means" means that he discerns the means for purification either through the practice of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, or through the knowledge of disenchantment and so forth, or by way of faith and conviction.
"He discerns the command" means that he discerns it either by way of the command to avoid evil, or by way of the command to regard the world as empty.
"He investigates the *anugīti*" means he investigates a corresponding song either by way of the songs already stated as *anugītis* or by way of the songs currently being spoken of as *anugītis*.
"He investigates all nine types of discourses" means he investigates the nine discourses— beginning with the *sutta*, *geyya*, and so forth—

either by way of direct statements, by way of sequential connections, by way of statements of explicit meaning (*nītattha*), by way of statements of implicit meaning (*neyyattha*), or by way of the sections dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so on.
Although the analysis of words (*padavicaya*) was explained first, because the Sutta must be analyzed word by word, the analysis of words is too burdensome and not easy;
therefore, setting that aside for now, he spoke the passage beginning with "In what way might it be? while analyzing the analysis of questions and answers (*pañhāvicaya-vissajjanavicaya*).
Therein, "In what way might it be" (*yathā kiṃ bhavē*) refers to the manner in which that analysis of questions [is conducted].
The meaning should be understood as follows: "It should be set forth" means that one should consider what kind of categories that [exposition] might be.
Just as the Venerable Ajita asks the Blessed One a question in the *Pārāyana* by way of a particular manner, so too should the investigation of the question be set forth by that same manner;
this is the meaning. In this context, "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment. "Ajita" refers to those who were the attendants of the brahmin Bāvari.
Ajita was one of the sixteen [questioners]. Regarding the term *pārāyana*: it is called *pārāyana* because by means of it one goes to or reaches the further shore (*pāra*), which is Nibbāna;
this is a designation for the sixteen discourses beginning with the Ajita Sutta.
“By what, indeed, is the world shut off? (Thus spoke the Venerable Ajita.)
“By what does it not shine?
What do you say is its defilement?
What is its great fear?”—with this verse, the Venerable Ajita asked: “By what phenomenon is the world, censured by the Noble Ones, shrouded and concealed?”
He asks: "For what reason does the world as previously described not shine forth? What is the defilement of that aforementioned world?
You say 'what,' and you say 'what is the great fear' for that aforementioned world? This is the meaning.
Thus, by this classification, these four lines of verse have been asked—that is, they were spoken by way of inquiry.
Or, while they may be illuminators of the meaning asked about, that [section] is nevertheless considered "one question" by way of its primary effort;

for although it should be called fourfold because it proceeds by way of asking four phrases, it is called "one question" because there exists only one intended meaning to be known. He stated the reason because he was told, "State the reason."

“‘Having a single subject-matter’ means this: although four matters—namely, warding off, clearing away, anointing, and great fear—are included in the question, it should be understood that because only one expressed meaning is grasped, it is taken as ‘one question’ by way of its primary significance.
[The interlocutor asks: “How are we to believe that there is a grasping of a single subject-matter?”

Because it is something that ought to be said, it is stated: "For thus he spoke. Thus, since the Blessed One spoke by means of grasping a single subject matter alone, it follows that you should have faith in this grasping of a single subject matter.
By the question, "By what is the world enveloped?", he asks about the concealment with reference to the world (*lokādhiṭṭhāna*), not with reference to various phenomena (*nānādhammādhiṭṭhāna*).
By the phrase “Why does it not shine?”, he asks about the non-shining of the world itself, not of phenomena that possess diverse intrinsic natures.
By the phrase “What do you say is its defilement?”, he asks about the defilement of the world itself, not of phenomena that possess diverse intrinsic natures.
By the phrase “What is its great fear?”, he asks about the great fear of that very world, not of phenomena that possess diverse intrinsic natures.

Therefore, the intention is that the question, “By what is the world shut in? and so forth, should be investigated as appropriate according to the following categories: among questions based on a single basis (*ekādhiṭṭhāna*) and those based on multiple bases (*nānādhiṭṭhāna*), it is one based on a single basis;

among those based on phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*) and those based on beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*), it is one based on beings; and among those that reveal the unseen (*adiṭṭhajotanā*) and so forth, it is a question that reveals the unseen, and so on.
This is because it must be stated that “the world which is taken as the ‘basis’ of the question is threefold. Regarding the word “world” (*loko*):
The passage beginning with “threefold” has been stated. Therein, it is “threefold” because this world consists of three modes.

A being of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-satta*) is defiled by means of passion and so forth, thus it is a “defilement” (*kilesa*); and since it is both a defilement and a world, it is the “world of defilement” (*kilesaloka*), namely, the being of the sense-sphere. For that [being] is called the “world of defilement” due to its abundance of defilements such as passion.
It exists through meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and insights (*buddhi*), thus it is “existence” (*bhava*). Existence...

And that world is the "existence-world" (*bhavaloka*), which refers to a being of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). For such a being exists by means of the notions of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and so forth.

One who is endowed with faculties (*indriya*) is called "facultied" (*indriya*); and that which is both facultied and a world is the "faculty-world" (*indriyaloka*), referring to a being of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).

For such a being possesses pure faculties due to an abundance of imperturbable concentration (*āneñjasamādhi*); thus, the designation "world" is applied by way of phenomena included within the mundane realm.
[The noble ones] have not been included because they are those who cause [the teaching] to proceed;
therefore, the teacher has analyzed the method of investigating the inquiry in the verse beginning with “By what is the world shut in?,” and this has been understood by us.
Since it must be asked, “In what [section] is the method of investigating the response analyzed?”—therein...
The passage beginning with “the answer” has been stated. Therein, “in that [context]” refers to that question, “By what indeed is the world enveloped?
and so forth—[to which the Blessed One replied]: “The world is enveloped by ignorance, O Ajita;
through craving and negligence it does not shine forth.”
"I call craving the defilement; suffering is its great terror"—this verse should be understood as the answer.

In this context, "the world is shrouded by ignorance" refers to [ignorance] being endowed with four factors, by way of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a dense forest thicket, the covering of a mass of clouds, and the middle of the night.

The world of beings is shrouded and concealed by ignorance (*avijjā*), which has the characteristic of obscuring the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), just as a multitude of chariots and other objects are hidden by darkness. Addressing him with the word "Ajita," the Blessed One said:
"Because of doubt (*vicikicchā*), which is a cause for negligence, the aforementioned world does not shine forth. [And] "craving" (*jappa*) refers to the thirst for the aforementioned world.

“I say it is ‘smeared with’,” said the Blessed One; the meaning is that the Blessed One said to Ajita, “I say suffering—the round of suffering beginning with birth—is the ‘great terror’ for this world as previously described.
Because it was necessary to ask, “How should one analyze this answer? [the text] says, “These four terms,” and so forth.
It has been stated. Therein, "these four phrases" refers to the verses spoken in the interrogative verse beginning with, "By what, indeed, is the world shut in?
They are answered by these four phrases spoken in the responsive verse beginning with, "The world is shut in by ignorance.
How so? The first phrase [is answered] by the first phrase, the second phrase...
The third term was answered by the second term, and the fourth term was answered by the third term.
In the first question, "By what is the world enveloped?", the first answer given was, "The world is enveloped by ignorance" (*avijjā*);
it was not stated in reverse order. Ignorance is the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*); therefore, the world would be one that does not know through ignorance.
"How is it covered so that it may be believed? To this he said: "The world is covered by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Considering the objection that, if this were so, the answer should have been "the world is covered by ignorance as a hindrance," he stated: "For all beings are hindered by ignorance. [To the question:
"By what statement can the fact that all beings are hindered by ignorance be believed?"
Because it ought to be stated, the passage beginning with “As the Blessed One said” was spoken.

“Monks, for all beings, for all living creatures, for all that have come to be, I declare, by way of analysis, there is only one hindrance, namely ignorance (*avijjā*). For all beings are hindered by ignorance. Of all ignorance, monks...”
“By means of cessation, fading away, and relinquishment, there is no hindrance for beings”—
this is the statement which the Blessed One spoke in such a way and by such a manner; by that statement thus spoken,
you should have faith in the state of being hindered by ignorance for all beings.
Considering the objection that the phrase “The world is enveloped by ignorance” (*avijjāya nivuto loko*) might not serve as a reply to the first question, “By what is the world enveloped?
(*kenassu nivuto loko*), but might also serve as a reply to the second question, “Why does it not shine forth?

(*kenassu nappakāsatī*), the words beginning with “And by that” (*tena cā*) were stated. In this context, by that phrase “The world is enveloped by ignorance,” [the answer to] “By what... [is provided].
The answer to the first phrase, “The world is enveloped,” is both appropriate and more appropriate;
because it is more appropriate, my intention is that the answer to the question “By what is the world enveloped? must indeed be stated as “The world is enveloped by ignorance.
As for the question “Why does it not shine forth?”, the answer is: “Because of craving and negligence it does not shine forth.”
It should be explained that because it proceeds through seclusion and due to negligence, the world does not shine forth—this is the meaning.
The answer, “The world is shrouded by the hindrance of ignorance; therefore the world does not shine forth,” must be provided.

Since it must be stated, “How is the answer ‘through seclusion and negligence the world does not shine forth’ given? the passage beginning with “the person who” is spoken. Therein, “whoever is an ordinary person (puthujjana)”—
The person is shrouded by the hindrance of ignorance; that person, being an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*), is distracted by distraction.
Since it must be asked, "What is the name of this distraction by which he is distracted?", it is said: "Distraction is called doubt (*vicikicchā*).
Since it must be stated, "Why does he not clarify [the truth] by means of that?", it is said: "He, being doubtful," and so forth.
It has been said: that person, being an ordinary worldling who doubts because of that [lack of faith], does not have conviction in what ought to be believed.
Not having conviction in what ought to be believed, he does not initiate the energy that should be initiated for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the realization of wholesome states.
Not initiating it, that person is devoted to negligence in this world.
Regarding the phrase "he dwells": a person who dwells in negligence, being negligent, does not produce the bright qualities (*sukka-dhamma*).
For that person who does not produce them, those bright qualities—remaining unproduced—do not shine forth; they do not proceed by way of manifestation.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that the answer should be given thus: "Because of separation and negligence, the world does not shine forth."

Because it must be asked, “By what word of ours can the fact that such bright qualities (*sukkadhamma*) are not manifested be believed? the passage beginning with “As the Blessed One said” was stated. Therein:
“The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himālaya mountain;
The non-virtuous are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.”
“They shine forth with those virtues, and by means of their renown and fame.”—
In whatever manner and by whatever mode of non-elucidation the Blessed One spoke this recitation of the verse, by that very recitation spoken in such a mode of non-elucidation,
you [should understand] the state of non-elucidation of the bright qualities (*sukkadhamma*) of such a person.
It must indeed be believed; therefore, the intention is that the answer should be given thus: "Because of doubt and negligence, the world does not shine.

As for the meaning of the verse: just as Mount Himavanta, though situated at a distance, appears as if manifest even to people with eyes who are themselves far away, so too do virtuous persons (sappurisa), even when standing at a distance, [shine] by virtue of their qualities and their fame.
They shine forth for the wise who stand far removed from fame, enjoyments, and retinues that proceed by way of [worldly] qualities;
just as arrows shot at night are not seen, so too in this world of beings, the unvirtuous are not seen as they dwell under the influence of sensual indulgence and negligence.
To show that those who are virtuous shine forth, it is said that those virtuous ones shine forth by way of their qualities.
It is said, “They shine by means of their qualities. Since qualities are born within [the person], one might ask, “How do they shine by means of qualities?

To answer this, it is said, “By means of fame and renown. Persons who shine by means of fame that proceeds from the power of their qualities, and by means of renown that proceeds from the power of their qualities, are to be described as “shining by means of their qualities.”
If [the world] does not shine forth due to the influence of seclusion and negligence, then the world remains shrouded;
therefore, considering that an answer must be given even for the first phrase, the words beginning with "And by that" (*tena ca*) were spoken.

Therein, "by that" refers to the phrase "it does not shine forth due to seclusion and negligence," which serves as the answer to the second phrase, "By what indeed does it not shine forth? (*kenassu nappakāsatī*).
The meaning is that the answer is both appropriate and more appropriately so. "By the word" means the answer is given by way of the meaning of the word (*padattha*).
"Of the word" should be understood as "of the meaning of the word" or "of that which is to be asked. This same method applies below and above.
Regarding the question, "What do you say is its defilement? the answer, "I say craving is its defilement," was given by Ajita.
[The words] are to be understood. Since it must be asked, "What is called 'craving' (jappā)?", it is said:
"Craving is called thirst (taṇhā). The construction is: "How is it known that this thirst smears over the world? Therefore it is said, "As the Blessed One has said," and so forth.
Therein, "as" (yathā) means by which manner of smearing—that is, by way of the state of being smeared by craving—...
“The lustful does not know the goal; the lustful does not see the Dhamma.
It is blind darkness then, when lust overcomes a man”—this is the verse spoken by the Blessed One.
The intention is that, as expressed by that verse through its quality of "smeared-ness" (*abhilepana*), it is understood that craving (*taṇhā*) smears the world.
In this verse: "one who lusts" (*rajati*) is *ratta*, meaning a being possessed of lust.
"Depending on a cause, the fruit arises"—this is the meaning; thus it is called "fruit" (*phala*). That which bears the fruit is the cause, and that cause is what is called "dhamma.

"Darkness" (*andhakāra*) means "blind" (*andha*). "When" (*yamhi*) refers to at which time. For "when" (*yamhi*) is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative. At which time lust [overcomes] a man...
The construction is as follows: "At that time, it becomes blind darkness, a blinding gloom," for it overcomes and masters one who possesses passion (*rāga*).
Alternatively, because passion overcomes a person, therefore at that time there is blind darkness;
or, for whichever person passion overcomes, for that person there is blind darkness at that time; or, passion overcomes—that is, masters—whichever person.
It brings about endurance and overcoming; or the construction may be: "that endurance and overcoming becomes blind, blinding darkness, and obscurity.
Since it must be asked, "If one who is lustful does not know what is beneficial and so forth, how then can craving be the 'smearing'?", it is said:
"That is craving," and so on. In that context, for one who possesses craving—who is full of attachment and full of clinging toward sense objects—
For an individual, this craving (taṇhā), by way of such manifold attachments, becomes an intense longing that persists as an obsession.
Having considered this, for this reason, the world of beings there is, as it were, smeared and defiled by some kind of glue;
thus the construction is: it is called "smeared by the ointment of longing" (jappābhilepana). [The verse continues: "The ointment of longing, even for one who does not reveal..."
Because it serves as the reason, one must say that there could also be a response to the meaning of the second phrase, "By what, indeed, would it not shine?
For this reason, the words beginning with "And by that" were spoken.
Regarding the fourth question, "What is the great fear for that world?", [the answer is]: "Suffering is the great fear for this world."
“This is the answer,” this is how it should be understood by Ajita. It is called *bhaya* (fear) because the world fears it; great fear is *mahabbhaya*.
Because it was asked, “How many kinds of suffering are there? it was stated, “Suffering is twofold,” and so forth.
That which has two modes (*vidhā*) of suffering is “twofold” (*duvidha*). Because it was asked, “What is the twofold suffering? [the following is stated].
It was stated: “Both bodily and mental. Since it must be asked, “Which is bodily? Which is mental? it was stated:
“That which is bodily is suffering (*dukkha*); that which is mental is grief (*domanassa*).
Disease and so forth, as well as weapons and other undesirable forms, may constitute a great terror for the world of beings; [the text asks]: “How is suffering a great terror?”
Because it must be said that "one should have faith," the passage beginning with "All beings" was spoken.
In this context, all beings are terrified by the aforementioned suffering;
there is no other fear for beings equal to suffering, nor how could there be a fear greater than suffering? Since there is none, therefore, from suffering...
The intention is that the statement, “Suffering is the great terror of the world,” should be believed because there is no other fear.
By the words beginning with “All beings,” he shows that undesirable things such as disease, weapons, and so forth, are merely the roots of suffering.

Suffering is twofold—bodily and mental—and it is simply painful feeling; this being so, how could the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*) constitute a great terror?
Because it must be said, "one should not fall [into such a state]," the passage beginning "the three kinds of suffering" was stated.
Since it must be asked, "Do the three kinds of suffering arise for all beings at all times, or do they sometimes not arise for anyone?
the passage beginning "In this regard, the world... was stated. Therein, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to within those three kinds of suffering. "The world" (*loko*)...
The world of beings is endowed with wealth and free from illness. From time to time, occasionally, it is liberated from the suffering of the nature of pain rooted in self-aggression;
from time to time, it is liberated from the suffering of the nature of pain rooted in aggression by others.
Likewise, from time to time, occasionally, the long-lived world is liberated from the suffering of change: "By what..."
Because it was to be asked, "By what cause is one liberated?", the phrase beginning with "For what reason? was spoken to set aside the question and demonstrate the cause.

In the world of beings, some are free from illness; because they possess wealth and are free from illness, they are liberated from the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*), especially those beings of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*). Some are also long-lived.
Because they are long-lived, they are liberated from the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-dukkhatā*);
specifically, beings of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*) are liberated because those beings frequently attain the meditative absorption of equanimity (*upekkhā-samāpatti*).
Their liberation from those types of suffering is not absolute; therefore, because they have not transcended them, it is not absolute.

"Release" has been spoken of by you and is known to us; however, because it must be asked, "Which one is absolute release?", the passage beginning with "But because of the suffering inherent in formations (saṅkhāradukkhatā)" was stated.
In that context, "because of the suffering inherent in formations" means that even painful feeling, being conditioned, is included within formations;
thus, the meaning should be understood as "due to such suffering inherent in formations. "The world" (loka) refers to—

An *arahant*. "Grasping" (*upādi*) refers to the pentad of aggregates consisting of the fourfold aggregate of fruition (*vipākakkhandhacatukkaka*) and the matter produced by past karma (*katattārūpa*).

That which is grasped is itself "residue of grasping" (*upādisesa*); this refers to the pentad of aggregates. Since that [pentad] does not exist for this element of Nibbāna, it is "without residue of grasping" (*anupādisesā*).

Having become the element of Nibbāna without residue of grasping within the element of Nibbāna without residue of grasping, one is liberated; [this is used] in the sense of a characteristic of having reached such a state.

And this is the exposition of the instrument (*karaṇaniddesa*). By the term "the element of Nibbāna" (*nibbānadhātu*), only the extinction (*nibbāyana*) of the pentad of aggregates is intended, not the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhatadhātu*).

Therefore, because it encompasses the entire world by virtue of pervading the whole world through the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*), the entire world is suffering on account of that aforementioned suffering inherent in formations; thus, having established this by way of the suffering inherent in formations...
Because the entire world is characterized by suffering, the Blessed One said, "Suffering is its great terror.
Since it is stated that "craving has feeling as its condition," there might be an apprehension that the answer to the third phrase, "What is its plaster?
could also be provided by the expression "suffering is its great terror"; therefore, [the author] says, "And by that, [there is no answer] to the fourth phrase..."

It was said: "The answer is appropriate. Since it must be asked, "By what means is the state of being more appropriately matched between the question and the answer to be known according to their sequence?

it was therefore stated: "For that reason, the Blessed One said... and so forth. Because the question and answer are more appropriately matched according to their sequence, the Blessed One—who knows what is more appropriately matched—spoke the words beginning with "The world is shrouded by ignorance"; therefore, this is the state of being more appropriately matched.
"You must understand this. And here, by one who does not know the hindrances and so forth of the world, and by one who has become familiar with the doctrines of the heterodox sects and other systems,
and who has fallen into doubt regarding both those other systems and the hindrances and so forth, [the teaching is given] solely by way of a reference to a sentient being (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*).

Because it is something that ought to be asked about, and because it must be answered exclusively from the standpoint of a sentient being (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*), it should be understood that this question is formulated from the standpoint of a sentient being.

Furthermore, this question is fourfold, corresponding to the fourfold nature of the subject matter—the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth—to be answered: for the sake of one who does not know, in order to bring about knowledge;
and for the sake of one who has arisen doubt, in order to dispel that doubt. Now, as for the hindrances and so forth...
Since the world is mentioned in the verse as the supporting basis for sense objects, it is said that "one question has been shown. This is the analysis of the question here;

however, the analysis of the answer should be understood according to the method stated in the analysis of the question, beginning with: "The answer that demonstrates what was not seen, the answer that cuts off doubt," and so forth.
The analysis of questions and answers based on a single basis has been explained by the teachers and is known to us.
However, as for the analysis of questions and answers based on multiple bases—that analysis which is worthy of being distinguished—how can that analysis be understood by us?
Therefore, it must be said: "For the sake of our understanding, please analyze that analysis [concerning] the question based on multiple bases. Thus, the question based on multiple bases.
Having brought him out, [the Blessed One] spoke thus to show him:
“The streams flow everywhere,” said the Venerable Ajita,
“what is the damming of these streams?”
"Tell me of the restraint of the streams; by what are the streams blocked?"—thus he spoke this verse.
First, the meaning of the verse should be understood. "Flow" means they stream forth; the sense is that they proceed.
"Everywhere" refers to all bases such as visible forms (*rūpa*), etc., which serve as the objects of craving and the rest. "Streams" refers to craving, covetousness, ill-will, and so forth.
"Sotas. Thus spoke the Venerable Ajita. "Of streams" means of the streams of craving, covetousness, ill-will, and so forth.
"What is the dam? means what kind of class of phenomena would be an obstruction, and what kind of class of phenomena would be a protection?
"Tell me the restraint of the streams" means the restraint, the obstruction, of the streams of craving, covetousness, ill-will, and so forth.
"Please tell us this collection of Dhamma for the benefit and welfare of all beings:
'By what are the streams closed?'—this asks by what abandoning-dhamma the streams of craving, covetousness, ill-will, and so forth, are closed by the wise; thus these questions were asked.
Regarding the verse "They flow... [and] are closed," which was spoken by way of response to those questions, how many words does it contain?
Because it must be asked, "How many questions were asked? it is said: "These four phrases were asked;

they constitute two questions. Since it might be argued, "If this verse, which proceeds by way of questioning, consisted of four phrases, then in that case there would also be four kinds of questions; why then are 'two' mentioned?", it is asked: "Why?"
"For these have been asked by means of many designations," it is said. These meanings taken up by this verse have been asked by means of many designations.

This is what is meant: "The two meanings—namely, mindfulness, which is reckoned as restraint, and wisdom, which is the cause for closing—that proceed based upon many words such as 'they flow'... 'they are closed'—these very two meanings are what have been asked."
"Therefore, two questions were stated according to their meaning.

Since it must be explained how the question has a twofold objective range, the passage beginning with "Of one who has thus attained" was stated in order to clarify that twofold objective range of the question.
Therein, "of one who has thus attained" refers to [one affected by] calamities known as the loss of relatives and so forth, which serve as causes for miserable rebirths.
Or, whether through calamities such as the slaughter of living beings, this world of sentient beings has equally or entirely been overtaken and overwhelmed;
thus, for one who is so overwhelmed or beset.

"Thus defiled" means that this world of sentient beings is defiled by the ten bases of defilement occurring through such things as the loss of relatives or the slaughter of living beings; thus, for one who is so defiled.

"And for the world" means: what kind of state of phenomena (dhammajāta) could there be that constitutes the purification or emergence of the world for one who has attained [meditative absorption] and has transcended it?

Thus, "for this is what was said in the *Ajita-sutta* regarding the truth"—this is the meaning in detail; the intention is that it should be understood that the scope of the question concerns two types of objects.
Because it must be asked, "Do the streams flow everywhere for everyone in the world, or only for some?", it is said:
"The streams flow everywhere; they flow for one who is not concentrated, who is full of covetousness, ill will, and negligence.
In this context, it refers specifically to one whose mind is distracted among various objects such as forms and so forth, due to being full of covetousness, ill will, and negligence.
The streams flow and proceed; the intended meaning should be understood as: [they do not flow] for one who is concentrated and free from covetousness, ill will, and negligence.

Because it must be explained what covetousness is, what ill will is, and what negligence is, it is said: "In that regard, whatever is covetousness," and so forth. Therein, "in that regard" (tattha) means among those [states], namely covetousness, ill will, and negligence. Whatever is covetousness...
This is greed (*lobha*), not merely covetousness; and greed is an unwholesome root (*akusalamūla*), not merely the state of being greedy.
That which is ill-will (*byāpāda*) is hatred (*dosa*), not merely the state of being malicious; and hatred is an unwholesome root, not merely the state of being corrupt.
That which is negligence (*pamāda*) is delusion (*moha*), not merely the lapse of mindfulness; and delusion is an unwholesome root, not merely the state of being bewildered. Thus, by this...

Because greed and the rest are unwholesome roots in the manner described, for one who is full of greed, ill-will, and negligence, and is unconcentrated, craving flows toward the six bases beginning with visible forms.
Since it must be stated, "Of how many kinds is that craving?", it is said: "Craving for forms... [and so on] ...craving for mental phenomena. "Of the six..."

Because it must be said, "By what statement should we believe [the existence] of craving for forms and so forth in the six bases of form and so on?", the passage beginning with "As the Blessed One said" was stated.
By the statement that the Blessed One spoke in such a way—that is, by the manner in which he said, "And it flows, monks... it strikes back"—according to the method thus described:

The intention is: "It must be believed by you. And here, because the eye and so forth function as the doors for the six streams—namely, craving for forms and the rest—the Blessed One spoke of the eye and so forth as if they themselves were flowing, by way of a metaphorical designation based on their support.
"Thus" means: in the manner thus described, it flows—that is, it proceeds—from all [the streams] and from every door, such as the eye and so forth.
The meaning is that it "flows" (*savati*)—that is, it proceeds—in every way (*sabbathā*), by way of craving, wrong adherence, arrogance, and so forth.

Because it must be stated, "Why does it flow and proceed from every door such as the eye, and how is the state of flowing to be understood as being in every way, by way of craving, wrong adherence, arrogance, and so forth?", the passage beginning with "Therefore he said" (*tenāha*) was spoken.
Therein, "therefore" (*tena*) refers to one who is not concentrated (*asamāhitassa*).

Because covetousness, ill will, and so forth proceed by way of craving and the like—arising from the doors of the eye and so on through the modes of yearning, wrong adherence, and inflation—the Blessed One, who knows their occurrence, said: "The streams flow everywhere.
By the question, "What is the damming of the streams? what does he ask? He asks: "What is the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of the streams?"
Since it ought to be asked, "Or is it the abandoning of transgression?", it was said: "What is the obstruction of the streams? It asks for the destruction of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
Since it ought to be asked, "Is this the purification that is the destruction of obsessions, or is it emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*)?", it was said:
"This is purification. Regarding the question, "Tell me the restraint of the streams; by what are the streams closed?"—what is meant by this?
He asks: "Does he ask about the obsession of the streams, or does he ask about their transgression, or does he ask about their eradication?
Because it must be said thus, it is stated: "The streams... are closed; he asks about the eradication of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
Because it must be said: "Is this purification the eradication of the underlying tendencies, or is it emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*)?"
“This is the emergence” has been stated.

The investigation of the inquiry beginning with “The streams flow everywhere” was spoken by the Teacher and is known to us; since it must be asked, “What is the investigation of the answer to that inquiry? the passage beginning with “In this regard, the answer” was stated. In that inquiry:
“The streams that exist in the world, (Ajita, said the Blessed One)”...
"Mindfulness is their prevention;
I call it the restraint of the streams. By means of wisdom, these are closed.
This should be understood as the response to the verse. In that verse, Ajita, regarding those streams that flow in the world:
The obstruction to those streams is mindfulness (*sati*); I say that they exercise restraint over those streams through that mindfulness.
The construction should be made thus: "These streams are closed by wisdom (*paññā*). In this context, "mindfulness" refers to the mindfulness associated with insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*).
"By wisdom" means by path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*). "Are closed" means they are closed and cut off by way of not allowing [the defilements] to arise.
“Mindfulness is the warding off of those streams; I call it restraint,” said the Blessed One. Since it must be asked:
