“Is the task of restraining the streams accomplished by any kind of mindfulness whatsoever? Is the task of restraining the streams accomplished by a distinguished kind of mindfulness?
By what kind of mindfulness is the task of restraining the streams accomplished?”—[the answer is: “By that which is directed toward the body (*kāyagatāya*... [he spoke].

"By mindfulness," and so forth, was said. Therein, "by mindfulness directed to the body" means by mindfulness associated with insight-knowledge that has proceeded by way of insight into the parts of the physical body, such as hair and so on, as impermanent and so forth.
"Developed" means by way of contemplation [of the body] as impermanent, suffering, non-self, as dispassion, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment.
...to that which has been cultivated. For in this way, one who contemplates as impermanent abandons the perception of permanence;

one who contemplates as suffering abandons the perception of pleasure; one who contemplates as non-self abandons the perception of self; by becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight; by becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust;
by bringing about cessation, one abandons origination; by relinquishing, one...
"He abandons grasping": "By means of frequent practice" means by practicing, in the manner already described, for a day, a month, a year, or even seven years.
"The eye" refers to the eye that stands as the gateway for the occurrence of covetousness and so forth;
it should be understood that the nasalization (*niggahita*) has been elided. "He does not crave" means [he does not crave] that which occurs at the eye-door together with covetousness and the like.
The construction is as follows: it does not drag along the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*) or the person possessing that continuum, nor does it yearn for agreeable forms.
It does not strike against disagreeable forms. When mindfulness directed to the body has been developed and cultivated, one does not yearn for sounds.
The construction—"it does not strike against disagreeable sounds," and so forth—should be applied according to what is possible.

He asks, "For what reason does he not pull back and does not strike back? He answers, "Because the sense faculties have been restrained and guarded, he does not pull back and does not strike back. He asks, "By what protection have they been restrained and guarded?
He answers, "They have been restrained and guarded by the protection of mindfulness. [The state of being restrained and guarded by the protection of mindfulness...]
"By whom should we believe this?"—because it was necessary to say this, he said "Therefore... and so forth. Therein, "therefore" (*tena*) means:
because they were guarded and restrained by the protection of mindfulness, the Blessed One—who knows that which has been guarded and restrained—spoke these words, "Mindfulness is their restraint.
By those words, you should believe in the state of being guarded and restrained through the protection of mindfulness.
In the preliminary stage, wisdom follows the truths; here, it should be understood that the function [of mindfulness] alone is predominant.
The Master has stated the detailed meaning of the answer, “Mindfulness is their warding off,” and this has been understood by us.
However, since the detailed meaning of the answer, “These two are covered by wisdom,” must be explained as to how it is to be understood by us, [the following is said].
To show the detailed meaning of the answer, “They are closed by means of wisdom,” he said, “By means of wisdom, the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are abandoned,” and so forth.

Therein, “by means of wisdom” means by means of the wisdom of the Path (magga-paññā). “Underlying tendencies” refers to the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the others, which are liable to arise upon obtaining their corresponding conditions.
“Are abandoned” means they are abandoned by way of total eradication; when the underlying tendencies have been abandoned by means of wisdom, the active outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna) are also [abandoned].

They are abandoned in terms of their meaning. Because of the abandonment of what are they said to be "abandoned"? It is answered: "The outbursts (pariyuṭṭhānā) are abandoned because of the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (anusaya).
Since it must be asked, "What is that abandonment of the outbursts through the abandonment of the underlying tendencies like?", [the text continues]: "That..."
It is as stated in the passage beginning, “Just as for a tree possessing trunks,” and so forth.

In that context, when the earth has been dug up with a spade or similar tool and the roots of a tree possessing trunks have been extracted without remainder, the continuity of that tree’s flowers, fruits, shoots, and sprouts is likewise utterly severed by the spade and other instruments;
even so, when the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have been abandoned by the knowledge of the path of Arahatship.
The continuity of the manifestation of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) becomes severed, closed off, and concealed.
By what is it severed? The construction of the meaning should be understood as: "It is severed by wisdom—that is, by the wisdom of the Path (*maggapaññā*).
Because it might be asked, "How is the state of being delimited by wisdom to be believed? the passage beginning with "By that" and so forth was stated. "By wisdom these... [is said].

The intention is that the fact that the latent tendencies (*anusaya*) have been delimited by wisdom through the cessation of their active manifestation (*pariyuṭṭhāna-santati*) must be trusted by the wise, based on the statement,
"they are closed off. In these answers to the questions, [this applies] to one who either does not know or is in doubt regarding the restraint and closing of the streams.
Because these [questions] are to be asked regarding the concealment by the vows (*saṃvara*), they are "questions based on the Dhamma" (*dhammādhiṭṭhānā pucchā*);

thus, the investigation of the question (*pucchāvicaya*) is to be understood. Furthermore, because these are to be answered through mindfulness and wisdom, the answer is "an answer based on the Dhamma" (*dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ vissajjana*); thus, the investigation of the answer (*vissajjanavicaya*) is to be understood.

And among these, the question beginning with "By what is the world enveloped? (*kenassu nivuto loko*) is fourfold, according to the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), negligence (*pamāda*), and longing (*jappa*).
One question is stated by way of the world as its basis (*lokādhiṭṭhāna*).

This being so, even the question beginning with “The streams flow everywhere” should be called “one question” by way of a single basis, taking both types—[the questions on] restraint and covering—as having a single meaning;
or it may be called “many questions” because of the multiplicity of the streams. And likewise...

Without referring to the *sota* (stream) itself, but by way of the *saṃvara-pidhāna* (restraints and coverings), it is stated in the passage beginning “The streams flow everywhere” that there are “two questions.
Following that same principle, in the passage beginning “By what is the world shut off?

it should likewise be said that there are “four questions” by way of the four [hindrances] such as the *nīvaraṇa* (obstructions), without referring to the world itself; this is how the demonstration of the method (*naya*) is to be understood.

The Master has analyzed the method of investigation (*vicayahāra*) for both the question asked according to his own composed system—without grasping the connection (*anusandhi*) of the doctrine taught at the time of the teaching—and the answer given without making a formal admission; and this we have understood.
[However,] it is [the method] that grasps the connection of the doctrine taught at the time of the teaching and [then addresses] the question asked...
Having set aside that question and having made a formal admission, as for the method of analysis (*vicayahāra*) which has been explained as the investigation of the answer, [one might ask:
"How is this method of analysis to be understood by us? For the sake of making it known to us, please analyze that analysis.

Because it must be said thus, in order to show the manner in which those [questions] are to be analyzed, immediately after showing the manner of analysis with the verse beginning "Those which are streams" (*yāni sotāni*), [the author says]: ... [the text continues] ...showing the manner of analysis through the verse beginning "Those which are streams."
He said, “Both wisdom and mindfulness,” and so forth.
In this regard, the meaning of the verse must first be understood:

that wisdom by which the cessation of the stream is stated through the abandoning of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), and that mindfulness by which the cessation of the stream is stated through the abandoning of obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*)—this is that wisdom.

"And both in the evening and throughout the day, whatever name and form arise together with those fifty faculties—where, O Blessed One, must all this cease without remainder so that it is utterly stopped? Sir, you have been asked by me;
please explain this cessation to me. Thus did the Venerable Ajita question the Blessed One.
Ajita, you have asked me about this question regarding cessation; I shall explain that cessation to you.

Where, with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form—which is accompanied by wisdom and mindfulness—ceases entirely together with the cessation of consciousness: in that cessation of consciousness, all this [ceases] through the cessation of consciousness.
In one instance, at one moment, it ceases simultaneously, neither before nor after;
this cessation of consciousness does not exceed the cessation of that name-and-form, and that respective cessation of name-and-form does not exceed the respective cessation of consciousness.
Regarding this question, Ajita, what is he asking? Is he asking about the very act of ceasing, or is he asking something else?
Regarding the statement, "He asks for the connection of the question," and so forth: therein, "this one" refers to the Venerable Ajita who asked the question;
"the question" refers to the question beginning with, "Both wisdom and mindfulness.
If he were asking for the connection, then, such being the case, would it not be improper for him to ask, "Where does this cease? It is not so, for [the answer] connects [to the previous].
"By this cessation" means "the connection," because that meaning is possible. Therefore it was said: "When asking about the connection, what...

[etc. ...is the element of Nibbāna? Since one asks even about the element of Nibbāna without residue by means of asking about the connection, the question "Where does this cease? is indeed appropriate.
Because it must be asked, "By what practice does one attain that nibbāna-element without residue which was inquired about?",
the passage beginning with "three truths" is stated in order to show the practice— consisting of the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths—
together with its object. Therein, "conditioned" means that suffering and the rest are produced by coming together and combining through conditions such as karma.
“Conditioned phenomena. Regarding the phrase “subject to cessation”: cessation (*nirodha*) is the act of ceasing;

a phenomenon (*dhamma*) is also something subject to cessation (*nirodhadhamma*). Therefore, the meaning to be understood is that those things—suffering and so forth—for which cessation is their inherent nature (*sabhāva*) are “subject to cessation.
To show the nature of these three truths, it is said: “Suffering, origin, and the path. These are the three truths of suffering, origin, and the path.
They were called "conditioned" because it was asked, "What is the truth of cessation? Therefore, it was stated that "cessation is unconditioned.
Here, it could also be said that "[it] has the nature of cessation. It is unconditioned because it is not conditioned by kamma and other such conditions.
It does not have the nature of cessation because there is an absence of arising and ceasing. Among the truths consisting of the abandoner and the abandoned, by which abandoner...
Because it must be asked, "What is to be abandoned? By which stage (bhūmi) is it abandoned?", it is said: "In that regard, origination [is abandoned] in two stages," and so forth.

In that context, "in two stages" means in the stages of seeing (dassana) and cultivation (bhāvanā). "Sensual desire" (kāmacchanda) is lust for sensual existence (kāmabhava). "Lust for form" (rūparāga) is lust for form-existence (rūpabhava).
"Lust for the formless" (arūparāga) is lust for formless-existence (arūpabhava). This is according to the classification by fetters (saṃyojana).
The construction is: "the ten fetters (saṃyojanāni) are abandoned.
12. The fetters to be abandoned have been analyzed according to the distinction between the plane of seeing (dassanabhūmi) and the plane of cultivation (bhāvanābhūmi), and these are also known by us;
however, because it remains to be stated how they are analyzed "according to the distinction of the faculties" (indriyabhedato), the passage beginning with "therein, three... was spoken. Now...
Or rather, because one must ask, "Among the fetters to be abandoned, which fetters cease by making which faculty their own abandoner?
it is said, "In that regard, three," and so forth. They cease by way of non-arising, having been resolved upon and made the abandoner of themselves. [The passage continues:
"The faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' and the faculty of final knowledge [abandon] the fetters..."

Since it must be asked, "Let [the faculty of] cessation be the cause; of what then is the faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya) the cause?", the passage beginning with "But that which...

is stated. Therein, that by means of which the Arahant knows, "Birth is exhausted for me"—this knowledge of exhaustion, which is the fruit of Arahantship occurring at the exhaustion of birth, is the faculty of one who has already known, being the cause of such knowing. That by which...

By means of the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*), the Arahant understands: "There will be no further state of being for me in this world. This understanding is the cause for the faculty of one who has already known.

Furthermore, it is said that the knowledge occurring in the fruit of Arahantship—regarding non-arising and non-origination—is the faculty of one who has already known, serving as the cause for knowing. Having made the faculties and knowledges the abandoners, the fetters cease.
Because it must be stated when those knowledges cease, the passage beginning with “In that regard, as for... was spoken. Since it ought to be asked:
“May the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown’ cease for one who attains the faculty of final knowledge; may the faculty of final knowledge cease for one who attains Arahantship;
but when does the faculty of one who has already known cease?”—therefore, [the text says] “In that regard...”

And that which was stated beginning with “and in the destruction,” etc.: therein, “two” means two according to the distinction of function (*kicca*), but in terms of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), it is indeed one.
Since it might be asked, “The function of understanding (*pajānana*) is also only one; how could there be two?”, the passage beginning with “Moreover” (*apica*) is stated.

What is meant is that two names are obtained through the distinction of the wisdom regarding the object (*ārammaṇa-paññā*). “That” refers to the wisdom mentioned in the preceding verse by way of its function of covering the ear.

That which was spoken of as wisdom (*paññā*) is called wisdom by virtue of its nature of knowing through various modes. Mindfulness (*sati*) is so called in the sense of not forgetting and in the sense of plunging into the object exactly as it has been seen.
Thus, the meaning of the phrase "both wisdom and mindfulness" has been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us; [and likewise] "both name-and-form."

Because it must be said, "How is the meaning of this term to be understood by us?", he analyzes name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and says, "Therein, those which are the five aggregates of clinging," and so forth.
Therein, "therein" refers to the three realms of existence (bhava), which are distinguished by the rounds of kamma and its result (vipāka).
"Therein" [also] refers to the collection of name-and-form comprised of the five aggregates of clinging. "The five faculties" refers to the five faculties beginning with the eye.
“Associated with consciousness” is not stated with reference to the state of being an associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*);
rather, it is stated with reference to the mere nature of what is easily grasped by ordinary people without analysis. However, those who know the distinctions should grasp it by analyzing:
“The mental is associated with consciousness, whereas the material is conascent but not associated with consciousness.”
“Of this” means of name-and-form accompanied by wisdom and mindfulness. “Cessation” refers to the element of nibbāna without residue.
While asking the Blessed One, the Venerable Ajita spoke thus in the *Pārāyana*: “Wisdom itself... where does this cease?
In the verse beginning with “Wisdom itself,” that element of nibbāna without residue which was asked about is the element of nibbāna without residue.

Since it must be asked, "By what realization is it to be attained?", [the answer is] that it is to be attained by way of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) and by way of the realization of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
Furthermore, the four faculties (*indriya*) are the roots for the cultivation of the four bases of psychic power;

therefore, having extracted those four faculties which constitute the root, [the author] says, "In this regard, mindfulness and wisdom," and so forth, in order to demonstrate them. [This concerns] the courses of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena...
When mindfulness is being thoroughly investigated and is becoming established, concentration must be brought to completion by means of it alone;

and by the mention of mindfulness, the abandonment of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) is intended in the verse. Since the function of concentration becomes manifest through the abandonment of the obsessions, he said:
"Mindfulness consists of two faculties: the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of concentration. [And] by means of wisdom, there is the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (anusaya).
It is accomplished by means of energy (vīriya) known as the four right strivings (sammappadhāna), and not without it; thus it is said:
"Wisdom consists of two faculties: the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) and the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya).
When these aforementioned four faculties are being accomplished either in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) or at the moment of the path (maggakkhaṇa), those [factors] associated with them—
That which is faith, that which is conviction, is established; this category of phenomena known as faith and conviction is established as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).

Since it must be asked, "When those root-faculties are established, which phenomenon is established by which faculty?", he says, "In that regard, that which is dominated by faith," and so forth, in order to show by this [passage] that this [phenomenon] is established.

“In each case” means among the Truths and so forth. “Having faith as its dominant factor” (saddhādhipateyya): since desire is established by means of faith acting as a condition, that desire is the dominant factor;
thus it is “having faith as its dominant factor. One-pointedness of mind that is to be exercised by means of that which has faith as its dominant factor is “having faith as its dominant factor.
“Concentration of desire” (chandasamādhi) refers either to concentration that has proceeded by making desire the primary factor, or to [concentration] associated with the dominance of desire.
The construction should be made thus: "Concentration occurring in the prior stage is concentration through desire (*chandasamādhi*);

it is the abandoning, the cause of abandoning. Regarding "abandoning" (*pahāna*), one should understand it in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*): that is, "it is called abandoning because by means of this concentration through desire one abandons—that is, suppresses—the defilements.
"By the power of reflection" means by the power of preliminary work (*parikamma*). "By the power of development" means by the power of sublime development (*mahaggatabhāvanā*).

Thus, because it must be stated that "the concentration of desire (*chandasamādhi*) itself is exclusively abandonment," the passage beginning with "therein, those in-breaths and out-breaths" was spoken.
Therein, the phrase "therein" (*tattha*) refers to that arisen state of consciousness when the mind is concentrated.

By the expression "in that arisen state of consciousness, there are in-breaths," etc., the formations of energy (*vīriya-saṅkhāra*) that produce the in-breaths and so forth are taken up by way of the in-breaths and out-breaths as their primary heads; and these [formations] persist until the completion of the development (*bhāvanā*).
They are "recollections" (*sara*) because they are recollected again and again, and "intentions" (*saṅkappa*) because they are intended again and again. Furthermore,
that which was previously described as "these formations are recollections and intentions"— namely, either the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*),

or the abandoning through the suppression of defilements and the abandoning by way of their specific factors (*tadaṅga-ppahāna*), or the primary cause for abandoning— [refers to] these aforementioned formations and so forth.
Because it was necessary to ask, "What is he developing?", the passage beginning with "these formations" and so forth was stated. Therein, the construction is as follows:

"He develops these formations and both of those [the mind and the concentration] as a basis for spiritual power (iddhipāda) that is endowed with the volitional formation of desire-concentration, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment."

“Endowed with the volitional formations of striving associated with desire-concentration” (*chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata*): desire itself is the dominant factor, thus it is “desire-dominance” (*chandādhipati*), which is “desire-dominance concentration” (*chandādhipatisamādhi*).
This was stated by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, making desire the dominant factor, attains concentration.
Alternatively, concentration caused by desire, or concentration beginning with desire, is “desire-concentration” (*chandasamādhi*). [This refers to] that which has desire as its dominant factor.
It is said that concentration is "arisen by way of conditions. The volitional formations that constitute the effort are "volitional formations of effort" (*padhāna-saṅkhārā*);
by the word "effort," conditioned formations and so forth are excluded. "Concentration through desire and volitional formations of effort" is *chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhārā*;
endowed with these is "one who possesses desire... [etc. ...endowed"; that... [etc. ...gone. It succeeds, it is accomplished, it is brought to completion—thus it is called "success" (*iddhi*).
*Iddhi-pāda*: *iddhi* is the factor (*koṭṭhāsa*), and since the factor itself is the foot, it is called a "basis of success" (*iddhipāda*). It is the fourth basis of success.

Alternatively, beings succeed, prosper, and reach excellence by means of it, thus it is *iddhi*. One goes by means of this, thus it is a *pāda*. A "basis of success" (*iddhipāda*) is the foot of success.

Although it is stated in its general sense as "basis of success," it is also said [specifically] as "endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving" (*chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata*).

Because it is so stated, only the basis of psychic power consisting of desire (*chandiddhipāda*) should be understood; the meaning is that one develops and increases that basis of psychic power, that basis of psychic power consisting of desire.

"Dependent on seclusion" and "dependent on dispassion" means: at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), it is dependent on seclusion as a factor (*tadaṅga-viveka*) by way of function, and dependent on seclusion as escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*) by way of aspiration;
however, at the moment of the path (*magga*), it is dependent on seclusion through eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*) by way of function, and [dependent on seclusion] by way of object (*ārammaṇa*).
"Dependent on seclusion as escape": at the moment of insight, this is dependent on "fading away" (virāga) by way of function, and dependent on "seclusion as escape" by way of aspiration;
however, at the moment of the Path, it is dependent on "fading away through eradication" by way of function, and dependent on "fading away as escape" by way of object.
"Dependent on cessation": at the moment of insight, this is dependent on "cessation by way of factor-substitution" (tadaṅganirodha) by way of function.
In terms of aspiration, it is based on the cessation that is deliverance; at the moment of the path, in terms of function, it is based on the cessation that is eradication;
and in terms of object, it is based on the cessation that is deliverance. Regarding the phrase "tending toward relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*):

here, relinquishment (*vossagga*) is twofold, by way of relinquishing (*pariccāga*), by way of launching forth (*pakkhandana*), and by way of relinquishment itself (*vossagga*). Among these, at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), there is relinquishing-relinquishment by way of its factor (*tadaṅga*); and by way of its inclination toward Nibbāna...

It should be understood by way of analysis as follows: there is the relinquishment consisting in leaping forward; at the moment of the Path, there is the relinquishment consisting in total eradication;
and through the act of making it the object, there is the relinquishment consisting in leaping forward into Nibbāna.

It is "tending toward relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*) because it turns toward the meaning of relinquishment as already stated, or because, having turned toward it, it ripens—that is, it brings about ripening. That which possesses this quality is "tending toward relinquishment."
The mode of development for the basis of psychic power consisting in concentration has been stated by the Teacher and is known to us.

Since it must be asked, "How is the mode of development for the basis of psychic power consisting in energy to be understood by us?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, that which is dominated by energy" was spoken.
Its meaning is to be understood according to the method already explained above. However, the text established in brief shall now be expanded in detail.
I shall set this forth.
How so?—“In that regard, the one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) dominated by energy is ‘concentration through energy’ (vīriya-samādhi).

When the mind is concentrated, the suppression of the defilements (kilesā) either by the power of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānabala) or by the power of cultivation (bhāvanābala) is ‘abandonment’ (pahāna). In that regard, those which...”
In-breathing and out-breathing are applied thought and sustained thought; perception and feeling are volition and intention—these are formations.

Thus, both the preceding energy and concentration, as well as the abandoning through the suppression of defilements and these formations, he develops as the basis of psychic power endowed with the formation of energy and concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
“In this context, that one-pointedness of mind which has mind as its dominant factor is ‘concentration of mind.
When the mind is concentrated, the suppression of the defilements—whether by the power of reflection or by the power of cultivation—is ‘abandoning.

In this regard, those in-breaths and out-breaths, applied thought and sustained thought, perception and feeling, and intentions accompanied by their own flavor, are ‘formations. Thus is the former [set].”

And there is mental concentration and the abandoning [of defilements] through the suppression of the afflictions (*kilesa*); these are the formations. One develops this basis of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) endowed with both the mental concentration and the volitional formation of striving, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
In that context, the one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) dominated by investigation is "concentration through investigation. When the mind is concentrated, the afflictions...
This is abandonment, whether by means of suppression, the power of reflection, or the power of cultivation.

In this context, those in-breaths and out-breaths, as well as the applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), perception (*saññā*), feeling (*vedayita*), and mental intentions (*saṅkappa*), are these formations (*saṅkhāra*).

Thus, both the preceding concentration through investigation (*vīmaṃsā-samādhi*)—which is abandonment by way of suppressing defilements—and these formations together constitute "concentration through investigation accompanied by the volitional formation of striving" (*vīmaṃsā-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra-samannāgata*).
“He develops a basis for spiritual power that is dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and results in relinquishment.

Now, this is the distinction: “Energy-concentration” (*vīriya-samādhi*) refers either to concentration that has proceeded by making energy the dominant factor, or to concentration occurring in the preliminary stage associated with energy as its predominant influence. “Mind-concentration” (*citta-samādhi*) refers to [concentration] where mind is the dominant factor.
Concentration that has arisen by making [energy] predominant, or concentration associated with the predominance of mind that arose in the prior stage,
is "concentration of mind" (*cittasamādhi*). Concentration that has arisen by making investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) predominant,
or concentration associated with the predominance of investigation that arose in the prior stage, is "concentration of investigation" (*vīmaṃsāsamādhi*).

Here, this brief commentary has been made according to one’s own strength and power; however, it should be understood in detail or in depth by those with profound knowledge, following the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*). 14.
It was stated: “Concentration through desire, concentration through energy, concentration through mind, and concentration through investigation.

When this is so, it follows that only concentration through investigation would have knowledge as its root, knowledge as its precursor, and would proceed in accordance with knowledge, while the other three [would not].

In order to show that all forms of concentration (samādhi) have knowledge (ñāṇa) as their root and so forth—since it would otherwise have to be said that "concentrations might have ignorance as their root, ignorance as their precursor, and proceed from ignorance"—it was stated: "All concentration has knowledge as its root," and so on.

In this context, "all concentration" refers to concentration through desire (chanda-samādhi), concentration through energy (viriya-samādhi), concentration through mind (citta-samādhi), and concentration through investigation (vīmaṃsā-samādhi).

Concentration is fourfold: 1. **Rooted in knowledge** (*ñāṇamūlaka*): This refers to that which occurs through the cognitive process of a single adverting moment (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*) or various adverting moments (*nānāvajjana-vīthi*), being rooted in access-knowledge (*upacāra-ñāṇa*).

2. **Preceded by knowledge** (*ñāṇapubbaṅgama*): This means that it has the knowledge of attainment (*adhigama-ñāṇa*) as its precursor; thus, it is "preceded by knowledge. 3. **Accompanied by knowledge** (*ñāṇānuparivatti*):

This means that it is accompanied by the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*); thus, it is "accompanied by knowledge. Alternatively, it may refer to the access-knowledge of various adverting moments.

Or, it is "rooted in knowledge" (*ñāṇamūlaka*) because its root is either the knowledge of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhiñāṇa*) or the knowledge of access (*upacārañāṇa*); it is "preceded by knowledge" (*ñāṇapubbaṅgama*) because its precursor is the knowledge of access;

and it is "concomitant with knowledge" (*ñāṇānuparivatti*) because it follows along with the knowledge of absorption (*appanāñāṇa*). Alternatively, it is "rooted in knowledge" because its root is the entire knowledge of access;

it is "preceded by knowledge" because its precursor is the knowledge of absorption; and it is "concomitant with knowledge" because it follows along with the knowledge of direct higher power (*abhiññāñāṇa*).

"Accompanied by knowledge" (*ñāṇānuparivatti*) means that it follows after knowledge, or "following after" (*anuparivatti*) is the act of following; thus, "that which follows after knowledge" is *ñāṇānuparivatti*.
Knowledge, moreover, is of the same kind as previously described.

"As before, so after" means that just as in the case of the fourfold concentration beginning with concentration through desire, [the recollection of past lives] possesses the state of being accompanied by the knowledge of the recollection of past lives.
In the past, even throughout incalculable births and aeons of cosmic contraction and expansion,
there is only the thorough penetration— never a lack of penetration— of both what is connected to one's own aggregates and what is connected to the aggregates of others; likewise,

by virtue of the subsequent revolving of knowledge regarding future states for one who possesses such concentration as described, it is the same in the future, even throughout incalculable births and aeons.

The meaning should be understood as follows: during the processes of world-contraction and expansion, there is indeed a thorough penetration of both that which is connected to one's own aggregates and that which is connected to the aggregates of others, and not a difficult penetration.

"As it was later, so it was before" means that, by way of following after the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) within the aforementioned concentration, [he knows] regarding future beings alone.
The meaning is that during those very days mentioned above, there is only the thorough penetration of the minds of other beings,
not a lack of penetration; likewise, during the seven days prior to the aforementioned attainment of concentration,
there is only the thorough penetration of the minds of other beings, not a lack of penetration.

"As by day, so by night": just as for beings with eyesight, during the daytime, because darkness has been dispelled by the light of the sun, a form that has come into the range of vision and is cognizable by the eye-consciousness is also easily cognizable by the mind-consciousness;
likewise, during the nighttime, even while the fourfold darkness prevails, for one who possesses the aforementioned concentration...
By virtue of its conformity with the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), there is indeed a thorough penetration of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), not a difficult penetration.

Just as at night, so too by day: just as during the night, even in darkness endowed with the four factors, there is indeed a thorough penetration of the sense-base of form by virtue of the aforementioned concentration’s conformity with the knowledge of the divine eye, not a difficult penetration.
Likewise, during the daytime, there is only the thorough penetration— and not a difficult penetration— of a subtle visible object,
or of a visible object hidden by something such as a wall, or of a visible object situated at a very great distance,
by means of the aforementioned concentration through its conformity with the knowledge of the divine eye; this is how the meaning should be understood.
Just as during the day, for one who possesses the aforementioned concentration, there is only thorough penetration— and not difficulty of penetration—
of the subtle sphere of sound due to its following upon the knowledge of the divine ear, or of a sphere of sound concealed by something such as a wall,
or of a sphere of sound occurring at a very great distance; so too during the night.

This method should also be applied as follows: for one possessing the aforementioned concentration, there is only thorough penetration—not difficult penetration—of a subtle sound-base, or of a sound-base concealed by something such as a wall, or of a sound-base occurring at an extremely distant place, because it functions in accordance with the knowledge of the divine ear (*dibbasotañāṇa*). Thus it is said in the Commentary:
Having stated, “‘As before’ means as [the concentration] was accompanied by the knowledge of recollecting past lives,” and so forth, he says:

“And just as it was explained regarding the sense-base of visible forms, so too should it be applied to the sense-base of sounds, because that concentration is accompanied by the divine ear-knowledge. [The question is:
“What does one develop by means of the concentration rooted in knowledge, etc., which is accompanied by the state of being followed by the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and so forth?”

Because it is to be asked, the words “thus with the opened” and so forth are spoken. Therein, “thus” means in the manner already described. “Uncovered” means by way of the removal of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so on.
“He develops the radiant mind” means he develops the path-consciousness associated with the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

For when the path-consciousness associated with the bases of psychic power arises, the wholesome states co-arising with that path-consciousness consist of the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
The five faculties arise. When the path-consciousness ceases, they cease by way of not arising, because they exist for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).
Thus, the construction is: "With the cessation of path-consciousness, wisdom and mindfulness also cease.
Since it must be stated, "With the cessation of what consciousness does name-and-form cease?", [the text says] "And name-and-form," and so forth.
It has been stated that with the cessation of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) also ceases; this is what is meant.
Alternatively, because it must be said that "with the cessation of consciousness, wisdom, mindfulness, and so forth—the five faculties thus cease"—name-and-form also ceases.
Furthermore, as name-and-form is ceasing, it [ceases] for the rebirth-linking consciousness.
In order to show that [it] ceases through cessation, it is said: "And name-and-form," and so forth.

Therein, "name-and-form" refers to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling—which is ready to arise when craving, ignorance, and the rest have not been cut off by the Path—as well as the primary elements and derived form.
"Conditioned by consciousness" means that the rebirth-linking consciousness, which is ready to arise, is the cause of this name-and-form; thus it is "conditioned by consciousness."
"Conditioned by consciousness, [name-and-form] is produced" means produced with consciousness as the condition.

"Of that" refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) which is about to arise. "Causes" refers to defilements such as craving and ignorance. "Consciousness" refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness which is about to arise.
"Without nutriment" means without a condition. "Not rejoiced in" means not to be rejoiced in by way of sensual craving and so forth. "Without rebirth-linking" means...
"Free from the reconnection to renewed existence": such is that consciousness. "Without cause" (*ahetu*):
there is no consciousness at rebirth-linking reckoned as a cause for this name-and-form; thus it is "without cause. "Without condition" (*appaccaya*):

due to the absence of companions, there are no volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) which serve as conditions for this; thus it is "without condition. In this way, with the cessation of rebirth-linking consciousness, name-and-form also ceases.
Because it must be asked, "How are we to have faith in the manner in which wisdom, mindfulness, and name-and-form cease as previously described?

it was said, "Therefore the Blessed One said," and so forth. In accordance with the manner of what must be said, the Blessed One—who knows the mode of cessation of wisdom, mindfulness, and name-and-form—revealed the manner of their cessation in the passage beginning: "That which is this... and ending with "...herein this."
He spoke this verse: “...is it ceased? By that statement of the verse, you must indeed have faith in the state of cessation as described by me.

Here too, because Ajita asked his question since he either did not know the cessation of the fifty name-and-forms or was in doubt regarding them, it is called “a question for the illumination of the unseen” or “a question for the verification of what has been seen.”

The investigation of the question should be determined as follows: "Is it a question from the standpoint of phenomena (dhamma) because wisdom and the other [faculties] have multiple meanings, or is it a question with multiple bases, or a question with phenomena as its basis? and so forth.

The investigation of the answer should be determined as follows: "Is it an answer that shows the identity [of the terms], or an answer with multiple bases, or an answer with phenomena as its basis? and so forth.
Thus, having separately demonstrated both the questions and answers based on the person (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) and so forth,
as well as those based on the phenomenon (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*) and so forth, the Teacher has analyzed the investigation of the questions and the investigation of the answers,
which we too have understood. [This applies] when the questions and answers based on the person and the phenomenon are shown together.

Because it must be asked, "How are the investigation of the question and the investigation of the answer to be understood by us?", he first brings forward a question framed in terms of both persons (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) and phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), and then, analyzing the investigation therein, he says:
"And those conditioned phenomena," and so forth. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however—

“Having thus shown the question concerning the sequence (*anusandhipucchā*), it was stated: ‘The questions based on beings (*sattādhiṭṭhānā*) and based on phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhānā*) were shown separately below; now, in order to show them together, the passage beginning with “And those who are conditioned phenomena” is commenced.

This is its meaning: here in this teaching, there are those Arahants who are conditioned phenomena, and many indeed—seven persons—are trainees (*sekkhā*) training in virtue and so forth; [the text describes] the conduct (*iriyaṃ*) of both those Arahants and the trainees.”
“Being asked about my practice, O Great One, you who are wise, please explain it to me, O Venerable Sir”—thus did the Venerable Ajita speak while posing his question.
In that verse, because it was necessary to state how many things were asked about, the words “these” (*imāni*) and so forth were spoken.

Because they were to be asked about in accordance with the meaning of the words, it was stated: “these three words were asked about. [This refers to] the verse beginning: “And those... O Venerable Sir.”
Regarding the questions asked, there are three questions. Because it must be asked, "Of what, by what reason, are there three?", it is said: "Of what... [etc. ...by way of connection" (*yogena*).

The noble ones in training (*sekha*) and the noble ones beyond training (*asekha*), as well as the abandoning preceded by insight (*vipassanāpubbaṅgama-pahāna*), constitute "the abandoning preceded by insight for those in training and beyond training";
the connection of these is "the connection for those in training... [etc.]".
By that [method], there are those in training... [and so on] ...by means of yoga. Indeed, because he spoke the verse beginning with "And those conditioned phenomena, O sirs...
according to this method of questioning, it should be understood that there are three questions.

By the phrase "And those conditioned phenomena," he asks about the arahantship of those beyond training (asekkha); and by "those many in training (sekha)... [he asks about the state of those in training].
By the word "here" (*idha*), he asks about the training of those in training (*sekkha*) and those beyond training (*asekkha*).

By the words "Tell me, O dear sir, being asked, their prudent conduct," he asks about the insight of those in training and those beyond training regarding the abandonment by means of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-ppahāna*) in the preliminary stage.
[This] is either a question for the illumination of what has not been seen, or a question for the corroboration of what has been seen; it is based on sentient beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*).
The investigation of the question (*pucchāvicaya*)—such as "Is it a question? or "Is it a question based on many foundations?"—is to be determined.
Having extracted a question based on the seven categories of phenomena (*sattadhammādhiṭṭhāna*), the Teacher has analyzed the investigation of the question, and we too have understood it.
Since one must ask, "In that question, which are the verses of the answer (*vissajjanāgāthā*)?", [the text begins] with "In that regard, the answer... and so forth.
It has been undertaken. "Therein" means in that verse. The verse of response, beginning with "In sensual pleasures... [and] wander forth," was spoken by the Blessed One.

"In sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*): they are called *kāmā* because they are desired; it means "in those sensual pleasures. Regarding objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāmā*), the wise should not covet them with the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*).
"With a mind not turbid" (*manasā nāvilosiyo*): this refers to ill-will thoughts (*byāpādavitakkā*) and so forth, as well as bodily misconduct and the like, which cause turbidity.
And while abandoning unwholesome states, the wise person, with an unclouded mind, should become well-composed.

"Skilled in all phenomena" means he is skilled and adept regarding the five aggregates—impermanence and so forth—because he has thoroughly examined all phenomena through their impermanence and other characteristics.
"Mindful" (*sato*) means one who remembers (*sarati*) things such as the head-hairs and so on. "Bhikkhu" means one who sees (*ikkhati*) conditioned phenomena with fear and so forth.

"Paribbaje" means that one should completely avoid (*pari-vajjeyya*) the defilement-desires and object-desires by means of their abandonment through substitution (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and eradication (*samuccheda*).
In the question-verse, the Blessed One—who was praised with the word "wise" (*nipaka*)—spoke the answer-verse;
that unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) of the Blessed One, which demonstrates his state of excellence through its supreme development, is [the subject].
Having thus analyzed [the Buddha’s actions] by way of the divisions of bodily action and so forth, he says: "All the bodily action of the Blessed One," and so on.
Therein, every bodily action performed after knowing with unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.

This same method applies to the remaining [actions] as well. "In the past" means in past existences; it is unimpeded by ignorance regarding the constituent parts (*koṭṭhāsa*), such as one's own aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
The Blessed One’s knowledge and vision. Regarding the phrase "in the future parts": it refers to the components such as the aggregates and so forth within a future existence.
Regarding "in the present parts": it refers to the components such as the aggregates and so forth within a present existence.
Since it must be asked, "In what [existence] is there an obstruction to knowledge and vision?", the question is set aside and the object of that obstruction is [explained].
The passage beginning with “And who” (*ko ca*) was spoken in order to show this. Alternatively, since it might be asked:
“In the present existence, regarding the constituent parts such as one’s own aggregates (*skandha*), there might be knowledge and vision even for others;

following that logic, in which of the past or future constituent parts would there be an obstruction of the knowledge and vision of others?”—the question having been thus set aside, [the text] states the object of that obstruction.
In order to demonstrate this by way of restriction, it was said: "And what? Therein, "And what?
asks: "At what time, in what circumstance, would there be an obstruction to the knowledge and vision of others?
The ignorance of others regarding the impermanent, the suffering, and the non-self—that which is their lack of vision—is what is termed "ignorance and lack of vision."
The intrinsic nature of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*) is the opposition [to the defilements], not merely the opposition to the perception of the aggregates and so forth belonging to others.

By this, he shows that the knowledge and vision occurring with respect to the three characteristics in terms of impermanence and so on is difficult for others to attain, and that the Blessed One’s knowledge and vision is not shared by others. For, through the manifestation of the three characteristics, the Blessed One’s...
Those capable of being trained (veneyyā) attain penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Since it must be asked, "By what simile is it made clear to us how the absence of obstruction to the Blessed One’s knowledge and vision implies the absence of obstruction to the knowledge and vision of others?", the passage beginning with "Just as here" was spoken in order to make it clear by means of a simile.
In that context, "here" refers to this world of beings, and "a man with eyes" refers to one who possesses sight.

Just as one might see stars in the sky but, due to a lack of numerical convention, would not know "there are this many," so too does this obstruction to the knowledge and vision of others have the nature of non-knowledge and non-vision.
However, because the Blessed One lacks such [obstructions], his knowledge and vision are unimpeded by any ignorance or lack of vision.

The meaning should be understood as "it exists. Since it might be asked, "Why should we have faith in the unimpeded nature of the Blessed One’s knowledge and vision?", it is said: "For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess unobstructed knowledge and vision.
[Thus,] the Blessed One’s unobstructed knowledge has been demonstrated by the Teacher through its divisions, such as bodily action and so forth, for one who is prudent... [and so on].

And since we ourselves have understood that, when questioned by the word "conduct" (*iriya*) in the subsequent verse, one must explain how the practices of those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*) are to be known, the passage beginning with "In this regard, by one in training" (*tattha sekhenā*) was stated in order to show the practice of those in training and those beyond training.
Therein, "in this regard" (*tattha*) refers to that response. "By one in training" (*sekhenā*) means by a person whose nature is to train regarding things that cause passion.
The mind must be guarded against greed for phenomena such as visible forms and their objects; the mind must be guarded against hatred toward the grounds for resentment that provoke obsession.
"Among those [faults of] greed and hatred, which one did the Blessed One intend to prevent when he spoke which word in the verse of response?"

Because it is to be asked, the passage beginning with “therein, whatever desire” is stated. Therein, “therein” refers to the faults of greed (*gedha*). “Desire” (*iccha*) is the desire of lust (*rāga*).
“Infatuation” (*muccha*) is the infatuation of delusion accompanied by greed and delusion. “Aspiration” (*patthana*) is the aspiration of lust.

“Endearment” (*piyayana*) is indeed the endearment of craving (*taṇhā*), not the endearment of loving-kindness (*mettā*). “Sporting” (*kīḷana*) is the sporting of greed; for these are synonyms for greed.
The Blessed One spoke thus in various distinct ways, saying "one should not covet sensual pleasures," in order to restrain that which is called greed, such as longing and so forth.

The construction is that the Blessed One spoke thus in various distinct ways, saying "one should be undisturbed in mind," in order to restrain the fault of the affliction of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
The Blessed One spoke these two phrases while restraining greed and hatred respectively.
It was asked, "In what sense should that be believed? Because it must be so stated, the passage beginning with "For thus the trainee" (*sekha*) was spoken.
One who is covetous toward things that provoke lust (*rajanīya*) generates unarisen defilements dominated by greed (*lobha*) and causes arisen defilements to increase and expand.
One who is turbid toward things that provoke obsession (*pariyuṭṭhānīya*) [generates] unarisen defilements dominated by hatred (*dosa*).
It gives rise to defilement, and it causes the defilement that has arisen to increase and expand;
thus, the intention is that my word should be believed in this sense of negation.
But does the trainee (sekha), being without greed and undisturbed, merely act to prevent grasping and hatred, or rather—

Because it must be asked, "Does he also fulfill the higher practice?", [the author] says, beginning with "But he whose intention is untroubled," in order to show that he indeed fulfills the higher practice as well.
In this context, "untroubled intention" (*anāvilasaṅkappa*) means one who has no intentions that cause turbidity—namely, intentions of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and intentions of cruelty (*vihiṃsā*);
thus he is "one of untroubled intention. This is due to the absence of greed for desires (*icchādigedha*).

Not being covetous, he exerts himself and initiates wholesome effort. Since it must be asked, "How does he exert himself?", the passage beginning with "He [strives] for those that have not yet arisen" and so forth is stated.
In this context, "he" refers to the trainee (*sekha*) who is practicing for the sake of the higher development of the path.
The meaning of the phrases beginning with "for those that have not yet arisen" can be understood from the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself; therefore, it has not been analyzed here.

16. By "that by which" (yena): the faculty characterized by the recollection of the foul (*asubha*) and so forth restrains the applied thought (*vitakka*) that arises simultaneously with sensual craving (*kāmatanha*) toward objects of craving.
This faculty, characterized by the recollection of the foul and so forth, is the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*).
That non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), having attained a state of loftiness, restrains the applied thought of ill-will (*byāpādavitakka*); this is what is termed [the faculty of concentration].
The faculty is the concentration faculty (*samādhindriya*). That right effort by which one restrains thoughts of cruelty—this faculty, termed right effort, is the energy faculty (*vīriyindriya*).
That faculty termed right view by which one does not tolerate [unwholesome states] as they arise...
and so forth—this faculty, termed right view, is the wisdom faculty (*paññindriya*). Arising together with these four faculties...
The faith that arises as conviction and trust, being free from turbidity, is this faculty known as faith, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
These are the five faculties of one in training (*sekkha*).
They would not attain preeminence over a single object; rather, they attain preeminence each within their own respective domain.

Because it is appropriate to ask, "Which faculty exercises the state of primacy in which object?", he spoke the words beginning with "In that regard, where is the faculty of faith to be seen," demonstrating that this faculty functions in this particular object.
Therein, the phrase "in those" refers to among those four faculties and four factors of stream-entry; [he states] that the faculty of faith exercises the state of primacy.
It should be understood that [these states] proceed. In the same way, this should be applied to the remaining cases as well.

Since it must be asked whether the trainee (*sekha*) was spoken of and praised by the Blessed One as being "heedful in the faculty of wisdom alone," or rather as being [endowed] with all wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*), the passage beginning with "Thus the trainee" is given to show that he was indeed spoken of and praised by the Blessed One as being endowed with all wholesome states, headed by the five faculties.

It has been said. In that context, by thus demonstrating the arising of the five faculties, the Blessed One spoke of and praised the person in training (*sekha*) as being "heedful through all wholesome states" (*appamatta*);

this is to be construed with the phrase "by means of a mind free from turbidity. Since it might be asked, "By what is the freedom from turbidity of one in training to be believed? it was therefore stated: "The Blessed One said, 'One should be undisturbed in mind.'"
Because the Blessed One said, “One should be undisturbed in mind,” the undisturbed state of the trainee (sekha) is to be believed by you.
The path that has reached its culmination for the trainee has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known by us;

however, since it must be explained how the path that has reached its culmination for the one beyond training (asekha) is to be known, [the following] regarding the culmination of the one beyond training...
In order to analyze and demonstrate the path (*paṭipadā*), he said, "skilled in all phenomena" (*kusalo sabbadhammānaṃ*), and so forth.

Therein, "in all phenomena" means that the Blessed One has spoken of and praised the one beyond training (*asekkha*) as being more skilled and proficient due to his mind being undisturbed by a path that has reached the pinnacle among all phenomena.
This was said with the intention of demonstrating the skillfulness of the one beyond training regarding all phenomena.

In order to analyze and demonstrate all phenomena (dhammas) that constitute the domain of that Kosala, [the author] first spoke the passage beginning with “The world, indeed,” by way of a reference to the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).
Therein, the construction is as follows: by the phrase “of all phenomena,” it is shown that what is called the world—consisting of the aforementioned phenomena—is threefold:
the world of defilements (kilesaloka), the world of existence (bhavaloka), and the world of faculties (indriyaloka). Among these, the meaning of limited phenomena (parittadhamma) is...

In the sense of generating defilements it is *kilesa* (defilement), and in the sense of the occurrence of the wholesome and so forth it is *loka* (world); thus it is the "world of defilements" (*kilesaloka*).
In the sense of sublime states it is *bhava* (existence) by way of being a state of becoming, and in the manner already stated it is *loka*; thus it is the "world of existence" (*bhavaloka*).

In the sense of states such as the faculty of faith and so forth, having become faculties through connection with the sense of predominance, and in the sense of reaching [their respective objects] such as the faculty of faith and so forth, it is *loka*; thus it is the "world of faculties" (*indriyaloka*).
Because it must be asked, "By which [person] in the three worlds does which [state] arise?", the words "Therein" (*tatthā*) and so forth were spoken.
Because it must be asked, "Who develops the faculties such as faith?", the words "He develops the faculties" (*so indriyāni nibbattetī*) were spoken.

Therein, "he" (*so*) refers to that person who, regarding the limited states known as the world of defilements (*kilesaloka*) and the exalted states known as the world of existence (*bhavaloka*), [proceeds].
And because he stands by way of accomplishing this or that [faculty], that person generates the faculties, such as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), within his own mental continuum (attasantāna).

Since it must be asked, "What wisdom arises when the faculties are being made to grow by way of their repeated generation within one's own mental continuum?", the passage beginning with "In regard to the faculties" (indriyesu) was stated.
Therein, "of the one to be led" (neyyassa) means of the one who is to be directly known through higher knowledge (abhiññeyya).

“Full understanding” (*pariññā*) is the wisdom that functions by way of discernment and so forth with respect to material and immaterial phenomena, according to their specific characteristics and their conditions.
Because it must be asked, “In how many ways should that full understanding be investigated? it is stated, “It is twofold,” and so on.

Therein, that full understanding should be investigated by the wise in two ways: by way of the full understanding of seeing (*dassana-pariññā*) and the full understanding of development (*bhāvanā-pariññā*).

"It should be understood" means that by "full understanding through seeing" (*dassana-pariññā*), the meaning of "full understanding through knowing" (*ñāta-pariññā*)—which generates the wisdom of the path of seeing—should be understood.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Full understanding through seeing is full understanding through knowing.

By "full understanding through development" (*bhāvanā-pariññā*), the meaning is "full understanding through abandoning" (*pahāna-pariññā*) together with "full understanding through investigating" (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), which generates the wisdom of the path of development.
Because it was said, "The meaning expressed by 'It is twofold,' etc., is too concise to be understood; please explain it in detail," the passage beginning with "For when" was spoken.
Therein, "when" (*yadā*) refers to the time when powerful insight (*vipassanā*) arises.

"A trainee" (*sekha*) refers both to the virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) and to those such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), owing to their habit of training (*sikkhanasīlatā*). "The knowable" (*ñeyya*) refers to form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are to be known.

"Volitional formations. "He fully understands" means he knows them after having grasped them by means of the knowledge of comprehension and so forth, accompanied by the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*).
"Of him" refers to both the noble ordinary person (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) and those such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*).
"Two states" refers to the state of powerful insight for the noble ordinary person and the state of powerful insight for those such as stream-enterers, respectively.

Skill in seeing is the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, and skill in development is the knowledge of the paths beginning with that of the once-returner; these proceed by way of causing [the factors] to arise within the mental continuum.
"The knowledge previously described as 'thorough understanding for one who is being led'—in how many ways is that knowledge to be understood?"
Because it is to be asked, it is said: "That knowledge is to be understood in five ways... [omission] ...realization. Because it is to be asked:

"Among those five—beginning with the higher knowledges—which are distinguished by the different types of insight (vipassanā)—which is the higher knowledge (abhiññā), which is full understanding (pariññā), which is abandoning (pahāna), which is development (bhāvanā), and which is realization (sacchikiriyā)?"—therefore, the passage beginning with "Therein, which... is stated.

It has been stated. Therein, "in each case" refers to the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth. "The knowledge of the specific characteristics of phenomena" means the knowledge that proceeds by way of taking as its object the specific characteristics of material phenomena, such as hardness and so on, and the specific characteristics of immaterial phenomena, such as contact and so on;

this is both the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*), which consists in knowing causes and knowing effects, and [the analytical knowledge of meaning], which consists in knowing effects and knowing causes.
And there is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*). This wisdom that knows cause and fruit together with their specific characteristics is called direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Having directly known by means of the knowledge of direct knowledge in the manner thus described—namely, that which is thorough understanding and so forth—one discerns:
"This is blameless and wholesome; this is blameworthy and unwholesome; this is blameworthy and productive of unwholesome fruition; this is productive of wholesome fruition."
"This is blameless; this is defiled and dark; this is undefiled and bright; this is wholesome, beginning with what is blameless, and should be cultivated;

this is unwholesome, beginning with what is blameworthy, and should not be cultivated. Thus, these conditioned phenomena—which have been grasped and comprehended by way of the comprehension of aggregates starting from impermanence and so forth, and which serve as the objects for insight—constitute the fruit of the knowledge of arising and passing away and the subsequent knowledges.
They gradually produce the benefits [of meditation]. Because it arises from that vipassanā which has been produced, they generate access concentration (*upacāra*).

Having thus delimited the meaning as "this is the penetration consisting in the awakening to the truths" regarding those knowledges of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth, which have been grasped and set in motion in due order, one should apply the following:
"This thorough understanding (*parijānanā*) that occurs is what is called 'full understanding' (*pariññā*)."

Having fully understood by means of the wisdom of full comprehension (*pariññā-paññā*) in the manner described above, three things remain: those states that are to be abandoned, those to be developed, and those to be realized. The wisdom that functions as the full comprehension, "Those which are unwholesome are to be abandoned," is abandonment (*pahāna*), the knowledge of abandonment (*pahāna-ñāṇa*).
The wisdom that functions as the full comprehension, "Those which are wholesome are to be developed," is [the knowledge of development].
The wisdom that functions as "that which is unconditioned is to be realized" is the wisdom of realization (*sacchikiriyā-paññā*);
having thus applied [the definitions], the meaning should be understood in accordance with the intention of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, without contradiction.
The fivefold wisdom beginning with direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known by us; [it is] by means of those full understandings (*pariññā*)...
Because it must be said that "the person who knows is called 'one who is praised' (thomīyati)," the passage beginning with "he who" was stated.

In this context, the person who knows in the manner thus described is called "skilled in the meaning" (*atthakusala*) and is praised because of his skill and proficiency regarding the phenomena arisen through conditions;
he is called "skilled in the Dhamma" (*dhammakusala*) because of his skill regarding the phenomena that serve as conditions.
Because he is skilled in the application of the four methods beginning with unity, he is called "skilled in excellence" (*kalyāṇatā-kusala*);

because he is skilled in the attainments of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*), he is called "skilled in fruition" (*phalatā-kusala*); because he is skilled in increases, he is called "skilled in gain" (*āya-kusala*); because he is skilled in decreases, he is called "skilled in loss" (*apāya-kusala*);
and when urgent business or danger arises, he is skilled in that business or danger.
Because he is skilled in the immediate causes for healing when capable of treating them, he is called "skilled in means" (*upāyakusala*);
and because he is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding the great [postures] such as advancing and so forth, he is said to be "possessed of great skill" and is thus praised.
Since it might be asked, "How is the state of skill regarding the meaning and other factors of that one beyond training (*asekkha*) to be believed?"—[the following is stated].
“Thus he said,” and so forth, was stated. The intention is that [the teacher] is to be trusted because it was said, “skilled in all phenomena.
Since the meaning of the phrase “skilled in all phenomena” has been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us, one might ask:
“How have we come to understand in detail the meaning of the phrase ‘a mindful bhikkhu should wander’? To this, it must be said:
“It is with mindfulness that a bhikkhu should wander,” and so forth, has been said. Alternatively, since it was asked by the Blessed One, “It is with mindfulness that a bhikkhu should wander;
endowed with what kind of knowledge accompanied by mindfulness, being mindful, for what purpose should he wander?”—the answer is:
“Endowed with this kind of knowledge accompanied by mindfulness as it occurs regarding these [objects], being mindful, he should wander for this purpose.”
Having thus restrained [the mind], he speaks the passage beginning with “A mindful bhikkhu should wander,” showing how it is to be practiced.
Therein, “by him” means by that bhikkhu who is possessed of mindfulness and wisdom as they occur during the acts of approaching and so forth;

by that bhikkhu who is an Asekha (one beyond training), because his training is fully perfected and he has no further purpose remaining, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life, when approaching... [and so on].
One should dwell in silence, being mindful and endowed with clear comprehension; one should carry out the dwelling known as the turning of the four postures.
“Regarding the paths of training and beyond training that have been explained, in brief, how many kinds are these paths of training and beyond training?”

Because these modes of conduct, termed "ways of practice" (*paṭipadā*), are to be inquired about, he said, "These two modes of conduct," and so forth, in order to show that they are, in brief, twofold according to the individual (*puggala*). Therein,
those modes of conduct which have been demonstrated through the classification of the wholesome qualities to be developed, or through the classification of skill in means (*atthakosalla*),
or through the classification of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) regarding the forward steps and so forth— these are the two modes of conduct authorized by the Blessed One.

It should be understood that there are two [types] by way of person: taught as a practice for those who have already purified themselves—the Arahants—and as a practice for those who are currently purifying themselves—the trainees (sekha).
Why is it that only the one beyond training (asekha) is described and praised with such terms as "he walks mindfully," and so forth, while the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana) is not?
Because it must be said that [the Buddha] is addressed and praised with the words, “He moves mindfully,” etc., the passage beginning with “having performed their duties” was stated.

The faculties of an Arahant have performed their duties; because the faculties have performed their duties, whatever question ought to be asked—all of that fourfold [task] is to be awakened to through the clear realization of the full understanding of suffering... up to ... through the clear realization of the actualization of cessation.

It should be understood as follows. This fourfold object of understanding (*bojjha*) is that which is to be understood (*bojjhitabba*). One who is an *asekha* (one beyond training), having attained full perfection of mindfulness, knows it thus through the realization of thorough knowledge (*pariññā-abhisamaya*) and so forth.

This *asekha* is, in the primary sense, said to be "one who approaches mindfully and departs mindfully for the sake of the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion," and he is thus praised.

The trainee (*sekha*) also knows, through his own direct realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*), that which has been described as the factor of enlightenment (*bojjha*) and that which is to be enlightened upon (*bojjhitabba*).
Therefore, it should be understood that he is called "mindful... [and] free from delusion," and is thus being praised. By this it is said: "Who are those who are purified? The trainees.

Why is it that for both trainees and non-trainees (*asekha*), there is the state of advancing and so forth by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), and the state of the destruction of lust and the other defilements?
Because it must be said that [this] is to be believed, it was stated: "Therefore the Blessed One said: 'A bhikkhu should wander mindfully.

By such statements as "All bodily action of the Blessed One is preceded by knowledge," [it is shown] his lack of craving for agreeable sense-objects, his mental clarity regarding disagreeable sense-objects, and his skillfulness regarding all phenomena for one endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Because it must be asked, "The state of wandering forth has been pointed out by the Teacher; why should we have faith in that [state] which begins with non-longing and so forth?", it was said:

"Therefore he said: 'In regard to sensual pleasures... [etc. ...one should wander forth. The investigation of the question and answer in this verse should also be understood according to the method previously explained in terms of the single foundation and so forth, and the foundation of the Dhamma and so forth.
In the *Vīmaṃsakaṇḍa* of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, having extracted the *Ajita-sutta*, the analysis of questions and answers was expounded by the Teacher and has been understood by us.
Since it must be asked, "What is the analysis of questions and answers among other discourses?",

one should extract the questions and answers from other discourses according to the method of the analysis of questions and answers found in the *Ajita-sutta*, and thus [expound] the analysis of questions and the analysis of answers.
To show that [the method] should be applied, it is said: "It should be asked in this way; it should be answered in this way.

However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, having thus far analyzed the Mode of Conveying Investigation (*vicayahāra*) by means of the *Ajitasutta*—and having thereby demonstrated the investigation of questions and the investigation of answers—the Elder now shows the method for the investigation of questions and answers in other discourses as well, stating: "In this way it should be asked..."
"It should be answered in this way," he said—so it is stated.

In that context, "in this way" means that by following the analysis of the questions as they were posed in the Ajita Sutta, one should extract the discourse proceeding according to those questions and analyze the analysis of the questions;
likewise, by following the analysis of the answers as they were given in the Ajita Sutta...
In other discourses as well, having extracted a discourse that proceeds by way of a response, the "investigation of responses" (*vissajjanavicaya*) should be analyzed.
The investigation of questions and responses has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known to us;

however, because it must be asked, "What is the 'investigation of the recitation following the discourse'? (*suttānugītivicaya*), the words "the recitation following the discourse" (*suttassa ca anugītī*) and so forth were stated. In that context, "of the discourse" (*suttassa*) refers to the discourse that has been extracted.
“Anugīti” refers to the *anugīti* (recapitulation) consisting of the teaching in another sutta. It should be made identical in both meaning and phrasing;

that is, it should be made similar to the sutta to be commented upon in terms of its meaning and its phrasing, or else the *anugīti* should be made identical to the meaning and phrasing of the sutta being commented upon. “In meaning... [and so forth].

Since it must be asked, "What fault indeed would there be in [the meaning] being dissimilar?", it is said: "For when the phrasing (byañjana) deviates from the meaning (attha), it becomes frivolous chatter (samphappalāpa).
Since it must be asked, "The fault has been stated regarding dissimilarity in meaning, and that is known by us;
but what fault indeed would there be in [the phrasing] being dissimilar in its verbal expression?", [it is replied]: "Even the meaning of a word or phrase that is poorly placed..."

"...it becomes a wrong interpretation," it is said. Therefore, because it contains faults, the *anugīti* (recitative verse) should be chanted together with the *sutta* (discourse), complete in both meaning and phrasing.
The analysis of the *anugīti* has been explained by the Teacher and is known to us; however, because it was asked, "What is the analysis of the *sutta*?", the words "the *sutta*...
and so forth were spoken. Therein, "the *sutta*" means the determined *sutta*. "This is the determined *sutta*."
One must investigate whether this was spoken by the Blessed One as a direct statement (*āhacca-vacana*), or whether it was spoken by those reciting it as a contextual statement (*anusandhi-vacana*);
one must investigate whether this determined sutta is of explicit meaning (*nītattha*) or of implicit meaning (*neyyattha*);
and one must investigate whether this determined sutta pertains to defilement (*saṃkilesa-bhāgiya*) or pertains to purification (*vodāna-bhāgiya*).
One must investigate: "Is this determined sutta partaking of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), or is it partaking of the state of one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*)?
Having investigated in this way, if it be a definitive statement (*āhaccavacana*), then, having determined it as "a definitive statement," it should be accepted.
If it be a sutta for those beyond training, then, having determined it as "a sutta for those beyond training," [it should be accepted].
It should be grasped; the meaning is "it is known.

Because it must be asked, "Having investigated the Sutta, having extracted all the truths that constitute the meaning of the Sutta, in which section are they to be seen?", he sets forth the question and then shows: "They are to be seen in this section."
It is said: “Wherein are all [the truths] of this sutta... up to the end?
