Therein, “of this sutta” means that since there is no meaning of a sutta apart from the Four Noble Truths, all the truths are to be seen within the beginning, middle, and end of that very sutta; such is the meaning.
Concluding the investigation of the discourses as they have been stated, he said: "In this way, a discourse is to be investigated.
Because it would be improper to say, "The state of being investigated regarding the questions and so forth as previously stated must be known or believed by us," he said:

"Therefore he said... [etc. ...the subsequent verse (*anugītī*). In that context, by means of that aforementioned state of the questions and so forth being to be investigated, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana [said]: "That which..."

By the words he spoke, beginning with "the question... and so forth, up to "...the sequel," it is meant that you should understand and have faith in the fact that the matter is to be investigated by means of that statement.
Furthermore, one should determine and apply whether the mode of investigation and the method of analysis (hāra) described above are complete, or whether there is something else as well.

Because it must be asked, "Is there [anything]? it is said: "The Mode of Conveying Investigation (vicaya-hāra) is applied. In this regard, the investigation of questions, the investigation of answers, the investigation of sequence, the investigation of repetition, and the investigation of the Sutta are analyzed according to their specific forms.
The intention is that by means of these, the remaining investigations—such as the investigation of gratification (assāda), and so forth—are to be appropriately determined and applied as is fitting.
Thus, the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Investigation has been composed in accordance with one's own strength and ability.
The Exposition of Analysis is finished.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
3. The Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Logical Reasoning (*Yuttihāra*).

18. By whichever specific mode of commentary consisting of the analysis of the "String of Investigation" (vicayahāra-vibhaṅga) the word-questions and so forth were investigated, that specific mode of commentary consisting of the analysis of the "String of Investigation" was completed. Because it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the 'String of Reasoning' (yuttihāra-vibhaṅga)?", it is said:
"In this regard, what is the 'String of Reasoning'? and so forth. Therein, "in those [cases]" (tattha tattha) refers to those [instances] already specified.
Among the sixteen modes (hāra), he asked: "Which specific exposition is the Mode of Reasoning (yuttihāra) and the Analysis of the Mode of Reasoning (yuttihāravibhaṅga)?

It should be understood that the detailed exposition beginning with "This is the Mode of Reasoning," which follows the summary description beginning with "Of all the modes," is what is called the Analysis of the Mode of Reasoning.
Therefore it was said: "In this context, 'Which is the Mode of Reasoning? and so forth, is the Analysis of the Mode of Reasoning."
"What is this Mode of Conveying a Reason (yuttihāra)? It asks what should be joined by way of the suitability or unsuitability of the meaning of the Thread.
Now, the meaning of a Thread is twofold: the meaning grasped in an incorrect manner, and the meaning grasped in the correct manner.
Among these, only the meaning grasped in an incorrect manner is to be joined by means of determining the reason according to reality; as for the other—

However, it should be applied merely by way of stating the facts. Since this exposition known as the "Investigation of Reasoning" (yuttigavesanā) cannot occur without the Great Authorities (mahāpadesā), therefore, while analyzing the Mode of Conveying Reasoning (yuttihāra), [the author] first pointed out its characteristic by saying, "The four great authorities," and so forth.
In that context, "great authorities" (mahāpadesā) refers to the great ones, such as the Buddha...
The reasons stated by way of reference, or the great references and foundations for the Dhamma. It is called a "reference" (*apadesa*) because it is referred to;
thus, "having the Buddha as its reference" means that the Buddha is the source of this reason, hence "Buddha-reference. The same method should be applied to the others as well.
Having said, "I heard this discourse (*sutta*) in the presence of the Buddha," regarding the text brought forward, [one should verify it] by means of the Suttas and the Vinaya.

The intended meaning is that the *mahāpadesa* (great reference) is the criterion for determining whether a teaching is "in accordance with the Dhamma" (*saṃsandana*) or "not in accordance with the Dhamma" (*asaṃsandana*). This refers to a text brought forward after stating:
"I have received this in the presence of the Buddha; I have received this in the presence of the Saṅgha;
I have received this in the presence of many elders; I have received this in the presence of a single elder."
Whatever phrases of phrasing and phrases of meaning there may be, those words and phrases should be introduced and inserted into the discourses taught by the Blessed One;

they should be shown and compared with the discipline (*vinaya*), that is, the discipline regarding passion and so forth. They should be placed alongside and included within the nature of things (*dhammatā*).
This applies if [they accord] with the meaning of the discourses, the meaning of the discipline, and the nature of things.

The intention is that, since they are not contradictory, those words and phrases brought forward by you should be accepted as being appropriate—this having been stated by those who make the determination.
[They] should be made to descend into, demonstrated in accordance with, and compared against the Sutta, the Vinaya, and the nature of the Dhamma; thus it was said by the Teacher.
Because it must be stated, "In which Sutta, in which Vinaya, or by what natural law (dhammatā) were they spoken?", the passage beginning with "In which Sutta" was stated.
Therein, "among the four Noble Truths" means among those Suttas that reveal the four Noble Truths.
"The subduing of lust" (rāgavinaya) refers to that by which lust is destroyed and pacified, such as the meditation on the foul (asubha); what is that? It is the sign of the foul and so forth.
"That which he possesses is the removal of lust (*rāgavinaya*). What is that? It is a specific type of discourse (*suttanta*) that shows the signs of foulness (*asubha*) and so forth.

This same method applies to "the removal of hatred" (*dosavinaya*) and the others as well. What is called "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is that which, avoiding the views of eternalism and annihilationism, demonstrates the nature of phenomena such as ignorance and formations by way of their being conditions and the states produced by those conditions, through the exposition of the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*) and so forth.
It was said: “In which natural law (dhammatā) should these [passages] be placed? In dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
Since it could be asked, “If they descend into the suttas and so forth, appearing there without contradiction, why would they not produce [conviction]?

the words beginning with “in the four” were stated. Therein, having said, “I have brought this from the presence of the Buddha and others,” the text thus brought is [to be applied] to the four noble truths.

If it descends [into the heart], then in that case the introduced text does not generate taints. If it is seen to accord with the discipline of the defilements such as lust, then in that case the introduced text does not generate taints.
And if it does not contradict the nature of phenomena (dhammatā), then in that case the introduced text does not generate taints;
this is how the meaning should be understood.
Since it must be asked, "For what purpose are the four great authorities (mahāpadesa) brought forward in the *Yuttihāravibhaṅga*?",

he says, "By means of the four great authorities," and so forth. In that regard, whatever kind of meaning or whatever kind of doctrine in the texts brought forward is consistent with the four great authorities,
that meaning or that doctrine should be taken from the suttas to be commented upon.
By whatever reason it accords with the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*), that specific reason should be grasped from the sutta to be commented upon by way of commentary.

In whatever manner it accords with the four great authorities, that specific manner should be grasped from the sutta to be commented upon by way of commentary. For the purpose of such grasping, the four...
The meaning is: "The great authorities have been brought forth.

19. Since it was stated by the Teacher that "whatever category of meaning is consistent with and not contradicted by the four great authorities (mahāpadesa) is to be accepted," and because it must be asked, "Where and by what means is the determination of consistency to be made?", [the text] says, "by one who asks a question," and so forth.

It has been stated: "The person who is asked a question must provide a reasoned determination. In this context, "question" (*pañha*) refers to the phenomenon (*dhamma*) possessing an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) that is to be questioned. "By the one who is asked" refers to the wise person capable of answering.
"Question" (*pañha*) refers to the text proceeding by way of inquiry. [One must first determine] how many words there are, word by word.
It should be thoroughly investigated, examined by means of reasoning, and scrutinized. Because it was asked, "How should it be examined?", the passage beginning with "If all [the terms]" was stated.

Therein, regarding the phrase "all the terms," if all the terms without exception in the questioned text express one and the same meaning, then, in that case, there is a single question by way of meaning. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
Therefore it was said: “Because of the desire to know that single meaning.
“Single” means a question of one kind according to its sense. By a person who is investigating, that which is unknown must be firmly known.
Since it must be asked, “What is the mode of understanding? he spoke the words beginning with “What are these phenomena? in order to show the mode of understanding.

In this context, the construction is: "Having investigated through reasoning—'Are these textual teachings (pariyattidhamma) which are to be praised different in meaning, or are they different in phrasing;
or rather, do these textual teachings have a single meaning and only the phrasing is different?'—they are to be understood.
[The question is: "What would the aforementioned question be?"
Because it was to be asked, in order to show a portion of the question as previously stated, he asked, "In what way might it be?
and then said, "In the same way as that," and so forth.
In that verse of inquiry—by what quality (*dhamma*) is one struck down, just as a thief is struck down by a man who is a murderer?
The world of beings is always beset; like a tree upon which the *māluva* creeper depends, it is surrounded and overwhelmed by its own support.
By what phenomenon is the world of beings always surrounded and overwhelmed?
Like one pierced and entered by a spreading arrow-head, by what arrow is the world of beings always pierced and entered? Of what, and by what?
The construction is: "For what reason is the world of beings always smoldering and tormented?
Because it was to be asked, "How many words are there in this verse of inquiry?", the words beginning with "These" were spoken.
Therein, "those which were asked" refers to the four words whose meanings were inquired after. Because it was to be asked, "How many questions are there?"...
“Those three questions,” it is said.

Since the Blessed One answers them for the sake of the deity, they are understood as “the three questions” by virtue of that answering. Because it must be asked, “What is the verse of the answer?”—[it follows]:
“The world is struck down by death, surrounded by old age;”
"Pierced by the dart of craving, one is always smothered by desire"—so it was said.
In that verse of response: just as a thief is struck down by an executioner, so too is the world of beings constantly struck down by death;
just as a tree upon which the *māluva* creeper depends is surrounded and overwhelmed by it.
The world of beings is always surrounded and overwhelmed by old age as if by a forest fire;
the world of beings is always pierced and entered by the arrow of craving, as if struck and penetrated by a spreading barb;
and the world of beings is always smoldering and tormented by desire—this is the construction of the meaning.
20. Because it must be asked, “What is death? What is aging?”, the passage beginning with “In that regard, aging... was stated. Therein, “in that regard” (*tattha*) refers to this verse of response.

Aging, which was mentioned in the second line, and death, which was mentioned in the first line—these two are the conditioned characteristics (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*) of the fivefold aggregate that is conditioned; they belong to the fivefold aggregate that is conditioned.
The meaning is that it is not perceived separately once released.
Because it must be explained how the distinction between aging and death—the characteristics of the conditioned—is to be known, it was said: "Of that which stands in aging," and so forth.

In this context, "the alteration of that which stands in aging" refers to the alteration of the continuity of the aggregates (*khandhappabandha*) while it persists; this is what is called manifest aging.
There is no aging in the duration of a moment. "Death is passing away" refers only to conventional death (*sammutimaraṇa*), that is, the falling away from existence;
it is not momentary death, nor is it death as annihilation. Therefore it is said: "Arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which persists is discerned.
If death were to occur only for that which persists, then, this being the case, the distinction between aging and death would not be logical; such a lack of logic [would result].
Since it would have to be said that even the statement "those three questions" would be inappropriate if [the former] existed, the passage beginning with "In that regard, by means of aging...
was stated. Therein, "therein" (tattha) means that in this verse of response, a difference in meaning between aging and death as they were stated is appropriate.
Because it must be asked, "For what reason is it logical? In what way should diversity be accepted?", it is said:

"For even those in the womb die. Since beings in the womb who have not yet reached old age nevertheless die, therefore diversity must be accepted. Because it must be asked, "Could those in the womb reach old age?"...
"And they do not become decayed," it is said. Even those who have reached old age die before reaching "decayed-old-age" because they have not yet become decayed;
thus, since death occurs here for one who is devoid of decayed-old-age as intended in this context, it should be understood that decay is one thing and death is another.
It is not only for those in the womb that there is death before reaching decayed-old-age.
Because it could be said that "others also have [death]," it was stated: "And there is death for the devas.
Because it could be said that "the devas too might reach old age due to their long duration of existence," it was stated: "Yet their bodies do not decay.
Because it could be said that "this alone is the reason for the difference between aging and death," the phrase beginning with "or they can" was used to show that there is another [reason] as well.
It has been said. In this context, the meaning is that while it is indeed possible to provide a remedy for old age and decay, it is absolutely impossible to provide a remedy for death;
for this reason as well, the distinction between aging and death must certainly be accepted.
Why was it stated, "it is not possible to provide a remedy for death"? Is it not because of the cultivation of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*)?
Reflecting on the admonition that if one attains mastery [over the mind], it is possible to perform a counteraction even against death, it was said:
"Except for those possessing psychic power (*iddhimanta*), within the domain of their psychic power.
The mutual distinction between aging and death has been shown by the Teacher and is understood by us; however, how...
Because it must be said that there is a difference between craving and aging-and-death, the passage beginning with "But as for what...

was stated in order to show the distinctness of craving from them. Since even those who are free from lust are seen to age and die even though craving is absent in them, the difference between craving and aging-and-death must be accepted.
“Since it must be said that ‘craving has the characteristic of aging and disintegration,’ what fault could there be in its being non-different from those [characteristics]?

To show the fault [in this view], the passage beginning with “And if” was stated. Just as aging and death are manifest by way of the characteristic of aging and disintegration, so too craving is manifest by way of the characteristic of aging and disintegration. And if this were the case; even for one who is in the prime of youth—
"All young men would be free from craving, yet they are not free from craving; therefore, diversity must be accepted.
To show that otherwise another fault would follow, it was said: "And just as craving is the cause of suffering," and so forth.

In this context, if aging and death were non-different from craving, then since craving is the craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*), there would be the origination of suffering through that very craving. Thus...
Aging and death could also be the origin of suffering. Since aging and death are not the origin of suffering, therefore the distinction between craving and aging and death must be understood.
To show that if there were no difference between them, this fault would also follow, [the text says]: "And just as craving is to be destroyed by the Path," and so forth.

It has been stated. In that regard, if there were no difference between craving (*taṇhā*) and those [factors] by way of that identity, then just as craving is to be abandoned by the Path, so too would aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) be to be abandoned by the Path.
Or, just as aging-and-death is not to be abandoned by the Path, so too craving would not be to be abandoned by the Path.
But such is not the case, because of their respective states of being abandonable and non-abandonable; therefore, [craving is distinct] from aging-and-death.

The diversity [between craving and aging-and-death] is to be understood. Since it must be stated that "the distinctness of craving from aging-and-death is to be sought through the very proof and reasoning expressed by the words 'If,
moreover,' etc.," the passage beginning with "By this reasoning" was stated in order to show that it is to be sought by other reasons as well.
In this context, "by this reasoning" means by this reasoning and justification stated as "If, moreover," and so forth.
The meaning is that the distinctness of craving from aging and death is to be sought through various reasons—that is, through various reasons in the form of justifications.
Why was it said, "It is to be sought through various reasons"?
Having taken to heart the objection that "a difference is indeed visible both in terms of reasoning and in terms of meaning," he says, "And if it is visible," and so forth.

The meaning of this is: if a difference from death and from craving is visible both in terms of reasoning and in terms of meaning, then a difference must certainly be sought even in terms of the phrasing (*byañjana*).
Because it must be stated, “How is difference to be sought according to the phrasing? the passage beginning with “Or ‘an arrow’” was spoken.

Therein, for these phenomena—namely, desire and craving—which are expressed by the two phrases “an arrow” (*salla*) or “smoking” (*dhūpāyana*), identity and sameness in meaning are appropriate, not difference. Whether as “an arrow” or as “smoking,” [they refer to the same thing].
Or rather, it is not logical for aging and death—which are spoken of by means of two distinct terms—to have identity with craving.

To clarify this very point, the passage beginning with “for it is not so” was stated. Therein, the construction is as follows: it is not logical that there is a difference in meaning between desire (*icchā*) and craving (*taṇhā*);
rather, their identity alone is logical. This is because, through desire and craving, the occurrence of aging and destruction [respectively] follows from aging and death.
Since it could be asked, "Why is distinctness appropriate when there is oneness through craving?
the passage beginning with "In the intention of craving" was stated. Therein, when the intention of craving is not fulfilled, anger arises and resentment arises regarding the nine grounds for malice;
and when aging and death are not fulfilled, anger arises regarding the nine grounds for malice.
...does not arise, and ill-will does not arise. Thus, by this reasoning, it should be understood that aging, death, and craving are indeed distinct in meaning.
If it were logical for desire and craving to be identical in meaning, then why did the Blessed One say, "Stricken by death..."?
In the verse beginning with “The world,” the statement “pierced by the dart of craving, always smoldering with desire” is expressed in two ways;
in order to avoid this objection, he says, “But that which was spoken by the Blessed One,” and so forth.
Therein, that which was designated by these two names—“desire” (*icchā*) and “craving” (*taṇhā*)—that designation was made by the Blessed One.

The meaning should be understood as follows: it is entirely appropriate that there is identity, not difference, because this [craving] is designated by the two names "desire" (icchā) and "thirst" (taṇhā) through the act of naming, based on the various objects such as visible forms—which are external things to be desired and longed for.
Thus, it is rightly considered a single entity.
Because it must be said, "By what means is it appropriate to believe that desire, craving, and so forth— which are spoken of as twofold by way of name—
are one and the same," the passage beginning with "by all" was stated. Therein, since all cravings such as desire, though differentiated by various names,
are indeed appropriate as having a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of clinging (*ajjhosāna*), therefore, even though they are divided by way of name—
It should be seen that unity is logically consistent with a single characteristic; it should be believed.

Because it must be asked, "In what way is it logical?", the words "Just as all... and so forth are stated. Therein, just as all fire—which is manifold by way of wood-fire and so on—is of a single characteristic through the characteristic of heat, so too [the five aggregates] are of a single characteristic through the characteristic of clinging (*ajjhosāna*); such is the construction. Of all fire...

The passage beginning with "Moreover" (*apicā*) was stated in order to show, according to their respective forms, the numerous names [given to craving] by way of its objects (*upādāna*). Its meaning is clear.

The construction should be understood as follows: craving has been designated by the Blessed One by various names according to its objects; likewise, fire has been designated by various names according to its fuel (*upādāna*).

Since it must be asked, "Is craving (taṇhā) expressed by the very names that appear in the verse of response?", the passage beginning with "It is also called 'desire' (icchā),' etc., was stated to show that it is expressed by many names.

Therein: it is called *icchā* because beings desire (*icchanti*) the objects to be desired, such as visible forms and other sense-objects; it is called *taṇhā* because they thirst (*tasanti*) by means of it; it is called *salla* because it pierces (*sallati*) or enters [the heart]."
They are "arrows" (*salla*) because they spread forth like an arrow; or else, they are "arrows" because they bring about or take up torment (*santāpa*);
or else, they are "arrows" because they bring about and cause torment to proceed. They are "fuming" (*dhūpāyanā*) because they fume, torment, and burn.

They are "streams" (*saritā*) because they flow, drag along, and carry away like a swift-flowing river; or else, they are "streams" because they flow and sting. They are "clinging" (*visattikā*) because they spread out.
It is called *sineha* (affection) because it moistens by way of attachment. It is called *kilamatha* (weariness) because it produces exhaustion in various states of existence (*gati*).
It is called *maññanā* (conceit) because beings conceive of objects such as forms through it. It is called *bandha* (bondage) because it binds one to existence (*bhava*).

It is called *āsā* (hope) because it is hoped for or desired; or alternatively, *āsā* is that by which one hopes or desires. It is called *pipāsā* (thirst) because one thirsts for it, or because one thirsts for the flavor of the object.
Thirst (*pipāsā*). "That which is to be delighted in" is delight (*abhinandanā*); or, that by which one delights is delight. It should be understood in detail according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Since it might be asked, "By whom can the state of being addressed by craving through its various modes such as 'desire' and so forth be believed?

the phrase beginning with "And as in the synonyms" was stated. In the analysis of the Synonyms Chapter (*Vevacanahāra-vibhaṅga*), that craving which is described as "longing and yearning... [etc. ...synonyms" is [craving].

Just as it was stated—in whatever manner it was stated—one should have faith that the state of being addressed by craving, through its various modes such as longing and so forth, is indeed as it was stated.
Because it might be asked, "Even though it was stated by the Teacher in the *Vevacanavibhaṅga*, how can one have faith in what was not stated by the Blessed One?
the phrase "just as the Blessed One said," and so forth, was stated. [The question continues: "In whatever manner the Blessed One..."
Regarding the statement beginning with “In form there is for her,” etc., it means that one should have faith in that word as it was spoken in such a manner.

“It is thus consistent” means that according to the method stated, because desire (*icchā*) and craving (*taṇhā*) are identical in meaning, and because aging, death, and craving are distinct in meaning, the statement “three questions” that was uttered is consistent; this is how the meaning should be understood.

21. Regarding the statement, “Three questions are stated in the verse beginning ‘By what is the world struck down? the teacher has analyzed the reasoning for the existence of these three questions, and we too have understood it.
Since it might be asked, “How is the reasoning to be known through other modes besides those?
he speaks the passage beginning with “All that is designated as suffering,” demonstrating the search for reasoning through other modes as well. Therein, *sabba*...

It is logical that "the range of suffering" (*dukkhūpacāra*) has its root in the formations (*saṅkhāra*) conditioned by craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*); however, it is not logical that "the entire range of disenchantment" (*nibbidūpacāra*) has its root in the requisites (*parikkhāra*) of craving for sense-pleasures.
As for the meaning of the words: the range (*upacāra*) of suffering is its occurrence (*pavatti*), thus it is "the range of suffering.

That which has as its root a formation occurring with craving for sense-pleasures as its condition is "rooted in the formations conditioned by craving for sense-pleasures. The range of disenchantment is its occurrence; thus...

It is the vicinity of revulsion (*nibbidūpacāra*). Because the object of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), which serves as the equipment for craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), is its root, it is called "rooted in the equipment of craving for sense-pleasures" (*kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlaka*).

In this context, while weariness characterized by dissatisfaction (*anabhirati*)—termed revulsion—is appropriately rooted in the equipment of craving for sense-pleasures, knowledge-revulsion (*ñāṇanibbidā*) is not appropriately so rooted;
therefore, the entire vicinity of revulsion is rooted in the equipment of craving for sense-pleasures.
However, it was stated that this is not tenable. For it must be asked:

"Is the very same reasoning explained by the Teacher regarding the absence of the threefold pentad and regarding the figurative usage of 'suffering' and 'disenchantment' to be observed, or should some other reasoning besides this one be sought? Thus it should be said.
In order to demonstrate this method, he said, "By this," and so forth. This is what is meant:

following this method of reasoning—which I have analyzed regarding both the threefold nature of the aggregates and the figurative application of the terms "suffering" and "disenchantment"—one should also seek out the underlying logic in various passages of the scriptures by means of their respective causes.

Because it must be said, “This demonstration of the method is concise; it is not possible to seek it in detail,” the following passage beginning with “Just as the Blessed One” was commenced in order to show that method of demonstration by analyzing it in detail.

Since the loathsome nature of the foul (asubha) is repulsive, the arising of lust is not appropriate; therefore, for a person of lustful temperament, the teaching on the foul is appropriate for the subduing of lust.

Because loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the direct antidote to hatred (*dosa*), the teaching on loving-kindness is appropriate for the subduing of hatred in a person of a hateful temperament (*dosacarita*).

Because dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is the domain of wisdom (*paññā*), the teaching on dependent origination is appropriate for the subduing of delusion (*moha*) in a person of a deluded temperament (*mohacarita*).
[An objection might be raised: "The teaching on loving-kindness and the like would also be suitable for one of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*), because it is common to all sentient beings."
Because it ought to be said, the passage beginning with "If indeed the Blessed One" was stated.

Since a person of sharp defilements and a lustful temperament (rāgacarita) is intended here, if he were to teach such a person the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti), then, because lust would arise even by way of loving-kindness, the teaching would not be appropriate.

Or, if he were to teach the pleasant path (sukhā paṭipadā), then, because a painful path (dukkhā paṭipadā) is appropriate for one of lustful temperament, [the teaching would likewise not be appropriate].

The teaching is not tenable. Or, even if one were to teach abandonment preceded by insight (vipassanā), since it is difficult for one of lustful temperament (rāgacarita) to practice insight-preceded abandonment while avoiding the contemplation of the foul (asubhānupassanā), the teaching is not tenable—this is the construction [of the argument].
By the passage beginning, “The Blessed One [taught] for one of lustful temperament,” the reasoning is not analyzed exhaustively; rather, it is merely a demonstration of the method (naya).
In order to show that other [methods] should also be sought by means of the method that has been demonstrated, it was said: "Thus, whatever...

and so forth. Whatever conformable abandonment of lust, whatever conformable abandonment of hatred, and whatever conformable abandonment of delusion has been taught—all that conformable abandonment, however many scriptural passages there may be [that describe it]...

The construction is as follows: having investigated by means of the method of investigation regarding those very [topics] which are the ground of knowledge, one should then apply them by means of the method of application (*yutti-hāra*).

Since it must be said that "the application should be sought by way of the abandoning of lust and so forth," the passage beginning with "of one who dwells in loving-kindness" (*mettāvihārissa*) is commenced in order to show the seeking of application by analyzing it further through other factors, such as mastery over the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) like loving-kindness, the fruit-attainments (*phala-samāpatti*), and the nine successive attainments (*anupubbasa-māpatti*). Therein, for one who dwells in loving-kindness...

For a person who actually exists and dwells in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*), the teaching that "ill-will (*byāpāda*) will persist, seizing the mind"—because loving-kindness is the direct opposite of ill-will—is not tenable;

however, the teaching that "for one dwelling in loving-kindness, ill-will is abandoned and passes away" is tenable. This applies likewise to one who dwells in compassion (*karuṇāvihāra*) and has attained the dwelling in compassion.
For a person who exists and is present, the teaching that "because compassion is the opposite of cruelty, cruelty will persist by seizing the mind" is not tenable;
however, the teaching that "for one who dwells in compassion, cruelty is abandoned and goes to destruction" is tenable.
This applies to a person who exists and is present, who dwells in sympathetic joy and has attained the dwelling in sympathetic joy.
Because joy (*muditā*) is the direct opposite of discontent (*arati*), the teaching that "discontent will persist by seizing the mind" is untenable;
however, the teaching that "for one who dwells in joy, the abandonment of discontent goes to its utter disappearance" is tenable.
For a person who dwells in equanimity (*upekkhā*), who has attained the dwelling in equanimity, and who exists [as such], equanimity is the direct opposite of lust (*rāga*).
The teaching that "lust will persist by seizing the mind" is not tenable; however, the teaching that "for one dwelling in equanimity, lust is abandoned and passes away" is tenable.
This applies to one who dwells in the signless, having attained the dwelling of the fruition-attainment by way of the contemplation of impermanence.

The teaching that "for a person who exists, consciousness proceeds by following signs—precisely by following those various signs of formations—with a sign abandoned regarding permanence and so forth" is not tenable;

however, because the contemplation of the signless is the antidote to the perversions of permanence and so forth, the teaching that "for one who dwells in the signless, the abandonment of the sign goes to its destruction" is tenable. "I am..."
The five aggregates, which are the objects of conceiving (*maññita*), are devoid of a self; I do not regard them thus: "This fivefold aggregate is I.
Yet, even while such a view is absent, the teaching would not be logical if the dart of doubt and perplexity—thinking "What am I?
and "How am I?"—were to persist, seizing hold of the mind. This is because [the teaching] serves as a means for the abandonment of doubt.
The teaching that “for one who does not regard this pentad of aggregates as ‘I am,’ the arrow of doubt and perplexity is abandoned and comes to an end” is appropriate. Since it must be said,
“The application [of the teaching] should be sought by way of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) alone,” it is also [appropriate] by way of the attainment of jhāna.
The passage beginning with "Or how, moreover, the first jhāna... was undertaken in order to show that the logical consistency (*yutti*) must be investigated;

or else, because it might be asked, "Should the logical consistency be sought only for one who dwells in the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*)," this passage was begun to show that the logical consistency must also be sought by way of the attainments of the jhānas. In that regard:

Just as the logical consistency must be sought for one who has attained the first *jhāna* and is dwelling in the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*), so too must the logical consistency be sought for one who dwells in the attainment of the *jhānas*. How so?
For one who has attained the first *jhāna*, for a person existing as a possessor of the first *jhāna*, sensual desire and ill-will [are absent] due to the suppression of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The teaching that [these] lead to the distinction of the second jhāna is not tenable; the teaching that sensual lust and ill will lead to the decline of the jhāna is tenable.

The teaching that perception and attention accompanied by applied thought, together with the phenomena of access concentration, lead to the decline of the second jhāna is not tenable; [rather, it is] those accompanied by applied thought...
The teaching that "perception and attention lead to distinction for the sake of higher jhāna" is appropriate.
For a person who has attained the second jhāna— one who exists and is present—

perceptions and attention accompanied by applied and sustained thought, together with the factors of access concentration, [lead] to distinction from the factors of the first jhāna for the sake of higher jhāna.

The teaching that [they] "conduce" is not tenable; however, the teaching that "perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by applied and sustained thought conduce to the decline of the non-applied jhāna" is tenable.

Alternatively, the teaching that "perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by equanimity, together with the factors of access, and the factors of the fourth jhāna, conduce to the decline of the jhāna" is not tenable; [rather, it is] those accompanied by equanimity...
The teaching that "perception and attention lead to distinction for the sake of higher jhāna" is appropriate.

In the remaining cases as well, the application should be made according to the meaning. "Citta" (mind) refers to that which is familiar through mastery over the aforementioned attainments—that is, familiar in its fitness.
One should not seek logical consistency only in this much; one should also seek the logic as it is found within the ninefold Suttanta.
To show that [the method] is to be performed, the words beginning with "Thus all" were spoken.

Since it might be asked, "By whom can the fact that all the *hāras*—whose stages and spheres of operation have been stated as such—are to be investigated by means of the method of investigation (*vicaya-hāra*) and then joined together by means of the method of reasoning (*yutti-hāra*) be believed?", the words beginning with "Therefore he said" were spoken.
In that context, by virtue of that necessity of being joined together, the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke the passage beginning with "Of all... and so forth.
What he says, by that word he is to be trusted— this is what is meant.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* composed in accordance with the power of the faculties, within the analysis of the "Jewel of Reasoning" (*Yuttihāravibhaṅga*).
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
4. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Footings (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra-vibhaṅga-vibhāvanā). 22.
By whichever specific method of exposition, which constitutes the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Logical Reasoning (*yutti-hāra*), such as the answering of questions and so forth...
The state of being appropriate or inappropriate has been analyzed; that analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reason (Yuttihāra), which constitutes a specific type of commentary, is now complete.
Since it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Footings (Padaṭṭhānahāra)?", the passage beginning with "In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Footings? is commenced.

Regarding the phrase "in this context" (*tattha*): among those sixteen modes of conveying taught, such as the Mode of Conveying Teaching (Desanāhāra) and the rest, what specific type of commentary is it?

He asks: “What is the ‘Analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Footing’ (padaṭṭhāna-hāra-vibhaṅga)? It should be understood that the specific detailed commentary now being stated by me—beginning with “This is the Mode of Conveying the Footing”—which follows the exposition beginning with “The Victor taught the Dhamma,” is the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Footing.
Therefore it was said: “In this context, what is the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Footing? And so forth.”
Having posed the question, "When this method of 'word-basis' (*padaṭṭhāna*), which is now being explained in detail,
is taught among the doctrines set forth in the Three Baskets (*piṭaka*), what kind of doctrine does it teach and what does it describe?",
and having determined that "this is the proximate cause for this proximate fruit," the passage beginning with "This is the word-basis" was stated in order to analyze it.
The meaning of this is as follows: Ignorance (*avijjā*) has the characteristic of the non-penetration of all knowable phenomena (*viññeyya-dhamma*) as they truly are;

thus it is "characterized by the non-penetration of the true nature of all phenomena. The proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), or immediate condition, for that ignorance is the perversions (*vipallāsa*), such as perceiving the "beautiful" (*subha*) in the unattractive (*asubha*).
When these perversions exist, ignorance proceeds, arising further and further and not diminishing.

Therefore, the perversions (vipallāsā) are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), that is, the immediate condition, for ignorance (avijjā). Since ignorance is the root of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa), it should be understood that the proximate cause is analyzed starting from that [ignorance].

Because craving (taṇhā) is likewise the root of the cycle of existence, immediately following that, the proximate cause of craving is analyzed with the words "characterized by attachment" (ajjhosānalakkhaṇā), and so forth.

It has been said. In that context, "the agreeable form" (*piyarūpa*) and "the pleasant form" (*sātarūpa*) refer to the class of phenomena beginning with the eye, which possess the nature of being dear and the nature of being pleasant.
When there exist such things as the eye that are dear and pleasant, craving (*taṇhā*) proceeds and arises repeatedly;
therefore, the agreeable form and the pleasant form constitute the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), the immediate condition, for craving.

When taking what is not given exists, greed proceeds; therefore, taking what is not given is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for greed. For even if taking what is not given occurs but once, it remains an immediate cause for greed because one fails to see its danger.

Likewise, although the perception of beauty (*subhasaññā*) operates toward unattractive things such as hair and so forth, lack of restraint (*asaṃvara*) regarding the eye-faculty and the rest is the proximate cause for that perception of beauty, because its characteristic consists in grasping the colors (blue, etc.), the shapes (long, etc.), and the secondary features (smiling, etc.).

Because it has the characteristic of approaching contact that is subject to taints (*āsava*), the perception of pleasure that occurs even regarding the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*) and so forth is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for the gratification found in form and the other aggregates.

Because it has the characteristic of not correctly discerning phenomena that possess the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*), the perception of permanence that occurs even regarding the impermanent aggregates of form and so forth is the proximate cause for the consciousness that grasps the aggregates of form and so forth as permanent.

Even though the perception of self occurs regarding the aggregates and so forth— which are characterized as impermanent, suffering, and non-self— the mental body (nāmakāya) that proceeds by way of "I" and "mine" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the perception of self, because the perception of impermanence and the perception of suffering lack the characteristic of observing [these aggregates] as such.
Having thus shown the proximate causes for unwholesome states such as ignorance, he now says, "characterized by the full penetration of all phenomena," etc.,
in order to show the proximate causes for the states such as true knowledge (vijjā), which are their opposites.

It has been said: because true knowledge (*vijjā*) occurring in relation to all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*) has the characteristic of penetrating all phenomena, all that is knowable is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for true knowledge.
Because serenity (*samatha*) has the characteristic of suppressing restlessness—which is defined as mental distraction—it [is the proximate cause].

The foulness that has become the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for serenity (samatha). For, since foulness is the antidote to craving, and serenity persists when craving is absent, [foulness serves as its basis].

Because non-greed, which occurs by way of abstaining from taking what is not given, has the characteristic of withdrawing the sphere of desire, abstaining from taking what is not given is the proximate cause for non-greed.
Abstention from taking life is the proximate cause for non-hatred, because non-hatred, which occurs by way of abstaining from taking life, has the characteristic of being free from malice.
Right practice is the proximate cause for non-delusion, because non-delusion, which occurs by way of right practice, has the characteristic of not erring regarding the true nature of things.

Disenchantment is [the proximate cause] for the perception of foulness, because the perception of foulness, which occurs by way of disenchantment, has the characteristic of apprehending a livid corpse, a festering corpse, and so forth.

The perception of the foul is the proximate cause for the knowledge of disenchantment; for through the knowledge of disenchantment, dissatisfaction arises, and with that dissatisfaction, the perception of the foul becomes established.

Feeling is the proximate cause for the perception of suffering, because the perception of suffering—arising by way of painful feeling—is characterized by the full comprehension of contact associated with the taints.

Because the perception of impermanence—which occurs by way of arising and passing away—has the characteristic of contemplating conditioned phenomena as they possess the characteristics of the formed, arising and passing away are the proximate cause for the perception of impermanence;
for it is by contemplating arising and passing away that the perception of impermanence proceeds.

Because the perception of non-self—which occurs by way of the perception of mere phenomena—has the characteristic of non-adherence to all phenomena, the perception of phenomena is the proximate cause for the perception of non-self.
Because sensual lust has the five strands of sensual pleasure—forms and so forth—as its object, the five strands of sensual pleasure are the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of sensual lust.

Because lust for form, which occurs with reference to the body known as "form," proceeds by way of the five sense-faculties such as the eye, the five faculties are the forms that serve as the proximate cause of lust for form.
The six sense bases (*chaḷāyatana*) are the proximate cause of lust for existence, which occurs by way of attachment to becoming. Thus it is said: "observing the becoming that has been produced."
Delighting in form that proceeds in such a manner as, “May such undesirable form not arise; may such desirable form arise; may such painful feeling not arise;
may such pleasant feeling arise”—this is the proximate cause for the five aggregates of clinging.

Because the knowledge of the ownership of kamma is accompanied by the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the vision of the knowledge of recollecting past lives is the proximate cause for the knowledge of the ownership of kamma.
Faith has "conviction" as its characteristic; thus, faith is characterized by conviction. Faith also has "resolute confidence" as its manifestation;
thus, faith is manifested as resolute confidence. Clarity is the characteristic of serenity.
"Clarity characterized by being undisturbed" is confidence (*pasāda*). Confidence that has "tranquillity as its manifestation" is confidence manifested as tranquillity.
Furthermore, that confidence should be understood as a specific state of faith (*saddhā*) itself.

Confidence of certainty (*aveccapasāda*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for faith characterized by longing; faith characterized by conviction (*okappana*) is the proximate cause for clarity characterized by being undisturbed.
The fourfold right exertion (*sammappadhāna*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for energy (*vīriya*), which has the characteristic of instigation;

the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) regarding the body and so forth are the proximate cause for mindfulness (*sati*), which has the characteristic of non-forgetfulness; the jhānas such as applied thought (*vitakka*) are the proximate cause for concentration (*samādhi*), because concentration accompanied by jhāna has the characteristic of one-pointedness;
and [the aggregates] are the proximate cause for wisdom (*paññā*), because wisdom has the characteristic of understanding the function and understanding the object.
The truths are the footing for wisdom.
Since it must be asked, "Of which phenomena are those beginning with ignorance—the footings of which were analyzed by the Teacher—their respective footings?
in order to show that those factors beginning with ignorance are likewise the footings of these phenomena:
“Another method,” etc., was said. Ignorance (*avijjā*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*), which is characterized by attending to gratification.
For it is through the concealment of danger that improper attention arises from ignorance.

Ignorance, characterized by delusion regarding the truths, is the proximate cause for the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable; these are the volitions belonging to the three planes, characterized by the sprouting of renewed existence.
Volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for resultant consciousness (*vipākaviññāṇa*).

Rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), which has the characteristic of being produced as the state of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*)—termed "arising" (*opapaccaya*)—is the proximate cause for mind-and-body (*nāmarūpa*).

Mind-and-body, which has the characteristic of being a composite of the mental body and the physical body, is the proximate cause for the six sense bases (*chaḷāyatana*), because it serves as a condition through such modes as co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth, for the six [faculties] beginning with the eye.

The six sense bases (*chaḷāyatana*) are the characteristic of the functioning faculties and, respectively, the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the sixfold contact, by way of being its supporting condition and so forth.
Sixfold contact has the characteristic of the conjunction of the sensitive eye-faculty, visible forms as objects, and eye-consciousness, and so on;
it is the basis for the sixfold feeling that is co-nascent with that sixfold contact. Thus, [it is the cause] for the sixfold feeling.

In due order: feeling—characterized as the experience of the desirable, the undesirable, and the experience of both—is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for craving, because it serves as a condition through its status as a co-nascent and other types of conditions;

craving—characterized by clinging to one’s own and others’ continua—is the proximate cause for grasping, because it serves as a condition through its status as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) and other types of conditions.

It is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of the fourfold clinging (*upādāna*) that proceeds by the power of that craving (*taṇhā*), because it serves as its decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) and so forth. There should be the reading: “That [clinging] is of feeling,” “that [craving] is of craving,” and “that [clinging] is of clinging”;
or else, it may be a description using a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
That clinging which is spontaneously arisen (*opapaccayika*) and productive of the aggregates of rebirth (*upapatti-kkhandha*) is [the cause] of the two-fold existence (*bhava*).
The proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). That kamma-existence which has the characteristic of bringing about the mental body and the physical body is the proximate cause of birth.
That birth, which is the state of rebirth and has the characteristic of the manifestation of the aggregates, is the proximate cause of aging.
That aging, which is decrepitude and has the characteristic of the maturation of the aggregates of the substrata, is the proximate cause of death.

Furthermore, that conventional death characterized by the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for that person’s sorrow (*soka*), because sorrow generally arises in one who contemplates the death of a loved one.

That sorrow which causes excessive longing for dear ones such as relatives is the proximate cause for lamentation (*parideva*). Lamentation, which consists of incessant wailing, is [the proximate cause for grief].
That lamentation is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of bodily pain.
That bodily pain, characterized by the oppression of the body, is the proximate cause of mental grief (*domanassa*).
That mental grief, characterized by the oppression of the mind, is the proximate cause of despair (*upāyāsa*). That despair is that which causes one to burn and does not allow one to cool down.
That despair (*upāyāsa*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the despair of existence—that is, for the continuity of existence which is the basis of despair.

To show what kind of existence is meant by "of existence," the passage beginning with "these" was stated. Therein, the "limbs of existence" (*bhavaṅgāni*) are the defilements that are limbs—meaning causes—of existence;
the rounds of kamma and its result (*kammavaṭṭa-vipākavaṭṭāni*) are the factors (*aṅgāni*) or constituent parts designated as "existence. When, at the time of the present and so forth...
When these arise together, then that collection of phenomena— comprising the round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), the round of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*), and the round of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*)—
should be understood here as "existence" (*bhava*). This triad of rounds consisting of defilement, kamma, and result,

termed "existence," is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), because the cycle of existence arises in an uninterrupted succession through each preceding round of defilements and so forth produced by birth.
That Noble Path which has the characteristic of leading out—that Noble Path is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for cessation, that is, Nibbāna, because it serves as the cause for its attainment.

One who is "learned" (*bahussuta*) is like a "ford" (*tittha*) because he is a foundation for all his disciples and others; he is called "one who knows" (*ñū*) from the root *jñā* (to know), and thus he is a "ford-knower" (*titthaññū*).
*Ñūti* means one who knows the landing-place (*titthaññū*). The state of being one who knows the landing-place is *titthaññutā*, which is right attendance.

That [right attendance] is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for knowing the drink (*pītaññutā*). For through right attendance upon one who is well-versed in the scriptures, joy connected with the Dhamma arises;

and through joy, the cultivation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) arises. Thus, because one knows rapture (*pīti*) by hearing the suitable Dhamma, one is "one who knows the drink" (*pītaññū*).

The state of knowing what has been attained is "knowledge of what has been attained" (*pattaññutā*); it is the cultivation of the meditation subject, and that is the proximate cause for knowledge of what has been attained.

For it is through the cultivation of the meditation subject that the state of knowing the attainment of development arises; thus, there is "knowledge of what has been attained. Knowledge of the attainment of development is the proximate cause for "self-knowledge" (*attaññutā*).
For it is through knowledge of the attainment of development that the state of knowing oneself—endowed with the five factors of striving—arises.
Self-knowledge is the proximate cause for having performed merit in the past.
For it is through the recognition of the factors conducive to striving that the performance of merit in the past arose;
and having performed merit in the past is the proximate cause for dwelling in a suitable locality. For it is by means of merit performed in the past that one obtains residence in a suitable locality.
Dwelling in a suitable locality is the proximate cause for relying on a true person. For by dwelling in a suitable locality, one gains reliance on a true person.
Relying on a true person is the proximate cause for right self-direction. For by relying on a true person, right self-direction arises.
Right self-direction is the proximate cause for moral virtues. By means of right self-direction...
For virtues are firmly established; virtue is the proximate cause for non-remorse. Indeed, when one reflects upon virtue firmly established within oneself, there is no remorse at all;
thus, through non-remorse, gladness arises. Therefore, non-remorse is the proximate cause for gladness.
Through gladness, rapture arises; therefore, gladness is [the proximate cause] for rapture.
The proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). From rapture, tranquility arises; therefore, rapture is the proximate cause of tranquility. From tranquility, happiness arises;
therefore, tranquility is the proximate cause of happiness. From happiness, concentration arises;
therefore, happiness is the proximate cause of concentration. From concentration, knowledge and vision of things as they truly are arises; therefore, concentration...
It is the proximate cause for knowledge of things as they truly are. Through the vision of knowledge of things as they truly are, the knowledge of disenchantment arises;

therefore, the vision of knowledge of things as they truly are is the proximate cause for disenchantment. From disenchantment, dispassion arises; therefore, disenchantment is the proximate cause for dispassion.
From dispassion, liberation arises; therefore, dispassion is the proximate cause for liberation.
Knowledge and vision of liberation arises from liberation; therefore, liberation is the footing for knowledge and vision of liberation.

Thus, in the manner already described, whatever state serves as a decisive support (upanissaya) or whatever state serves as a condition (paccaya), all such states should be understood as the footing for the state that arises conditioned by them.

Because it must be asked, "By whom is the state of being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of a supporting condition (*upanissaya-dhamma*), a conditioning factor (*paccaya-dhamma*), or a conditionally arisen factor (*paccayuppanna-dhamma*) to be believed?",
the passage beginning with "Therefore he said" (*tenāha*) was stated. In that context,
"thereby" (*tena*) refers to the state of being the proximate cause of any supporting condition, conditioning factor, or conditionally arisen factor.

By the words spoken by the Venerable Mahākaccāna, beginning with “The Victor teaches the Dhamma,” one should have faith in the fact that these [words] serve as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for those phenomena that are the supporting condition (*upanissaya-dhamma-paccaya*).

Since it must be asked, “Is the method of the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna-hāra*) as it has been stated complete, or is there another that should be extracted and applied?”—it is said: “It is established.”

It is said: "The Mode of Conveying the Footing (padaṭṭhāna-hāra). Here, although not explicitly analyzed in the text, the Mode of Conveying the Footing should be drawn out and applied according to what is available; that is to say, it should be analyzed.
Thus, this analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Footing has been composed in accordance with one's own strength and ability.
The exposition of the "Chain of Characteristics" (Lakkhaṇahāra) is completed.
However, the wise should grasp its profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
5. Exposition of the Analysis of the Chain of Characteristics.

23. By whichever specific mode of commentary consisting of the analysis of the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) the proximate causes of ignorance and the rest have been analyzed, that specific mode of commentary—the analysis of the "conveying of the proximate cause" (*padaṭṭhānahāra*)—is complete.
Because it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the 'conveying of characteristics' (*lakkhaṇahāra*)?", it is said:
"In this regard, what is the conveying of characteristics? and so forth. Regarding the word *tatra tatra* (in this regard):

The meaning has already been stated. He asks: "What is the specific distinction of the commentary that is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra), the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics?

It should be understood that the specific distinction of the detailed commentary beginning with "Those phenomena" (*ye dhammā*), which is now being stated by me, for the exposition beginning with "When one phenomenon has been stated," is called the Mode of Conveying Characteristics, the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics. Therefore it was said: "In this regard, what is..."
"The section on the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra) begins with 'The characteristic is the string,' and so forth.
Now, this Mode of Conveying Characteristics, which is being explained in detail, asks: "Among the teachings (dhammas) taught in the Three Piṭakas, what teaching is to be characterized?
Having asked this, in order to show briefly those teachings investigated within the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics, it says: "Those teachings," and so forth.

It has been stated. Therein, "those phenomena" (*ye dhammā*) refers to those phenomena that constitute a collection. "Having a single characteristic" (*ekalakkhaṇā*) means having an identical characteristic. "Of those phenomena" (*tesaṃ dhammānaṃ*) refers to those phenomena of a collection that have an identical characteristic;

this is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*). "In one phenomenon" (*ekasmiṃ dhamme*) means in one phenomenon that has an identical characteristic, provided it has been mentioned by the Blessed One in the Canon.
When such a phenomenon has been mentioned, [the term refers to] those remaining phenomena of an identical characteristic [other than the one already mentioned].
The meaning is that phenomena (dhammas) are spoken of by way of their common characteristic (*samānalakkhaṇa*).

Having established that when phenomena are explained in detail within this Dhamma according to the scope of the "conveying of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇahāra*), these phenomena possessing a common characteristic are also thereby explained, [the author] says "Just as what would it be? and so forth, in order to demonstrate this. Its meaning is: just as...

He asks: what is that manner in which they are said to be so? The meaning is: by whatever manner they are said to be so, that manner is "having the same characteristic" (*samānalakkhaṇa*). What did the Blessed One say?
The Blessed One said, "Bhikkhus, the eye," and so forth. In the passage beginning, "Bhikkhus, the eye is unstable," and so on—
When it is said, "The ear, monks, is unstable," and so forth, that statement has already been made.

Alternatively, because they share the same characteristic by virtue of having characteristics such as instability, or because they share the same characteristic by virtue of being internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana), it must be stated that they have a single characteristic precisely by way of the sense bases (āyatana).
Thus, it should also be stated that they have a single characteristic by way of the aggregates (khandha).
To demonstrate this, it was said: "And as it has been said," and so forth. When it was said: "Rādha, one should be indifferent toward past form; do not delight in future form;
practice for the sake of revulsion toward, dispassion toward, cessation of, relinquishment of, and letting go of present form," [it was further said]:
"Rādha, one should be indifferent toward past feeling; do not [delight in] future feeling..."
It would have been said: “One should practice for the sake of revulsion toward present feeling, for its fading away, for its cessation, for its relinquishment, and for its abandonment,” and so forth.

Or rather, it is because they share the same characteristic by virtue of having the characteristic of being not to be looked back upon, or because they share the same characteristic by virtue of having the characteristic of the aggregates (*khandha*).

Because it must be stated that "the aggregates and bases should be spoken of as phenomena having a single characteristic," it is said "as it was said" (*yathāha*) and so forth, in order to show that they may also be spoken of by way of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). In this context, the meaning is:

"In whatever way—that is, by virtue of which single characteristic—the Blessed One spoke, in that same way and by that same single characteristic, even those phenomena not explicitly mentioned become as if they were spoken of."

The Blessed One spoke thus: "Those individuals who are practitioners of insight (vipassaka), who are constantly and well-exerted regarding the five aggregates and constantly develop mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati)—those practitioners of insight do not engage in what is not to be done, such as [the perception of] beauty and pleasure, or in activities such as farming and trade;
rather, they are constant in their practice toward what is to be done, namely, the foul, the unpleasurable, and the body, etc. This is the construction of the meaning.

And here, there is the elision of one of the two instances of the word *iti*. Thus, when the verse beginning with “*yesañca*” has proceeded regarding mindfulness directed toward the body starting with the hair,
and that mindfulness has been stated by the Blessed One in its own form as being present, then the remaining mindfulness directed toward feelings,
mindfulness directed toward the mind, and mindfulness directed toward phenomena are stated as having the single characteristic of being the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
"In brief, it should be said: 'Constantly and well-undertaken mindfulness directed toward the body... constantly mindfulness directed toward feelings...
constantly mindfulness directed toward the mind... constantly mindfulness directed toward mental phenomena.
Because it must be stated that 'all phenomena have a single characteristic by way of the foundations of mindfulness' (satipaṭṭhāna), [the text says] 'likewise, whatever... etc.
It has been stated. In that context, since the Blessed One has explicitly mentioned the triad of "seen" and so forth— namely, whatever form-object (*rūpāyatana*) is seen by eye-consciousness,
whatever sound-object (*saddāyatana*) is heard by ear-consciousness, and whatever odor, taste,
or tangible-object (*gandha-rasa-phoṭṭhabbāyatana*) is sensed by the triad of consciousnesses beginning with nose-consciousness— it follows that whatever remains beyond these...

The meaning is that whatever is cognized (viññāta) included within the objective sphere of mental phenomena (dhammārammaṇapariyāpanna), namely form (rūpa), is stated by the Blessed One because it possesses the single characteristic of being an object to be taken as a support (ālambitabbabhāva).

Alternatively, when "whatever visible form-sphere (rūpāyatana) has been seen" is stated by the Blessed One, since that has been stated, the remainder—such as what is heard and so forth—is also thereby stated;
thus the sense of "and so forth" (ādi) should be applied individually to each.
Therefore it was said: “Whether seen, heard, or sensed.

Since it must be asked, “When mindfulness directed to the body has been mentioned, should only the remaining [factors] such as mindfulness directed to feelings be mentioned?”—the passage beginning with “And as the Blessed One said” is given to show that the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are also thereby included.

It has been said. In that regard, the meaning is as follows: just as the Blessed One spoke by way of the characteristic of leading to liberation (*niyyānika-lakkhaṇa*) and by way of their having a single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇatta*), so too they are spoken of by way of that same single characteristic.
"Therefore, O bhikkhu, because you have been overcome by covetousness and dejection (*abhijjhā-domanassa*) here in my teaching, you must be ardent..."

“Being mindful and clearly comprehending, having removed and eliminated covetousness and dejection regarding the world— whether by abandoning them through their constituent parts (*tadaṅgappahāna*) or by suppressing them (*vikkhambhanappahāna*)—
dwell contemplating the body in the body, that is, dwelling as one who contemplates the body of physical form consisting of head-hairs and so forth,” when this was said by the Blessed One,
[the Buddha continued]: “Therefore, bhikkhu, you should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings.”
“Dwell ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Therefore, monk, dwell contemplating the mind in the mind… [as before] …regarding displeasure;
therefore, monk, dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena… [as before] …regarding displeasure. This is how the meaning should be understood in brief.
Since the detailed meaning has been explained in many ways in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, we have not elaborated upon it here.

To address the objection, "If one foundation of mindfulness is mentioned, why should four foundations of mindfulness be taught?", the passage beginning with "‘Ardent’ (*ātāpī*) refers to the faculty of energy" (*vīriyindriya*) was stated.
In that context, by the word "ardent," [the faculty of energy] is [applied] to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena...

The faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is said to be active [with respect to the body]. By the term "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*), the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) active with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is expressed.
By the term "mindful" (*satimā*), the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*) active with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is expressed.

By the phrase "having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world" (*vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ*), [the faculty of concentration active] with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is expressed.
The faculty of concentration has been described as occurring not in the body alone. If it were said that, in this manner,
the four foundations of mindfulness reach the fulfillment of their development for the practitioner who contemplates the body in the body,

then— since the four faculties of energy, wisdom, mindfulness, and concentration possess a single characteristic by virtue of being the means of accomplishing the four foundations of mindfulness— [the faculties would be identical to the foundations].
The construction is: "They reach fulfillment because they possess identical characteristics (*samānalakkhaṇattā*). Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"Because these faculties have no difference in their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) when accomplishing the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), they possess identical characteristics.

24. "Even if this were said, only the four foundations of mindfulness would have been mentioned; how then [are] the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) [accounted for]?"
Because it must be stated [in this way], the words "In the four foundations of mindfulness" and so forth were spoken.
Therein, when the four foundations of mindfulness are being cultivated by a practitioner (*yogāvacara*), that practitioner’s four right efforts reach the fulfillment of their cultivation.
The same application should be made for the remaining [categories] as well. Awakening to the four truths is "awakening" (*bodha*), which is the knowledge of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga-ñāṇa*).

They are called "leading to enlightenment" (*bodhaṅgamā*) because they go toward enlightenment. They are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiyā*) because they exist on the side of enlightenment, that is, the knowledge of the Noble Path.
Since it must be asked, "Are only wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) extracted by virtue of having a single characteristic, or are unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*) also [extracted]?
the passage beginning with "In this way, unwholesome states too... was stated. Therein, just as wholesome states are determined by virtue of having a single characteristic, [so too are the others].
The meaning is that unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*) must likewise be determined by way of their single characteristic.

Since it is asked, "How are they to be determined?", he says, "Because they have a single characteristic, they go to destruction through abandonment," showing that they are to be determined by way of being factors to be abandoned together.
In that context, "because they have a single characteristic" means because they have a common characteristic by virtue of being factors to be abandoned together.
Because it must be asked, "What is the abandonment that goes to disappearance?", it is said: "In the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth.

Therein, regarding the phrase "they go to full understanding": when the foundation of mindfulness directed to the body is being cultivated by a practitioner (yogāvacara), through that mindfulness, the perversion (vipallāsa) of perceiving as "beautiful" the unattractive physical body consisting of hair and so on is abandoned by that practitioner. As for him... [text continues]
For the practitioner of yoga, edible food comes to be fully understood;

because it has been said, "With the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form," for one who abandons desire and lust for the material body, desire and lust for its source—edible food—are also abandoned.
When the foundation of mindfulness regarding feelings is cultivated, the perversion that perceives suffering as pleasure is abandoned.
For that practitioner of yoga, the nutriment of contact (*phassāhāra*) comes to be fully understood;
because it has been said, "With contact as condition, feeling arises," when he abandons desire and lust for feeling, his desire and lust for its condition—the nutriment of contact—is abandoned.

When the foundation of mindfulness directed toward the mind is cultivated, the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent is abandoned; for that practitioner of yoga, the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*)...

It goes toward full understanding (*pariññā*). When the foundation of mindfulness directed toward phenomena (*dhammā*) is cultivated, the perversion that perceives a "self" in what is not-self is abandoned;
for this practitioner, the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*) goes toward full understanding.

Having stated each of the things to be abandoned individually, one should understand the meaning as follows: by stating one thing to be abandoned, the remaining things to be abandoned are also stated, because they share the single characteristic of being "to be abandoned."
Regarding the statement, “And his [cravings for] nutriment go to full understanding,” the meaning taken is that the lust, hatred, and delusion directed toward nutriments have been brought to an end.
For as long as lust for sensual pleasures exists with respect to physical (edible) nutriment, there is no full comprehension of that physical nutriment;
however, when that lust for sensual pleasures is abandoned, full comprehension arises. This applies to the comprehension of the remaining nutriments as well.

The same method applies here. For that practitioner of yoga in whom the foundations of mindfulness have been developed, in whom the perversions have been abandoned, and in whom the full understanding of nutriment has arisen—that practitioner of yoga becomes free from clinging through the clingings.

Since sensual clinging especially arises toward the body designated as "beautiful," the body designated as "beautiful" is the basis for sensual clinging; thus, it should be contemplated with mindfulness directed to the body.
That which is perceived as foul, such as hair and so forth, is certainly not the basis for the clinging to sensual desire (*kāmupādāna*).
Because the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) arises through the gratification found in pleasant feeling, feeling perceived as pleasant is the basis for the clinging to views;

however, feeling that is to be contemplated within mindfulness directed toward feelings is certainly not the basis for the clinging to views. [Likewise,] the thought "the mind is permanent" [is not the basis].
Because of the grasping at views, there is a misapprehension that "purity comes about through this or that personal rule and observance";

thus, the mind is the basis for the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*). However, the mind that is to be contemplated by means of mindfulness directed toward the mind is certainly not the basis for the clinging to rules and observances.
Regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), for one who does not see them as they truly are through the discernment of name-and-form, [there arises clinging] to phenomena...

The phrase "there is adherence to a self" means that phenomena are the basis for the clinging to a doctrine of self; however, when mindfulness is directed toward phenomena, those very phenomena are not at all the basis for the clinging to a doctrine of self.
Therefore, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: when the four foundations of mindfulness are cultivated, one becomes free from clinging through those very objects of clinging.

Because it must be asked, "The practitioner by whom the foundations of mindfulness have been developed becomes, through those very clingings, one who is without clinging," the phrase "and detached from the bonds" and so forth was stated in order to show that he also becomes dissociated from the bonds and the rest.
Therein, "from the bonds" means from the bond of sensual desire, the bond of existence, the bond of views, and the bond of ignorance. "Detached" means...
