The meaning is that it has "vanished" by way of the abandoning of its constituent parts, the abandoning through suppression, and the abandoning through eradication, and thus it is "liberated.

For the material body, which is perceived as beautiful, is the basis for sensual lust; however, the body that is to be contemplated through mindfulness directed to the body is certainly not a basis for sensual lust.
Or else, existence (bhava) is to be understood as "pleasure" or "the cause of pleasure."
The object of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is the basis; however, when existence is contemplated through mindfulness directed toward feeling, it is no longer a basis for craving for existence.
The mind that is to be adhered to as "self" is the basis for the bond of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*);
however, when the mind is contemplated through mindfulness directed toward consciousness, it is no longer a basis for the bond of views. This is because it is difficult to effect their separation.

Because they are difficult to penetrate as mere phenomena (*dhammamattatā*), they cannot be separated; because they are not penetrated as mere phenomena, these phenomena become the basis for the bond of ignorance (*avijjāyoga*).
However, when phenomena are contemplated with mindfulness directed toward them, those phenomena do not become the basis for the bond of ignorance.
Therefore, one who contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness is "disjoined from the bonds."
It has been said. This method should also be applied here [to the following]: "He becomes free from taints (*āsava*) by means of the taints, and he has crossed over the floods (*ogha*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he becomes dissociated from the knots (*gantha*)," here the body of form (*rūpakāya*) perceived as beautiful is the basis for the bodily knot of covetousness;
however, the body of form which is to be contemplated through mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatā sati*) is the basis for the bodily knot of covetousness.
It does not exist. Feelings that consist of the suffering of pain, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations serve as the basis for the bodily tie of ill will;
therefore it is said: "In painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent.
However, when mindfulness is directed toward feelings, the feelings to be contemplated do not serve as the basis for the bodily tie of ill will. [The view] "The mind is permanent" ...

Through the influence of dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*), there arises the misapprehension of eternalism, such as: "Purification comes through one's own moral conduct (*sīla*), purification comes through vows (*vata*).
Therefore, the mind grasped as "permanent" is the basis for the bodily tie of clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa-kāyagantha*);
however, the mind that is to be contemplated by means of mindfulness established in the mind is not the basis for the misapprehension of rules and observances. Of phenomena...
Because one does not see the nature of name-and-form as conditioned, there arises the view of existence and the view of non-existence; therefore,

those phenomena which are to be adhered to with the thought "this is the truth" are the basis for the bodily tie of adherence to the view that "this is the truth," whereas those phenomena which are to be contemplated by mindfulness directed toward phenomena are not the basis for the bodily tie of adherence to the view that "this is the truth."
Therefore, one who contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness is said to be "dissociated from the knots.
The body, when perceived as beautiful, is the basis for the arrow of lust; however, the body contemplated through mindfulness directed toward the body does not become the basis for the arrow of lust.
There is hatred toward feeling when it is perceived as pleasant; therefore, feeling is the basis for the arrow of hatred.
As for the basis (*vatthu*): feeling (*vedanā*) is not the basis for the arrow of hatred when it is being observed by mindfulness directed toward feeling.
Mind (*citta*) is the basis for the arrow of conceit (*mānasalla*) that proceeds by grasping mind as "self" and thinking "the self is superior," and so forth;
however, mind is not the basis for the arrow of conceit when it is being observed by mindfulness directed toward mind. As for phenomena (*dhammā*):...
Because one does not understand the nature of name-and-form together with its conditions, phenomena are the basis for the arrow of delusion;
however, when mindfulness is directed toward phenomena, those phenomena are no longer the basis for the arrow of delusion.
Therefore, one who contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness is said to be "without arrows, free from arrows."
The teacher stated, “And his nutriments go to full understanding. Since it must then be asked, “Do only the nutriments of this practitioner go to full understanding, or are there others as well?
it was said, “And his stations of consciousness go to full understanding,” in order to show that the stations of consciousness also go to full understanding for this practitioner.
If it were said that for the practitioner by whom the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed,

only body, feeling, mind, and phenomena would reach full understanding (*pariññā*), but not the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*), [this would be so] because through the contemplation of the body and so forth,

once body, feeling, mind, and phenomena have been fully understood, perception (*saññā*) must also be fully understood; for that [perception] is included within the phenomena comprised of feeling and mind when they are fully understood.
"By way of invariable concomitance, they have fully understood":
the practitioner who has developed the four foundations of mindfulness is one who is without clinging through the modes of clinging,
detached from the bonds, dissociated from the aggregates, free from taints through the taints, crossed over the floods, and without thorns through the thorns.

It is said that "he becomes [such]," but since it must be asked, "Does he become exactly like that, or otherwise as well?"—in order to show that he does not go even to what is not a path, he said, "And by reason of going to what is not a path, he does not go to what is not a path.

With regard to the material body designated as "beautiful" and so forth, a person goes astray through favoritism; therefore, the material body designated as "beautiful" and so forth is specifically [the object of such attachment].

The basis for bias through desire exists; however, the body—consisting of inhalation and exhalation and so forth—which is to be contemplated by means of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body, is not a basis for bias through desire.
Therefore, a person who develops the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body does not fall into bias through desire.
By experiencing [feeling] through the relish of pleasant feeling, one [falls into] ill will due to the absence of that [pleasant feeling].
That which "comes" is the basis for falling into the error of defilement (*dosāgati*)—namely, pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*).

However, the feeling that is to be contemplated through the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*) is not a basis for falling into the error of defilement.

Therefore, a person who cultivates the development of the foundation of mindfulness of feelings does not fall into the error of defilement. That which has been grasped as "permanent" and "stable" by way of the density of continuity (*santatighana*)...
The mind is the basis for delusion; however, the mind that is to be contemplated through the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the mind is not a basis for delusion.
Therefore, a person who develops the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the mind does not fall into the wrong course of hatred.
Fear arises in one who does not know the specific nature of phenomena after having analyzed them; thus, "having analyzed... [is said].

Phenomena that are alien by nature are objects of fear; however, the phenomena that are to be contemplated and analyzed through the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*) do not become objects of lust.

Therefore, a person who cultivates the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena does not fall into the state of fear. Thus, even regarding unwholesome states, which share the single characteristic of being to be abandoned—

Having extracted the factors (dhammas), it is now stated once more in order to conclude: "In this way, even unwholesome factors reach abandonment and disappearance because they share a single characteristic.
When certain portions among the factors to be developed have been mentioned, the remaining factors to be developed are also [implied] because they share a single characteristic.

Having extracted [the examples], they should be stated. Regarding the phenomena to be abandoned (*pahātabba*), when even a single portion has been mentioned, the remaining phenomena must also be stated after being extracted, because they share the same characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇa*);

this was taught by the Teacher and is known by us. "If there are other ways in which they should be stated, you should state those as well"—thus, the extraction of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇahāra*) may also be done by another method.
In order to show examples, the passage beginning with "Or where" was stated.

Therein, "where" means in that teaching on a portion of form (*rūpa*), the eightfold faculty—beginning with the eye-faculty and ending with the life-faculty—is taught by the Blessed One as a portion of form characterized by being affected (*ruppana-lakkhaṇa*).
In that very same teaching on a portion of form, the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*) is also characterized by being affected.

The tenfold material element (rūpadhātu), beginning with the eye-element and ending with the tangible-object-element, is taught as having a single characteristic because it possesses the single characteristic of being subject to change (ruppanalakkhaṇa).

And the entire aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is taught [in this way]. Furthermore, the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana), which has the characteristic of being subject to change and consists of ten types of sense-spheres beginning with the eye-sphere and ending with the tangible-object-sphere, was taught by the Blessed One as having a single characteristic because it possesses the single characteristic of being subject to change.

Furthermore, in whatever teaching on a portion of feeling where pleasant feeling was taught by the Blessed One, there both the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) were taught;
and the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering was also taught, because they share the same characteristic by way of being pleasant feeling. Or, wherever...

However, in that teaching on a portion of feeling where painful feeling was taught by the Blessed One, therein—in that teaching on a portion of feeling—the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*) was taught and the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) was also taught; and the noble truth of suffering (*dukkha-ariyasacca*) was taught as well, because they share the same characteristic by way of being painful feeling.
Or rather, in that teaching on a portion of feeling where neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling]...

The Blessed One has taught feeling; therein, within that teaching on a portion of feeling, both the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*) and the entire dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) have been taught—this is how the connection should be made.
In whichever teaching non-painful-and-non-pleasant feeling is taught, in that teaching the faculty of equanimity is taught.
Because they share the same characteristic, it may be asked, "By whom was dependent origination taught?
Having thus asked "by what cause," the passage beginning with "in the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling]" is stated in order to show the reason.
Therein, because ignorance underlies the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, therefore ignorance is taught. Regarding ignorance...

The intention should be understood as follows: when dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), which has ignorance as its root, is taught, it is indeed taught in its entirety by the statement, “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise... [and so on] ...there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
Thus, the dependent origination that proceeds in forward order (anuloma) as “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise... [and so on] ...there is the arising” is what is intended.

"Taught" means spoken by the Teacher. Having taken to heart the objection—"If that dependent origination as it occurs [in the forward order] is taught, then it cannot be said that 'all dependent origination is taught'"—the words "And that...
and so forth were stated. Therein, that which occurs in the forward order belongs to the side of defilement (*saṃkleśapakṣa*) characterized by lust, hatred, and delusion.

It is to be abandoned. Furthermore, that which proceeds in reverse order, beginning with “With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations,” is to be abandoned by means of the noble qualities of being free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion.
And that which proceeds both in forward and reverse order is to be abandoned by means of both of those. Therefore, it should be said: “The entire dependent origination has been taught.”
The intended meaning must be grasped.

"Whatever method of application regarding characteristics has been stated by the Teacher— beginning with 'When a single characteristic is stated for those phenomena that share a single characteristic, the remaining phenomena are thereby stated'— that alone should be applied, and not otherwise."

To show that the application of the method of characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāra*) must indeed be performed in another way as well because of the nature of what is to be asked, it was said: "In this way, those phenomena...

and so forth. Therein, those material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) such as earth and so on, and those immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) such as contact and so on, which possess a single characteristic by virtue of their functions—such as supporting and so on, or impinging and so on—when one of those material or immaterial phenomena is mentioned, the remainder...

Material and immaterial phenomena are thereby stated. Those material phenomena such as earth and so forth, and those immaterial phenomena such as contact and so forth—which possess a single characteristic by virtue of their characteristics of hardness and so forth, or touching and so forth—when one of these material or immaterial phenomena is stated, the remaining material and immaterial phenomena are thereby stated.
Those phenomena which, by way of the commonality of being subject to transformation...

They possess a single characteristic either by way of the commonality of being nameless, or by way of the commonality of impermanence and so forth, or by way of the commonality of the aggregates, bases, and so on;
thus, when one conditioned phenomenon among those conditioned phenomena has been stated, the remaining phenomena are thereby stated.
Those conditioned phenomena are conditioned by way of arising and dissolution, or by way of death and rebirth, or by way of the conditioning of simultaneous cessation and arising.

They have a single characteristic in terms of death and rebirth; the construction of the meaning should be understood as follows: when one conditioned phenomenon among those conditioned phenomena is stated, the remaining conditioned phenomena are thereby stated.
Furthermore, in the phrase "by function and by characteristic," etc., the word "and" (ca) includes concomitance, having a common cause, and so forth.

They are to be seen. And as for what should be said regarding their association and so forth, that has already been stated in such passages as, "Those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, through non-attention to diverse perceptions," where it was explained that by way of association, the phenomena concomitant with perception (*saññā*) have been determined, and so on. [Question:
When one phenomenon is stated in its own form, by what means is the fact that the remaining phenomena are also stated—by virtue of having a single characteristic and so forth—established?
Because it must be said, "It is to be known and believed by us," the words beginning with "Therefore" were spoken. In this context,
by the statement "When one dhamma has been spoken," etc., which the Venerable Mahākaccāna uttered because the remaining dhammas have also been spoken,
it is meant that you should know and believe that the remaining [dhammas] have likewise been spoken.
“Thus far the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra) is complete;

there is no other to be assigned,” because it must be said thus, it is stated: “The Mode of Conveying Characteristics is assigned. In that regard, in whatever textual passage (pāḷi), when one phenomenon has been stated, the remaining phenomena are also determined by means of that Mode of Conveying Characteristics—in that textual passage, that Mode of Conveying Characteristics is assigned, having been determined.
The meaning should be understood as "joined.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Exposition) composed according to the strength of one's faculties, within the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāra-vibhaṅga*).
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
6. Exposition of the Analysis of the Fourfold Array (Catubyūhahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā).
25. By whichever specific mode of commentary, namely the analysis of the Mode of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāra), the meanings of the discourses are identical in meaning;...
The analysis of the string of characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅga*), which constitutes a specific kind of commentary, has been fully explained.
Because it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the fourfold array string (*catubyūhahāravibhaṅga*)?", it is said: "In this context, what is the fourfold array? and so forth.

Therein, "in those" (*tattha*) refers to those sixteen modes of exposition, such as the string of teaching (*desanāhāra*), that have been pointed out. "What" (*katamo*) means: what specific kind of commentary is the fourfold array, the analysis of the fourfold array?
It is to be understood as "name. Therefore it was said: "In this context, what is the 'Fourfold Array' method? It is the analysis of the Fourfold Array method.
Because it must be asked, "By means of this Fourfold Array method, which [of the four]—etymology and so forth—should be sought?"—the words "by the phrasing," etc., were stated.
Therein, "by the phrasing" refers to the specific nature of the analysis of the phrasing (*byañjana*) of the Sutta that constitutes the Fourfold Array method.

“By means of ‘phrasing’ (*byañjana*)”—the meaning is that by this fourfold method of expansion (*catubyūhahāra*), those who comment upon the etymology of the discourse (*sutta*), the intention of the discourse, the source of the discourse, and the connection between what precedes and what follows in the discourse must investigate it.
Regarding the etymologies and so forth to be investigated by the fourfold method of expansion: which among them is the etymology of the discourse that must be investigated?
Because it is to be asked, the passage beginning with "In this context, what is etymology (nerutta)? was stated. Its meaning is as follows:
If one were to ask, "Among those things—etymology and so forth—to be sought by means of this fourfold method, which is the etymology, that is, the derivation (nibbacana), of the sutta?
then the etymology of the sutta, which is its designation of intrinsic nature (sabhāvapaññatti) stated after having been determined, is to be sought.
This etymological explanation (nibbacana), which constitutes the natural language (sabhāva-nirutti), is called *nerutta*.

Since it might be asked, "What is that *nirutti* which is called *nerutta*?", it is stated: "It is the connection of words (*padasaṃhitā*). That which is connected (*saṃhitā*) and joined (*yuttā*) within words is the "connection of words.
It is that natural language (*sabhāva-nirutti*) by which the meaning of the Sutta should be expressed in whatever way is appropriate.
The construction is as follows: that which is the "occurrent" (pavattā) is precisely the "intrinsic linguistic expression" (sabhāvanirutti), and it is this that is called "language" (nirutti).
Since it must be asked, "What then is that intrinsic linguistic expression?", it is stated: "It is the knowledge of phenomena by way of their names.

By means of that name-designation (nāmapaññatti), which serves as the instrumental cause, there is the knowing of phenomena—whether they be objects of comprehension—by way of their names, such as the name "earth," or the name "contact," or the name "aggregate," and so forth.
The knowledge of a person skilled in meanings, phenomena, and so forth, proceeds by means of various names;

that which serves as the cause is the "designation by name" (*nāmapaññatti*), meaning it is called "natural terminology" (*sabhāvanirutti*). The word "which" (*yā*) is a change of gender; the sense is "by which. This is because one must say:
"Explain, having opened up the knowledge proceeding by way of names for things according to their gender, nature, and phenomena."
The passage beginning with “yadā hi” has been stated [above]. However, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

“By the words ‘yadā hi bhikkhu,’ etc., he explains the meaning of the phrase ‘knowledge of phenomena by way of name. Since its meaning has already been explained in detail in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is not further investigated here.
26. The etymological analysis (*nerutta*) has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known by us; [the question remains: “Which [meaning] of the Blessed One’s [words] is to be sought in the Sutta?”
Because it was necessary to ask, "What is the underlying intention (*adhippāya*)?", the passage beginning with "In this regard, what is the underlying intention? was stated. Its meaning is clear.

Furthermore, in such passages as "The Dhamma indeed protects," the Blessed One’s intention is that the person who desires to be protected by the Dhamma—which must be protected by oneself—will protect the Dhamma. This applies to whichever person wishes to be liberated from an unhappy state.
"He will protect the Dhamma"—this is the Blessed One’s intention.

In such passages as "Just as a thief caught at the opening of a tunnel," the Blessed One’s intention is that the thief who wishes to be released from execution will no longer commit the work of a thief.
Likewise, the person who wishes to be released from the suffering of the woeful states and so forth will [abandon] evil karma.
"He will not do it"—this is the Blessed One’s intention.
Regarding the passage beginning "Those who desire happiness," the Blessed One’s intention is that those persons who desire happiness will avoid harming others.
Regarding the passage beginning "When one is drowsy and a great eater," [the intention concerns] those persons [who fail to escape] from the repeated occurrence of birth, aging, and death.
The Blessed One’s intention was: “Those who desire liberation will be moderate in eating, they will be contented, they will be pure in livelihood,
they will be endowed with the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, they will be untiring, they will be practitioners of insight,
and they will be respectful and deferential.”

In such passages as "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless," the Blessed One’s intention is that those persons who fear death and desire Nibbāna will become heedful in the practices of giving, virtue, and mental development. 27.
The teacher has analyzed how the intention in a sutta is to be sought, and we have understood it;
because it was asked, "What is the source (nidāna) of the sutta to be sought?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is the source? was stated. Therein:

*Nidāna* means "cause" (*kāraṇa*). It is called *nidāna* because it gives forth the fruit after having brought it out. What is that? It is the cause. *Dhaniya* means one who is intent upon the cause for the increase of wealth;
thus he is *dhaniya*. *Gopālaka* means one who protects and guards cows by way of lordship; thus he is a cowherd (*gopālaka*). *Upadhīhi* refers to [possessions] such as sons, oxen, and so forth.
*Narassa* (of the man) refers, according to the context of the respective cases, either to a man who has sons or to a cowherd.
Whether by way of majority, or as it has come down in the verse, it should be understood that there is indeed delight (*nandanā*) for women through acquisitions (*upadhī*).

"By this basis" means by this very basis consisting of acquisitions, namely children, cattle, and so forth. A "basis" (*vatthu*) is that wherein delight dwells or occurs, such as children, cattle, and so on.
Having extracted the delight, one gives away children, cattle, and so forth; this is the "source" (*nidāna*).
Having grasped the meaning as "delight for a man arises from acquisitions," Dhaniya said: "From acquisitions comes a man's delight.

The Blessed One, however, having grasped the meaning as "herein, with the objects such as sons and cattle, sorrow dwells and proceeds; it brings forth sorrow, and sons, cattle, and so forth are the source [nidāna]," said:
"From acquisitions comes a man's sorrow. It is that which is grasped that is called an acquisition (pariggaha). What is that?
He calls that possession consisting of children, oxen, and so forth "an acquisition" (*upadhi*), but not the acquisition of defilements or the acquisition of the aggregates.
"In acquisitions" means in bodies reckoned as aggregates. He calls the body "an acquisition," but not children, cattle, and so forth, nor possessions.
"In external objects" means in objects such as jewels, earrings, children, wives, and so forth.

"Sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukha*) refers to craving (*taṇhā*) that occurs by way of the enjoyment of desirable objects. "Craving with external objects as its basis" (*bāhiravatthukāya taṇhāya*) means craving that occurs by way of the enjoyment of external objects that are desirable.
"With internal objects as its basis" (*ajjhattikavatthukāya*) means [craving] that occurs by way of delighting in the internal object comprised of the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
Again, "with internal objects as its basis" (*puna ajjhattikavatthukāya*) means [craving] that occurs by way of affection for the internal object comprised of the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).
The source (*nidāna*) to be sought has been analyzed by us and is known;

because it was asked, "Which is the connection between what precedes and what follows (*pubbāparasandhī*) that is to be sought?", the passage beginning with "In this regard, which is the connection between what precedes and what follows? was stated. Therein, "in those" refers to those [topics] of etymology, intended meaning, source, and the connection between what precedes and what follows.
"As" means by whatever nature—such as darkness—that the Blessed One [described] sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) in the verse: "Blinded by lust... [they do not see] their mother."
He said: This verse, beginning with "Blinded by desire... [and] their mother," was spoken because sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) has such a nature as that darkness and so forth;

this is the construction of the meaning. As for the meaning of the verse: it desires, thus it is "desire" (*kāma*), which is sensual craving; they are "blind by desire" (*kāmandhā*) because, through desire, they do not know the goal and do not see the Dhamma.
By means of the net known as sensual craving, through the non-knowing and non-seeing of the goal and the Dhamma...

"Covered and enveloped" means covered by a net. "Shrouded by the shroud of craving" means that those very same persons are covered and obstructed by the covering known as craving, due to their lack of knowledge and vision regarding the meaning and the Dhamma.
Bound by the bond of negligence—known as heedlessness—toward the meaning and the Dhamma, such persons who ought to be bound pursue aging and death, like fish caught in the mouth of a net.
Just as fish follow after death, and just as a milk-drinking calf follows after its mother, so too should it be understood that aging and death follow [beings].
By this teaching or verse—“Blinded by sensual desire... [and] the mother”—it is shown that sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) is what is expressed. This is the teaching, this is the verse.

Because it must be asked, "With which other teaching does this [verse] correspond?", and having asked thus, the words beginning with "By which one" were spoken in order to show that it corresponds with this teaching or with the verse. In that context, "that" refers to the teaching—"Blinded by desire...
they wander on"—or the verse. "By what precedes and follows" means by the preceding words of the teaching from that [verse].
“By a verse statement” means either by another statement of the teaching or by a verse statement. He asks: “It is fitting; it goes to what is fitting;
it accords. “In what way? means by that which causes blindness and so forth. Regarding the verse statement spoken by the Blessed One, “One who is lustful... [etc.]... a man,” the construction is:
it is fitting in that way, by that which causes blindness and so forth, through that verse statement. As for the meaning of the verse: one who is lustful, being impassioned... [etc.]... a man.
The person does not know the goal—the purpose of one’s own welfare or the purpose of the welfare of others.
Being impassioned and being inflamed with passion, he does not see with the eye of wisdom the cause of the aforementioned goal.
It should be understood that when passion overcomes a man, then for that man there arises blindness, a darkness, a gloom, which is ignorance.
*Iti* means "thus. *Andhatāya* means by way of blindness, by way of causing blindness; by way of obscuration, by way of causing obscuration.

"That very same craving" refers to that which was spoken of as sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) in the verse passage: "Blinded by sensual desires... [and so on] ...the mother. That very same sensual craving is what is meant.
"Expressed" means it was designated and made known by the Blessed One through the designation in another verse passage: "The man who is impassioned... [and so on]. Of that which has been expressed—
What is meant is that the identity of the subject matter makes the subsequent teaching consistent with the preceding teaching.
Since it must be asked, "In which words of the two verses is that very same craving expressed?", the passage beginning with "And that which...
was stated in order to show, having determined it, that it is expressed by these [words]. Therein, in the first verse, [it says]: "Blinded by desire... covered."
And as for the phrase he spoke in the second verse, "one who is lustful...

does not see," by means of these phrases—"blinded by sensual desire... does not see"—which illuminate obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), that very same craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*) mentioned in the first verse was expressed by the Blessed One.
Because it must be asked, “What is that darkness which was mentioned? And what is that craving for renewed existence which was mentioned?
the passage beginning with “That which is darkness” is stated. Therein, the construction is as follows: “The ignorance that was called darkness is the origin of suffering in becoming;
and the craving for renewed existence that was mentioned is also the origin of suffering in becoming.”
Regarding the phrase “sensual pleasures” (*kāmā*) which the Blessed One spoke: by that term, these defilement-sensualities (*kilesakāma*) are meant.
Regarding the phrase “covered with a net” (*jālasañchannā*) which the Blessed One spoke:

by that term, the Blessed One shows the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of those very same defilement-sensualities through their application (*payoga*) and manifestation (*samudācāra*). Therefore—because in whichever continuum craving has arisen, that continuum...
Without allowing one to escape from *saṃsāra*, it remains by seizing the mind with defilements while enticing it with visible objects and so forth;
therefore, because craving remains within the continuum having seized the mind, [it is said to be] "by way of defilement.

"By way of transgression" means by way of the defilement that constitutes the actual transgression. "By way of obsession" means by way of its arising before reaching the point of transgression. "Those" refers to persons similar to those accompanied by the aforementioned kind of craving.
Bound by the fetters of craving, such individuals as these pursue aging and death; they are unable to transcend aging and death.
The construction of the sentence is as follows: the non-occurrence of aging and death is shown by the Blessed One through this expression, "they pursue aging and death."
The connection between the preceding and following verses—beginning with "kāmandhā" and "ratto"—has been analyzed by the Teacher and is understood by us.

However, because it must be explained how the connection between the preceding and following verses in the stanzas beginning with "yassa papañcā ṭhitī ca" is to be discerned by us, the passage beginning with "yassa papañcā" was stated. Regarding that verse: for which sage...
There is no proliferation (*papañca*), nor craving, conceit, or views; there are no formations conditioned by craving, conceit, and views;
there is no persistence, nor underlying tendencies, nor craving; there is no obsession by craving like a tethering post, nor delusion like a crossbar.
That sage, having transcended all such things as proliferation, is said to have "gone beyond. He is free from craving.
The meaning is: "The world together with its gods does not recognize that Sage who wanders in the world free from conceit, wrong view, attachment, and obstacles.
In this verse, since the Blessed One has mentioned "proliferation" (papañca) and so forth, and it must be asked, "Which are these?", [the text continues] with "Proliferation is called... and so on.

It has been said: craving, conceit, and views—which cause one’s own personal substrate to wander long in *saṃsāra*—and the formations (*saṅkhārā*) conditioned by those cravings, conceits, and views, whether by way of co-arising or by way of support, are called "proliferations" (*papañca*).
In the sense of being unabandoned within the continuum, they are "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*); craving is called "stability" (*ṭhiti*) because it is the cause for the persistence of beings.
The obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of craving as it occurs, and the various wanderings (*vicarita*) of the thirty-sixfold net of craving that have been described—
all this is called a "shackle" (*sandāna*) because, in the sense of binding,
it is like a tether for the person who is its own support. Delusion (*moha*), because it prevents the person who is its own support from entering the city of Nibbāna, is like a crossbar.

“Bar” (paligha) is the name [of a specific obstruction]. Because it must be asked, “He for whom conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) and the rest do not exist—what has he transcended?”, the passage beginning with “And those which...

is stated. Those formations (*saṅkhāra*) of the aforementioned kind that are conceptual proliferations, that station (*ṭhiti*) of the aforementioned kind, that tether (*sandāna*) of the aforementioned kind, and that bar (*paligha*) of the aforementioned kind which were mentioned as not existing—all this, beginning with conceptual proliferation, [is what he has transcended].
The sage who has completely transcended [these] should be understood as the sage "free from craving" (*nittaṇha*).
28. In the verse beginning with "For whom there are no conceptual proliferations" (*yassa papañcā*), regarding those formations (*saṅkhāra*) stated to be caused by craving, conceit, and views:
when do they, and in how many ways, yield their fruit? And when does the craving associated with those formations yield its fruit, and in how many ways?

Because it must be asked, "Does it give fruit?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, the formations of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna-saṅkhārā*)" was stated. Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) means among those formations of proliferation (*papañca-saṅkhārā*) and so forth.
"Formations of obsession" refers to unwholesome formations consisting of volition (*cetanā*) that manifest as obsessions by way of transgression.
"To be experienced in the present life, etc. (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādi*) [refers to] in the present life (*diṭṭha*), meaning in the visible state, that is, in the individual existence (*attabhāva*).

It is "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) because it gives its fruit in this very life; or alternatively, it is "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" because one experiences its fruit in the present state (*diṭṭhe dhamme*). What is that?
It is the first impulsion volition (*paṭhamajavana-cetanā*) occurring through excessive misconduct, etc., toward those who are not to be offended, and so forth.

It is "to-be-experienced-after-rebirth" (*upapajjavedanīya*) because one experiences its fruit upon rebirth; it is the seventh impulsion volition. [It is] "to-be-experienced-in-a-subsequent-becoming" (*aparāpariyāyavedanīya*) because its fruit [is experienced] in a future personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Feeling it" refers to the five impulsion-consciousness volitions that occur in the middle [of the cognitive process], which are to be experienced either subsequently or in a later succession (*aparāpariyāyavedanīya*).
Formations (*saṅkhāra*) are threefold by way of yielding three kinds of fruit. Thus, the threefold craving associated with this threefold volition of formations yields a threefold fruit:

either in the present life (*diṭṭhe va dhamme*) within one's own personal existence (*attabhāve*), or upon rebirth (*upapajje*) in the immediately following existence, or in a subsequent succession (*apare vā pariyāye*).
"He gives existence; he produces it"—thus the Blessed One spoke either of the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) that produce the fruit, or of the craving associated with them.

Since it must be asked, "By which other mode of teaching does that teaching or verse which speaks of the volitional formations that produce the fruit correspond?", [the text] says, "Whatever kamma one performs consisting of greed," and so forth.
It has been said. Both this teaching—"For whom... the world..."—and that teaching—"Whatever action is performed out of greed...
or by other methods"—which have been spoken, these two teachings of the Blessed One are mutually consistent with one another;
the former with the latter and the latter with the former, they join, they come together, they accord, just as the waters of the Gaṅgā do with the waters of the Yamunā.
The waters of the Yamunā also flow together and merge with the waters of the Gaṅgā. The teaching beginning with “For whom...
the world” merges and accords with the teaching beginning with “That which is fashioned by greed... by way of synonyms”; likewise, the teaching beginning with “That which is fashioned by greed...

by way of synonyms” also merges and accords with the teaching beginning with “For whom... the world. This is how the meaning should be understood. [The question] “How is this consistent? [is thus answered].

Because it is something that ought to be asked, the passage beginning with "therein, obsession" was stated; what is meant is that it is appropriate in the sense of producing the triad of fruits, such as those to be experienced in this very life.
Having extracted each respective discourse taught by the Blessed One that is consistent from beginning to end, [one should apply it].

The phrase beginning with “As it has been said” was stated in order to show the connection between what precedes and what follows. The manner of this connection should be understood according to the method already explained.
Therein—referring to those manifestations (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), and the wanderings of craving (*taṇhā-vicarita*).

“Manifestation” is the movement of craving within the continuum of a being, directed toward objects such as visible forms through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). “By the power of reflection” (*paṭisaṅkhāna-bala*)...

That which is to be abandoned by means of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*) through the power of seeing [things] as impure, impermanent, and so forth, refers to the formations (*saṅkhārā*) that are to be abandoned by vision.
"By the power of vision" means they are to be abandoned by the power of the knowledge of the first path, which is designated as vision.
"The thirty-six modes of craving's wandering" refers to the remaining thirty-six modes of craving's wandering, excluding those modes of craving's wandering that are to be abandoned by vision.

He from whom craving has departed is "craving-free" (*nittaṇha*); the state of being craving-free is "craving-freeness" (*nittaṇhatā*). What is that? It is the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining (*saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).

Although the triad of delighting in the conditioned, conceptual proliferation, and formations is identical in meaning, the phrase beginning with "Moreover" (*apicā*) was stated to show that there is a distinction in terms of the phrasing and syllables of the teaching.
Since it must be asked, "In how many ways is this connection between what precedes and what follows analyzed by the Teacher?", he says: "That..."
And thus it was said: “This is the connection between what precedes and what follows,” and so forth. However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“The connection between what precedes and what follows is not merely the correlation with other suttas; rather, it is said ‘this is that,’ etc., to show that there is another kind as well.

In that context, “connection of meaning” (*atthasandhi*) refers to the connection of one meaning with another by way of action, agent, and so on. “Connection of words” (*padasandhi*) refers to [the connection] of noun-phrases and the like...

Connection by way of names, phrases, and so forth is *sandhi*. Connection of teaching (*desanāsandhi*) is the connection between one mode of teaching already mentioned and another mode of teaching already mentioned.
Connection of exposition (*niddesasandhi*) is the connection between one exposition already mentioned and another exposition already mentioned.

Furthermore, there is no distinct dharma of intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) called "connection" apart from meaning and the rest; because meaning and the rest are included within the six meanings, the six phrases, and so forth, it is said: "The connection of meaning consists of the six phrases," and so on.
The connections of meaning and the connections of phrasing have been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us;
however, because it was necessary to ask, "What is the connection of the teaching? it was stated: "The connection of the teaching is not the earth," and so forth.

In that context, regarding the passage, "The meditator does not meditate depending on the earth, yet he meditates": here, the "meditator" (*jhāyī*) is the person (*puggala*) possessing absorption (*jhāna*), who, having depended upon—that is, taken as an object—the earth...

And it should be understood that he does not meditate [on those things], but rather, having relied upon and taken as his object Nibbāna—which is detached from all conditioned phenomena—he meditates on and attains the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
This same method should also be applied to the passages beginning with "he does not fall" (*na ca āpanti*).
For a person possessing the attainment of fruition, having set aside earth and the other elements, takes Nibbāna alone as the basis for the attainment of fruition.

"He enters" (*samāpajjati*). Herein, the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) are included by way of the great elements such as earth, because their subsistence is bound up with form.

The immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) is also included by way of the base of infinite space and so forth. The intention is that one meditates (*jhāyati*) having abandoned these three types of existence.
If one does not meditate by depending on earth and so forth, yet still meditates, then [this refers to] the continuity of beings known as this world.

Because it might be suspected that a meditator meditates by depending on either the world beyond, or the continuum of beings known as the "other world," or a continuum devoid of faculties, he says "nor this world" and so forth to avoid such a misconception.
Therein, "this world" refers to the visible personal existence (attabhāva) known as this world, which is spoken of as the continuum of beings;
the meditator does not meditate by depending on that, nor does he meditate [by depending on those other things].
"Another world" (*paraloka*) refers to the continuity of a being (*sattasantāna*) distinct from this world, designated as a transition between states of existence (*bhavantara*).
Relying upon that, the meditator does not meditate, yet he meditates.
Regarding the passage beginning with "this both," etc.: having excluded this pair consisting of this world and the other world, that which...
The visible base is seen, and that is the visible base itself. The audible base is heard, and that is the audible base itself.
The olfactory, gustatory, and tactile bases are touched, and those are the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile bases themselves.
That which is cognized—the water element, the space element, the characteristic-forms, and the form included in a portion of the mental-object base known as nutritive essence—is the cognized.
That too includes the materiality that is a portion of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), such as the water element and so forth;

it also includes the physical basis (*vatthu*) that has been sought after or not sought after, and which has come into proximity; it also includes the physical basis that has been obtained or not obtained, which has been sought after or is worthy of being sought after, and which is beautiful;
and it also includes the physical basis that has been thought about and should be taken as an object by way of thinking.
"Also the basis": that basis which has been examined and should be taken as an object by way of repeated reflection—that basis too;
and that basis which has been mentally contemplated by the mind alone and should be taken as an object by way of further contemplation—that basis too.
The construction should be made thus: "the meditator does not meditate, nor does he meditate, depending upon that basis."
In this context, only external form—beginning with what is seen—is to be understood, because it is non-sensory-bound form that is intended.
Therefore, the commentator said: “The continuity of form that is non-sensory-bound is distinct from both of those.
“If a person who meditates does not meditate by depending on the earth and so forth as previously described, but rather the meditator meditates [independently], then this being the case...”

Because it must be asked, "Is this meditating person known by anyone in the world as 'he meditates depending on this [object],' or is he not known?"—in order to show that he is not known, the text says, "In this world with its devas," and so forth.
Therein, when this person whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is meditating by means of the attainment of fruition-jhāna (phalasamāpatti-jhāna), in this world with its devas...
[and so on] ...in whatever place among the generation of devas and humans, he is not known.
"He meditates with a mind independent" means that in the world with its devas—and so on—among the generation of devas and humans, he is not known by anyone.
Therefore it was said:
"Homage to you, O noble steed among men; homage to you, O supreme among men."
“We do not know what it is that you rely upon as you meditate.
Since it must be asked, “By which sutta is the state of being unknown to anyone made clear?
this is shown by the Godhika Sutta with the words, “Just as Māra the Evil One,” and so forth. However, in the Commentary, [it says]: “Now...”

It is said that the passage beginning with “Just as Māra... was spoken in order to clarify, by means of the Godhika Sutta and the Vakkali Sutta, the state of non-reliance in any respect whatsoever on the part of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
In this context, he is called Māra because he kills or obstructs those who perform meritorious deeds such as giving, or merit itself;
or alternatively, he is Māra because he kills both self-interest and the welfare of others. He is called Pāpimā (the Evil One) because of his possession of an evil mind. In a previous existence...

Because he was the slayer of Godha, the noble son who had acquired the name "Godhika" was not known or seen by Māra while searching for the consciousness of that noble son at the moment of his final Nibbāna, nor for any rebirth-linking consciousness thereafter.

To address the question, "Why does Māra, who knows the minds of others, not know [this]? it is said: "For he... and so forth. For that Godhika was, indeed, beyond conceptual proliferation (*papañca*).
Therefore, since Godhika has no basis for views because craving has been abandoned, he does not know [the future].
Because it must be asked, "It is to be made clear by the Godhika Sutta itself," the passage beginning with "And how" was stated.
"By the Godhika Sutta and the Vakkali Sutta, the state of being independent of the element of Nibbāna without residue is made clear; likewise, regarding the element of Nibbāna with residue..."

Because it would have to be asked, "By what means is the state of non-dependence known?", it was stated, "by the world together with its devas," and so forth, in order to show that even then it is not known.

In this context, when these "destroyers of the taints" (khīṇāsava) meditate through the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti-jhāna) in the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining, they meditate with minds unattached to anything; thus, they are not known by the world together with its devas.
The construction should be made as follows: "They are not known by the world with its Māras... including gods and humans.

Regarding the phrase "With unattached minds they are not known," the negative particle *na* here should not be connected to the word "jhāyamānā" (meditating), because the sense of "not meditating" would be possible [if so connected].
However, it should be connected to "na ñāyanti" (they are not known), as stated in the sub-commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) below: "By anyone in the world..."
Because it is said, "it is not known. This "connection of the teaching" (*desanāsandhi*) is determined by way of the mutual correlation of the meanings of the *Godhika-sutta* and the *Vakkali-sutta*,

just as the correlation of the meaning of the teaching beginning with "and not depending on earth" and the teaching beginning with "and not this world" is determined by that very correlation of meaning.
In this teaching, wherever it may be, whatever [object] a meditator might rely upon, they do not meditate; rather, relying upon Nibbāna, the meditator meditates.
This is determined by way of its purpose (atthavasena). This should be understood as the "connection of the teaching" (desanāsandhi), meaning a coordination.
The connection of the teaching has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known by us; therefore, one must ask: "What is the 'connection of the exposition' (niddesasandhi)?"
Regarding this, it is said: “What is the ‘explanatory connection’ (niddesasandhi)? It is ‘the mind that is dependent,’ and so forth. Herein, the phrase “therein” (tattha) means:

among those four—namely, the connection of meaning, the connection of phrasing, the connection of teaching, and the explanatory connection—it asks which of these connections designated as the “explanatory connection” is [to be] explained by way of exposition.
“The mind that is dependent” (nissitacitta) refers to [the mind] through its association with craving and views.
Or, by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), those ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) whose minds are dependent [on such things] are "those of dependent mind.
By this teaching, individual persons (*puggala*) are to be demonstrated, because this teaching is based on individuals (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).

If the teaching were based on phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), then in these sections of the Sutta, it would be the dependent mind itself that is taught; thus, "those of dependent mind" would be for the purpose of knowing the dependent mind.
The sections of the Sutta have been taught. "Those noble persons whose minds are independent" means they possess independent minds;
by this teaching, the noble persons are to be demonstrated, because it is a teaching focused on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).

However, in the case of a teaching focused on the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), the sections of the Sutta have been taught for the purpose of knowing the independent mind—that is, those sections of the Sutta where the independent mind is taught.

Because it must be asked, “By what exposition should those with supported minds (*nissitacitta*) be explained, and by what exposition should those with unsupported minds (*anissitacitta*) be explained?,” it is said:
“Those with supported minds are to be explained by way of the unwholesome side (*akusalapakkha*),” and so forth. They are to be explained by an exposition according to the unwholesome side.

This same method should also be applied to the phrases “by way of the wholesome side” (*kusalapakkha*) and so on. [They are to be explained] by means of the general characteristics of the unwholesome side and the general characteristics of the wholesome side.
Having shown [the unwholesome], in order to show the specific distinctions between the unwholesome and the wholesome, it was said:

"With minds dependent, through defilement," and so forth. This is the "connection of exposition" (*niddesa-sandhi*): this linking together of the preceding exposition beginning with the side of the unwholesome by means of the subsequent exposition beginning with defilement, by way of the "dependent mind," is called the connection of exposition. [This applies] to that which begins with the side of the wholesome...

This correlation and connection of the exposition should be understood by analyzing it as follows: the correlation between the preceding exposition, characterized by purification and so forth, and the subsequent exposition, characterized by the mind being independent, is called a "connection of exposition" (*niddesa-sandhi*).

Furthermore, it should be understood through the distinctions of the fourfold method (*catubyūha-hāra*)—namely, etymology (*nerutta*), intention (*adhippāya*), source (*nidāna*), and the sequence of what precedes and follows (*pubbāpara-sandhi*)—as well as through the distinctions of the connections of meaning (*attha-sandhi*), phrasing (*byañjana-sandhi*), exposition (*niddesa-sandhi*), and teaching (*desanā-sandhi*).
Because it must be said, "By whom is the state of being thus to be analyzed by us to be known and believed?",
the passage beginning with "Therefore he said" was spoken. Therein, by that statement which the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke— namely,
"The intention of the etymological analysis (nirukti)" and so forth— by that statement, the state of the Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra) being to be analyzed in such a manner is to be known by you.
"It is to be believed" is what is meant.
Because it must be said that "to this extent the Fourfold Array (catubyūha-hāra) is complete;

there is no other [array] to be applied," it is stated: "The Fourfold Array is concluded. In this regard, whatever fourfold [analysis] occurs in whichever portion of the scripture (pāḷi), each such instance is the Fourfold Array.

And it should be understood that the meaning is: having been extracted and applied in each respective textual passage according to its availability, that fourfold fourfold-analysis method (catubyūhahāra) has been thus arranged and joined.
Thus ends the analysis of the fourfold-analysis method (catubyūhahāravibhaṅga), composed in accordance with the strength of one's faculties.
The Exposition of the Modes of Penetration is finished.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
7. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Conversion.
29. By whichever specific exposition, namely the analysis of the Fourfold Array (catubyūhahāra), the Nairuttika and other [methods] were analyzed, that...
[the analysis of the Fourfold Array] is complete. Because it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the Conversion (āvaṭṭa-hāra)?", it is said therein:
"What is the conversion method? and so forth. Therein, "therein" refers to those sixteen [methods] thus specified.

Among the modes of conveying the teaching (*desanāhāra*) and so forth, he asks: "Which specific method of commentary is the 'Turning' mode (*āvaṭṭahāra*), and what is the analysis of the Turning mode (*āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅga*)?

The specific method of detailed commentary beginning with "Exert yourselves! and so forth—which is now being stated by me as the explanation for the instruction beginning with "In one footing" (*ekamhi padaṭṭhāne*)—is taken to be the analysis of the Turning mode.
In that regard, within the teaching, when there is one footing upon which the teaching is based...
Because it must be said: "He seeks the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the remainder; having sought it, he applies it to the opposite side [of the teaching] by means of the verse:
'Exert yourselves! Strive! Apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching!
Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut.'"

The verse has been stated. Here, it is said that when one word-base (*padaṭṭhāna*) in a verse has been introduced in the teaching, one seeks out the remaining word-bases. As for the meaning of the verse, it is explained in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

Since it must be stated, "In which word-base among the verses beginning with ‘Exert yourselves’ (*ārambhatha*) has the teaching been introduced, and what remaining word-base does one seek out?", it was therefore said: “‘Exert yourselves, strive!’—this is the word-base for energy (*vīriya*),” and so forth.

In this context, although it is stated in general terms as "the footing of energy," the energy known as the element of instigation (*ārambha-dhātu*) is the footing for the energy known as the element of exertion (*nikkama-dhātu*);
the energy known as the element of exertion is the footing for the energy known as the element of perseverance (*parakkama-dhātu*);
and the energy known as the element of perseverance is the footing for the energy associated with the development of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*).
By the phrase "the proximate cause" (*padaṭṭhāna*) and so forth, it is to be understood that [the cause] should be sought—that is, grasped.

The energy accompanied by the cultivation of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*), which was expressed by the word "exert yourselves" (*yuñjatha*), is the proximate cause for the exalted concentration (*mahaggata-samādhi*) expressed by the phrase "in the Buddha’s teaching.

Furthermore, other proximate causes such as happiness (*sukha*) and so forth, which have appeared in the teaching, should also be sought. By the phrase "shake off the army of Death" (*dhunātha maccuno senaṃ*).
The energy accompanied by insight taken up here is the proximate cause for wisdom capable of shaking off the defilements;
one should also seek other proximate causes, such as concentration and so forth, which have been included in the teaching.
If it is argued that the energy mentioned in the passage beginning with "Exert yourselves" refers only to energy, concentration, and wisdom in their general sense...
Since it must be said, "If this were the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), then how would they cut off the root of the round and reach the cessation of the round?";
it is therefore stated again: "Exert yourselves, strive! This is the proximate cause of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*)," and so forth.

Because it is the proximate cause for those individuals among practitioners who possess a preponderance of energy and are engaged in its governing function (*ādhipaccakicca*), those practitioners who exert themselves cut off the root of the round and—
What is meant is that they lead to turning away from the round of existence (*vivatta*). However, since the passage beginning with “Exert yourselves!

(*ārambhatha*) and so forth is a teaching concerning the basis for the arousal of energy and other such factors, one might raise the objection: “Are not the bases for exertion and so forth themselves the proximate cause (*padatthāna*)?
Bearing this in mind, he said: “These proximate causes are the teaching. Thus, the teaching beginning with “Exert yourselves! consists of the aforementioned proximate causes.
It is not the basis for the arousal of energy and so forth; therefore, it should be understood that only its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) has been commented upon.
Thus, the meaning of the teaching beginning with "Exert yourselves" has been analyzed by way of its proximate cause, and this has been understood by us.
Since it must now be stated, "How is the meaning of that very same teaching to be analyzed by way of its opposite?", [the text says]: "For those who do not apply themselves..."

The passage beginning with “or” has been stated. In that context, for those beings who have not applied themselves to yoga—that is, to meditative development—and whose wisdom is immature, the teaching beginning with “Exert yourselves!
was undertaken for the sake of future knowledge, by way of the portion dealing with the influence of latent tendencies (vāsanā) as the cause of application in yoga.

For those beings who have applied themselves and whose wisdom is mature, [the teaching] was for the sake of full comprehension in this very life, by way of the exertion itself as the cause of exertion.
The teaching beginning with “Exert yourselves! was commenced.
Therein, among those beings—whether they were applying themselves or not, and whether their knowledge was matured or immature—those beings whose knowledge was immature did not apply themselves;
being rooted in negligence, those beings of immature knowledge [failed] in yoga and in meditation through that negligence.
They do not apply themselves; that negligence is twofold: negligence rooted in craving and negligence rooted in ignorance.

Among these two kinds of negligence, the being who is shrouded by ignorance—that is, the one whose negligence is rooted in ignorance—does not, through that negligence, understand the object of knowledge (*ñeyyatthāna*), namely:
"These five aggregates, subject to arising and passing away, are called the object of knowledge. This [negligence] has ignorance as its cause.
Negligence has ignorance as its root; such is negligence. That negligence which has craving as its root is threefold:
first, the negligence that a craving-afflicted being falls into while seeking the arising of wealth not yet arisen;
and second, the negligence that a craving-afflicted being falls into for the sake of guarding wealth already arisen, by means of protection.
There is this negligence (*pamāda*): when a craving-afflicted being, while enjoying established wealth, falls into negligence for the sake of enjoyment, this is negligence.
Thus, there are three kinds. So, in the world, this negligence is fourfold:
one kind of negligence has ignorance (*avijjā*) as its basis, and three kinds of negligence have craving (*taṇhā*) as their basis; thus it is fourfold.
In this context, among those [factors] of ignorance and craving, the "name-body" (nāmakāya)—the collection of names such as contact and so forth—is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for ignorance;
the "form-body" (*rūpakāya*)—the collection of forms such as earth and so forth—is the proximate cause for craving. This is what is meant:

the fourfold negligence (*pamāda*), which is the opposite of energy (*vīriya*) characterized as the element of exertion (*ārambhadhātu*) and the element of setting out (*nikkamadhātu*), must be eliminated. Having eliminated it, [one should understand] the single type of negligence...
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of the threefold negligence; craving (*taṇhā*) is the proximate cause of the threefold negligence.

The mental body (*nāmakāya*) is the proximate cause of ignorance, and the physical body (*rūpakāya*) is the proximate cause of craving. Having thus applied this to their opposites, the proximate causes should be sought.
[One might ask: "Why is the mental body the proximate cause of ignorance, and the physical body the proximate cause of craving?"
Because it is something that ought to be asked, he asks, "For what reason? and replies, "Attachment to the realms of form, and delusion regarding the formless realms.

Since attachment—consisting of craving and dogmatic adherence—towards the phenomena of form within the realms of form occurs by way of the notions of "I" and "mine" established among sentient beings, therefore the material body (*rūpakāya*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for craving. For, in the beginningless cycle of existence...

In saṃsāra, women and men become mutually delighted by each other’s forms. Since delusion is established among beings due to the subtle nature of the formless [aggregates] such as contact (phassa) and so forth, the construction should be made thus:
"therefore, the mental body (nāmakāya) is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for ignorance.
This is what is meant: craving, by way of making the mental body and the physical body its object, [arises].

Because the material body arises from craving and the mental body arises from ignorance, it should be brought out that the material body is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for craving, and the mental body is the proximate cause for ignorance.
Since it must be asked, "What is the material body? What is the mental body?", it is said: "Therein, the material body is the aggregate of form;
the mental body is the four immaterial aggregates. Therein, among those two—the material body and the mental body—the material body...
The aggregate of form is called the "collection of form," and the "mental body" or "collection of name" refers to the four immaterial aggregates.
These five aggregates might be considered "with clinging" because they are the objects of ignorance and craving;
therefore, since it must be asked, "By what kind of clinging are they possessed of clinging?", one asks that very question and answers: "These five aggregates..."
"By means of which clinging are they 'with clinging'? It is said: "By craving and by ignorance. In this context, the construction should be made as follows:
"By means of craving, which is itself a form of clinging, and by means of ignorance, which is itself a form of clinging, these five aggregates come to be called 'with clinging'. [One might ask:
"How many types of clinging are there that are called craving, and how many types of clinging are there that are called ignorance?"
Because they are to be questioned, it is said: "Therein, craving is twofold," and so forth. "Therein" means within those [factors of] craving and ignorance.

The two types of clinging—clinging to sense pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) and clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*)—are called craving. For it is by way of craving that there occurs the misapprehension: "My virtue! My vow!
The two types of clinging—clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) and clinging to the doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*)—[are likewise explained].
Ignorance (avijjā) indeed comes to be. For it is through the influence of ignorance that both the view of eternalism and views such as "I" and "mine" arise.
Because it must be asked, "Among the four truths, how many truths are comprised by the aggregates with clinging (saupādānakkhandhā) due to these four types of clinging?
the words beginning with "by these" were spoken. Those mundane aggregates which are aggregates with clinging...
For it is through clinging that even the aggregates themselves become "with-clinging"; this pentad of aggregates with clinging is called suffering, the truth of suffering.
Those four types of clinging which are the causes of suffering—this tetrad of clinging is the origin, the truth of the origin.
"The five aggregates" refers to the five aggregates with clinging, because they constitute the basis for suffering.
“Suffering”: this refers to the five aggregates together with their clinging (*saupādāna*). “He teaches the Dhamma”:
the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma—beginning with “Exert yourselves! and so forth—in accordance with those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Although it was stated previously in general terms, it is stated again as “for the full understanding of suffering and for the abandoning of its origin” in order to show the specific purpose.
30. The first two truths were determined by the Teacher by way of negligence (*pamāda*), which is the opposite of exertion (*ārambha*), and we too have understood them.

To address the question, "How should the other two truths be determined?", it was said, "In that regard, that which is threefold," etc., in order to show that even those two must be determined by way of negligence.
Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) means among those [truths] rooted in craving (*taṇhā*) and rooted in ignorance (*avijjā*).
Regarding "negligences": "of that" refers to the threefold negligence rooted in craving.
"By penetration" means by the full understanding of gratification and so forth. "Guarding" is defined as the guarding of one's own mind.
"Withdrawal" is the removal or casting aside of that negligence mentioned by the word "of that," through the application of diligence which is its opposite.
"There is this development known as 'withering' (khepana), which proceeds by means of the application of heedfulness (*appamāda*) as the antidote to negligence (*pamāda*);
thus, having turned back once more by way of the antidote to negligence, serenity (*samatha*) is determined.
Since it must be asked, "How does that serenity come about, and by what means?", one asks accordingly and [explains] the means.
To show this, the passage beginning with “How so? was stated. Therein, “how” means by what means.

It refers both to the gratification (*assāda*) arising in dependence on the two kinds of sensual pleasures (*kāma*) described as “sensual pleasures are so called because they are desired, or because they are desirable,” and to the danger (*ādīnava*) arising in dependence on sensual pleasures that yield little gratification, according to such statements as “Sensual pleasures have little gratification and much suffering.”

"Of sensual pleasures" (*kāmānam*) is a genitive case used in the sense of the object. Therefore it is said: "dependent on sensual pleasures. Because of the statement, "The escape from sensual pleasures is this:
renunciation," "escape" here refers to the first jhāna. In the word *vokāra*, the letter *va* is an augment;
the syllable *o* signifies the state of being inferior. "Blessing" (*ānisamsa*) refers to the fourfold purification of virtue and so forth. When...
The meaning is that when one knows [the object], then through that means calm (*samatha*) comes to be.
Calm has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known by us; however, because it must be asked, "What is insight (*vipassanā*)?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, whatever investigation...
was stated in order to analyze insight. Alternatively, when one knows the gratification (*assāda*) and so forth of sense-desires—
At that time, it is said that "tranquility (samatha) exists. Since one must ask, "When that tranquility is present, what [wisdom] exists?", it is stated:
"In that regard, whatever investigation... and so forth. Therein, "in that regard" means:

when that tranquility is present, whatever investigation, examination, or wisdom regarding impermanence and so forth there is concerning gratification and the rest—this is the wisdom of investigation. Specifically, it is distinguished as follows:

"Insight" (vipassanā) is so called because of seeing. Alternatively, the teacher has stated that "tranquility" (samatha) is the protection and withdrawal [of the mind] through the thorough penetration of the threefold negligence rooted in craving;
since it was necessary to ask, "What is insight?", he said, "In that regard, that which is investigation," and so forth.
Therein, "in that regard" (tattha) means when that aforementioned tranquility exists, regarding that which was aforementioned...

The investigation and examination by means of wisdom regarding negligence through such aspects as impermanence and so forth—this wisdom of investigation and examination is called *vipassanā* because it sees with distinction. The distinction is that while investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is weak, examination (*upaparikkhā*) is powerful.
Thus, the two phenomena of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) have been determined by the Teacher: "These two phenomena have been determined."
Because it was necessary to state, "What goes?", the words "These two," and so forth, were spoken. Tranquility (samatha) reaches the fulfillment of the cultivation of tranquility;
insight (vipassanā) reaches the fulfillment of the cultivation of insight.

Because it was necessary to state, "When these two phenomena are being cultivated, which fetters are abandoned by the practitioner (yogāvacara)?", the words "In these," and so forth, were spoken. [This refers to] in the phenomenon of tranquility...
When craving is being abandoned by the practitioner through its cultivation, and ignorance is being abandoned by the practitioner through the cultivation of insight—
these two states to be abandoned, namely craving and ignorance, are thus abandoned. Since it must be asked,
"When these two states are being abandoned, which states cease?", it follows that clinging and the other factors also cease.
Demonstrating the cessation of all suffering in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*), he said, "When these two states have been abandoned," and so forth. Therein,
when craving is being abandoned through the development of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*) and ignorance is being abandoned through the development of insight (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*),

and when these two states have been abandoned by means of these two developments, the four types of clinging— beginning with sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*)— are [abandoned] by way of suppression and complete eradication.
They cease, not by way of the moment of dissolution.

Here it may be asked: "Since it has been stated that 'with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging,' the statement that 'when craving is being abandoned, clingings cease' is appropriate; but how is it that when ignorance is being abandoned, clingings cease?"

Regarding the reading, “With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging”: since the sense is possible that the cessation of clinging occurs through the cessation of craving accompanied by ignorance, one should understand it thus.
For just as ignorance accompanied by craving is the condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), so too craving accompanied by ignorance is the condition for clingings;
therefore, the sense that the cessation of clinging results from the cessation of craving accompanied by ignorance is indeed possible.
"Through the cessation of clinging by way of suppression and eradication, there is likewise the cessation of existence"—this same method applies to the remaining [links] as well.

Here too, in the phrase "the cessation of this entire mass of suffering," it should be understood that the cessation of formations and so forth is included, resulting from the cessation of ignorance together with craving.
"Thus" (*iti*) means in this way, by way of turning back [the mind] from both dissimilar and similar phenomena.

The first two truths have been determined; these two factors—serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*)—are the path and the truth of the path, while the cessation of the round and the truth of the cessation of the round are *nibbāna*. Thus, the four truths have been determined.
[This is done] either by way of the states such as negligence that are opposed to energy (*vīriya*), or by way of the states such as negligence that are of the same nature [as the defilements].
Because it must be said, "By what means can we be made to believe the state of the four truths having been determined by [the Buddha] after having turned [our minds] toward them?",
the passage beginning with "Therefore he said" was spoken. By that state of having been determined in such a way, the Blessed One spoke the words of the verse beginning with "Exert yourselves,
strive," and by those words of the verse beginning with "Exert yourselves, strive," [the meaning is established].
Thus, it is said that you must have faith in the fact that the four truths are to be determined.
Since it was asked, "Having set forth only the side of purification with the words 'Exert yourselves! Strive!
and so on, and having turned that very side of purification toward its own discordant and concordant factors, the determination of the four truths should be made," [the following is stated].

Having set aside the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*) and having turned back toward that very defilement by way of both dissimilar and similar phenomena, he spoke the words of the verse beginning with "Just as at the root" (*yathāpi mūle*) in order to demonstrate the extraction of the Four Noble Truths. In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it says:
"Thus, having set aside the side of purification (*vodānapakkha*), [he speaks] by way of its dissimilar phenomena and by way of its similar phenomena..."

It is said: “Having thus shown the turning-back (*āvaṭṭana*) by way of the side of defilement, he now, having set aside that side of defilement, spoke the verse beginning with ‘Just as at the root’ (*yathāpi mūle*) in order to show the turning-back by way of both dissimilar and similar states.
The meaning of this verse is also stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). Nevertheless, for the sake of those who are slow-witted, we shall explain it according to the Commentary itself.
A tree is a collection. It is called a "root" (*mūla*) because by means of this part situated in a portion of the earth, it establishes itself (*patiṭṭhāti*).
