What is that? It is the part of the tree designated as a root, situated in a portion of the earth; [the phrase refers to] "in that root. It is "unassailable" (*anupaddava*) because there is no calamity—that is, no obstacle such as being cut with an axe—against that root.
It is "firm" (*daḷha*) when, due to the absence of calamities, it is stable by its very nature. It is "cut" (*chindīyati*).
"Severed"—what is that? It is a portion of a tree together with its root established in the earth, not a portion of a tree taken after having been severed.
It is called a "tree" (*rukkha*) because it grows and increases; and that portion of a tree together with its root established in the earth is called a "tree," just as one says, "the ocean was seen.
Furthermore, the phrase "it grows again" is said with reference to the production of a new sprout.
Regarding "the underlying tendency of craving" (*taṇhānusaya*): it refers to the root of the tree known as the individual existence (*attabhāva*).

"When it has not been uprooted" means that while it remains unsevered by the knowledge of the path to arahantship, this suffering known as individual existence—along with its cause—continually arises again and again without interruption and simply does not cease; such is the meaning of the verse.

“Here, in this verse, that underlying tendency of craving (*taṇhānusaya*) which is called the root for the production of suffering because it has not been eradicated—of what kind of craving is this underlying tendency?

Thus he asks. He answers, “It is the underlying tendency of the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), because craving is manifold through its divisions such as the craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*) and so forth, [and this refers to] the state of craving for the relish of existence. This is the underlying tendency.
This is the condition for this phenomenon known as craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*); this latent tendency (*anusaya*) is the latent tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*).
Since it must be stated, "The latent tendency is of many kinds; why should it be accepted as the latent tendency of ignorance?", it was said:
"For craving for existence has ignorance as its condition. Because ignorance is the condition for craving for existence, the latent tendency of ignorance should be accepted.
For it is through the non-perception of the danger in states of existence (bhava) due to ignorance that craving for existence arises.

Following the method explained previously in the passage beginning "These two defilements," one should determine the four truths and understand the engagement with both dissimilar and similar phenomena;
however, only those forms of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) associated with the path (magga) should be taken here.
The connection (*anusandhi*) for the passage beginning with “*sabbapāpassa*” has been explained in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). “*Sabbapāpassa*”:

of all unwholesome states (*akusala*), both those that have reached the state of courses of action (*kammappaṭha*) and those that have not, without exception. “*Akaraṇan*” means non-arising within one’s own continuum and that of others. “*Kusalassa*”:

of wholesome states (*kusala*), both those belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) and those that are supramundane (*lokuttara*), whether they have reached the state of courses of action or not. “*Upasampadā*” means by way of causing them to arise within the continuum.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: "Accomplishment" (*sampadā*). One's own mind is "one's own mind" (*sacitta*); the purification (*pariyodāpana*) of that mind is "cleansing" (*vodāna*), which refers to the arising of the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*).
Furthermore, the arising of the Path of Arhatship is included by the phrase "the accomplishment of the wholesome" (*kusalassa upasampadā*).
This teaching and instruction of the Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, is the illumination of these three points of non-doing. This is the meaning of the verse.

In this verse, that which was stated as "the non-doing of evil" is explained by way of the courses of action consisting of misconduct (*duccarita-kamma-patha*) with the words, "all evil," and so forth.
"Arisen from hatred" is stated by way of what is most frequent; it may also be arisen from greed (*lobha*).
"Arisen from greed" is also stated by way of what is most frequent; it may also be arisen from hatred. It may also be arisen from delusion (*moha*).
It has been stated in that very way. It should be understood that origination from greed and origination from hatred are also possible.

Since it might be asked, "Is all evil analyzed solely by way of the divisions of the courses of misconduct (*duccarita-kammapatha*), or should it be analyzed by something else?", [the text] begins with "whatever covetousness...
and so forth, in order to analyze it further by way of the unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*) and the going upon wrong paths (*agatigamana*).
This has been stated. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the connection between the sections is explained as follows:

“Having thus analyzed ‘all evil’ by way of the classification of misconduct, unwholesome courses of action, and kamma, the passage beginning with ‘unwholesome root’ is now stated in order to show the classification of going to a bad destination (*agatigamana*) by way of the unwholesome roots.
For one who, through delusion (*moha*), does not know the true nature (*sabhāva*)...
Because it arises from fear—that which one goes to a wrong course through both fear and delusion—it is said to be "originating from delusion.

All evil has been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us; since it was asked, "What is the non-doing of all evil?", it was stated therein: "Greed [is abandoned] by means of the meditation on the foul," and so forth.
However, in the Commentary, after showing what evil is in the phrase "the non-doing of all evil" up to this point, it now says, while demonstrating the non-doing of that evil:

It is said: “By means of the three roots of the wholesome—namely, non-greed, non-hatred, and wisdom—one speaks of the non-doing and non-arising of all evil through the abandoning of the three roots of the unwholesome.
Greed, which proceeds by way of being intent upon the beautiful, [is abandoned] by means of the foul, that is, by the meditation on the foul proceeding in such a manner.

Hatred, which proceeds by way of anger and malice toward living beings, is abandoned through non-greed by means of its abandonment via substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*); likewise, delusion,

which proceeds by way of confusion regarding both living beings and conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), is abandoned through wisdom— the wisdom of investigation— by means of its abandonment via substitution of opposites and suppression.
And it is abandoned through the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaggapaññā*) by means of abandonment as a factor (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and eradication (*samuccheda*).

To the objection, "If the unwholesome roots are abandoned by the wholesome roots alone, then equanimity (*upekkhā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and gladness (*muditā*) would be purposeless," it was said: "In that way, greed [is abandoned] by equanimity," and so forth. Regarding "by equanimity":
“By means of equanimity (upekkhā) developed through such [meditations] as ‘all beings are owners of their karma,’ one pacifies discontent (arati);
then, reflecting that one abandons even delusion (moha), which is the root of discontent, it is said: ‘Delusion goes to its destruction and disappearance through sympathetic joy (muditā).
[One might ask: ‘By what means should we believe that the unwholesome roots are to be abandoned by the wholesome roots?’”

Because it ought to be stated, the words beginning with “Therefore he said” were spoken. By virtue of that which is to be abandoned in such a manner, the Blessed One uttered the statement, “The non-doing of all evil.
By this statement, “The non-doing of all evil,” it is meant that you must have faith in that which is to be abandoned in such a manner.
31. "To this extent, all evil has been analyzed, and its non-performance should also have been analyzed;

yet, if that were so, the non-performance of the eight forms of wrongness would remain unprohibited. Because it must be stated thus, it is said: "All evil consists of the eight forms of wrongness," and so forth.
Wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*) is the occurrence of unwholesome states proceeding by way of recollecting and contemplating things such as the impermanent as "permanent."
The non-doing of all evil has been explained in many ways by the Teacher, and it has been understood by us.

However, because it must be stated how the accomplishment of the wholesome (*kusala*) is to be analyzed and understood, he says, "When the eight wrongnesses (*micchatta*) have been abandoned," and so forth, showing the analysis of the accomplishment of the wholesome.
The "eight rightnesses" (*sammatta*) are right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) and right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*).

Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these eight factors of rightness are established by way of the transformation of their opposites.
"Of the past" means taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One of the past;
for this verse for reciting the Pātimokkha belongs to the Blessed One Vipassī. "When the mind has been purified."
The five aggregates, which are bound to the mind, also become purified.
To the question, "How are we to have faith in the purification of the five aggregates through the purification of the mind?

it was said, "For in this way," and so forth. In the manner thus described, the Blessed One [taught] that for the sake of the purification of the mind, O monks, the holy life is lived under the Tathāgata...
By saying the words, “...is lived,” it is meant that you must have faith in those words: “the mind... is lived.
Since it ought to be asked, “In how many ways does purification occur? the reply “It is twofold,” and so forth, was given.
[This refers to] the abandoning of the hindrances through serenity and insight, as well as the uprooting of the underlying tendencies through the cultivation of the Noble Path.
Because purification is twofold, the meaning is that the five aggregates become purified. For individuals who have abandoned the hindrances and underlying tendencies possess a pleasing appearance.
Since it is asked, "What are the stages of purification? the reply begins with, "There are two stages of purification," and so forth.

It has been said. Since it must be asked, "Among the teachings taught in the verse beginning with ‘The non-doing of all evil,’ which is the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), which is the truth of origin (samudayasacca), which is the truth of the path (maggasacca), and which is the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca)?", the passage beginning with "Therein, that which by penetration...
was stated. "Therein" means among the teachings taught in the verse; [it refers to] that pentad of aggregates (khandhapañcaka).
One purifies this pentad of aggregates through penetration and the clear realization of full understanding; thus, this pentad of aggregates is suffering, the truth of suffering.
Since one purifies the pentad of aggregates from the defilement of craving, this defilement of craving is the origin, the truth of the origin.
That noble path-factor by which one purifies it is the noble path, the truth of the path. That which...
When a person has realized the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), that which is purified by him—this unconditioned-element phenomenon, cessation—is the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca).
These four truths have been determined by way of the application of similar and dissimilar phenomena among the teachings taught in the verse.
The meaning of the passage beginning with "Therefore it was said" should be understood according to the method explained below.

The four truths were determined by the Teacher through the application of similar and dissimilar phenomena to the teachings set forth in the verse beginning, “The non-doing of all evil,” and these have been understood by us as well. [As it is said:
“Indeed, Dhamma protects the one who lives according to Dhamma, like a great umbrella during the rainy season.
This is the benefit when Dhamma is well-practiced: the one who lives according to Dhamma does not go to a state of misery.”

Because it must be stated how the four truths are determined by way of turning toward the teachings taught in the verse—both those that are dissimilar and those that are similar—he said, "The Dhamma indeed... and so forth.

Showing the teachings taught in that verse by analyzing them, he said, "As for what is called 'Dhamma'... and so forth. Therein, "as for what is called 'Dhamma'" means the meritorious Dhamma (*puññadhamma*).
"Restraint of the faculties" (*indriyasaṃvara*) refers to all forms of restraint, beginning with the virtue of restraint of the six faculties, including the mind as the sixth. Therefore it is said:

"In this context, it should be understood that by way of the heading 'restraint of the faculties,' all morality (*sīla*) is included. The four states of deprivation (*apāya*) are called "bad destinations" (*duggati*) because they are the destinations for those who have committed misdeeds.
However, all rebirths are characterized by the suffering of pain (*dukkhadukkha*), the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*).
Because it is a state of going, it is called "an evil destination" (*duggati*).
Since one must ask, "In which of these two kinds of phenomena does the phenomenon of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) abide? How is it well-practiced?
From what does it protect?"—therefore, it was said: "In that regard, as for the virtue of restraint," and so forth. "In that regard" (*tattha*) means in those two kinds of phenomena.
One who stands in the virtue of restraint (*saṃvara-sīla*) and acts without breach—this is to be done by way of being unbroken.

One who stands in the virtue of restraint and has well cultivated and practiced the dharma of merit protects the person who is their own support from the four states of misery (*apāya*) with absolute certainty;
however, even the dharma of merit, when protected only in an uncertain manner, [does not provide such security].

The meaning should be understood as "he protects. Furthermore, the phrase "from the states of misery" (*apāyehi*) is stated by way of primary importance; however, he also protects from obstacles such as disease and so forth.
Alternatively, it should be seen that the term *apāyanto* (the state of being gone away) is included because obstacles such as disease have departed (*apagata*) from him who is *ayata* (intent).
Since it might be asked, "How can we believe that he protects in such a way?", the passage beginning with "Thus the Blessed One" was spoken.
By the statement the Blessed One made—“Monks, there are these two destinations for one who is virtuous:

gods and humans”—which demonstrates the manner of the characteristics in the way already described, it is meant that you should have faith in him through that very statement: “There are these two... [and] humans.
For one established in the virtue of restraint, the meritorious dhamma that must be practiced unbrokenly and well-performed—

Because it must be asked, "By which sutta is the state of absolute certainty regarding protection from the states of misery (apāya) illustrated?", the passage beginning with "And thus in Nāḷandā" was spoken.
Therein, by the phrase "and thus" (evaṃ ca), the meaning described in the manner just stated should be understood even according to the mode that is now being explained. "In Nāḷandā" means:
in the market town named Nāḷandā, there sat a village headman (gāmaṇi), the eldest son of one named Asibandhakaputta.
Addressing the Blessed One, he spoke these words beginning with, “Venerable sir, O Brahmins.

“Brahmins” refers to the non-Buddhist brahmins. “Venerable sir” (bhante) is how the village headman addresses the Blessed One. “Those from the western lands” refers to those seated in the western direction. “They cause to go forth” means they cause them to go upward from the human world to the heavenly world;

they lead them there. “Idhassa” means that such a person might exist here in this world. The construction is: “A person might be a taker of life... [and so on] ...might be one of wrong view. The remainder should be understood according to the text itself and following the sequence stated therein.

32. Because it must be asked, "By what means can we believe that the four Truths have been determined by way of turning toward [the Truth] through phenomena that are dissimilar and similar?", it was said: "Therefore, Mahākaccāna said: 'In one footing...
And because it must be stated, "To this extent the Mode of Conveying Turning (āvaṭṭa-hāra) is complete;
no other is assigned," it was said: "'The Mode of Conveying Turning is assigned. Whichever Mode of Conveying Turning has been applied in whichever textual passage, according to its availability—
In each respective textual passage, the meaning should be understood as follows: that particular "turning" (āvaṭṭa) method of exposition has been extracted and applied accordingly.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* composed according to one's own strength, within the analysis of the "Turning" method of exposition (*āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅga*).
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail precisely according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
8. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Analysis (Vibhattihāra). 33.

By whichever specific mode of commentary consisting of the analysis of the "Turning-back" (Āvaṭṭahāra) the proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna) and so forth are to be turned back, [those should be understood].

The analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis (*vibhattihāravibhaṅga*), which constitutes a specific form of commentary, is complete. Because it must be asked, "In that regard, what is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Analysis?
is stated. Therein, "in those" refers to those sixteen modes of teaching, such as the Mode of Conveying Teaching (*desanāhāra*) and so forth; [the question asks]:
"Which specific form of commentary among them is the Mode of Conveying Analysis, and what is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis?"

"Name" he asks. The meaning to be understood is this: the specific commentary on the exposition beginning with "Two Suttas," which is now being stated by me as the detailed expansion of the summary beginning with "The Dhamma, the proximate cause, and the plane," is called the Mode of Analysis (vibhattihāra) and its analysis (vibhattihāravibhaṅga).

Since it must be asked, "How many suttas are those for which these stages of the foundations of Dhamma (dhammapadaṭṭhāna) spoken in the suttas have been analyzed by this method of classification?"—in order to first show those suttas, it is said:
"There are two suttas: that partaking of purification through habituation (vāsanābhāgiya) and that partaking of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya).
Therein, "partaking of purification through habituation" refers to the habituation of meritorious cultivation; [the word] "habituation" (vāsanā)...

*Vāsanābhāgiyaṃ* means a portion or a section that belongs to the category of *vāsana* (habitual tendencies). A discourse (*sutta*) is called *vāsanābhāgiya* because it is connected to the category of *vāsana* by way of being its designator.
What is that? That discourse in which the three bases for meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*) are taught by the Blessed One is a *vāsanābhāgiya* discourse.

*Nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ*: "Penetration" (*nibbedha*) is the piercing through and the shattering of the mass of greed (*lobhakkhandha*) and so forth. [A discourse is called *nibbedhabhāgiya*] because it pertains to that penetration.

The "portion of penetration" (*nibbedhabhāga*) is a part or division of penetration; a discourse (*sutta*) that is connected to the portion of penetration by way of expressing it is called "pertaining to the portion of penetration" (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).

Which one is that? That discourse in which the qualities of those in training (*sekkha*) and those beyond training (*asekkha*) have been taught by the Blessed One—that discourse pertains to the portion of penetration.
Because it must be asked, "What are the practices by which the individuals who receive those discourses succeed?", it is said, "There are two practices," and so forth.
Those practices that exist in the portion of merit consisting of giving, virtue, and cultivation are "conducive to merit" (*puññabhāgiyā*).
Those practices that exist in the portion of the fruit are "conducive to the fruit" (*phalabhāgiyā*). "Established in which virtues the recipients..."
Because it must be asked, "How many are those virtues (sīla) that they practice?", it is said: "There are two kinds of virtue," and so forth.

That by which one restrains oneself is restraint (saṃvara). This restraint is fivefold: the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the restraint of mindfulness, the restraint of knowledge, the restraint of patience, and the restraint of energy.
All of these are called "restraint" because they restrain evil; furthermore, they are so called because they serve as the basis for mundane and supramundane success.
"Virtue" (sīla) is the name [of the first factor]. That by which one abandons what is to be abandoned is "abandoning" (pahāna);

or, abandoning itself is "abandoning. And that abandoning is fivefold: abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandoning by tranquillization (paṭipassaddhi-pahāna), and abandoning by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna).
Therein, excluding abandoning by escape, there are four kinds of abandoning.
Virtue is as described by the method already stated.
Since it must be asked: "Among those [categories] such as the Suttas, which Sutta does the Blessed One teach by which practice;
and established in which virtue does a person become a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī) by means of which virtue?", [the text] analyzes it accordingly.

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “Therein, the Blessed One” was stated. Therein, among those discourses categorized as pertaining to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*) and so forth, the discourse pertaining to purification is that which the Blessed One teaches to a person via the path of merit (*puññabhāgiyā paṭipadā*) among those paths such as the path of merit;
that person who receives the discourse pertaining to purification is, therein, [established] in the virtues of restraint (*saṃvara-sīla*) and so forth.

Having established himself in the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), through that holy life (*brahmacariya*) known as the morality of restraint—the supreme conduct—he becomes a practitioner of the holy life who fulfills the highest practice.

In this context, among those discourses (*sutta*) such as those pertaining to spiritual cultivation (*vāsanā-bhāgiya*) and so forth, there is the discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedha-bhāgiya*);

therein, among those modes of practice (*paṭipadā*) such as those pertaining to merit (*puñña-bhāgiya*) and so forth, [it refers to] the mode of practice pertaining to the fruit (*phala-bhāgiya*) for whichever person...

The Blessed One teaches; the person who receives this discourse conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta), having established himself therein—in the morality of restraint and so forth—within the morality of abandonment by way of complete cutting off, tranquility, and abandonment, becomes a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī) through that distinguished holy life (brahmacariya) known as the Path, which is synonymous with abandonment. This is how the construction [of the sentence] should be understood.

Since it was asked, "Among the discourses conducive to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya-sutta*) and so forth, which is the discourse conducive to purification?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, which...

was stated. In that context, "in those" refers to those discourses conducive to purification and so forth. "Discourse on giving" (*dānakathā*) is the discourse on the giving of a true person (*sappurisa*), the fruit of giving by a true person, the giving of an untrue person, and the fruit of giving by an untrue person.

"Discourse on virtue" (*sīlakathā*) is the discourse on the five precepts and so forth, and the fruit of virtue. "Discourse on heaven" (*saggakathā*) is the discourse on the excellence of heaven and its happiness, as well as—

And there is the discourse on merit that brings about rebirth in heaven. "Disadvantage" refers to a sutta that shows disadvantage. "Advantage" refers to a sutta that shows advantage. The construction is:
"a sutta pertaining to the stage of purification by habituation.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "In this context, what is...", the meaning of the connection follows the method already stated. As for the teaching that reveals the Four Noble Truths:
The construction is: "That teaching is called a discourse (sutta) pertaining to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya).

Having considered the objection that, if this were the case, even a discourse pertaining to purification by habituation (vāsanābhāgiya) would necessarily become a discourse pertaining to penetration because it reveals the Four Truths, he said:

"In a discourse pertaining to habituation," and so forth. In a discourse pertaining to habituation, the understanding is insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), which serves as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the Noble Path.
There is no wisdom, there is no path—the Noble Path—and there is no fruit—the Noble Fruit.
However, in suttas pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), there is understanding and so forth; in suttas pertaining to mere habituation (*vāsanābhāgiya*), these are not present.

By the passage beginning with "understanding," the exposition of the Four Truths—such as the discourse on giving—is included within suttas pertaining to penetration; the other type alone is called a sutta pertaining to habituation.
...shows. Why, if they were to ask, "Why are only two suttas singled out," when there are not only two suttas in which the stages that serve as the foundations for the Dhamma-padas are analyzed?
It is because the stages serving as the foundations for the Dhamma-padas, as stated in the suttas, are easy to understand when analyzed without confusion.
"If this is so, then the suttas dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) and those dealing with the state beyond training (asekkhabhāgiya)..."
If they were to say, "They have been determined because they are unmixed," [we reply: they have not been determined separately.

When the sutta dealing with the side of spiritual cultivation (*vāsanābhāgiya*) has been determined, the sutta dealing with the side of defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) is also thereby determined, because those phenomena that have escaped from the nature of defilement are precisely the phenomena belonging to the side of spiritual cultivation.

And when the sutta dealing with the side of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) has been determined, the sutta dealing with the side of the Adept (*asekkhabhāgiya*) is also thereby determined, because there is no difference between them.
Because it must be asked, "The stages of the foundations of the Dhamma-padas taught in the Suttas have been analyzed according to their classification;
with which fruit (*phala*) should those Suttas be connected?", it was said, "These four Suttas," and so forth.

Therein, "these four Suttas" refers to the Suttas pertaining to the side of purification by habituation (*vāsanābhāgiya*) and the side of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), as they have been determined.
And by means of that specific determination, the discourses pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and those pertaining to the state beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*) are also determined;

thus, these four discourses, when guided by the method of teaching of these very four discourses, should be applied in every way and in all their aspects to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) consisting of the virtue of restraint and the virtue of abandonment. And while applying them in every way and in all their aspects—

The meaning to be understood is this: having analyzed the fruit—such as the virtue of restraint (saṃvara-sīla) and so forth—by means of the method of analysis beginning with the words [of the Suttas], and having sought out the appropriate fruit by means of the method of reasoning, one should apply the Suttas individually to their respective fruits, thinking, "This fruit is the fruit for this person; this fruit is the fruit for this Sutta."
Because it must be asked, "To what extent should they be joined with the fruit of the holy life? it is said: "To whatever extent is the range of knowledge.

By means of the *Vāsanābhāgiya-sutta* taught by the Blessed One, it is established that to whatever extent the stages of practice conducive to merit (*puññabhāgiya*) and so forth constitute the range of analytical knowledge (*vibhajanā-ñāṇa*), and are worthy of becoming its objective supports (*ārammaṇa*), [the practitioner should proceed] by means of those stages.

The *Vāsanābhāgiya-sutta* should be applied [to this]. As many stages as are established by the *Nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta*—beginning with the "way leading to the fruit" (*phalabhāgiyā paṭipadā*)—and are worthy of becoming the grounds and objects for the knowledge of analysis (*vibhajanā-ñāṇa*), the *Nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta* should be applied to that many stages.
The other two suttas should also be applied according to their respective possibilities.
By this, he demonstrates the manifold nature of the knowledges, the planes, and the meanings of the suttas. 34.

The phenomena taught in the *Vāsanābhāgiya-sutta* and others have been analyzed by the Teacher according to their status as belonging to the side of purification through habituation (*vāsanābhāgiya*) or to the side of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), and they have been understood by us;
[now we shall consider] how they belong to the side of defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) or to the side of those beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*), and their common or uncommon status.
Because it was asked, "They should be analyzed," the passage beginning with "In this regard, which phenomena are common" was commenced. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), it says:

"Having thus analyzed the phenomena by way of their being conducive to purification through habituation (*vāsanā*) and conducive to penetration (*nibbedha*), [the author] now analyzes them by way of their being conducive to defilement (*kilesa*) and conducive to the state beyond training (*asekha*), and by way of their being common or uncommon. In this regard, which..."
"...the passage beginning with 'Dhammas are common' has been commenced"—so it is said.
Therein, "therein" means: regarding those dhammas stated in the Sutta that are to be analyzed by way of classification, he asks, "Which dhammas are common?
and he answers, "Two dhammas are common. Those two dhammas...
In order to show them according to their nature, it is said:
"common in name and common in substance. Therein, "common in name" means they are common or identical by way of name—that is, by way of designation (nāma-paññatti).

For example, twenty-one types of consciousness are identical under the name "wholesome" (kusala), and twelve types of consciousness are identical under the names "unwholesome" (akusala) and so forth; they are to be expressed by the verbal designations of "wholesome" and so on.
It is said that meanings are common to names such as "wholesome" (kusala) and so forth. Therefore, in the *Ṭīkā* it is stated:

"Name is a designation by name; through that very medium, the meaning is understood from the word. And by means of the word, the apprehension of such an object occurs solely by way of its general form (*sāmañña-rūpa*), not by way of its specific form (*visesa-rūpa*).
Consequently, meanings expressed by words are [designated] by names whose form is common, because they must be apprehended in dependence upon them."
"Common by name" has been stated.
"Common by basis" means common by way of the basis that serves as their foundation.

Those phenomena which proceed within whichever continuum serving as the foundation—whether that be the mental continuum or the initial arising of consciousness—and so forth, those phenomena [are said to be common] with that continuum or basis.
The meaning is that they are common or identical by virtue of that arising of consciousness and so forth.

Although they are distinct in their intrinsic nature—such as contact and the rest—because they fall within a single continuum, they possess a common basis and thus have an identical object; this is what is meant by saying "having analyzed them by way of classification. [One might ask:
"Are only those things that are common by name and common by basis to be analyzed, or is there nothing else to be analyzed?"
Because it was necessary to ask [further], the passage beginning with "or whatever else" was stated. Whatever other category of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) there may be—
whether characterized by commonality of function, commonality of conditions, or commonality of opposites— that belongs to this same class, that is, possesses a common nature,
all of that should be investigated by means of analysis and sought out by means of reasoning as being appropriate.

The intention is that [the kamma] common [to all] must be divided according to the method of division. Since it must be asked, "Among those [categories] beginning with 'common by name' (nāmasādhāraṇa), which are common by name and which are common by basis (vatthusādhāraṇa)?

it is said: "Of beings fixed in falsehood," and so forth. This refers to the six types of beings fixed in false destiny—namely, the matricides and others who commit such deeds—as well as those in miserable destinies, those in happy destinies without roots, those with two roots, and those with three roots.

The defilements to be abandoned by vision (*dassanapahātabba*) that occur in the mental continua of the four types of worldlings (*puthujjana*) and of beings whose karma is undetermined (*aniyata-kammakara*) are common to those [defilements] to be abandoned by vision;

for although they differ in nature according to the categories of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rites and rituals (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), they do not transcend the designation "to be abandoned by vision.
This applies to the aforementioned types of beings, whether their destiny is determined or undetermined.

The meaning is that they share a common basis (*vatthusādhāraṇā*) and have a common object (*samānavatthukā*), because they serve as the foundation and substrate for those defilements that are to be abandoned by vision.

The defilements of sensual lust and ill will occurring in the mental continuum of both an ordinary person (*puthujjana*)— who consists of four types of beings such as those bound for the miserable states and those without roots of merit—

and a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), are non-common in terms of their names (as "sensual lust" and "ill will"), yet they are identical in nature according to whether they are to be abandoned by the path of the once-returner or the path of the non-returner.

Because even though their natures are different, they do not transcend sensual lust and ill will. Furthermore, the meaning should be understood as follows: for the ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) of the type described, these fetters have a common basis and a common object, insofar as they serve as the foundation and the objective ground for sensual lust and ill will.
As for the higher-tier fetters (*uddhaṃbhāgiya-saṃyojana*) that occur in the mental continuum of the ordinary person and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*):

They are "common" (sādhāraṇā) by way of the name *uddhaṃbhāgiya* (higher-fetter), because that designation does not transcend [the category of] higher-fetters even though they differ in intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) due to [their objects such as] attachment to the form realm and so forth.

Furthermore, the meaning should be understood as "having a common basis" (*samānavatthuka*), in the sense of having a common objective basis (*vatthusādhāraṇa*), because they serve as the objective ground for the higher-fetters of both the worldling (*puthujjana*) and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "For of those [fetters] to be abandoned by vision..."
It is said: "Just as beings fixed in wrongness have a common locus for their activity, so too do those who are unfixed.

In brief, however, it should be understood that on the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*), the defilements that function to abandon [the wholesome] are common by way of name, while the defilements that function simultaneously [with the object] are common by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*).
Those common to the side of defilement have been analyzed by the Teacher and are known by us; but how [are they] on the side of purification (*vodānapakkha*)?
Because it was to be asked, "Are they shared and divided?", the passage beginning with "Whatever a noble disciple" was stated.
Therein, by the general term "whatever," only mundane attainments such as the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth are included.
"A noble disciple" (ariyasāvaka) refers to one who is a disciple of the Noble One, the Blessed One; thus he is called a "noble disciple" (ariyasāvaka), specifically one who has attained the jhānas.
And the person established in the fruit, not one established in the path. For one established in the path does not enter any mundane attainment whatsoever.

All that mundane attainment—whether it be the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, the divine abodes, the sublime abodes, the attainment of the first jhāna, and so forth—is common to those who possess it, whether they are free from lust or not.
They are "shared" because they do not transcend worldly attainments (*lokiya-samāpatti*) and because they can be entered by both those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) and those who are not.
To the objection that must be raised—"When a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) enters a worldly attainment, he does so in specific instances;
this being the case, how can it be believed that they are shared with those free from passion?"—the text says, "For these are shared phenomena," and so forth.

It has been stated. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: “Having kept in mind the inquiry—‘How have these [factors] been taken specifically? Or should they be taken specifically? How are they common?’—and clarifying that, he said:
‘For common factors are thus mutually... and so forth.”
In this regard, those states which are to be attained individually by those who are both free from lust and not free from lust—
namely, the various classes of phenomena occurring successively one after another— are called "worldly attainments" (*lokiya-samāpatti*).
Because they do not overstep their respective fixed domains while remaining mutually related, it should be understood that they are common [to all].
The meaning is "should be grasped. Because it must be explained how one who enters each successive attainment does not overstep [the limit], the passage beginning with "He who...

was stated in order to make this non-overstepping clear. Whether he be a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) or one not yet free from lust (*avītarāga*), if he is endowed with these mundane attainment-states (*lokīya-samāpatti-dhamma*), then that noble disciple or one not yet free from lust, even while entering each successive attainment, [remains within] that state...
It does not transcend the mundane state of attainment; the meaning is that it does not overstep by approaching something else.
Those mundane states of attainment with which one is endowed—these mundane states of attainment should be regarded as common [to all].
"Those states mentioned in the discourses such as the *Vāsanābhāgiya* have been analyzed according to this method of analysis; among those states..."
Because it must be asked, "Which phenomena are uncommon? the passage beginning with "In that regard, which phenomena are uncommon?
and so forth was stated. Therein, among those phenomena to be analyzed, he asks, "Which phenomena are uncommon?
Having asked, one should seek the uncommon phenomena in accordance with the teaching, such as "those of the trainee and those beyond training."
They should be investigated as to whether they are "capable" (*bhabba*) or "incapable" (*abhabba*).
Alternatively, they should be investigated as "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) with reference to the teaching as far as it is stated:

"The trainees and those beyond training are capable or incapable. How are they to be investigated? By way of the qualities of the trainees and those beyond training among the Noble Ones, the name "trainee" (*sekha*) is unshared with the one beyond training (*asekha*), and the name "one beyond training" (*asekha*)... [is unshared with the trainee].

Or, it should be investigated whether the name "those capable" (*bhabbā*) among the ignoble ones is not shared with those who are incapable (*abhabba*), and whether the name "incapable" (*abhabbā*) is not shared with those who are capable.
Because sensual lust and ill will have not been abandoned, they arise in the form of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*);
thus, for the person on the path of the eighth [stage] and for the stream-enterer, these fetters (*saṃyojana*) [remain].
The states of those established in the fruit are common [to both], whereas the natural law (*dhammatā*) and the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) are uncommon. This is what is meant:

"For the eighth-rank person (*aṭṭhamaka*), being established on the path of stream-entry is uncommon to the stream-enterer; for the stream-enterer, being established in the fruit of stream-entry is uncommon to the eighth-rank person established on the path of stream-entry.
Or, for the eighth-rank person, the state of defilements currently being abandoned..."
“The qualities unique to a stream-enterer, and the state of having abandoned the defilements, are not shared with the candidate for the first fruit (the *aṭṭhamaka*).
Because the higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) have not been abandoned and are liable to arise in the form of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*),

they are [present] in the candidate for the first fruit and likewise in the candidate for the path of non-returning who resembles the candidate for the first fruit, as well as in the non-returner established in the fruit.”
And some are common, while the nature of phenomena (dhammatā), the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva), is uncommon. This is what is meant:

"The state of being on the path of non-returning for one who is an eighth-person (aṭṭhamaka) is uncommon to one who stands in the fruit of non-returning; and the state of being in the fruit of non-returning for a non-returner is uncommon to the eighth-person.
Or, the state of having defilements currently being abandoned by the eighth-person is uncommon to the non-returner."
“The state of having abandoned defilements in one who stands at the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is not shared with one who is still a worldling (aṭṭhamaka).

It is also appropriate to say: “The state of standing on the path (maggaṭṭhatā) is not shared with the state of standing at the fruit (phalaṭṭhatā), and the state of standing at the fruit is not shared with the state of standing on the path.
The name “trainee” (sekha) is common to all seven types of persons who are trainees. This is the nature of things (dhammatā).
"Unshared" means that the state of being on each respective path among the four path-states is unshared with one another;
likewise, the state of being in each respective fruition among the three lower fruition-states is unshared with one another.
The meaning is that the four path-states and the three lower fruition-states are mutually unshared.
It is also appropriate to say: “For those in training (sekha), being on a particular path is not common to their being on a particular fruit;
and being on a particular fruit is not common to their being on a particular path. Regarding “of all those who are practicing” (sabbesaṃ paṭipannakānaṃ):
they are called “practitioners” (paṭipannaka) because they practice for the sake of the fruit; this is the name for the four types of persons (puggala) who possess the path.
The name is common, but the specific state of being established on this or that path is unique.
The virtue of all trainees—the seven types of persons who are in training—is common; however, the specific state of being established on this or that path or fruit is unique.

This applies both to those factors such as "to be abandoned by vision" mentioned in the discourses dealing with defilement and the portion concerning perfuming, as well as to those mentioned in the discourses dealing with penetration and the portion concerning those beyond training.

It should be understood that the intention is that the states beginning with those of the trainee (sekha) are to be analyzed according to the method of classification by way of the distinction between common and uncommon. By the passage beginning with "Of the eighth-rank person" (aṭṭhamakassa),
the teacher has analyzed those [states] among the noble persons (ariya-puggala) that are uncommon, and we [shall analyze] them as well.

Since it must be asked, "How are they distinguished as not shared among the non-noble ones?", the passage beginning with "Thus, by one who perceives the distinction" was stated to show that, following the method explained for the noble ones, they should be sought by distinguishing them among the non-noble ones as well.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it says: "Thus, by [the phrase] 'of the eighth person,' etc., the quality not shared among noble individuals..."
Having thus shown [the method for the noble ones], it was said, beginning with “one who perceives the distinction in this way,” for the purpose of showing the method for the others.
Thus, according to the method stated for the noble ones, a wise seeker— one who perceives the distinction among those capable and incapable,
and among those who are not noble, by way of their non-commonality— should [perceive] the inferior, superior, and middling even among those capable and incapable.

It should be sought by way of its dependence. How so? For those who possess the seventh impulsion-moment of consciousness associated with aversion and associated with wrong view—which arises through such acts as matricide and is fixed in the state of falsehood—the first impulsion-moment of consciousness and subsequent states that arise in that manner are indeterminate (*aniyata*) phenomena.

These are common to [all] in their quality of being associated with aversion and so forth; however, the phenomena fixed in falsehood are [distinctive] because they belong to a single specific arising of consciousness.

They are uncommon (*asādhāraṇā*). For just as consciousness cannot be called "associated with consciousness" (*cittasaṃsaṭṭha*), so too those states fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*) cannot be called "common to what is fixed in falsehood.

Even among those fixed in falsehood, for those who possess the seventh impulsion-moment consciousness associated with view—their view being fixed—those first impulsion-moment consciousnesses associated with view that are not fixed (*aniyata*) [do not share in that fixed nature].

Phenomena (dhammas) are common because they are associated with wrong view and so forth; however, fixed wrong view is uncommon because it exists only in association with a single moment of consciousness.
Therefore, the commentator said:
"For those fixed in falsehood, the non-fixed phenomena are common, while the phenomena fixed in falsehood are uncommon."
“Even among those fixed in the wrong way (*micchattaniyata*), the indeterminate states (*aniyata-dhamma*) are common to those fixed in wrong view, while the fixed wrong view itself is uncommon;
this is how it should be understood by one who perceives the distinction according to this method.
In that context, by the phrase “by this method,” it refers to the indeterminate states capable of arising for those fixed in the wrong way.
Those phenomena that are incapable of arising are taken to be "unshared" (asādhāraṇa) because they are indefinite (aniyata). Therefore it is said: "those who are capable and those who are incapable.
For likewise, for one who is inferior, the inferior is shared by virtue of its inferiority, while the middling and superior are unshared.
For one who is middling, the middling is shared, while the inferior and superior are unshared. For one who is superior, the superior is shared by virtue of its superiority...
They should also be sought out as common, or as inferior, middling, and uncommon. Therefore he said: "They should be sought out by way of the inferior, the superior, and the middling.
Having thus analyzed the states (dhammas) through various methods of classification, such as: "In this context, which states are common? and so forth.

These have been shown and understood by us. Since one might ask, "How were the planes and the bases analyzed and shown by way of analysis and method?"—and because it is appropriate to ask this—it is after the analysis of the phenomena that he analyzes and shows the planes and bases, saying:
"The plane of seeing," and so forth. Therein, "the plane of seeing" means that seeing occurs here in the first path.
The plane of seeing is the path of stream-entry. Regarding "entry into the certainty" (*niyāmāvakkanti*): "certainty" (*niyāma*) means being fixed; what is it? It is the certainty of attainment.
"Entry" (*avakkanti*) means entering; it is the fruit of stream-entry. "Entry into certainty" is the entry into that certainty; by means of that.

The path of stream-entry, named the plane of seeing, is the proximate cause for the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, named the entry into certainty. [This refers to] one who possesses the first path.
For while a person is said to be "entering the fixed course" (*niyāma*) when they are about to enter it, one who possesses the fruit (*phalasamaṅgī*) is said to have "entered the fixed course.
Therefore, by the term "entry into the fixed course," the arising of the first fruit is intended. "The planes of development" (*bhāvanābhūmi*) refers to the three higher paths.
"Of those that follow" means for the attainment of the respective fruits that proceed from each respective path; it is their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
Each should be applied individually.
The painful practice with slow direct knowledge, arising for one of dull wisdom, brings about serenity and thus becomes the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of serenity;
the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge, arising for one of superior knowledge, brings about insight.

Having established that insight (vipassanā) is the proximate cause [for the path], it should be understood that the remaining two modes of practice are also proximate causes for serenity (samatha), because they arise even in one who is not particularly wise.
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "But the other three modes of practice bring about serenity," and so forth.
The basis for meritorious action consisting in giving is itself an absolute prerequisite for hearing the Dhamma.
It does not serve as the proximate cause (*padatthāna*). However, acts such as paying homage, making requests, and asking questions do serve as its proximate cause;
therefore, by way of these factors acting together, the voice of another becomes the proximate cause. And the voice of another occurs through such means as hearing the Dhamma and answering questions.
For, at times when one gives away material gifts or pays homage and makes requests, people generally teach the Dhamma.
And at times such as when asking questions, they provide answers, or engage in cross-examination and discussion.

The basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue, by being common to gladness, rapture, tranquility, happiness, and concentration through its state of being their proximate cause, becomes the proximate cause for wisdom born of reflection.
For when one who possesses virtue reflects upon that virtue—
Joy and the other [factors] arise, and one who is concentrated is capable of reflecting on the Dhamma.
"The basis for meritorious action consisting in development" means that the preceding development of serenity (*samatha*) and the development of insight (*vipassanā*),
acting in common with the causes such as giving and virtue, lead to the wisdom consisting in development.
It is the proximate cause for each respective development of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*) and insight (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*). Therefore, it is said in the Commentary:

"Common" means that it is not exclusive (*āveṇika*)—like a seed is to a sprout, or like the stage of seeing and so forth are to the entry into the path of assurance (*niyāmāvakkanti*) and so forth—but rather it is common even with other causes. [It is the basis] for the bases of meritorious action consisting in giving, morality, and mental development.

Since the Master has explained that the state of being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for wisdom derived from the voice of another, wisdom consisting of reflection, and wisdom consisting of cultivation exists [only] in that way, one might object:

"If that were so, then the state of being the proximate cause for generosity and the other perfections would not exist respectively as the study of the scriptures, proficiency in learning, application to the meditation subject, and right view on the path.
In order to show that they do indeed function as proximate causes in such a manner, [the author] says:
“It is said: ‘The basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting in giving arises from the voice of another and from wisdom born of hearing,’ and so forth.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is stated:
‘Now, since giving, virtue, and mundane development do not arise solely from the aforementioned voice of another and so on…’”

It is said: "Furthermore, since [the practice] is also a condition for the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), proficiency (*bāhusacca*), application to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-anuyoga*), and right view regarding the path (*maggasammādiṭṭhi*) in their proper order, he therefore extended the teaching again with the words 'consisting of giving' (*dānamaya*) and so forth, in order to show that method as well.
In this context, the state of being a common proximate cause (*sādhāraṇapadaṭṭhāna*) for the voice of another regarding the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting of giving is as follows:

This should be understood according to the method explained below. However, after giving a gift and hearing the teaching, for one who reflects by expanding upon it according to what was heard, the wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī-paññā*) that arises serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), being common to acts such as paying homage and making requests.
Likewise, the basis of meritorious action consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*) also serves as a proximate cause common to the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-paññā*).
This has already been stated. However, for one who reflects thus—“Relying on purified virtue, I shall produce jhāna;
I shall produce the path and its fruit”—the appropriate attention that is occurring serves as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) by being common to gladness and the other [factors].
Furthermore, it also serves as the proximate cause common to the basis of meritorious action consisting in development and to the wisdom consisting in development.

It has already been stated. However, right view—whether it proceeds by taking as its foundation the jhāna known as the development of serenity (samatha-bhāvanā), or by relying on the ripening state of insight (vipassanā)—serves as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) when it is accompanied by purified virtue and the other factors.
The status of the bases for meritorious action consisting of giving, etc., and of the voice of another, etc., as proximate causes has been explained by the Teacher again and again.
[The Master said: "This has been analyzed and understood by us: 'Dwelling in a suitable locality and so forth are also the proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna) of these qualities.

Therefore, you should analyze and demonstrate them in such a way that they may be analyzed and understood by us. Because he was thus addressed, [the Elder] spoke the words beginning with "dwelling in a suitable locality" in order to analyze and demonstrate them as well.
However, in the Commentary, it says: "In that same way, dwelling in a suitable locality and so forth..."

It is said: "The phrase 'dwelling in a suitable locality' and so forth was spoken to demonstrate this method—that [these factors] serve as the causes for bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and the rest.
This is because, for one dwelling in dependence upon a suitable locality, bodily and mental seclusion increase, and concentration increases;
thus, dwelling in a suitable locality [is the cause] of bodily and mental seclusion, as well as access concentration and absorption concentration, along with virtue and the other [requisites].

The proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is common [to all]. "Dependence upon a true person" (sappurisūpanissaya) refers to the confidence (pasāda) that arises from attending upon a true person and can be taken as an object;

or, it refers to the prior confidence that arose in the continuum of those who attended upon him after obtaining dependence upon him—such being the dependence upon a true person for one endowed with faith who attends upon the Three Jewels.

The proximate cause for the three kinds of confirmed confidence (*aveccappasāda*) is, in common with the qualities of the Triple Gem and so forth, the service rendered to a true person (*sappurisa*) who bestows the signs for attaining serenity (*samatha*);

having relied upon that true person and abiding by the method given by him, the practice of serenity—which must be set in motion—has as its proximate cause, in common with joy in virtue, rapture, and so forth, the reliance upon a true person (*sappurisūpanissaya*). For one who has rightly directed oneself...
Because it gives rise to disgust for evil and so forth, right self-direction— being common to those who reflect on their birth,
age, and other factors— is the proximate cause for moral shame (*hirī*); and because it gives rise to disenchantment and so forth in one who has rightly directed himself,
it— being common to virtue and the rest— is the proximate cause for insight (*vipassanā*).
The relinquishing of unwholesome states by way of their factors and so forth, being common to the knowledge of disenchantment and others,
is the proximate cause for the wisdom of wholesome investigation, for the contemplation of reflection, for the noble path-concentration faculty,

and for the planting of the roots of the wholesome that result in mundane and supramundane success through following the hearing of well-expounded teachings. This well-expounded nature of the Dhamma is the planting of the roots of the wholesome.
It is the proximate cause for that [faith] and for the attainment of fruition through such roots of merit.

The Saṅgha’s state of being well-practiced is the proximate cause for the Saṅgha’s excellence, for the excellence of those who attend upon the Saṅgha, and for the state of receiving words with respect and deference.

The perfection of the Teacher is the proximate cause for the lack of knowledge regarding the virtues of the Teacher himself, as well as the Dhamma and so forth, and for the lack of confidence [in them].
It is the proximate cause for the increase, growth, and further development of faith in those who already have faith, as well as for the increase of even slight faith.
Unimpeded observance of the Pātimokkha is for the purpose of restraining individuals who are stubborn, sullen, and immoral within the midst of the Saṅgha or the assembly;
and it is for the comfortable dwelling of individuals who are amiable and endowed with virtue, such as restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
And it is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). However, it should be understood that in being such, it exists as common to other appropriate causes.

Because one might ask, "By whom can we know or have faith in the manner of analyzing the divisions of the dharma-bases and proximate causes mentioned in the *Vāsanābhāgiya-sutta* and other texts?"—therefore, the passage beginning with "Therefore he said" was spoken. Its meaning is as follows:
It is to be understood according to the method already stated.
Because it must be said, “At this point the Mode of Conveying Analysis (vibhattihāra) is complete;
no other is assigned,” it is therefore stated: “The Mode of Conveying Analysis is concluded. Wherever in whichever suttas whatever phenomena and so forth are mentioned, there—

The meaning should be understood as follows: whatever method of analysis was applied to those various phenomena and so forth mentioned in the Suttas, according to their availability—that very method of analysis has been extracted and properly applied.
Thus, this analysis of the method of analysis (vibhattihāra-vibhaṅga) has been composed in accordance with one's own strength and ability.
The analysis of the Mode of Conveying Investigation is finished.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
9. Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reversal.

35. By whichever specific commentary—that is, by whichever analysis of the "Modes of Conveying" (hāra)—the phenomena and so forth mentioned in the Sutta have been analyzed, that specific commentary of analysis is complete. Because it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reversal?
it is said: "In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Reversal? and so forth. Therein, "in this regard" (tattha) means among those [modes].

Among the sixteen modes of conveying the teaching (desanāhāra) and so forth that have been pointed out, he asks: which specific method of exposition is the "mode of transformation" (parivattano hāro), known as the "Analysis of the Mode of Transformation" (parivattanahāravibhaṅgo)?

The specific method of detailed exposition beginning with "of a person possessing right view" (*sammādiṭṭhissa purisapuggalassa*), which is now being stated by me following the summary indication (*niddesa*) beginning with "wholesome and unwholesome phenomena" (*kusalākusale dhamme*), is the mode of transformation, the analysis of the mode of transformation.
The meaning "name" (nāma) should be understood here.

Since it must be asked, "When the sutta is being commented upon, what is the counteragent to which cultivated wholesome state that has been specified, and how is it to be reversed?", [the answer is: this is the counteragent to this cultivated wholesome state.
Showing that it must be turned over by way of its state of being abandoned, he said, “Of a person with right view,” and so forth.
In the commentary, however, it says:
“In this regard, because when a sutta is being expounded, [one considers] those wholesome and unwholesome states as they have been specified, which stand as opposites...”
It is stated: “The determination [of the person] by way of the state of being abandoned and so forth among unwholesome and wholesome phenomena is a reversal from the perspective of their opposites;
therefore, the passage beginning ‘For a person of right view, wrong view is worn away’ has been commenced.
For there is a determination of the abandoning agent (the dhamma that abandons) by way of its state of being the abandoner, and [a determination] of that which is to be abandoned.
The determination by way of the state of abandoning the Dhamma is called "reversal from the opposite.

In this context, "of right view" (*sammādiṭṭhissa*) means that person whose view (*diṭṭhi*) is right, beautiful, and praised; thus he is one of right view. For this teaching has the person as its proximate cause (*puggala-padaṭṭhāna*).
Therefore it is said: "of the person, the individual" (*purisa-puggalassa*). Furthermore, that right view arises through the conviction in karma, the fruit of karma, and so forth.
Or, [the insight] occurring by way of insight into impermanence and so forth, or by way of the right view of the path, is taken as being entirely included.
"By the development of which right view wrong view is abandoned and worn away":
if only wrong view itself were worn away, then while that might be so, the remaining unwholesome states would not be worn away.
Because it ought to be said, "They would come to be," it was stated: "And those various evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view...
These various evil, unwholesome states would arise, or rather, they would be such as to be liable to arise;
yet for this person endowed with right view, those unwholesome states have been worn away, are fit to be abandoned, and are of a nature not to arise again.
Thus it is. Therefore the Blessed One said: “With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence.

[An objection: “If, for a person of right view, wrong view is eliminated along with the unwholesome states conditioned by it, then in that case, wholesome states conditioned by right view would not be possible.”
Because it ought to be stated, the words "conditioned by right view" and so forth were spoken.

For that person endowed with right view, numerous wholesome states—whether serenity and insight, or factors conducive to enlightenment—which are appropriate to arise conditioned by right view, do indeed come into being;
and once arisen, those states belong to that person endowed with right view.
They reach the fulfillment of development by way of recurring occurrence within the mental continuum.
The teacher has analyzed, and we have understood, the state of being the opposite of right view—namely, wrong view—and of the unwholesome states conditioned by it;
[likewise] the state of being the opposite of the phenomenon of right intention...
Because it must be asked, "How is it to be reversed?", the passage beginning with "of a person who possesses right intention" was stated.

The meanings of the terms *yojana* (connection) and so forth should be understood according to the method already explained. One whose speech (*vācā*) is right, beautiful, or praiseworthy is "one of right speech" (*sammāvāca*);
[the text refers to] that one of right speech. The meaning of the terms "person" (*purisa*), "individual" (*puggala*), and so forth should also be understood by the same method already explained.

This, however, is the specific meaning: one who possesses the knowledge and vision of liberation that is right and non-perverted is called "one possessing right knowledge and vision of liberation" (*sammā-vimutti-ñāṇadassana*).

For such a person, who is endowed with the knowledge and vision of reflective awareness regarding that right knowledge and vision of liberation, there exists a "wrong knowledge and vision of liberation" (*micchā-vimutti-ñāṇadassana*) that proceeds by way of a false adherence, thinking, "We are liberated," when in fact we are not liberated.
It becomes worn away and vanished. The connection and so forth for the phrases beginning with “And those which” should be understood according to the method already stated.

36. Since it must be asked, “By the phrase ‘of one with right view,’ etc., the unwholesome factors such as wrong view, which are the opposites of the wholesome factors such as right view, are to be substituted as the objects to be abandoned,” [the text continues] with the abstinences from killing living beings, etc.
In order to show that unwholesome states such as killing living beings—which are the opposites of the wholesome—must also be abandoned and turned away from, it is said:

"Or for one who abstains from killing living beings," and so forth. In the Commentary, however, after thus showing wrong view and so on by way of right view and so on, [it continues] again by way of abstinence from killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and so on.

It is said that the passage beginning with “yassā” (of whom) was commenced in order to show the reversal of killing living beings and so forth. It is abandoned by way of its constituent parts (*tadaṅga*) and so on.
Regarding the term “kālavādissa” (one who speaks at the right time): he is a speaker at the right time because it is his habit to say what ought to be said at the time when it ought to be said;
[the text refers] to him. Since it was asked, “They must be reversed in the very manner already described,” it follows that they may also be reversed in another manner.
The passage beginning with “And whoever... was spoken in order to demonstrate this. However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“By the words ‘And whoever... and so forth, he demonstrates by another method the reversal of wrong view and the rest through right view and the rest themselves.
In that context, certain individuals who possess wrong view, wrong intention, and so forth, [act] toward other noble ones...
They censure the Noble Eightfold Path. "Visible here and now" (*sandiṭṭhika*) means connected with what is visible.
"Those who speak in accordance with the Dhamma" (*sahadhammika*) refers to those who proceed together with the Dhamma by way of reason. "Censurable" (*gārayha*) means engaged in modes of censuring.
"Disputes and counter-disputes" (*vādānuvādā*)—those venerable ones censure both right view and the Dhamma. By means of that censure.
They are not worthy of honor, nor are they to be honored; they are not praiseworthy, nor are they to be praised.

In such statements as "Thus," etc., they censure either right intention individually, or right speech and so forth individually, or both right intention and those venerable ones together as the Dhamma.
Therefore, those who possess wrong intention are not worthy of honor or praise... [and so on] ...nor do they possess right liberation.
Those venerable ones censure the Dhamma. Therefore, those who speak with wrong view are not to be honored or praised by you.
And since those venerable ones censure the Dhamma of right liberation through knowledge and vision, therefore those who possess wrong liberation are not to be honored or praised by you.
[And so too regarding] right liberation through knowledge and vision...

Those venerable ones criticize the Dhamma. Therefore, the construction should be made thus: "Those who possess wrong knowledge and vision regarding liberation are not to be honored or praised by those venerable ones.
There is also a reading: "micchāvimuttiñāṇadassanā" (those with wrong knowledge and vision regarding liberation).
Furthermore, through the very act of criticizing the Noble Path, right view, and so forth, wrong view and the rest are to be understood as being reversed; it does not refer to anything else.

Because it must be stated [as] "by way of praise," in order to show that even by way of praising sensual pleasures (*kāma*) and so forth, their opposites—abstinence and the like—are also to be reversed, it was said: "And as for those who say thus... and so on.

Therein, regarding the terms "sensual pleasures to be enjoyed," "sensual pleasures to be consumed," "sensual pleasures to be cultivated," and "sensual pleasures to be indulged in": they are called *kāmā* because they are desired (*kamyante*).
Regarding "kāmā": by way of the instrumental sense of "action" (*kamma-sādhana*), "objects of desire" (*vatthu-kāmā*) are intended. One should enjoy desires that are not too refined;
one should enjoy very refined desires on all sides (*pari*); one should intensely (*ā*) cultivate desires that are even more refined than those, and they should be cultivated with certainty.

Furthermore, in the phrases "desires should be developed" (*bhāvayitabbā kāmā*) and "desires should be practiced frequently" (*bahulīkātabbā kāmā*), the term *kāmā* is used in the sense of the instrumental of the agent (*kattusādhana*), meaning "those who desire."
The defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) are grasped; the defilements of sensual desire are to be cultivated, increased, and set in motion by way of repeated arising;
the defilements of sensual desire are to be performed, increased, and maintained by way of the repeated arising of many [instances].
This refers to certain worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are subject to sensual desires and have spoken thus regarding those worldlings subject to sensual desires.

The intention should be understood as follows: abstaining from such sensual pleasures—which consist of wholesome volition—would, by way of its opposite, result in what is called "unrighteousness" (*adhamma*) that ought not to be practiced.
To demonstrate the turning away from the two extremes, the passage beginning with "or whatever... was stated. [This refers to] the pursuit of self-mortification.

Regarding the phrase "the Dhamma is leading-out": those who practice the five-fold heat (pañcātapa) and so forth have said that for those practitioners of the five-fold heat and so on, the Dhamma that leads out—the Noble Path accompanied by insight, which is reckoned as the Middle Way—would result in being called "not the Dhamma," "not leading out," and "not to be cultivated.
There is also a reversal [of the meaning] by way of pleasure and pain.

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “But those who... was stated. [The objection is: “The practice of self-mortification and so forth, which proceeds for those who have undertaken it with the thought ‘We shall wear away evil,’ is a painful state that torments the body;

yet they claim this state is leading-out (niyyānika). Furthermore, for those who practice in such a way, the pleasant state that consists in the alleviation of bodily suffering—which proceeds by means of the enjoyment of blameless requisites—would result in being called ‘not-Dhamma’ (adhamma) and thus ought not to be practiced.”
The teacher has analyzed the transformation by way of the two extremes and so forth, and this has been understood by us.

However, because it must be asked, "How should one transform by way of the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) and so forth?", the passage beginning with "Or else" was stated to show how the perception of beauty (subha-saññā) and the rest are to be transformed by way of the perception of foulness and so forth.
In the Commentary, however, [it says]: "Now, by way of the perception of foulness and so forth..."
It is said that the passage beginning with “Or alternatively” was stated in order to show the transformation of the perception of beauty and so forth.

“In all formations” means in the formations belonging to the three planes. For to one who has commenced insight meditation, phenomena of the three planes appear as foul because they are characterized by the oozing of the impurities of the defilements.

“If these were not to be exchanged because they are of the same nature—such that ‘these are the opposites of those’—then, this being the case, it would be impossible to exchange all opposites without exception; how then can they be exchanged?

Since it was necessary to state this, he spoke the passage beginning with “whatever...,” in order to show the characteristic of exchange. In that context, whatever phenomenon, whether wholesome (*kusala*) or unwholesome (*akusala*), [is taken]...
One who wishes to turn back, the teacher approves with his mind and approaches with his view.

Whatever is the opposite of that particular state—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that which has been approved and approached is an "untrue state" (*asaddhamma*), because it is undesirable, contrary, offensive, and fully understood. Whether desirable or undesirable...
Or rather, whatever phenomenon (*dhamma*) a teacher desires to master by means of his mind and approaches through his view—

whether it be desirable or undesirable— whatever is its opposite, that opposing phenomenon becomes for him mastered through full understanding (*pariññāta*), because it is undesirable, contrary, and has been overcome by one who wishes to master it.
The characteristic of the opposite is stated as “the reversal should be made by way of the opposites corresponding to the desired qualities.
By this, it is said in the Commentary: “It makes manifest the characteristic of the opposite.
To the question, “How are we to believe in such a form of reversal as has been described? the passage beginning with “Therefore he said” was spoken.
Because it must be said, “To this extent the Mode of Conveying Reversal (parivatta-hāra) is complete;

there is no other [mode] to be applied,” it is stated: “The Mode of Conveying Reversal is applied. In whatever sutta wholesome and unwholesome states are demonstrated, whichever Mode of Conveying Reversal is applicable is applied by way of extracting the opposites. Having extracted them by way of the opposites in that sutta which has been demonstrated...
The method of reversal (*parivattanahāra*) is concluded; the meaning should be understood as "extracted," "joined," and "applied.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Exposition) composed according to one's own ability on the analysis of the method of reversal.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
10. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Synonyms (*Vevacanahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā*).
37. By whichever specific mode of commentary consisting of the Mode of Occurrence (*pavattanahāra*), the meanings of the discourses (*sutta*) are to be turned over [into analysis].

The analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (*vevacana-hāra-vibhaṅga*), which constitutes a specific kind of exposition, has been completed following the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reversal (*parivattana-hāra*).
Because it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms?", it is said: "In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms? and so forth.

Regarding that, the phrase "in those" (*tattha*) refers to those sixteen Modes of Conveying, beginning with the Mode of Conveying Teaching (*desanā-hāra*), which have been specified. What specific exposition among them is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms, or the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms?

He asks, "What is the name?
