[The answer is: "The meaning should be understood as follows: the specific detailed commentary now being stated by me—beginning with 'One Dhamma, O Blessed One'—which belongs to the exposition beginning with 'There are many synonyms,' is called the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (vevacana-hāra) or the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (vevacana-hāra-vibhaṅga). This is because one must ask:
'Regarding those synonyms that have been determined, what are those synonyms?'"

“Just as one,” and so forth, is what was said. The meaning is that one should understand those synonyms by the various modes and synonyms through which the Blessed One explains a single phenomenon to be known—a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma), or a phenomenon to be made known—in such ways.
Since it might be asked, “What did the Blessed One say those synonyms are? [the following is stated].
“It was said by the Blessed One,” and so forth, is what was stated. For example, there are various synonymous expressions:
“Hope, longing, and delight—these cravings are established among the manifold elements;
these yearnings, which arise from the root of ignorance, have all been eradicated by me along with their roots.”
The Blessed One said: the meaning is that those various synonymous terms (vevacana) are to be understood.
The fruit of explaining a single dhamma by means of numerous synonymous terms used as alternative modes of exposition has been stated in many ways in the Aṭṭhakathā;
therefore, it has not been shown by us here. This is because one must ask: "What is hope (āsā)? What is longing (pihā), and so forth?"
“It is called ‘expectation’ (āsā),” and so forth, was said.
That longing for a future object—the expectation that it will certainly come to pass—which arises in a person who is hoping, is called “expectation.
Furthermore, the aspiration that arises in one who is currently aspiring, or upon seeing something else that is superior—
The longing that arises in one who longs, thinking, “May I become such,” is called *patthanā* (aspiration); it is also called *pihā* (longing).
Craving directed toward a future object is called *āsā* (hope), while craving directed toward both future and present objects is called *pihā*.
Nevertheless, because they are identical in their nature as craving, they are one and the same phenomenon.
The accomplishment of the desired goal is "accomplishment of the goal" (*atthanipphatti*). One protects by means of this craving, hence it is "protection" (*paṭipālanā*).
The protection of the accomplishment of the goal is "protection of the accomplishment of the goal" (*atthanipphattipaṭipālanā*).
That craving which arises in that person who is thus protecting is called "delight" (*abhinandanā*).
Because it must be asked, "What is that accomplishment of the goal which is to be maintained by craving?
he spoke the passage beginning with "a dear relative or a dear thing," showing that accomplishment of the goal by analyzing it into either a being (*satta*) or a formation (*saṅkhāra*).
In this context, by the word "relative" (*ñāti*), friends, kinsmen, and so forth are also included. [The word] "thing" (*dhamma*)...
Furthermore, that craving by which one who possesses craving delights in the sixfold objects of affection,

such as pleasant forms and so forth, is called "delight" (*abhinandanā*). That craving by which one who possesses craving, through the influence of perversion, delights in a repulsive relative or phenomenon as being non-repulsive—
either by way of perversion regarding a repulsive relative or phenomenon, or by way of its intrinsic nature regarding a non-repulsive relative or phenomenon— is [likewise called delight].
The meaning should be understood by connecting it thus: "That craving is called 'delight' (abhinandanā).

Since it must be asked, "In which various elements (dhātu) is the aforementioned kind of craving called 'lust' (sara) by the Blessed One? Which are those elements?", the passage beginning with "the eye-element" is stated in order to show those elements in their own form.
Since it must be asked, "In which element among those elements does which lust reside and proceed?", [the answer follows] with this...
Having determined that "this craving proceeds established upon the element," it was said:
"Craving: some are intent on form," and so forth. Therein, "some" refers to persons who are characterized by craving in the form of craving for form (*rūpatanha*).
"Intent on form" means they are devoted to and attached to the object known as the form-element. By this phrase, craving in the form of craving for form is indicated.

It is understood that those established in the form-element (rūpadhātu) are those who proceed [therein]; likewise, by the phrases "some are intent on sounds" and so forth, the various cravings—comprised of craving for sound and the rest—which are established in and proceed within the sound-element and the others, are also understood as "cravings.

Regarding the phrase "some are intent on mental objects" (dhammādhimutta), by the inclusion of the term "mental objects" (dhamma), the eye-element, ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, body-element, the seven consciousness-elements, and the mental-object-element (dhammadhātu) are included.
Since they have been included, it should be understood that although eighteen elements are included by way of being their bases, they are nonetheless included as sixfold.

Because it must be asked, "In the case of those intent on forms (*rūpādhimutta*) and so forth, how many terms belong to the side of craving (*taṇhāpakkha*) and are synonyms for craving?", [the author] establishes and shows that such and so many terms belong to the side of craving and are synonyms for craving, saying: "Therein..."
And it is said, beginning with, “those six based on the household life. Therein means: among those six [objects], form and so forth.
“The six griefs based on the household life” refers to the six types of grief that arise depending upon craving and affection directed toward the six objects, form and so forth.

This same method applies to the remaining [feelings] as well. One might ask: “Six equanimities based on the household life were also spoken of by the Blessed One; why are they not included? To address this, [the text says]: “As for the six equanimities...”
It is said, "This side of views is based on the household life"; the meaning is that it is not included because it belongs to the side of views.
38. Since it must be asked, "How is it that craving alone is taken in the manner described?", it is said, "That very [craving] by way of aspiration," and so forth.
That very craving, in the manner described, is expressed by terms such as "longing" (*āsā*) and so on, because it proceeds in the mode of aspiration.
Because it delights in phenomena that have form and so forth as their object, it is figuratively called "delight in phenomena" (*dhammanandi*);

because it remains clinging to phenomena that have form and so forth as their object, as if swallowing them and reaching a final conclusion, it is figuratively called "clinging to phenomena" (*dhammajjhosāna*).
Therefore, these are synonyms for craving (*taṇhā*).
The synonyms for craving have been pointed out by the Teacher and are known to us;

however, because it was asked, "Which are the synonyms for consciousness?", the passage beginning with "consciousness (citta), mind (mano)" was stated. The meaning—namely, "it thinks of an object, thus it is consciousness;
it cognizes, thus it is mind; it discerns, thus it is consciousness"—has already been explained in the treatises, and therefore we have not elaborated upon it here.

These are synonyms; we shall explain only as many as there are, saying, "These are the synonyms for this. Terms such as "the faculty of wisdom" (*paññindriya*) and "the power of wisdom" (*paññābala*) are synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*).
Terms such as "the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One" (*araham sammāsambuddho*) are synonyms for the Buddha. Since it must be asked, "Where were these taught? [the following is said].

“And as it is stated in the *Buddhānussati*,” and so forth, was said. In the teaching on *Buddhānussati*, whatever kind of synonym has been stated by the Blessed One as “Thus indeed is the Blessed One, the Arahant... [etc.
...of the Blessed One,” this kind of synonym should be understood as a synonym for *Buddhānussati* and a synonym for the Buddha. “And as in the *Dhammānussati*...”
The same method of application should be made for the passages beginning with "vuttaṃ" and so forth.

The meaning of the connection and so forth for the passage beginning with "tenāha," as well as the meaning of the connection and so forth for the passage "the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (vevacana-hāra) is concluded," should be understood according to the method already stated.
Thus, the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms has been composed in accordance with one's own strength and ability.
The exposition of the method of analysis (*vibhāvanā*) is concluded.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
11. The Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Description (*paññatti-hāra-vibhaṅga-vibhāvanā*).
39. By whichever analysis (*vibhaṅga*), which constitutes a specific mode of exposition, synonyms are analyzed, that specific mode of exposition as an analysis is complete.
Because it must be asked, "Which is the analysis of the Mode of Description (*paññattihāra-vibhaṅga*)?", it is said: "In this regard, what is the Mode of Description?
and so forth. Therein, "in each case" (*tattha tattha*) refers to those sixteen modes of teaching, beginning with the Mode of Teaching (*desanāhāra*), which have been pointed out.
He asks: "What is the specific exposition of the Mode of Conveying Descriptions (paññatti-hāra), known as the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Descriptions?

One should understand that the detailed exposition now being stated by me—beginning with "The teaching which is the natural discourse" (*yā pakatikathāya desanā*) and so forth—is the specific exposition of the Mode of Conveying Descriptions, known as the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Descriptions, in reference to the instruction beginning with: "The Blessed One teaches one Dhamma through various descriptions."
Because it must be asked, "By which various designations does the Blessed One teach a single Dhamma? What are those various designations?", it is said:

"That which is by way of natural discourse," and so forth. Therein, "by way of natural discourse" means by way of a discourse that proceeds according to the essential nature of the meaning, without determining specific details of the word-meanings such as gratification and so on;
[it refers to] a discourse on the Dhamma characterized by careful attention.
Teaching (desanā) deposits, establishes, and makes known in a specific manner the intended meaning within the mental continuum of those to be trained;
therefore, it is a "presentation by way of deposit" (nikkhepapaññatti). The meaning is that one teaches the Dhamma by means of that presentation.
Since it must be asked, "What is this presentation which is called 'teaching by way of natural discourse'?", he asks thus and then shows it in detail:
The passage beginning with “And what is the teaching by way of the natural exposition? has been stated. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:

“Thus, in order to analyze in detail the meaning that was stated in brief as ‘the teaching by way of the natural exposition,’ [the author] asked, ‘And what is the teaching by way of the natural exposition?
and then replied, ‘The four truths,’ and so forth. In that context, although there is a distinction between the teaching and the subject to be taught, [the text continues:]
By way of figurative designation (*abhedopacāra*), it is said: "The teaching is the four truths. The meaning is that the designation of the four truths is what is called "the teaching.
Since it must be asked, "In what manner did the Blessed One state that designation of the truths?", it is therefore said: "In the manner that the Blessed One stated it.
In whatever way—that is, by whichever method—the Blessed One stated each particular designation, in that very same way is that designation [to be understood].
It should be understood thus: the designation spoken by the Blessed One as "This is suffering" is a designation for the presentation of the five aggregates,
a designation for the presentation of the six elements, a designation for the presentation of the eighteen elements,
a designation for the presentation of the twelve bases, and [a designation] for the ten faculties.
The construction should be understood as "the designation by way of grouping. The aggregates (khandhas), elements (dhātus), bases (āyatanas), and faculties (indriyas) are exclusively mundane.

Having brought them to a state of unity through their commonality of being characterized by oppression, being conditioned, being afflicted with heat, and being subject to change, they are declared as "this is suffering. Regarding "of the ten faculties": this refers to the ten faculties consisting of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, life, mind, and feeling faculties.
Because they share a single characteristic by virtue of having the characteristic of experiencing, the feeling faculty is taken as one; [so too are] the faith faculty and the others.
However, because they are included within the path (*maggapariyāpanna*), they are not taken [here].

Regarding "in edible food" (*kabaḷīkāre*): although it is designated by way of its location (*ṭhānūpacāra*) as the nutriment consisting of nutritive essence (*ojā*), there is delight (*nandī*)—whether by way of underlying tendency (*anusaya*), or by way of hope (*āsā*), or by way of aspiration (*patthanā*)—because lust (*rāga*) is not to be abandoned by the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
"There is craving" (*atthi taṇhā*): here too, [the same applies].

The same method applies here. "Established and grown" should be understood as being both established and grown because it has reached the state of being capable of drawing in rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Of formations" (*saṅkhārānaṃ*) means of those formations which are the causes for the production of existence (*bhava*) that brings about renewed becoming.
"Birth, aging, and death": birth has the characteristic of actualizing [existence].
It is not arising alone; aging has the characteristic of ripening. It is not stability alone; death has the characteristic of breaking up.
It is not dissolution alone. Therefore it is said: "accompanied by sorrow, accompanied by fear, accompanied by despair.
"Monks, if in the nutriment of contact... [and so on] ...if, monks, in the nutriment of mental volition... [and so on] ...in consciousness..."
“Bhikkhus, regarding this nutriment, there is lust... [as before] ...so I say. This is a designation called a “designation of origin,” because it designates the origin and the source of suffering.

The classification of designations according to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known by us; but how [is it classified] according to the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*)?
Because it must be stated that "the classification of designations is analyzed," it was said: "If, monks, there is no lust for physical nutriment...

and so forth. This designation—namely, "In physical nutriment... I say there is no despair"—is called a "designation of full understanding" because it designates the full understanding of suffering, and a "designation of abandoning" because it designates the abandoning of its origin.

It is called a "description by way of development" because it makes known the path and its development; it is called a "description by way of realization" because it makes known the cessation and its realization. 40.
The classification of descriptions by way of turning away has been analyzed by the Teacher and is understood by us. How, then, [is it] by way of comprehension?
Because it must be stated that "the classification of designations is analyzed," it was said: "Bhikkhus, develop concentration... and so forth.

This statement—"Bhikkhus, develop concentration... [as far as] ...he understands things as they really are"—is called a "designation of development" (*bhāvanā-paññatti*) because it designates both the path and its development; it is also a designation because it designates the full understanding of suffering.
It is called a "description by full understanding" because it describes full understanding; it is called a "description by abandoning" because it describes the abandoning of the origin;
and it is called a "description by realization" because it describes the realization of cessation.
The classification of descriptions by way of comprehension has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known to us. [But] how is it [described] by way of the aggregates of clinging?
Because it must be stated that "the classification of designations is analyzed," it was said: "Disperse form, Rādha," and so forth.
This designation—beginning with "Disperse form, Rādha... [up to] Nibbāna"—is called a "designation of cessation" because it makes known the cessation of the obstruction known as craving;
it is called a "designation of disenchantment" because it makes known disenchantment with gratification.
It is called a designation by name; it is called a designation of full understanding because it makes known the full understanding of suffering;
it is called a designation of abandonment because it makes known the abandonment of the origin; it is called a designation of development because it makes known the development of the path;
and it is called a designation of realization because it makes known the realization of cessation.

Because it must be asked, "What does he understand when he scatters, destroys, and renders playthings of the mind the form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, practicing for the destruction of craving through wisdom?", it is said: "He understands as it really is:
'This is suffering'... [and so on] ...the way leading to its cessation."
"One understands it as it really is"—this is called a "penetration-designation" (paṭivedha-paññatti) because it designates the penetration of the truths;

it is called a "presentation-designation" (nikkhepa-paññatti) because it designates the presentation of the plane of vision; it is called a "cultivation-designation" (bhāvanā-paññatti) because it designates the cultivation of the path;
and it is called a [realization-designation] because it designates the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
This is called a "description by way of realization" (*sacchikiriyā-paññatti*). The description: “He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’...

[and so on] ...he understands as it really is: ‘The taints cease without remainder’”—this is called a "description of arising" because it describes the arising of the knowledge of destruction (*khaye-ñāṇa*), and it is called a "description of opportunity" because it describes the opportunity for the knowledge of non-arising (*anuppāde-ñāṇa*).

It is called a "description by way of cultivation" because it makes known the cultivation of the path; it is called a "description by way of full understanding" because it makes known the full understanding of suffering;
it is called a "description by way of abandoning" because it makes known the abandoning of the origin;
it is called a "description by way of undertaking" because it makes known the undertaking of the faculty of energy; and [it is so called] because it makes known the removal of the gadflies.
It is called a "definition by bringing forth" because it makes known the stage of development; it is called a "definition by presentation" because it makes known the presentation [of the path];
and it is called a "definition by striking down" because it makes known the striking down of evil, unwholesome states.
(41) Or else, it is [defined] by way of the round of existence, or by way of the cessation of the round, or by way of the investigation of phenomena, or by way of the aggregates of clinging.
The various classifications of designations regarding the truths, whether by way of their manifestation or by way of their comprehension, have been analyzed by the Teacher and are known to us.

Since it must be explained how the classification of designations regarding the truths is analyzed by way of the three turnings, the passage beginning with "This, O monks, is suffering" was commenced in order to show that classification of designations regarding the truths by way of the three turnings. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

However, it is said: “Having thus shown the classification of designations among the truths by way of the cycle of existence and its cessation, and by way of the aggregates of clinging as objects of comprehension, [the Buddha] now began with the words, ‘This, monks, is suffering,’ etc., in order to show them by way of the three turnings.

In that context, “previously” means starting from the point of full understanding (*parijānana*). “In what has not been heard before” (*ananussutesu*) means in regard to those things not heard through the process of full understanding.
Regarding the four truths and phenomena: "Eye" (*cakkhu*) is so called in the sense of seeing Nibbāna for the first time.
"Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) is so called in the sense of fully understanding their essential nature and function, and in the sense of full realization through direct experience.

"Wisdom" (*paññā*) is so called in the sense of understanding after having penetrated the full comprehension of their essential nature and function, and so forth. Likewise, it is "clear vision" (*vijjā*) in the sense of making things known as they truly are. It is "light" (*āloka*) in the sense of producing illumination.
“Light” is a name. All this, beginning with the eye, is merely a synonym for wisdom (*paññā*). The expression, “‘This is suffering,’ O monks... [etc.
...arose in me,” is called a “declaration of teaching” (*desanā-paññatti*) because it makes known the truths through their teaching;

and it is called a “declaration of presentation” (*nikkhepa-paññatti*) because it presents the application of wisdom consisting in what is heard (*suta-mayī paññā*); [and it is the basis] of the faculty of “I shall come to know the unknown” (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*).

It is called "description by realization" because it is described for the sake of realization; it is called "description by setting in motion" because it is described for the sake of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
The statement, “Now this suffering is to be fully understood... [and so on] ...it arose,” is a description of the cultivation of the path.
It is called "description by way of development" because it describes through the wisdom consisting of reflection;

it is called "description by way of presentation" because it presents the presentation [of the truths] through that same wisdom; and it is called "description by way of realization" because it describes the realization of the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*).
The statement, “This suffering has been fully understood... [and so on]... [the knowledge] arose,” is the description of the path by way of its development.

It is called "description by way of development" because it describes through the wisdom consisting in development; it is called "description by way of presentation" because it presents the presentation of wisdom consisting in development;
it is called "description by way of realization" because it presents the realization of the faculty of one who has known;
and it is called "description by way of setting in motion" because it presents the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma.
The various classifications of designations regarding the Truths according to the threefold rotation were analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us;

however, because it must be explained how the classifications of designations for the Dhamma taught by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth were analyzed, the passage beginning with "the measurable and the immeasurable, and their arising" was stated.
Alternatively, the classification of designations in the *Dhammacakka Sutta* [was analyzed] by the Teacher...

It has been analyzed and understood by us. Because it must be explained how the distinction in designation is analyzed in the verse beginning with “The measurable and the immeasurable,” the passage beginning with “The measurable and the immeasurable” is stated. That which is weighed and delimited is *tulaṃ*; this refers to sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) karma.

That which has no other worldly (*lokiya*) karma as its equal or counterpart is *atulaṃ*; this refers to sublime (*mahaggata*) karma, namely, form-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and formless-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) karma.
It is "origination" (*sambhava*) because renewed existence arises through this formation; that is, origination. It forms renewed existence, thus it is the "formation of existence" (*bhava-saṅkhāra*).
One who delights within by means of insight is "delighting within" (*ajjhattarata*). One who concentrates by means of serenity is "composed" (*samāhita*).
That which originates within oneself is "self-origination" (*attasambhava*); that is, self-origination. The Sage, the Fully Awakened One, [knows] that origination...
The construction should be made thus: "He relinquished both the measurable and the immeasurable formative forces of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*);

delighting within himself and concentrated, he shattered his own origin as if breaking through armor, and having shattered it, he destroyed it. Alternatively, the Sage, the Fully Awakened One, [realized]:
"The five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change; but Nibbāna is permanent, blissful, unconditioned, and not subject to change."
Weighing the measurable against the immeasurable, having seen Nibbāna, he abandoned through the Noble Path the arising of existence and the formative forces of becoming.

How did he abandon them? For that Sage, being inwardly delighted by means of insight (vipassanā) and concentrated in both access and absorption through serenity (samatha), shattered [the fetters] as if piercing armor; thus, he [abandoned] the arising from self—that which was born within himself.
The meaning of the verse should be understood as: "He broke and shattered the defilements; by the absence of defilements, he abandoned karma.
Regarding the phrase "the measurable and the immeasurable arising": it is called a "direct-knowledge designation" (*abhiññā-paññatti*) because it designates all phenomena through direct knowledge;

it is called a "positional designation" (*nikkhepa-paññatti*) because it designates the presentation of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-patisambhidā*). [And he] "cast off the formative force of existence."
The designation "a sage" (*muni*) is called a "designation of relinquishment" because it makes known both the origin [of suffering] and relinquishment;
it is called a "designation of full understanding" because it makes known the full understanding of suffering;

and the designation "delighting in the internal, concentrated" is called a "designation of development" because it makes known the development of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*). [This applies also to] one-pointedness of mind...
It is called a "description of stability" because it describes stability; it is called a "description of emergence" because it describes the emergence of the mind, as in the description:
"He shattered the source of selfhood like a coat of mail"; it is called a "description of clinging" because it describes both omniscience and clinging;
and it is called a "description of shattering" because it describes the shattering of the eggshell of ignorance.
Regarding the name: since it must be asked, "By whom can the aforementioned classification of designations be believed?

the passage beginning with "Therefore he said" was stated. Because the aforementioned classification of designations is possible, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "The equal and the unequal";
and because it is possible in that way, the aforementioned classification of designations should be believed on account of the verse as it was spoken.
In the verse beginning with “The comparable and the incomparable,” the classification of designations has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known to us:
“He who has seen suffering and its source—how could that person bow down to sensual pleasures?
Having understood that in the world sensual pleasures are a snare, the mindful one should train for their subduing.”
Since it must be asked, "In this verse, how is the classification of designation analyzed?", it is said: "He who has seen suffering," and so forth.
That person who has begun insight (vipassanā) and has seen that all suffering belonging to the three planes—arising from whatever source—is the result of causes;
that person who has begun insight, how could he incline toward sense pleasures? He is not fit to incline toward them. Sense pleasures...

Since that which is seen as "attachment" (*saṅga*) in the world is therefore not fit to be approached, one who has understood this state of suffering and its cause as suffering should—mindful and endowed with mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*)—train in the three trainings for the sake of the removal and pacification of those sensual desires;
such is the meaning of the verse to be understood in brief. However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it says:
It has been described in detail.

The designation "that which is suffering" is both a designation of synonyms and a designation of full understanding, because it designates a synonym for suffering and because it makes full understanding known.
The designation "from whatever source" is [a designation] of the origin and of its arising, and of its abandonment.

And because it makes known both the origin and the abandoning [of suffering], the designation “he saw” (*addakkhi*) is both a designation of synonyms and a designation of penetration, since it makes known the synonym for the eye of knowledge and for penetration.

The designation “how could that person incline toward sensual pleasures? is a designation of synonyms and a designation of non-adherence, since it makes known the synonym for sensual craving and for non-inclination.
And because it makes known [the meaning], it is both a designation by synonyms (*vevacanapaññatti*) and a designation of non-adherence (*anabhinivesapaññatti*).

The designation, “Having known that sensual pleasures are a snare in the world,” is called a designation of vision (*dassanapaññatti*), because it makes known the vision of sensual pleasures as enemies.
For sensual pleasures are like enemies, in that they are understood to bring about harm.

Because it must be asked, "In what way do they produce harm?", it is said, "Sensual pleasures (kāmā)," and so forth. Sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing embers because they burn from within through the fire of passion and the like;
they are like a piece of putrid meat because they lead to a state of decay;
they are like a mass of blazing flames because they burn by means of something external; and they are like a precipice because they lack any firm foundation.

They are called "comparable to snakes" because they injure others through defilements such as hatred that are like venom. They are called "designations of diminution" because they designate the abandoning and the diminution of those [defilements] by means of the phrase "mindful of them.
They are called "designations of relinquishment" because they designate the relinquishing of mindfulness directed to the body.
They are called "designations of development" because they designate the development of the path.

“Name”: “One should train for the sake of discipline” is called a manifestation of penetration (*paṭivedha-paññatti*), because it makes known the penetration of the removal of passion, the removal of hatred, and the removal of delusion.
“A person” (*jantu*) is called a manifestation of synonyms (*vevacana-paññatti*), because it makes known a synonym for a practitioner (*yogī*).

Because it must be asked, "Why should the word *jantu*, which denotes a sentient being in general, be understood as denoting a practitioner (*yogin*)?", the passage beginning with "When indeed" (*yadā hi*) was stated.

When—at whatever time—the practitioner understands that sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) are a fetter (*saṅga*), then at that time, for the sake of the non-arising of sensual pleasures, that practitioner generates wholesome states (*kusale dhamme*) such as mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) and so forth; he [generates] those wholesome states...
As the practitioner brings them forth, he exerts himself for the arising of unarisen wholesome states and performs wholesome energy;
therefore, the word *jantu* should be understood as a designation for the practitioner (*yogī*).

This designation “*jantu*” is called a “designation of effort” because it designates the effort made for the attainment of wholesome states such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) that have not yet been attained; it is [a designation] pertaining to the mundane.
Because it establishes non-contentment and the laying down [of the burden], it is called a "description by way of laying down" (*nikkhepa-paññatti*).
The description, “He makes an effort for the arising of unarisen wholesome states,” is a “description by way of effort” (*vāyāma-paññatti*).
Since one must ask, “What kind of description is this description that ‘he makes an effort for the stability of arisen wholesome states through their cause’?”—therein, he...
The passage beginning with "of those that have arisen" and so forth has been stated. Therein, regarding that [passage] beginning with "of those not yet arisen":

the designation "he exerts himself for the stability of wholesome states that have arisen" is called a *paññatti* (designation) of diligence (*appamāda*), because it designates both cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and diligence;
and it is called a *nikkhepa-paññatti* (designation of presentation), because it designates the presentation of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*).
It is called a "designation by protection" because it makes known the protection of wholesome states;
it is called a "designation by stability" because it makes known the stability of the training in higher consciousness.
Since it must be asked, "By whom is this aforementioned classification of designations to be believed? the passage beginning with "Therefore he said... was stated.
The classification of designations in the verse beginning with “He who has seen suffering and its source” has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known to us.
“The world is bound by delusion, yet it appears as if it were capable [of liberation];
the fool is bound by acquisitions and enveloped in darkness.”
"It appears like a corpse; for one who sees, there is nothing.
Since it must be asked, "How is the classification of the designation (paññatti) analyzed in this verse?", it is said: "Bound by delusion," and so forth.
Therein, "bound by delusion" means bound by fetters (saṃyojana) that have delusion as their cause. "The world" refers to one whose fetters have not been abandoned.

The world of beings (*sattaloka*). "It appears as if capable" means that even though the self (*attā*) is incapable, it appears to fools who lack insight as if it were capable and of a nature that is capable.

"Bound by acquisitions" (*upadhibandhana*) means one who is to be bound by the acquisitions of the defilements (*kilesa*). For the suffix *-yu* is prescribed in the sense of the object (*kamma*). Alternatively, "bound by acquisitions" refers to a fool for whom there is a binding of defilements within the acquisitions.
A fool (*bāla*) is one who takes or seizes two kinds of non-prosperity (*avaḍḍhi*).
Enveloped and shrouded by darkness—that is, by delusion—he appears and presents himself as if he were without glory, like one bereft of splendor in the presence of the wise who possess insight.
For the wise person who sees with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), there is nothing whatsoever; such is the meaning to be understood in brief.

“The world is bound by delusion”: this is called a *desanā-paññatti* (teaching-designation), because it is a designation established through the teaching of the perversions (*vipallāsa*) grasped under the heading of delusion.

“Only one fit [to be enlightened] is seen”: this is called a *viparīta-paññatti* (perverse designation), because it is a designation established for the world as it appears in a perverted manner. “The fool is bound by acquisitions (*upadhi*): this is a designation...
It is called a "description of origin" (*pabhava-paññatti*) because it makes known the source of evil desires and their range.

The description "The fool is bound by acquisitions" is called a "description of function" (*kicca-paññatti*) because it makes known the binding function of the unwholesome states that constitute the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
The description "The fool is bound by acquisitions" [also illustrates] the binding power and the deluding power of the defilements (*kilesa*).
The designation "the fool is bound by acquisitions" is called a *balapaññatti* (designation of power), because it designates the growth of formations.
The designation "enveloped in darkness" is called a *viruhanāpaññatti* (designation of growth), because it designates the teaching of the darkness of ignorance;
it is also called a *desanāpaññatti* (designation of teaching), because it designates the teaching of the darkness of ignorance and its synonyms.

This is called a designation by way of synonyms (*vevacanapaññatti*). The designation “it appears like a horse” is called a designation of seeing (*dassanapaññatti*), because it designates the act of seeing by means of the divine eye.

The designation “it appears like a horse” is called a designation of presentation (*nikkhepapaññatti*), because it designates the presentation of the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). The designation “for one who sees, there is nothing whatsoever” is...
It is called "description by penetration" (*paṭivedhapaññatti*) because it makes known the penetration of the Noble Ones among beings.

Because it must be asked, "What is the 'something'? it is said, "Lust is the something," and so forth. Because it must be stated, "How are we to have faith in the aforementioned divisions of description?
it is said, "Therefore he said," and so forth. [This refers to] the aforementioned divisions of description.

Since it is possible that the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with “The world is bound by delusion,” the various classifications of designations as stated therein should be accepted according to that verse and following its sequence.
The classification of designations in the verse beginning with “The world is bound by delusion” has been analyzed by the Teacher, and by us as well.

Since it must be asked, "How is the classification of the designation [of the term] ‘there is, monks, that which is unborn,’ etc., analyzed?", he states the Pāli passage beginning with "There is, monks.
If one were to ask, "For what purpose was that Pāli passage spoken by the Blessed One?", [the answer is:
because Nibbāna does not exist in an ultimate sense (paramatthato), it is said, "Nibbāna does not exist"; therefore, [the Buddha spoke thus] to show that "Nibbāna exists" [in a conventional sense].

It should be understood that these were spoken by the Blessed One in order to refute the false doctrine of those who claim that speech is as useless as the talk of one with horns, being merely conventional expression (*vohāramatta*).

Because it is not born from anything and has never come into being, it is "unborn" (*ajāta*) and "unbecome" (*abhūta*); because it is not produced by conditions, it is "unmade" (*akata*); and because it lacks the nature of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*), [it is unconditioned].
Unconditioned Nibbāna exists. If this Nibbāna, characterized by being unborn and so forth, did not exist, then an escape would not be discernible;

for Nibbāna is the object of the Noble Path and its Fruits, and because the Path and the Fruits sever and pacify the defilements, and through that severance bring about the non-rolling back of the threefold cycle of existence.
It should be understood that Nibbāna, characterized by non-arising and so forth, truly exists.
The designation, “Bhikkhus, there is the unarisen… [and so on] …the unconditioned,” is both a teaching-designation for Nibbāna and a synonym-designation for Nibbāna.
The designation, “For one who has arisen here… [and so on] …it would not be discerned,” is this [teaching-designation].
There is both a designation of synonyms for the conditioned and a designation that brings the conditioned near. The designation, “Because...
[as far as] ...the unconditioned,” is both a designation of synonyms for Nibbāna and a designation that illuminates Nibbāna.
The designation, “Because of what is born... [as far as] ...is made known,” is a designation of synonyms for Nibbāna.
Furthermore, the path is a designation of deliverance from saṃsāra and a designation of escape;
thus, this distinction of designations must be discerned and grasped by the wise.
To the question, "By whom should this aforementioned classification of the designations of Nibbāna be believed? it was said: "Therefore he says..."

The passage beginning with "the Blessed One" has been stated. The meaning of the connection and so forth for the passage beginning with "Therefore the Venerable One said," as well as the meaning of the connection and so forth for the statement "the Mode of Description (paññatti-hāra) is concluded," should be understood according to the method already explained.
Thus, in this analysis of the Mode of Description, [this work] has been composed in accordance with the strength of one's faculties.
The Exposition of the Mode of Conveying Analysis is finished.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
12. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Ways of Entry.

42. By whichever specific exposition—that is, by whichever analysis of the modes of presentation (*paññatti-hāra-vibhaṅga*)—the various presentations have been analyzed, that specific exposition of the analysis is complete.
Because it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the modes of entry (*otaraṇa-hāra-vibhaṅga*)?", it is said:
"In this regard, what is the mode of entry? and so forth. Therein, "in those" (*tattha tattha*) refers to those sixteen [modes] already specified.

Among the modes of conveying the teaching (*desanāhāra*) and so forth, he asks: "Which specific mode of exposition (*saṃvaṇṇanāvisesa*) is the Mode of Entry (*otaraṇahāra*), and what is the analysis of the Mode of Entry?

[The answer is: This specific mode of exposition consisting of the detailed commentary beginning with "Above, below, and everywhere completely freed," which is now being stated by me as the explanation for the summary beginning with "And that which is dependent origination," should be understood as the Mode of Entry and the analysis of the Mode of Entry.
In that regard, since it must be asked in the text, "Having distinguished which [factors] such as dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda),
by means of which distinguished phenomena does one enter?",

it is said, "Released above, below, and in every way," and so forth, in order to show that having distinguished these factors such as dependent origination in this text, one enters by means of these distinguished phenomena.
In this context, *uddhaṃ* (above) refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*), which function above and beyond the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).
*Adho* (below) refers to the sense-sphere realm, which functions below the form realm. *Sabbadhi* (everywhere) means throughout all three realms—the sense-sphere, form, and formless realms.

*Vippamutto* (completely liberated) refers to one who is liberated because of the non-occurrence [of defilements] by way of rebirth-linking; this is the *asekha* (one beyond training). This *sekha* (one in training), by means of the path of seeing...
Because of the uprooting of the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), he dwells without regarding [anything] as "I am.

Thus, by means of both the liberation of one in training (*sekkhā vimutti*) and the liberation of one beyond training (*asekkhā vimutti*), the one who is both in training and beyond training—having been liberated so as not to undergo renewed existence—has crossed over the flood never before crossed;
such is how the meaning of the verse should be understood.
In that recitation of verses, because it must be asked, "Having set aside which [factors], does one descend by means of which?", it was said:

"Above" (*uddhaṃ*) refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and so forth. Since the meaning could also imply that those above the human world—such as the Cātumahārājika gods and others—are included, in order to exclude that, it was said:
"the form realm and the formless realm" (*rūpadhātu arūpadhātu*). "Below" (*adho*) refers to the human existence.
Because the four lower planes of misery (apāyabhūmi) are also included [in the term "all"], the word "the realm of sense-desire" (kāmadhātu) is stated in order to exclude them.
Because the meaning "in all four planes" is possible, the word "in the three realms" (tedhātuke) is stated. This is the liberation of one beyond training (asekkha);
that which is the state of detachment (virāgatā) belonging to the liberated one beyond training—this too is the liberation of the fruit of one beyond training.
The meaning is that this *asekkhā* (beyond-training) liberation, described in the passage beginning “Released above, below, and everywhere,” has been thus determined.

Those very five faculties beginning with faith which were determined in relation to the determined *asekkhā* liberation become the five *asekkha* faculties themselves. This is the aforementioned method of entry into liberation by means of the faculties.
"Entry" (otaraṇā) means "penetration" (pavesanā).

Those same five faculties of one beyond training (asekkha) become "true knowledge" (vijjā) because they are conducive to true knowledge, or because they are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for wisdom (paññā).
Through the arising of such true knowledge—that is, through its arising as the cause of arising—there is the cessation of ignorance (avijjā).
There is cessation... [and so on] ...there is the cessation of the mass of suffering; this aforementioned mode of entry is called "entry by means of dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

Those same five faculties of one beyond training (*asekha*) are comprised within three aggregates: because faith and energy give rise to virtue, and because mindfulness follows along with wisdom. The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained.
Having extracted the meaning from the reading, "Released above, below, and everywhere," the Master has analyzed the modes of entry.
Regarding our own understanding of the reading, "not contemplating 'I am this'," it must be stated which [factors] are excluded and by which modes of entry one enters;
therefore, it was said: "'Not contemplating 'I am this' refers to the personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)," and so forth.
As for that trainee (sekkha) who does not contemplate "I am," the eradication of that trainee's personality-view—[this is what is meant].
There is that which is called liberation by eradication (*samugghāta-vimutti*), which is the liberation of one in training (*sekkhā-vimutti*);
those five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*) that have been determined for that liberation of one in training are themselves the five faculties of one in training.
This aforementioned method of entry is called "entry by way of the faculties. The remaining [methods] should be understood according to the manner already explained.
43. In the verse beginning with “Above and below,” the method of entry (*otaraṇā*) has been analyzed by the Teacher and is understood by us.
Regarding the reading beginning with “The wavering of one who relies,” it must be asked: “Having excluded which [terms], does one enter by means of which?

Therefore, it was said: “There is wavering for one who relies; there is no wavering for one who does not rely. For a person (*puggala*) who relies, there is *calitaṃ*, which is to say, wavering (*calanaṃ*).
There is no wavering, no fluctuation, for a person who is independent. When there is no wavering, no fluctuation, there is tranquility;
when tranquility exists, there is no inclination. When there is no inclination, there is no coming and going;
when there is no coming and going, there is no passing away and rebirth. When there is no passing away and rebirth...
Here, one does not see a self in the six internal bases; nor does one see a self in the six external bases beyond;
nor, having excluded both, does one see a self in the phenomena consisting of the collection of contact and so forth.
This very dependent origination—beginning with "from the cessation of ignorance"—brings about the end and the final conclusion of suffering; this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "the wavering of one who is dependent" (*nissitassa calitaṃ*): since it must be asked here, "How many kinds of dependence (*nissaya*) are there?", the passage beginning with "The wavering of one who is dependent—dependence is called...

and so forth was stated. In that context—referring to those two types of dependence, namely dependence on craving (*taṇhā-nissaya*) and dependence on views (*diṭṭhi-nissaya*)—that volition (*cetanā*) which has been determined for a person who is lustful is this factor of volition called "dependence on craving. That volition...
These have been determined for the person who is confused. This phenomenon of volition is called "the support of views.

That volition is twofold, and it is indeed called "formations" (*saṅkhāra*). With formations as condition, consciousness arises... [and so on]... the entire dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) has been determined.
This aforementioned mode of entry is called "entry by way of dependent origination."
"In that regard" means: among those bases of craving and views, that feeling which has been determined for a person who is attached is pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*).
That volition (*cetanā*) which has been determined for a person who is deluded is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*).
For the most part, the remaining [feelings] are to be understood according to the method already stated.
44. The introduction to the passage beginning with “For one who is dependent there is wavering,” etc., has been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us.
[It is as stated in the verse: “Whatever sorrows or lamentations... [etc.
...one should not hold anything dear anywhere in the world.”
In the recitation of the verses, because it must be asked, "Having excluded which [factors], does one descend by means of which?", it is said:
"Whatever sorrows," and so forth. Whatever sorrows, whatever lamentations, or whatever various kinds of sufferings arise in the world—these sorrows and the rest originate dependent upon the beloved;
when the beloved is absent, these sorrows and the rest do not come to be.
Therefore, since sorrow and the like do not exist when there is nothing dear, those who are free from sorrow—whom there are none anywhere in the world—become happy and free from grief.
Thus, because those free from sorrow are endowed with happiness, the meaning of the verse is:
"A true person, aspiring for that which is sorrowless and stainless, should not hold anything dear anywhere in the world."

Regarding the passage: “Whatever sorrows or lamentations there are, and whatever various forms of suffering exist in the world, all these arise dependent upon what is dear,” the feeling (*vedanā*) determined here is painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*). The remaining [feelings] are to be understood according to the method already explained.

The teacher has analyzed the entry points into the verse beginning with “Whatever sorrows...,” and we too have understood them; however, regarding the verse beginning with “One who desires sensual pleasures...,” it must be stated:
“Having determined which [terms], by means of which [methods] does one enter?”
“*Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassā*,” etc., has been stated. The meaning of that verse has already been explained above.
In that context, regarding the reading “*pītimano hotī*,” the state of being joyful (*pītimanatā*) which was mentioned and determined is *anunaya* (attachment).
Regarding the reading “*sallaviddhova ruppatī*,” the deformation (*ruppana*) which was spoken of is *paṭigha* (aversion).
The meaning is that favoritism (*anunaya*) and aversion (*paṭigha*) have been determined.
Since it must be stated, "When favoritism and aversion have been determined, what dhamma has been determined?", it is said:
"But favoritism and aversion belong to the side of craving (*taṇhā*). Because they belong to the side of craving, craving itself is determined.
If it should be argued: “Let *anunaya* (attachment) belong to the side of craving (*taṇhā*), but *paṭigha* (aversion) should not; [we reply:
because *paṭigha* proceeds by way of self-attachment (*attasineha*), *paṭigha* also belongs to the side of craving. Because it must be asked, “When craving is excluded, what is excluded?
the passage beginning with “And furthermore, by craving... was stated. [This refers to] the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Because craving is the proximate cause, the ten material bases (rūpāyatana) are determined.
This aforementioned method of entry is called "entry by way of the bases" (āyatana-otaraṇā).

The dependent origination and other doctrines found in the Sutta are determined by that specific method of commentary, or they are determined by way of the meaning of the Sutta; thus, regarding the dependent origination and so forth determined by that method... [etc.]

The intended meaning should be understood as follows: that particular method of commentary which descends, enters, and converges—either by way of expressing its meaning or by way of making its meaning known—is called the "Method of Descent" (*otaraṇa-hāra*).

In the remaining [methods] as well, the descents should be grasped according to the stated method. The phrase "Therefore the Venerable One said," etc., refers to the connection between the sections and so forth; thus it is concluded.
The meaning of the "Entry" (otaraṇa) method, including its connections and so forth, should be understood according to the manner already described.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* composed in accordance with one's strength and ability, within the analysis of the "Entry" method.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
13. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification (Sodhanahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā). 45.
By whichever specific mode of commentary, namely the analysis of the Mode of Entry (*otaraṇahāra*), the meanings of the discourses (*sutta*) are to be entered; [those meanings are to be understood].
The *Vibhaṅga*, which constitutes a specific kind of commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanāvisesa*), has been fully analyzed.

Because it must be asked, "What is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification (*sodhanahāravibhaṅgo*)?", the passage beginning with "In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Purification? and so forth was stated.

Therein, the phrase "in those" (*tattha*) refers to those sixteen Modes of Conveyance, such as the Mode of Conveying Teaching (*desanāhāra*), etc., that have been specified; and "what specific commentary" (*katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso*) refers to the Mode of Conveying Purification, the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification (*sodhanahāravibhaṅgo*).

“By name” he asks. Now, this specific detailed commentary being spoken by me—beginning with “Just as the Venerable Ajita”—which follows the exposition starting with “When the question has been answered,” should be understood as the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification (*sodhana-hāra-vibhaṅga*).
Because it must be stated how the Mode of Conveying Purification is to be understood regarding that question, the passage beginning with “Just as the Venerable... was spoken.

Just as the Venerable Ajita asked the Blessed One a question in the *Pārāyana* in a certain manner, so too, when that question is answered in that same manner, this "mode of purification" (*sodhana-hāra*) is to be understood.

Because it was said, "Having determined, analyze," the words beginning with "By what? were spoken in order to analyze after having determined [the subject]. The meaning of the verse has already been stated.
“By what is the world enveloped? By what does it not shine forth?
What do you say is its defilement? And what is its great terror?”—thus, in the verse that proceeds by way of inquiry.
“The world is shrouded by ignorance,” said the Blessed One,
“and due to craving and negligence it does not shine forth.
I call longing its defilement, and suffering its great terror.”
And in these two verses— namely, the verse that presents the question and the verse that provides the answer—
when the question is asked with the line, "By what is the world enveloped?", the Blessed One purifies that line by removing the stains of ignorance,
doubt, and so forth regarding its meaning, through the line, "The world is enveloped by ignorance. Regarding its meaning...

For when the meaning has been answered, because ignorance, doubt, and so forth are absent, the meaning is said to be clarified; and when the meaning is clarified, the word itself is likewise clarified.

Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Because of the answering of its meaning," and in the *Ṭīkā* it is stated: "It clarifies by removing the stains of ignorance, doubt, and so forth regarding that object.
However, one does not begin to ask about every single word of the verse that ought to be asked, [but rather focuses on] the meaning of the verse.

Or rather, because the answer to every intended meaning is not yet concluded by the mere statement "The world is shrouded by ignorance," the Blessed One clarifies it with this much alone. This same method applies to the others as well.

When the question was asked by the phrase "What is its great fear?", the Blessed One’s intended meaning—to be known through the phrase "Suffering is its great fear"—becomes pure and clarified. This same method applies to the remaining verses as well.
In whatever question the undertaking is thus purified and cleansed by way of a complete answer, that question is answered and cleansed.
In whatever question the undertaking remains unpurified and uncleansed by way of a complete answer, to that extent that question is not answered and not cleansed; such is the construction.

The meaning of the connection and so forth for the passage beginning with “Therefore it was said,” as well as the meaning of the connection and so forth for the statement “the Mode of Conveying Purification (sodhana-hāra) is thus applied,” should be understood according to the method already stated.
Thus, the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification has been composed in accordance with one’s own strength and ability.
The exposition of the method of analysis (*vibhāvanā*) is completed.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*).
14. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Terms of Expression (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-vibhaṅga-vibhāvanā*).
46. By whichever analysis (*vibhaṅga*), which constitutes a specific mode of exposition (*saṃvaṇṇanāvisesa*), the questions and so forth are clarified, that specific mode of exposition is complete.
Because it must be asked, "Which is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Basis (*adhiṭṭhānahāra*)?", it is said: "In this context, what is the basis? and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in each of those" (*tattha tattha*): among those sixteen modes of conveying the teaching (*desanāhāra*) and so on that have been specified, which...?
He asks: "What is the specific excellence of the commentary on the Mode of Conveying the Terms of Expression (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra), known as the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Terms of Expression?

The answer is: The specific excellence of the detailed commentary—beginning with "Those phenomena which are shown by way of unity, and those which are shown by way of diversity," and so forth—which is now being spoken by me, and which states, "Those which were shown therein should be retained accordingly," and so on, is to be understood as the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Terms of Expression.

"Since it must be asked: 'Are those phenomena (dhammas) which are taught in the discourses (suttas) by way of both unity and diversity to be retained exactly as they are, or should they also be conceptualized otherwise?'—therefore, the words 'Those therein,' and so forth, are stated.
In that context, among those discourses, those phenomena such as the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) and the rest, which are taught by way of both unity and diversity..."
Those phenomena, beginning with the truth of suffering, should be held and characterized according to their unity and their diversity, and not otherwise conceptualized. [One might ask:
"In what sense is there unity, and in what sense is there diversity, given that they do not persist as mere conventional designations through the application of commonality?"

Because it is to be asked, it is said: "Suffering is a unity," and so forth. That which was stated as the general nature of suffering (*dukkhasāmaññatā*), without regard for specific distinctions such as birth and so on—that general nature of suffering is what is called the "unity of suffering" (*dukkhassa ekattatā*).

Having been asked, "In that regard, what is suffering?", [the answer]—taking into account specific distinctions such as birth—is given: "Birth is suffering, aging is suffering... [and so on]... consciousness is suffering."
That which was stated as the specific nature of suffering is this very "specificity of suffering," meaning the diversity within suffering.
"Therein" refers to those phenomena such as suffering that were mentioned in the Sutta; it means with respect to those meanings, beginning with suffering.
"The origin of suffering" refers to the general quality of being an origin, stated without regard for the specific qualification that "craving leads to renewed existence."
This aforementioned "sameness of origin" (*samudaya-sāmaññatā*) is what is called the "oneness of origin" (*ekattatā*).

Having asked, "In this context, what is origin?", and having stated the specific distinction—"that which is this craving... [etc. ...craving for non-existence"—the "particularity of origin" (*samudaya-visesatā*) that was thus described is what is called the "diversity of origin" (*vemattatā*).

Regarding "the cessation of suffering": this commonality of cessation—which was stated without regard for its specific distinction as "the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving"—is what is called the unity of cessation. Having asked, "In this context, what is the cessation of suffering?", [it is answered]:
"It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving; it is relinquishment, surrender, liberation, and non-attachment."
The specific nature of cessation that was mentioned in consideration of its particular distinctions is what is called the "differentiation" (*vemattatā*) of cessation.

As for "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering": the general nature of the practice leading to cessation that was mentioned without regard to the specific distinctions such as right view and so forth is what is called the "unity" (*ekattatā*) of the path. "In this context, which is..."
Having asked, "What is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?", [the Buddha replied], "It is this very Noble Eightfold Path... pe ... right concentration.

This specific quality of being the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—which was stated in reference to the distinctions of right view and so forth—is what is called the "differentiation of the path" (*maggassa vemattatā*).
The term "path" (*magga*) refers to the state of being a path in general, without regard for specific distinctions such as the path leading to hell;
this state of being a path in general is what is called the "unity of the path. Having asked, "In that regard, what is the path? and then stated, "the path leading to hell...
[and so on] ...the path leading to Nibbāna," the state of being a path with specific distinctions is referred to; this is the "specificity of the path."
This is what is called the diversity of the path.

As for "cessation," setting aside specific distinctions such as analytical cessation (*paṭisaṅkhā-nirodha*) and so forth, that which is described as the general state of cessation—this general state of cessation is what is called the unity of cessation.
Having asked, "In this context, what is cessation?", it is stated: "Analytical cessation... [and so on]."
The specific state of cessation that is spoken of in relation to distinctions such as the cessation through reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā-nirodha*)—
namely, "the cessation of all defilements"— is what is called the diversity of cessation (*nirodha-vemattatā*).
The general nature of form (*rūpa-sāmānya-rūpatā*) that is spoken of without regard for distinctions such as the four great elements (*cātumahābhūtika*) is this very general nature of form.

The unity of form (rūpassa ekattatā) is as follows: having asked, "In that regard, what is form?", and then stated—having regard for the distinctions such as the four great elements—that "it is composed of the four great elements...
[and so on]... it causes the mind to fade away from the air element," whatever specific nature of form was thus described is called the diversity of form (rūpassa vemattatā).

48. Regarding "ignorance" (*avijjā*): the general nature of ignorance that was stated without regard for specific distinctions such as ignorance regarding suffering (*dukkhe aññāṇa*) and so forth—this general nature of ignorance is what is called the "oneness" (*ekattatā*) of ignorance. Having asked, "In this context, what is ignorance?

and then [answering] by referring to specific distinctions such as ignorance regarding suffering and ignorance regarding the origin of suffering—up to—"ignorance is delusion (*moha*), the underlying tendency to ignorance, the unwholesome root"—[the oneness is established].
That which was stated as the specific nature of ignorance is this specific nature of ignorance, called the diversity (*vemattatā*) of ignorance.

That which was stated as the commonality of true knowledge (*vijjā*), without regard for its specific distinctions such as the knowledge of suffering, is this commonality of true knowledge, called the unity (*ekattatā*) of true knowledge.
Having asked, "In that regard, what is true knowledge? it is said: "Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering..."

When it is said, “Knowledge... [and so on] ...the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment is a path-factor included in the path,” that specific quality of clear vision (vijjā) mentioned in relation to the distinction of knowledge regarding suffering and so forth is what is called the "variety of clear vision" (vijjāvemattatā).
When it is said, "Attainment," that general state of attainment mentioned without regard for the distinctions such as the attainment of perception and so forth—[is what is meant].
The state of being a common attainment (*sāmañña-samāpatti*) is called the unity of attainment.
Having asked, "In this context, what is attainment?", and having stated, "The attainment of perception (*saññā-samāpatti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaññā-samāpatti*), ... [and so on] ...

the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)," the specific state of attainment mentioned in consideration of these distinctions such as the attainment of perception and so forth is called the diversity of attainment (*visesa-samāpatti*). This state of specific attainment is what is meant by the diversity of attainment.
The term "one who meditates" (*jhāyī*) refers to the commonality of meditation without regard for specific distinctions such as the meditator in training (*sekkha-jhāyī*).

This commonality of meditation is called the "unity of the meditator. Having asked, "In this context, what is the meditator?", it is explained—taking into account distinctions such as the meditator in training and the meditator beyond training—that there is "the meditator in training, the meditator beyond training... [and so on] up to] the meditator preeminent in wisdom."
That which was stated as the distinction among meditators is this: the distinction among meditators is called the diversity of the meditator.

Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*), setting aside the specific types such as protective concentration (*saraṇa-samādhi*) and so forth, that which was stated as the commonality of concentration is this:
the commonality of concentration is called the unity of concentration. Having asked, "In that regard, what is concentration? it says: "Protective..."

The specific nature of concentration that has been described— referring to the distinctions such as "concentration with conflict" (*saraṇa-samādhi*) and so forth, up to "wrong concentration" (*micchā-samādhi*) and "right concentration" (*sammā-samādhi*)—
is what is called the "variety of concentration. The commonality of the path that has been described—
without regard for the distinctions such as the "arduous path" (*āgāḷha-paṭipadā*) and so forth— is this commonality of the path.
The unity of the way is called *paṭipadā-ekattatā*. Having asked, "In this context, what is the way?", the specific nature of the way that is described—

taking into account the distinctions such as the "difficult way" (*āgāḷha-paṭipadā*), the "arduous way" (*nijjhāma-paṭipadā*), and so forth, up to the "pleasant way with quick direct knowledge" (*sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā*)—
this specific nature of the way is called the diversity of the way (*paṭipadā-vemattatā*).
"Body" (*kāya*) refers to the commonality of being a body, spoken of without regard for specific distinctions such as the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and so forth;
this commonality of being a body is what is called the "unity of the body. Having asked, "In that regard, what is the body? and then stated, "The mental body, the material body...
[etc. ...this is the mental body," the specific distinction of the body spoken of with reference to specific distinctions such as the mental body and so forth is this "distinction of the body."

The construction should be made as: "the diversity of the body" (*kāyassa vemattatā*). The specific distinctions regarding the meaning of the words and so forth have been explained in detail in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
To show, by way of conclusion, the characteristic of unity and so forth of the phenomena (dhamma) of the kind already described—namely, suffering, its origin, and so on—it was said:
"Thus, whatever phenomenon... and so forth. Therein, by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), [it refers to] what has been stated by me as "suffering."

Unity. In that context, what is suffering? It is by such statements as: "Birth is suffering, aging is suffering," and so forth. "Whatever phenomenon" refers to any particular phenomenon such as birth, aging, illness, and so on.
"Of whatever phenomenon" refers to another particular phenomenon, such as aging, distinct from that [preceding] particular phenomenon of birth and so forth.
"The state of being the same" refers to the state of the particular phenomenon of aging being identical to the particular phenomenon of birth and so forth.
The state of being common [to all] by way of the nature of suffering (*dukkha*). "Of that phenomenon" means of the specific phenomena such as aging and so forth.
"By way of unity" means by way of the unification of the states of suffering, origin, and so forth, through their commonality as suffering, origin, and so forth.

"It becomes one" means that although it is manifold due to the distinctions of specific categories such as birth and so forth, it becomes one by being denotable by the single term "origin of suffering" and so on. Or else, by whichever...
It is dissimilar; it goes to a state of difference by means of this or that [characteristic].

Whatever phenomenon, such as birth, is dissimilar and distinct from another phenomenon, such as aging, by way of its specific nature—such as the nature of production or maturation—that phenomenon of birth, etc., through that very nature of production, maturation, and so forth, attains a state of difference from the phenomenon of aging, etc.

The meaning should be understood as follows: although birth and other phenomena are identical in being the origin of suffering and so forth, they attain a state of distinction relative to aging and other phenomena.
The unity and diversity of the phenomena of the origin of suffering and so forth have been analyzed by the Teacher and are known by us; "by that... [the text continues].

When it is asked, "Where, when a question regarding unity or diversity has arisen, should the resolution be investigated?"—in order to show that it should be investigated when a Sutta or other such text is questioned, it is said:

"Thus, when a Sutta is questioned," and so forth. Therein, "thus" means in the manner described; when a Sutta is questioned, or when a Veyyākaraṇa (Exegesis) is questioned, or when a Gāthā (Verse) is questioned...
When this has been asked, the determination must be investigated. The construction is as follows:
if one should ask, "What is to be investigated?", it should be investigated whether he asks about unity (*ekattatā*) or whether he asks about diversity (*vemattatā*).
In the Commentary, however, in order to first apply and demonstrate the scope of unity and diversity, it says: "In the Sutta or in the Vyākaraṇa..."

The phrase "or" and so forth is stated [in the text]. Because it must be explained how the question was asked and how the answer should be given, the passage beginning with "If by way of unity" and so forth is stated.

Furthermore, the connection and so forth for the phrase "Therefore he said," as well as the connection and so forth for the statement "The Mode of Conveying the Foundation is concluded," are to be understood according to the method already described.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Exposition) composed in accordance with one's own strength and power within the *Adhiṭṭhānahāravibhaṅga*.
However, the wise should grasp its profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the *Aṭṭhakathā* and the *Ṭīkā*.
15. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Requisites (Parikkhārahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā) 49.
That particular mode of exposition by which the unity and other characteristics of the truth of suffering and the rest are analyzed—that particular mode of exposition is complete.
Since it must be asked, "What is the analysis known as the Mode of Conveying Requisites? [the following is stated].
“Among these, what is the ‘Requisite’ Mode of Conveying (parikkhāra-hāra)? and so forth is stated. Therein, “among these” (*tattha*) means:

among those sixteen modes of conveying taught, such as the Mode of Conveying the Teaching (*desanā-hāra*), he asks: “Which specific exposition is the Requisite Mode of Conveying, known as the Analysis of the Requisite Mode of Conveying (*parikkhāra-hāra-vibhaṅga*)?
Regarding the exposition beginning with “Those phenomena which produce this phenomenon,” that which is now being stated by me is: “That which... [and so on].

The detailed exposition of the cause and condition that serves as an equipment—beginning with, "Whatever phenomenon produces a phenomenon, that [phenomenon] is its equipment"—is called the *Parikkhāra-vibhaṅga*.
Because it was asked, "What kind of equipment is to be expounded?", the passage beginning with "Whatever phenomenon... was stated. Therein:

Whatever kind of state that functions as a cause-condition (hetupaccaya) produces or has produced a state that constitutes its fruit, that state acting as the cause-condition is called the "requisite" (parikkhāra) for that resultant state.
Since it was necessary to ask, "What is the characteristic of a requisite?", the passage beginning with "What is its characteristic?
was stated in order to show the specific characteristic after having asked thus. [This is] in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

However, it is said: “Having stated there, in brief, the characteristic of a requisite—that ‘whatever phenomenon generates another phenomenon, that [former] is its requisite’—the passage beginning with ‘What is its characteristic?
was spoken in order to demonstrate that through analysis. Since it must be asked, “How many phenomena generate [it]?
it is said: “Two phenomena generate it: the cause (hetu) and the condition (paccaya).”
And it has been said: "The cause (*hetu*) is a reason (*kāraṇa*), and the condition (*paccaya*) is also a reason; therefore, by what characteristic are these reasons stated to be twofold?
Because this must be explained, it was said: "In that regard, what is its characteristic? and so forth.

The cause has a characteristic not shared with other fruits than the fruit to be produced, whereas the condition has a characteristic shared with all fruits. By means of this specific characteristic...
The meaning is that it should be stated in two ways. Since it must be asked, "What kind of distinction between the common and the uncommon would there be?", one asks, "In what way would it be?

and then says, "As in the case of the sprout," and so forth. The meaning is: "In whatever manner that distinction between the common and the uncommon exists, in what respect would that distinction between the common and the uncommon be like what? [This refers to] the production of the sprout.
Just as the seed is unique [to a specific sprout], so too the cause would be unique for the production of its fruit.
Just as earth and water are common conditions for the production of a sprout, so too the condition would be common for the production of the fruit.
Because it is the condition for all fruits, the seed is the unique productive cause of the sprout.
Because it must be asked, “How is it to be believed that earth and water are common causes for production? the passage beginning with “For the sprout” was stated.
That which brings about an equal or identical fruit is the *sabhāva* (intrinsic nature); what is it? It is the seed itself, which is the cause. [One might ask:
“Is the distinction between the cause and the condition to be shown by the simile of the seed and the sprout alone, or should it also be shown by another simile?”
