In order to show the distinction [between them] by means of another simile as well—since it ought to be stated—the passage beginning with "Or, for example" was spoken.
The intention is that through this simile too, the distinction between causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*paccaya*) should be understood.
The distinction between the causes and conditions that serve as external requisites for the seed, the sprout, and so forth, has been analyzed by the Teacher.
And because it was to be asked, "How is it distinguished among internal [factors]?", the passage beginning with "For this is the cycle of existence" (ayaṃ hi saṃsāro) was stated.

Alternatively, because it was to be asked, "While it may be appropriate as a causal condition consisting of requisites among external things, how is it appropriate among internal things?", the passage beginning with "For this is the cycle of existence" was stated.
However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it says: "Thus, the external..."
It is said: "Having shown the analysis of the condition of cause (hetupaccaya), this [passage] beginning with 'For this saṃsāra' was stated in order to show the internal [condition].
Because saṃsāra comes to be together with the conditions of cause, it is "with-cause-condition" (sahetupaccaya).

Since this saṃsāra has arisen having become possessed of the condition of cause, therefore it is indeed appropriate that the condition of cause, which serves as an accessory (parikkhāra), exists even within the internal [person].
The intended meaning is that it "should be seen.
If the Blessed One has stated that this saṃsāra possesses causes and conditions, then it must be accepted by us;
because it was asked, "How is it to be accepted?", the words beginning with "For thus" were spoken. By the word "thus," [it refers to] ignorance and so forth.
By stating that "the entire dependent origination is saṃsāra" and "is produced," the Blessed One has declared that saṃsāra possesses causal conditions;
therefore, this should be believed. While ignorance and the rest may serve as conditions for volitional formations and the rest, because it was asked, "What is the cause of ignorance?
it was stated: "Thus, ignorance is the cause of ignorance. [And when asked: "What is the condition for ignorance?"...
Because it was to be asked, it was said: "Inappropriate attention is the condition. Because it was to be asked, "What is ignorance?
Of what ignorance is it the cause?", it was said: "Prior ignorance is the cause of subsequent ignorance.
Because it was to be asked, "What is prior ignorance? What is subsequent ignorance?", it was said: "Therein," and so forth.

Because it must be asked, "Is the prior underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), which serves as the cause for the manifestation of ignorance, an immediate cause, or is it also a remote cause?", it is said:
"Just like a sprout from a seed," and so forth. "A sprout from a seed" (*bījaṅkura*) means a sprout of seeds;
just as a sprout is produced by virtue of being the immediate cause of the seeds. In the case of a tree or similar [growth],...
Regarding the fruit that is produced, this seed becomes the cause for that fruit produced on the tree or other such object by way of being a successive cause (*paramparahetutā*).
To address the objection, "But the seed is only one; how can it be said to be twofold?", he says, "For it is twofold," and so forth.
The meaning is that, as stated, the cause is likewise twofold through the distinction between immediate time and successive time.

Just as the seed-like cause is twofold, so too the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), which serves as the cause for ignorance, is twofold according to the distinction of time: it is both an immediate cause and a successive cause.
The immediate underlying tendency to ignorance [is the cause] of the immediate manifestation of ignorance (*avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna*).
It is an immediate cause. A prior underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) is a successive cause for a subsequent manifestation of ignorance (*avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna*).

Thus, just as the distinction is evident—that the seed is the uncommon cause while the earth, water, and so forth are the common conditions—likewise, the underlying tendency to ignorance is the uncommon cause, and improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is the common condition.
The term "condition" (paccaya) should be understood as a distinction.

Because it was necessary to state that "the distinction between the root-cause (hetu) and the condition (paccaya) should be explained by this much alone," the passage beginning with "Or, just as a bowl...
was stated. However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is said: "By the words 'Or, just as... and so forth, [the author] shows precisely the classification of the root-cause and the condition."

It has been stated. Therein, the construction is as follows: the bowl, the wick, and the oil, which serve as conditions for the lamp, are not the "cause of its own nature" (*sabhāvahetu*) nor the "identical cause" (*samānahetu*) of the lamp.
Since it might be asked, "Why should one believe that even though the bowl and so forth are conditions for the lamp, they are not the cause of its own nature?
the phrase beginning with "for it is not possible" was stated. [This concerns] the lamp.

Since it is impossible to illuminate or kindle a bowl, a wick, and oil that serve as conditions but lack fire—that is, are devoid of fire—the former lamp is like the natural cause (*sabhāvahetu*) of the subsequent lamp;
likewise, the bowl and so forth are not the natural cause. Thus, being of such a nature, the lamp is the cause.

Just as there is a cause that is an internal specific nature (*sabhāva*) and a condition that is an external dissimilar factor—as in the case of a bowl or similar objects—so too does the internal specific nature function as the cause, while the external dissimilar factor functions as the condition.

The productive underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) is the cause of the manifestation of ignorance (*avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna*), whereas the supporting and stabilizing factors are the conditions. This cause is not shared with other fruits.

Having connected this with the statement that it "is a condition common to all fruits," the intention is that the distinction between the root-cause (hetu) and the condition (paccaya) should also be understood through the simile of the lamp.

The teacher has stated that the cause (kāraṇa) is the classification of the root-condition (hetupaccaya) and its equipment (parikkhāra); the state of being a cause (kāraṇabhāva) belongs to that cause.
And because one does not expect a fruit, it must be asked: "In what manner does the state of being a cause exist?
What is that state of being a cause? What is that manner? And because it must be asked: "What is the fruit that exists with a particular distinction?
What is that fruit? What is that distinction? And [because it must be asked]: "What is the connection between the cause and the fruit..."
Because it was necessary to ask, "What is that connection? and in order to clarify all of that, it was stated: "The meaning is non-interruption," and so forth.

This is the meaning of the transition (*anusandhi*) as explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Now, since the cause has been called 'requisite' (*parikkhāra*), and the state of being a cause is in relation to its fruit, therefore, what the state of being a cause of the cause is, how that state exists, and what..."

It should be understood that this was stated by the words "the meaning of non-interruption," etc., in order to clarify all of the following: the fruit, its specific distinction, and the relationship between the cause and the fruit.
In that context, there exists the meaning of non-interruption belonging to the cause—which consists of the root-cause and the conditions—that has not been interrupted.
Thus, the meaning of "continuity" (santati) is the meaning of "non-interruption," because there is a connection with the fruit;
and that cause which, having arisen as the producer and supporter of its own fruit, ceases, is indeed called "uninterrupted.
Furthermore, when a fruit ceases after having become the cause for another, if that [subsequent fruit] is uninterrupted, it too has the meaning of continuity.
However, that fruit which ceases without having become the cause for another fruit is "severed," such as the death-consciousness of an Arahant.
Whatever purpose of production exists for a fruit produced from a cause, that purpose of production is the "fruit-purpose.
The purpose of rebirth—the purpose of reconnecting—of the aggregates of rebirth-linking is [the rebirth-purpose].

That which is the meaning of rebirth-linking for the defilements—the meaning of arising within the continuum, the meaning of renewed existence—is the meaning of renewed existence. That which is the meaning of obstruction for the defilements is the meaning of obsession.
That which is the meaning of non-eradication by the Path for the defilements is the meaning of underlying tendency. [Regarding] ignorance, of the four...
The meaning of non-penetration that exists among the truths is the meaning of ignorance.
Through the path of Arahantship, the meaning of non-full-understanding that exists is the meaning of the seed for consciousness—that is, for rebirth-linking consciousness.
To this extent, the teacher has analyzed the state of being a cause and the mode of being a cause, as well as the fruit and the distinction of the fruit.
And because it was understood by us that it ought to be asked, "What is the meaning of 'successive cause-condition' (paramparahetupaccaya), and what is the meaning of 'connection' (sambandha)?
the passage beginning with "where there is no interruption" was stated.

Where—in whatever occurrence of material and immaterial phenomena—there is an uninterruptedness of the cause, which is the various types of cause-conditions, that non-interruption exists therein in that [occurrence].

In the occurrence of both the material and the immaterial, there is a continuity (*santati*). Wherever and in whichever occurrence of the material and immaterial this continuity exists, that continuity is the arising within that occurrence of the material and immaterial;
having applied [the analysis] in this manner and so forth, the successive causes and so on are to be understood.
"The aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandha*) refers to the perfectly pure aggregate of virtue. "Of the aggregate of concentration" (*samādhikkhandhassa*) refers to the exalted aggregate.
For a sublime state has concentration as its proximate cause. "The aggregate of wisdom" refers to the aggregate dominated by the wisdom of the path and fruition;
for that is the condition for the aggregate of reviewing knowledge known as the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The meaning of "skill in landing places" and so forth has already been explained in the commentary on the *Padatthāna*, *Hāra*, and *Vibhaṅga*.
The teacher stated that "intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is the cause.
Because it must be asked, "What kind of intrinsic nature is the cause?", he said, "Or rather, depending on the eye... and so forth.

Eye-consciousness arises depending upon—that is, taking as its support—the eye and the eye-faculty, and depending upon—that is, taking as its object—visible forms. In this context, regarding the eye and the others...
The eye-faculty is a condition for eye-consciousness by way of being a dominant condition (*ādhipateyyapaccaya*) and a faculty condition (*indriyapaccaya*);

the visible form object is a condition by way of being a pre-arisen object-condition (*purejātārammaṇapaccaya*); and light is a condition by way of being a support (*sannissayatā*) and a decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).
While being such a condition, it is not the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) [of the consciousness] because it is not identical with its fruit, the eye-consciousness.

There is the condition, and there is attention (*manasikāra*). However, because the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) shares the same nature as the resultant eye-consciousness in its status as consciousness, it is a cause by way of its own-nature (*sabhāva-hetu*);

likewise, because the formations (*saṅkhārā*) share the same nature as consciousness in their status as the mental aggregate (*nāmakhandha*), they are causes of consciousness by way of their own-nature.
Consciousness [is related] to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) by way of sharing the same continuity (*ekasantati*).

The intrinsic nature (sabhāva) that serves as a condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the cause (hetu). By this method, the meaning should also be understood in such passages as "name-and-form [is the condition] for the sixfold sense base" (nāmarūpaṃ saḷāyatanassa), and so forth.

Thus, any kind of supporting condition (upanissaya)—whether it be a producing condition (janaka-paccaya) or a consolidating condition (upatthambhaka-paccaya)—that is a strong condition (balava-paccaya), all such things constitute the causal condition (hetupaccaya) which is both producing and consolidating for that which is to be produced and consolidated.
Because it prepares and conditions the fruit, it is called "requisite" (parikkhāra) in the primary sense.
To the objection, "By what means are we to believe that the cause-condition (hetupaccaya) of the aforementioned type is called a 'requisite'?
the passage beginning with "Therefore it was said" was stated. By that reason—that is, by the fact that every cause-condition possesses the nature of a requisite—
The Venerable Mahākaccāna said the words, “Those phenomena which produce that phenomenon. By those words, it is to be believed;
the intention is that you should observe [the matter] based on the statement, “Those phenomena which produce that phenomenon.

Because it must be stated, “Only this much is the Mode of Conveying Requisites (parikkhāra-hāra) to be applied,” it is said, “The Mode of Conveying Requisites is concluded. Whatever Mode of Conveying Requisites is to be applied, each such Mode of Conveying Requisites is to be extracted and applied accordingly.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* composed in accordance with one's own strength and ability within the analysis of the requisites for the Path.
However, the wise should grasp its profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
16. Exposition of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Coordination (Samāropanahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā) 50.
By whichever analysis of the mode of conveying requisites—which constitutes a specific form of commentary—the causal condition for the meaning of the Sutta has been analyzed, that...
[is] complete; because it must be asked: "What is the analysis of the mode of conveying coordination?"

“In that regard, what is the ‘Method of Coordination’ (samāropana-hāra)? and so forth is stated. Therein, among those sixteen modes of exposition (desanā-hāra) and so on that have been pointed out, he asks:
“What specific mode of commentary is the ‘Method of Coordination,’ known as the ‘Analysis of the Method of Coordination’? [The answer is:
“Regarding the exposition beginning with ‘Those phenomena which have this as their root,’ that which is now being stated by me—‘In one footing, however many... [and so on].
The detailed specific commentary beginning with “the word-bases descend” is called the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Coordination (*samāropana-hāra-vibhaṅga*).
Because it must be asked, “When how many word-bases are stated in the Sutta, how many word-bases are to be coordinated?
the passage beginning with “in one word-base” is stated. When one word-base is stated in the Sutta, as many [unstated ones] as there may be— (End of fragment)

The word-bases enter into and converge; all those word-bases, even if not explicitly stated, should be brought forward by way of selection as if they were stated in the Sutta and applied to the teaching.
Because it must be asked, "Like what should they be applied?", it is said: "Just as in the Conversion [Method]," and so forth.
For in the Conversion Mode of Conveying (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*), when a single word-base is stated in the Sutta...
When many word-meanings (*padatthāna*) not explicitly stated in the Sutta enter [into its interpretation], those many word-meanings must be sought;
likewise, in the method of coordination (*samāropanahāra*), the meaning is that many word-meanings must be coordinated with the teaching.
But should the coordination be performed solely by way of word-meanings, or should it also be performed by way of something else?
Because it must be stated, "How is it to be done?", the application (*samāropanā*) may also be performed by way of other factors. Therefore, showing that the application is fourfold, he said:
"In this regard, the application is fourfold," and so on. Therein, "in this regard" (*tattha*) refers to those applications to be applied:
the application of the basis (*padaṭṭhāna-samāropanā*) is the basis, and the application of the synonym (*vevacana-samāropanā*) is the synonym.
Development is the application of development; abandoning is the application of abandoning. Thus, by this classification, the application should be made fourfold.

Since it must be asked, "Among those four kinds of applications, which is the application of the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*)?", having asked thus, the passage beginning with "In that regard, which...
was stated in order to show the application of the proximate cause as taught in the Sutta.
He asks: "How is the application of the word-meanings (*padaṭṭhāna*) made for those word-meanings not explicitly stated in the sutta? [The answer is:
That which is the non-doing of all evil, of the unwholesome, and the teaching that exists as the cause for such non-doing—this teaching is the instruction (*ovāda*) of the Buddhas;
or alternatively, that teaching which exists for the purpose of non-doing is the [instruction] of the Buddhas.
“Instruction” (*sāsana*) means advice; the meaning is that it is not instruction for just anyone.

For the word *akaraṇa* is used here in the sense of the recipient (dative), as in the nominative case, just as in the expressions “for what purpose? (*kissa atthāya*) or “what is the aim? (*kimattha*).

That instruction which exists for the attainment of the wholesome—that is the instruction of the Buddhas. “The cleansing of one’s own mind” (*sacittapariyodāpana*) is for the purpose of cleansing one’s own mind.
Whatever teaching exists, that is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Thus, he asks again for the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) of that teaching described in such a manner—the proximate cause of the distinction—asking: "What is the proximate cause of this teaching, this instruction?
This triad of good conduct (*sucarita-ttaya*) is the proximate cause of the teaching, the instruction; by means of the triad of good conduct...
It should be understood as being by way of cause for the teaching (*sāsana*), just as in the expression “he lives by means of food,” and so forth.

Since it must be asked, “When the three types of good conduct have been stated as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), which proximate cause is to be superimposed [upon the teaching]?”—therefore, it is said: “In that regard, that which is bodily...,” and so forth.
This triad of aggregates is to be superimposed as the proximate cause of the teaching; [this is stated] regarding the triad of aggregates.
Since it must be asked, "When the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) has been superimposed, what is to be superimposed?", it is said: "Therein, the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha)," and so forth.
This pair of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) is to be superimposed as the proximate cause of the Dispensation (sāsana).
[Furthermore,] since it must be asked, "When the pair of serenity and insight has been superimposed as the proximate cause, what proximate cause is to be superimposed?"

Because it is to be asked, it is said: "In that regard, the fruit of serenity," and so forth. These two fruits are to be superimposed as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
Having determined that the proximate causes of the Dispensation are to be superimposed, they have been analyzed by the Teacher; we [have followed suit].
And because it must be asked, "Now, which [factor] should be assigned as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for which?

it is said, "The forest is the proximate cause of the thicket," and so forth. This fivefold set of sensual qualities is the "forest" that serves as the proximate cause for the "thicket" consisting of craving, because it is the basis for craving;
or rather, it is the grasping at signs known as "woman" or "man."

This forest should be understood as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the thicket (*vanatha*) known as the grasping of the secondary characteristics of various limbs and members—such as "O, what an eye! O, what an ear! O, what a nose! O, what a tongue! O, what a body!
Furthermore, this forest, known as the twelve sense bases (*dvādasāyatana*), when not fully understood (*apariññāta*), is the proximate cause for the thicket known as the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

It should be superimposed [upon the sense bases]. Because fetters arise dependent upon the sense bases, this "forest" (vana), which is designated as the underlying tendencies (anusaya), should be superimposed as the proximate cause (padatthāna) for the "thicket" (vanatha) designated as the outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna).

To the objection, "By what means are we to believe that the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth have the nature of a forest, and that craving and so forth have the nature of a thicket? it was said: "Therefore he said..."

The passage beginning with “the Blessed One” has been stated. By that means—namely, by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) and so forth being the "forest" (*vana*), and by way of craving (*taṇhā*) and so forth being the "thicket" (*vanatha*)—the Blessed One spoke the words, “Having cut down both the forest and the thicket. One should have faith in those words of the Blessed One, following the literal sense of the speech.
This refers to this very commentary beginning with “in one footing” (*ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne*). Regarding the phrase “by way of the footing” (*padaṭṭhānena*):
By each individual *padatthāna* (basis of the word). "Superimposition" (*samāropanā*) means the superimposition of other *padatthānas*. The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
it is called "superimposition" because by means of this commentary they are superimposed—that is, they are to be superimposed. (1) 51.
The superimposition by way of *padatthāna* has been pointed out by the Teacher and is understood by us. [Now,] which is that by way of synonyms (*vevacana*)?
Since it was necessary to ask, "What is 'co-ordination'? the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is [co-ordination] by means of synonyms? was stated. "In that regard" (*tattha*) means:
among those four types of co-ordination—beginning with the co-ordination of the footing—he asks which is the co-ordination of various synonyms for each individual synonym.
"The fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāga*), "the liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*), and "the fruit of training" (*sekkhaphala*)... [are examples].

Furthermore, these three terms—“the fading away of ignorance,” “liberation through wisdom,” and “the fruit of the one beyond training”—are synonyms for the fruit of non-returning because they refer to the state of being a non-returner.

Likewise, these three terms—“the fading away of ignorance,” “liberation through wisdom,” and “the fruit of the one beyond training”—are synonyms for the fruit of arahantship because they refer to the state of being an arahant.
Following this method, the application [of the analysis] should be made to the remaining cases as well. (2)
The teacher has demonstrated the application (*samāropanā*) by means of synonyms, and this is understood by us;

however, because it must be asked, "What is the application regarding development (*bhāvanā*)?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is [the application] regarding development? was stated. "In that regard" (*tattha*) means:

among those four types—application as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna-samāropanā*), and so forth—which of the taught developments and which of the untaught developments are the applications of development? Thus he asks.
The meaning is that just as the Blessed One spoke of a particular meditation in a certain manner— namely, "Therefore, bhikkhu, dwell contemplating the body in the body,
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world"—
in that same manner and by means of that meditation, other meditations should also be superimposed.
In the passage beginning with “Therefore, then,” since it must be asked, “What did the Blessed One say regarding meditation? the words beginning with “ardent” (*ātāpī*) are spoken.

By the word “ardent,” the Blessed One spoke of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*). By the word “clearly comprehending” (*sampajāno*), the Blessed One spoke of the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).

By the word “mindful” (*satimā*), he spoke of the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*). [And] by the phrase “having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world” (*vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassam*).

By this statement, he has spoken of the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*). Since it must be asked, "When this has been said, what kind of development (*bhāvanā*) is to be superadded?", it is stated:
"For one who dwells thus contemplating the body in the body, the four foundations of mindfulness reach the fulfillment of their development.
Thus, when the development of the faculties of energy (*vīriyindriya*) and so forth has been described, the four foundations of mindfulness are to be superadded.

The meaning is as follows. He asks: "By what cause do they reach the fulfillment of development? He answers: "Because they possess a single characteristic by way of being faculties among the four faculties, or by way of being that which is to be developed.
Since it must be asked, "When these have been superimposed, which ones are to be superimposed?", he says "In the four," and so forth. In the four...
When the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are being developed and applied, the four right efforts (sammappadhāna) reach fulfillment of their development;
thus, "to be applied" is the meaning. In the remaining [foundations] as well, they are to be applied in exactly the same way.
The application through development has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known by us. [Now, one may ask: "What is the application by means of abandoning?"
Because it was necessary to ask [this question], the passage beginning with “In that regard, which... was stated. “In that regard” means:

among those four—namely, the application of the foundations of mindfulness (*padaṭṭhāna-samāropana*) and so forth—which taught abandonment, does which application of the abandonment belong to which untaught abandonments? He asks this.

By the teaching, “Dwelling contemplating the body as the body, one abandons the perversion (*vipallāsa*) of perceiving the beautiful in the ugly,” [the following is shown]: by the [abandonment] taught as “the beautiful,”...

By means of the abandoning of the perversions through the full understanding of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), the abandoning of the defilements and clinging to sensual desire (*kāmupādāna*) which act as obstacles,

and so forth, should also be superimposed. By means of the abandoning of the perversion that [perceives] pleasure in what is suffering— taught in the passage, “Dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings, one abandons the perversion of [perceiving] pleasure in what is suffering”—

the abandoning of the defilements and clinging to existence (*bhavupādāna*) which act as obstacles to the full understanding of contact-nutriment (*phassāhāra*), and so forth, should also be superimposed.
By the teaching, “Dwelling contemplating mind as mind, one abandons the perversion of [perceiving] the impermanent as permanent,” the abandoning of the defilements,

views, and clinging that act as obstacles to the full understanding of consciousness as nutriment (*viññāṇāhāra*) should also be understood as included in the abandoning of the perversion of [perceiving] the permanent as “permanent.
By the teaching, “Dwelling contemplating phenomena as phenomena, one abandons the perversion of [perceiving] the non-self as self,”...
“Is it by the abandoning of the perversion [of ‘self’] that there is full understanding of the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*)?”—
the intention is that the abandoning of the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*), which is a defilement obstructing the full understanding of the nutriment of mental volition,

and so forth, should also be superimposed [upon this]. (4) As for the Mode of Abandoning (*pahānahāra*), however, since it has already been explained in the commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāra*), we shall not discuss it here.

Because it must be asked, "By what means can we understand and have faith in the process of correlating the foundations and so forth that are not explicitly taught in the Sutta with each foundation and so forth that *is* taught?
he said, "Therefore the Venerable One... and so on. By means of that process of correlation, the Venerable Mahākaccāna—
"Those phenomena which have a certain root, and those which are explained by the Sage as having a single meaning—these should be subsumed;
this is the Mode of Conveying Subsumption (samāropana-hāra).
By the statement he has uttered, it is meant that you should understand and have faith in the manner of such subsumption according to that statement and following its sequence.
"Is the Mode of Conveying Coordination (samāropano hāra) complete at this point, or is there nothing else to be assigned?"—because it must be stated thus, it is said:

"The Mode of Conveying Coordination has been assigned. By means of the method taught in the Sutta through such factors as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), those proximate causes that have not been taught must be coordinated;
[likewise] by means of those respective proximate causes and so forth, the untaught proximate causes and so forth [are to be supplied].
The application-mode of interpretation (*samāropana-hāra*) has been concluded; the meaning should be understood as that which is to be applied after having been extracted.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Exposition) composed according to one's own strength and ability, within the analysis of the application-mode of interpretation.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
These sixteen aforementioned specific modes of exposition are called "modes" (*hāra*) because they carry away and remove ignorance and doubt regarding the meanings to be expounded.
The explanation of the section on the analysis of the modes is concluded.
1. The Elucidation of the Comprehension of the Modes of Exposition (Desanāhāra).

52. By whichever specific mode of commentary—such as the analysis of the modes of exposition (desanāhāra) and the analysis of the modes of treatment (hāra)—the various meanings of the Suttas, beginning with the "tastes" (assāda), have been analyzed, that specific mode of commentary consisting of the analysis of the modes of exposition and the analysis of the modes of treatment is complete.
"First, the sixteen modes; having surveyed the directions by way of 'surveying the directions' (disālocana);..."
“Having condensed it, one should point out the Sutta by means of the hook and the three methods”—this verse was spoken by the Teacher in the Section on Exposition (Niddesa-vāra).
The exposition of that verse has not been analyzed at the beginning of the Section on the Analysis of the Modes (Hāra-vibhaṅga-vāra);
where has it been analyzed? It has been analyzed either in the Section on the Convergence of the Modes (Hāra-sampāta) or in the Section on the Origination of the Methods (Naya-samutṭhāna-hāra).

Or rather, because it was necessary to ask "How is it divided?", the passage beginning with "The first sixteen strings" was stated in order to inform you that it should be seen by you as being divided at the junctions of the strings (*hārasampāta*).
Alternatively, it is like various sections of well-adorned suttas that resemble a well-prepared ground, upon which [the commentary] is to be embellished like flowers of various colors and fragrances.
Having joined the sixteen strings (hāra) by way of commentary, the Teacher has analyzed the sixteen strings; likewise,
having joined the sixteen strings by way of commentary upon the various passages of the Suttas— which are like ornaments of Jambūnada gold well-examined by a teacher skilled in his craft—
the sixteen strings have been analyzed as being like various jewel-gems emitting networks of diverse rays, even as he turned over the great earth.
Just as feeding someone with *pappaṭaka* (mushroom) is exceedingly difficult,
so too is the act of making [the meaning] understood by one who explains the ultimate truth (*paramattha*) through the sixteen modes (*hāra*) in various praised passages of the Sutta—
this being like the exceedingly difficult task of squeezing a *yojanika* honey-bundle and making [the person] drink its exquisite sweetness. And likewise, among the various [texts]...

And by the Master, who provides an explanation— difficult as drinking milk— for those passages of the Sutta that are to be praised, using the sixteen modes (*hāra*) which are sweet in their ultimate meaning;
and having applied the sixteen modes to many passages of the Sutta to be praised by way of commentary, the sixteen modes have been analyzed and are known by us in various types of Sutta passages.
Having joined them by way of being commentaries, are the sixteen modes of conveyance (*hāra*) analyzed?
Or rather, having joined even a single passage of a sutta that is to be commented upon by way of being a commentary, are the sixteen modes of conveyance analyzed?

Since it must be stated [in response] that they are indeed analyzed by joining even a single passage of a sutta that is to be commented upon by way of being a commentary, he analyzes them accordingly: "The sixteen modes of conveyance..."
He states the section on the "Convergence of Modes of Conveying" (Hārasampātavāra) beginning with "The first," and so forth. Now, one might ask:

"Should not the teacher, wishing to explain the section on the Convergence of Modes of Conveying, have stated such words as 'In this regard, what is the convergence of the mode of conveying by teaching' and so on?
Why, then, does he state 'The sixteen modes of conveying are the first,' and so forth? [The answer is: It is stated in the *Niddesa*:

The section on the analysis of the modes (*hāravibhaṅgavāra*) does not apply the verse beginning with “The sixteen modes first,” because its subject matter is scattered and because the investigation of the methods (*naya*) intervenes.
However, the section on the convergence of the modes (*hārasampātavāra*) does apply that verse, as its subject matter is not scattered.
Therefore, in order to inform [the reader] that one should look for the exposition of that verse in the section on the convergence of the modes by referring back to it, [the text says...]
“‘The sixteen modes of conveyance come first,’ and so forth, must indeed be stated. However, in the Commentary it says:

‘Just as one scatters various colored jasmine flowers upon ground that has been well-prepared, or as one sets various precious gems—blazing with networks of diverse rays—into highly polished golden ornaments designed by a master craftsman of well-trained skill.’”
Just as one might turn over the great earth and make it eat the sap of the *pappaṭaka* plant,
or as one might press a *yojanika* honey-ball and make [the world] drink its most delicious juice, so too the Venerable Mahākaccāna,

while citing various sections of the Suttas and analyzing them according to the sixteen modes (*hāra*), now demonstrates the section on the convergence of modes (*hārasampātavāra*) by applying them all to a single Sutta.
One should begin. And while beginning, one should—according to the section on exposition which states:
“First, the sixteen modes of conveying; having surveyed the directions by way of discerning the directions;
then, having condensed [the meaning] with the hook, one should expound the discourse by means of the three methods”—proceed accordingly.

The verses have been stated. Because that section on the analysis of the strings (*hāravibhaṅgavāra*) does not apply them—since its subject matter is scattered and because the investigation of the method (*naya*) intervenes—the section on the analysis of the strings consists simply in showing the classification of the strings through numerous scriptural passages.
However, the section on the convergence of the strings (*hārasampātavāra*) does apply them, having applied sixteen strings within a single scriptural passage.

Because the exposition of the "arising of the method" (nayasamutthāna) was spoken immediately after that. Therefore, having referred back to the verse, “The sixteen modes of conveyance are first,” it was said:
“Where is its detailed exposition (niddesa) to be found? It is stated: ‘In the *Hārasampāta*’.
The meaning of the verse has already been explained in the *Niddesavibhāvanā*. As for the verse beginning, “The sixteen... [up to] the Sutta,” which appears in the *Niddesa*:
When asked by the Teacher, "Where is the exposition of that verse to be found?
Was it not analyzed by the Teacher at the beginning of the *Hāravibhaṅga*, or is it to be understood as having been analyzed by referring back to the *Hārasampāta*?

Or is it to be understood as having been analyzed by referring back to the *Nayasamuṭṭhāna*?"—he asks, "How so? [The answer is: "It is to be understood as having been analyzed by referring back to the *Hārasampāta*."
“It is to be seen” is the answer.

The teacher stated that the exposition of that verse is to be seen within the "convergence of the modes" (hārasampāta). That convergence of the modes is sixteenfold, being divided by the convergence of the modes of teaching (desanāhāra) and so forth;
for it must be asked therein: "In this context, what is the convergence of the modes? What is the convergence of the modes of teaching? Thus, in this [text]...

When a Sutta is to be expounded, that specific mode of exposition which, being analyzed by me, constitutes a particular application of the modes (hāra) and is termed the "application of the modes of teaching" (desanā-hārasampāta), is thus analyzed with the words: "In this context, what is the application of the modes of teaching? and so forth.

"In this context" (tattha) means within that sixteenfold application of the modes beginning with the application of the modes of teaching. What kind of application of the modes is it? It is that which constitutes the application of the modes.
He asks: "What is the specific excellence of the commentary called the 'arrival of the sustenance of the teaching'?
[It is as follows: "With an unguarded mind, struck by wrong view, and overcome by sloth and torpor, one falls under the power of Māra."

In the Sutta, having asked, "What does one confess by means of an unguarded mind?", the specific commentary stating, "One confesses negligence," and so forth, is called the "descent of the nutriment of the teaching. The meaning of the verse is analyzed in the Aṭṭhakathā;
however, the sense of the construction is as follows: by means of an unguarded mind, a person possessing an unguarded mind falls under the power of Māra, the Death-deity.
A person possessed of perversion, being struck by wrong view, falls under the power of Māra.
A person possessed of that mind—whose mind is overcome by sloth and torpor, and which is both prompted and indolent—falls under the power of Māra, namely the defilement-Māra.
Since it must be stated for whom that state of negligence, taught by the phrase "with an unguarded mind," constitutes a footing.
It was said, “That is the path of Death. The meaning taught by this passage from the Sutta, “By an unguarded mind,” has been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us.

However, since it must be explained how the meaning taught by the passage from the Sutta, “And by one struck down by wrong view,” is analyzed, the words beginning with “And by one struck down by wrong view” were spoken.

When one perceives what is impermanent as "permanent" by means of a particular perversion (*vipallāsa*), that perversion occurring at that time is called "struck down by wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi-hata*).
Since it must be asked, "What is the characteristic of that perversion?", having asked thus, it is stated:
"Perversion has the characteristic of grasping things in a distorted way."
“Characterized by grasping what is contrary” means that perversion (*vipallāsa*) has the characteristic of grasping the beautiful and so forth in the very things that are ugly and so forth;
it is called “perversion” because the sense of its activity—namely, “it causes one to become perverted”—is possible. What is this perversion characterized by grasping what is contrary?
That perversion perverts perception (*saññā*), it also perverts the mind (*citta*), and it also perverts view (*diṭṭhi*). Thus, it perverts these three states.
Because there are three kinds of things that can be distorted, the distortions themselves are also threefold.

Among them, the distortion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*) is weak and feeble, because it consists merely in grasping an appearance as it presents itself through such [erroneous] modes as "beautiful" and so forth.

The distortion of mind (*citta-vipallāsa*) is stronger than the distortion of perception, because it is the definitive judgment (*sanniṭṭhāna*) regarding the aggregates of form and so forth—which present themselves as beautiful and so forth—as being indeed beautiful and so forth.

Because of grasping by way of view. The perversion of view is stronger than the perversions of perception and consciousness, because it grasps whichever object appears in the mode of being beautiful and so forth by adhering to that very object as eternal and so on.
Therefore, the perversion of perception is mentioned first, followed by the perversion of consciousness, and after that—
The perversion of view has been stated. In detail, however, because each one is fourfold by way of grasping at the beautiful, the pleasant, the self, and the permanent, they become twelvefold.
The perversions have been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us; [now we shall consider] "which are the bases and objects for the occurrence of the perversions?"
Because these bases of personal existence (*attabhāvavatthu*) are objects for the occurrence of perversion (*vipallāsa*), it is said:

"In what does he become perverted? In the four bases of personal existence. In the four bases of personal existence—consisting of the material body (*rūpakāya*), feeling (*vedanā*), mind (*citta*), and mental phenomena (*dhamma*)—all that perversion, namely perception (*saññā*), mind (*citta*), and view (*diṭṭhi*), becomes perverted. "How does one who views them..."
Because it must be asked, "Does it cause perversion? the following was said: "One regards form as self," and so forth.
That person who regards form as self, or regards a self possessed of form as self, or regards form within the self as self, or regards a self within form as self—in this way, for him...
For a person who views [them] thus, perversion perverts the perception, mind, and view regarding the material body.
This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.
Since it must be asked, "Among those—the material body and so forth—which is the basis for which perversion?"—for one proceeding in this manner:
In order to analyze which of these is the basis for which perversion, it is said, "Therein, form... and so forth.
"Therein" means that among those four—form and the rest—the first, form, should be understood by way of analysis as the basis for the perversion occurring as "the beautiful in the ugly.
This same method applies to the remaining [perceptions] as well. Thus, "in the ugly..."
The perversions (vipallāsā) are fourfold, such as [the perception of] "the beautiful" (subha) and so forth.
This has been shown by the Teacher after analyzing it as "this is the basis for this," and it is known by us;
however, because it must be asked, "Which phenomena are the root causes of those perversions?", it is said: "Two phenomena," and so forth. These are the defilements of the mind (cittasaṃkilesā).
Craving and ignorance—these two factors constitute the root causes of the perversions.

Since it must be stated whether these two factors together or individually serve as the root cause of the perversions, the passage beginning with “enveloped by craving” is spoken in order to analyze them separately. There is no such thing as craving that is devoid of ignorance.
Therefore, should it not be said that [the world] is "shrouded by craving and ignorance"?
No; because craving is the predominant condition. For through predominant craving, people regard even the unattractive as "attractive" and even suffering as "pleasurable.
Since it is stated as "craving and ignorance," it should be said to be "shrouded by ignorance"; why then is it said to be "shrouded by views"? Because of ignorance...
The phrase "shrouded by views" (*diṭṭhinivuta*) is stated by taking ignorance (*avijjā*) under the heading of "views," meaning it should be understood as "shrouded by ignorance.
However, if one were to say simply "shrouded by ignorance," ignorance devoid of views might also be included;
for it is through ignorance accompanied by views that people regard even the impermanent as "permanent" and the non-self as "self."
Because it must be explained how perversion (vipallāsa) proceeds with craving as its root, and how perversion proceeds with ignorance accompanied by views as its root, it is said:
“In that regard, that which is the perversion of view,” and so forth. “In that regard” means among those [perversions] rooted in craving and rooted in ignorance accompanied by views.
“Perversion of view” refers to the perversion rooted in ignorance accompanied by views. “One regards past form as self” means...
Even though it is not a material thing, it is spoken of as if it were a material thing. "Perversion rooted in craving" refers to a perversion based on craving accompanied by views;

one rejoices in future form by way of delighting through views. Thus, the distinction in the mode of occurrence should be understood according to the division between the contemplation of the past and the rejoicing in the future.
"The defilement of the mind consists of only two factors: craving and ignorance."
If it is asked, "Since there are ten defilements as well, why are only two mentioned?", it is said, "Two things are corruptions of the mind," and so forth.
Craving and ignorance—these two things alone [are mentioned] because they are the root causes of the most blameworthy perversion.
When the mind is purified of those two, craving and ignorance, it is purified of all defilements; therefore, specifically...

It is said that there are two things that are defilements of the mind. For when craving and ignorance have been abandoned by the path of Arahantship, there is no defilement whatsoever that remains unabandoned.
Why is it that craving and ignorance, in the manner described, are the root causes of the perversions in the manner described?
Or rather, since it must be stated whether they are the root cause of the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*),

the statement beginning with "of those" was made to show that just as craving and ignorance of the aforementioned types are the root causes of the aforementioned [defilements], so too are they the root causes of the entire cycle of existence.
In that context, for those individuals whose minds are unprotected and struck by wrong view...
There are those persons for whom no prior limit is discerned to their hindrance of ignorance and fetter of craving;
for those persons wandering and transmigrating through saṃsāra with that hindrance of ignorance and fetter of craving,
there occurs at one time the wandering and transmigrating by going to the realm of Māra in hell, and at another time [the wandering and transmigrating] into the animal womb.
"Running and wandering" means that there is once running and wandering in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya),
once running and wandering in the host of asuras, once running and wandering among the devas,
and once running and wandering among human beings; such is the meaning.
The meaning taught by the passage from the Sutta beginning with “by one struck down by wrong view” has been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us;

however, because it must be stated how the meaning taught by the passage from the Sutta beginning with “by one overcome by sloth and torpor” is analyzed, the words beginning with “by one overcome by sloth and torpor” were spoken.
It is the lack of health of the mind, which is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha).
There is unworkability; this lack of fitness, this unworkability, is called *thina* (sloth).

That which is the sluggishness of the body and the sluggishness of the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling—that is the sluggishness of the body, called *middha* (torpor). Thus, the specific nature of *thina* and *middha* has been stated.
However, the state of the mind being overcome by these two—sloth and torpor—and so forth, is not mentioned because it is easily understood.
Even for those persons whose minds are overcome by sloth and torpor,
the nature of their running and wandering through saṃsāra— by means of that mind, under the heading of "mind," bound by fetters, and going under Māra’s control—
must be understood in detail as having a terminal state.
Because it must be explained how the meaning taught by the scriptural passage, “He goes under the power of Māra,” is analyzed, it is said: “He goes under the power of Māra.
In that context, regarding “of the defilement-Māra”: defilement is called “Māra” in the sense that it kills (māreti) or obstructs merit such as giving; thus, it is the defilement-Māra.
By means of this [term], the formative-Māra, the aggregate-Māra, and the death-Māra are also included, because they function in dependence upon the defilement-Māra.
And they are included, or it should be understood that they are included by the word "and" (ca). "Of the Māra of Beings" means of the Devaputta-māra.

Alternatively, because it is stated as "of the Māra of Beings" rather than saying "of the Devaputta-māra," whoever—such as kings, thieves, and so forth—who destroys [the practice of] giving and so on, or who destroys sovereignty, wealth, and so on, each such king, thief, and so forth is also included; therefore, for anyone whatsoever...
The meaning is "of the Lord of Beings. "They dwell" means [they abide by] desire, greed, intention, preference, longing, command, and injunction.
"He goes" means he approaches, attains, follows, pursues, and does not transgress; such is the meaning. Because it must be asked, "Why does he go under their control?
the passage beginning with "For he... is stated. It refers to that being whose mind is unprotected and whose mind is struck down by wrong view.
And he possesses a mind overcome by sloth and torpor;

because that being, being shrouded by the hindrance of ignorance and the rest, faces toward *saṃsāra* rather than facing toward the dismantling of formations (*visaṅkhāra*), he therefore falls under the power of Māra—this is the meaning.
By means of this sutta, the meaning of which has been analyzed starting with the words "By the unprotected," etc., [the point is established].
Because it must be stated, "How many truths were taught by the Sutta?", the passage beginning with "These two truths were taught by the Blessed One" was spoken.
By the Sutta beginning with "By one who is unguarded," these two truths—suffering and its origin—were taught by the Blessed One. How were they taught?
They were taught both through discourse based on the Abhidhamma and through discourse based on the Sutta. Of those discourses, regarding that based on the Abhidhamma:

When this discourse is taught, by the phrase "with an unguarded mind," the Blessed One teaches and makes known that there is an unguarded mind when it is lustful, an unguarded mind when it is hateful, and an unguarded mind when it is deluded.
Therein, a lustful mind is eightfold by way of the arising of consciousness accompanied by greed; a hateful mind is [eightfold] by way of the arising of consciousness associated with aversion.
It should be understood that there are two kinds [of unguardedness]: the bewildered mind and the state of utter delusion (*momūha-citta-ppāda*).

For, by way of these mental states, whatever lack of guarding and non-protection arises regarding the eye-faculty and so forth, through that lack of guarding and non-protection, the mind itself becomes unprotected by way of figurative designation (*phalūpacāra*).

By the phrase “by one struck by wrong view,” a consciousness associated with wrong view is taught; this should be understood as fourfold, according to the types of consciousness-arising associated with views.
For that [consciousness] is called “struck by wrong view” because it follows the influence of wrong view due to its state of being conjoined with wrong view.
By the phrase “overcome by sloth and torpor,” [a consciousness] conjoined with sloth and torpor [is taught].
The mind has been explained; it should be understood as fivefold by way of the arising of prompted consciousness (*sasaṅkhārika-cittuppāda*).
For that [consciousness], because it is associated with sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) and follows the influence of sloth and torpor, it is called "overcome by sloth and torpor.
Thus, regarding the twelve unwholesome states of consciousness mentioned in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*: "Which states are unwholesome? At whatever time an unwholesome..."
“...a state of mind arises,” and so on; these twelve unwholesome types of consciousness should be understood as having been taught by the Blessed One through three phrases.
By the word “of Māra,” the five Māras are included. Among them, the defilement-Māra consists of:
the four taints (*āsava*), the four floods (*ogha*), the four yokes (*yoga*), the four knots (*gantha*), the four clingings (*upādāna*), and the eight...

The Mara of the Hindrances is taught as "the five hindrances" and "the ten defilements. The Mara of Volitional Formations is taught as "wholesome volition, unwholesome volition, wholesome karma, unwholesome karma," and so forth.
The Mara of the Aggregates is taught as "the personal existence consists of the five aggregates," and so forth.
The Mara of Death is taught as "passing away, the state of vanishing," and so forth. Thus, first, regarding that which is based on the Abhidhamma...
The meaning taught by the discourse should be understood as follows:
when a teaching based on the Suttantas is given, it says: "Having seen a form with the eye, one grasps at its signs and grasps at its secondary characteristics;
because the faculty of the eye remains unrestrained while he dwells thus, covetousness and dejection..."
Evil, unwholesome states might flow in upon him; he does not practice for their restraint,

he does not guard the eye faculty, and he does not achieve restraint over the eye faculty… [and so on] …he does not achieve restraint over the ear faculty… he does not achieve restraint over the nose faculty… he does not achieve restraint over the tongue faculty… he does not achieve restraint over the body faculty.

"He attains restraint... he does not attain restraint over the mind-faculty"—thus, that six-door consciousness which was spoken of by way of reference to the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) is taught by this phrase "with an unguarded mind.
As for those wrong views, whether by way of conceptualizing the past, or by way of conceptualizing the future, or by way of conceptualizing both the past and the future—

Or, for one who adheres wrongly or emerges from reflection in an improper manner, there arise views such as "the world is eternal" or "the world is not eternal," or "the Tathāgata does not exist after death.

By means of those views—or by those views which [are enumerated] in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and other discourses as "these four theories of eternalism... [and so on] ...up to the theory of Nibbāna in this very life"—[one is bound].
That consciousness which is associated with those views is taught by the phrase "by one struck down by wrong view.

Furthermore, regarding sloth (*thina*) and torpor (*middha*): some say that "sloth is the unserviceability of the mind, while torpor is the unserviceability of the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling";
others say that "sloth is the sinking due to a lack of exertion, while torpor is the impairment of the power of exertion. These are what are meant by sloth and torpor.
Those states have been described; that mind which is overcome and overwhelmed by those states of sloth and torpor is taught by this phrase: "by one overcome by sloth and torpor.
As for the term "power" (*vaso*)—which has been stated as "desire, greed, intention, preference, longing, command, and injunction"—that which is called power is...
By the word “dwells,” this is taught. As for the Māra mentioned—namely, the five Māras:

the Māra of the aggregates (*khandhamāra*), the Māra of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāramāra*), the Māra of death (*maccumāra*), the Māra of the son of a god (*devaputtamāra*), and the Māra of defilements (*kilesamāra*)—that Māra is taught by the phrase “of Māra.
As for the person mentioned who “goes, approaches, attains, follows, pursues, and does not transcend,” he is...
The person is taught by this [statement]: “He goes. Among the phenomena thus taught, the unwholesome are the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*).
By the phrase “he goes under the power of Māra,” the person—who is designated in dependence upon the five aggregates of clinging—is mentioned;
those five aggregates of clinging are the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). Thus, two truths are taught. For what purpose are these two?
Because it was asked, "Were the truths taught?", the passage beginning with "To them, the Blessed One...

was stated. The meaning is that for the full understanding and the abandoning of those two truths, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma beginning with "By the unprotected," and he makes those two truths known by means of the teaching beginning with "By the unprotected."
Since it must be asked, "Of which of those two truths does he teach for full understanding, and of which for abandoning?
it is said: "For the full understanding of suffering, and for the abandoning of its origin. Since it must be stated, "Which truths are taught by means of full understanding and abandoning?
it is said: "And by which... and so forth. [It refers to] that path of arahantship by which one fully understands...
That which is abandoned by means of the path to arahantship—this path to arahantship is called the truth of the path.
That state of Nibbāna, with reference to which the abandoning of craving and ignorance has occurred—this state of Nibbāna is cessation, and it is called the truth of cessation.
Thus were the four truths taught by the Blessed One.
Because it must be stated, "By whom is the state of having taught the four truths to be understood?", the words beginning with "Therefore he said" were spoken.
Among those four truths, gratification (*assāda*) is grasped by the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*); danger (*ādīnava*) is grasped by the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*);

and escape (*nissaraṇa*) is grasped by the truths of the path (*maggasacca*) and cessation (*nirodhasacca*). Through the abandoning of the origin, there is the relinquishing of all destinations (*sabbagati*).
The phrase "the abandoning of all destinations has arisen" is taken to mean the fruit.
That by which the abandoning of all destinations has arisen—namely, the guardedness of mind and so forth—is taken as the means.

And the instruction of the Blessed One, which consists in the directing toward guardedness of mind and so forth by way of prohibiting unguardedness of mind and so forth, is taken as the injunction; thus it is understood through the method of teaching in various Suttas.
The gratification and so forth that have been shown have been extracted and presented within a single sutta beginning with the words "by one who is unprotected.
Since it might be asked, "By what means is the fact that the gratification and so forth have been extracted and shown to be known or believed?

the passage beginning with "Therefore he said" was stated. And here, by means of this particular method of commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanāvisesa*), the gratification and so forth have been extracted and shown across various suttas.
That specific method of commentary is called the "Analysis of the Nutriments of Teaching" (*desanāhāravibhaṅga*).

That specific method of commentary by which the gratification and other [characteristics] are extracted and demonstrated within a single sutta is to be understood as the "Convergence of the Nutriments of Teaching" (*desanāhārasampāta*).
Because it must be said that "this much alone constitutes the complete convergence of the nutriments of teaching," it is stated: "The convergence of the nutriments of teaching is concluded."

It has been stated. In each individual sutta, the gratification and so forth have been extracted and shown as appropriate through various specific modes of commentary consisting of a sequence of teaching-materials;

the meaning understood here is that those respective specific modes of commentary consisting of a sequence of teaching-materials must be applied by extracting them appropriately according to their respective contexts.
Thus concludes the *Vibhāvanā*, composed in accordance with the strength of one's faculties during the course of the exposition.
It should be mastered by the wise... [as follows]... and grasped.
2. Analysis of the Convergence of the Mode of Investigation (Vicaya-hāra-sampāta-vibhāvanā) 53.
That convergence of the mode of teaching by which the teacher has analyzed the gratification and so forth, and which we have understood—that convergence of the mode of teaching is complete.
Since it must be asked, "What is the convergence of the mode of investigation?", [the text] begins with: "In this regard, what is the convergence of the mode of investigation? and so forth.

It has been stated. Therein—referring to those sixteen modes of conveying the teaching (hārasampāta) such as the mode of conveying the teaching, the mode of conveying the nutriment, and so forth—he asks: "Which specific method of commentary is called the 'mode of conveying investigation' (vicayahārasampāta)?

Having determined that "among these phenomena, that specific method of commentary by which this phenomenon is to be investigated is called the 'mode of conveying investigation'," he proceeds to analyze it, saying: "Therein..."
“Craving,” and so forth, has been stated. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), it says:
“Having thus shown the sequence of the mode of teaching (*desanāhāra*), he now shows the sequence of the mode of analysis (*vicayahāra*).

Since the mode of analysis consists in the investigation of the meaning of the terms in the mode of teaching, therefore, by way of investigating the classification of craving—such as its wholesome and other qualities—as determined in the mode of teaching through its status as a cause for perversion (*vipallāsa*)...”
It is said: "In order to show the application of the mode of investigation (*vicaya-hāra*), the passage beginning with ‘Therein, craving is twofold’ is commenced.

Regarding that, the phrase "therein" (*tattha*) refers to those unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) described by the application of the mode of teaching (*desanā-hāra*) in the Sutta beginning with "With an unguarded mind," wherein "craving" (*taṇhā*) is determined as all craving. "Wholesome too" (*kusalāpi*) refers to [craving] belonging to the four planes.
Craving that arises directed toward wholesome states is also [included]. "Unwholesome" means craving that arises directed toward unwholesome phenomena;
thus it should be analyzed as being twofold. Therefore, it is said in the *Ṭīkā*:

"‘Having wholesome phenomena as their object’ is said with reference to the mere fact of arising directed toward wholesome phenomena, not because they serve as an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) here; for ‘wholesome’..."
Because the term "dhammas" is intended to include supramundane dhammas as well.
Alternatively, because it was asked, "Where does wholesome craving lead? Where does unwholesome craving lead?", it was stated that "unwholesome [craving] leads to saṃsāra," and so forth.
Or else, because it was asked, "What is the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome craving?", it was stated that "unwholesome [craving] leads to saṃsāra," and so forth.
It has been said: "Let craving be that which leads to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra); how can it lead to diminution?
Because this must be addressed, it is called "craving for abandonment" (*pahānataṇhā*). The meaning is: craving that serves as the cause for abandonment is "craving for abandonment.

It is said that one goes to diminution by means of that abandonment which is to be practiced in dependence upon the craving that is to be abandoned; that is, by means of the abandonment to be practiced.
Since it must be asked, "Is craving alone twofold—wholesome and unwholesome—or is there something else that is also twofold—wholesome and unwholesome?
it was said, "Pride also," and so forth. Since it must be asked, "Which pride is wholesome? Which pride is unwholesome? it was said:
"That pride by relying upon which one abandons pride is wholesome; however, that pride which produces suffering [is unwholesome]."
"This conceit is unwholesome" is what was said. In that context, regarding the statement "which conceit... is wholesome":
by relying upon and depending upon which conceit the abandonment [of other conceits] is set in motion, one abandons through that abandonment the conceit capable of arising within the continuum;

this conceit, being a condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*), is called "wholesome" by way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*) for its result. However, regarding the statement "but which... is unwholesome": as for the conceit that, by way of harming others and so forth, [is unwholesome].
Having arisen, it produces suffering for both oneself and others; thus, after investigating it, this conceit (māna) should be understood as unwholesome (akusala).
This is because one must ask: "Among those cravings (taṇhā) that lead to the diminution of saṃsāra, which craving leads to diminution and is wholesome?"
In order to show the specific nature of that craving which was referred to as "wholesome" (*kusala*), it is said: "Therein, that which is based on renunciation," and so forth.
"Therein" (*tattha*) means among those wholesome and unwholesome states consisting of craving that lead to the diminution of *saṃsāra*. The connection is: "This craving is wholesome.
"The noble persons, having realized and attained the peaceful sphere, which is the state of the fruit of the noble ones..."
As that noble son, aspiring, "When shall I dwell having realized for myself that sphere which is the Dhamma of the Noble Fruits?
conceives a longing for those Noble Fruits, the mental distress that arises conditioned by that longing is called "based on renunciation. This [distress] regarding the Noble Fruits—
It should be investigated that craving, known as *pihā* (delight), is wholesome and blameless because it proceeds with reference to the blameless dhamma of the Noble Fruit (*ariyaphala*).
Since it must be stated how it proceeds, the words "fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāgā*) and so forth are spoken.

That craving which proceeds by resorting to that liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) which is to be attained through the fading away of lust is wholesome and blameless; likewise, that which [proceeds] through the fading away of ignorance (*avijjāvirāgā*)...

Liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) is to be attained. Having come to that liberation by wisdom, one must investigate that craving which proceeds with it as its object, [realizing] that it is wholesome and blameless.
By way of that liberation by wisdom, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, the range of right intention..."
“With right view as his foremost priority, having understood arising and passing away, the bhikkhu who has overcome sloth and torpor shall abandon all miserable destinies.
In this verse, the phrase “shall abandon all miserable destinies” is stated; [it refers to] the investigation pertaining to that liberation through wisdom (*paññāvimutti*).
Since it must be asked, "What is that investigation?", the passage beginning with "What is its investigation? was stated.

If one should ask, "What is the investigation of that liberation by wisdom?", the investigation is: "The eight factors of the path—right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
It is to be understood. Because it must be asked, "Where is that investigation to be seen?", the passage beginning with "Where is that? is stated.

He asks: "In what phenomenon (dhamma) is that investigation of liberation through wisdom (paññāvimutti) to be seen? It is to be seen in the fourth jhāna, when the perfection has reached its peak through the cultivation of the fourth jhāna.
In order to explain the meaning stated in the phrase “in the perfection of the fourth jhāna,” it is said: “For in the fourth jhāna,” and so forth.

That person who has attained the fourth jhāna possesses a mind endowed with eight factors in the fourth jhāna: utterly pure, luminous, stainless, free from secondary defilements, pliant, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability.
He cultivates it; that person who has attained the fourth jhāna achieves the eightfold knowledge-and-conduct (*vijjācaraṇa*) therein.
What is the eightfold? The construction is: "He achieves the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and two special qualities.

The five beginning with the modes of psychic power (*iddhividhā*) are the mundane direct knowledges, and together with the wisdom of the path of arahantship, these constitute the six direct knowledges. [The sixth is] mind-made psychic power (*manomayiddhi*).
Thus there are two distinctions: [the fourth jhāna] itself and insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).

Because it must be asked, "From what is that fourth-jhāna consciousness purified... from what has it reached imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*)?", it is said, "That consciousness is purified from which," and so forth. That consciousness is [purified] from the state of purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi*).

It is purified; because of the state of purity of equanimity and mindfulness, it is bright. Because of the absence of blemish due to the destruction of the conditions for pleasure and so forth, it is unblemished;
because of that state of being free from passion and other blemishes, it is free from defilements.
Because of the state of being well-developed, it is malleable; because of that state of being well-developed, it is wieldy. Because of [the state of] being purified and so forth...

It is "steadfast" (*ṭhita*) because of its state of stability; therefore, the construction "it has reached imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*) because of its state of stability among the purified states and so forth" is also appropriate, as it is handed down in pairs in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

It has reached imperturbability because it is embraced by the radiance of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. For a mind embraced by faith does not waver (*iñjati*) toward its opposite, lack of faith.
It moves: the mind embraced by energy does not waver in the presence of its opposite, laziness;
the mind embraced by mindfulness does not waver in the presence of its opposite, negligence; the mind embraced by concentration does not waver in the presence of its opposite, agitation;
the mind embraced by wisdom does not waver in the presence of its opposite, ignorance; it has become luminous.
The mind does not waver in the darkness of the defilements. Thus, the fourth jhāna consciousness, when embraced by these six factors, has reached imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*).

Because it is thus endowed with eight factors, the fourth jhāna consciousness is the means for attaining the six kinds of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), as well as the knowledge of the mind-made body (*manomaya-iddhi*) and the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*);
therefore, that cultivation of liberation through wisdom occurs in the fourth jhāna.

“It should indeed be seen” is the summary meaning. As for the detailed explanation, it has already been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* either by way of the passage beginning “therein, by virtue of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness,” or by way of the passage beginning “another method”; therefore, we have not stated it here.

[It refers to] that which is “without blemish” (*anaṅgaṇa*) due to the absence of those stains (*aṅgaṇa*) such as lust, and which is [free from defilement] due to the absence of those secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*) such as covetousness.

Because it must be asked, "By which side do those stains (aṅgaṇa) and defilements (upakkilesa)—such as lust and so forth—belong [to this mind] which is free from defilement, which stands by virtue of the absence of any state that would cause the mind to stand [unsteadily], and which has reached imperturbability (āneñja) by virtue of the absence of agitation? it is said: "In that regard, the stains... and so on.

"In that regard" (tattha) means: among those stains and defilements such as lust; "stains" (aṅgaṇa) refers to the stains of lust and so forth, and "defilements" (upakkilesa) refers to the defilements of covetousness and so forth.
And there are these two: the pair consisting of the stains such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth, and the secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*) such as covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and so forth.
These belong to the side of craving (*taṇhā*), because the stains such as lust have the nature of craving, and because the secondary defilements such as covetousness are in conformity with craving.

Whatever agitation (*iñjanā*) and trembling (*phandanā*) there is, and whatever non-stillness and instability of the mind there is—this agitation and instability belong to the side of views (*diṭṭhi*).
And an investigation should be made as follows:

"Is it because of its being endowed with eight factors that the fourth jhāna consciousness is the means for attaining the six kinds of direct knowledge (abhiññā), namely, the knowledge of supernormal power (iddhi) consisting of mind-made bodies and the knowledge of insight (vipassanā)?
Since this question must be asked, [the text states] "the four faculties."
It is said: “For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, four faculties—the faculty of pain, the faculty of grief, the faculty of pleasure, and the faculty of joy—cease in that fourth jhāna.

For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the faculty of equanimity remains; therefore, the consciousness of the fourth jhāna [is associated] with the eight [mental factors] of the aforementioned kind.”
[The opponent might argue: "Knowledge is the means for attainment, and that status of being a means for attainment would belong only to one who has attained mastery (*ciṇṇavasī*);
how then could one who has merely attained the fourth jhāna possess mastery? To this it must be said:
That attainer of the fourth jhāna does not remain in the fourth jhāna alone, but likewise produces and develops the formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*) by doing so; therefore—
In order to show that he has attained mastery (*vasībhāva*), it is said: "He [emerges] from the higher attainment," and so forth.
The meaning of this has been explained in detail in the *Aṭṭhakathā*; therefore, we shall provide only a brief summary.
That practitioner who has attained the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) emerges from the attainment of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere and [enters] the higher...
He attends to the attainment of the base of infinite space as more peaceful than [the previous state].
As he attends to the aforementioned higher attainment as more peaceful, for that practitioner who has attained the fourth jhāna,
the perception within the fourth jhāna— being dominated by perception— becomes established as if it were gross, and the perception of resistance becomes weariness.
Having become dissatisfied, he remains firm; and the practitioner of yoga, attending to it by the method already described,
through the complete and total surmounting of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity,
attends to "space is infinite" and attains the meditative absorption of the base of infinite space as it proceeds.

Having realized it and attained it, he dwells therein. Perception of form (*rūpasaññā*)—that is, perception pertaining to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*)—is the launching point for the fivefold direct knowledge (*pañcavidha-abhiññā*).
Perception of diversity (*nānattasaññā*) occurs as an unwholesome differentiation among various objects.
Thus, seeing the danger in the fine-material-sphere jhānas, that meditator transcends those perceptions of form and perceptions of diversity regarding the object. For that practitioner:

And the perception of resistance passes away. Thus, for the practitioner who is concentrated by means of this aforementioned method of transcendence, and who is concentrated by means of the peaceful conduct of formless-sphere absorption, the radiance—the radiance of the fine-material-sphere jhānas—disappears.
The construction is that the seeing of forms—that is, the forms of the kasiṇas—by means of the eye of jhāna also disappears.

Because it must be asked, "With how many factors is that concentration endowed by which, for one who is concentrated, the radiance and the seeing of forms disappear, and how is that concentration to be reviewed?",
the passage beginning with "That concentration" was stated. "That concentration" refers to that fine-material and immaterial-sphere concentration by which one has become concentrated.

Both kinds of concentration should be repeatedly reviewed, contemplated, and observed as being endowed with six factors: three accessory factors consisting of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and the arousal of energy;
two requisites consisting of tranquility and mindfulness; and one essential factor consisting of non-distraction. How and where should this be reviewed?
