Because it was necessary to ask [this question], it was said: "My mind is not accompanied by covetousness toward the whole world," and so forth.

Because it was necessary to ask, "Of those six factors, how much is serenity (samatha) and how much is insight (vipassanā)?", it was said, beginning with "Therein, that which... in order to analyze: "This much is serenity; this much is insight."

54. Regarding what was called “liberation by wisdom,” the preliminary practice consisting of serenity and insight for that concentration of the fruit of arahantship was explained by the Teacher by way of concentration.
Since it must be asked, “By how much is the concentration of the fruit of arahantship to be understood as obtainable through that practice? [the answer is: “That concentration is fivefold.”

It is said, "it should be understood. That concentration of the fruit of arahantship which is to be obtained through the practice of serenity and insight—that concentration of the fruit of arahantship is to be understood by means of fivefold knowledge and vision.
Since it must be stated, "How does the fivefold knowledge and vision become manifest?", [the text says] "This concentration," and so forth.
It has been said. This concentration of the fruit of arahantship is pleasant in the present because of the bliss of the attainment of the fruit at every moment it is entered;
thus, for that arahant who reflects upon it, a personal knowledge and vision becomes manifest.
This concentration of the fruit of arahantship is [the basis] for the concentration of the fruit of arahantship to be attained in the future.
Because it is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), it has a pleasant ripening in the future; for one who reflects thus... [as before] ...it comes to be.

This concentration of the fruit of Arhatship is "noble" (*ariya*) because it is far removed (*āraka*) from the enemies that are the defilements, and it is "free from worldly bait" (*nirāmisa*) due to the absence of the bait of sensual pleasures, the bait of existence, and the bait of the world; for one who reflects thus... [as before] ...it comes to be. This is the concentration of the fruit of Arhatship.
Because it is practiced by those who are not base persons—namely, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddhas—it is "practiced by the noble.

When he reviews this... [and so on] ...it occurs. This concentration of the fruit of Arahatship is both peaceful because of the pacification of the fever of the defilements that are its constituent parts, and sublime because it brings no satiety even to one who enters it during the day; it is further characterized by the subsiding of the defilements.

It is "attained through subsiding" because it is obtained by a person who is an Arahant; it is "attained through unification" because it is reached by means of one-pointedness known as the concentration of the path of Arahantship;
it is "attained with effort and application" because it is reached by exerting oneself against opposing states such as the hindrances;
and it is "attained by warding off other defilements" because it is reached after having restrained other corruptions.
Because it proceeds precisely as the state of the path and fruit of arahantship, it has reached the stage of being restrained by the suppression of formations;
thus, for this Arahant who reviews [this], knowledge and vision become established within himself.
Therefore, that concentration of the fruit of arahantship should be understood as having been investigated by means of fivefold knowledge and vision.
Because it must be asked, "In the concentrations consisting of present happiness and so forth, how much is serenity (samatha) and how much is insight (vipassanā)?", it was said:

"Therein, that concentration which is pleasant in the present," and so on. By "serenity" and "insight," only the serenity and insight of the fruit of Arahantship are intended, not the serenity and insight of the preliminary stage.
The concentration of the fruit of Arahantship should be understood as fivefold.

Because it must be asked by the teacher, “To what extent should the concentration spoken of in the preliminary practice for the attainment of the fruit of arahantship be understood? it is said: “That concentration is to be understood in five ways.
That which was spoken of as the fourth-jhāna concentration of the fine-material sphere in the preliminary practice—that is the fourth-jhāna concentration of the fine-material sphere.
It should be understood in five ways. Since it was asked, "By which [five]? the passage beginning with "the pervasion by rapture" (pītipharaṇatā) was stated.
In the first and second jhānas, wisdom is the pervasion by rapture. In the first, second, and third jhānas, wisdom is the pervasion by bliss.
In the fourth jhāna, the wisdom of the knowledge of others' minds is the pervasion by mind. The wisdom of the divine eye...
There is the pervasion by light. The wisdom occurring after reflecting upon the jhāna is the sign of reflection.
Thus, it should be understood as having been investigated by way of these five modes of wisdom.

Because it must be asked, "Among those five modes, how much is serenity (samatha) and how much is insight (vipassanā)?", it was said: "In that regard, that which is the pervasion by rapture," and so forth.
55. Concentration has been analyzed by the Teacher according to its association, and this is understood by us.
Since it must be asked, "How is it analyzed according to its object?", the passage beginning with "the ten kasiṇa bases" was stated.
Concentration should be understood by investigating it through these ten kasiṇa objects. [One might ask: "Among those ten, how much is serenity (samatha) and how much is insight (vipassanā)?"
Because it is something that ought to be asked, the passage beginning with “And therein, whatever... was stated.

The term *kasiṇa* refers to the *kasiṇa*-disk, the preliminary work (*parikamma*), the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*), and the jhāna arisen in regard to that counterpart sign; however, here only the jhāna together with its associated mental factors is intended.
[One might ask: “But is only the kind of concentration already described to be joined with serenity and insight, or should something else also be joined?”

In order to show that the entire Noble Path—divided into numerous categories by way of its preliminary stages such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth—should also be investigated and applied, it was said, "Thus all... and so on. Therein, "thus" means according to the method stated by me;
following that method, "all" refers to the entirety without exception, divided into numerous categories by way of its preliminary stages such as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.

The Noble Path should be applied. How? By whichever aspect of non-covetousness and so forth, or by whichever aspect of present happiness and so forth, concentration has been described by me, by that very aspect of non-covetousness and so forth, or that very aspect of present happiness and so forth, whichever Noble Path is possible to be joined with serenity—that Noble Path should be investigated by means of serenity.
It should be joined. The meaning to be understood is that whichever noble path is possible to join with insight (vipassanā), each such noble path should be joined with insight again and again.
"Those bases of serenity (samatha) and states of insight (vipassanā-dhamma) by which it should be joined... [and so forth].
Since it was asked, "By which phenomena are they comprised?", it was stated: "They are comprised by three phenomena:
by impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Those phenomena of insight based on serenity are comprised by the three modes of contemplation:
"by the wisdom of impermanence, by the wisdom of suffering, and by the wisdom of non-self."

The meaning is "to grasp. Because it occurs in association with impermanence and the other [characteristics], the wisdom of contemplation (*anupassanā-paññā*) is also called "impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

Since it must be asked, "What does that yogin, that person who is cultivating insight based on serenity (*samatha*), cultivate?", it was said: "That person, while cultivating serenity and insight," and so forth. A person cultivating serenity, insight, and so on, is of three types:
one whose temperament is dominated by lust (*rāga-carita*), one whose temperament is dominated by hatred (*dosa-carita*), and one whose temperament is dominated by delusion (*moha-carita*).
“In this regard, which person is led out by which gate of liberation;
training in what and in what; abandoning what and what; not approaching what and what;
fully understanding what and what; casting off what and what; shaking off what and what?”

Because it must be asked, "Blowing out what, what? Uprooting what, what? Unraveling what, what does it lead away?"—the passage beginning with "a person of lustful temperament" (rāgacarito puggalo) was stated. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it says:
"Now, for which persons, training in which [teachings], are there specifically the gateways to deliverance (niyyānamukhāni), and which defilements (kilesā) do they serve as the antidotes to?"
It is said that the three doors to liberation were mentioned [in the preceding text] in order to show those [three aggregates] together with them;
the meaning of this has also been stated in the Aṭṭhakathā itself.
Since it might be asked, "Why does one who develops the three doors to liberation develop the three aggregates?", it is said: "In that regard..."
"The door to liberation that is emptiness," and so forth, is said. "Therein" means among those three doors to liberation.

The door to liberation that is emptiness is the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha), because it has the predominance of wisdom through the contemplation of non-self (anattā). The door to liberation that is the signless (animitta) is the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), because it has the predominance of concentration through the contemplation of impermanence (anicca).
The door to liberation that is the desireless (appaṇihita) is the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), because of the contemplation of suffering (dukkha).

Because of the predominance of virtue (*sīla*). Thus, because the three aggregates (*khandha*) are comprised within the three gateways to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*), it is stated in the Commentary that when that practitioner-yogi develops the three gateways to liberation, he is indeed developing the three aggregates;

this is the state of having wisdom (*paññā*) as the predominant factor. Developing the three aggregates, he develops the Noble Eightfold Path (*ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga*). [Question: "Why does he develop it?"
In order to show the reason why this must be stated, it was said, “Therein, that which...,” and so forth.

While the nature of the three aggregates as the Noble Eightfold Path has been analyzed and understood by us, since it remains to be asked, “How is their nature as serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) to be known?”—it was said [further] to show the nature of the three aggregates as serenity and insight: “Therein...”

And so it was said: “The aggregate of virtue,” and so forth. Since it must be asked, “For that yogic person who develops serenity and insight, which of the factors of existence (bhavaṅga) do they proceed toward through that development?”—therefore it was said: “For him who develops serenity and insight,” and so forth.
Both body and mind are two factors of existence for the existence at rebirth (upapatti-bhava).
They proceed toward cultivation and increase. Both virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*)—these two factors, these two feet—are the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;
they proceed toward cultivation and increase.
Because it must be explained how they proceed, the passage beginning with "He is a bhikkhu" was stated. "One who has cultivated the body" means one whose body has been cultivated.
The body refers to bodily conduct or bodily restraint by which a bhikkhu is one whose body is developed.

This same method applies to the others as well. When the body, or bodily conduct, or bodily restraint is being developed, two factors—right action and right effort—come to be cultivated, because they consist in virtue regarding bodily conduct. Or, [they are included] under virtue by way of verbal restraint and livelihood restraint.
When virtue is being cultivated as it occurs, two factors—right speech and right livelihood—attain cultivation because they consist of the virtue of restraint in speech and so forth.

When the mind is being cultivated as it occurs through the restraint of the mind, two factors—right mindfulness and right concentration—attain cultivation because they consist of the virtue of restraint of the mind. [Likewise,] when wisdom is being cultivated...
Right view and right intention are two factors that proceed toward development because they are equal and mutually supportive.
For as one repeatedly intends with right intention, wisdom increases. [The question arises:
"Right action and right effort—these two factors—are to be analyzed and understood as being distinguished solely by way of the body?"
Or rather, because it was asked, "Are they to be analyzed and investigated by way of the mind? the following was stated:
"In that regard, whatever is right action," and so forth. That which is right action consisting of volition for good bodily conduct, and whatever right effort is associated with it, may be bodily;
and that which is right action consisting of abstinence, and whatever right effort is associated with it, may be mental.
Therein, among those factors consisting of the bodily and mental [aggregates],
that right action and right effort which are comprised within the body— when right action and right effort are developed in the body,

in bodily conduct, or in bodily restraint, they come to fulfillment through development. That right action and right effort which are comprised within the mind— [that right action and right effort...]
The construction is: when the restraint of the mind has been cultivated within the mind, it reaches its full development (*bhāvanā*).

Because it must be investigated as to "how much attainment does that yogi person reach while cultivating serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*)?", the passage beginning with "he, cultivating serenity and insight...
was stated. This is in order to show the fivefold attainment of the Noble Path (*ariya-magga*).
“Quick attainment,” and so forth, has been stated. Its meaning is analyzed in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Since it must be asked, “By what means does which attainment occur?,” it was stated, “Therein, by means of serenity (*samatha*),” and so forth. 56.
The meaning of the sutta beginning with “With an unguarded mind,” etc., was explained by the Teacher by way of the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship for those to be trained.
This has been investigated and analyzed, and it is known by us that, because it must be asked, "How are the ten powers of the Teacher who possesses the ten powers to be investigated?
it was said: "In this regard, he who teaches is one endowed with the ten powers," and so forth.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—
Thus, the Great Elder, by means of the verse beginning “Therefore,

for one whose mind is guarded,” demonstrated the application of the method of investigation (*vicayahāra*) through the gateway of liberation consisting of the fruit of Arahantship; and, owing to his skill in teaching,

having shown the method of investigation in its various modes by way of analyzing the specific stages of development and the benefits of development for that preliminary practice through numerous scriptural passages, he [proceeded].
"Now, in order to demonstrate that [the Teacher's excellence] by way of the ten powers of a Tathāgata as well, it was said: 'In that regard, he who teaches...
and so forth. Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) means among those who are being trained and those who train, while they are developing serenity and insight.
The Teacher, the instructor endowed with the ten powers, teaches the Dhamma beginning with "with an unguarded mind," and does not deceive his disciples through his exhortation.
The construction is: "The ten powers of that Teacher, the Desika, are to be investigated.
Because it must be asked, "In what manner does he teach?", it is said, "He is threefold," and so forth.
Among those ten powers of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of what is possible and impossible is called the first power of a Tathāgata; [the question arises: "How is that power to be investigated?"
Because it was to be asked, it was said: “Thus exhorted,” and so forth. The meaning has been stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and is also clear from the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Knowing that “this possibility does not exist” is called the knowledge of the impossible (*aṭṭhānañāṇa*); knowing that “this possibility exists” is called the knowledge of the possible (*ṭhānañāṇa*).
Thus, the first power of the Tathāgata, which is the knowledge that discerns what is possible and what is impossible, should be investigated.
The underlying intention must be understood.
(1) 57. The first Tathāgata-power, the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa*), has been investigated and analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us;
[now we consider] how the second Tathāgata-power, the knowledge of the way leading everywhere (*sabbatthagāminipaṭipadāñāṇa*), is to be investigated.
Because it is to be inquired into, it is called "the state of what is possible and what is impossible.

The knowledge that discerns the path leading everywhere—namely, the knowledge that "this practice leads to this state of existence" and "this practice leads to that state of existence"—is called the knowledge of the path leading everywhere (*sabbatthagāminipaṭipadāñāṇa*).
The intention is that this second power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the path leading everywhere, should be investigated. (2)
59. The second power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the way leading everywhere (*sabbatthagāminipaṭipadāñāṇa*), has been investigated by the Teacher and understood by us.

Because it must be asked, "How is the third power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the various elements and their diversity (*anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇa*), to be investigated?", the passage beginning with "Thus, the way leading everywhere... was stated. "This is an element and this is an element... [and so forth].

“Furthermore, that which is called ‘the manifold element’—this element and that element are called ‘diverse elements. Thus, the knowledge that knows the manifold and diverse elements is called the “knowledge of the manifold and diverse elements.
This knowledge of the manifold and diverse elements, the third power of a Tathāgata, should be investigated. (3) 60.
The third power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the manifold and diverse elements, has been investigated and analyzed by the Teacher.
And because it was asked by us, "How is the fourth power of a Tathāgata—
the knowledge of the various inclinations of beings— to be investigated?", the passage beginning with "Thus, of this world with its many elements and its manifold elements" was spoken.
The knowledge that knows the inclinations of beings— [knowing] "these beings are inclined thus, these beings are inclined thus"— is [the knowledge of the diversity of elements].
"The knowledge of the diversity of inclinations of beings" means that the fourth power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations of beings, must be investigated.
(4) The fourth power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations of beings, has been analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us;
however, because it must be asked, "How is the fifth power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the diversity of the ripening of kamma, to be investigated? [the following is stated].
Thus it was said: “And according to their inclinations,” and so forth. The knowledge that discerns the diversity of results—such as, “For beings who are thus inclined, this karma is dark;

this is the result of that dark karma; this karma is bright; this is the result of that bright karma”—is called the knowledge of the diversity of results (*vipākavemattatāñāṇa*). This is the knowledge of the diversity of results.
"The fifth power of a Tathāgata is to be investigated. 62.
The knowledge of the diversity of karmic results (*vipākavemattatāñāṇa*), the fifth power of a Tathāgata, has been investigated by the Teacher and is understood by us. [Now we consider:

"How is the sixth power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence regarding the meditative absorptions (*jhāna-saṃkilesa-vodāna-vuṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*), to be investigated?"
Because they are to be questioned, it is said: “Thus, for those who have undertaken [the practices] in such a way,” and so forth.
“For actions, jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments undertaken in this manner, this is the defilement, this is the cleansing, this is the emergence;
thus they are defiled, thus they are cleansed, thus they emerge”—[this refers to] the defilement, cleansing, and emergence of the jhānas.
Unobstructed knowledge is called "knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence of the jhānas.
Thus, the sixth Tathāgata-power, which is the knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence of the jhānas, should be investigated. (5) 63.
The sixth Tathāgata-power, the knowledge of the defilement of the jhānas, has been investigated by the Teacher; [how so? "How...?"
Because it must be asked, "The seventh power of the Tathāgata, the knowledge of the diversity in the faculties of others, should be investigated," it is said:

"Thus, of that very concentration... and so forth. Along with the knowledge that "the faculties are thus in the sense of predominance" and "the powers are thus in the sense of unshakability," [he knows]:
"This one has dull faculties, this one has medium faculties, this one has sharp faculties."

The knowledge that knows the dullness, mediocrity, and superiority of the faculties, powers, and so forth of other beings and other persons is called the "knowledge of the differentiation of the degrees of others' faculties.
Thus, the seventh power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the differentiation of the degrees of others' faculties, should be investigated. (6)
64. The seventh power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of others (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*), has been analyzed by the Teacher.
Because it must be asked, "How is the eighth power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), to be analyzed?
How is the ninth power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*), to be analyzed?", [the text] begins with "In this regard, that which is of many kinds... and so forth.

It has been said: "The knowledge that knows, without remainder, various past lives—characterized by their specific modes such as 'one birth' and so forth, or by their details such as 'of such a name' and so forth, including the experience of names, clans, complexions, food, pleasure, and pain, and their limits—is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa).
Thus, the eighth [knowledge] is the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
"The power of a Tathāgata is to be investigated.

(7) The knowledge that knows, without exception, the passing away and rebirth of beings—whether they are passing away or being reborn, inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly, in a happy state or a miserable state, according to their respective kamma—is called the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*). This is the ninth [power].
“The power of a Tathāgata is to be investigated.
(8–9) The eighth and ninth powers of a Tathāgata, beginning with the recollection of past lives, have been investigated and analyzed by the Teacher.
Because it must be asked, “How is the tenth power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the destruction of all taints (*āsrava*), to be investigated? it is said therein: “Thus, in that regard...”
The passage beginning with "yaṃ... has been stated. At the foot of the Bodhi tree, the knowledge that strikes down the Māra of defilement (*saṃkilesamāra*) arose;

this knowledge that strikes down the Māra of defilement is called the knowledge of the destruction of all taints (*sabbāsavakkhayañāṇa*). Thus, the tenth Tathāgata-power, the knowledge of the destruction of all taints, should be investigated—this is the summary meaning.
However, in detail, according to both the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is clear even to those who are like young elephants.
Thinking that [it] might be [otherwise], it was not shown.
Because it must be said, "This much is the complete arrival at the Mode of Conveying Investigation," it is stated: "The Mode of Conveying Investigation is concluded.
Whatever meanings of the various passages of the Sutta have been stated, those very meanings of the passages of the Sutta [are established] by whichever specific method of commentary...
It should be investigated by means of the application of the method of investigation (*vicayahārasampāta*).

The meaning to be grasped is that this application of the method of investigation—which consists of various specific commentaries—has been set forth; it must be extracted as appropriate and applied accordingly.
Thus, the application of the method of investigation has been composed in accordance with the strength of one's faculties.
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Investigation is finished.
But by the wise... [as before] ...it should be grasped.
3. The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synthesis.

65. Whatever method of investigation the teacher has employed to investigate the meaning of the passage of the Sutta, and whatever we ourselves have understood, that method of investigation is complete. Because it must be asked, "What is the method of reasoning (*yuttihāra*)?", it is said:
"In this regard, what is the method of reasoning? and so forth. In the Commentary, however: "Thus, by various methods..."

Having expanded upon the application of the mode of investigation (*vicaya-hāra*), it is said that [the following] was begun in order to show the application of the mode of reasoning (*yutti-hāra*) and the others: “In this regard, what is the application of the mode of reasoning? and so forth. “In this regard” (*tattha*) means:

among those sixteen applications of the modes, beginning with the application of the mode of teaching (*desanā-hāra*), he asks which specific exposition is called the application of the mode of reasoning; having asked, [he proceeds].
In order to extract that passage from the Sutta where the logical consistency of the points stated therein should be investigated:
"Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, whose range is right intention,
who is intent upon right view, and who has understood arising and passing away..."
“A bhikkhu overcome by sloth and torpor would abandon all miserable destinies.

Thus it was said. In that verse, because one whose mind is unprotected follows the sway of Māra, a bhikkhu should have a protected mind by means of the restraint of mindfulness, the restraint of the sense faculties, and so forth;
therefore, because one whose range of activity consists of wrong intentions such as sensual thoughts follows the sway of Māra...
A bhikkhu should have the domain of right intention by way of the intention of renunciation and so forth;
therefore, because one whose mind is struck by wrong view follows the power of Māra, a bhikkhu, having understood rise and fall through careful attention, should have right view as his primary aim;
therefore, because one whose mind is struck by sloth and torpor follows the power of Māra, a bhikkhu [should act] by way of energy.
One should understand that the meaning is: “May he be one overcome by sloth and torpor; such a bhikkhu shall abandon all miserable destinies—he will abandon them.
Since it was asked, “How should the logical consistency of this verse be examined? the passage beginning with “Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded” was stated.
The meaning—that for one whose mind is guarded, there will be the range of right intention—is indeed logical; it is not otherwise.

This is logical. It is logical that by abandoning even wrong intentions (*micchā-saṅkappa*), one who dwells with right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) as the foremost will penetrate arising and passing away (*udaya-vaya*), because the contemplation of arising and passing away is possible for one who has right view as the foremost.
It is logical that one who penetrates arising and passing away will abandon all miserable destinies (*duggati*), following the sequence of the contemplation of arising and passing away.

Because it arises from the Noble Path; because he abandons all miserable destinies, it is appropriate to say that he will transcend all fears of miserable destinies and states of ruin, since all such fears of miserable destinies and states of ruin no longer arise.
Since it must be said that "this much is the complete application of the method of reasoning," it concludes: "The application of the method of reasoning is concluded."

It has been stated: "By whichever specific method of exposition (*saṃvaṇṇanāvisesa*) consisting of the 'method of reasoning' (*yuttihārasampāta*), the logical consistency of the meaning of the various passages of the Sutta must be investigated—that specific method of exposition consisting of the method of reasoning must be applied after having determined it appropriately for each case;
this is the sense that should be grasped."
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā*, composed according to one's own strength and ability at the junction of the *Yuttihāra* section.
However, it should be mastered by the wise... [and so forth]... as follows.
4. Analysis of the Conveying of the Basis (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra-sampāta-vibhāvanā) 66.

Whatever conveyance of the method (yutti-hāra-sampāta) by which the Master has analyzed the reasoned nature of the meaning of the passage from the Sutta, and which we too have understood—that conveyance of the method is complete.
Because it must be asked: "What is the conveyance of the basis? [the following analysis is undertaken].
Therein, he asks: "What is the 'source of the method' (padaṭṭhāna-hārasampāta)?
Having asked this, in order to extract that specific portion of the sutta in which the bases of the method have been set forth, it is said:
"Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, the range of right intention... This is the verse. The meaning of the verse is as follows:
It has already been stated. Since it must be asked, "Which verses are the footing for which phenomena?", the passage beginning with "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded" was spoken.

The state of guarding the doors of the sense faculties—which constitutes the meaning of the scriptural passage "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded"—is called the "footing" for the three types of good conduct, because it is the proximate cause for the fulfillment of good conduct.

“Having right intention as one’s range”: the right intentions, such as the intention of renunciation, which constitute the meaning of this passage from the Sutta, are called the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of serenity (*samatha*), because they are the immediate conditions for the suppression of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) such as sensual desire.

“Having right view as one’s foremost concern”: the right view of being the owner of one’s kamma and the right view that sees name-and-form together with their conditions, which constitute the meaning of this passage from the Sutta, [are the proximate cause of insight].
And it is called the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for insight (*vipassanā*) because it is the specific condition for the contemplation of impermanence and the other [contemplations].

The wisdom consisting in the contemplation of rise and fall, which constitutes the meaning of the scriptural passage, “Having known rise and fall,” is called the proximate cause for the plane of seeing, because it is the immediate condition for the attainment of the first path.
[This applies to] the scriptural passage, “The bhikkhu who has overcome sloth and torpor... [and so forth].
The overcoming of sloth and torpor is called the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for energy because it is its immediate condition.

The cultivation of the Noble Path is called the proximate cause for the cultivation of abandoning that which is to be abandoned— the meaning of the scriptural passage “one should abandon all miserable destinies”— because the completion of the cultivation of the Noble Path occurs through the abandoning of what is to be abandoned.
Because it must be said that "the sequence of the modes of conveying meaning (hārasampāta) consisting of the footing (padaṭṭhāna) is thus complete," it is stated:

"The sequence of the modes of conveying meaning consisting of the footing is concluded. Whatever specific mode of commentary, consisting of the sequence of the modes of conveying meaning as the footing, has extracted the footings—the meanings of the sections of the Sutta—that specific mode of commentary consisting of the sequence of the modes of conveying meaning as the footing is concluded.
The meaning to be understood is that one should apply oneself after having determined [the application] as appropriate.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Exposition), composed according to the strength of one’s faculties, within the *Padatthāna-hāra-sampāta* (The Convergence of the Modes of Conveying the Footings).
"But by the wise... [it] should be grasped.
5. The Analysis of the Convergence of the Modes of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāra). 67.

Whatever modes of conveying the basis (padaṭṭhāna) have been determined by the teacher through the convergence of the modes of conveying the basis for the meanings of various sections of the Sutta, [those should be understood].
These have been understood by us, and that "mode of conveying the basis" (*padaṭṭhāna-hāra*) is complete.
Because it must be asked, "What is the mode of conveying characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*)?", it is said: "In this context, what is the mode of conveying characteristics? and so forth.

Therein, among those sixteen modes of conveying—beginning with the mode of conveying the teaching (*desanā-hāra*)—he asks: "Which specific method of commentary is called the mode of conveying characteristics?"
Because it must be asked, "By which meanings of the Suttas do which phenomena (dhammas) of identical characteristic [of the mind] become included?", the passage beginning with "Therefore" is stated.
By this phrase from the Sutta, "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, the range of right intention," this guarding is understood as the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya).
When the faculty of mindfulness is included, the five faculties beginning with faith (saddhā) are thereby included.
Because they have the same characteristic in the sense of being faculties (*indriya*). By the scriptural passage “having right view as its precursor,” right view is included;
when right view is included, the Noble Eightfold Path is thereby included.
He asks for the reason with the words “For what reason? Having asked, he states the reason with the words beginning “Because of right view. That is, because of the cause that is right view.
Since right intention arises from that, therefore; since right speech arises from right intention, therefore;
since right action arises from right speech, therefore; since right livelihood arises from right action, therefore;
since right effort arises from right livelihood, therefore; [since right mindfulness arises] from right effort, therefore...
Since right concentration arises from right mindfulness, since right liberation arises from right concentration,
since the knowledge and vision of right liberation arises from right liberation,
and since the Noble Eightfold Path is thereby encompassed; therefore, it is so stated.
Because it must be said that "the application of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra-sampāta) is thus complete," it is stated: "The Mode of Conveying Characteristics is concluded.

That specific application of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics, which constitutes a particular method of exposition, by which the meanings of various portions of the Sutta are grasped through their common characteristics—that specific application of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics is what is meant.
The meaning taken here is that "being applied" means having been extracted according to what is appropriate, it should then be joined [to the subject].
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Exposition), composed in accordance with the strength of one's faculties upon the convergence of the Modes of Conveying (*hāra*) and the Characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
"But by the wise... [as before] ... it should be grasped. 6.
Analysis of the Convergence of the Fourfold Array Method (Catubyūhahāra). 68.
By whichever convergence of the characteristic method (*lakkhaṇahāra*) the meanings of the passages of the Sutta are grasped through a common characteristic, that—
The *lakkhaṇa-hāra-sampāta* (the convergence of the mode of characteristic) has been completed.
Because it must be asked, "What is the convergence of the fourfold array (*catubyūha-hāra-sampāta*)?", the text says, "In this context, what is the convergence of the fourfold array? and so forth.
Therein, among those sixteen convergences of modes beginning with the convergence of the mode of teaching, he asks which specific method of commentary is called the convergence of the fourfold array.

Because it must be asked, "In which sutta are which etymologies, intentions, causes, and connections between preceding and following passages determined?", the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmā*) was stated.

Regarding the phrase "of one whose mind is guarded" (*rakkhitacittassa*) in that portion of the sutta, he shows the etymology (*nirutti*)—namely, that "guarded" (*rakkhita*) means "that which is protected"—by means of the synonym "it is thoroughly preserved. Because the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with," [it implies] "he thinks" (*cinteti*).
It is called *citta* because it accumulates its own continuum; it is called *citta* because it is built up by conditions; it is called *citta* in the sense of being variegated (*vicitta*);
it is called *citta* in the sense of making thoughts (*cittakaraṇa*). One whose mind is guarded is "one of guarded mind" (*rakkhitacitto*).
One who intends rightly is "right intention" (*sammāsaṅkappo*). A place where cattle graze is a "pasture" (*gocaro*); like a pasture, it is a "pasture" (*gocaro*). Right intention is the pasture.
"Assa" means having right intention as one's range. "Sammā passati" means right view; "sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāro" means having right view as one's primary concern.
"Jānāti" means having known. "Udayo ca vayo ca" is "udayabbaya" (arising and passing away).
"Thinamiddhaṃ" is sloth and torpor; "abhibhū" means one who overcomes; thus, "thinamiddhābhibhū" means one who has overcome sloth and torpor. "Bhikkhati" means he begs.
The term "bhikkhus" has also been derived through etymological analysis (*nirukti*). Therefore, it was said: "The word *iti* has the sense of 'beginning'.
This aforementioned mode of designation is what is called "etymological analysis" (*nirukti*).
If one were to ask: "What is the Blessed One’s intention here in this passage of the Sutta? [the answer is: those who are true persons [are freed] from all miserable destinies (*duggati*).
The intention is this: those who desire to be fully liberated will become true persons (sappurisa) who practice in accordance with the Dhamma and possess guarded minds.
Here, the intention of the Blessed One is to be drawn out from the passage in the Sutta beginning with, "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded.
If one should ask, "What is the causal occasion (nidāna)? [the answer is]: Kokālika, having failed to guard his mind toward the two elders, Sāriputta and Moggallāna...
Because he was reborn in the Mahāpaduma hell after having harbored ill will, and because the Blessed One, being endowed with the protection of mindfulness,
abandons all states of woe, therefore a virtuous bhikkhu who wishes to abandon all states of woe should have a guarded mind;
thus the introductory context should be drawn out.

If one should ask, "What is the connection between what precedes and what follows?"—the statement in the Sutta, "The mind should be guarded by mindfulness," being the preceding word, this passage from the Sutta, "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded... [etc.
...may he abandon all miserable destinies," connects with and accords with it; thus, the connection between what precedes and what follows must be determined.
Because it must be said that "this much alone constitutes the complete arrival at the fourfold method of exposition," it is stated:

"The fourfold method of exposition is concluded. That specific mode of exposition, consisting of the fourfold method of exposition by which etymology, intention, cause, and the sequence of what precedes and follows are to be determined, is each such specific mode of exposition concluded as appropriate.
The meaning is that, having extracted [the essential], one should apply oneself;
this is the sense to be grasped. Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Elucidation), composed according to the strength of one's faculties, upon the convergence of the fourfold modes of conveyance.
"But by the wise... [it] should be grasped.
7. Exposition of the Convergence of the Modes of Conversion. 69.

By whichever convergence of the fourfold mode of conversion the etymological derivation (*nirukti*), intention (*adhippāya*), source (*nidāna*), and the sequence of what precedes and follows (*pubbāparānusandhi*) are analyzed, [that is the convergence].
Since the application of the fourfold method (*catubyūha-hāra*) has been completed, and because it must be asked, "What is the application of the turning method (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*)?", it is said:
"In this regard, what is the application of the turning method? and so forth. Therein, he asks: "What is the specific excellence of the commentary called the application of the turning method?

Since it must be asked, "Which meanings of the Sutta are to be turned, and how are they to be turned?", it is said: "Therefore," and so forth. [He is one] who abounds in right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*), which consists of the intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
By means of the kasiṇas and so forth, and by means of loving-kindness and so forth— which abound in right intention characterized as non-harming—
one who establishes the mind in the one-pointedness of mind thus attained is said to have "a guarded mind" because it is protected from defilement.

When "a guarded mind" has been stated in this way by the phrase, "Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, the range is right intention," that one-pointedness which must be directed toward [the object] is [implied].

This one-pointedness is serenity (*samatha*). When it is said, "having right view as the foremost," the wisdom that must be turned toward that which has right view as its priority is this wisdom of insight (*vipassanā*).

When it is said, "having known arising and passing away," the full understanding of suffering that must be turned toward that which is endowed with the knowledge of arising and passing away is this full understanding of suffering.

The full understanding of suffering (*dukkhapariññā*). By the phrase “a monk who has overcome sloth and torpor,” the overcoming of sloth and torpor spoken of with reference to a person is the abandoning of the origin (*samudayappahāna*).

By the phrase “he shall rightly abandon all miserable destinies,” the non-arising (*anuppāda*) spoken of as the abandonment of all miserable destinies is this cessation (*nirodha*). Thus, through the full understanding of suffering...
The truth of suffering, which is to be fully understood, is to be turned toward; the truth of the origin, which is to be abandoned through the abandoning of the origin, is to be turned toward;
the truth of cessation, which is to be realized through cessation, is to be turned toward;
and the truth of the path, which is to be developed through serenity and insight, is to be turned toward—thus these four truths are to be turned toward.
Because it must be said that "the application of the method of turning (āvaṭṭa-hārasampāta) is thus complete," it is stated: "The application of the method of turning is concluded.

The meaning to be understood is this: whichever specific mode of commentary consisting of the application of the method of turning—such as *samatha* and so forth—is by means of which the subjects are to be turned, each such specific mode of commentary consisting of the application of the method of turning is "concluded"; having determined them as appropriate, they are to be applied accordingly.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā*, composed according to one’s own strength and ability upon the arrival of the method of turning back (*āvaṭṭahāra*).
It should, however, be mastered by the wise... [as follows].
8. Analysis of the Convergence of the Mode of Conveying Analysis (Vibhattihārasampātavibhāvanā) 70.

Whatever convergence of the mode of conveying turning-back (āvaṭṭahārasampāta) by which the meanings of the Sutta are to be turned back, that convergence of the mode of conveying turning-back is complete.

Because it must be asked, "What is the convergence of the mode of conveying analysis?", [the text begins] with: "In this regard, what is the convergence of the mode of conveying analysis? and so forth.
It has been stated. Therein, he asks: "What is this specific distinction in the commentary called the 'Method of Analysis' (*vibhattihārasampāta*)?
Because it must be asked, "Which meanings of the Suttas are analyzed where?", the passage beginning with "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded...
is stated. In that verse which was spoken—namely, "Therefore... [the range of] the domain"—the wholesome factor (*dhamma*) is stated therein.

The phenomenon of restraint through mindfulness should be demonstrated and analyzed by way of the wholesome side of phenomena, and it should be demonstrated and analyzed by way of the unwholesome side of phenomena. How so?
The wholesome side of the phenomenon of restraint through mindfulness, expressed by the phrase “of one whose mind is guarded,” consists of “restraint at the eye-door,” and so forth.
“Restraint of the mind-door” is to be demonstrated and analyzed by way of the sixfold wholesome category of phenomena.

The wholesome category of phenomena called “right intention,” expressed by that term, is to be analyzed by way of the threefold wholesome category of phenomena: “the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty.”

The categories of wholesome phenomena described by the phrase “having right view as the foremost” are: knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering,
knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the past limit, knowledge of the future limit,
knowledge of both the past and future limits, and knowledge regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.
“Knowledge” (*ñāṇa*) should be analyzed by way of the eightfold wholesome side of the Dhamma.

The knowledge of the rise and fall of the wholesome side, expressed by the phrase “having known the rise and fall,” that class of Dhamma should be analyzed by way of the fiftyfold knowledge of rise and fall on the wholesome side.
The overcoming of sloth and torpor, expressed by the phrase “overcoming sloth and torpor,” [should be analyzed].

The class of wholesome phenomena (*kusalapakkha*) should be analyzed by way of the fourfold division of the wholesome side as: "the overcoming of the stream-entry path, the overcoming of the once-returning path, the overcoming of the non-returning path, and the overcoming of the arahant path.
Wholesome restraint of mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*) is twofold: "mundane restraint of mindfulness" and "supramundane restraint of mindfulness."

"It should be analyzed" means: mundane restraint of mindfulness, which belongs to the sense-sphere, should be analyzed as being of one kind. Supramundane restraint of mindfulness should be analyzed as being of two kinds:
"the plane of seeing" and "the plane of development. Sense-sphere restraint of mindfulness should be analyzed as:

"restraint of mindfulness through contemplation of the body, restraint of mindfulness through contemplation of feelings, restraint of mindfulness through contemplation of the mind, and restraint of mindfulness through contemplation of phenomena."
It is to be analyzed in four ways. The supramundane restraint of mindfulness is likewise to be analyzed in four ways.
Right intention and right view are also to be analyzed according to the mundane and supramundane distinction, and so forth, by way of their twofold classification and others.
They are also to be analyzed by way of their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), according to the method stated in the "Conveying of Proximate Causes" (*Padaṭṭhānahāra*).
Non-restraint, expressed by the phrase "with an unguarded mind" under the side of the unwholesome, is to be analyzed as eightfold: "non-restraint of the eye...
[and so on] ... non-restraint of the body, non-restraint of the physical body, non-restraint of speech, and non-restraint of the mind.
Wrong intention, included by the phrase "struck by wrong view," consists of "thought of sensual desire, thought of ill will, and thought of cruelty."

It is to be analyzed in three ways. The wrong view expressed by the term "wrong view" is to be analyzed in eight ways—as "ignorance regarding suffering," and so forth, up to "ignorance regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions"—and it is also to be analyzed in sixty-two ways as the sixty-two types of views.
Sloth and torpor are to be analyzed in five ways according to the method of being prompted (sasaṅkhārika).
Because it must be said that "the application of the method of analysis (vibhatti-hāra-sampāta) is thus complete," it is stated: "The application of the method of analysis is concluded.

Having determined each instance as appropriate, one should understand that whichever specific mode of commentary—by means of which application of the method of analysis—the meaning of the sections of the Sutta was analyzed, that specific mode of commentary, being an application of the method of analysis, is "concluded" (niyutta).
The meaning is that it should be applied;
it should be grasped. Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā*, composed according to the strength of one's faculties upon the convergence of the methods of analysis.
"But it should be grasped by the wise... [etc.
9. Exposition of the Convergence of the Modes of Analysis (Vibhattihārasampāta): 71.
By whichever convergence of the modes of analysis a portion of the meaning of the Sutta has been analyzed, that is the convergence of the modes of analysis.

Because it was necessary to ask, "What is the sequence of the mode of conveying by way of reversal? [the text] states, "In this regard, what is the sequence of the mode of conveying by way of reversal? and so forth.
Because it was necessary to ask, "Which portions of the Sutta's meaning are to be reversed, and how? [the text] states, "Therefore," and so forth.

Regarding the verse stated as “Therefore… [is] the range,” the serenity and insight that have been determined by that verse—when that serenity and insight have been developed—their fruit and purpose is the cessation of unwholesome states. One should reflect:
“Suffering has been fully understood, its origin has been abandoned, and the path has been developed. This is by way of the counter-agent.
However, it should be reversed as follows: "Because serenity and insight have not been developed, there is no cessation of unwholesome states;
suffering is not fully understood; the origin has not been abandoned; and the path has not been developed.
Since it must be stated that "this much constitutes the complete set of the modes of the reversal method," it is said: "The set of the reversal method is concluded."

It has been stated: "The meaning should be understood as follows: whichever specific method of commentary, consisting of the application of the mode of 'reversal' (*parivattana-hāra*), is required to reverse the meaning of the passage from the Sutta, that specific method of commentary consisting of the application of the mode of reversal must be applied by extracting it appropriately.
This is the sense to be grasped.
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā*, composed according to the strength of one’s own faculties upon the arrival of the method of the "turning-back" (*parivattana-hāra*).
It should, however, be mastered by the wise... [as follows]... and grasped.
10. Analysis of the Convergence of the Mode of Synonyms (Vevacanahārasampātavibhāvanā) 72.
That convergence of the mode of synonyms by which the meanings of various passages of the Sutta are to be exchanged is complete as the "mode of exchange.
Since it must be asked, "Which is the convergence of the mode of synonyms?", [the text continues]: "In this regard, which..."
The passage beginning with “the synonym is the convergence of the strands” has been stated.
Since it must be asked, “Of which portions of the Sutta’s meaning, or of which words of the Sutta, are these synonyms?

the passage beginning with “Therefore” has been stated. Regarding the verse that was spoken, namely, “Therefore... the range,” by means of that verse [the phrase] “of one whose mind is guarded” [is explained].
Regarding the word *citta* spoken [in the phrase] "of one whose mind is guarded" (*rakkhitacittassa*), the statement "mind... [etc.

...the state of being cognizant" (*vijānitattam*) which is spoken here is a synonym for that word *citta*; furthermore, terms such as "mental faculty" (*mānasa*) and "heart" (*hadaya*) are also synonyms for *citta*.
Regarding the phrase "having right intention as its range" (*sammāsaṅkappagocaro*), "right intention" (*sammāsaṅkappa*) refers to the intention of renunciation (*nekkhammasaṅkappo*).
Regarding the statement, "the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-cruelty," this is a synonym.
Furthermore, the expression "reasoning, applied thought," and so forth, is also a synonym for right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*).
In the phrase "having right view as one's foremost," the term "right view" refers to the sword of wisdom, the blade of wisdom, and the jewel of wisdom.
Regarding the statement, “Wisdom is a goad, wisdom is a palace,” this statement is a synonym;
likewise, the statement beginning with “wisdom, understanding, investigation” is also a synonym for the term right view.
Regarding the statement: “Sloth is slothfulness, the state of being slothful, the mind’s lack of health, unwieldiness, obstruction, envelopment, and inward contraction.”
That which was stated—this statement is a synonym for *thina* (sloth).
That which was stated as “the body’s lack of fitness, unwieldiness, physical laziness, sleep, sleeping, and the state of being sleepy”—this statement is a synonym for *middha* (torpor).
That which was stated as “a mendicant, a monk,” and so forth—this statement is a synonym for the term *bhikkhu* (monk).
“‘An unhappy destination, a state of deprivation, a fallen state, the suffering of the round, and saṃsāra’—this statement that has been spoken is a synonym for the term ‘unhappy destination.
Thus, the synonyms have been brought forth.
Since it must be said, ‘The application of the method of synonyms is thus complete,’ it is concluded: ‘The application of the method of synonyms is finished.’”

It has been stated: "By whichever specific method of commentary, consisting of a collection of synonyms, the synonyms have been brought forth, that specific method of commentary consisting of a collection of synonyms is applied;
the meaning taken here is that it should be joined by bringing them forth as far as possible."
Thus ends the *Vibhāvanā* (Elucidation), composed according to one's own strength and ability upon the convergence of the method of Synonyms (*vevacanahāra*).
But by the wise... [as before] ...it should be grasped.
11. Analysis of the Convergence of the Mode of Conveying Descriptions (Paññattihārasampātavibhāvanā) 73.
By whichever convergence of the mode of conveying synonyms (vevacanahārasampāta) the synonyms have been determined, that convergence of the mode of conveying synonyms is complete.

Since it must be asked, "What is the convergence of the mode of conveying descriptions? the passage beginning with "In this context, what is the convergence of the mode of conveying descriptions? has been stated.
Because it must be asked, "What is the designation that constitutes a portion of the Suttas, and of which phenomena is it the designation?", the passage beginning with "Therefore" is stated.
"Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded": this is a designation by way of the foundation of mindfulness (*satipadaṭṭhāna*), because it designates the mind that is to be guarded;
thus it is called a "designation by way of the foundation of mindfulness. For the mind is to be guarded by means of mindfulness.
Mindfulness is called its proximate cause and its foundation. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary:
"The mind, being guarded by mindfulness which has established itself [as a foundation], becomes as if it were the foundation for that mindfulness.

"Having right intention as its range" is a designation for the development of serenity, because it is designated through the cultivation of serenity; thus, it is called the "designation of the development of serenity. "Having right view as its priority..."
"Having known arising and passing away" is called a "definition by way of presentation" because it presents the presentation of the stage of seeing through wisdom.
"The monk who has overcome sloth and torpor" is called a "definition of complete abandonment" because it presents the complete abandonment of the origin [of suffering].
"He should abandon all miserable destinies" is a definition because it presents the cultivation of the Noble Path, which is the path.

This is called the "description by way of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-paññatti*). Because it must be said that "the arrival at the method of description (*paññatti-hāra*) is thus complete," it is stated: "The arrival at the method of description is concluded.
By whichever specific method of description, which constitutes a particular mode of commentary, the various classifications of description [are established]...

The meaning should be understood as follows: having determined each respective category according to its fitness, it must be applied; that is, the inclusion within the method of exposition (*paññatti-hāra*), which constitutes a specific type of commentary, has been set forth, and it should be joined after being determined as appropriate.
Thus, this inclusion within the method of exposition has been composed in accordance with the strength of one's faculties.
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Penetration is finished.
However, it should be grasped by the wise... [as follows].
12. Analysis of the Convergence of the Modes of Entry.
74. By whichever method of the modes of presentation (*paññattihārasampāta*) the various classifications of presentation have been determined, that method of the modes of presentation is complete.
Because it must be asked, "Which is the method of the modes of entry (*otaraṇahārasampāta*)?", he said: "In this regard, which is the method of the modes of entry?
and so forth. "In this regard, having determined which faculties (*indriya*) in that verse, and by means of which determined phenomena..."
Because it must be asked, "Does he descend?", the passage beginning with "Therefore" is stated.
In that verse which was spoken, beginning with "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded," right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is included by way of the scriptural passage:
"...therefore... [and] priority. When right view is included, the five faculties—the five faculties beginning with faith—are thereby included.
Those same five faculties beginning with faith become "true knowledge" (vijjā) because they are either conducive to true knowledge or its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

From the arising of such true knowledge, through its arising as a cause, the cessation of ignorance (avijjā) occurs; from the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of volitional formations (saṅkhāra) occurs...
and so on... from the cessation of birth, the cessation of aging and death occurs. This is the entry point.
This is called the entry into the five faculties by means of dependent origination.
Those same five faculties are comprised within the three aggregates— the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom—
because virtue arises from faith and energy, and because mindfulness follows after wisdom.
This is the entry-point by way of the aggregates; it is called the entry-point of the five faculties.

Those same five faculties, when included within formations (*saṅkhāra*), become such that those formations which are without taints (*anāsava*) do not become factors of existence (*bhavaṅga*) or causes of existence;
those taintless formations are comprised within the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*).
Because it is included within the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*). This is the entry by way of the elements, known as the entry into the five faculties.

That taintless element of mental objects is comprised within the base of mental objects; whatever base is taintless does not become a constituent of existence (*bhava*) nor a cause for existence. This is the entry by way of the bases, known as the entry into the element of mental objects.
Because it must be said that "this much constitutes the complete set of modes of entry," it is stated: "The set of modes of entry is concluded."

It has been stated: "By whichever specific mode of commentary, as a particular method of introduction (*otaraṇa-hāra*), the meaning of the passages of the Sutta is to be introduced, that respective specific mode of commentary, as a particular method of introduction, having been determined as appropriate, should be applied; such is the meaning to be grasped.
Thus, this compendium of methods of introduction has been composed according to the strength of one's faculties.
The Investigation (vibhāvanā) is finished.
However, it should be understood by the wise...
[as follows]. From this point onward is the connecting meaning beginning with "In that regard, what is...", and at the conclusion is the connecting meaning beginning with "It is concluded."
And this should be understood according to the method already stated. In certain passages where the meaning is not manifest, we shall explain it to the best of our ability.
13. Analysis of the Convergence of the Modes of Purification (Sodhanahārasampātavibhāvanā) 75.
"Wherein" means in which question. The undertaking is the purpose; when that is pure and complete, that question is exhaustive.

It is answered. However, if in a question the undertaking, the purpose, or the purity is incomplete or imperfect, and there remains something yet to be answered, that question has not yet been answered.
15. The Analysis of the Occurrence of Requisites and Nutriment.
77. Regarding the phrase “therefore for one whose mind is guarded,” the restraint of mindfulness (satisaṃvara) that is spoken of is a requisite for serenity (samatha).
Regarding the phrase “having right intention as its range,” the right intention (sammāsaṅkappa) that is spoken of is a requisite for insight (vipassanā);
thus it should be applied after making this distinction.
16. Analysis of the Convergence of the Mode of Conveying Ascertainment (Samāropanahārasampātavibhāvanā) 78.
Regarding the phrase “therefore, for one whose mind is guarded,” that which is called “guarded mind” is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*).
When right view has been developed, the Noble Eightfold Path [is established].
The path is cultivated because it is to be cultivated on one side, and because it serves as the proximate cause. Therefore it was said:
"From right view," and so forth. That Arahant who possesses liberation through concentration is the person of the Arahant without residue;
this liberation through concentration is the element of Nibbāna without residue.

Regarding the statement, "By what means can we believe in this sixteenfold classification, by which the sequence of the 'modes of conveying' (hārasampāta)—beginning with the 'mode of conveying through exposition' (desanāhāra)—is established after having determined the meaning of the sections of the Sutta?"—in response to this, the words "Therefore he said...
and so forth were spoken. By that sixteenfold classification, the Venerable Mahākaccāna [stated] the passage: "Sixteen... pe ...sutta."
He said: "By that statement, you should have faith in its sixteenfold classification.
Because it must be said that 'the arrival at the modes of exposition (hāra) is thus complete,' it is stated: 'The arrival at the modes of exposition is concluded.
By whichever specific mode of exposition among the various types of commentary—the arrival at the modes of teaching—the meanings of the portions of the Sutta have been determined, that..."

The meaning should be understood as follows: that which constitutes a specific mode of commentary—the transition from the "nutriment of teaching" (*desanāhāra*) to the "nutriment of exposition" (*īhāhāra*)—is established;
having been extracted accordingly, it must be applied. And in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is likewise extracted and applied.
Thus, in the transition from the nutriment of teaching to the nutriment of exposition, according to the strength of one's faculties...
The exposition of the method of origin (*nayasamuṭṭhānavibhāvanā*) is completed.
However, the wise should grasp its profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
The Exposition of the Method of Origin.

79. By whichever specific mode of commentary—such as the convergence of the modes of teaching (*desanāhāra*) and so forth—one has analyzed and explained the meaning of a portion of a single sutta by extracting it, that specific mode of commentary consisting of the convergence of the modes of teaching and so forth is complete.
Because it must be asked, "What is the arising of the methods (*nayasamuṭṭhāna*)?", [the text begins] with: "In this regard, what is the arising of the methods? and so forth.

It has begun. However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Having thus demonstrated the investigation of the *hāras* by way of various suttas and by way of a single sutta, [the text] now begins with ‘In this regard, what is the origination of the methods (*naya*)? in order to demonstrate the investigation of the *nayās*.
Why is it that, instead of beginning with ‘In this regard, what is the *nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*?’, the text begins with ‘In this regard, what is the origination of the methods? and so forth?"
The reason for this has already been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Regarding the phrase "in each case" (*tattha tattha*):

among those methods such as the *hāras* and so forth, whatever method of meaning (*atthanaya*) has been demonstrated by means of the method of commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanānaya*), he asks for the source-ground (*samuṭṭhāna-bhūmi*) of that very method of meaning, asking, "What is the source of the method?
Although [the meanings] have been demonstrated by the method of commentary, nevertheless, the distinction between the method of meaning and the method of commentary is made clear.

We shall explain it further. The specific method of commentary characterized by the guidance of the meaning of the Sutta belonging to the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*) through the application of the Four Truths by means of craving and ignorance,

as well as the specific method of commentary characterized by the guidance of the meaning of the Sutta belonging to the side of purification (*vodānapakkha*) through the application of the Four Truths by means of serenity and insight,
is called the "Method of the Conversion of Relishing" (*nandiyāvaṭṭo nayo*).
The specific mode of commentary characterized by the guidance of the meaning of the Sutta concerning the side of defilement through the three unwholesome roots—

greed and so forth— by way of its connection with the Four Noble Truths, as well as the specific mode of commentary characterized by the guidance of the meaning of the Sutta concerning the side of purification through the three wholesome roots—
non-greed and so forth— by way of its connection with the Four Noble Truths, is the "Three-Forked" (Tipukkhalo).

"Method" (naya) means: a specific mode of commentary characterized by the application of the four truths to the meaning of the entire mass of defilements (*saṃkilesa-pakkha*) through the four perversions (*vipallāsa*),

such as the perception of beauty, etc., and likewise [characterized] by the application of the four truths to the meaning of the side of purification (*vodāna-pakkha*) through the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) free from perversion, such as the perception of foulness, etc., or through the faculties of faith (*saddhindriya*).

The specific method of commentary characterized by the "eye" (nayanalakkhaṇa) is called the "Lion’s Play" (sīhavikkīḷita) method; thus, these methods are known as "methods of commentary" (saṃvaṇṇanānaya).
He asks regarding the origin of those methods of commentary: "What is the origin of the methods?
For the methods [arise] from the application of the Four Truths through the root-terms such as craving (taṇhā), ignorance (avijjā), and so forth, which have been extracted from various Suttas.
The meaning of suffering and so forth is being fully understood. For that [meaning] leads and brings one to attainment by means of path-knowledge;
thus it is called a "method" (*naya*). This is what is known as the method of meaning (*atthanaya*). He asks about the origin of that very method of meaning: "What is the origin of the method?

Therefore, it is a method because, through the grasping of the method by way of application to the Four Truths, one is led and questioned. What is it? It is that which consists in the meaning of the discourses (*sutta*).

The meaning is suffering and so forth. Or, it is called a "method" (*naya*) because it leads (*nayati*) and brings about path-knowledge; thus, the meaning is suffering and so forth. Therefore he said: "The meaning of suffering and so forth is being awakened to.
For that which leads and brings about path-knowledge is the method. It is called the "source" (*samuṭṭhāna*) because methods arise from it; what is that?
It is the cause consisting of ignorance, craving, and so forth, as well as the commentary that illuminates it.

For the methods of meaning, such as suffering and so forth, arise through ignorance, craving, and the rest. Alternatively, the "origination" (*samuṭṭhāna*) refers to the application of the Four Noble Truths by means of ignorance, craving, and so on.
Thus it was said: "What, then, is that? It is the application of the Four Noble Truths by means of their respective root-terms.
When the meaning is grasped in this way, the methods of exposition (*saṃvaṇṇanā-naya*) are also included; the "origination of methods" (*nayasamuṭṭhāna*) is the source from which the methods arise.
Regarding that "arising from the method" (*nayasamuṭṭhāna*):

since it must be asked, "What is the arising from the 'turning of delight' method? (*nandiyāvaṭṭanayasamuṭṭhāna*), the passage beginning with "The prior limit is not discerned" was stated in order to first show the arising from the "turning of delight" method. Of that which constitutes the arising from the "turning of delight" method...

The construction is as follows: because there is no beginning, it is not known whether the prior limit of ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*) arose at the time of the appearance of such-and-such a Buddha, the Blessed One, or at the time of the appearance of such-and-such a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
Since it must be asked, "Between ignorance and craving, which is the hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*) and which is the fetter (*saṃyojana*)?", [the text continues]: "In that regard, ignorance..."
It is said: "The hindrance is craving; it is a fetter. Therein—referring to those two, ignorance and craving—ignorance is a hindrance because it conceals danger.
Craving is a fetter because it binds one to states of existence. [As it is asked: "How do beings wander about hindered by ignorance?
How are they described? How do beings wander about fettered by craving? How are they described?"
Because they are to be questioned, it is said: "Beings are hindered by ignorance," and so forth. They are "hindered by ignorance" (avijjānīvaraṇā) because ignorance acts as a hindrance for them.
Beings proceed as if bound by ignorance; they proceed as if bound to the objects of adherence through ignorance.
They wander among objective bases such as form, which have become bases for adherence to permanence and so forth, due to the perversion belonging to the side of ignorance.
Various beings move about and proceed, wandering while adhering to [views] such as permanence;
they are called "those of speculative temperament" (*diṭṭhicarita*). Those for whom the fetter of craving (*taṇhāsaṃyojana*) exists are "those with the fetter of craving" (*taṇhāsaṃyojana*).

Beings who proceed as if bound by craving, or who proceed as if bound to the objects of sense-pleasure (*vatthukāma*) which have become the objective supports (*ārammaṇa*) of craving, are—by way of craving—[characterized] by the eight hundred types of craving-conduct (*taṇhāvicarita*).
The meaning is that they wander and proceed within the objective basis (vatthu) which has become their cognitive object (ārammaṇa).
Because it must be asked, "What kind of practice do beings of speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita) dwell devoted to?

What kind of practice do beings of craving-temperament (taṇhācarita) dwell devoted to?", the passage beginning with "beings of speculative temperament" was stated. Beings of speculative temperament...

Even though they have gone forth outside this teaching, they dwell devoted to the practice of self-mortification—such as the discipline of the five fires and so on—while reflecting: "There is no happiness to be attained through ease; rather, there is happiness to be attained through suffering.
Likewise, beings of craving-temperament who have gone forth outside this teaching [reflect]: "In sensual pleasures..."

“By enjoying [these things] and increasing the world, they increase much merit”—thus reflecting, those of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) dwell devoted to the practice of devotion to the pleasure of sense desires (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*).
Why do those of speculative temperament dwell devoted to such a practice? And why do those of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*)...
Because it was necessary to ask, "They dwell devoted to such a practice," the passage beginning with "What is the reason for that?

was stated. "Therein" (*tattha*) means among those [persons] characterized by views (*diṭṭhicarita*) and craving (*taṇhācarita*). He asks what the reason is—that is, for what cause they dwell—by saying, "For what reason" (*yaṃ...
kāraṇā*). Outside of this Dispensation (*sāsana*), for those persons there is no definitive establishment of the truths (*saccavavatthāna*).
There is no such thing; how could there be the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths? And how could there be skill in serenity and insight, or the attainment of the bliss of peace?
Those persons, being unacquainted with the bliss of peace and possessing perverted minds, have said:
"There is no bliss to be attained through bliss; there is indeed bliss to be attained through suffering."
Having such perceptions and such views, and yearning for happiness through suffering, they dwell devoted to the practice of self-mortification.
Outside of this teaching, for those individuals who lack the definition of the truths, how could there be any proclamation of the Four Noble Truths?
And how could there be skill in serenity and insight, or the attainment of the bliss of peace? Such are those individuals.
Lacking direct knowledge of the bliss of tranquility and having a perverted mind, they said: "He who indulges in sensual pleasures increases the world;
he who increases the world generates much merit. The construction should be understood as follows:
being thus percipient and thus viewing, they dwell devoted to the pursuit of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, having the perception of pleasure in sensual pleasures.
Because it must be asked, "What do they increase by dwelling in such a way?", it is said: "Those who are well-versed in that [method] increase only disease.
Because it must be asked, "By increasing in that way, do they increase the medicine for diseases and so forth, namely, serenity and insight?", it is said:
"Those pierced by disease, oppressed by abscesses, and transfixed by arrows [fall] among the denizens of hell, the animal realm, the hungry ghosts, and the asuras..."
It is said: "While performing plungings and emergings, and experiencing the rising and falling [of breath], they do not find the medicine for the mass of diseases, the boils, and the arrows.
However, the meaning is explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Since it must be asked, "Which are the defilements and purifications?
Which are the diseases and so forth? What is the medicine?", it was stated: "In that regard, devotion to self-mortification," and so on.
"In that regard" means among those things such as defilement and purification, disease and medicine. Devotion to self-mortification and devotion to sensual pleasures are defilement;
serenity and insight are purification. Devotion to self-mortification is a disease; serenity and insight are the medicine that destroys the disease.
… [and so on] … serenity and insight are the medicine for extracting the arrow.
Because it must be asked, "Which [truth] is which?", it is said: "In that context, defilement is suffering," and so forth.
"In that context" means among those factors beginning with defilement; defilement is, by way of its partial aspect, suffering, namely the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
"Attachment thereto" refers to the mundane dhamma that proceeds like attachment toward that defilement; this is the truth of suffering by way of its entirety.
Or else, craving—which occurs as if it were an attachment to that suffering—is the origin of suffering, the truth of the origin.
The cessation of craving is the cessation of suffering, the truth of cessation. Tranquility and insight are the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, the truth of the path.
Having thus determined these four truths, they should be applied. "Among those four..."
