Because it must be asked, "Among the truths, which is to be fully understood, which is to be abandoned, which is to be developed, and which is to be realized," it was stated:
"Suffering is to be fully understood," and so forth. 80.
For those whose temperament is dominated by views or by craving, the four truths are determined by way of the pursuit of self-mortification and so on.

Since it must be asked, "How are the four truths determined by way of the different modes of occurrence in the view of self-identity (*sakkāyadassana*) for those of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) and craving temperament (*taṇhācarita*)?", the passage beginning with "Therein, those of speculative temperament... was stated.

Alternatively, since it must be asked, "What is the difference in the mode of occurrence in the view of self-identity for those of speculative and craving temperaments?", [the text] states that this is the difference in the mode of occurrence in the view of self-identity for these two.
In order to show [this] by way of analysis, it was said: “Therein, those of speculative temperament,” and so forth. Therefore it was stated:

“Now, in order to show the difference in the mode of occurrence regarding the perception of a personal identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) for those of speculative temperament and those of craving-temperament, it was said: ‘Those of speculative temperament,’ etc. Therein means:
among those of speculative temperament and those of craving-temperament. Persons of speculative temperament approach form as “self,” as a self... and so on.
Those of a speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita), because their adherence to a self is powerful, approach consciousness as "self" and grasp it as self.
Those of a craving temperament (taṇhācarita), however, approach either form as "self," or a self possessing form, or form within the self;
or they approach the self as being in form... and so on, up to: or they approach the self as being in consciousness.
This is because those of craving-temperament possess a powerful adherence to the notion of "mine" regarding themselves.
Since this wrong view has twenty bases—being fourfold in relation to each of the five aggregates of clinging—it is called "personality-view" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
Thus, the meaning is that the different modes of activity in the perception of a personality should be understood for those of view-temperament and craving-temperament.
Because it must be asked, "What is the antidote to the view of a personal entity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)?", it is said, "The antidote to that," and so forth.
Supramundane right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is the antidote by way of abandoning that view of a personal entity;
and those phenomena that follow along with and function in accordance with that right view are also antidotes by way of abandoning the view of a personal entity.
[They] exist. Because it must be asked, "Which phenomena are the followers?
[the text] says, "Right intention," and so forth. Right intention... pe ...right concentration—these phenomena are the followers.
This Noble Eightfold Path, beginning with right view, is the antidote to that identity-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), because it is its abandoner. "Those [factors], right view and the rest..."
Because it must be asked, "How many aggregates (khandhas) do the phenomena (dhammas) consist of?", it is said: "Those are three aggregates," and so forth.

Because it must be asked, "Which aggregate is serenity (samatha), and which aggregate is insight (vipassanā)?", it is said: "The aggregate of virtue (sīla-khandha) and the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-khandha) are serenity;
the aggregate of wisdom (paññā-khandha) is insight. [And because it must be asked,] "Among the categories such as personality-view (sakkāya), which one is which truth?"...
Because it must be asked, "Which [truth] is which?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, personality-belief (sakkāya)" was stated.
Because it must be explained, "For those of speculative temperament and craving temperament, the four truths have been determined by way of their opposites to personality-belief;
how then were the two extremes and the middle way determined?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, those who [regard] form as self... was stated.

It has been stated. Regarding the phrase "therein": among those persons of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) and craving temperament (*taṇhācarita*), those persons of speculative temperament approach form as "self," and so forth...
they approach consciousness as "self. These persons of speculative temperament [hold that] "form and the rest are the self;
because form and the rest are impermanent, and because the self is also impermanent, the self is annihilated; the self..."
Because they adhere to the view that "the self perishes; there is no self after death," they are called "annihilationists.
Those individuals of craving-temperament who approach form as "self" or approach a self possessed of form...
[and so on] ...or approach consciousness as "self" or approach a self possessed of consciousness; or [they hold] consciousness in the self, or the self in consciousness.

They approach [them] as a self. These persons of craving-temperament (taṇhācarita), because of their dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) that "the self is other than form and so forth" or "the self is other, different, permanent, and eternal," are called "eternalists" (*sassatavādin*).
Among those persons—the annihilationists (*ucchedavādin*) and the eternalists—the doctrines of annihilationism and eternalism that operate therein are both extremes.
There are practices leading to the two extremes. This practice of the two extremes is the process of saṃsāra because it serves as the cause for the turning of saṃsāra.
The Noble Eightfold Path, known as the Middle Way, is the antidote to that practice of the two extremes, because it abandons them. This path is for the cessation of saṃsāra.
Through the state of causality, there is the turning away from saṃsāra. In that regard, concerning the occurrence and the cessation of saṃsāra:

"occurrence" refers to the occurrence of saṃsāra, which is suffering and the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); "clinging to that" means clinging to that suffering, which is craving, the origin and the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*);
the cessation of craving is the cessation of suffering, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and the Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
The path is the truth of the way; thus these four truths have been determined. The meaning is exactly as stated in the passage beginning with "Suffering is to be fully understood.
Since it must be asked, "How many divisions are there of annihilationism and eternalism, and how many for the path?", the passage beginning with "Therein, annihilationism and eternalism" was stated.
Therein, regarding annihilationism, eternalism, and the Noble Path, the view of annihilationism and eternalism is, in brief, by way of summary—
The view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) consists of twenty bases. Annihilationism is fivefold because it occurs in dependence upon the five aggregates of clinging;
the view of eternalism is fifteenfold because it arises in three ways regarding each aggregate. Thus, there are twenty types.

In detail, there are sixty-two positions of views (*diṭṭhigata*). Which are they? The four theories of eternalism, the four theories of partial eternalism, [the four theories of finite and infinite, the four theories of neither finite nor infinite, the two theories of chance-origination, the seventeen theories concerning the past, and the sixteen theories concerning the future].

The sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) should be understood as follows: four theories of finitude and infinity, four theories of evasive equivocation (*amarāvikkhepa*), two theories of fortuitous origination, sixteen theories of a self possessing perception (*saññīvāda*), eight theories of a self lacking perception (*asaññīvāda*), eight theories of a self with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*), seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), and five theories of Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*).
However, in detail, they are found in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
They have arrived. For those views of annihilationism and eternalism, the path that serves as their antidote consists of forty-three factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).
Which are the forty-three? "The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, and the perception of non-self"—these three perceptions;
and "the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation"—these three perceptions; thus, these six perceptions; and "the four foundations of mindfulness..."

The four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight path factors—these forty-three states conducive to enlightenment are called the "path as the antidote" by way of insight (*vipassanā*).
Since it must be stated, "What is the antidote by way of serenity (*samatha)?", the passage beginning with "the eight liberations" was spoken. Eight...
The liberations (vimokkha) are manifest. The ten bases of totality (kasiṇāyatana) are called the path that is the antidote by way of serenity (samatha).
Because it must be asked, "What knowledge is the shatterer of what phenomenon?", it is said: "The sixty-two types of views," and so forth.
The types of views that operate in one of a view-temperament (diṭṭhicarita) are delusion (moha); the types of views that operate in one of a craving-temperament (taṇhācarita) are...
The net (*jāla*). Delusion (*moha*) that proceeds from beginninglessness; the net that proceeds without end.

Having entered upon the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) and having blazed forth [the mind], there is the sharp knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the Noble Path (*ariya-magga-ñāṇa*), which is called the "diamond-knowledge" (*ñāṇavajira*) because it is the footing for the knowledge of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).
Delusion and the net are "delusion-net" (*mohajāla*). It "shatters" (*padāleti*), hence "shattering" (*padālana*); the suffix *yup* is used in the sense of the agent.

"Breaking the net of delusion" means the breaking of the net of delusion (*mohajālapadālana*). Breaking is twofold: breaking by suppression (*vikkhambhanapadālana*) and breaking by eradication (*samucchedapadālana*).
Breaking by suppression should be understood as occurring in the preliminary stage through serenity and insight; breaking by eradication should be understood as occurring at the moment of the Path.
"Therein" refers to that net of delusion; ignorance is delusion, and craving for existence is...
*Jālaṃ*. It is *moha* (delusion) because it deludes its own support, the individual, regarding the eight points such as suffering.

First, it is called *jāla* because, having caught hold of the *jaṭā* (tangle), it proceeds by way of that tangle; or it is *jāla* because it takes (*lāti*) or seizes the fish, birds, and so forth born within itself, or causes them to be taken or seized;
or it is *jāla* because it is like a net (*jāla*). Therefore it is said: "In those things divided into past and so forth..."
“Because it functions by way of binding together [beings] to form and so forth, as well as to one’s own personal existence and so forth, craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) is a net.

Since it must be asked, “How and by whom can it be believed that the selection of the defilement-side factors, such as devotion to self-mortification, has been made by means of ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*)?
it is therefore said: “The prior limit of ignorance is not known.”
and craving for existence. Thus it was said. 81.
Since it must be asked: “Outside this Dispensation, the methods and so forth for those of speculative temperament and craving temperament have been determined;
how then should the methods and so forth for those of speculative temperament and craving temperament within the Dispensation be determined?”—the following is stated: “The side of defilement...”
Because it must be stated, "How should the meaning of the suttas on the side of purification be shown by the teacher?", it was said:
"In this regard, one of speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita) [in this teaching]," and so forth. "In this regard" means among those of speculative temperament and craving temperament.
A person of speculative temperament, having gone forth in this teaching, maintains a conduct that is continuously refined regarding the four requisites.
It occurs. Why? Because he has intense reverence for effacement; therefore, it is due to his intense reverence for effacement.
A person of craving temperament, having gone forth in this teaching, becomes one whose conduct is continuous with the training. Why? Because he has intense reverence for the training;
therefore, it is due to his intense reverence for the training. A person of view temperament [enters] the fixed course of rightness...

Having entered the state of certainty, a person of speculative temperament becomes a follower by Dhamma. Why? Because their wisdom functions in a manner similar to that of right view regarding the objects of view.
A person of craving-temperament, having entered the state of certainty in the rightness [of the path], becomes a follower by faith.
Why? Because of their wrong resolution due to the influence of craving. A person of speculative temperament enters the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge...
And it leads out by way of the pleasant path with quick direct knowledge, because it is capable of suppressing the defilements with ease.
A person of craving-temperament leads out by way of the painful path with sluggish direct knowledge;
and it leads out by way of the painful path with quick direct knowledge, because it is capable of suppressing the defilements with difficulty.
Because it must be asked, “Why does he depart in that way? the passage beginning with “What is the reason for that? is stated.

He asks: “By what reason does he depart?”—that is, what is the cause? Since sensual pleasures are not abandoned with ease by one of craving-temperament, therefore, because sensual pleasures are not abandoned with ease, he departs in that manner.
Thus, one whose temperament is dominated by craving, when being secluded from sensual pleasures— both the objects of desire (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of desire (*kilesakāma*)—
withdraws with difficulty and understands the Dhamma, the Dhamma of the Four Truths, only slowly. However,
this person whose temperament is dominated by views is, from the very beginning, indifferent to sensual pleasures, both the defilements of desire and the objects of desire.

He exists as one whose temperament is dominated by views (*diṭṭhicarita*). When he is separated from those sensual pleasures, he quickly and easily relinquishes them and quickly understands the Dhamma.

"One whose temperament is dominated by craving (*taṇhācarita*) goes forth by means of a painful practice and slow direct knowledge; one whose temperament is dominated by views [goes forth] by means of a pleasant practice."
Because it must be said that "it leads out by means of swift direct knowledge," it is stated:
"The painful practice is twofold—both slow-direct-knowledge and swift-direct-knowledge; the pleasant practice is also twofold—both slow-direct-knowledge and swift-direct-knowledge.
[Objection: "If that were so, it would follow that a single [path] leads out by means of two distinct practices each."

Because it ought to be stated, the words “beings also” and so forth were spoken. The construction should be made as follows: beings of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*) are of two kinds—those with dull faculties (*mudindriya*) and those with sharp faculties (*tikkhindriya*);
beings of view-temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) are also of two kinds—those with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties.
Those who are of craving-temperament or view-temperament and possess dull faculties emerge from them slowly, and they [emerge] slowly...
They understand the Dhamma. Those who are of craving-temperament or view-temperament and possess sharp faculties quickly relinquish [their defilements] and quickly understand the Dhamma;
therefore, it is appropriate that for each [type of person] there is a single path.
"By means of these paths they indeed go forth; it would be a logical error to claim that 'they have gone forth' or 'they will go forth' using the present tense."
Because it must be stated that they have been demonstrated, the words "these four," and so forth, were spoken. The meaning should be understood as follows:
in the past, people went forth by means of these four ways; in the present, they are going forth; and in the future, they will go forth—just as one says, "the mountain stands."
"In this way"—that is, in the manner thus described—the noble persons (ariyapuggalā) prescribe the fourfold path as the method of practice.
Since it must be asked, "For what purpose do they prescribe it?", the phrase beginning with "cultivated by ignorant people" is stated. This is called the ground of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method;
it consists of the application of the Four Truths to the side of defilement through craving and ignorance, as well as [the application] to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
By way of this [method], the application of the Four Truths to both sides of the purification category has also been shown.
This fourfold application of the Four Truths is the ground for the arising of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, because it constitutes its source.

To the question, "By what can the fact that such an application of the Four Truths serves as the ground for the arising of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method be believed? it was said, "Therefore he said," and so forth.
82. “The ground that serves as the source for the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method has been shown; however, it must be stated:
‘In what [context], by which direction, and to what extent should that Nandiyāvaṭṭa method be examined? Because of this, the passage beginning with ‘In the Veyyākaraṇas’ was spoken.
The word ‘hi’ (for/indeed) has the sense of introducing an alternative point. Those phenomena such as nutriment and so forth, which constitute the directions, in the Veyyākaraṇas...”

It is said, “wholesome and unwholesome. Those phenomena, such as the nutriments, which have become the directions, are to be examined and scrutinized in two ways: “These are unwholesome phenomena, phenomena of defilement; these are wholesome phenomena, phenomena of purification.
Since it must be asked, “In what two ways? [the answer is: “Those that follow the worldly cycle (saṃsāra) and those that follow the turning away from the world (nibbāna).”
It was stated [thus]. Because it must be asked, "What is the round (vaṭṭa)? What is the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭa)?
it was stated: "The round is saṃsāra; the turning away from the round is Nibbāna. Because it must be asked, "What is the cause of saṃsāra? it was stated:
"Kamma and the defilements (kilesa) are the cause of saṃsāra. [If one asks], "What is called kamma? Is volition (cetanā) alone what is called kamma, or rather..."

Since it was necessary to ask, "What is the mental factor (cetasika), and what is the action (kamma) that is capable or incapable of yielding a fruit? the passage beginning with "In this context, kamma... was stated.
"In this context" means among those [factors of] kamma and defilements (kilesa). If one were to ask, "How, in what manner, should that kamma be regarded?
[the answer is: in whatever way, by whatever accumulation (upacaya), the performed kamma becomes capable of yielding a fruit, in that very accumulation...
That is how action is to be seen. If one should ask, "By which phenomena are those defilements to be demonstrated?", all defilements are to be demonstrated by means of the four perversions.
If one should ask, "Where are those defilements to be seen?", those defilements are to be seen in the ten-based mass of defilements.

If one should ask, "What are the ten bases?", it should be understood that the ten bases are: the four nutriments, the four perversions, the four clingings, the four yokes, the four ties, the four taints, the four floods, the four arrows, the four stations of consciousness, and the four ways of going to a bad destination. Of these four...

Because of their unity by way of function. And herein, even the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements themselves are the basis for defilements (*kilesavatthu*), because each preceding defilement serves as a condition for each subsequent defilement.
Since it must be asked, "Which [object] is the basis for which [defilement]?", the text says, "In the first nutriment," and so forth.
It has been said. Regarding the first object to be grasped, edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), the first perversion—“form is beautiful”—occurs by way of taking it as its object.
Regarding the second object to be grasped, contact-food (*phassāhāra*), the second perversion—“feeling conditioned by contact is pleasant”—occurs.
Regarding the third object to be grasped, mind-food (*cittāhāra*), the third perversion—“the mind is permanent”—occurs.
Regarding the fourth nutriment, mental volition (*manosañcetanā*), which is to be taken as an object, the perversion that "phenomena (*dhamma*) are self" occurs by way of making them its object.

Regarding the first [nutriment], form (*rūpa*), which is to be taken as an object, the perversion that "form is beautiful" occurs as the first clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) by way of making it its object.
In the remaining cases as well, the meaning should be understood by applying the method accordingly.
83. Since it must be stated, "Among those [nutriments, etc.], which one is the defilement for which person?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, whichever...
is spoken. "In that regard" means among those nutriments, etc., or among those of craving-temperament and view-temperament.
Because intense desire and lust arise toward form and feeling in one of craving-temperament, "whichever is the physical nutriment and whichever is the nutriment of contact" [is mentioned].
These, namely the food of edible morsels and the food of contact, are the defilements for a person of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*).
Because a strong adherence to the notion of self and permanence arises toward mental phenomena in one of view-temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*),
the food of mental volition and the food of consciousness that proceed are these two— the food of mental volition and the food of consciousness— for a person of view-temperament.

Thus there are secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*). In this regard, the meaning should be understood according to the method explained in the passage beginning with, "In that [context], one who perceives the beautiful in the ugly," and so forth.

This is because the first two pairs have craving (*taṇhā*) as their primary element and the nature of craving, while the latter two pairs have views (*diṭṭhi*) as their primary element and the nature of views.

84. Because it must be asked, "In which nutriment, beginning with the first, does which perversion, beginning with the first, occur?", [the text] determines it by name, starting with "Therein, in the case of physical nutriment," and shows the very same meaning as previously stated.
Because it must be asked, "Abiding in which perversion does one grasp what?", [the text states] "In the first perversion..."
“Established,” and so forth, has been stated. A person established in the first perversion (vipallāsa) grasps at sense pleasures by means of a particular clinging;

this clinging is called “clinging to sense pleasures” (*kāmupādāna*). The application [of the terms] to the remaining [perversions] should be made according to this same method. The application should be made as follows:

“That clinging to sense pleasures by which a person is bound to sense pleasures—this phenomenon of clinging to sense pleasures is called ‘the bond of sense pleasure’ (*kāmayoga*),” and so on. The meanings of the applications for the rest are clear from the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
85. Because it must be asked, "Among the nutriments and so forth, which is which direction?", it is said: "In this regard, these are the four directions," and so on.
Therein, among those ten tetrads beginning with the tetrad of nutriment, each first [tetrad] beginning with physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) is the first direction;
each second [tetrad] beginning with contact-nutriment (*phassāhāra*) is the second direction; each third [tetrad] beginning with consciousness-nutriment (*viññāṇāhāra*)...
The third direction, and likewise the fourth, beginning with the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*), should be understood as the fourth direction. Since it must be asked,
"Among those four directions and among those phenomena such as the nutriment of physical food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), which phenomena are the defilements (*upakkilesa*) of which [direction]?",
these phenomena— beginning with the nutriments— are explained to show that they are the defilements of this person.
“In this regard, the physical nutriment of morsels... [and so on]... these are the defilements of one of proud speculative temperament,” it is said.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: “The passage beginning ‘Physical nutriment is nutriment’ was undertaken to demonstrate, by way of analysis, which among the nutriments and so forth are the defilements for each particular individual.
Of the ten suttas, those that constitute a portion of the ten...
“Of the suttas. “Meaning” (*attha*) refers to a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), for the referent of a word (*saddattha*) is not uniform.
By the phrase “only the phrasing is different,” he demonstrates the diversity of the referents of words.

Because it must be asked, “Among the types of nutriment such as physical food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), which nutriments and so forth reach full understanding (*pariññā*) and abandonment (*pahāna*) by means of which gateway to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*)?”—therefore, the passage beginning with “In that regard, that which is physical food” was stated.

*Iti*: thus, of the kind already described. *Sabbē*: all phenomena, beginning with the nutriments, follow along with the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). *Tē*: those same phenomena, beginning with the nutriments.
*Lōkā*: from the world, that is, from the cycle of existence. They lead out by means of the three doors of liberation, such as the contemplation of impermanence and so forth. 86.
Having extracted them, the Teacher has identified ten tetrads of phenomena, beginning with the fourfold sets of nutriment, which constitute the directions on the side of defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
These have been shown and are known to us. Since it must be asked, "Which factors on the side of purification are the directions?
the passage beginning with "four modes of practice" was stated in order to show the factors that serve as directions on the side of purification.
"Four abidings" refers to the four abidings: the divine abidings, the sublime abidings, the noble abidings, and the imperturbable abidings. Among these, the attainments of the fine-material sphere...

The divine abodes, the four immeasurables as the sublime abodes, the four attainments of fruition as the noble abodes, and the four formless attainments as the imperturbable abodes—these are the four wonderful and marvelous qualities.
These four wonderful and marvelous qualities consist of the abandoning of conceit, the uprooting of attachment, the abandoning of ignorance, and the pacification of existence. The four...

The foundations (*adhiṭṭhānāni*) are the four foundations: the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*), the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*), the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*), and the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*).

The four developments of concentration (*catasso samādhibhāvanā*) are the development of concentration through desire (*chandasamādhibhāvanā*), the development of concentration through energy (*vīriyasamādhibhāvanā*), the development of concentration through mind (*cittasamādhibhāvanā*), and the development of concentration through investigation (*vīmaṃsāsamādhibhāvanā*). The four conducive to happiness (*cattāro sukhabhāgiyā*)...
Restraint of the sense faculties, austerity, the factors of enlightenment, and the relinquishing of all acquisitions—these four are conducive to happiness. The remainder are obvious.
Because it must be asked, "Among the four sets beginning with the 'way of practice' (paṭipadā), which way of practice, etc., comes first for each set, such as the foundations of mindfulness?
it was stated: "The first way of practice has the first foundation of mindfulness," and so forth. [The passage continues: "The ways of practice, etc."

"Since it must be said that 'the foundations of mindfulness and so forth have wisdom as their proximate cause (padatthāna), whereas the foundations of mindfulness and so forth have mindfulness as their proximate cause,' the construction should be made thus:

'The first way of practice fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness,' and so on; therefore, it was stated: 'The first way of practice, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness,' and so forth—this being because of the relationship between the fulfiller and that which is to be fulfilled."
The intention is that the construction [of the sentence] should be made thus.

Alternatively, because it must be asked, "Which practices, when developed and cultivated, fulfill which foundations of mindfulness and so forth?", it was said: "The first practice, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness," and so on.
87. Since it must be asked, among those ten sets of fourfold paths and so forth, "Which phenomena belong to which direction?
Which phenomena belong to which direction?", it was said: "In that regard, these first path, the first foundation of mindfulness, and so forth are the four directions.
Here, "in that regard" means among those ten sets of fourfold paths and so forth. "These" refers to the first path and so forth being spoken of by me.
There are four directions.

Since it must be asked, "Among those four things that constitute directions—such as the fourfold path and so forth—which direction-constituting meaning is the medicine for which type of person?", [the text states]:
"In this regard, the first path... [is for] one of exalted temperament whose conduct is dominated by views."
It is said, "medicine.
Since it must be asked, "Among those ten sets of four, such as the way of practice (*paṭipadā*) and so forth, which [way] is which door to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*)?", it was stated there:
"The way of practice that is painful," and so on. However, the meaning is explained in detail in the *Ṭīkā*.

This has been explained clearly. On the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*), the ten tetrads beginning with the fourfold food (*āhāracatukka*), which constitute the directions, have been determined by way of their being to be transcended and abandoned;

on the side of purification (*vodānapakkha*), however, the ten tetrads beginning with the fourfold way (*paṭipadācatukka*), which constitute the directions, have been determined by way of their being the means of transcending and abandoning.
"The sport (*vikkīḷita*) consisting of the transcending and abandoning of those ten tetrads beginning with the fourfold food..."

Since it must be asked, "Of which persons does this threefold play (vikkīḷita) become a play—namely, that which consists of the cultivation of the ten tetrads beginning with the fourfold path, and that which consists of the realization [of the fruits]?"—therefore it is said, "the play of those. Alternatively: "By means of the aforementioned modes..."
In investigating those Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples who were liberated through the gateways to liberation:
"Is it the sport of the Buddha alone? Or is it the sport of the Paccekabuddha alone?
Or is it the sport of the disciple alone? Or rather, is it the sport of all—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples alike?"—so one should reflect.

It is said that this is "the sport of those [beings]" in the sense of possibility. It is the sport of those Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples who were liberated by means of the doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha) of the aforementioned types.

This refers to the transcendence and abandoning within one's own and others' continuums of the ten tetrads beginning with the fourfold food, as well as the practice of the ten tetrads beginning with the fourfold path.

The accomplishment of development and the accomplishment of realization regarding the fourfold sets within one's own continuum and that of others—this is all what is called "sport" (*vikkīḷita*); this is the meaning.
[It refers to] all ten fourfold sets, beginning with the fourfold set of nutriment, as well as all ten fourfold sets, beginning with the fourfold set of the path.
Since the consideration might arise as to whether they are opposites [in general], or rather whether the sets of four are opposites of the sets of four respectively,

he says, "The four nutriments have their opposite in the four paths," and so forth, demonstrating that the sets of four are opposites of the sets of four respectively by way of the relationship between that which is to be abandoned and its abandoner. In the commentary...

However, it is said: "Now, showing how the transcendence of food and so forth occurs by means of the [four] ways and so on, he spoke the words beginning with ‘The four foods have their opposites in the four ways.
In that context, regarding the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*), those four foods which have been determined—of those four foods, on the side of purification (*vodānapakkha*)—

Regarding the four modes of practice that have been determined: those four modes of practice are the antidote because the nutriments are to be abandoned, whereas the modes of practice are the abandoners.

Even though the nutriments themselves are not to be abandoned, it is stated that they are to be abandoned by way of abandoning desire and lust for them, since they are the objects of insight; such is the construction to be made.
“Sīhā” (Lions) means those similar to lions: Buddhas are like lions, Paccekabuddhas are like lions, and disciples are like lions;
thus, those who are like lions should be applied separately. However, since there are also disciples whose lust, hatred, and delusion have been destroyed, one might think they too are “lions”;
therefore, to exclude them, it is said “those who have destroyed lust, hatred, and delusion. They are called “destroyed” (hatā) because they are to be destroyed; [and] lust and hatred...

Delusion (*moha*) and lust-and-hatred-and-delusion (*rāgadosamoha*); those disciples by whom lust, hatred, and delusion have been destroyed are "those who have destroyed lust, hatred, and delusion" (*hatarāgadosamohā*).
The construction should be made as "the disciples," because it is only with respect to the disciples that the possibility of deviation [from this state] exists. Of those lions, the Buddhas;
of those lions, the Paccekabuddhas; of those lions, the disciples—the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of those things to be cultivated on the side of purification (*vodānapakkha*)...
The development and increase of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā), the realization of those things to be realized within the side of purification—
namely, the fruits and Nibbāna— and the thorough elimination of those things to be abandoned within the side of defilement,
which is termed abandonment: these constitute what is called "sport" (vikkīḷita).
"Foundation of the faculties" (*indriyādhiṭṭhāna*) means the foundation, the occurrence, the cultivation, and the realization of the faculties, beginning with the faculty of faith.
"Non-foundation of perversions" (*vipariyāsānadhiṭṭhāna*) means the non-occurrence and non-arising of the perversions (*vipallāsa*) by way of their abandonment;
this is briefly taken as what is called "sport. The faculties, such as the faculty of faith, have the true Dhamma as their domain.
The objects belonging to the side of purification of the True Dhamma are intended as the causes for its maintenance.
The perversions and distortions, which are the objects of the defilements, are intended as the objects of the side of corruption and the causes for its maintenance.

By means of the passage beginning with “the four nutriments,” ten tetrads—such as the tetrad of nutriments and so forth on the side of corruption, as well as the craving-character and others—are [discussed].
This is that determination which was made by the Teacher by way of the removal of the defilements of the four types of persons;

and this is that determination which was made by the Teacher by way of the manifestation of the purification of the four types of persons— such as those of craving-temperament and so forth— through the ten tetrads beginning with the "four modes of practice" (*catasso paṭipadā*) and others on the side of purification.
Because it must be asked, "Of which method is this extraction (niddhāraṇā) said to be the origin and the ground?
it is stated: "This is called the ground of the Lion’s Play (sīhavikkīḷita) method.
In that context, "this" refers to this twofold extraction performed according to the method already described; that twofold extraction belongs to the Lion’s Play method.
The construction should be made thus: "The 'source' (*samuṭṭhāna*) is the place where the method (*naya*) occurs; it is so called by persons skilled in the arising of methods.

Since it must be asked, "Why is the state of being the ground (*bhūmibhāva*) of the method distinguished in the manner already stated known?", the passage beginning with "Therefore he said" was spoken.
By that [statement], through the state of being the ground of the method distinguished in the manner already stated, [it is said]: "He who leads... [and] those who are skillful."
"By whatever word the teacher has spoken, it is understood through that very word.
The stage of the Lion's Play method (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*) has been elucidated by the teacher and understood by us;

since it must be asked, "What is the stage of the Three-Forked method (*tipukkhalanaya*)?", he spoke the passage beginning with "In that regard, those who [follow] the painful way of practice," desiring to elucidate the stage of the Three-Forked method.
This being so, the Teacher should have stated only such words as, “This is defilement: the three unwholesome roots,” and so forth;

why, then, did he state the words, “In that regard, those who follow the painful way,” and so on? True; however, the cultivation of the ground of the Tipukkhalanaya proceeds by way of the three types of persons—the one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (ugghaṭitaññu), and so on.
Therefore, [he spoke thus] for the sake of the three types of persons beginning with the ugghaṭitaññu.

In order to clarify this, the statement beginning with “Therein, those who [follow] the painful way” was spoken. Even so, one might ask: why was the statement beginning with “Therein, he who sets out by the pleasant way with quick direct knowledge is one who understands through a condensed presentation (ugghaṭitaññū)” not simply stated instead? It is true; however, the three types of persons, beginning with the one who understands through a condensed presentation, [are distinguished as follows: [The text continues: ...the one who understands through a condensed presentation is one who, having heard the teaching once, attains realization. The one who understands through expansion is one who, having heard the teaching twice or thrice, attains realization. The one who understands by inquiry is one who attains realization after asking questions about the meaning of the teaching.

These three types of persons are established based on their respective faculties and the manner in which they attain realization. Therefore, while it would have been possible to state the matter more succinctly, the specific classification of the paths and fruits was taught in order to demonstrate the diversity of the means for attaining liberation according to the varying dispositions and capabilities of individuals. Thus, the statement beginning with “Therein, those who [follow] the painful way” was indeed necessary to fully elucidate the distinctions among these practitioners.

However, because the Tipukkhalanaya emerges from and issues forth according to the method of the Lion’s Play (Sīhavikkīḷitanaya), it is determined within the exposition of the stages of the Lion’s Play by way of the analysis of the path and the analysis of the fourfold types of persons.

To first expound the fourfold types of persons analyzed by way of the analysis of the path in the exposition of the stages of the Lion’s Play, [it says]: "In that regard, those who [are intent] on suffering..."
The passage beginning with “the way” has been stated. Regarding the word *tattha*:
it refers to that tetrad of ways which was determined in the analysis of the stages of the Lion’s Play method (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*). Regarding the word *ye*:

those persons of dull and keen faculties who are of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) emerge respectively by means of the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge and the pleasant way with quick direct knowledge.

Thus, two types of persons have been determined. Since it must be asked, "What is the defilement of those four persons?", the passage beginning with "This is the defilement of those four persons" was stated in order to provide the answer:
"This is the defilement of those four persons. The four nutriments have been determined... [and so on] ...the four ways of going to ruin.
These have been determined; thus, this tenfold set of four—beginning with the fourfold nutriment—is the defilement of those four types of persons. Since it must be asked, "What is their purification?
after the teacher has determined the defilement of those four types of persons, it was stated:
"This is the purification of those four types of persons," and so forth. The four...

The way of practice has been determined, and the four immeasurables have been determined; thus, this set of tenfold phenomena, consisting of the tetrad of ways of practice and so forth, constitutes the purification for those four types of persons. 88.
Among those four types of persons, which person is one who understands through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), and which person is one who understands through an elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*)?
Because it was necessary to ask, "What kind of person is one who is to be led (*neyya*)?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, those who... was stated. If one should ask:

"Previously, four types of persons were also determined by means of the phrase 'In that regard, those who...'; why then are four types of persons determined again by the phrase 'In that regard, those who...'?"—the answer is:
previously, defilement and purification were determined from the perspective of their ownership (*sāmibhāvena*).

However, the specific meaning should be understood as follows: they are determined later by way of being a collection of the components, such as those who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth.

In that context, regarding the phrase "these two persons," the method of application (*yojanattha*) is similar to what was stated previously. "Therein" (*tattha*) means among those four types of persons.

"He" refers to one of lofty temperament (*udātta*) whose conduct is dominated by views (*diṭṭhicarita*). "This one" refers to this very person of fixed destiny who is of lofty temperament and whose conduct is dominated by views.
"Puna yeva" (again, indeed) refers specifically to one who is dull-witted and characterized by craving (*taṇhācarita*) as well as one characterized by views (*diṭṭhicarita*).
"By way of the common [path]" means by way of the painful practice with quick direct knowledge and the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge.

"The three types of persons beginning with the one who understands through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*) have been determined by the Teacher; among those three types of persons, for which one..."
Because it must be asked, "Which [type of person] does the Blessed One point out as which [type of practice]," the passage beginning with "In this regard, the Blessed One...
was stated. Alternatively, because it must be explained, "The distinction among persons has been clarified by the Teacher by way of the distinction of the path;

how, then, is the distinction among persons clarified by way of the distinction of the teaching?"—in order to clarify the distinction among persons even by way of the distinction of the teaching, it says: "In this regard..."

The passage beginning with “the Blessed One” has been stated. Regarding the phrase “therein”: it refers to those three types of persons, namely the *ugghaṭitaññū* (one who understands from a condensed statement) and the others.

Since it must be said that “the distinction between persons is elucidated precisely through the division into the teaching of serenity (*samatha*) and the teaching of insight (*vipassanā*),” the passage beginning with “therein the Blessed One” was stated in order to further elucidate the distinction between persons by means of the division into the teaching of the easy dhamma (*mududhamma*) and the teaching of the difficult dhamma (*tikkhadhamma*).
The same connection of meaning (*anusandhi*) should be stated in the remaining cases as well.

In order to clarify that, having become four by way of the distinction of the individual paths, they become three—both individually and collectively—by way of the distinction of the paths and the distinction of the teaching, it was said again, beginning with "Therein, those which... and concluding with "Thus, having been four, they become three.
In this context, the expression "four... three" is a description employing a change of grammatical gender (liṅgavipallāsa).
However, the description of their natural gender should be made as "four and three.
Because it must be asked, "Of those three persons, what is the defilement?", it was said: "This is the defilement of those three persons," and so forth.
In that context, "this is the defilement" refers to: "The three roots of unwholesomeness... [etc. ...failure in virtue."
This collection of unwholesome states—namely, "failure in view" and "failure in conduct"—which were thus determined, constitutes defilement (*saṃkileso*).
Since it must be asked, "The defilement of those three types of persons has been determined by the Teacher;
how then should their purification (*vodāna*) be determined?", it was said: "This is the purification for those three types of persons," and so forth.

In this context, "this purification" refers to the collection of wholesome states determined as follows: "the three roots of the wholesome... [and so on]... the three gateways to liberation: the void, the signless, and the desireless. This class of phenomena constitutes purification.
It has been elucidated by the Teacher that, according to the manner described, there are three persons who become four; and having been three, they become—
Because it must be stated how many types of persons there are, it was said: "Thus, having been four, they become three;
having been three, they become two: the one of craving-temperament and the one of view-temperament.
Here, "thus" means that in the manner described below, having been four each, they become three each; having been three each, [they become] the one of craving-temperament...
And there are two types of persons: one of speculative temperament and one of view-temperament.
Because it was necessary to state, "Which is the defilement of these two persons?", it was said: "This is the defilement of these two persons," and so forth.
In that context, "this defilement" refers to: "Craving and ignorance... [and so on] ...the eternalist view."
And the view of annihilationism—this collection of unwholesome states thus determined constitutes defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
Since it must be asked, "The defilement of these two types of persons has been determined by the Teacher; how then is purification (*vodāna*)?
it was said: "This is the purification of those two types of persons," and so forth. This purification is "serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*)."

And... [as before] ...the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining and the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining—this collection of wholesome states thus determined constitutes this "arising of phenomena" (dhammajāta) as purification.
By means of such passages as "The three unwholesome roots," etc., there are two groups of twelve [factors], beginning with the triad of unwholesome roots, on the side of defilement.
The determination made by way of the manifestation of defilement regarding the three types of persons— namely, those who attain knowledge through what is condensed (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and so forth—

by means of the triads beginning with "the three roots of unwholesomeness" and so on; and the determination made by way of the manifestation of purification regarding the two sets of twelve triads on the side of purification,
such as the triads of wholesome roots, and the three types of persons beginning with those who attain knowledge through what is condensed.
Having connected this— namely, that the ground, the source, and the cause of occurrence for the previously described selection of the Tipukkhalo method and the Aṅkusas method—
is "craving and ignorance," and so forth— one should apply it to the fifteen dyads on the side of defilement, such as the dyads of craving and ignorance,
and to the two types of persons characterized by craving and characterized by views.
The determination made by way of the manifestation of purification— namely, the nineteen dyads beginning with serenity and insight within the side of purification,

as stated in the passage beginning “serenity and insight,” and the determination made by way of the manifestation of purification for the two types of individuals characterized by craving and by views— this is the Nandiyāvaṭṭa in the manner described.
The phrase "the stages of the method" (*nayassa bhūmi*) should also be extracted and applied [to the following].

For, by way of referring to persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), the Lion’s Play method (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*) arises from the Hook-turning method (*nandiyāvaṭṭanaya*), and the Three-peaked method (*tipukkhalanaya*) arises from the Lion’s Play method.
However, by way of referring to phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), the Three-peaked method arises from the Lion’s Play method.
And from the Tipukkhalanaya, the Nandiyāvaṭṭanaya arises. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary:
"At the end, by means of the passage beginning 'Craving and ignorance,' the ground for the method of serenity (samatha) is shown. For that very reason it is stated:
'Having been four, they become three; having been three, they become two.'"

"However, why is it that the state of being the ground for this aforementioned type of selection (*niddhāraṇā*), as well as for the *tipukkhalo* method and the *aṅkusako* method, is to be understood?"—because there was a need to state this, the words beginning with "Therefore he said" (*tenāha*) were spoken.

By means of that aforementioned state of being the ground for the selection, the Teacher [stated] the following passage: "That which is unwholesome... [and so on] ...and by the discernment of directions."

He said: by that statement, through the selection (*niddhāraṇā*) of the aforementioned kind, the meaning is that the state of being the ground (*bhūmibhāva*) for *tipukkhala*... [and so on]... is understood.

Because it must be stated that "to this extent the arising of the method (*nayasamuṭṭhāna*) is complete, there is nothing further," it is said: "the arising of the method is concluded" (*niyuttaṃ nayasamuṭṭhānaṃ*).
By whichever arising of the method [it may be], whether on the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkhe*) or the unwholesome (*akusala*)...

The meaning to be understood is this: having determined the states (dhammas), or having determined the wholesome states on the side of purification, one should apply them after determining each respective origin of the method (naya) as is appropriate.
However, I shall show it briefly by way of the sequence of methods: two persons, three persons, four persons.
Persons are divided into three groups; likewise, directions are divided into three groups: four directions, six directions, and eight directions.
In this context, "two persons" refers to two types of persons: the person of craving-disposition (*taṇhācarita*) and the person of view-disposition (*diṭṭhicarita*).

"Three persons" refers to three types of persons: the person who understands through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), the person who understands through an expanded explanation (*vipañcitaññū*), and the person who is led to understanding (*neyya*).

There are four types of persons (*puggala*). By way of the division into those with a painful practice and sluggish direct knowledge (*dukkhāpaṭipadā-dandhābhiññā*), and so forth, there are four persons:

the person of dull faculties who is driven by craving (*taṇhācarita*), the person of dull faculties who is driven by views (*diṭṭhicarita*), the person of sharp faculties who is driven by craving, and the person of sharp faculties who is driven by views. "In the four directions" refers to the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*).
Two directions each—two directions on the side of purification—make four directions.
Six directions means three directions each on the side of defilement and three directions each on the side of purification; thus they become six directions.
Eight directions means four directions each on the side of defilement and four directions each on the side of purification; thus they become eight directions. Among these:
Two types each of persons characterized by craving and characterized by views arise from the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method based on the four directions.

Three types of persons—those who understand through a condensed statement, those who understand through elaboration, and those who require guidance—and six directions give rise to the Tipukkhalā method.

Four pairs of persons—distinguished by the path of practice being difficult and the direct knowledge being sluggish, etc.—consisting of those with dull faculties characterized by craving, those with keen faculties characterized by craving, those with dull faculties characterized by views, and those with keen faculties characterized by views [are treated similarly].
The arising of the Lion’s Play method occurs by way of both individuals and the eight directions.
When each individual method of arising is analyzed, the methods of arising for the Directional Survey and the Hook are also thereby analyzed.
If one should ask, "How does the arising of the Joyful Turnabout method occur? [the answer is: "Craving, ignorance, and moral shamelessness..."
Lack of moral dread, lack of mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, improper attention, laziness, difficult-to-correctness,
the conceit "I am," the conceit "mine," lack of faith, negligence, not hearing the true Dhamma, lack of restraint, covetousness, ill will,
the hindrances, the fetters, anger, resentment, contempt, domineering, and envy.
And stinginess, deceit, fraud, the view of eternalism, and the view of annihilationism.

Thus, this collection of unwholesome states, which constitutes the directions, has been taught by way of pairs. Having joined them to the side of defilement by virtue of their common nature as defilements—saying that they constitute the corruption of persons of the two temperaments, those of craving-conduct and view-conduct—one [should understand] these fifteen...
Having mentally observed the unwholesome states—which have become directions by way of being taught individually—as having the nature of directions, [one considers]:
"This, this first unwholesome state is called the first direction on the side of defilement for a person of craving-temperament; this, this..."
"Each second unwholesome state is called the 'second direction' on the side of defilement for a person of speculative temperament.

Having thus applied [the terms] individually, and having extracted the truths of origin and suffering as appropriate, that specific method of exposition by which the intrinsic nature of the phenomena to be analyzed is demonstrated—
that specific method of exposition originates from the "Nandiyāvaṭṭa" (The Conversion of Relishing) method.
That specific mode of commentary by which his observation is shown,
that specific mode of commentary originates from the method of "surveying the directions. Likewise,

that specific mode of commentary by which he leads individuals toward the specific Dhamma that constitutes the particular direction after having observed thus, that specific mode of commentary originates from the method of the "goad."
“Tranquility and insight, moral shame and moral dread, mindfulness and clear comprehension, appropriate attention and the arousal of energy,
readiness to listen and knowledge of the Dhamma, knowledge of conformity, knowledge of destruction,
knowledge of non-arising, faith and heedfulness, hearing the true Dhamma and restraint, non-covetousness and non-ill will.”
And the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, and the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance;
realization and fewness of wishes, contentment and non-anger, non-malice and non-insulting speech, non-defamation and the abandoning of envy, the abandoning of stinginess, and true knowledge;
liberation and the liberation having a conditioned object, and the liberation having an unconditioned object, and that with a residue remaining.

And the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining, and the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining. Thus, this collection of wholesome states that constitute the directions has been taught by way of triplets and dyads;

and since it serves as the purification for persons of the two temperaments—those of craving and those of views—it is joined to the side of purification by virtue of its commonality with purification.
Regarding these nineteen dyads... [or by way of triplets and dyads...]

Having mentally observed the phenomena that have become directions among the desired phenomena, thinking, "Which specific wholesome phenomenon is the direction for which specific person?", [one sees]:
"This first, first wholesome phenomenon is called the first direction on the side of purification for a person of craving-temperament;
this second, second wholesome phenomenon is [the direction] for a person of view-temperament."
Having applied [the terms] individually, stating, “For a person on the side of purification,

this is called the second direction,” and having extracted the Truth of the Path and the Truth of Cessation as appropriate, that specific method of exposition by which the state of being a phenomenon to be analyzed is shown—
that specific method of exposition arises from the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method (the turning of joy), and the observation of that [method] is by which...
It is demonstrated by a specific method of exposition; that specific method of exposition arises from the principle of "orienting the directions.
Having thus observed, the guidance of individuals toward the specific Dhamma that constitutes the particular direction is led by whichever specific method of exposition it employs;
and that specific method of exposition arises from the principle of the "goad."
“If one should ask, ‘How does the Tipukkhalanaya arise? [one should reply: ‘There are three roots of unwholesomeness:
the root of unwholesomeness that is greed, the root of unwholesomeness that is hatred, and the root of unwholesomeness that is delusion. There are three types of misconduct:
bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. There are three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, ill-will thought, and...’”
The thought of cruelty. Three unwholesome perceptions: the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of cruelty.
Three inverted perceptions: the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, and the perception of self.
Three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Three kinds of suffering: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and...
The state of suffering due to change. Three fires: the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion. Three arrows:
the arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, and the arrow of delusion. Three tangles: the tangle of lust, the tangle of hatred, and the tangle of delusion.
Three unwholesome investigations: unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and unwholesome mental action. Three failures.
—“Failure in virtue, failure in view, and failure in conduct. This collection of unwholesome states, which is like a direction, has been taught by way of these triads.

Having applied it to the side of defilement by way of its commonality as defilement—thinking that it constitutes the corruption of the three types of persons, namely those who understand through a brief indication, those who understand through elaboration, and those who are capable of being guided—it is asked:
“Among these twelve unwholesome states taught by way of the triads of triads, which...”
"Which unwholesome state is the 'direction' for which person? Having thus observed with the mind by way of the nature of directions and states, [he understands]:
"This, this first unwholesome state is called the first direction on the side of defilement for the person who gains knowledge through a brief indication (ugghaṭitaññū).
This, this second unwholesome state is [the second direction] on the side of defilement for the person who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū)."
"The second direction is named [the second]. This, this third unwholesome state is named the third direction on the side of defilement for a person who is to be guided.

Having thus applied [the terms] individually, and having extracted the truths of the origin and suffering as appropriate, that specific mode of commentary by which the nature of the phenomena to be analyzed is shown—that specific mode of commentary [is what follows].
And it arises from the Tipukkhalanaya. The specific mode of commentary by which its observation is shown, and that specific mode of commentary itself, arises from the Disālocananaya.

Furthermore, the leading of persons toward the specific Dhamma that constitutes the particular direction—having observed thus—and the specific mode of commentary by which one leads them, that specific mode of commentary [arises from the same source].
It arises from the method of the hook. “There are three roots of the wholesome:
the root of the wholesome that is non-greed, the root of the wholesome that is non-hatred, and the root of the wholesome that is non-delusion.

There are three types of good conduct: good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind. There are three wholesome thoughts: the thought of renunciation, [the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-cruelty].”
The thought of non-ill will; the thought of non-cruelty. Three kinds of concentration: concentration with applied thought and sustained thought;
concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only; concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought. Three wholesome perceptions:

the perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, the perception of non-cruelty. Three unerring perceptions: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self.
Three skillful investigations: skillful bodily action, skillful verbal action, and skillful mental action.
Three purities: purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind. Three accomplishments:

accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in concentration, and accomplishment in wisdom. Three trainings: the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
The three aggregates—the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom;

the three gateways to liberation—emptiness, the signless, and the desireless. This collection of wholesome states, which constitutes the directions and has been taught by way of these triplets, serves as the purification for the three types of persons—the one who gains knowledge through a condensed presentation, the one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition, and the one who is capable of being guided—by virtue of its commonality with purification within the side of purification.

Having applied [the analysis] and mentally observed these twelve wholesome states—which have been taught according to the system of triads within two groups and which function as directions—as being both directions and phenomena, one considers:
"Which specific wholesome state is the direction for which specific person?
Thus, one sees that "this and this first wholesome state belongs to the side of purification for the person who gains knowledge through a condensed teaching."
"This is the first direction. This and this second wholesome state is called the second direction for a person of the 'to-be-developed' (vipañcitaññu) type on the side of purification.
This and this third wholesome state is called the third direction for a person of the 'to-be-guided' (neyya) type on the side of purification.
Having thus associated them individually as directions, [he taught] the truth of the path and the truth of cessation as appropriate.
The nature of the dhamma to be analyzed after it has been extracted is shown by a particular method of exposition;
that particular method of exposition arises from the Tipukkhalanaya (the Three-Pointed Method). Furthermore, the observation of that [nature] is shown by a particular method of exposition;
that particular method of exposition arises from the Disālocananaya (the Direction-Finding Method). Having observed in such a manner, of that which constitutes the specific direction...
The specific method of commentary by which one guides both the Dhamma and individuals—that specific method of commentary arises from the Hook Method (*aṅkusanaya*).
If one should ask, "How does it arise from the Lion’s Play Method (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*)?", [one would say]: "The four nutriments, the four perversions..."
The four kinds of clinging, the four yokes, the four ties, the four taints, the four floods, the four arrows,
the four stations of consciousness, and the four ways of going a bad way— this set of fourfold unwholesome states, taught according to their respective groups of four,
constitutes the direction of "the painful way with slow direct knowledge."
[The path] leading to liberation for one of dull faculties and craving-temperament, which is painful practice with quick direct knowledge;
[the path] leading to liberation for one of sharp faculties and craving-temperament, which is pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge;

[the path] leading to liberation for one of dull faculties and view-temperament, which is pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge; and [the path] leading to liberation for one of sharp faculties and view-temperament...
Having thus applied [the analysis] to the side of defilement by way of the commonality of defilement among the four types of persons— thinking,
"Among these ten tetrads taught by way of groups of four, which unwholesome state is the 'direction' for which type of person?"—
one should mentally establish them as the states that constitute directions on the side of defilement.

Having observed this, [he understands]: "This, this first, first unwholesome state is called the 'first direction' for a person of dull faculties, of craving-temperament, who is intent on the path of suffering with sluggish direct knowledge.
This, this second, second unwholesome state is [the second direction] for one intent on the path of suffering with swift direct knowledge, of keen faculties..."

For a person of craving-temperament, this is called the second direction. This, this third, third unwholesome state—for a person of dull faculties, of view-temperament, who is destined for deliverance by the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge—this is called the third direction.
This, this fourth, fourth unwholesome state—for [a person] by the pleasant way with swift direct knowledge...
Having applied [the terms] individually as directions— namely, "the fourth direction" for a person who is one to be led out, possesses keen faculties,
and is of a speculative temperament— and having extracted the truths of the origin and suffering as appropriate,
that specific mode of exposition by which the intrinsic nature of the phenomena to be analyzed is shown is the Lion’s Play method (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*).
There is. That specific mode of commentary by which his observation is shown, and that specific mode of commentary itself, arises from the method of "surveying the directions.

Having observed in such a manner, that specific mode of commentary by which he leads the Dhamma—which constitutes the specific direction—and leads individuals [to it], and that specific mode of commentary itself, arises from the method of the "goad."
“Four ways of practice, four foundations of mindfulness, four jhānas, four abidings, four right endeavors,
four astounding and wonderful qualities, four determinations, four developments of concentration,
four things conducive to happiness, and four immeasurables”— this is taught by way of sets of four.
The category of wholesome phenomena that has become the directions—namely, for one of dull faculties and temperament of craving who is destined for the painful practice with slow direct knowledge;
for one of sharp faculties and temperament of craving who is destined for the painful practice with quick direct knowledge;
and for one of dull faculties and temperament of views who is destined for the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge.
“For one who is of quick direct knowledge, of easy progress, with keen faculties, and of speculative temperament”—thus there is the purification for four types of persons.
Having thus applied them by way of their commonality of purification within the side of purification, [one asks]:
"Among these ten tetrads of wholesome states taught by way of groups of four, which specific wholesome state..."
Having observed with the mind alone, according to the nature of the directions, for which specific individual each direction applies, [he understands]:

"This and this first, first wholesome state is called the 'first direction' for a person of dull faculties, of craving-temperament, who is destined for emergence via the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge. This and this second, second wholesome state..."
For a person of keen faculties whose temperament is dominated by craving, who possesses a path that is painful and leads to swift direct knowledge, this is called the second direction.

This and this third wholesome state, which leads to a pleasant path and sluggish direct knowledge for a person of dull faculties whose temperament is dominated by views, is called the third direction. This and this fourth...

"The fourth wholesome state is called the fourth direction for a person of sharp faculties, of a view-character, who is destined for deliverance by means of a pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge.
Having thus applied [the states] individually according to their directional nature,
and having extracted the Truth of the Path and the Truth of Cessation as appropriate, [he explains] the intrinsic nature of the phenomena to be analyzed by which...
It is shown by a specific method of commentary. That specific method of commentary arises from the *sīhavikkīḷita-naya* (the lion’s-play method).
And its observation is that by which it is shown through a specific method of commentary. That specific method of commentary arises from the *disālocana-naya* (the method of determining directions).
Having observed in such a manner, the leading of the various directions of the Dhamma and of individuals is that by which it is [shown] through a specific method of commentary.

He leads [the meaning]; and that specific excellence of exposition arises from the method of the goad (*aṅkusanaya*). Thus, it should be understood that the arising of methods occurs in brief by way of the sequence of methods.
Thus, in the section on the arising of methods, this has been composed according to the strength of one's own capacity.
The Exposition of the Analysis is finished.
However, the wise should grasp the profound meaning by analyzing it in detail according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
Thus ends the Exposition of the Foundation of the Dispensation.

89. Regarding the passage beginning with “In this context, what is the ‘arising of the methods’? and so forth, the Teacher has established the arising of the methods in every respect, and we too have understood it.
However, since it must be asked, “How are the eighteen root-terms analyzed among the sixteen modes of nutriment, the five methods, and the eighteen root-terms?
Where are they to be seen by us?”—therefore, [the question arises: “In that regard, where are the eighteen root-terms?”

The passage beginning with “should be seen” has been stated. Regarding the phrase “therein”: among those sixteen nutriments, five methods, and eighteen root-terms, he asks by which term the eighteen root-terms were analyzed by the Teacher, and where they should be seen by us in detail.
The eighteen root-terms were analyzed by me in the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*; they should be seen by you in detail in the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*.
"It should be seen" is the answer. For it is precisely the eighteen root terms (*mūlapada*) that have been analyzed which are what "should be seen. However, in the Commentary it says:

"Having thus analyzed the arising of the methods in every way, now, while analyzing the *Paṭṭhāna* of the Dispensation—since in the sections on Compendium and so forth the *Paṭṭhāna* was not shown in its own form by being condensed under the root terms alone—therefore, as follows..."
It has been said: "The *Paṭṭhāna* should be extracted from the root-terms; likewise, the root-terms should be extracted from the *Paṭṭhāna*.
To demonstrate this, it was stated: 'Where are the eighteen root-terms to be found? In the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*.
Thus the Teacher stated that the eighteen root-terms are to be found in the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*. Which one is that?"
Because it was asked, "What is the *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*? [the following] was stated: "In this context, what is the *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*? and so forth. "In this context" (*tattha*) means:
among those eighteen root-terms of the *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*, which one is that *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*? He answers:

the discourse taught by the Blessed One—which is now being determined by me—beginning with the section on the side of defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), is called the *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*. "Sāsana" means...

The *pariyatti-sāsana* (the teaching as scripture). Regarding *paṭṭhāna*: it is the "establishment" (*paṭṭhāna*)—that is, the basis or occurrence—of that *pariyatti-sāsana* through various modes such as its being conducive to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*);
however, here the sūtra that illustrates this is what is called *paṭṭhāna*. Therefore it was said: "A sūtra conducive to defilement," and so forth.
Alternatively, *sāsana* refers to the threefold training (*sikkhattaya*) consisting of higher virtue (*adhisīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).
The "Dispensation" (sāsana) is that by which one is established in the three trainings and by which one is protected from defilements and so forth; thus it is a "foundation" (paṭṭhāna).

The foundation for the Dispensation of the three trainings is the "Sāsanapaṭṭhāna. Furthermore, the Sutta that serves as its basis is also called "Sāsanapaṭṭhāna" by way of metaphorical designation (ṭhāny-upacāra).
To show that Sāsanapaṭṭhāna Sutta according to its actual form:
“A discourse dealing with defilement, a discourse dealing with purification, a discourse dealing with penetration, a discourse dealing with the state of one beyond training,
a discourse dealing with both defilement and purification, a discourse dealing with both defilement and penetration,
a discourse dealing with both defilement and the state of one beyond training, [and] a discourse dealing with both defilement and penetration.”

A discourse pertaining to the state of one beyond training; a discourse pertaining to defilement, a discourse pertaining to purification, and a discourse pertaining to penetration; a discourse pertaining both to purification and penetration;

a discourse pertaining to the defilement of craving, a discourse pertaining to the defilement of views, a discourse pertaining to the defilement of misconduct, and a discourse pertaining to the cleansing of craving.
It is said: “The discourse on purification of view, and the discourse on purification of misconduct.

Since it must be asked, “Among those discourses, regarding the defilements and so forth spoken of by the Blessed One, how much is there of defilement among those defilements and so forth?”—it is stated:
“In that regard, defilement is threefold: the defilement of craving, the defilement of views...”
“...the corruption of misconduct,” it is said. “Therein” means among those phenomena such as corruption and so forth mentioned in the Suttantas.
Since it must be asked, “Of those three kinds of corruption, by what wholesome state is the corruption of craving purified? it is therefore stated:
“Therein, the corruption of craving is purified by serenity (samatha). “Therein” means in that [context of] the threefold corruption beginning with the corruption of craving.
Since it must be asked, "To which aggregate does that serenity (samatha) belong?", it is stated: "That serenity is the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-khandha).
Since it must be asked, "By what is the corruption of views (diṭṭhi-saṃkilesa) purified?", it is stated: "The corruption of views is purified by insight (vipassanā).
Since it must be said, "To which aggregate does that insight belong?", [it is stated]: "That insight is the aggregate of wisdom (paññā-khandha)."
It was stated [previously]. Since it must be asked, "By what is the corruption of misconduct purified?", it was stated, "The corruption of misconduct is purified by good conduct.
Since it must be asked, "To which aggregate does that good conduct belong?", it was stated, "That good conduct is the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
Since it must be asked, "What happens to the person established in that virtue?"...
The passage beginning with “For one established in virtue” has been stated.
