For that virtuous person established in virtue—meaning the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) characterized as good conduct—if attachment to existences (bhava), that is, the aspiration for existence within the realms of sense-desire, form, and formlessness, should arise, [the phrase] “thus they flow toward him” (*evaṃ sāyanti evaṃ assa āyanti*) is the word-division. This being so, for him who is established in virtue:
This attachment is a longing for existence (*bhavapatthanā*) and constitutes a basis for meritorious action consisting in the cultivation of serenity and insight;
by the word "and," the meaning that it also constitutes a basis for meritorious action consisting in giving and morality is included. "Therein" means:
among those [three], the realms of sense-desire, fine-material, and immaterial existence, it leads to rebirth.

Since it must be stated, "How many are those suttas by which defilement and so forth are shown?", it was said, "These four suttas," and so on. There are four suttas that are unique: the sutta dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), the sutta dealing with purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*), the sutta dealing with penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), and the sutta dealing with the state beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*).

There are also two suttas that are common: the sutta dealing with both defilement and purification (*saṃkilesabhāgiya-vāsanābhāgiya*), and the sutta dealing with both defilement and penetration (*saṃkilesabhāgiya-nibbedhabhāgiya*).

The *saṃkilesabhāgiya* (pertaining to defilement) and *asekkhabhāgiya* (pertaining to the beyond-training) discourses, when mixed with the *vāsanābhāgiya* (pertaining to purification) and *nibbedhabhāgiya* (pertaining to penetration) discourses, become four.
Thus, there are eight discourses. These very same discourses, according to the manner described, constitute the eight discourses.
Or, they are shared as the *vāsanābhāgiya*, *asekkhabhāgiya*, *nibbedhabhāgiya*, and *asekkhabhāgiya* discourses.

The suttas pertaining to defilement, the suttas pertaining to purification, and the suttas pertaining to penetration; the suttas pertaining to defilement, the suttas pertaining to purification, and the suttas pertaining to the state beyond training;

the suttas pertaining to defilement, the suttas pertaining to penetration, and the suttas pertaining to the state beyond training; the suttas pertaining to purification, the suttas pertaining to penetration, and the suttas pertaining to the state beyond training;

the suttas pertaining to defilement, the suttas pertaining to purification, the suttas pertaining to penetration, and the suttas pertaining to the state beyond training; and the suttas that pertain to neither defilement nor purification.
When the discourses pertaining to the parts, the parts leading to penetration, and the parts pertaining to those beyond training are combined, they constitute eight discourses;

thus, there are sixteen discourses in total. Among those sixteen discourses, four single-discourse (ekaka) suttas, four double-discourse (duka) suttas, and two triple-discourse (tika) suttas are found in the Canon (pāḷi);
likewise, two double-discourse suttas and two triple-discourse suttas [are also included].
The tetrads and the suttas have been included in the commentary.

If it were argued that "only the sixteen suttas described according to the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* have been analyzed, then in that case the entire teaching of the scriptures (*pariyatti-sāsana*) consisting of nine divisions, such as the Sutta and Geyya, would remain unanalyzed by the method of the *Paṭṭhāna*," [the author] says: "By these..."

"By means of the sixteen suttas," and so forth, it is said. By these sixteen suttas analyzed according to the *Paṭṭhāna* method, the entire ninefold scripture (*pariyatti*) becomes differentiated, having been analyzed by that very same *Paṭṭhāna* method.

A verse should be inferred from a verse through its classification as "conducive to defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so on; a prose exposition (*veyyākaraṇa*) [should be inferred] from a prose exposition through its classification as "conducive to defilement" and so on.
It must be inferred. Indeed, by means of a discourse classified as pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth, one discourse must necessarily be inferred from another.
90. Since it was asked, "Among those sixteen discourses—pertaining to defilement and so forth—which is the discourse pertaining to defilement?", it was stated:
"In this regard, which is the discourse pertaining to defilement? and so on. "In this regard" (*tattha*) means among those [sixteen].
Among the sixteen suttas beginning with those "pertaining to defilement" (saṃkilesabhāgiya), he asks: which sutta is called a "sutta pertaining to defilement"?
“Blinded by desire, shrouded in a net, covered by the veil of craving;
bound by the fetters of negligence, like fish in the mouth of a trap.”
“They follow after old age and death, like a suckling calf following its mother.
This sutta is called a *saṃkilesabhāgiya* (discourse on the side of defilement) because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the aspect of defilement.
Those beings who are blind with desire, blinded by craving, covered by the net, shrouded by the veil of *taṇhā*, and bound by the fetter of negligence...
Bound and to be bound—those beings follow after aging and death. Just as those fish caught at the mouth of a net follow after aging and death, even so do those beings follow after aging and death.
The construction should be made thus: "Just as a suckling calf follows its mother, even so do those beings follow after aging and death. Now...

Or, just as a calf raised on milk follows its mother, and as fish caught at the mouth of a net follow after old age and death, so too those beings who are blinded by craving and bound by the fetter of negligence—those beings follow after old age and death; such is the construction of the meaning.
Because it must be stated that "this is indeed a sutta"—
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of going astray. What are the four?
One goes astray through desire, one goes astray through hatred, one goes astray through delusion, and one goes astray through fear. These, bhikkhus, are the four ways of going astray.
This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:”
“Whoever transgresses the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
his fame diminishes like the moon in the dark fortnight.
This is a sutta dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*).

It has been said: "Whether it be a king or one such as a master of the Vinaya who, out of desire for the sake of desire, out of hatred for the sake of hatred, out of fear for the sake of fear, or out of delusion for the sake of delusion,
oversteps and transgresses the Dhamma— the Dhamma of the Noble Ones— their fame, reputation, retinue, and wealth diminish."
The construction is: “Just as the moon wanes in its radiance during the dark fortnight, so too does he wane.

Because it must be stated that “only this much [is said],” it is said: “‘Mind precedes all phenomena... ... ‘Like the wheel of a moving cart’—this is a discourse dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya). The meaning is clear and has been analyzed in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) as well:
“When one is slothful, gluttonous, sleeping, and rolling about in bed...”
“Like a great boar fattened on fodder, the dull-witted one enters the womb again and again.
This sutta is called a *saṃkilesabhāgiya-sutta* (a discourse pertaining to defilement) because it functions as both an expression and an indicator regarding the domain of the side of defilement.
A great boar fattened on fodder—that is, a village pig—is by nature prone to sleep and rolls about while sleeping.

It is as if this were so: when a dull-witted being is a great eater, that dull-witted being—having become drowsy and overcome by sloth and torpor—sleeps on a bed of soft touch, being caressed by soft hands, and turning over again and again in his sleep, enters the womb once more;
such is the construction of the sentence.
“Just as rust arising from iron consumes that very iron from which it sprang, so too do one’s own deeds lead a person who behaves with excessive license to a state of misery.
This sutta is also called a discourse dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya-sutta*). Rust arises and is produced from iron; for that very reason, it consumes it.
Then, having risen from that iron [cauldron], as if it were eating him, even so, having passed beyond the person of excessive self-indulgence,
one's own unwholesome kamma committed by oneself leads the person of purified conduct to a state of misery— this is the construction.
"Just as a thief caught at the mouth of a tunnel is struck and bound by his own deed;"
"Thus, having passed away, this person in the next world is struck and bound by their own karma.
This sutta is also called a "sutta dealing with defilement.
Just as a thief caught at the entrance of a dwelling by royal officers and others is struck and bound by his own karma—that is, by the criminal act he himself committed—so too is this evildoer.

The construction is as follows: having passed away from this world to the next world, living beings are themselves slain by their own performed unwholesome karma with swords and the like, and they are bound with fetters, ropes, and so forth.
"He who harms with a rod those beings who desire happiness..."
“Seeking his own happiness, he does not find happiness after passing away.
This sutta is also called a “discourse dealing with defilement.
A being who, seeking—constantly seeking—his own happiness, harms other beings who desire happiness with a stick, that harmful being, having passed away to the next world, finds no happiness.
The construction is: "he does not obtain.
"If among cattle that are crossing over, the leader goes crookedly, they all go crookedly when the leader has gone crookedly."
“In the same way, among humans, whoever is considered the best—
if he practices unrighteousness, how much more so the rest of the people?
The entire kingdom lies in suffering if the king is unrighteous.”
This sutta is also called a "sutta dealing with defilement. Just as when cattle crossing a river, if the bull goes crookedly, all those cows go crookedly because their leader has gone crookedly;
even so, among men, if the king who is esteemed as the best practices unrighteousness (*adhamma*), then when the king practices unrighteousness—
While others are practicing [righteousness], the rest of the people practice unrighteousness even more so, right from the very beginning.
If the king is unrighteous, then while the king is unrighteous, the entire kingdom lies in suffering—this is the construction of the meaning.
"Truly, these people are in a miserable state; they commit evil deeds, being attached to worldly acquisitions."
“They go to the abode of many people, to Avīci hell, which is bitter and terrifying.”—This sutta is also called a “sutta dealing with defilement.

Those people who, being attached to acquisitions—that is, the acquisitions consisting of the strands of sensual pleasure—and being overcome by lust, perform evil unwholesome kamma; these people who perform evil kamma are truly miserable.
The construction is as follows: "Alas, how truly difficult it is for those people who have committed evil deeds to reach [liberation];
they go to the Avīci hell, which is bitter, terrifying, and crowded with many beings.
"The fruit indeed destroys the plantain tree; the fruit destroys the bamboo, the fruit destroys the reed."
“Honor kills the base man, just as the fetus kills the mule”—
this sutta is also called a sutta dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*). Just as the fruit of the plantain tree invariably destroys the plantain tree itself,
and just as the fruit invariably destroys the bamboo, and just as the fruit invariably destroys the reed...
The construction is as follows: just as a fetus invariably destroys its mother, the mare, so too does honor invariably destroy a base person.
“A bhikkhu who values anger and slander, who values gain and honor...”
“Just as a rotten seed does not sprout even in a fertile field, so too [one who is corrupted] does not flourish in the True Dhamma.
This sutta is also called a “discourse dealing with defilement.

Just as a rotten seed cast even into a beautiful, fertile field does not grow, so too, that bhikkhu who possesses gain, honor, and respect, and who harbors anger—anger characterized by the quality of being prone to wrath—[does not flourish].
He practices while holding malice—characterized by the smearing away of the virtues and conduct of others—in high esteem;
the construction is that such a practicing bhikkhu does not take root in the True Dhamma. 91.
"In this case, bhikkhus, having encompassed with my own mind the mind of a certain person whose mind was corrupted, I [saw]..."
“I understand... [and so on] ...thus have I heard”—this sutta is also called a sutta dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*).

“Monks, here in this teaching, or in the world, I understand a certain person of corrupted mind by encompassing his mind with my own mind, having delimited it with the Buddha-eye. If one asks, “How do I understand it? [the answer follows].
One might ask: "In what way does this person practice a wrong course and ascend a wrong path;

and by means of that wrong course and that wrong path, at this time, at this moment, when it is a time for practicing wrongly, how does this person—who has practiced wrongly and ascended a wrong path—conduct himself and proceed?"
If that person should die, then just as the object brought [as a gift] was placed [in the bowl], so too is he placed in hell.
Why is that? Monks, it is because that person’s mind has become corrupted and defiled;
therefore, he is placed there. Thus, in this teaching or in the world, some [beings] are [reborn in such states] due to the corruption of the mind.
"I understand that beings, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm.
This is what the Blessed One said. In this regard, in that sutta, this statement of a verse is spoken thus: "Having known the mind to be corrupted... he reappears in hell."
The Teacher, having recognized a certain individual whose mind was corrupted either in this Dispensation or in the world, explained this matter in the presence of the bhikkhus:
"If this person were to pass away at this very moment, being possessed of such a corrupted mind, he would be reborn in hell; for the mind of this person has indeed been corrupted."
It exists; therefore, one might be reborn there. Sentient beings go to an evil destination because of mental corruption (*cetopadosa*).
Just as one would deposit a heavy burden, even so that foolish person with a corrupted mind, upon the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in hell.
This meaning was also spoken by the Blessed One; such is the connection [of the passage] as it was heard by me.
“If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you,
do not perform an evil deed, whether openly or in secret.
And if you have performed an evil deed, or are performing one— ”
“There is no release from suffering for you, even if you were to fly away.
This sutta is also called a “sutta dealing with defilement. "O noble ones, you [are subject to] the eightfold suffering:

the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, the suffering of the states of deprivation, the suffering rooted in the past round of existence, the suffering rooted in the future round of existence, and the suffering rooted in present nutriment. Thus [it is said].
If you fear suffering, and if this eightfold suffering is indeed unpleasant to you, then—whether in public or in private—do not commit an evil deed; do not do it.
Noble persons, if you were to commit an evil deed in public or in private, or if you are committing one now—this being the case—
The construction is as follows: whether by chance or intentionally, for you who are fleeing, there is no release—no liberation from the eightfold suffering that consists of suffering itself.
"Having acquired wealth by unrighteous means, and both [parents] by falsehood..."
"‘It is mine,’ so fools imagine; how indeed will that come to be?
‘There will surely be obstacles; what has been gathered will perish.
Those who have died do not go to heaven; are they not destroyed by this much alone?’"
This sutta is also called a "sutta dealing with defilement" (saṃkilesabhāgiya).

As for those fools who, through unrighteousness and by means of false speech, acquire all kinds of wealth—both animate and inanimate—and having obtained that wealth, think of both types of property as "my wealth," how and in what manner will that wealth of theirs belong to them? [It will not,] because it was acquired through unrighteousness.
Because it has been accumulated, it does not endure for long. Obstacles—such as obstacles from kings and the like—will arise for those fools.
By means of that unrighteous conduct and so forth through which the wealth was accumulated, that accumulated wealth will perish.
When they die, those fools do not go to heaven or a happy destination.
For "Sugati" (the happy destination) is intended here as "Sagga" (heaven), because it is the foremost among beautiful states of existence due to its excellent enjoyments.

To this extent—by means of this much—the foolish ones are indeed slain and ruined through the loss of their own welfare pertaining both to the present life and the future life; such is the construction of the meaning.
"How does one dig up oneself? How does one grow old with one's friends?"
“How does one turn away from the Dhamma? How does one not go to heaven?
“Through greed one harms oneself; the greedy man wastes away his friends.
Through greed one turns away from the Dhamma; through greed one does not go to heaven.”
This sutta is also called a "sutta dealing with defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*). The meaning of the application [of the terms] is clear.
"Fools of little intelligence wander about as if with themselves as their own enemies, performing evil deeds that bear bitter fruit."
“That deed is not well done which, having been done, one regrets;

that whose result one experiences weeping with a tearful face.”—This sutta is also called a sutta dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*). The dull-witted, the unwise, the foolish [suffer] evil at the hands of their enemies.
As if the deed were already done: thus, those who perform an evil deed that will result in bitter fruit for themselves go about their way having committed that wicked action.
That deed which, having been performed, one regrets while doing it—that performed deed is not good.
The construction is: "That deed whose ripening one experiences weeping, with a tearful face, crying out—that performed deed is not good."

“Difficult to do and difficult to endure... [as far as] ‘one who is not free from lust’”—this sutta is also called a sutta dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*). The meaning of this sutta is explained in detail in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
“One who would measure the immeasurable, O Wise One, would be full of conceit;
I consider him to be shrouded, O Seer, who measures that which is immeasurable.”
This sutta is also called a "sutta dealing with defilement.

Herein, who among ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) could attempt to measure a person whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), who is immeasurable and possesses immeasurable qualities, by saying, "This person whose taints are destroyed has such-and-such virtue, such-and-such concentration, and such-and-such wisdom"? One who would attempt to measure an immeasurable person whose taints are destroyed is indeed measuring what should not be measured.
The construction is as follows: "I think, I consider that this worldling—who is shrouded, whose wisdom is inverted, who lacks insight, and who is without discernment—is such.
For it is said: "When a man is born, an axe is born in his mouth, with which the fool cuts himself by speaking ill."
“Indeed, neither a well-sharpened sword nor even the halāhala poison brings such ruin when missed as does ill-spoken speech.
This sutta is also called a sutta dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*). Ill-spoken speech refers to harsh words characterized by reviling the Noble Ones (*ariyūpavāda*).
As a foolish, wicked man speaks again and again, he cuts himself with that ill-spoken speech which is like an axe;
that ill-spoken speech, resembling an axe, arises in the mouth of the person as it is born.
That ill-spoken speech seems to arise in the mouth; however, such a well-sharpened weapon does not arise in the mouth in the same way.
Hālāhala poison does not arise in the mouth; rather, it is ill-spoken speech that, like a person who has failed, causes one to fall into the states of misery (*apāya*).
Just so, a well-sharpened sword does not cause one to fall into the states of misery, nor does Hālāhala poison cause one to fall into the states of misery—this is the construction [of the verse].
“He who praises one who deserves blame, or blames one who is worthy of praise;”
He gathers misfortune with his mouth; through that misfortune, he finds no happiness.
"This is but a minor misfortune, this defeat of wealth at dice;
but this is the far greater misfortune: to lose everything, even one's very self."
“He who harbors malice toward the Sugatas—
having directed evil speech and mind toward them— goes to hell for a hundred thousand *nirabbudas*, thirty-six and five *abbudas*.”
This sutta is also called a "discourse dealing with defilement.
The person who praises an individual who is blameworthy, of bad conduct, and immoral—that praising person gathers and accumulates misfortune with his own mouth;

because of that misfortune, he does not find happiness. But as for the one of good conduct and virtuous character who is worthy of praise—whether it be that person of good conduct or the virtuous one...
The person who reviles another person, that reviling person gathers and accumulates misfortune (*kali*) with his mouth;
because of that misfortune, he finds no happiness.
Even in relation to one's own self, or even by way of all one's wealth, that loss of wealth which occurs at dice—this is *kali*.
This defeat of wealth is insignificant. For that person who harbors malice toward the Sugatas, whatever misfortune (kali) befalls them, this very misfortune is far greater. Why?
Because when a person who reviles the Noble Ones, having directed their speech and mind [toward them], enters the evil hell at that time—
That time is equal to a period “in which thirty-six *nirabbudas*, five *abbudas*, and one hundred thousand *nirabbudas* are counted”;
therefore, the construction is that [the latter] is even greater than that.
“He who is devoted to the qualities of greed…” and so forth.
"You are indeed going to the precipice for a long time.
This sutta is also called a "sutta dealing with defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*).
A person who is devoted to the qualities of greed, who is repeatedly and continuously attached to them, that person reviles other persons with words; he is faithless, miserly, and ungenerous.
He does not understand the exhortations of the Buddhas; he is miserly and devoted to slander.

O foul-mouthed one, uneven-mouthed one, ruined one, one devoid of spiritual beings, ignoble one, destroyer of beings, evil doer of misdeeds, man-ant, man-like, unlucky one, ill-fated one, base-born son—you are destined for hell. Here...
Now, do not be a talkative person.
Do not scatter or cast upon yourself the dust that leads to harm. You are a doer of evil;
you revile individuals who are virtuous and whose taints are destroyed, and you practice many deeds of misconduct. Having practiced them, for a long time you will be deprived of joy.
"You will surely fall into hell, you go to the abyss"—this is the construction.

Various types of discourses dealing with defilement have been determined by the Teacher and understood by us; because it must be asked, "Which is the discourse dealing with purification through habituation?
[the text begins] with "In this regard, which is the discourse dealing with purification through habituation? and so forth.

It has been stated. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*): among those sixteen discourses beginning with the "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), he asks which discourse is called the "partaking of purification" (*vāsanābhāgiya*) discourse.

The verse beginning, “Mind precedes all phenomena... [and] like a shadow, never departing,” is called the "partaking of purification" discourse because it functions as a speaker and indicator regarding the domain of the partaking of purification—that is, the partaking of merit (*puññabhāga*). The meaning is clear.
93. “Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One...

‘...a death that is not evil’”—this sutta is called a *vāsanābhāgiya-sutta* because it functions as a communicator and indicator regarding the category of purification (*vāsanābhāga*) and the category of merit (*puññabhāga*). The meaning is clear:
“He who does not harm beings who desire happiness with a stick...”

“Seeking his own happiness, he obtains happiness after passing away”—this sutta is also called a sutta pertaining to the portion of purification by habituation (*vāsanābhāgiya*). The meaning is clear.

“If [a leader] of a flock of cattle rushing forward... [and] if he becomes a righteous king”—this sutta is also called a sutta pertaining to the portion of purification by habituation. The meaning is clear.
94. “The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī... ‘He understands thus’”—this sutta also [illustrates] the latent impression (*vāsanā*)... this is called a sutta. The meaning is clear. One might ask:
“For what reason does the Blessed One wander on tour through the countryside? Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on tour through the countryside for seven reasons. What are the seven?
For the sake of training those who are to be trained (*veneyya*) who have gone to other regions;... [and so forth].
Therein, it was for the purpose of inspiring zeal in those who were already established there; for the purpose of preventing his disciples from being bound to a fixed residence in one place;

for the purpose of demonstrating his own lack of attachment to living there permanently; for the purpose of establishing the status of the locations as *cetiyas* by virtue of being places where a Perfectly Enlightened One had dwelt;
and for the purpose of generating a flood of merit for many beings through seeing him, approaching him, and so forth.
The reason for traveling through the countryside should be understood as being due to these seven causes:
[the first] being for the purpose of pacifying calamities such as drought.
“Having sacrificed a single flower, for ten million eons...”
“Both gods and humans, through the remainder, have attained final Nibbāna.”—This Sutta is also called a *vāsanābhāgiya* Sutta.
“A thousand crores of eons” means a thousand crores of individual existences (*attabhāva*).
“In Assattha trees, green and shining, with their foliage fully grown...”
“Mindful, I attained a single perception directed toward the Buddha.
For thirty kalpas from then on, I do not recall ever being reborn in an unhappy state;
the threefold knowledge has been realized through the impression of that perception.”
This sutta is also called a "sutta pertaining to the stage of purification by habituation" (*vāsanābhāgiya*). "Haritobhāse" means "in a green radiance. "Alabhiṃhaṃ" means "I obtained.
"The city of Kosala for alms... [etc] ...the result is inconceivable"—this sutta is also called a "sutta pertaining to the stage of purification by habituation.
The Supreme Person, the compassionate one, the Sage who has destroyed craving, the Fully Awakened One, before his meal, went for alms from house to house.
In order to receive [it], he entered the city of Kosala.
That man who had a flower-ornament (*vaṭaṃsaka*)— adorned with all kinds of flowers—
in his hand was this very person entering the city of Kosala by way of the royal highway, preceded by the community of monks and honored by gods and humans.
He saw the Perfectly Enlightened One; having seen him, he was thrilled and his heart was filled with serene confidence. Having inspired confidence in the Perfectly Enlightened One, he approached him.
Having approached and become full of faith, he offered that fragrant, beautiful, and delightful ear-ornament (*vaṭaṃsaka*) to the Perfectly Enlightened One with his own hands.
Then, from between the lips—the mouth—of the Buddha, rays of light like crests of fire issued forth in a thousand beams.
A light issued forth from his mouth like lightning flashing from a cloud;
thus, a thousand-rayed radiance emerged from the mouth of the Kinsman of the Sun, circumambulated his head three times to the right, and vanished back into his head.

Having seen this wondrous, marvelous, and hair-raising miracle, Ānanda adjusted his robe over one shoulder and said this: "Great Sage, what is the cause of this smile? Explain that cause, for it shall become a light of the Dhamma."
The Blessed One, whose knowledge regarding all phenomena is ever-active, the Sage who has transcended doubt, spoke thus to the elder Ānanda, who was still doubting and perplexed:
"Ānanda, that person who has placed confidence in my heart shall not go to an evil destination for eighty-four thousand eons; among the devas he will enjoy divine splendor and celestial sovereignty."
Having governed the kingdom among men throughout the entire realm, that lord of men shall become a king.
That man, having gone forth for the final time and realized the nature of Dhamma, will become a Paccekabuddha named Vaṭaṃsaka, with his passions shaken off.
Whether it be toward a Tathāgata, a Sammasambuddha, a Paccekasambuddha, or a disciple of such a Tathāgata, when the mind is full of faith, there is no gift that is considered small.
The Buddhas are thus inconceivable as to how much they are. The Buddha-qualities and Buddha-attributes are thus inconceivable as to how much they are.
For those who have faith in what is inconceivable, the ripening of merit—the result of that merit—is thus inconceivable as to how much it is; this is the construction of the meaning he spoke. 96.
“In this case, monks, I [see] a certain person...pe... ‘This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One,’ so I have heard.”
"Learned" (*suta*): this refers to a discourse belonging to the category of "conducive to purification through habituation" (*vāsanābhāgiya-sutta*).
"Monks, here in this teaching, with my own mind I encompass the mind of a certain person and, with the Buddha-eye, I understand it thus:
in whatever manner and by whatever means this person has practiced the path of giving and so forth..."
And when one has ascended the path of vision and so forth, and practices and maintains that way and that path—
if this person were to die at this very moment, then just as a deposited object is placed in its proper location,
so too would he be self-deposited in heaven by means of that practice and that path. That.
"For what reason? Monks, because the mind of that person is serene and has been made serene, therefore he would be deposited here, either in this teaching or in the world.

And furthermore, monks, I understand it thus: some beings and persons, upon the breakup of the body, after death, arise in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, precisely because of their serenity of mind."—Thus spoke the Blessed One.
He spoke this matter. In that context, regarding that meaning, what is spoken as the verse statement beginning with “Having known the mind to be serene...
he is reborn in heaven” is said by way of its inclusion. The construction is: “This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus it was heard by me.”
“The one who has performed merit obtains such a boat with a golden canopy…”—this Sutta is also called a Sutta pertaining to the stage of purification by habituation (vāsanābhāgiya).
A celestial maiden, having boarded a boat with a golden canopy covered in golden ornaments, stands there;
she plunges into a lotus pond, a divine lotus pond, and plucks a lotus with her hand.
"Deity, by what karma does such beauty, such majesty, and such radiance belong to you?
Deity, by what karma do those enjoyments that you desire with your mind arise for you?
Deity, being questioned by me, explain; explain how all this is the fruit of which karma? Thus Sakka asked.
Questioned by the King of the Gods, that daughter of the gods, being delighted at having been asked the question, answered Sakka:
"O King of the Gods, while traveling along a long road, I saw the delightful stupa of the illustrious Blessed One Kassapa;
having seen it, I set my heart upon that stupa with faith. With my own hands, being full of faith, I offered lotus flowers."
"I worshipped. All this is the fruit and the result of that very deed.
"I, having performed merit, obtained such a fruit"—thus he explained to Sakka. "Thus have I heard," says Mahāmoggallāna; such is the construction of the sentence.

Since it must be stated that "only those suttas already determined [in the previous section] are the suttas pertaining to the stage of purification through habituation (vāsanābhāgiya), complete in themselves," there follows the "Discourse on Giving" (Dānakathā).
It is said: "Discourse on virtue, discourse on heaven, discourse on merit, and discourse on the result of merit—this is the portion dealing with moral permeation (*vāsanā*)," and so forth.
In this context, that teaching by which both giving and the fruit of giving are shown is called "discourse on giving" (*dānakathā*).
That teaching by which both virtue and the fruit of virtue are shown is called "discourse on virtue" (*sīlakathā*). That teaching by which [heavenly] realms...
The discourse that demonstrates the karma which causes rebirth in the heavens is called the "Discourse on Heaven" (saggakathā).
The discourse by which the tenfold meritorious action—consisting of giving, virtue, mental development, and so forth—is demonstrated is called the "Discourse on Merit" (puññakathā).

The discourse by which the various results of such meritorious action are shown, having determined them as "this is the result of this merit," is called the "Discourse on the Result of Merit" (puññavipākakathā).

The construction is as follows: those people who are full of faith toward the stūpas built for the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, the possessors of the Ten Powers—stūpas constructed with sand after having placed the bodily relics within them—having performed meritorious deeds of service at those stūpas, arise in the heavenly realms and rejoice.
This is a discourse... [pe] ...a discourse.

97. "With the complexion of a son of the gods, with a complexion like that of a son of the gods, with a beautiful form, and a shape endowed with good fortune—let all people moisten the dust with water and increase the stupa. Whose stupa is this? he asks.
"O deity of beautiful limbs and lovely body, these gods and humans, having faith in that stupa, are performing meritorious deeds."

"Having offered [this], one is liberated from aging and death. This stūpa is to be known as the stūpa of the Great Sage, the Sugata who possesses the Ten Powers and upholds the Dhamma"—such is the construction of the meaning. This is a *sutta*... [etc. ...a *sutta*.
"By me, who offered four blue lotuses and a garland to the stūpa of the Great Sage—" by that [merit] of mine...
"That merit was indeed sublime. From that eon until today, for thirty eons, having honored the Teacher’s stupa, those [beings] endure;
"I do not know such a state of woe, nor do I go to the lower realms"—this is the construction.
This is a sutta... [etc. ...a sutta.
I worshipped the stupa of the Lord of the World, who possesses the thirty-two marks, who is endowed with the thirty-two marks, and who has conquered all conquerors;
having worshipped it, I remained joyful for a hundred thousand aeons throughout the duration of my life.
By whatever merit I have performed, through that merit, may I not fall into the lower realms, and without falling there, may I attain the splendor of the devas.
I have brought about both prosperity and those divine kingdoms; or rather, divine splendor has been brought about by me, and kingdoms have been ruled by me.

In the teaching of the Tamer of the Untamed, that eye—the eye of wisdom—that was established, and likewise that mind—the liberated mind—that was established, all that eye of wisdom and liberated mind has been attained by me.
I am one whose craving, known as the "waving creeper," has been shaken off.
The construction is: "Having offered [the gift], we said, 'We are those whose minds are liberated and who are endowed with minds liberated by the fruit. This is a sutta...

[etc. ...a sutta. 98. To one whose mind was liberated, who was endowed with a mind liberated by the fruit, who was unblemished, free from the five mental stumps, free from taints, dwelling in non-conflict, habituated to dwelling in non-conflict, whose mind was unattached and unclinging—to that Paccekabuddha, I gave a mere offering of millet porridge and water.

In that Pratyekabuddha, I placed my confidence in the supreme Dhamma, the Dhamma of Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, believing: "That supreme Dhamma exists. Thus, I directed my mind toward that Dhamma, thinking:
"May I come to have association with Pratyekabuddhas who dwell in such noble abodes; and may I never again be possessed of longing [for worldly things]."
“I too might realize the Dhamma attained by this Paccekabuddha,” I thus made a mental aspiration.
As the result of that very deed performed toward the Paccekabuddha, I was reborn among the long-lived Kurus of Uttarakuru—
beings who are without possessiveness, who lack the sense of "mine" or "my belongings," and who are distinguished and free from deficiency.
A thousand times you were reborn among beings with hands; a thousand times I was reborn there.

Through the ripening of that very same karma, having attained a distinguished body as the glorious god Tidasa, surrounded by a retinue and adorned with various garlands, ornaments, and ointments, you were reborn a thousand times.

Through the ripening of that very same karma, I became one whose mind is liberated, free from the stake, and taintless—having transcended both the wholesome and the unwholesome, which are the basis for benefit and harm.
“I had a meeting with these Paccekabuddhas who were bearing their final bodies, or with the disciples of the Buddha.
‘Whatever is desired by one of virtuous conduct succeeds’— the Tathāgata, the Conqueror, spoke this very statement after having made it manifest,
for in whatever way and by whatever means it was conceived in my mind, it came to pass exactly so.”
It becomes prosperous in each respective way. The construction is: "This existence is the final existence. This is a sutta... [pe] ...a sutta.
In the thirty-first aeon, the Victor Anejo (the Unshakable), named Sikhī and possessed of infinite vision, appeared.
Of that Blessed One as well, the king was his brother; and during the time of the Buddha named Sikhī and of the Dhamma of that Blessed One—

And having full confidence in the Leader of the World, after that Great Seer— the God beyond gods, the Supreme among men— had attained final Nibbāna, I had a vast and great stupa built, measuring a league in circumference on all sides. A man,
having taken jasmine flowers born of their own season, joyfully brought an offering of worship to that stupa and paid homage.
A single flower fell upon that man after being struck by the wind.
I took that fallen flower and gave it to its owner.
That man, the owner of the flower, became deeply inspired with faith and said to me, "You yourself should offer this single flower."

"I gave. In the word *dadāsī*, the letter *da* is an augment (*āgama*). Having taken that single flower and recollecting again and again the Buddha and the qualities of the Buddha, from the aeon in which I offered it until today, thirty aeons have passed.
During those aeons, I do not recall being born in an unhappy destination, nor did I go to a state of ruin; this is the fruit of worship at a stupa.
"They bear fruit," is the connection [of the phrase]. This is the Sutta... [etc. ...the Sutta.
Kapila by name was the city of King Brahmadatta—so called because of his name Brahmadatta—which was well-laid out, meaning it was properly divided into sections;
it possessed great highways, was crowded, and was filled with people of various kinds.
It was prosperous and flourishing.
There, in that most excellent city of the Pañcālas, I was selling sour gruel.
There, near the illustrious Upariṭṭha, I saw a self-enlightened Buddha (paccekabuddha) named Ariṭṭha; having seen him, my heart was filled with joy.
Having pleased that supreme among men, I invited Ariṭṭha— who was always provided with a regular meal in my home—
to that very same regular meal. And when the month of Kattika arrived, on the fifteenth day when the moon was full, on that full-moon fifteenth day,
I took a pair of new garments and presented them to Ariṭṭha, the Paccekabuddha named Ariṭṭha.
The supreme man, compassionate, merciful, the destroyer of craving, the Sage, the Paccekabuddha, having perceived my devout mind, accepted [the offering].

Having performed that wholesome deed praised by the Buddhas, I wandered through the realms of gods and humans; then, passing away from there, I was reborn as the only son of a wealthy merchant in a noble family in the city of Bārāṇasī, and I was dearer to them than their own lives.
Then, having attained full consciousness at that time and being exhorted by the son of a god, I descended from the palace and approached the Blessed One Gotama, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Out of compassion for me, that Blessed One Gotama, the Perfectly Awakened One, taught the Dhamma: suffering and the truth of suffering;
the origin of suffering and the truth of its origin; the transcendence of suffering and the noble eightfold path, which is the truth of cessation.

The Sage, the Blessed Gotama, taught the four truths: the path leading to the subsiding of suffering and the truth of the path itself; he did not teach any other doctrine that produces those [truths].
Having heard the word of that Blessed Gotama, I dwelt delighting in his teaching; untiring by day and night, I penetrated *samatha*.
“Whatever taints there were internally and whatever taints there were externally, all those taints have been utterly destroyed by the Path; they have been found within me and shall never arise again.
Suffering has been brought to its limit—that is, ‘the suffering of which [I have made] an end’—this heap, this cycle of birth and death, has become final and last.
Now, immediately following this present existence, there is no further becoming for me,” he said.

The Exposition (*yojanā*). That various kinds of discourses pertaining to the portion of habitual tendencies (*vāsanābhāgiya*) which have been determined by way of illustration—this various discourse is called "pertaining to the portion of habitual tendencies" because it functions as both an expresser and an indicator with respect to the category of merit that constitutes the portion of habitual tendencies.
Various kinds of discourses pertaining to the portion of habitual tendencies have been determined by the Teacher and are known by us. "Which [one]..."
Because it was asked, "What is a discourse partaking of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta*)?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is a discourse partaking of penetration?
was stated. Therein, among those sixteen discourses—beginning with those partaking of defilement—he asks: "Which discourse is called a discourse partaking of penetration?"
Above in the Brahma-world and below in the sense-sphere existence—liberated in every respect from all states of existence, the Arahant does not regard [anything] as "this is the Dhamma, I am this.
Thus liberated, the Arahant has crossed over the flood never crossed before, for the sake of no further becoming;
"he has crossed over" is the construction. This Sutta concerns the state of training (sekha-dhamma) within the sphere of penetration (nibbedha-bhāga).
It is called a discourse conducive to penetration because it proceeds by way of making known and causing understanding.
Because it must be stated as "only this much," the words beginning with "for one who is virtuous" are spoken.
Ānanda, for a person who is virtuous, no volition need be made nor should it be performed in the form: "How might remorse not arise or occur in me? Ānanda, [this is so].
When non-regret arises and proceeds in one who is virtuous, this is the natural law (dhammatā) regarding the arising and proceeding of non-regret.
Ānanda, a person who is without regret need not form the intention, "How might joy arise and proceed for me? For in a person without regret, joy [arises naturally].

It would arise and proceed; this is the natural law regarding the arising and proceeding of gladness. The method of application for the remaining [factors] should be understood by following this same method of application.
This discourse is also known as a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta*).
For a brahmin who is ardent, endowed with right exertion through the burning away of the defilements, and who is meditating, thus meditating...

When, at whatever time, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhammā*)—which are the means for realizing the mode of conditions in conformity with the Dhamma of one who has cast off evil and whose taints are exhausted—manifest or arise with absolute certainty;

or alternatively, when the Dhammas, namely the Dhammas of the Four Noble Truths, manifest, are made clear, and become evident through the process of direct realization (*abhisamaya*); or else, at the time of their manifestation, for him...
For the ardent, meditating brahmin whose taints are exhausted, all doubts fade away, depart, and cease.

Why? Because he understands, knows, and penetrates the dhamma of the mass of suffering—which arises together with its causes such as ignorance, consisting of formations and so forth, and which is unmixed with pleasure—therefore they fade away.
The construction is: "they depart" and "they cease. This sutta is called a sutta pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).

In the second verse, however, the construction is: "Since he has known, understood, and penetrated the destruction of conditions—that is, Nibbāna, which is termed 'destruction'—therefore all doubts have vanished.
This sutta is a sutta pertaining to penetration. "Tissa, why are you angry? Do not be angry, Tissa; for you, non-anger and the absence of malice are better and supreme."
"Is it true, Tissa, that you lead the holy life for the sake of subduing anger, conceit, and malice?"—this is how the Blessed One spoke.

The construction is as follows: [he asked this] of Nanda, who was at that time subsisting on a mixed meal obtained through the effort of wandering for alms by means of "gleaning"—that is, by standing in an order of houses while remaining unrecognized and unobserved.
"I would see," he said—this is the construction. This sutta is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
"Gotama, what is it that, having been cut and struck down by one who strikes, does not burn with the fever of anger, and thus one sleeps in comfort?
What is it that, having been cut and struck down by one who strikes, has its sorrow destroyed through the destruction of anger?"
"Having offered it, one does not grieve, Gotama; what single thing do you approve as its slaughter and destruction? thus the brahmin asks.

"Brahmin, by cutting off and slaying anger, by destroying it, and by not being consumed by the fever of anger, one sleeps and lies down in happiness; by cutting off and slaying anger, by destroying it, through the destruction of anger—"
Having destroyed his mental distress, he does not grieve;

the Noble Ones—the Buddhas and others—praise the slaying, the striking down, of anger, which has its root in poison, is like poison, is the source of suffering, yet has a sweet tip, being designated as "sweet" because it ends in pleasure.
For it is true that by cutting off and destroying that anger and the act of being angry, [one attains peace].

The construction is as follows: "Vadhanto" means that having become one whose mental distress (*domanassa*) is destroyed by the destruction of anger, he "lies," that is, he rests. Regarding the term *madhuragga*:

it should be understood as a compound meaning "having sweetness as its peak," where "sweetness" (*madhura*) refers to mental happiness (*cetasika-sukha*), and "peak" (*agga*) refers to the excellence or conclusion of that anger.
For in one who is angry—after reviling, abusing, and striking—the enjoyment of mental happiness occurs at the very end.
"It arises. This discourse is a discourse pertaining to penetration.
"O Gotama, what is it that the wise man, when striking, should strike down as it has arisen?
What is it that the wise man, when dispelling, should dispel once it has been born? And what is it that the wise man, when abandoning, should abandon?"
“The realization of what Dhamma is bliss for a wise person? asks the deity.
“Devaputta, the wise person, destroying, should destroy arisen anger; he should destroy it as one who destroys. Dispelling, the wise person should dispel arisen lust;
he should dispel it as one who dispels. Abandoning, the wise person should abandon ignorance; he should abandon it as one who abandons. [This is] the realization of the True Dhamma.”
"Direct realization is happiness," said the Blessed One—this is the construction [of the sentence]. This discourse is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*). 101.
Just as a man struck by a spear, pierced from above down to below, exerts effort for the removal of that spear;
or just as a man whose head is burning with fire, with his head ablaze, exerts effort for the extinguishing of that fire...

The deity spoke thus: "As if exerting himself, a bhikkhu who is being consumed by sensual lust should wander and dwell mindful, possessed of mindfulness, and diligent, striving for the abandoning of sensual lust and the suppression of sensual lust.
However, the Blessed One said, "As if struck by a sword," and so forth, in order to show that "exertion must be undertaken for the sake of eradication."
Devaputta, just as a man struck by a spear exerts effort to cast off that spear, or as a man whose head is burning with fire exerts effort to extinguish that fire,
so too a monk overcome by the view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is diligent for the sake of abandoning that view of a personal body— its abandonment through the path and its total eradication.
"The Blessed One said: 'Exerting himself, being mindful and possessed of mindfulness, one should wander and dwell'—this is the construction [of the sentence].
This sutta is called a sutta pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
All accumulations of wealth end in exhaustion and have exhaustion as their conclusion; all elevated states of phenomena end in falling."
They end in falling; for all beings, in light of death, life is unstable.

Thus, considering this aforementioned danger, its cause—death—and looking toward conventional death, the wise person performs meritorious deeds consisting of giving, virtue, and meditation, which bring about happiness pertaining to the present life and happiness pertaining to future lives.
"Let him do so," the deity said.
"Son of the gods, all accumulations of wealth end in exhaustion; all lofty structures end in falling;
for all beings, in the face of death, life is unstable."

Thus, regarding this aforementioned fear and its cause—death—the wise person, looking toward peace and desiring *nibbāna*, which is the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), should abandon the bait of the world, namely the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "He should abandon it," so said the Blessed One; such is the construction [of the sentence].
This discourse is known as a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta*).
Those sages whose minds delight in meditation, who find joy in meditation, sleep happily and do not grieve. The wise person—
possessed of wisdom regarding the path, well-concentrated, energetic, resolute, with a mind directed toward Nibbāna—
crosses over the flood of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross.

The construction is as follows: one who is detached from the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*), whose mind has departed [from it], who is an *āsava*-destroyer (*khīṇāsava*) having transcended all fetters (*saṃyojana*), who has transcended all fetters by means of the path of *arahantship*, and for whom delight in existence (*nandibhava*) has been utterly exhausted—that *āsava*-destroyer does not sink in the deep ocean of *saṃsāra*.

"Delight-existence" (*nandibhava*) refers to craving (*taṇhā*)—which is designated as "delight"—as well as the existence of sense-sphere becoming (*kāmabhava*), fine-material becoming (*rūpabhava*), and immaterial becoming (*arūpabhava*).
The compound *nandibhavaparikkhīṇo* should be understood as "one for whom craving and existence have been completely exhausted," referring to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
This discourse is known as a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta*).

[It concerns] the Dhamma of the Arahants—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which are divided into categories such as right conduct and so forth.
The wise person who has faith in the Dhamma, and having become one who has faith, being heedful and discerning for the attainment of Nibbāna, should be one who desires to hear;
such a wise person obtains wisdom—both mundane and supramundane wisdom.
That energetic individual who acts in a suitable place, not neglecting the factors of place, time, and so forth, [practices] that which is appropriate to the mundane and supramundane Dhamma...
He applies the means for realization; being "steadfast" through mental energy, he does not cast off his burden;
being "an ariser" by virtue of physical energy, he is endowed with exertion. Such a person of energy finds and attains wealth—both mundane and supramundane wealth.
Through truth, both in terms of verbal truth and ultimate truth, the true person, established in the Dhamma of truth, is headed by the Buddha and others.
He attains fame. By giving—by bestowing whatever is desired or wished for, by practicing and employing the four bases of sympathy—the true person binds and secures friends who are exclusively loyal.
Thus, endowed with these four qualities of truth, dhamma, virtue, and generosity, that true person, having passed away from this world to the next world, [is freed] from the cause of absolute sorrow.
The construction is: "Because of non-existence, he does not grieve.

Gotama, you, the ascetic who has abandoned all fetters, who is liberated from the three states of existence, mindful and possessed of mindfulness—whatever instruction you give, whatever teaching you perform for others such as gods and humans, that instruction belongs to one who has abandoned all fetters.
“A recluse who is liberated from the three states of existence— it is not right for you [to address him thus],” said the yakkha named Sakka,
a follower of Māra, addressing him with this verse:
“O Sakka, yakkha named Sakka, with any man whatsoever, out of compassion, for whatever reason...”
Living together in one place gives rise to companionship;
a wise person ought not to fail to feel compassion in their mind for that companion who has come to live with them, but rather ought to show compassion.
Whatever compassion, pity, kindness, loving-kindness, and gladness have arisen—by means of that compassion, pity, kindness, loving-kindness, and gladness.
And the Blessed One said that when a wise and virtuous person, with a mind uplifted and serene, instructs others— whether gods, humans, or others—
and gives them such instruction, that wise and virtuous person, through that instruction,
is not bound by an unfavorable bond consisting of the fetters such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). This is the construction of the sentence.
“Ascetic, from what source do these two states—lust and hatred—arise; what is their origin, what is their condition?
And from where do these three arise, and from where do they come: discontent, delight, and horripilation?
It is as if young boys were to catch a hawk or a crow, bind its feet with a long string, wind the end of the string around their finger, and let it go.”
"From where do mental thoughts arise and cause the mind to be released? Thus the yakkha Sūciloma asked the Blessed One.
"Lust and hatred—these two states arise from this source, from this personal existence.
Discontent, delight, and horripilation—these three arise from this, from this self. It is like young boys who, having caught a hawk or a crow..."
Just as they might bind [something] to the foot with a long thread, wrap the end of the thread around a finger, and let it go,
so too do mental thoughts arise from this selfhood and let the mind go.
Just as shoots growing from the trunk of a banyan tree are produced upon its branches, or as the *māluvā* creeper grows by depending on a tree in the forest.
Just as a creeper, having completely overspread that tree, stands there spread out and entwined on all sides, even so, O Yakkha, listen:
those manifold kinds of mental thoughts born of affection— that is, born from the moisture of craving, produced within oneself, arisen within oneself—
including both evil mental thoughts and the defilements associated with them— remain stuck, attached, and entangled in sense pleasures, that is, in objective sensual desires.
Those wise ones who understand the thicket of defilements— the truth of origination— as the source from which this personal existence arises,

thinking, "What is the cause of this personal existence?"— those wise ones dispel that thicket of defilements, which is the truth of origination and the source of the truth of suffering known as personal existence,
by means of the truth of the path. This is for the sake of non-renewal of existence, for the sake of the truth of cessation known as non-renewal of existence.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "The Blessed One said that they are crossing this fourfold flood of defilement, which is difficult to cross and which has never before been crossed even in a dream throughout the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra.
"Blessed One, the performance of the ascetic’s duty is indeed difficult; Blessed One, the performance of the ascetic’s duty..."

"Indeed, it is very difficult, truly most difficult," said one son of good family who, having gone forth and practiced the duty of a recluse, died before reaching the stage of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi) and was reborn in the world of the gods. That son of the gods approached the Blessed One and said:
"O Giver of Desires, even for the seven types of persons in training (sekkhā), who are established through concentration in virtue and whose nature is stable, it is indeed difficult."

“They perform the duties of a recluse (samaṇadhamma). For one who has entered the homeless life, who has attained the state of renunciation, and who is a wanderer, contentment with the four requisites brings happiness,” said the Blessed One.
“Blessed One, this contentment which brings happiness—this contentment is difficult to find,” said that son of the gods.
“Kāmada, those trainees whose minds, by day and by night, delight in meditation and delight in the stilling of the mind,
those trainees obtain satisfaction even when it is difficult to find,” said the Blessed One.
“Blessed One, this very mind that delights in meditation is difficult to concentrate,” he replied.
The son of the gods said: "O Kāmada, those noble ones who delight day and night in the tranquility of the faculties—those noble ones, O Kāmada, compose even a mind that is difficult to compose;
having cut through the net of Māra, the net of defilements, those noble ones proceed upon the path.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
“Blessed One, that path which is uneven by way of the preliminary practice is a difficult path to traverse,” said that son of the gods.
“Kāmada, the noble ones travel even on a path that is difficult to traverse or uneven; the ignoble ones fall headlong upon an uneven path.
For that path of the noble ones becomes level, not uneven. Indeed, truth is the level ground for those whose bodies are free from attachment.”
"The Noble Ones become equanimous," thus spoke the Blessed One—this is the construction [of the verse]. 103.
That Jeta’s Grove, frequented by the assembly of seers and inhabited by the King of Dhamma—that very Jeta’s Grove produces joy for me; it is indeed a producer of joy (*pīti-sañjanana*).
Action (*kamma*) is the volitional action of the path, and knowledge (*vijjā*) is the wisdom of the path; the Dhamma is concentration (*samādhi*) as well as the factors conducive to concentration.
And the Dhamma is virtue; for one established in virtue, life is supreme. By means of this Eightfold Path, beings are purified;
beings are not purified by lineage or by wealth.
Therefore, seeing and perceiving his own welfare, a wise person [should strive] because it is by the Path alone that beings are purified.
One should investigate, investigate thoroughly the Dhamma—the factors conducive to enlightenment—by means of systematic method.
When there is such investigation, a person investigating therein within the Noble Path is purified.
Just as Sāriputta has gone to the further shore by means of virtue and tranquility, so too a bhikkhu who [possesses] virtue and tranquility...

The construction is as follows: "And having gone to the further shore—that bhikkhu would be the very highest, equal to Sāriputta"—thus spoke the divine son named Anāthapiṇḍika after approaching the Blessed One. This discourse is known as a *nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta* (a discourse pertaining to penetration).
One should not follow after the past—the five aggregates of the past—by means of craving or views; nor [should one follow] the future—the five aggregates of the future.

One should not long for or yearn for things through craving and views. Since that which is past has been abandoned, ceased, and come to an end, one should not pursue it because it has been abandoned, ceased, and come to an end.
Since that which is future has not yet arrived, one should not long for it.

The five aggregates of the present are subject to decay; wherever they arise—whether in this or that continuity (*santāna*) or in this or that forest and so forth—one contemplates those present phenomena with the contemplations of impermanence and so on.
By means of those contemplations of impermanence and so on, one [realizes] Nibbāna.

It is unshakable by lust and the other defilements, and it is unshakeable; that is Nibbāna. A person who possesses insight, being wise, should cultivate and increase it by entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object.
Diligence (*ātappa*)—the energy that scorches away the defilements—is such that one must do what is to be done this very day, for tomorrow there may be life or death.

Or who could know? One should not give rise to the thought, "I will perform meritorious deeds such as giving tomorrow," but rather one should exert effort with the resolve, "I shall do it this very day.

For indeed, by its nature as the cause of death, that Death possesses a great army consisting of many forces such as snakes, scorpions, poison, and weapons; therefore, one must act [now], for there is no way to cultivate friendship with him, nor can one bribe him with gifts.
"There is no bargain [to be struck].

Having thus attended to this in mind, the Sage, being peaceful, definitively declares that the true person who dwells practicing in this way—ardent, untiring day and night, not lazy, and diligent—is "one who has a single auspicious night" (*bhaddekaratta*). This is the construction: he indeed declares him as such.
The discourse beginning with "These four, monks... is well known from both the Pāḷi text and the commentary.
104. Various discourses pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) have been determined by the Teacher and are known to us;

however, because it must be asked, "Which discourse pertains to the state of one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*)?", it is said: "In this regard, which discourse pertains to the state of one beyond training? and so forth. "In this regard" (*tattha*) means:
among those sixteen discourses beginning with those pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), which discourse pertains to the state of one beyond training?
He asks: "What is called a 'sutta'?

That supreme person whose mind is like a rock—steadfast and unshaken by the winds of worldly conditions—and who is detached from gain and other things that cause passion, does not become angry at those things that provoke anger, such as loss and the like; of him...

The mind of the Supreme Person has been thus developed through [contemplation of] impermanence and so forth. How could suffering—caused by the transcendence of worldly conditions—come to that Supreme Person whose mind is so developed?

This is the construction of the sentence. This sutta is called "pertaining to the stage of one beyond training" (*asekkhabhāgiya*) because it functions as an expression and an indicator regarding the domain of the stage of one beyond training. This same method should be understood for those [suttas] that follow.

Because it must be stated that "this very discourse belongs to the category of those pertaining to the Asekha (the One Beyond Training)," the passage beginning with "And of the Venerable One" was spoken.
That brahmin who, by having banished evil states, has become one whose evil states are banished; who, by being free from the sound of "hum," has become one without the "hum";
who, by being free from the stains of the defilements, has become one without stain; and who, through the restraint of virtue, possesses a mind that is self-controlled—[he is truly a brahmin].

That brahmin would be one who has reached the end; because he has gone to the end, Nibbāna, through the knowledge of the four paths, he would be a "one who has reached the end of knowledge" (*vedantagū*).
Because he has lived the holy life according to the Dhamma, he would be "one who has lived the holy life" (*vusitabrahmacariyo*).
That brahmin in whom there are no excesses anywhere in the world—no excess of lust, no excess of hatred, no excess of delusion, no excess of conceit, and no excess of views—that brahmin...
The construction is: "The Blessed One said, 'One should utter the speech of a Brahmavādin, saying, "I am a brahmin.

Those Buddhas who, having banished evil and unwholesome states, always proceed mindful and possessed of mindfulness, with their fetters destroyed—they, those Buddhas, are indeed spoken of as "brahmins" in the world; this is the construction of what was said.
Wherein in Nibbāna neither water, nor earth, nor fire, nor wind finds a footing or establishes itself—therein...
In Nibbāna, the bright planets and stars do not shine;
there in Nibbāna the sun does not radiate, there in Nibbāna the moon does not gleam, and there in Nibbāna darkness is not found.
When a brahmin himself, as a sage, through his sagehood, has known, found, and attained that Nibbāna.

The construction is as follows: "He penetrates; then, at the moment of penetration, that brahmin is liberated from forms as form-phenomena and from the formless as formless-phenomena, and from pleasure and pain as pleasure and pain," he said.
O Yakkha, that brahmin [is liberated] from his own personal phenomena, from the aggregates of clinging, from the truths, and from phenomena...
And having reached the further shore, at the very moment of crossing over, that brahmin said:

"This *ajakalāpaka* mentioned by you, this *pisāca*—the *pisāca* of the defilements—and the confusion (*akkula*) created by you, which is further intensified (*pakkulakaraṇa*), he has transcended. This is the construction of the sentence.
As for the monk who [sees] his former wife coming toward him, or another woman approaching:

The construction is as follows: "I call that bhikkhu a 'brahmin' who does not rejoice in his mind over his former wife departing, nor does he grieve in his mind over another woman departing—him who is freed from attachment even from the fivefold attachment and who has conquered in battle. Thus he spoke.
The construction of the sentence is as follows: "In this river many people bathe, yet those many bathers do not become pure by means of water or by bathing in water.
But that person in whom truth and all other virtues exist—that person is pure, and that person is a brahmin," so he said.
The distinction between the pure and the impure has already been explained in detail in the commentary (*ṭīkā*).

When, for a brahmin who is ardent and meditative, the phenomena that are the true Dhamma become manifest in their absolute entirety—at that moment, at the time of the manifestation of the Dhammas—that brahmin stands dispelling, utterly dispelling, the army of Māra.
Because it must be asked, "Like what? it is said: "Like the sun illuminating the sky. The sun [illuminates] the sky.
"Shining as it were, he stands"—thus is the construction: "he stands in this manner.
That bhikkhu who is a wearer of rag-robes (paṃsukūlika), having transcended all four bonds (yoga), moves about in this world devoid of possessions (akiñcana) among those with possessions;
he conducts himself in the four modes of deportment (iriyāpatha). He is of a nature not subject to abandoning, meaning his essential state is such that he cannot be abandoned by any path.

With a body that has not yet reached [the goal], he has not yet reached the state of one possessing the threefold knowledge; yet, see that rag-robe wearing bhikkhu moving about with tranquil faculties.

Many sublime deities, having approached his Brahma-palace, [behold] that rag-robe wearing bhikkhu—a thoroughbred man, a noble steed of a person, who has suppressed the power of birth—[one] who suppresses the power proceeding from mere birth by saying, "I am a brahmin by birth. Here...
Having developed a mind of confidence toward the Teaching or the Brahma-palace, they pay homage. And here, the letter *na* is an augment (*āgama*). The construction is as follows:

"O Noble Steed among Men (*purisājañña*), let there be homage to you from us; O Supreme among Men (*purisuttama*), let there be homage to you from us. Since we do not recognize the support (*nissaya*) upon which you rely, upon what person do you meditate? Thus they spoke.

Those monks who from time to time, by way of hearing the Dhamma, have been meeting together for a long time—these monks are indeed companions. For these companion monks, the True Dhamma meets within the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha.

Well-trained in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble One, those companion monks, having conquered Māra along with his army, bear their final bodies as individual existences; such is the construction of the meaning.
If one applies lax energy, this Nibbāna—the liberation from all suffering—cannot be attained by the practitioner; nor can this Nibbāna be attained with only slight strength.
And as for this young bhikkhu practitioner: he who, having conquered Māra together with his host, bears his final body and personal existence—he is indeed a supreme person (*uttamapurisa*).
This is the construction of the passage. Where "person" (*purisa*) should have been said, "human being" (*porisa*) is used for the sake of guarding the meter.
The construction of the sentence is as follows: "Mogharāja, that bhikkhu— ugly, wearing coarse robes, always mindful and possessed of mindfulness, with taints destroyed, detached,
having done what was to be done, free from taints, possessing the threefold knowledge, attained to psychic power, and skilled in the penetration of minds—
having conquered Māra together with his host, bears his final body," he said.

105. In such passages as “The Tathāgata,” the application [of the terms] is evident. This discourse is called an "asekkhabhāgiya-sutta" (a discourse pertaining to the stage of one beyond training) because it functions by way of expressing and indicating the portion or the object pertaining to the Asekhas (those beyond training). 106.
Various types of *asekkhabhāgiya* discourses have been determined by the Teacher and are known to us.

Since it must be stated, "Which is the discourse pertaining both to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*)?", [the text continues]: "In that regard, which is the discourse pertaining both to defilement..."

And it is said: “The discourse pertaining to defilement and the discourse pertaining to purification,” and so forth. Therein, among those sixteen discourses beginning with the discourse pertaining to defilement, he asks:
which discourse is called the discourse pertaining both to defilement and to purification?

[It is that which describes] a bhikkhu who, having committed six kinds of offenses, conceals them; while he is concealing them, the rainy season—[originally] for six days—overflows, and the open space...
When a monk who has committed an offense confesses it openly while declaring it, the rain of *dukkaṭa* and other offenses does not fall upon him;
therefore, because the rain falls excessively upon that which is concealed but not upon that which is open, one should uncover what is concealed—confess, declare, and reveal the offense.
When there is such an uncovering, the rain of *dukkaṭa* and other offenses does not fall upon that monk who is uncovering it.
The construction is: "It does not rain excessively.

Since it must be asked, "In this sutta, by how much is defilement (saṃkilesa) shown, and by how much is the latent tendency (vāsanā) shown?"—the phrase "It rains excessively on what is covered" shows defilement;
"It does not rain excessively on what is open" shows the latent tendency; therefore, "Open what is covered."
Thus it was said: “In this way, the rain will not soak it. By the words “The covered is soaked by the rain,” defilement (*saṃkilesa*) is shown.
By the words “The uncovered is not soaked by the rain,” the latent tendency (*vāsanā*) is shown.
By the words “Therefore, uncover what is covered; in this way, the rain will not soak it,” both this defilement and this [tendency] are shown.

And the *vāsana* (habitual tendency) is also shown. This Sutta, “When it is covered... it rains,” is called both a *saṃkilesabhāgiya* (pertaining to defilement) and a *vāsanābhāgiya* (pertaining to purification) Sutta, because it functions as both an expresser and an indicator with respect to the domain of the side of defilement and the domain of the side of purification.
Since it must be stated that “the Suttas pertaining to defilement and the Suttas pertaining to purification are only this many,” [it is said]: “These four...”

The passage beginning with “Great King” was spoken. Because it must be asked, “Among those four types of persons, which persons partake of defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), and which persons partake of purification through habituation (vāsanābhāgiya)?”, the passage beginning with “In that regard, whichever person... was spoken.

“In that regard” (tattha) means among those four persons, such as those who go from darkness to darkness (tamotamaparāyana). Its meaning is clear. This refers to the passage beginning with “These four.”

Because it proceeds by way of both expressing and indicating the two types of persons who partake in defilement and the two types of persons who partake in purification, the discourse is called "the discourse partaking in defilement" and "the discourse partaking in purification.
Various kinds of discourses partaking in defilement and purification have been determined by the Teacher; [these] have been [presented] by us.
And since it must be asked, "Which is the discourse (sutta) that pertains both to defilement and to penetration?", it is therefore stated there:
"Which is the discourse that pertains both to defilement and to penetration? and so forth. Its meaning should be understood according to the method already explained.
Whatever bond there is in the world made of iron, whatever bond made of wood, and whatever bond made of rattan— the wise ones,
the Buddhas and other learned persons, do not call those bonds of iron and the like "a firm bond.
Rather, it is that longing for jewels and earrings, for sons, and for wives— which is intensely passionate, colored by powerful passion— that they call a firm bond in the world.
"That which exists—this bond of lust known as infatuation and longing—the wise, those men of discernment, have called it a 'firm bond.
By this passage from the Sutta, this unwholesome state known as infatuation and longing is shown to be a defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
Since it must be stated by what penetration (*nibbedha*) is shown, the words beginning with "this" (*etam*) were spoken. The wise, those men of discernment, [regard] this...
They say that the bond of lust is a "firm bond. This bond of lust is "downward-leading" because it carries one away to the lower realms.
It is "loose" because, in its place as a bond, it does not disturb the skin and other parts of the body.
It is "difficult to release" because, through the power of greed, even a single instance of the bond of lust that has arisen is hard to untie.
Wise men, having severed even this aforementioned bond of lust by means of the Path, go forth as wanderers, abandoning sensual pleasure and becoming free from longing.
Thus, by this passage of the Sutta, this Path is shown as penetration (*nibbedha*).
This Sutta beginning with "This is not for me" (*idam ayasaṃ*) pertains both to the sphere of the defilements such as lust and to the sphere of the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Because it proceeds by way of the relationship between the signifier and the signified, it is called a discourse dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and a discourse dealing with purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
(107) "Monks, whatever one intends and whatever volition one brings forth, whatever one plans and whatever planning one performs,
whatever one underlies and whatever underlying tendency there is— this is volition, this is planning."
The underlying tendency is the objective condition for the persistence of consciousness. When the objective condition exists, there is a foundation for that volitional consciousness.

When that volitional consciousness is established and has grown, there is the production of renewed existence in the future, which is the production of consciousness and so forth. From the production of renewed existence in the future...
When there is [this], birth, aging, and death come to be in the future. In the future, sorrow... [and so on] ...there is an origination.
Monks, if one does not intend, if one does not plan, yet if there is still a latent tendency, that latent tendency exists;
