thus, this latent tendency becomes the objective support and condition for consciousness, for the volitional-formative consciousness... [and so on].
...there is an origin. Thus, by this passage from the Sutta, this aforementioned unwholesome state consisting of volition and so forth is shown as defilement (*saṃkileso*).
Since it must be asked, "By what is penetration (*nibbedho*) shown?", the words beginning with "And from which" (*yato ca*) were spoken.
"Monks, when one who possesses the Noble Path neither wills (*ceteti*), nor intends (*pakappeti*), nor underlies [with latent tendencies] (*anuseti*), that is non-willing, that is non-intending..."
The non-inclination (*an-anusayana*) is not a condition for consciousness—that is, for the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*)—as its object...
[etc. ...in the future, birth, aging, and death cease; in the future, sorrow... [etc. ...cease... [etc. ...there is cessation.
Thus, by this passage from the Sutta, this Noble Path is shown as penetration (*nibbedha*). This refers to the section beginning with "And what, monks... (*yañca bhikkhave*).

Because it functions as both an expressive and an indicative discourse regarding the portion of defilement and the portion of penetration, it is called "discourse pertaining to the portion of defilement" and "discourse pertaining to the portion of penetration. 108.
The Teacher has determined various kinds of discourse pertaining to the portion of defilement and the portion of penetration.
And because it was asked by us, "Which is the discourse that pertains both to defilement and to the state of one beyond training (asekkha)?
the passage beginning with "In this regard, which is the discourse that pertains both to defilement and to the state of one beyond training? was stated.
Its meaning should be understood according to the method already explained.
“Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of the ocean, the watery sea, as ‘the ocean, the ocean.
In what sense does he speak thus? He speaks of it as ‘the ocean’ in the sense of being difficult to fill, in the sense of its vast expanse, and in the sense of its being difficult to cross.
This being so, monks, this watery sea, the ocean, [is not the ocean] of the Noble One, the Blessed One.”
In the sense described in the Vinaya, it is not an ocean. Monks, this is a water-ocean, a great mass of water, a great expanse of water.
Monks, the eye is an ocean for a person; its current consists of forms, consisting of the form-base.
In what sense? From the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world, there is the objective support of forms such as blue and so forth.

The eye itself is the ocean, in the sense that it is difficult to fill even as it flows in, and in the sense that it is difficult to cross over due to wandering through the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

The blue and other forms (*rūpāyatana*) themselves are the surge, in the sense that they wander with an immeasurable force consisting of immeasurable waves of blue and other forms. Thus, by this passage from the Sutta, this eye—
The ocean is shown as form, the surge, and the cause of defilement.
Since it must be asked, "By what is the one beyond training (asekkha) shown?", the passage beginning with "He who... is stated.
Established in that fruit of Arhatship, the Arhat endures that surge consisting of form: lust for agreeable forms, hatred toward disagreeable forms, and [aversion] toward indifference.

"Without giving rise to delusion, he endures through the state of equanimity; this Arahant, monks, is said to have crossed the ocean of the eye, which has its waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons.
Having crossed over and reached the further shore, he stands on dry land—he is called a brahmin.
By this passage from the Sutta, this Asekha who has attained the fruit of Arahantship is shown.
In such passages as “The ear, monks,” etc., the meaning should be understood according to this same method as applicable in each case.

This discourse beginning with “The ocean” is called both a discourse on the side of defilement and a discourse on the side of the Adept, because it functions by way of expressing and indicating both the sphere of the side of defilement and the sphere of the side of the Adept.
Because it must be said that "it is only this much," the words "these six," and so forth, are spoken.
Monks, these six hooks—which I am about to describe—exist in the world for the ruin, the disadvantage, and the affliction of living beings. What are the six?
Monks, those things cognizable by the eye, cognizable by visual consciousness, which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, agreeable, and provocative of lust.
There exist forms that are lovely, pleasant by nature, connected with sensual desire, accompanied by the defilements of sensual desire, and alluring—namely, objects such as blue and other colors.
If a bhikkhu delights in such a form, he rejoices facing it with craving accompanied by rapture;
if he welcomes it, he welcomes it by way of craving, causing himself to say, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!"
When he remains clinging to it, as if having swallowed it and brought it to completion—being thus, monks, this bhikkhu is called "one who has swallowed the hook...
[and so on] ...of the Evil One. And here, although the plural designation "forms that are desirable...

[and so on] ...enticing" is used because of their manifold nature through distinctions such as blue and so forth, it is nevertheless by way of being the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) and the object of form (*rūpārammaṇa*)...
And because it does not transcend its singlefold nature by way of being cognizable by the eye, it should be understood that the singular designation “it” (*taṃ*) is employed.
In such passages as “There are, monks, [sounds] cognizable by the ear,” the meaning should be understood according to this same method, as applicable.
Thus, by means of this portion of the Sutta, this sixfold hook consisting of what is cognizable by the eye and so forth—
Defilement and the cause of defilement have been shown.
Since it must be asked, "By what is the state of one beyond training (asekkha) shown?", the passage beginning with "And there are" was stated.
"He broke," "he split," "he broke all around. Thus, by this portion of the Sutta, this [state] consisting of the fruit of Arhatship—

The one beyond training (asekkha) has been shown. This sutta beginning with “These six,” etc., is called a sutta dealing with defilement and a sutta dealing with the state of one beyond training according to the method already stated.
109. The teacher has determined various suttas dealing with defilement and dealing with the state of one beyond training, and we have understood them.
[Now,] which is the sutta dealing with defilement, dealing with penetration (nibbedha), and dealing with the state of one beyond training?

Because it was necessary to ask, "What is the discourse (sutta) that pertains to defilement, pertains to penetration, and pertains to the state of one beyond training (asekkha)? the following was stated: "In this regard, what is the discourse that pertains to defilement, pertains to penetration, and pertains to the state of one beyond training?
This world—the world of sentient beings—is born of torment; it is born of the torment of grief through such things as the loss of kinsmen, and it is [also] born of passion and so forth.
Afflicted by the burning heat of fever, overcome by contact, and overwhelmed by manifold painful sensations, he weeps and cries out.
What does he say? Being unable to endure the suffering that has touched him because his body has not been cultivated, he weeps and laments, saying:
"Alas, what suffering! May such suffering never befall even my enemy," and so forth.
Because it must be asked, "Why does he speak thus?", the passage beginning with "In whatever way they conceive [it] as self" is stated.

These beings, by whatever manner—such as through attachment to sensual pleasures—they conceive of a remedy for suffering as being the self, that suffering must indeed be treated in a way other than that manner, by means of another method; for such is the case.

"Subject to change" (*aññathābhāvī*): because one who is weeping speaks while weeping, or whatever manner of harming others and so forth by which they imagine or hope for their own increase, from that very manner there occurs only non-increase.
Since that which is hoped for is subject to change—that is, it results only in non-increase—therefore, regarding both what is imagined and what is hoped for...
Because his nature is to exist otherwise [in another state], he speaks while weeping; this world of beings speaks while being in a state of weeping.
Because it is something that ought to be asked, "What? the passage beginning with "attached to existence" (bhavasatto) was stated.

Attached to existence—meaning the world is bound and fastened to the states of existence such as the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava)—the world rejoices only in existence, that is, in the states of existence such as sense-sphere existence. Whatever existence one rejoices in, because it is followed by many calamities such as aging and death...
It is "fear" in the sense of being terrifying. That from which one fears—such as aging, death, and so forth—is "suffering" because it serves as the basis for suffering, such as aging and death;
thus it is called the "basis of suffering. Therefore, by this passage from the Sutta, this defilement consisting of torment and the rest, along with its cause, is shown.
The defilement has been shown; since it must be stated by what penetration is shown, the passage beginning with “for the sake of abandoning existence” (*bhavavippahānāya*) was spoken.

Indeed, for the sake of abandoning existence—that is, for the purpose of relinquishing existence such as sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*)—this very holy life (*brahmacariya*), which is the path attained by me, is lived.
Thus, by this portion of the Sutta, this [path] which constitutes the holy life...
The path of penetration has been shown.
By the words beginning with “for the abandoning of existence,” the teacher has shown the path that leads exclusively to liberation as penetration, and this has been understood by us;
however, because it must be asked, “Which is the path that does not lead to liberation? the passage beginning with “Whatever recluses or... was spoken.
The word *hi* has the sense of eloquence in speech. Whatever recluses or whatever brahmins have declared liberation from existence— that is, from existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*)—

or have declared liberation from existence by means of existence— that is, from both existence in the realm of sensual desire (*kāmabhava*) and existence in the realm of form by means of existence in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*)—
all those recluses or all those brahmins [have spoken falsely].
"I say that they are 'beings' because they are not liberated from existence (bhava) of the kind already described.

Since it must be said that "those who claim liberation from existence such as the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) by means of existence such as the fine-material existence (rūpabhava)," the passage beginning with "But those who...
was stated in order to show that they claim the escape from existence by means of non-existence (vibhava). "And whatever recluses... [the text continues].
Or whatever brahmins have declared that liberation from existence— that is, from the existence of the cycle of rebirth— is through non-existence or the view of annihilation,
I say that all those recluses or all those brahmins remain indeed unliberated from existence,
from the existence of the cycle of rebirth. Because it must be asked, "Why are they unliberated?", [the following] is stated to show the reason for their lack of liberation.

“‘Upadhiṃ hi’ and so forth was said. This suffering—the suffering of saṃsāra—arises because it comes into being dependent upon *upadhi*, namely the aggregates (*khandha-upadhi*), the defilements (*kilesa-upadhi*), and volitional formations (*abhisankhāra-upadhi*);
therefore, they are not free from them. Thus, by this passage from the Sutta, this corruption known as wrong view is shown.

Since corruption has been shown by the words ‘whosoever,’ etc., one must state by what penetration (*nibbedha*) is shown; hence, ‘Through the destruction of all clinging (*sabbupādānakkhayā*),’ and so forth.”
It has been stated. Through the total destruction of all clinging, by means of the Noble Path, there is no arising of suffering—that is, the suffering of saṃsāra.
Thus, by this passage from the Sutta, this Noble Path is shown as penetration (*nibbedha*).
To show that it is also shown by another passage from the Sutta in the manner already described, the words beginning with "this world" (*lokaṃ imaṃ*) were spoken. [The word] *puthū*...

O my mind, look upon this world: the five aggregates, which are individually overcome and overwhelmed by ignorance, delighting in beings—men and women who delight in one another—and being unliberated from existences.
Whatever existences there may be, whether they be of brief duration or long-lived, whether they be pleasant or unpleasant.
The five aggregates as existence (*bhava*) occurred everywhere—in all these [directions] "above, below, and across"—by way of being in all places and by way of their state as everything.
All those existences of the aforementioned kind were impermanent because they are devoid of permanence and stability;

they were suffering because they are oppressed; and they were subject to change because of their nature of transformation. Thus, by this passage from the Sutta, this defilement beginning with ignorance is shown.
By the passage beginning with “This world,” defilement has been shown. Since it must be asked, “By what is penetration shown?

the passage beginning with “Thus this” is stated. For a person who sees this fivefold aggregate as it really is with right wisdom—either by means of his own path-wisdom or insight-wisdom—in the manner thus described, craving for existence...
It is abandoned. Seeing the five aggregates as they truly are with right wisdom, one does not delight in or long for the view of annihilationism (*vibhava-uccheda-diṭṭhi*).
For that person, through the complete destruction of all cravings, there is cessation—the cessation known as the total fading away—by means of the path termed the total fading away;
this is Nibbāna, this is extinction (*nibbuti*). Thus, by this...
This path of penetration (*nibbedha*) is shown by a passage from the Sutta.

Penetration is shown by the words beginning with "Thus it is" (*evametam*); since it must be stated by whom the state of one beyond training (*asekkha*) is shown, the words "of him who has attained extinction" (*tassa nibbutassa*) and so forth are spoken.
Because that bhikkhu—who has attained extinction regarding craving and views—does not produce further defilements or volitional formations through clinging (*anupādā*).

Because of non-grasping, there is no further existence; by such a noble person (ariyapuggala), the fivefold Māra that previously overcame him has been conquered. This noble person has won the battle against the five Māras.

In that battle—or regarding the desirable and undesirable and so forth—the noble person, being "such-like" (tādī) and having attained the characteristic of being "such-like," has transcended all states of existence.
"He was born having transcended. Thus, by this passage from the Sutta, this Asekha (one beyond training) is shown.

This aforementioned type of Sutta—beginning with "This world"—is both *saṃkilesabhāgiya* (concerning defilement) and *nibbedhabhāgiya* (concerning penetration), because it functions, even partially, as a speaker and indicator regarding the domain of defilement, the domain of penetration, and the domain of the state of one beyond training.
And there is the discourse pertaining to those beyond training (*asekkha*). Because it must be stated that "it is only this much," the passage beginning with "These four" was spoken.

The blind worldling is called one who goes with the stream (*anusotagāmī*) because he proceeds in accordance with the current of saṃsāra; the noble worldling, however, [proceeds] by means of the contemplation of disenchantment with the current of saṃsāra and so forth...
It is called "going against the stream" because it proceeds by way of the repulsive (paṭikkūla).

The trainee (sekkha) is called "steadfast in self" because his nature is established through the possession of unshakable confidence and so forth. The one beyond training (asekkha) is said to "stand on firm ground" because he stands having gone to the further shore of saṃsāra.
Regarding those four types of persons, since it was necessary to state which person belongs to the category of defilement and so forth, the passage beginning with "therein, whichever... was spoken.
110. Various suttas pertaining to defilement, pertaining to penetration, and pertaining to the state beyond training have been determined by the Teacher and are known to us.

Since it was necessary to ask, "Which is the sutta pertaining to defilement, pertaining to habituation, and pertaining to penetration?", the passage beginning with "In this regard, which... was stated.
There are six classes of persons found in the world. One born into a dark, low-born family is "dark by birth";

or, being dark due to being endowed with dark qualities, having become dark by birth, he gives birth to and produces the tenfold dark quality of immorality—such a person exists. By the manner described, he is dark and dark by birth.
Having sacrificed the tenfold dark dhamma, one is reborn into the bright; such a person exists.
Having been dark and born into the dark, one attains Nibbāna—which is neither dark nor bright, has neither dark nor bright fruition, and is seen absolutely—such a person exists.
By reversing what was stated, three other persons are to be understood.
Because it must be stated, beginning with, “Among those, which persons partake of defilement? and so forth, the passage beginning with “In that regard, whoever...
was spoken. Because it must be stated, “only this much,” the passage beginning with “These four... was spoken. 111.
The Teacher [has] explained various types of discourses (sutta) that partake of defilement, partake of purification through habituation, and partake of penetration.

This has been determined and understood by us. Because it must be asked, "Which suttas belong to the category of spiritual cultivation (vāsanābhāgiya) and which belong to the category of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)?", it was said:
"In that regard, which are those belonging to the category of spiritual cultivation and those belonging to the category of penetration?
Having attained the state of a human being—the human condition—there are two things: what is to be done (kicca) and what is not to be done (akicca). There are indeed two duties.
[These] are to be performed. Therefore, the commentator says: "He shows [what is] 'to be performed'.

Because it must be asked, "What is the duty to be performed?", he says "and what is a good duty," etc., in order to show the duty to be performed (*kattabbakicca*). The construction is as follows: meritorious deeds (*puñña*) are indeed a good duty because they are to be performed;
or, the abandoning of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) is called a good duty because it is to be performed.

Since it must be stated, "In this sutta, which one is shown by which?", it is said: "The 'habitual tendencies' (vāsanā) are both 'well-performed deeds' and 'meritorious acts,' while the 'abandoning of fetters' (saṃyojana-vippahāna) is 'penetration' (nibbedha).
Since it must be stated, "It is only this much," it is said: "Having performed meritorious acts," and so forth.
Having performed meritorious acts, persons who have done merit go from heaven to heaven. Through the abandoning of fetters, the Noble Ones are completely liberated from old age and death.

Since it must be stated, "In that sutta, which one is shown by which?", it was said: "'Having performed meritorious deeds, those who have done merit go from heaven to heaven' refers to *vāsanā* (habitual tendency);
'Through the abandoning of the fetters, they are fully liberated from aging and death' refers to *nibbedha* (penetration).

Since it must be stated, "Is it only this much?", it was said, "These two," and so forth. Since it must be stated, "In that case, which one is shown by which?", it was said: "In that regard, that which... [etc. ...this is *nibbedha*."

The teacher has determined various suttas pertaining to the side of purification through habituation (*vāsanā-bhāgiya*) and the side of penetration (*nibbedha-bhāgiya*), and these have been understood by us.
Since it was necessary to ask, "Which among them is the sutta pertaining to the defilement of craving (*taṇhā-saṅkilesa-bhāgiya*)?", it was said:
"Among those, that which pertains to the defilement of craving," and so forth. "Among those" (*tattha*) refers to those sixteen suttas beginning with the side of defilement.
The Sutta should be demonstrated by way of craving alone; what is meant is that we shall determine and explain it after delimiting its many objects.

Since it must be stated in what manner it is to be demonstrated, the words "by three kinds of craving," and so forth, are spoken. "By craving for existence" means by craving for existence in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*).
"By craving for non-existence" means by craving for existence in the immaterial realm (*arūpabhava*). Or else, by whatever object—
"Adhered to by way of craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) and so forth, through objects such as the varieties and the cutting off of craving;

or rather, in various ways, by means of craving and so forth, or by means of objects such as the varieties and the cutting off of craving—one should point out a discourse belonging to the category of the defilement of craving (*taṇhā-saṃkilesa-bhāgiya*).
A discourse belonging to the category of the defilement of craving should be pointed out solely from the side of craving; thus it was stated by the Teacher, and by us..."
And because it must be stated, "By which side should a discourse dealing with the corruption of views (*diṭṭhisaṃkilesabhāgiya*) be demonstrated?", it was said:

"In that regard, [a discourse] dealing with the corruption of views," and so forth. Or rather, "by whatever basis" means by a basis such as the various types of views, the "immovable vacillation" (*amarāvikkhepa*), and so on.
The Teacher has stated that a discourse dealing with the corruption of views should be demonstrated specifically by way of the side of views.

And we have observed that because it must be stated, "In what manner should the discourse dealing with the corruption of misconduct (*duccarita-saṅkilesabhāgiya*) be demonstrated?", the words "Therein, [the discourse] dealing with the corruption of misconduct," and so forth, were spoken.
Likewise, because it must be stated in the same way, the words "Therein, [the discourse] dealing with the purification of craving (*taṇhā-vodānabhāgiya*)," and so forth;
"dealing with the purification of views (*diṭṭhi-vodānabhāgiya*)," and so forth; and "dealing with the purification of misconduct (*duccarita-vodānabhāgiya*)," and so forth, were spoken.

112. Regarding that *sāsanapaṭṭhāna* in which eighteen root-terms (*mūlapada*) are to be seen, that *sāsanapaṭṭhāna* has been analyzed by way of partial extraction through the sixteen suttas beginning with the "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), and this we know.
But is that *sāsanapaṭṭhāna* to be analyzed only by those sixteen [suttas] beginning with the "partaking of defilement"?

Since it must be stated, "Or should it be analyzed by means of other suttas as well?", it was said—"In that regard, what are the eighteen root-terms? Mundane and supramundane," and so forth—in order to analyze it by means of those other twenty-eight suttas. [Objection:
"If it is to be analyzed by the other twenty-eight suttas as well, then in that case only the statement 'mundane' and so forth should have been made; why [were the others mentioned]?"

If it is asked, "In that regard, which are the eighteen root-terms?"—the analysis of the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna* is comprised of eighteen root-terms, and those eighteen root-terms are to be seen within the analyzed *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*;
therefore, the root-terms have indeed been analyzed. To analyze those root-terms, [it is said]: "In that regard, which are the eighteen root-terms?"
Thus it was said. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), it is stated:

"Having thus analyzed the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna* by way of sixteen modes through examples from various suttas, now, in order to show the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna* by way of twenty-eight modes, since this division of the *Paṭṭhāna* [is also] by means of root-terms..."
There is not even a single portion of this that is not included by them;
therefore, in order to show the root-terms and their classification, the root-terms are first extracted by way of the question, “In this regard, what are the eighteen root-terms?
and then the twenty-eightfold *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*—consisting of nine triads such as “mundane and supramundane,” etc., plus the *Thava* (Praise)—is enumerated.
It has been stated. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*): among those sixteen modes of nutriment, fivefold systems, and eighteen root-terms, he asks which terms constitute the "root-terms.

That which is connected with the world and possesses an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is "mundane" (*lokiya*). Alternatively, that whose intrinsic nature is known by the wise in the world is also "mundane.
Since this particular discourse possesses such a mundane intrinsic nature, that particular discourse is "mundane."

[This is] the name. This same method should be understood for [terms such as] "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) and so forth. It is called *ñāṇa* (knowledge) because it knows; it is called *ñāṇa* because this specific discourse possesses knowledge.
They are called *ñeyya* (the knowable) because they are to be known; it is called *ñeyya* because this specific discourse possesses the knowable.
This same method should also be understood here in the phrase "knowledge and the knowable. It is called *dassana* (vision) because it first sees Nibbāna; that is, the knowledge of the first path.
It is "vision" (*dassana*) because this particular discourse possesses vision as its meaning; it is "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) because this particular discourse possesses cultivation within its text.
This same method should be understood here for the phrase "vision and cultivation.
"One's own" (*saka*) means one's own statement; "one's own statement" (*sakavacana*) means the word of the Blessed One. "Another's statement" (*paravacana*)...
*Paravacanaṃ*: "To be answered" (*vissajjanīya*) means that there exists a specific sutta for it that provides an answer;
"not to be answered" (*avissajjanīya*) means that no such specific sutta providing an answer exists. "Action" (*kamma*) means that there is an action associated with this specific sutta.

"Result" (*vipāka*) means that there is a result for this passage. In the remaining cases as well, the sense of "belonging to" (*assa*) should be understood. Alternatively, it may have the sense of "worldly" (*lokiya*) and so forth.

The primary meaning [is the subject], and the sutta expressing that is spoken of by way of metonymy (*ṭhānyupacāra*). It is called *thava* because one praises the qualities of the Buddha and others by means of this portion of the sutta;
thus, it refers to a portion of the sutta. "Among those twenty-eight types of suttas of the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*, including the mundane (*lokiya*) and so forth, which sutta is mundane?"
Because it was necessary to ask, "Which is the *sutta*? the passage beginning with "In that regard, which is the mundane (*lokiya*) [sutta]? was stated. "In that regard" (*tattha*) means:

among those twenty-eight kinds of *sutta* on the foundations of the teaching (*sāsanapaṭṭhāna*), such as the mundane and so forth, he asks: "Which *sutta* is the mundane foundation of the teaching? [The Buddha replied:
"Monks, the fresh milk flowing from a cow's udders is not released and does not transform at the very moment it flows out."

Just as milk does not reach the state of curd by abandoning its own nature [immediately], but rather abandons its state as milk and reaches the state of curd only after coming into contact with sour substances such as buttermilk,
so too, the evil deed committed by a fool does not ripen at the very moment of its performance by producing the suffering of the woeful states for that fool. But on the second [occasion]...
Or it ripens in the third or subsequent existence. Just as a smoldering fire covered by ashes and concealed by cinders does not burn a person at the moment they step upon it,
but rather burns them after a lapse of time once the cinders have been heated,
so too, the evil deed committed by a fool does not produce the suffering of the woeful states and so forth at the very moment of its performance.

Having burned [the fool] once, it does not follow him. Or rather, the construction is: having burned—that is, burning—that fool by way of producing the suffering of the states of misery (apāya) and so forth in a second or third future existence, it follows him.
This Sutta, beginning with “For... pe... fire,” is called "worldly" (lokiya) because it functions as both a speaker and an indicator regarding worldly matters.
Because it must be said that "this much alone is mundane," the passage beginning with "These four conceits... was stated. The meaning is clear.
This Sutta—“These four... like the moon in the dark fortnight”—is called mundane because it functions as both an expression and an indicator regarding mundane matters.
Because it must be stated that "thus, the mundane is indeed twofold," the passage beginning with "These eight, monks, are worldly conditions" was spoken.
The meaning is clear. This sutta beginning with "These eight" is called mundane because it functions as both a designation and an indicator among the eight kinds of mundane objects.
Various types of mundane [suttas] have been determined by the Teacher and are known to us;

because it must be stated, "Which sutta is supramundane?", the passage beginning with "In this regard, which is supramundane? was spoken. This same method should be understood for what follows as well.
"Therein" means among those twenty-eight kinds of suttas, such as the mundane and so forth.
Just as well-tamed horses have reached a state of tranquility through a skillful charioteer,
so too the six faculties— the eye-faculty and the others— of that stainless bhikkhu who has abandoned conceit and abandoned the ninefold conceit have reached a state of tranquility.
Of that stainless bhikkhu who is "such-like" (tādī), endowed with the characteristic of being such-like, both devas and humans...

The construction is: "they cause [others] to shrink away. This sutta beginning with “yassindriyāni” is called *lokuttara* (supramundane) because it functions as an indicator and communicator regarding supramundane meaning.

Because it must be stated as “only this much,” the passage beginning with “pañcimāni bhikkhave indriyāni” was spoken. This sutta beginning with “pañcimāni” is also called *lokuttara* because it functions as an indicator and communicator regarding supramundane meaning. (1)
The two verses beginning with “Having attained human status, there are two things: what is to be done and what is not to be done” were spoken.

Herein, regarding these verses, the phrase “meritorious deeds are indeed good to be done” and the phrase “Having performed meritorious deeds, those who have done merit go from heaven to heaven”—this verse-phrase [functions] by way of expressing and indicating the mundane meaning.
That which proceeds [in the world] is called mundane (*lokiya*). Here,
in these verses, the verse-line "or the abandoning of the fetters" and the verse-line "through the abandoning of the fetters, they are liberated from aging and death"—
these verse-lines are supramundane (*lokuttara*) according to the method already stated.
This refers to both the mundane and the supramundane, as described in the passage beginning with "having obtained" (*laddhāna*).
Monks, when there is desire and lust for the nutriment of consciousness—which is bound up with nutriment—there is the descent of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The statement, "In consciousness...
[there is] the descent," is mundane according to the method already explained. The statement, "In consciousness... [there is] cessation," is... [supramundane].
The *sutta* is called supramundane (*lokuttara*). This *sutta*, beginning with "If, monks, in consciousness...
and so forth, pertains both to the mundane and the supramundane, because it functions—by way of partial expression or indication—with respect to both mundane and supramundane meanings. (2) 113.
Having wandered through every direction in the world of beings, in no direction whatsoever does one find anything dearer to oneself than one's own self by means of the mind.
He found nothing else at all dearer than himself; even so, for each and every other being, their own self is individually dearer.

Therefore, because one's own self is dearer, the wise world of beings—desiring themselves and desiring their own welfare—should, taking oneself as the analogy, not harm another, nor should they cause harm. This refers to the verse beginning with “all directions.”
The *sutta* is called "having beings as its subject" (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) because it proceeds by way of expressing and making known [the state of] beings.
Whatever individuals have exhausted their taints (*khīṇāsava*), having already been so, will not [again] come to be;

all those individuals who have exhausted their taints, having abandoned the body and the personal existence (*attabhāva*), will go to Nibbāna. And whatever beings, such as worldlings (*puthujjana*), will exist in future births—
All those beings, beginning with worldlings (*puthujjana*), will abandon their bodies—their personal existence—and go to the next world;

that "loss of all" (*sabbajāni*) is the death of every being, or its destruction. The skilled person who understands this "loss of all," having understood that loss of all, should practice the holy life (*brahmacariya*) with ardor—this is the construction of the meaning. This refers to the passage beginning with "whosoever."
According to the method already stated, this is an exposition based on the person (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*).
A virtuous friend endowed with seven factors should not be abandoned by a person seeking what is wholesome for as long as life lasts.
With which seven? Because they are endowed with the perfection of pure virtue and the perfection of pure view.
He is beloved and worthy of being loved; he is as venerable as a stone parasol; he is one to be cultivated through esteem;

and having established within himself the five qualities beginning with "I speak at the proper time, not at the improper time," he stands as one who provides guidance, support, and instruction to his fellow celibates or students, and is thus addressed by those fellow celibates.
Or, when being spoken to by disciples and others, he is easy to speak with and patient with their words;

he is capable of delivering profound discourses on such topics as truth and dependent origination, or other profound subjects, because he elucidates them precisely through the Dhamma and Vinaya; and he does not direct one toward what is inappropriate.
A spiritual friend endowed with these seven qualities should [be relied upon] for as long as life lasts.
It should be abandoned. This is the statement beginning with "With seven" that the Blessed One spoke.
Having spoken this statement beginning with "With seven," the Sugata, the Teacher, then spoke this further verse. What did he say?
"Dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem, one who speaks and is patient with what is said;..."
The Teacher spoke this verse: "One who speaks profound words, and does not urge one toward what is improper—that friend should be served even for as long as life lasts by one who desires a friend.

This is the construction of the statement. There is also the reading "na ca aṭṭhānayojako" (and not urging toward what is improper). This statement beginning with "by seven," etc., is based on the number seven.

The construction is as follows: whatever sensual pleasure exists in the world and whatever divine pleasure exists here, these pleasures of sense and the pleasures of the devas do not equal even a sixteenth part of the pleasure of the destruction of craving (*taṇhākkhayasukha*).
This sutta beginning with "And what... (*yañcā*) is expressed in terms of the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*). The construction is as follows:

that Nibbāna where suffering ceases—taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One, sorrowless, stainless, and secure—that Nibbāna is indeed a supreme happiness (*susukha*). This sutta beginning with "Supreme happiness" (*susukha*) is also expressed in terms of the Dhamma. (3)

Because it causes beings to be born within the three realms of existence, craving—which is designated as the "mother"—and because pride arises in dependence upon the father, which is designated as the "father," [the two views] are like the world’s resorting to the king, the lord of the realm;

for among all possible positions of view, the two views of eternalism and annihilationism are the most frequently resorted to. Thus, regarding those designated as the views of eternalism and annihilationism...
The two Khattiya kings and the man who accomplishes his purpose wander through the kingdom;

likewise, because one wanders among the twelve sense-bases (*dvādasāyatana*) through the craving for delight (*nandirāga*), the "kingdom" designated as the twelve sense-bases is the place where that which is reckoned as craving for delight occurs.
When the Brahmin who is an *Arahant* (one whose taints are exhausted) slays [these], that Brahmin, having slain them, becomes free from affliction and free from suffering.

The construction is "he goes. Here, in this verse beginning with "Having killed his mother," the statement of the verse—"having killed his mother... [etc.]"—is a formulation based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna).
The statement of the verse—"the brahmin goes free from distress"—is a formulation based on a being (sattādhiṭṭhāna).
Thus, this sutta beginning with "his mother" is both a formulation based on a being and a formulation based on phenomena.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*); this statement from a portion of the Sutta is expressed by way of the Dhamma.

A person endowed with these four bases of psychic power immerses and directs the mind—the foundational meditative absorption (*pādakajjhānacitta*)—into the body, that is, the physical body made of kamma.
That person, wishing to go with a visible body, directs the foundational meditative absorption mind toward the destination of the physical body.
He exercises resolve. He merges and inserts the body—the physical body made of kamma—into the mind, specifically into the foundational jhāna-consciousness.
That person, desiring to go quickly to another place, resolves the physical body made of kamma so that it follows the course of the foundational jhāna-consciousness.
In the body—the physical body made of kamma—he perceives pleasure, perceives a state of ease, perceives lightness, and perceives the capacity for swift movement.
Having descended [from the divine realm], desiring another destination or desired place, he goes there in a single moment of consciousness and, having attained it, dwells therein.

This passage from the Sutta beginning with "He... is expressed by way of a person (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*). This Sutta beginning with "These four... is expressed both by way of a person and by way of the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*). (4)
114. That which is omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*), which stands having transcended and overcome the world by being supramundane (*lokuttara*);
that omniscient knowledge by which the Blessed One is called "Omniscient" (*sabbaññū*)—there is no decline of that omniscient knowledge.

The construction is as follows: that omniscient knowledge functions at the time of adverting (*āvajjana*) in order to know all things at all times. This passage beginning with "That which... refers to the meaning of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
It is called "knowledge" (ñāṇa) because it proceeds by way of both expressing and making known.

The construction is as follows: that wisdom of the path leading to Nibbāna, by which one understands the exhaustion of birth and death—that wisdom of the path leading to Nibbāna is the best and most praised among all mundane forms of wisdom. This refers to the passage beginning with "wisdom indeed... and so forth.
Knowledge is as described by the aforementioned method.

“Dhotaka, I shall proclaim your peace,” the Blessed One said. “A practitioner (yogāvacara), while walking about—having become endowed with mindfulness such as the contemplation of impermanence regarding what is present in this very life (diṭṭhe dhamme), or regarding phenomena beginning with suffering, or regarding the personal existence (attabhāva)—”

“Having known through the Noble Path that which is beyond tradition—that peace, that Nibbāna—one should cross over, one should transcend the craving that clings to and spreads through the world, the world of saṃsāra,” the Blessed One said.
Dhota spoke to the Blessed One: “O Great Seer, O Gotama, you who possess the great aggregate of virtue and the like, being mindful—”
“Having become endowed with the refuge that begins with ‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,’ as the practitioner (yogāvacara) goes about his course,
he shall cross over, he shall transcend the attachment— that is, craving— within the world, the world of saṃsāra, having realized through the Noble Path that supreme peace which is Nibbāna.
O Great Sage, I rejoice in and aspire toward both that word and that peace, Nibbāna.
“You, and that which you clearly understand,” Dhotaka said to the Blessed One.
Addressing him as “Dhotaka,” the Blessed One spoke to Dhotaka: “Above, what has not yet come; below, what is past;
across, in the middle, and in the present—everywhere in the world, in the world of saṃsāra, this is craving for becoming and non-becoming.”
The construction is as follows: "Having understood that attachment is a clinging for the sake of small and great states of existence, as you wander, do not create craving;

do not create it!"—thus the Blessed One spoke to Dhotaka. This [verse] beginning with "I shall proclaim" is called "the knowable" (*ñeyya*), because it functions by way of denoting and indicating the object of knowledge, which is the meaning.
Because it must be stated that "it is just this much," the passage beginning with "Bhikkhus, of the four" was spoken. Bhikkhus, through the non-awakening,
the failure to awaken to, the non-penetration, and the failure to penetrate the Four Noble Truths—
the truths that produce the state of a noble one— it is for this reason that this long journey, this wandering, has been undergone both by me and by you.
“This has been wandered through, this wandering has occurred,” monks, today this Noble Truth of suffering has been fully awakened to and penetrated by me...
[and so on] ...today this Noble Truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering has been fully awakened to and penetrated by me;
my craving for existence has been cut off, the craving that leads to becoming has been exhausted; now—
"I have no further existence"—this is what the Blessed One said, beginning with "of the four.
Having spoken this beginning with "of the four," the Sugata, the Teacher, then spoke this subsequent verse beginning with "of the four";
thus the application should be made accordingly within the verse. This beginning with "of the four" is to be understood according to the method already stated. (5)

One sees: “This feeling is impermanent,” thus one sees feeling; “This perception is impermanent,” thus one sees perception;
“These formations are impermanent,” thus one sees formations; “This consciousness is impermanent,” thus one sees consciousness.
Thus, this discourse is called "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) because it functions as both a designator and an indicator regarding the knowledge that perceives form and the other aggregates.
The construction is as follows: "The noble disciple, seeing in such a manner as 'form is impermanent' and so forth, is liberated from form and from lust for form...
[and so on]... he is liberated from consciousness and from lust for consciousness; thus, I say, he is liberated from suffering.
This Sutta beginning with "he is liberated" functions as both a speaker and an indicator with respect to both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
There is both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
All five aggregates are *saṅkhārā* because they are conditioned by conditions;

they are impermanent because they possess a beginning and an end, because they are subject to absolute change, because they exist only for a time, and because they are momentary and limited. This is what is meant by "All *saṅkhārā* are impermanent."

The statement from the Sutta passage is to be understood according to the method already explained. When, at the time of practicing insight (vipassanā), one sees with wisdom—that is, with the wisdom of insight—one sees impermanence and so forth. This statement from the Sutta passage, "when one sees with wisdom," is called knowledge (ñāṇa).
Then, at the moment of seeing, the practitioner of insight becomes disenchanted with the five aggregates as suffering; becoming disenchanted, [he becomes dispassionate].
A person penetrates the four truths by way of knowing suffering and so forth; this penetration of the four truths is the path for the sake of purification and for the state of purity.
This passage from the Sutta beginning with "Then," etc., constitutes both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
"Soṇa" is an address to Soṇa. "Ascetics" refers to non-Buddhist ascetics; "brahmins" refers to brahmins by birth, [who perceive] form as impermanent.
Regarding form that is suffering, form subject to change, they regard it thus: "I am better than others, I am superior," or they regard it thus:
"I am equal to others," or they regard it thus: "I am inferior to others, I am base.
Apart from this failure to see things as they truly are, what other cause could there be?
It may be that there is no other cause for the non-comprehension of things as they truly are than the very absence of such vision;

thus, it should be understood that the absence of seeing things as they really are is itself the cause. In the cases of "of impermanent feeling," and so forth, the application should be made according to the method already stated and following the same principle.
This should be known as the statement from the passage of the Sutta beginning with "Whosoever... and so on.
The "bright side" (sukkapakkha), beginning with the words "And whoever," should be understood as the opposite of what was stated [in the preceding dark side].
This passage from the Sutta beginning with "And whoever" is called "knowledge" (ñāṇa).

This Sutta beginning with "For whoever" is both knowledge and the knowable (ñeyya), because it functions by way of being both the expresser and the indicator regarding the meanings of both knowledge and the knowable. (6)
The Teacher has determined various kinds of knowledge and the knowable in the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna-sutta*, and we have understood them;
because it was necessary to ask, "What is vision?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is vision? was stated. "In that regard" (*tattha*) means:
among those twenty-eight kinds of suttas in the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*—such as the mundane and so forth—which sutta is [meant]?
He asks: "What is meant by 'vision'?

[The answer is: Those Noble Persons who have cultivated their meditative development clarify, through the illumination of wisdom, the Noble Truths that were well-taught by the Omniscient Buddha of profound wisdom—taught thoroughly through various methods such as concise and detailed expositions.
Although those noble persons who have cultivated spiritual development may become greatly negligent upon encountering occasions for heedlessness—
such as the sovereignty of the gods or the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch— nevertheless, because they have cultivated spiritual development, those noble persons,

through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry and the cessation of volitional consciousness, have brought to an end the name-and-form that would otherwise arise in the eighth existence and beyond.
The construction is: "They do not take up an eighth existence by way of eight times.

This Sutta beginning with "Those who [know] the Noble Truths" is called "seeing" because it functions as a declarative and indicative means regarding the knowledge of the first path at the moment of seeing.
For the purpose of strengthening the door-posts of a city gate, [one digs] into the earth inside the threshold to a measure of eight or ten cubits.
Just as a post made of heartwood, fixed in the earth, supported by the earth, and embedded deep within the earth, might be set up in a pit and, because it is raised up in that pit,
would be unshakable and impossible to shake by the winds coming from the four quarters—
the great winds— just so is that noble person who sees the Noble Truths through direct knowledge.
The construction is: "I say that the true person (sappurisa) is comparable to that [pillar], because of his unshakability by the winds of the doctrines of all other sectarians.
This Sutta beginning with "Just like a pillar" (*yathindakhīlo*) is, according to the method already stated, called "Vision" (*dassana*).
"Monks, the noble disciple endowed with the four factors of stream-entry [is established] in the noble Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened One..."
A disciple, desiring to explain [his attainment], would himself personally declare of himself:
"O sir, as for my self, I have now exhausted hell; I have exhausted the animal womb... [and so forth]... I shall bring an end to suffering.
To show the conformity with the four factors, it was said, "By which four? and so on. This is what is called the "vision" beginning with "by four."
Having determined various kinds of "seeing," because it must be asked, "What is development? the passage beginning with "In this regard, what is development? was stated.

Herein, in this Dispensation, for whichever noble disciple there is the abandoning of the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) that cause rebirth within the internal sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), and [the abandoning] of the higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) that cause rebirth externally in the fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpārūpabhava*).
And by way of abandoning, the faculties— the faculty of faith and the others—
become well-developed through the cultivation of the Noble Path; that cultivated path is developed, and that tamed noble disciple,
having become disillusioned with this world and the world beyond, and having penetrated them, at the time of death, at the passing away, [attains finality].

The construction is: "or he desires, he longs for. This passage beginning with "yassindriyāni" is called *bhāvanā* (development) because it functions as both an expression and an indicator of development.

The "verses of the Dhamma" (*dhammapadāni*) are the constituent portions of the phenomena consisting of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), the fruits (*phala*), and Nibbāna. Non-covetousness is a verse of the Dhamma.

The section consisting of the factors of dhamma—namely, jhāna, vipassanā, the path, and nibbāna—is attained through the desire for non-covetousness. This same method applies to the remaining [factors] as well.
This passage beginning with "four kinds of conceit" refers to what is called "cultivation" according to the method already stated.
(7) A person who severs the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) severs them by means of the three lower paths.
One who cuts off, one who abandons, should abandon the five higher fetters by means of the path of Arahatship;
one who cultivates, one who develops, should further develop the five faculties beginning with faith.

A bhikkhu who has transcended the five attachments—one who has transcended the attachment of lust, the attachment of hatred, the attachment of delusion, the attachment of conceit, and the attachment of views—is one who has crossed the flood.
The construction is as follows: “one who has crossed the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance” is what is said, that is, what is spoken.
The statement “one should cut off five, one should abandon five” is called *dassana* (vision). The canonical passage beginning with “five more than those...
[etc. ...is said” is called *bhāvanā* (cultivation). Thus, this sutta beginning with “five” constitutes both vision and cultivation.
In passages such as “These three, monks,” the application [of the terms] is evident. (8) 116.

“The non-doing of all evil... this is the teaching of the Buddhas”—this sutta is called “our own word” (*sakavacana*) because it is the speech of the Fully Enlightened One. The meaning has already been stated above.
Monks, the characteristics of a fool, the causes for identifying a fool, the signs of a fool—[by which one knows] “this person is a fool.”
The causes for being grasped are the deeds of a fool, the ancient and long-established deeds of a fool—those characteristics of a fool by which wise people recognize a fool as "a fool.
These three characteristics of a fool that I am about to describe are as follows:
Monks, a fool is one who thinks evil thoughts; he thinks evil thoughts, namely covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
He is one who thinks ill; he is a speaker of what is ill-spoken, speaking falsehood and the like.
He is a doer of what is ill-done, performing such deeds as the taking of life and so forth. Monks, these three "gifts of a fool" have been spoken of by me for the fool...
[as follows]. The bright side, however, should be understood by reversing what has been stated.
This statement beginning with “Bhikkhus, these three... is called our own teaching (*sakavacana*) because it is the word of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
There is no awakening as vast as the earth. Because one obtains water abundantly when it has rained in the morning, it is called *pātāla*;
there exists no depression equal to the *pātāla*. There is no height equal to Mount Meru; there is none like a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
The construction is: "There is no person [to equal me]. This statement beginning with "equal to the earth" is the speech of another because it is the speech of the other god.

Having said, "O Lord of the Devas, victory comes through your well-spoken words," and having said, "Vepacitti, let victory come through your well-spoken words," he said, "Vepacitti, you recite a verse; recite it! Monks, then...
The asura lord Vepacitti spoke this verse as it was being recited:

“If there were no one to restrain them, and if such a person did not exist, then fools would become even more agitated; therefore, a wise and learned man should restrain a fool with a severe punishment.
Monks, when this verse had been spoken by the asura lord Vepacitti, the asuras rejoiced, while the devas remained silent.
They were thus. Monks, then Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, spoke these words to Sakka, the lord of the devas:
"Lord of the devas, recite a verse; recite it! Monks, then Sakka, the lord of the devas, spoke this verse: "The warding off of a fool is the supreme adversary..."
"Knowing one is provoked, the wise person who is mindful and alert pacifies their anger; I consider that for such a wise person, this very state is the supreme peace.
Monks, when these verses were spoken by Sakka, Lord of the Devas, the devas rejoiced, while the asuras remained silent.
They were. Monks, then Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke these words to Vepacitti, lord of the asuras:
"Vepacitti, you recite a verse. Monks, then Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, spoke this verse: "Vāsava, when one practices patience, then that person who is practicing patience..."
The fool thinks, "He endures this out of fear of me," yet I see this very thing as a fault in his endurance.
Vāsava, just as a herd of cattle tramples upon a cow that tries to flee, even so does the dull-witted man further assail and overwhelm one who is patient.
Monks, when this verse was spoken by Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, the asuras applauded, while the devas remained silent.
...they were. And when the bull-fight begins, first only two bulls fight; however, the herd stands watching until one bull flees.
When one bull flees, then the entire herd falls heavily upon that fleeing bull—such is the nature of a bull-fight to be understood. "Then..."
The meaning of the connection of the words beginning with "kho" is evident.
O Vepacitti, whether a person who practices endurance thinks of that patient individual, "This person endures out of fear of me," or does not so think—that conceiving is entirely fruitless.
One's welfare has as its supreme goal one's own true welfare.
There exists no goal for oneself greater than patience and forbearance.
Regarding one who, being strong, endures the weak—the noble ones call that endurance of the strong "supreme patience. The weak person always simply forgives.
As for the fool who possesses the strength of a fool, the noble ones call that "strength of a fool" "no strength" at all.
For one who is guarded by the Dhamma, whatever power he possesses, there exists no one who can oppose or counteract that power of his who is guarded by the Dhamma.
Vepacitti, that person who, when another is first angry, returns anger for anger— by returning anger, he...
By that act of returning anger, that person would become even more wicked, more evil, and more base than that wicked person who first became angry.
Vepacitti, it is the true person who, being mindful and alert, knowing that another is provoked, [remains calm] toward the one who first became angry.
One who does not retaliate in anger is indeed a true person; he is said to conquer the battle that is difficult to win.
He practices for the welfare of both himself and others.
For those who seek to heal both themselves and others, the anger of both subsides—those people who [abide] in the Dhamma...

Those who are unskilled in the meaning of the Dhamma of patience, or in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, think of a good person who is patient, "This one is a fool. For those unskilled people, that thought is fruitless.
Regarding these verses, monks, spoken by Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, the devas rejoiced, but the asuras remained silent.
The construction is: "they were. This statement beginning with "furthermore, fools" is called the "speech of another" because it is the speech of Sakka and his followers. (9) 117.
That which has been attained now—the requisites for sensual pleasure—and that which is to be attained and has been attained in the future...
There are the requisites for sensual pleasure; both of these are strewn with dust—that is, strewn with the dust of passion and so forth.
To one who is afflicted and who trains under other afflicted persons, as they train, these become the essence of their training:
namely, virtue, observance, livelihood, and the holy life. These stand before them as the essence of their training; thus, they are those for whom standing [in service] is the essence.
These individuals stand having grasped [these things] as essential. Herein, "virtue" (*sīla*) means abstaining [from unwholesome deeds] with the thought, "I shall not do it.

"Vow" (*vata*) refers to the performance of duties such as the meal-time observances. "Livelihood" (*jīvita*) means one's mode of living. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) should be understood as the specific state of abstaining from sexual intercourse.
For those individuals who hold attendance upon these [things] as essential, this doctrine is the first extreme, which is inferior. Those...
And there are persons who, having held such a doctrine and such a view as "there is no fault in sensual pleasures," remain established in them;
for those persons, this doctrine is the second inferior extreme. Thus, both these extremes are proponents of extremes—persons who increase the cemetery, who increase the cemetery of views.
These two extremes are: devotion to self-mortification and devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure.
The construction is: "Some individuals lag behind due to lack of direct knowledge (*anabhiññāya*); some individuals run too far ahead.
This statement beginning with "And what has been attained" and so forth is called "the speech of others" because it consists of the words of other persons.
Furthermore, those persons who possess right view, having directly known both extremes—the devotion to self-mortification and the devotion to sensual pleasure—[do not fall into them].
And therein, at the end, they did not exist. By that very higher knowledge, those two extremes were not conceived;
for those individuals of right view, there is no threefold round for the manifestation of the round. Thus, this statement beginning with "And those who...
is called the Blessed One’s own word because it is the speech of the Blessed One. This is the *udāna*: "And that which has been attained... [etc. ...for the manifestation."
This *udāna* is, according to the method already stated, both our own statement and the statement of another.
King Pasenadi of Kosala, the lord of Kosala, spoke this speech to the Blessed One:
"Here, venerable sir, when I am alone and in seclusion, my mind... [and so on] "...to them, the self is dear. Venerable sir, here, when I am alone and in seclusion, my mind...
A reflection arose in my mind: "Of which beings is the self dear, and of which beings is the self not dear? It was this very reflection that arose in me, venerable sir:
"Whatever beings engage in misconduct by body... [and so on] ...engage in misconduct by mind."

Indeed, for those beings, the self is not dear. Although those beings who engage in misconduct might say, "Our self is dear," nevertheless, for those beings engaging in misconduct, the self is indeed not dear. Why is that?
Because one who is not dear would do what is harmful to one who is not dear; such is the misconduct they commit.
"Those beings, while practicing misconduct, do so by themselves and of their own accord;
since they act for their own harm, therefore, as they practice misconduct, the thought occurred to them: 'To us, our own self is indeed unlovely.
Venerable sir, whatever beings practice good conduct with the body... [and so on] ...practice good conduct with the mind."
For those beings who practice good conduct, their own self is indeed dear.
Even if those beings practicing good conduct were to say, "Our self is not dear," nevertheless, for those beings practicing good conduct, their self is indeed dear.
Why is that? Because one would practice good conduct for the sake of what is dear to oneself; such is good conduct.

Since those beings, while practicing good conduct, act for their own welfare by themselves and of their own accord, therefore, as they practice good conduct, the thought occurred to them: "The self is dear.
This is the construction of the sentence: "He spoke this word."
Having first stated the words, “It is even so, Great King,” the application of the same method should likewise be made to the words spoken by the Blessed One beginning with, “For whoever...
In the verses, however, if a wise man should know himself as “dear,” then that wise man would not—nor would he cause himself to—be bound by an evil deed;
for that statement is true: one’s own self is dear and easily accessible.
For one who commits misdeeds, happiness is not easily obtained.
For that being who has been seized by the Ender, Death, who is abandoning and relinquishing human existence and stands at the mouth of death—what belongs to him?
And what does that being standing at the mouth of death take with him to the next world?
Just as a shadow follows a moving being without ever leaving it, so too does something follow that being who has gone to the next world.
Thus the Blessed One asks this question, and having asked it, he speaks the words of reply beginning with "Both.
Whatever merit and whatever evil—both these karmas—a mortal performs here in this world, they follow him when he has gone to the next world.

That pair of merit and demerit belongs to the mortal as his own. Having gone to the world beyond, the mortal goes to that other world taking with him that very pair of merit and demerit, just as a shadow follows a being who moves without ever leaving him;
even so, for that mortal who has gone to the world beyond, that same pair of merit and demerit follows after him.
Therefore, a wise person, acting as one who accumulates a virtuous store that produces fruit in the future life, should do so for the sake of the next world.
"Meritorious deeds are the foundation for living beings in the world beyond"—thus the Blessed One spoke; this is how the construction should be understood.
This sutta, beginning with "King Pasenadi," is the speech of another because it consists of the words of the King of Kosala.
“It is so, Great King; it is so, Great King. Such verses of recitation (*anugīti*), being the words of the Blessed One, constitute his own statement (*sakavacana*).
This pair—both his own statement and the statement of another—is what constitutes speech.
(10) 118. When a question is asked: “This truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*); this truth of origin (*samudayasacca*) is to be abandoned (*pahātabba*).”
"This is the truth of the path that must be developed; this is the truth of cessation, or the fruit that must be realized;

these are wholesome and unwholesome states, grasped as such by way of their wholesomeness or unwholesomeness, or by way of being blameless or blameworthy, or by way of having pleasant or painful results;
this produces a desirable result, this produces an undesirable result"—thus it is for those states so grasped.
Of those wholesome and unwholesome states, this is their increase, which is their benefit; this is their decrease, which is their loss.

Thus, this sutta beginning with “When a question is asked,” etc., is called *vissajjanīya* (to be answered) because it functions as an indicator and an explainer regarding the meaning that is to be answered.
By means of the phrase “The Buddha, the Blessed One, is sublime,” one should point out the sublimity of the Buddha exclusively and by way of a single portion.
By the phrase “The Dhamma is well-expounded,” one should describe the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma exclusively and as a single category.
By the phrase “The Saṅgha is practicing the good way,” one should describe the Saṅgha’s practice of the good way exclusively and as a single category.
By the phrase “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” one should describe the impermanence of conditioned phenomena exclusively.
By the phrase “All conditioned phenomena are suffering,” one should point out the suffering inherent in formations with absolute certainty.
By the phrase “All phenomena are non-self,” one should point out the selflessness of phenomena with absolute certainty.
By stating “All phenomena are non-self” instead of saying “All formations are non-self,” this phrase indicates that which is other than formations.
Alternatively, there exists that class of phenomena consisting of the path, the fruit, and the attainment of cessation;

and since even that class of phenomena consisting of the path, the fruit, and the attainment of cessation is of such a nature and must be answered categorically in this way, the construction is that the selflessness of even that class of phenomena consisting of the path, the fruit, and the attainment of cessation is demonstrated categorically.
This refers to the Sutta beginning with "Exalted" (*uḷāra*), which is to be explained in relation to the exaltedness of the Buddha and so forth.
It is called "to be answered" because it proceeds by way of the relationship between the questioner and the respondent.

O Charioteer who tames men, all beings—gods, humans, and every living creature—would not know, nor could they know, that object of knowledge (*ñeyyadhamma*) contemplated by the mind of the Blessed One, which is endowed with the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). [This refers to] the peaceful, conflict-free concentration (*samādhi*).
Even all beings together would not know, nor could they know, what has been mentally contemplated by that Blessed One as he practices;
or even with wisdom having the *kasiṇa* as its object, they would not know, nor could they know it.

Regarding the phrase "even all together" (*kasiṇāpi*), although it should have been stated as "even all [of them] together" (*kasiṇāyapi*), it is expressed as "even all together" (*kasiṇāpi*) by means of the elision of the letter *ya*. Alternatively, it refers to "whatever he desires, whatever desire... [and so forth].
The construction is as follows: when asked the question, "What is that desire which one performs?", it becomes unanswerable because it is outside the scope of others.
This Sutta beginning with "of one who desires" is called "unanswerable" (avissajjanīya) because it functions by way of expressing and indicating a subject matter that is unanswerable.
The Blessed One, by reason of the aggregate of virtue, is to this extent and of this measure; the Blessed One, by reason of the aggregate of concentration, is to this extent and of this measure;
the Blessed One, by reason of the aggregate of wisdom, is to this extent and of this measure;
the Blessed One, by reason of the aggregate of liberation, is to this extent and of this measure. The Blessed One...
In the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, by reason of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, it is so much, of such measure;
O Blessed One, in conduct, that is, in the deportment of body and speech, by reason of the deportment of body and speech, it is so much, of such measure;
O Blessed One, in majesty, by reason of power, it is so much, of such measure; O Blessed One, in benevolence, by reason of loving-kindness, it is so much, of such measure.
The construction is as follows: "The Blessed One, in his compassion, [is] this much, this limited in measure;
the Blessed One, in his supernormal power, [is] this much, this limited in measure"—thus he is "inexhaustible" (*avissajjanīya*).
This Sutta beginning with "this much" is called "inexhaustible" because it functions by way of expressing and indicating that which is inexhaustible.

"Monks, through the arising of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One in the world, and by reason of that arising, the arising of the Three Jewels occurs: the arising of the Buddha-jewel occurs for the future;
for it is said 'for the future' because while one Buddha-jewel is present, another Buddha-jewel does not arise. [Likewise] the Dhamma-jewel..."
The arising of the Buddha occurs, the arising of the Dhamma occurs, and the arising of the Saṅgha occurs—thus there are the Three Jewels.

When it is asked, "What is the measure of those Three Jewels in terms of their qualities? the construction is that one should not answer by saying, "Those Three Jewels are of such-and-such a measure in terms of their qualities.
This Sutta beginning with "Of the Tathāgata... concerns a subject that is not to be answered definitively.
It is called "unanswerable" because it proceeds by way of being a signifier and a signified.

A question concerning the domain of the Buddha that is person-centered or focused on individuals is unanswerable; likewise, the knowledge of the relative distinctions between persons within the domain of the Buddha is unanswerable.
"Monks, for beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, no prior limit is discerned."
Once for beings running and wandering through hell; once for beings running and wandering through the animal realm;
once for beings running and wandering through the sphere of hungry ghosts; once for beings running and wandering through the realm of asuras;
once for beings running and wandering among the devas. Once...
"For beings wandering and transmigrating among humans, a prior limit is not known, is not seen, and is not found.
When someone asks, "What is that prior limit?", it is an unanswerable question because a prior limit of *saṃsāra* does not exist; thus, it remains unanswerable.
The statement "it is not known" was made by the Teacher [the Buddha] due to the deficiency of knowledge in his disciples.

It is not because of a deficiency in his own knowledge. Regarding the objection that the teaching "it is not discerned" might have been made due to a deficiency in the knowledge of himself and his disciples, it was said:
"The teaching of the Blessed Buddhas is twofold," and so forth.
That teaching to which one is led by oneself is *attūpanāyikā* (leading to oneself). That teaching to which another is led is... [parūpanāyikā].

Regarding "referring to others" (*parūpanāyikā*): because it was asked, "What is a teaching referring to oneself (*attūpanāyikā*), and what is a teaching referring to others (*parūpanāyikā*)?", the passage beginning with "it is not discerned" (*na paññāyati*) was stated in order to define and demonstrate them.

"It is not discerned" means that because the teaching was taught according to the disciples who were to be guided, it is called a "teaching referring to others"; for there is no [need for such guidance] for the Blessed Buddhas.
“Non-knowing” (*avijānanā*): This teaching is called a "teaching directed toward oneself" (*attūpanāyikā*) because it is taught by way of what is to be led back to oneself.
Because it is stated that "there is no non-knowing in the Blessed Buddhas," it is understood that it is not discerned precisely because of the absence of a prior limit (*pubbā koṭi*).
It is not discerned because one is unable to establish the knowledge of the Blessed One.
Therefore, it is not understood; thus, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Regarding the phrase 'there is no non-knowing on the part of the Blessed Buddhas,' this shows that because of the very absence of a prior limit (*purimāya koṭiyā*), it is not perceived, and not because there is an obstruction to knowledge therein. However, since it must be asked: "In what way, then, is the state of non-existence of non-knowing on the part of the Blessed Buddhas to be known?"
In order to make known the state of non-existence through non-cognition, it was said: "Just as the Blessed One [knew] the bhikkhu Kokālika," and so forth.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "But that which exists, even if immeasurable to others, is not immeasurable for the Blessed One;
thus, in order to show the Blessed One’s unimpeded knowledge regarding all things, [it says]: 'Just as the Blessed One [knew] the bhikkhu Kokālika'..."

It is said: "He spoke beginning with the words ‘Concerning...’. Having asked the question, "Venerable Sir, how long indeed is the lifespan in the Paduma hell?", the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu who was sitting nearby, saying, "In such a way...
having struck him... and so forth. Then, because of his lack of understanding regarding that manner [of rebirth], [the Blessed One spoke].
The meaning to be grasped is that the state of non-existence must be understood.
Bhikkhu, you should observe this: suppose a Kosalan sesame-cartload of twenty khārīs were heaped up in a pile, and from that sesame, a person were to remove a single seed every hundred years.
Just as a Kosalan cartload of twenty khāris of sesame seeds might, by this method of removal, more quickly reach exhaustion and depletion,
a single Abbuda hell would not reach exhaustion and depletion in that same amount of time.
Twenty Abbuda hells might, in that same amount of time, reach exhaustion and depletion.
In the same way, even a single *nirabbuda* hell would not reach its exhaustion or termination in that much time;
this same principle applies to the others as well. "Having harbored malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the bhikkhu Kokālika was reborn in the Paduma hell;
you, bhikkhu, should observe it thus," so said the Blessed One—this is the construction of the sentence. The Blessed One...
He said nothing such as, “This is immeasurable” or “This is incalculable. When someone asks, “In that which is immeasurable, what is immeasurable?
In that which is incalculable, what is incalculable?”—because this falls within the domain of the Buddhas, it is not to be answered.
This *Appameyya-asaṅkhyeyya Sutta* is, according to the method already stated, not to be answered. (11)
119. In passages such as “When that Upaka...,” the construction is clear.
Regarding the question posed by Upaka, “In what way, in what manner is he a Jina?”—this is a "vissajjanīya" (to be answered) because it is to be answered thus:
“He is a Jina by way of the abandoning of the defilements. Regarding the question posed by Upaka, “In what manner is he a Jina?”—[the answer is: “By way of [the destruction of] evil things...”

Because it can be answered by the statement, "He is the Victor (Jina) due to having conquered all phenomena," it is answerable (*vissajjanīya*). Because it is impossible to answer the question, "Who is the Victor?
by either saying, "The Victor is form and so forth," or "The Victor is someone other than form and so forth," it is unanswerable (*avissajjanīya*).

[Likewise for: "What is the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*)? What is the destruction of lust (*rāgakkhaya*)? What is the destruction of hatred (*dosakkhaya*)? What is the destruction of delusion (*mohakkhaya*)?"... [and so on].

The question, "The destruction of delusion," is to be answered by such responses as "Nibbāna is the destruction of the taints," or "The path of arahantship is the destruction of the taints," or "The fruit of arahantship is the destruction of lust," and so forth; therefore, it is "to be answered. [As in:
"How much is the destruction of the taints? How much is the destruction of lust? How much is the destruction of hatred? How much is the destruction of delusion?"
The question is "Is the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) of such and such a measure? and so forth; it is "unanswerable" (*avissajjanīya*) because it cannot be answered in that way.
This type of discourse mentioned above is, according to the stated method, both answerable and unanswerable.
(12) The question "Does a being (*satta*) exist as a Tathāgata? [is answered by saying] "A being should be designated in dependence upon the five aggregates."
It is "to be answered" because it is to be answered [with the word] "it exists. The question posed as "Does form exist?
is "to be answered" because form is being answered [affirmatively] with "Yes (āmantā). The question posed as "Is the Tathāgata form?
is "not to be answered" because it cannot be established as such [an identity]. This same method applies to questions such as "Does the Tathāgata possess form? and so forth.
