It should be applied according to what is possible. This type of discourse mentioned above is both answerable and unanswerable according to the method stated.

For instance, regarding the question posed: "Does the Blessed One see... [as far as] ...he understands beings as faring according to their karma?"—this is answerable because it can be answered either by "The Blessed One sees" or "...the Blessed One understands."

The question, “Who are beings? Who is the Tathāgata? is unanswerable because it cannot be answered from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), as [the referents] are not to be found there.
The question, “Does the Tathāgata exist? is answerable according to the method explained below.
As for the question, “Does the Tathāgata exist after death?”—if one were to answer, “The Tathāgata exists after death,”...
If one were to answer, "The world here is itself the world beyond," one would fall into the position that there is no other world beyond;

and if, when answering "there is no Tathāgata after death," one were to say, "the world beyond is different from this world," one would fall into the position that there is another world. Therefore, because it is not to be answered, it is "unanswerable" (*avyākata*).
This type of discourse mentioned above functions as both a communicator and an indicator with respect to both the domain of what is answerable and the domain of what is unanswerable.
Because it proceeds [in this way], there is both that which is to be answered and that which is not to be answered.

120. The Teacher has determined various suttas concerning what is to be answered and what is not to be answered; we too have understood them. Since it was necessary to ask, "Which sutta is 'kamma'?", the passage beginning with "In this context, which is kamma?
was stated. In such passages as "Of one seized by the Ender," the meaning is clear because it follows the method explained below: "Of one overcome by death... [etc.]"
The shadow that never departs”—this Sutta is called *kamma* because it functions as both a declarer and an indicator regarding the two types of action, merit and demerit.
“Monks, you should further observe action: [the case of] one who is sick from lack of exertion, for whom a chair is brought when he is sick from lack of exertion;
for one who has climbed onto a chair, a child is brought; for a child, a bed is brought; and for one who has climbed onto a bed...”
When a fool is lying on the ground— that is, lying upon the earth—
another fool, by means of his body, speech, and mind, performs evil deeds; those evil deeds which were previously performed by that fool in the past,
during former times, or over many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, are those very evil deeds [that now afflict him].
At that time— when he has climbed onto the seat and so forth— his past kamma presents itself as if hanging down, presents itself as if hanging down deeply,
and presents itself as if hanging down all around. Monks, just as the shadows of great mountain peaks hang down, hang down deeply,
and hang down all around upon the earth at the time of sunset, so too do his kamma-presentations appear.
Just as, monks, so too does one cling to a fool... [as before] ...they take hold of him.
Monks, in that situation, because of that mode of appearance, a thought occurs to the fool who has committed evil:
"Alas, I have not done what is good; alas, I have not done what is wholesome; alas, I have not provided a refuge for the fearful; alas, I have done what is evil."

“Alas, I have done what is cruel! Alas, I have done what is wicked! O good man who is not ill, I am one who has not performed what is beautiful, who has not performed what is wholesome, and who has not created a refuge from fear; whereas you have committed evil, practiced cruelty, and done what is wicked.
To whatever destination there is—a bad destination—I shall go to that destination after passing away. Such is the reflection that arises. Thus...
The construction is as follows: "While reflecting, that fool sorrows, suffers, laments, beats his breast, wails, and falls into delusion.
Regarding the shadows of mountain peaks: although they hang over the earth even at the time of sunrise, those shadows hang in a manner that diminishes;
however, at the time of evening, those shadows hang in a manner that increases. In the same way, kamma-actions also [behave].
At that time, they appear by way of increase; therefore, it is with reference to that very appearance of increase that "in the evening" is said.
The application for the bright fortnight (sukkapakkha) should also be made according to the application for the dark fortnight (kaṇhapakkha).
This pair of suttas beginning with "Furthermore... serves as both an indicator and an explainer regarding wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
It is called "kamma" because it proceeds.

Various kinds of kamma have been determined by the Teacher and are known to us; however, because it must be asked, "What is its result (vipāka)?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, what is the result?
and so forth was stated. Therein, among those twenty-eight types of mundane and other [states] in the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*...
"What is the result? he asks. "Monks, those things you have obtained—human birth, the acquisition of faith, and so forth—are indeed gains for you.

Furthermore, that which you have attained by going forth and fulfilling the fourfold pure virtue (*cātupārisuddhisīla*) and the rest—that fulfillment of the fourfold pure virtue and so forth [is the result]."
"It is a great gain for you, monks! You have obtained the ninth moment, which is the arising of a Buddha;
that ninth moment of a Buddha's arising has been acquired by you for the sake of living the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Monks, I have seen the hells called 'the six bases of contact' (*chaphassāyatanika*); having seen them, [I know] those who dwell in those six bases of contact..."
In the hells, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only an undesirable form, not a desirable form;
one sees only an unpleasing form, not a pleasing form; one sees only an unpleasant form, not a pleasant form.

Whatever sound one hears with the ear... [and so on] ...whatever odor with the nose... [and so on] ...whatever taste with the tongue... [and so on] ...whatever tangible object with the body... [and so on] ...whatever mental phenomenon...
One cognizes by means of the mind; one cognizes only that which is undesirable, not that which is desirable. One cognizes only that which is unlovely, not that which is lovely.
The reading “one cognizes only that which is disagreeable, not that which is agreeable” is appropriate.
The reading “one cognizes only an undesirable form, not a desirable form,” etc., is inappropriate in certain parts of the Canon.
An incorrect reading has been observed. The application [of the commentary] should be made by reversing the method stated for the bright side (the wholesome).
This aforementioned passage beginning with “A gain for you, monks,” is called *vipāka* (resultant) because it functions precisely as that which expresses and indicates the result.

“O Noble Ones, sixty thousand years have been fully completed for us while being cooked in hell, sinking and surfacing completely; when, at what time, will there be an end to the inside of this hell?”
There is no end, no limit to hell. How could there be an end or a limit to hell? An end or a limit to hell is not perceived by us.
O venerable ones, when you and I were born as the sons of merchants, then evil was indeed committed—done in various ways—by you and by me.
"Therefore, the end or limit of hell is not seen by us"—this reading is called "result" (*vipāka*) because it functions as that which expresses or indicates the result. (13) 121.
Since a person who acts unrighteously is indeed heedless regarding wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), therefore he is one who acts unrighteously.
Wherever and to whatever miserable destination a heedless man goes, that very unrighteousness practiced by himself destroys that man who lives unrighteously.
How does it destroy him? Just as a black snake caught by oneself destroys the person who caught it, even so does the unrighteousness practiced by oneself destroy the one who lives unrighteously.
The meaning of the verse beginning with “For what is Dhamma is not non-Dhamma” is clear.
These two Suttas constitute both action (*kamma*) and its result (*vipāka*), because they function as both the expression and the indicator of action and its result.
“O monks, do not fear meritorious deeds (*puñña*); O monks, that which is designated by the term ‘meritorious deeds’...”
This is a designation for "meritorious deeds"; it is a designation for that karma which is desirable, lovely, dear, agreeable, pleasant, and which produces a pleasant result.
"Bhikkhus, I recall that for a long time I have experienced what was desirable, lovely, dear, and agreeable, as the long-term fruit of meritorious deeds performed over a long period. How..."

If he should ask, “Do you recall this? one should say: “I do recall it. Having previously developed for seven years a mind of loving-kindness, a second jhāna-mind associated with loving-kindness, I did not return to this world—the world of human beings—for seven aeons of dissolution and evolution (*saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappa*).
Herein, by the inclusion of “dissolution,” the period of subsistence during dissolution is included; by the inclusion of “evolution,”...
It should be understood that those who abide during the period of evolution (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) are also included. The same should be understood for the others as well.
"Monks, when the eon was contracting, I went to the Ābhassara realm; when the eon was evolving, I was reborn in an empty Brahmā-vimāna.
Monks, because of being reborn there in that Brahmā-vimāna, and by reason of being reborn there, I became Brahmā, while others [became so] through great power."
Because I have overcome others, I am a conqueror; because I cannot be overcome by others, I am unconquered as a Great Brahmā.
Indeed, I am unilaterally a Daśa, a wielder of power.
Monks, I was Sakka, the lord of the devas, thirty-six times—a righteous king who ruled according to the Dhamma.

Monks, as a universal monarch who had conquered the four quarters, established his sovereignty over the realm, and was endowed with the seven treasures beginning with the wheel-treasure, I have been such a king hundreds of times;
what need is there to mention my status as a king of a local principality?
Monks, while I was that universal monarch, this reflection occurred to me: "By whatever fruit..."
“By what ripening of karma am I now so powerful and so majestic? Of what action is this the fruit? Of what action is this ripening?
Such was my reflection, monks, as I was pondering: “By what fruit...”
"By whatever ripening of karma I am now so powerful and so majestic, this that has come about is the fruit of three kinds of karma;
indeed, this is the ripening of three kinds of karma. Of which three kinds of karma is it the fruit and ripening?
It is the fruit and ripening of three kinds of karma: namely, of giving, self-control, and restraint. Thus [he spoke] regarding the three kinds of karma.
The construction is: "He said that this reflection was 'the fruit, the result'.

In that regard, in the sutta beginning with "Monks, do not fear meritorious deeds," whatever giving, restraint, and self-control exist—this triad of giving and so forth is *kamma*; the sutta which expresses and indicates that is also *kamma*.
The term "resultant" (*vipāka*) refers to that kamma-condition which has arisen as a conditionally produced state and has been experienced;
this resultant fruit must also be included. Furthermore, the textual passage that expresses and indicates that resultant is also called "resultant.
Likewise, the *Cūḷakammavibhaṅga* (Shorter Exposition of Kamma) should be described as the "Cūḷakammavipākaputhuttavibhāga" (Analysis of the Diversity of the Resultants of Kamma).
Regarding the discourse taught by the Blessed One to the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya:
therein, those phenomena such as the destruction of life which lead to short or long lifespans;
those phenomena such as violence which lead to much sickness or little sickness; and those phenomena such as envy which lead to being of little influence or great influence.
They lead [to these results]: those states such as anger which lead to being ugly or beautiful;
those states such as lack of respect which lead to being born into a low family or a high family; those states such as stinginess which lead to having little wealth or great wealth;
and those states such as lack of discernment which lead to being witless or possessed of wisdom. This is...
The act of taking life together with its seven factors is *kamma*; the Sutta that expresses or indicates that is also called *kamma*.
In this regard, the short or long lifespan mentioned in the Subha Sutta—and likewise the lack of wisdom or possession of wisdom mentioned there—is the result (*vipāka*);
the textual passage that expresses or indicates that [result] is also the result. Thus, this Subha Sutta pertains both to wholesome and unwholesome *kamma* and to their results.
And because they function through the relationship of the signifier and the signified, there is both karma and its result.
(14) 122. That person who, by avoiding verbal misconduct, would guard their speech; who, by not giving rise to covetousness and so forth, would be restrained in mind;
and who, by abandoning the killing of living beings and so forth, would commit no unwholesome deed with the body—thus [these] three...
The construction is as follows: "One who purifies these courses of action (kamma-patha) shall attain, or may attain, the path proclaimed by the seers—the Noble Eightfold Path.
This discourse, beginning with the words "guarding speech," is called "wholesome" (kusala) because it proceeds by way of teaching and making known what is wholesome.

The construction is as follows: "That person for whom there is no bodily misconduct leading to an unhappy destination, no verbal misconduct, and no mental misconduct—who is restrained in these three bases of arising—I call that person a ‘brahmin’.
This statement in the verse is wholesome according to the method already explained.
“Bhikkhus, there are these three... [as before] ...wholesome roots. This statement is wholesome according to the method already explained. The construction is as follows:
“Bhikkhus, for the attainment of wholesome states, clear knowledge (*vijjā*) is the precursor, and moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) follow along.
This statement is called wholesome according to the method already explained.
Just as a *māluvā* creeper causes a *sāla* tree that has bent down to fall to the ground, so too,
a person who possesses extreme immorality throughout two or three existences makes themselves visible falling into the states of misery (*apāya*).
Just as a person who desires harm intends it, so too does such a person act to bring about that very harm.
The construction is: "The immoral person brings harm upon himself. This statement beginning with "of whom" (yassā) refers to unwholesome [action] according to the method already stated.

Just as a diamond made of stone—meaning composed of a stone-gem—is used to crush or shatter a diamond-gem known as the source of diamonds, so too does one [crush oneself] by that which is produced by oneself, born of oneself, and originating from oneself.
The construction is: "Evil crushes the evil person who commits evil. This statement beginning with "By oneself" and so forth refers to unwholesome [action] according to the method already explained.
O deity, having practiced and performed the ten unwholesome courses of action, which are avoided by the wholesome, they become censurable and subject to reproach.
The construction is: "One of childish mind and dull intellect falls into the hells. This discourse beginning with "the ten courses of action" is unwholesome according to the method already stated.
This statement, "Bhikkhus, there are these three... [etc. ...unwholesome roots," is unwholesome according to the method already stated. (15)

Just as whatever seed one sows, one reaps a fruit corresponding to that very seed, so too does the wise person who performs wholesome deeds reap a wholesome fruit, while the foolish person who performs evil deeds reaps an evil fruit—this is the construction [of the meaning].
In this regard, regarding the words beginning with "yādisaṃ" (of such a kind) in the Sutta, the statement "the doer of good [reaps] good" is what was said. This statement...
“Wholesome. As for the statement he spoke, “The evil-doer is evil,” this statement is unwholesome. These two statements, according to the method already explained, are both wholesome and unwholesome.
Those who do good, the true persons, go to—meaning they travel to—a happy destination by means of beautiful karma; those who do evil, the base persons...
By means of unwholesome karma, they go—that is, they travel—to the plane of misery;

yet, through the exhaustion of that karma—specifically of the karma accompanied by the formative consciousness (*abhisankhāra-viññāṇa*)—those true persons, with minds liberated by way of exhaustion, with minds liberated by way of total eradication and by way of subsiding, are extinguished in the foul.
How are they extinguished? Just as a fire is extinguished through the exhaustion of fuel, so too are those true persons extinguished.
The construction is: "They go out (nibbanti) because of the destruction of karma, due to its destruction without remainder.

In that regard, within the statement of the verse beginning with "By the beautiful," namely the phrase "by the beautiful... [and so on]... to a happy destination" (*suggati*), this phrase "by the beautiful... [and so on]...
to a happy destination" is called "wholesome" (*kusala*) because it functions as a designator and indicator of the wholesome. As for the phrase "to the plane of misery by unwholesome karma":
This statement, “...by means of action,” is called unwholesome because it functions as a designator and indicator of unwholesomeness.
This verse passage beginning with “By the beautiful,” etc., is both wholesome and unwholesome according to the method already stated.

(16) 123. “Just as a bee [takes nectar from] a flower... the sage should wander”—this verse passage is called permitted because it functions as a designator and indicator of wandering that has been permitted.
The "bee" refers to the honey-bee and similar insects that move about for the purpose of gathering flower-nectar.
While collecting the nectar, it moves with slow speed, not destroying the flower’s color or fragrance;
having drunk as much nectar as it requires and gathered enough nectar for the purpose of making honey, it flies to a forest thicket, which is its place for making honey.
The color and fragrance of the flowers remain as they naturally were. In the same way, the sage entering the village for alms,
having produced a pleasing look, a glance, a manner of walking, a manner of standing, and so forth, and having generated a serene confidence accompanied by joy and gladness,
accepts the food offering given out of faith— just enough for his sustenance— and having departed from the village, he takes his medicine in the forest at a place convenient for water.

The intended meaning should be understood as follows: having reflected upon the alms-food as if one were licking honey from a blade, or as if one were eating the flesh of one's own son in the wilderness,

and having consumed it like a bee making honey in the forest, one should wander through the village after entering a grove suitable for the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) in order to practice the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) for the sake of producing the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the paths (*magga*), the fruits (*phala*), and Nibbāna.
“Bhikkhus, there are these three duties for bhikkhus... These, bhikkhus, are the three duties for bhikkhus.
This discourse is called “prescribed” because it functions as an indicator and communicator regarding the conduct and purpose permitted by the Blessed One.
In that discourse, the bhikkhu who guards—that is, protects—his virtue (*sīla*) [is so called] because of such protection.

That bhikkhu is indeed a "boat" (pāti). Since that virtue (sīla) delivers the bhikkhu from the suffering of the woeful states and so forth, it is called the *Pātimokkha* by way of delivering (*mocana*).

Since by means of that virtue the bhikkhu restrains the eye-faculty and the rest which ought to be restrained, it is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) by way of performing restraint; thus, the *Pātimokkha* itself as restraint is the *Pātimokkha-saṃvara*.
Being restrained and endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, he moves about in the four postures because of that very restraint;
thus, by virtue of such restraint, a bhikkhu is said to be "restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint. He dwells, meaning he proceeds within the four postures.

Having avoided improper movement (*vāritta-cāra*), he takes up the conduct of proper behavior (*cāritta-sīla*); this "conduct" (*cāra*) is "behavior" (*ācāra*). Having avoided improper resort (*agocara*),...
“Walking in the range is the range. If the meaning were to be explained in full detail, it would become excessively prolix;
therefore, after saying just a little, we shall explain its status as a *sutta* established in the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
Because it must be stated that “only this much of a *sutta* is to be determined as ‘authorized,’” [the Blessed One said]: “Monks, these ten...”
It is said: "The states (dhammas) should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth," and so forth.
This Sutta beginning with "The ten" is called "authorized" because it functions as an expression and indicator of the ten kinds of states that should be reflected upon which have been authorized.

This Sutta beginning with "These three... [are] to be practiced" is likewise [called authorized] because it functions as an expression and indicator of the three kinds of good conduct that have been authorized.
That which is permitted is so called because it has been set forth.

Various kinds of permitted suttas have been determined by the Teacher and are known to us; therefore, because it was necessary to ask, "Which sutta is prohibited?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, which is prohibited? was stated.
"There is no love equal to that for a son; there is no wealth equal to cattle."
“There is no radiance equal to the sun; there is no lake equal to the ocean.
Rejecting these words of the young god, the Blessed One said:
“There is no love equal to that for oneself; there is no wealth equal to grain.”
“There is no radiance equal to wisdom; indeed, rain is supreme among waters”—thus he spoke this verse.
Herein, regarding these two verses, that which precedes them, beginning with “There is no love equal to that for a son,” is the speech of the young deva.
Because it was rejected by the Blessed One, [the latter part] begins with “There is no love equal to that for a son.”
It is called "rejected" because it proceeds toward a rejected object.
Or, in times of famine or in the wilderness, parents—even by killing their own sons and daughters—nurture only themselves;
therefore it is said: "There is no love equal to that for oneself. In times of famine and so forth, [one values] bullion, gold, and the like.
Even oxen, buffaloes, and the like, having been given to the owners of the grain for the purpose of harvesting it, take only the grain;

therefore it is said, "There is no wealth equal to grain. While the light of the sun and other such sources dispels only a portion of the darkness of the present moment, wisdom is capable of making even the ten-thousandfold world-system a single radiance and a single light.
It also dispels the darkness of the defilements that conceals even the categories of phenomena past, future, and present;
therefore it is said, "There is no radiance equal to wisdom. The ocean rests upon only a single portion of the earth, and if there were no rain from the heavens, it would be liable to exhaustion;
yet even when rain falls across hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems, [the ocean does not diminish].
Even up to the Ābhassara Brahma-worlds, they become full; therefore it is said, "Rain is indeed the supreme treasure.
Because it must be stated that "this very thing [rain] is what should be excluded and determined," the passage beginning with "Monks, there are these three... was spoken.
This sutta beginning with "These three... also functions as both an indicator and an expresser regarding the misconduct that has been excluded.
"Prohibited" means [as follows]. (17) 124.

Various kinds of prohibited items have been determined by the Teacher and are known to us; because it was necessary to ask, "Which are both permitted and prohibited?", the passage beginning with "In this regard, which are both permitted... was stated.
O Gotama of vast wisdom, you who possess vast wisdom—O Gotama of vast wisdom, I ask you that. In this world...
The multitude of people who are afraid—of what nature would that multitude be? And the path which is said to have many entrances—of what nature would that path be?
"In what state established would a person not fear the next world?"—this is the construction of the question, asking whether one should or should not fear.
O Devaputta, there is one person who, having resolved upon right speech and having resolved upon right intention, does not commit evil deeds with the body;
this is one. There is another who dwells in a house abundant in food and drink; this is one. There is another who is faithful, endowed with faith, and supple through the pliancy of his mind;
this is one. There is another who is generous, knowing how to speak to supplicants in accordance with their requests.

"And having offered [the sacrifice], one should be one who shares"—this is the first. Thus, the construction is: "A person established in these four qualities, being established in those qualities, would not fear the world beyond; he should not fear.
Since it must be asked, "In that sutta, what is permitted and what is prohibited?", [it says] "therein..."

The passage beginning with "What [did he say]? has been stated. Therein, in the response to the question "What indeed [did he say]?", regarding the statement "Having directed speech and mind rightly," that which the Blessed One said—"speech and mind...
rightly"—is called "authorized" (*anuññāta*), because it functions as a speaker and an indicator with respect to the meanings such as what is to be spoken, which have been authorized.

Regarding the statement, “Not committing evils with the body,” this is called “prohibited” because it proceeds according to the method stated for the prohibition of one who commits evil, as in the passage beginning, “With the body … not committing. Regarding the statement,

“Abounding in food … he should not fear,” this is called “permitted” because it proceeds according to the method stated for what is permitted, as in the passage beginning, “Abounding in food … he should not fear.”
This statement beginning with “speech” is both permitted and prohibited according to the two methods already described.

The meaning of the passage beginning with “the non-doing of all evil” is as previously stated. Since it must be explained what is permitted and what is prohibited regarding that passage beginning with “all evil,” the words beginning with “therein, which” were spoken.
O Lord of the Devas, I also declare bodily conduct to be twofold—that is, bodily conduct which is to be cultivated and is blameless.

“I say,” [the Blessed One said], “I declare that even bodily conduct that is blameworthy is not to be cultivated. The same method of application should be followed for verbal conduct and the others as well.
Because it must be stated why bodily conduct and so forth are described in terms of what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, the passage beginning with “In dependence on what?
was spoken. [This refers to] the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states.
One should observe that bodily conduct and so forth are not to be practiced when they depend on [conditions] that do not increase wholesome states and do not cause unwholesome states to decline;
whereas bodily conduct and so forth are to be practiced when they depend on [conditions] that increase wholesome states and cause unwholesome states to decline. (18) 125.
Various things both permitted and prohibited have been determined by the Teacher and are known to us.
Because it must be asked, “What specific type of sutta is the *thava* (praise)?”, having asked thus, the passage beginning with “In that regard, what is the *thava*?
was stated in order to make known that this specific type of sutta is called *thava*. Therein, the phrase “in that regard” (*tattha*) asks:
among those twenty-eight kinds of suttas of the Dispensation, such as the worldly and so forth, which specific type of sutta is called *thava*?
Among paths— such as the path for the legs, the path for views, and so forth— the eightfold path, consisting of the factors beginning with right view,
is the best and supreme. Among truths— such as verbal truth, conventional truth regarding kshatriyas and the like,
and ultimate truth— the four noble truths, by way of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the practice leading to its cessation, are the best and supreme.
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*) that possess causes, fading away (*virāga*)—which is to say the unconditioned Nibbāna—is the supreme and most excellent phenomenon.
Among bipeds, including all gods and humans, the Visionary—the Blessed One who possesses the fivefold vision—is the supreme and most excellent;
such is the construction [of the verse]. This is the specific meaning of the Sutta beginning with "Of paths, the Eightfold," intended for recitation.
It is called *thava* (a hymn of praise) because it proceeds by way of expressing and making known [the virtues of others].
Since it must be said that "this very specific type of discourse is a *thava*," the passage beginning with "These three, monks... was stated.
As for those without feet, such as snakes and fish; those with two feet, such as humans, birds, and various species of fowl; or those with four feet, such as elephants, horses, cattle, and buffalo.
Or those with many feet, such as centipedes and the like; or material beings of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere; or immaterial beings of the immaterial sphere;

or percipient beings, which are the sentient beings existing in the seven stations of consciousness; or non-percipient beings, which are the non-percipient beings; or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient beings, which are the beings reborn at the peak of existence—whatever beings exist, for all those beings, whether footless and so forth, to that same extent...

That is to say: this Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who has arisen, is declared to be the foremost among the foremost, the best among the best, the most excellent among the most excellent; this is the first foremost.
Whether it be of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*)—which possess the nature of having conditions—or of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṅkhata*), which are not constructed by conditions.
Regarding those phenomena which consist of mere designations (*paṇṇattimatta*), to whatever extent and by however many designations they are conventionally expressed—
those conditioned and unconditioned phenomena that are to be designated by such designations: namely, this "subduing of intoxication" … [as described] … this "cessation," which is Nibbāna,
the objective support for the path and the fruits— that is this "subduing of intoxication" and so forth.
The Dhamma is declared to be the foremost, the supreme... [as before] ... this is the second foremost.
Among all designations of communities (saṅgha), as far as they are designated; among all designations of groups (gaṇa), as far as they are designated;

among all designations of large assemblies of people, as far as they are designated and are used in common parlance—of those communities, groups, and so forth that are to be defined by such designations, these [which follow]...

There are four pairs of persons, eight types of individuals... [as before] ...this Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples, which exists as this field of merit for the world, beginning with the four pairs of persons, is declared to be the foremost, the most excellent...
[as before] ...it is declared; this is the third excellence. These three—namely, the Tathāgata, Nibbāna, and the Noble Saṅgha—are the excellences.

The Teacher is supreme over the entire world, transcending the world of all beings beginning with those without feet; the Dhamma is supreme by virtue of being on the side of the wholesome and being blameless;
and the assembly of the Teacher, the Lion among Men, is likewise supreme—thus these three jewels of the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Assembly are the foremost.
These three jewels—the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Assembly—are distinguished, for they excel by way of their qualities.

Just as a beautiful lotus growing in a lake is the most excellent among flowers, so too there are three supreme jewels in the world that transcend all others: the Saṅgha, which is a collection of beautiful lotuses of ascetics;

the sublime Dhamma; and the Buddha, the All-Enlightened One, who possesses the eye, is honored by the wise, and is the tamer of the best of men—the subduer and further tamer of kings, deities, humans, ministers, and others. These three jewels—the Saṅgha, the Dhamma, and the Buddha—are the highest in the world.
The Teacher who is peerless, the one free from burning and devoid of the fuel of craving, and all the Noble Dhamma along with the excellent Saṅgha—
these three supreme jewels of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha... indeed, these three excel, they do excel beyond all doubt.
He is named Truth because his teaching is non-false and true; he is Peaceful;

he is the All-Conqueror, for although he does not actually conquer all beings—such as humans and gods—he is called the All-Conqueror because he proceeds as if conquering them through the excellence of his qualities; he is the Victor;
and he is the Truth of Dhamma because his intrinsic nature is non-false. He is the supreme, the highest, of that Truth of Dhamma.
There is no other phenomenon that is eternally honored and worthy of worship by the wise; thus, the Noble Saṅgha constitutes three things that are supreme and unsurpassed in the world.

The meaning of the term *ekāyana-pada* has been explained in many ways in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). [He is] one who sees the destruction of birth, who is compassionate and seeks the welfare of others.
The Blessed One understands the path that goes alone.
Because it must be stated what one crosses by means of that path which he understands, the words beginning with "by this path" were spoken.
By this very path which the Blessed One knows, the noble ones—the Buddhas and others—crossed the flood, the flood of saṃsāra, in the past; [they will cross it] in the future...
Those who will cross over, as well as those Buddhas and others who arise in the present—they too, the Buddhas and others in the present, are crossing over.
Beings who look for purity, looking toward purity, pay homage to such a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), the best among gods and humans, who possesses the aforementioned qualities.
Thus, this various collection of specific suttas is also a praise of the Three Jewels.

And because it proceeds by way of both expressing and indicating the qualities of the Triple Gem, it is called a "praise" (*thava*). Thus, this particular commentary, which demonstrates specific suttas of the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*, should also be understood as being named the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*.
Our teacher [taught] to you, and by our teachers, the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna* sutta consisting of sixteen divisions, beginning with that pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), and so forth.
The twenty-eightfold *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna-sutta*, beginning with the mundane (*lokiya*), has been determined and is known by us.

Since it must be stated, "Among those specific *suttas* of the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*—such as those dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth—which specific *sutta* should be demonstrated by correlating it with which other specific *sutta*?", the passage beginning with "In that regard, the mundane *sutta*" is commenced. [End of] the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

However, it is said: “Having thus analyzed both types of the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna* by citing various sūtra passages, [the author] now commenced the section beginning with ‘The worldly sūtra’ in order to demonstrate them by correlating them with the portions dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth.
In that context, the phrase “in those” refers to those specific sūtras of the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna* among the sixteenfold divisions beginning with the portion dealing with defilement.

Furthermore, among the twenty-eight types of suttas—such as those concerning the mundane and so forth within the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*—the mundane sutta occurring on the side of the unwholesome accords with the *saṃkilesabhāgiya* (corrupting) sutta by virtue of having an identical meaning;
the mundane sutta occurring on the side of the wholesome accords with the *vāsanābhāgiya* (purifying) sutta by virtue of having an identical meaning. Therefore...
The mundane discourse, though of one kind, is to be demonstrated by two discourses: that dealing with defilement and that dealing with purification.
The supramundane discourse occurring on the side of vision accords with the discourse dealing with vision through their identity of meaning;
the supramundane discourse occurring on the side of development accords with the discourse dealing with development through their identity of meaning.
It is "concordant" (*saṃsandati*); that is, a supramundane sutta occurring on the side of the Asekhas is concordant by virtue of having an identical meaning with what pertains to the Asekhas.
Therefore, even a supramundane sutta should be demonstrated by means of three suttas: those pertaining to vision, those pertaining to development, and those pertaining to the Asekhas.
Following the method already stated, the application of concordance should be made for the remaining cases as well.
"O our teacher, you have demonstrated the correlation of specific discourses by way of showing their underlying principles through your own teachers, and this has been understood by us.

However, when it must be asked, 'For what purpose did the Blessed One speak [these discourses], having classified them into categories such as those dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) and so forth?', [the answer is given:
'A discourse dealing with purification (vāsanābhāgiya) is for the purpose of counteracting a discourse dealing with defilement,' and so on."
It has been stated. And here, the meanings of the suttas are taken according to the suttas themselves.
Since it must be asked, "By how many suttas should that which was determined by the Teacher as being expressed in terms of beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna) be analyzed and demonstrated?", [the answer is:
"The supramundane sutta expressed in terms of beings is [demonstrated] by twenty-six..."

It is said, "They are to be demonstrated by way of individuals. Since it must be stated, "Those twenty-six individuals are to be sought after by means of how many suttas?", it is therefore said, "By three," and so forth.

By three suttas—namely, that which pertains to the side of vision (dassanabhāgiya) with reference to persons (sattādhiṭṭhāna), that which pertains to the side of development (bhāvanābhāgiya) with reference to persons, and that which pertains to the side of the adept (asekkhabhāgiya) with reference to persons—those twenty-six [individuals] [are to be sought].
“Persons are to be investigated.
Because it must be stated, “By which [persons] should which suttas be demonstrated? it is said: “In that regard, ‘pertaining to vision’ (*dassanabhāgiya*), etc.
Therein, “in those” (*tattha*) refers to those three suttas beginning with “pertaining to vision. Alternatively, “therein” (*tattha*) refers to those twenty-six [suttas].

Regarding individuals: the discourse pertaining to the portion of vision (*dassanabhāgiya*), which is based on a partial aspect of the person-as-a-being (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*), is to be demonstrated by means of the individual who is a "single-seeder" (*ekabījī*)... and so on...

up to the individual who is a "follower of the Dhamma" (*dhammānusārī*). Thus, the discourse pertaining to the portion of vision, based on a partial aspect of the person-as-a-being, is to be demonstrated by these five types of individuals.
And here, by the mention of "vision," even those established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) [are included].
Since they are included, those established in the fruit who are "one-seeders," "clansmen," or "seven-times-at-most" are also included.
As for the faith-follower (*saddhānusārī*), he is the person who, making faith the primary factor at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), realizes the path of stream-entry;
at the moment of realizing that path of stream-entry, such a person is called a "faith-follower" because of his attainment through faith.
One who recollects [the Buddha] through faith and by means of this recollection enters the path of stream-entry is called a *saddhānusārī* (follower by faith).

At the moment of the fruit of stream-entry, because that person is liberated through faith, they become one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*) and becomes one who has at most one more birth, or one who goes from family to family, or one who is reborn seven times at most.
However, as for the person who, during the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), makes wisdom their primary focus and realizes the path of stream-entry—
At the moment of generating the path of stream-entry, that person is called a "follower by Dhamma" (*dhammānusārī*);
he recollects the attainment through the Dhamma and through wisdom. Thus, because of this recollection of the attainment through the Dhamma and through wisdom, he is called a follower by Dhamma.
At the moment of the fruit, that person, having attained cessation through view and wisdom, becomes one who has "reached through view" (*diṭṭhippatto*).

The "single-seeded" one... [and so on] ...is supreme. And here, by "Dhamma," wisdom (paññā) is intended. Thus, according to their classification, there are two who stand at the stage of the path and six who stand at the stage of the fruit;

therefore, the discourse pertaining to the portion of vision should be demonstrated by means of eight noble persons (ariyapuggala), or, when combined, by five noble persons, as a partial illustration based on the category of beings.

Because these individuals, beginning with the "one-seeded" (ekabījī), constitute a portion of those defined by way of beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna) and possess the quality of being on the side of vision (dassanabhāgiya), the Teacher analyzed [the passage] by determining that the Sutta concerning a portion of those defined by way of beings and on the side of vision must be illustrated by these many individuals;
and this has been understood by us as well: "a portion of those defined by way of beings and on the side of vision..."
Because it must be asked, "By how many types of persons is the discourse (sutta) to be demonstrated?", [the text says]:
"The discourse pertaining to development (bhāvanābhāgiya) is to be demonstrated by twelve types of persons:

one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning, a once-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning, a non-returner, and one who attains final nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyin)."

“The discourse on the factors conducive to development should be demonstrated by these twelve persons: one who attains final nibbāna upon landing, one who attains final nibbāna without exertion, one who attains final nibbāna with exertion,
one who goes upstream bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm, one liberated by faith, one attained to view, and the body-witness.”
It has been stated. Therein, too, it should be understood that the portion concerning beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) within the section on development (*bhāvanābhāgiya*) is the discourse (*sutta*).
By one who has entered the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*), by a person established in the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-phala*);

by one who has entered the path of non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*), by a non-returner (*anāgāmi*) established in the fruit of non-returning; [and] in the five Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), such as the Aviha realm...

By means of the nature of attaining final nibbāna after reaching arahantship without exceeding the midpoint of the lifespan, as an anāgāmin named "one who attains nibbāna in the interval" (antarāparinibbāyī);

by means of the nature of attaining final nibbāna after reaching arahantship having exceeded the midpoint of the lifespan, as an anāgāmin named "one who attains nibbāna upon landing" (upahaccaparinibbāyī);
and by means of the nature of attaining final nibbāna after reaching arahantship without exertion or effort, as one named "one who attains nibbāna without exertion" (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī).
by means of a non-returner who, through effort and exertion, attains Arahantship and attains final Nibbāna—known as a "non-returner who attains Nibbāna with exertion";

by means of a non-returner known as an "upstream-bound" (uddhaṃsota) who, through the stream of rebirth from the Aviha realm upwards into the Atappa realms and so forth, attains Arahantship and attains final Nibbāna;
and by means of one who, having gone to the Akaniṭṭha realm, attains Arahantship and attains final Nibbāna.
And by these eleven persons who have attained the jhānas—namely, the non-returner named Akaniṭṭhagāmī; the non-returner named Saddhāvimutta, so called because he is liberated through faith;

and the non-returner named Diṭṭhippatto, so called because he has reached cessation through view—Nibbāna is realized immediately after the formless jhānas that were touched by the body within the mental body (nāmakāya).
He realizes it; thus, by way of realization, it is to be demonstrated by twelve types of persons, including one who has attained jhāna and is known as a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī).

Since these aforementioned types of persons constitute a portion of the "person-centered" (sattādhiṭṭhāna) category and possess the quality of being conducive to development (bhāvanābhāgiya), the discourse that is person-centered and conducive to development is to be demonstrated by this many types of persons.

Having been determined and analyzed by the Teacher, and being known by us as to how many persons should be stated to demonstrate the portion of the *asekkha* (one beyond training) suttas that belong to the category of beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*), it is said:
"The *asekkha*-portion sutta is to be demonstrated by nine persons: by one liberated through faith (*saddhāvimutta*), by one liberated through wisdom (*paññāvimutta*),..."

It is said: “The discourse pertaining to the state of one beyond training (asekkhabhāgiya) should be demonstrated by these nine persons: by one liberated through voidness, one liberated through the signless, one liberated through the desireless, one liberated both ways, one who has attained even-mindedness, the paccekabuddhas, and the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

In this context, it should be understood that the discourse pertaining to the state of one beyond training is to be demonstrated as referring to a portion of those who are defined by the category of beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna).
At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, because he is liberated from the defilements through faith, he is an arahant liberated by faith; [he is addressed] as "by that one liberated by faith.
At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, because he is liberated through wisdom, he is an arahant liberated by wisdom; [he is addressed] as "by that one liberated by wisdom.

Because he is liberated through the contemplation of non-self known as emptiness-vipassanā, he is an arahant liberated by emptiness; [he is addressed] as "by that one liberated by emptiness. Through the contemplation of the signless...
Because he is liberated through the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), the Arahant is "liberated by the signless" (*animittavimutta*); thus, by that one liberated by the signless.

Because he is liberated through the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), which is termed the contemplation of the wishless (*appaṇihitānupassanā*), the Arahant is "liberated by the wishless" (*appaṇihitavimutta*); thus, by that one liberated by the wishless.

Because he is liberated from both sides—from both the body of form (*rūpakāya*) and the body of name (*nāmakāya*)—the Arahant is "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*); thus, by that one liberated in both ways.

The first five types of persons are taken as those who have attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*); however, the one liberated both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) is taken as one who has attained meditative absorption.

There are three kinds of those called "equal-headed" (*samasīsī*): equal-headed in terms of posture (*iriyāpatha*), equal-headed in terms of illness (*roga*), and equal-headed in terms of life-span (*jīvita*).
Among these three types of equal-headed ones, the Arahant who has attained Arahantship in each of the four postures is [the first].
The Arahant who, without shifting to another posture, attains final Nibbāna in that very posture is called an Arahant "level-headed with respect to postures" (*iriyāpathasamasīsī*).

The Arahant who, when a certain illness has arisen, attains Arahantship and, without rising from that illness, attains final Nibbāna in that very illness is called an Arahant "level-headed with respect to illness" (*rogasamasīsī*). The Arahant who...
After the cognitive process of review, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) descends;

from there, immediately following the final impulsion process at the moment of death, one attains Parinibbāna. This Arahant is called "one who reaches the end of life simultaneously with the path" due to the equality of the number of impulsions.

The "equality of the number of impulsions" refers to the fact that the final process at the moment of death follows the process of review because it conforms to the path-process, even though it occurs immediately after the process of review.
It should be said that it proceeds immediately after the path-process; therefore, this is called "immediate succession" (*vīthianantaratā*) and "equality of the turn" (*vārasamatā*).
And because of that equality of the turn, he is described as one who reaches the same conclusion as his life.
In the phrase "he attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)," here too, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) follows immediately after the process of reviewing.
Having descended from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and emerged from it, the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidāñāṇa) proceed through the active cognitive process (pavattavīthi).

Because they follow immediately after the cognitive process in the manner described, and because they occur simultaneously with the [other] analytical knowledges, it is said: "together with the analytical knowledges.

The omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) of the Blessed One likewise descends into the life-continuum and emerges from the life-continuum immediately after the cognitive process of review (paccavekkhaṇavīthi).
It should be understood that [the path] occurs first. By means of these nine persons— namely, this one who has life as his goal, all the paccekabuddhas,
and all the perfectly enlightened Buddhas— the portion of the discourse concerning the Asekha (the one beyond training) within the section on beings should be demonstrated.

Because these persons have the meaning of being a partial basis for the designation "sentient being" (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) and because they possess the quality of belonging to those beyond training (*asekkha*),

the supramundane [discourse] is— by way of these twenty-six noble persons mentioned in this manner through the phrases beginning with "the supramundane discourse has the sentient being as its basis"— [designated as such] by means of the discourses pertaining to vision, cultivation, and the state beyond training.
The Sutta that is partially based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhānekadesa) must be demonstrated.

Because these twenty-six types of persons constitute both the meaning of the entire supramundane Sutta and the meaning of the Sutta that is partially based on beings, it is the supramundane Sutta that is partially based on beings. [This] is what must be demonstrated by means of these persons; thus [it was said] by the Teacher.

Having established and analyzed [the matter], and because it was understood by us that one must state how many individuals (*puggala*) are required to illustrate a mundane sutta that is partially based on sentient beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*), it was said:
"A mundane sutta based on sentient beings is to be illustrated by nineteen individuals," and so forth.
"Which phenomena do those nineteen mundane individuals consist of?"
Because it must be stated that "they are to be sought out as they have been described," the passage beginning with "by their conduct" (*caritehi*) was spoken.
This means that those nineteen worldly individuals are to be sought out as they were described by way of their conduct—that is, by specific types of conduct.

Because it must be stated how they are described by way of conduct, the passage beginning with "some are of lustful temperament" (*rāgacarita*) was spoken. [This refers to] those of lustful temperament, those of hateful temperament, and so forth.
By way of their temperaments, nineteen types of worldly persons are specified: those of lustful temperament, some of hateful temperament... [and so on] ...up to those of deluded temperament.
Thus, by means of these nineteen specified types of persons, a portion of the discourse concerning worldly beings should be demonstrated.
Although it is stated in general terms as "worldly," it is specifically referred to as "the worldly pertaining to the side of defilement."
It should be understood specifically as follows:

the mundane discourse (*sutta*) that partially adopts the perspective of sentient beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) has been defined and analyzed by the Teacher, specifying that it is to be demonstrated by means of so many individuals;
and this we too have come to know: "The discourse pertaining to the stage of purification by habituation (*vāsanābhāgiya*) is one that partially adopts the perspective of sentient beings."
Because it must be stated with which persons [the teaching] is to be demonstrated, the words beginning with “pertaining to purification by habituation” (*vāsanābhāgiya*) were spoken.

It should be connected thus: the discourse pertaining to purification by habituation, which is a partial reference to sentient beings, is to be demonstrated by means of both virtuous persons and [virtuous] phenomena.
Because it must be stated how many virtuous persons there are, it was said: “Those virtuous persons are five. How many...
Because it is to be spoken of as "states" (*dhammā*), the terms "natural virtue" (*pakatisīla*) and so forth are stated. This is what is meant:

there are five types of persons—those possessing natural virtue, those possessing undertaken virtue, those possessing confidence of mind, those possessing serenity, and those possessing insight—and there are five corresponding states:
the state of natural virtue, the state of undertaken virtue, the state of confidence of mind, the state of serenity, and the state of insight.
And "the Dhamma of insight"— thus, by means of these five persons and these five Dhammas,

the Sutta that pertains to the portion of purification (vāsanābhāgiya), which is based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna) and partially based on Dhamma, should be demonstrated in due order. The Sutta pertaining to the supramundane (lokuttara) that is based on beings is [demonstrated] by means of the Sutta pertaining to the portion of vision (dassanabhāgiya), the Sutta pertaining to the portion of purification (vāsanābhāgiya), and the Sutta pertaining to the portion of the Adept (asekkhabhāgiya).
"Should be demonstrated" means that which has been determined and analyzed by the Teacher and understood by us.

Because it must be stated, "By how many suttas is a sutta that is supramundane and based on the Dhamma to be demonstrated?", it was said: "A supramundane sutta based on the Dhamma... [etc. ...is [demonstrated] by that which pertains to the Asekha."

Since it must be asked, "By how many [categories] should the mundane and the supramundane, as well as those based on a being (sattādhiṭṭhāna) and those based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), be demonstrated?", it is said:

"The mundane...pe... should be demonstrated by both. "By both" means that they should be demonstrated by both the mundane and the supramundane, and by both the basis on a being and the basis on phenomena, because they share the same meaning.

Because it must be stated, "By how many [terms] is knowledge (*ñāṇa*) to be demonstrated?", it was said: "Knowledge is by means of wisdom (*paññā*)," and so forth. In whichever sutta knowledge has appeared, in that very sutta knowledge is to be demonstrated by way of its synonyms, such as wisdom, and so on.
Because it must be stated, "By how many [terms] is the knowable (*ñeyya*) to be demonstrated?", it was said:
"The knowable is by means of the past, future, and present," and so forth. In whichever sutta the knowable has appeared, in that very sutta the knowable is to be demonstrated by way of its synonyms.

Because it must be stated, "By how much are both knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) to be demonstrated?", it was said: "Both knowledge and the object of knowledge are [demonstrated] by both of them," and so forth.
In whichever sutta knowledge and the object of knowledge have been mentioned, in that very sutta they are to be demonstrated by way of the method of knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Having reflected upon how they were demonstrated in the *Dassana-sutta*, they are to be demonstrated as being obtainable [therein]. In the *Bhāvanā-sutta*...
Having considered it exactly as it has been demonstrated, it should be demonstrated according to what is obtainable.
Both of these—seeing and cultivation—should be demonstrated according to what is obtainable by considering them exactly as they have been demonstrated in the Sutta.
In cases such as "one's own statement" and "another's statement," it is likewise both individually and collectively, exactly as demonstrated in the Sutta.
Having understood it in this way, the construction should be made as follows: "It should be demonstrated by way of what is being obtained.
Because it must be stated that "only this much should be demonstrated," the passage beginning with "or else" (*yaṃ vā pana*) was spoken.

Because it must be stated that "for the result, the cause is karma alone," the passage beginning with "the cause is twofold" (*duvidho hetū*) was spoken. [The defilements are treated] according to the *Saṃkilesabhāgiya-sutta*.

They should be demonstrated by way of their identical meaning. Either the origin consisting of craving, or the origin consisting of defilements, or the origin consisting of unwholesome states, should be demonstrated by way of their identical meaning with the Discourse on the Section Dealing with Corruption (*saṃkilesabhāgiya-sutta*).

Or else, the origin consisting of mundane wholesome causes, or the origin consisting of mundane wholesome states, [should be demonstrated] by way of their identical meaning with the Discourse on the Section Dealing with Morality (*vāsanābhāgiya-sutta*).
It is to be demonstrated by way of its having the same meaning as a sutta.

Since it was analyzed in general terms—stating that both action (*kamma*) and its result (*vipāka*) are to be demonstrated by whatever sutta is applicable according to the case—the question "By what [sutta] is the wholesome (*kusala*) to be demonstrated?
must be addressed; therefore, the passage beginning with "Therein, the wholesome... is stated. "Therein" (*tattha*)...

Among those twenty-eight suttas on the foundations of the Dispensation (*sāsana-paṭṭhāna*), the wholesome (*kusala*) should be demonstrated through its state of having the same meaning as four suttas.

Since it must be asked, "By which four?", the phrase beginning with "by that which pertains to purification by means of spiritual cultivation" (*vāsanābhāgiyena*) was stated. Mundane wholesome [states] are to be demonstrated by that which pertains to purification by means of spiritual cultivation because of their identical meaning;
supramundane wholesome [states] are [to be demonstrated] by that which pertains to vision (*dassanabhāgiya*) and by that which pertains to purification by means of spiritual cultivation.

And it should be demonstrated by way of its having a corresponding meaning with that which pertains to the Asekhas, as appropriate. Having determined that the wholesome (kusala) is to be demonstrated by so many [factors], it has been analyzed;
because it must be stated, "By what is the unwholesome (akusala) to be demonstrated?", the passage beginning with "The unwholesome" is spoken.
Because it must be stated, "By what are both the wholesome and the unwholesome to be demonstrated?"...
It is said: "The wholesome and the unwholesome are to be demonstrated by both of them.
In whichever sūtra both of these have appeared, they are to be demonstrated by those two as they appear in that respective sūtra.
Because it had to be stated, "By what is 'the permitted' (anuññāta) to be demonstrated?", the passage beginning with "the permitted" was spoken. The permitted...
That which is permitted by the Blessed One should be demonstrated by means of what is similar to it.

Because it must be asked, "In how many ways is there that which is permitted?", it is said, "It is fivefold," and so forth. Whatever is permitted that is seen in various planes (bhūmi), that which is permitted should be demonstrated by means of what is similar to it—namely, by what is allowable and conformable to the rules—as it occurs in those respective planes.
Having determined and analyzed it by the Teacher with the words, "That which is permitted is to be demonstrated by this," he stated, "By whom is that which is prohibited to be demonstrated?
because it must be so stated. Thus, "It was prohibited by the Blessed One" and so forth was said.

That which was prohibited by the Blessed One is to be demonstrated by the reason for its prohibition—namely, by the case (vatthu) as it appears in the Sutta, through the relationship of cause and effect.

Whatever is prohibited that appears in various levels [of the Vinaya], that prohibition must be demonstrated by means of what is permitted and what is similar to the unallowable (akappiya) as it occurs in those respective levels.
Because it must be stated, "By what are both the permitted and the prohibited to be demonstrated?", [it is said: "The permitted and the prohibited..."

"It should be demonstrated by both of those," it is said. In whichever sutta both what is permitted and what is prohibited has come down, it should be demonstrated by both as they appear in that respective sutta.
Since it must be asked, "By what is 'praise' (thava) to be demonstrated?", it is said: "'Praise' is [to be understood] from 'commendation' (pasaṃsā)," and so forth. In whichever...
In whichever discourse whatever praise has come down, the praise found in each respective discourse is to be demonstrated.
Since it must be asked, "That praise which is to be demonstrated—by how many kinds is that praise to be demonstrated?", it was said, "It is fivefold," and so forth.
This includes both the praise of the Blessed One and the praise of the Dhamma.
It should be understood as fivefold: the praise of the Noble Saṅgha, the praise of the training in the Noble Dhamma, and the praise of the attainment of mundane qualities.
Thus, in the manner described, the praise should be demonstrated as fivefold.
"Our teacher has stated that the eighteen root-terms are to be seen in the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*."
Because it was asked, "What are those eighteen root-terms?", the passage beginning with "the stage of the faculties" (*indriyabhūmi*) and so forth was stated.
In the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*, the stage of the faculties—the stage of the faculties such as faith-faculty (*saddhindriya*) and the rest—is that which is to be demonstrated by nine terms;
likewise, in the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*, the stage of defilements (*kilesabhūmi*) is that which is to be demonstrated by nine terms. Thus, in this manner, these...
There are nine root-terms that are wholesome terms and nine root-terms that are unwholesome terms; thus, there are eighteen root-terms.

They are to be seen in the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*. Because it must be stated, "By what reason is it known that the eighteen root-terms are to be seen in the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*?", the words beginning with "For thus" (*tathā hi*) were spoken. "For thus" (*tathā hi*) means for that very reason.
Since the eighteen root terms (*mūlapada*) are to be found in the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*, the statement, "Where are the eighteen root terms to be found?

In the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*," is understood by that very statement. To the question, "By what means is the state of being eighteen of these root terms understood, given their division into nine wholesome terms and nine unwholesome terms? it is said: "Therefore he said," and so forth.
It has been said. Because the root terms consist of nine wholesome terms and nine unwholesome terms, the Venerable Mahākaccāna stated:
“By nine terms the wholesome [states] are joined, and by nine the unwholesome side;
these indeed are the root terms, which become eighteen terms.”

By the statement he made, namely, “by nine... [etc.]... terms,” it is understood through that expression that the root terms possess the nature of eighteen, by way of being the nine wholesome terms and the nine unwholesome terms.

Whatever sixteenfold *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*—beginning with that pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*)—and whatever twenty-eightfold *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*—beginning with the mundane (*lokiya*)—has been determined by the Teacher, this much alone is complete; there is no other *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*.
Because it must be said that "having extracted [the meaning], there is nothing further to be joined," it is stated: "The *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna* is fully joined.

The meaning should be understood as follows: whatever other *sāsanappaṭṭhāna* has been extracted from the *sāsanappaṭṭhāna* as thus extracted, each of those other *sāsanappaṭṭhānas* is to be joined by being extracted appropriately and fully joined.
Regarding the statement, “Whatever the world honors... [etc. ...is applied as the foundation of the Teaching,” one might ask:
“Is the *Netti* complete with this much sequence of words, or is it incomplete? To address this, the words beginning with “to this extent” were spoken.
The *Netti* that was spoken by the Venerable Mahākaccāna was approved by the Blessed One; it is included in the Root Recitation (*mūlasaṅgīti*).

The *Netti* which was chanted by the bull-like elders—that *Netti* is completed and perfected by this sequence of words ending with: "That which the world honors... [etc. ...is applied as the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*.
Thus, in the original recitation (*mūlasaṅgīti*) spoken by the Venerable Mahākaccāna and approved by the Blessed One, it is complete.
This commentary on the meaning of the *Nettippakaraṇa*, which was sung by the preeminent elders (*therāsabha*),
has been composed for the benefit of the sons of the Conqueror (*jinaputta*) by the Great Elder, the Preceptor of the Great Dhamma King, named Saddhammapālana.
It was completed at the time of sunrise on the ninth day of the waxing moon in the month of Sāvaṇa, in the nine hundred and twenty-sixth year of the Sakkarāja era.
Thus ends the exposition composed according to one's strength and ability within the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*.
This is the concluding discourse.
The Protector, supreme among all beings, the Leader, arose in the world—
the Fully Enlightened One, Gotama, the Victor, adorned with manifold virtues.
The teaching of that Most Excellent One has lasted for more than eight hundred years.
When the stainless, beautiful, and expanding bowl had reached two thousand [years],
then the great King of Dhamma, the lord of the earth possessed of great psychic power,
caused those kings who did not submit to him to tremble by means of his wheel of command.
Having obtained an excellent white elephant that causes wonder in the world,
the Great Hero, being heedful, rejoices after having performed meritorious deeds.
On the ninth day of the month of Sāvaṇa in that very year—
At the time of the rising of the sun, this *Vibhāvanā* has been brought forth.
To the extent that the Dispensation remains, to that extent has it been composed by me.
May this *Nettivibhāvanā*, which brings benefit to the sons of the Conqueror, endure!
Thus, by composing this, merit has been attained by me;
by the power of that merit, may all beings— kings, queens, sons,
grandsons, great-grandsons, and their kinsmen— partake in liberation.
May all, having established themselves in the happiness of sovereignty, live happily practicing their proper conduct.
May the rain-god send rain in due season, may all the people of the kingdom be happy,
and may they, not harming one another, be dear to each other and bring each other welfare.
The *Nettivibhāvinī* is completed.
